Brilliant Game. Many Mods and so many content, you can play this forever. Factorio is an economic building strategy game comparable to Anno, the Settlers or Simcity but with much more complexity and with a strong technical affinity (think of redstone circuits in minecraft for example).
The Story is simple: crashed on an alien inhabited planet your mission is surviving and building a rocket for escape. To do so you need to mine and refine ores, gases and oil, built automated machines and operate science with 'em. The economic drive leads to pollution, which doesn´t please the alien inhabitants and causes them to attack your fortified settlement. Last but not least you can do all this together with your friends in the well functioning multiplayer with up to 200+ Players on an automaticly enlarging, randomly generated map.
Upshot: Stongly recommented!

The game might look compelling at a glance, but ultimately, there are only three core activities to do in it:
A) Trade goods. Buy low, sell high, through an extremely simple interface. Not engaging whatsoever.
B) Do missions. Every one reduces to generic "go to place X". It involves no thought beyond finding multiple ones along the same route.
C) Fight. Regrettably, this is extremely simple, doesn't involve much agility, and is largely decided by who has more and better ships and guns.
On top of that, the game presents its content poorly: rather than making it seem like you modify your ship and trade cargo, the activities feel respectively like purchasing generic upgrades and clicking a "make money" button.
Last but not least, the game has major technical and design issues: First 365 days involve losing money everyday to pay off your debt, landing on a planet resets the system, and saving the game doesn't actually save your current game, but rather the last time you were landed on a planet.
If you want to play an actually good game of its kind, try Transcendence, which is also free, but far better in every respect.

Legend of Grimrock is an old-school RPG that harkens back to old first-person dungeon crawlers such as the venerable Eye of the Beholder series, the older Might and Magics or the Wizardry series.
My first playthrough on normal difficulty took close to 20 hours and this was considering that i had skipped a couple of puzzles and also had to consult the net for solutions to some of them.
Puzzles are the core of the game. Some of them are essential for game progression, most are optional, and ALL of them are very cleverly crafted and are absolutely fun and challenging. You will definitely get a sense of satisfaction if you manage to solve it without any help.
However because of this, I personally felt that the game focused too much on puzzle solving, and the game sometimes felt more like a puzzle game with RPG elements instead of an RPG with puzzles.
Instead of having puzzles subtly presented like in the old Eye of the Beholder series, Grimrock literally hands you a puzzle room and even puts out a label of the puzzle's name.
On the whole, this makes the whole game feel more like 13 levels of puzzle rooms where you just need to solve it to progress instead of an RPG with a coherent story that gives context to the puzzles.
Story is definitely not Grimrock's strong point, and it only provides an introductory excuse to let the player know why he is in a dungeon. As a game touted as an RPG, the treasure and loot selection are unfortunately not exciting. There are only a couple of limited choices. This game also features the most rediculous looking final boss in an RPG ever.
Music is very well done and sounds appropriately cinematic and epic. However, there are only 2 tracks in the whole game. The art style while looking very modern, recycles alot of textures and makes every dungeon level feel the same as the earlier ones.
The main gripe I had was the magic system, which was overly complicated and too frustrating to use. It actually requires you to remember spell combinations and click on them fast during battle. I felt that they should have had a simpler approach to this, or at least provide a simpler alternative style. (Eg: why can't we right click on the mage's hand, choose the spell i want and just cast it?)
Despite its flaws, Legend of Grimrock is still a very good game and is a worthy addition to the past glorious dungeon-crawlers. The fact that the entire game was made by only a 4 man team with a limited budget really blows the mind. Whats more, they even allowed player modding on this game which is probably a first time for games of this type and genre.
For veterans of old-school RPG dungeon-crawlers, this game is a definite must buy. For newer gamers who have never experienced such old-school gameplay before however, it is better to review the gameplay videos before deciding if this game is for you. The play style in this game may not appeal to modern gamers.
Overall Rating: 8.0 / 10

I have a very strong love-hate relationship with this game. At it's best you're running through beautiful dungeons with awesome music in the background, taking in the sights, and battling epic monsters and primals. But at it's worst you're slogging through dreary areas and content trying to get to the good stuff, this lack of consistency in content have given me a sweet and sour view on the game in general.
There are things I wish this games could do better, like the duty roulette system, and the open world levelling system. Participating in fates pre-SB is counterproductive to your levelling, and the hunting log system is the only thing that gives you enough exp to actually be worth doing, so you're either stuck doing monotonous side quests with barely engaging stories, with early game dungeons that after completing once or twice, tend to make you want to fall asleep at the keyboard. It doesn't help that with the duty roulette system, most of the time you're stuck doing boring content, even with the post lvl 50 options. Queuing up for trials and you want to get something like Singularity Reactor? Tough luck pal, you're getting Bowl of Embers hard.
Enough about the bad of this game, let's get to the good. The content that has kept me stuck into this game includes but is not limited to the story past A Realm Reborn. Heavenswards writing has got to be the best writing I've ever seen in an MMO to date. The characters are very engaging and it's been so long since I've actually cared about the characters of an MMO's story. People like Haurchefant, Alphinaud, Thancred, etc, make the game an absolute pleasure to play. The music is breathtaking, with tracks like The Hand that gives the Rose, Knights of the Round, to name a few, Yukiko Takada, Nobuo Uematsu, and mainly Masayoshi Soken all did great work composing a soundtrack that inspires a range of emotions in the listener. The visuals of the game tend to swing back and forth in quality, but for the most part, they're great to look at, areas like Dravania, Coerthas, La Noscea and Gridania being very scenic, and good to screenshot.
Now the community is probably the best thing about my experience with FF14, while playing on Kujata, while there's mainly a japanese speaking playerbase, I found a nice tight knit english FC that helped me through my new player phase, teaching me what I needed to know, etc, and giving me a pleasant experience overall.
If you're thinking about buying this game, just ask yourself a few questions. Are you okay with possibly not getting on a server you want, because of congestion? Are you okay with slogging through the early game, without seeing much good content for up to 150hrs, depending on how fast you play the game? Are you okay with shelling out up to 20 bucks a month, depending on where you live? Are you okay with getting possibly hour long queue times, if you play DPS? If the answer to some or all of these is yes, then I say go nuts. Thanks for reading, and good luck on your adventures.

I give this game a recommendation with the clause you buy it on sale.
My synopsys of this game is: "It's alright".
More in-depth: There's nothing particularly broken in the game IMO. The combat is serviceable, the limb cutting is fun, the weapons look cool - but nothing really makes it to the point where it's very compelling. To me there's a few things really holding the game back.
1) I really dislike the sort of "rustic sci-fi" with chunky, scrapy designs that more things seem to be adopting. Dead space had elements of it, borderlands had a ton of it, and this game has it too.  IMO it's just unappealing looking as the environments are quite literally just heaps of garbage.
There's nothing drawing the player with a sense of curiosity. Souls had gorgeous environments begging the player to explore and marvel at them despite the immense danger. The world was beautiful - at least for the most part. However, in the Surge there is nothing I want to go investigate. Big broken cement tubes, collapsed factories, dirt, patches of weeds, and chunks of metal collapsed everywhere. If I wanted to walk around broken factories with collapsed scaffolding I would just go visit Detroit for a weekend.
As far as I know, the environments do not change either. The souls games had incredible environmental and variety to keep it fresh - this just doesn't.
Further, this odd "mad max sci fi" look leads to a very odd juxtaposition in the lore where software and chemistry are so advanced you can implant chips in your brain that enhance your body, but mechanical engineering somehow stopped in the 1980s with hydraulic powered legs made of steel welded together. We have the technology to revive people from the dead but still haven't developed light-weight yet sturdy materials that are more practical than half a ton of steel on your legs?
I really think the game would have appealed to me more if it was a more sleek, advanced sci-fi theme with cool looking armor. Here you can really only choose between one chunk of dinged up scrap metal or another.
2) The combat could really use some tweaking. While it works, i just feel it's worse than the souls game. You cannot dodge out of any attacks. You cannot move while blocking. The arm lock-on sometimes does weird♥♥♥♥♥♥like you're aiming at the head and press down to target the body but instead it targets a leg. It just feels incredibly chunky, just like the rest of the game. I really wish some of the fluidity of souls combat was present.
In addition to this, the weapons are extrodinarily slow. I also don't really like the weapon proficiency scaling as it really discourages the player from trying new weapons - though that said there really aren't many weapon types, and what there are seem to all attack the same. Gone are the weapon specific movesets from the souls game, which really limits the utility of a weapon and that means you're basically just going to pick whatever gives the highest stats and use that.
I level these criticims cause there really is a good game in here, it just sucks it seems to fall short. It certainly does enough differently from souls and has some neat ideas - but in places where the comparisons are obvious it does worse than its inspiration in every single case.

It's Dark Souls! It isn't Dark Souls! People can't seem to make their minds up about this one. The truth is:
It isn't Dark Souls, but the DNA runs pretty deep. It's an action-RPG where every enemy poses a threat and has to be approached carefully. You loose your money/exp on death and have to go and pick it up in person. You have light and heavy attacks. You have a stamina bar.
But it isn't quite the same. You move differently, more like a traditional action game. You can target individual body parts. Blocking is de-emphisized, in favor of dodging. it feels different, and looks different.
But if you like Dark Souls, you'll probably like The Surge. I do.

If you like tweaking at the microscopic level and trying to squeeze out that little extra bit of performance, this game is for you. You can figure out optimal designs for producing a given amount of each resource as fast as possible and using as little space/materials as you can.
If you like large scale planning and architecting, this game is also for you. From the map view, that shows each section of your factory and how they all fit together geographically, to the production statistics that let you monitor graphs of your production/consumption of each resource and product, this game gives you the tools necessary to make sure your overall factory design does what you need.
This game has perfected automation. There are so many layers and aspects to it, but it all amounts to building machines that help you build more machines. The rate at which you are able to rework, expand, and optimize increases seemingly exponentially. Once you have perfected your assembly layout for a given resource, blueprint it and then have your construction robots automatically construct additional facilities to increase your production. Factorio demands thoughtful design at both the small and large scales.

They've not forgotten the lessons learned in the Wargame series, but this time with less micromanagement and a clearer focus on what makes that series' gameplay unique. Eugen is an outlier in this business, and they are prone to taking missteps, but this time all big decisions they have taken regarding this game are spot on. Now, if they just had brought back the war room ambience when you zoom out the map like they did in Ruse, it'd be simply perfect. As it is, it's bloody brilliant.

So, first things first - 1) It's in beta, and balance hasn't finished yet. 2) Only 4 out of the 18(?) divisions are in the game yet. 3) It's in beta.
It's a great game in my opinion. It's very wargame / company of heroes -esque without being as nitpicky as I found wargame or as... RTS'y as I found CoH (I know, that sound stupid, bear with me) -
The game is not based around your usual kind of win conditions - the conquest variant is dictacted by the amount of territory you control which can vary a lot during the game especially since you effectively dictate where the fights take place. There aren't control points to fight over (although there are towns and such, but they hold no intrinsic value other than cover). In fact, sticking to one point on the map will probably result in the enemy investing in artillery to pound you to dust.. or flanking you... or ignoring you completely and taking the rest of the map. And this is where the great strength of the game comes into it's own - the variability.
There's a meta of sorts when you just consider the battlegroup formation - you make your army out of 'cards' from possible selections within a particular division. You can't take all of them so do you take more infantry or more tanks, and then each division has a certain amount of slots for each type of unit, so one may have 6 infantry, 4 tanks, and another might have 8 infantry, 2 tanks. Then on top of that, some units activate in certain phases (A, B or C) so do you bring more infantry early and save for late tanks, or bring an early heavy tank and hope you don't get eaten up by anti-tank... the choices are effectively endless.
Ultimately it's a strategy game that isn't based around bases or control points but rather what army you bring and how you plan on playing it versus whatever the enemy brings. There's a lot of room for depth and I am certainly looking forward to the full release and the new divisions it will bring with it.
Tl;dr, not an easy game, but has a lot of depth and looks to become a real strategy gem.

This is a nice way of getting you to learn the mechanics of the game without taking too many risks. There's a lot to like about that: exploring the galaxy, figuring out which supplies to sell at a profit later, and plotting your flight path to maximise how much you can get done.
That was fun for a while, but after I'd paid my loan off and bought some new ships so that I could start doing some combat missions, I realised I didn't like the combat in this game. Sure, I'd been instantly blown up previously by extremely overpowered enemies when I wasn't even looking for a fight, but even when I'd built up my fleet and could hold my own, I just didn't find the combat fun at all. But others will have a great time with it, and I definitely recommend the game. It's free, so you've really nothing to lose.

I've only been playing this game for about a week, and I'm already addicted. This game rekindled my love for MMO's that I had grown out of quite a few years ago.
It's perfect for both new players or returning ones - There are tutorials that I've found are more useful than ones I've seen in any other games. It explains dungeon roles in details so that new players won't feel lost, and there's a chat dedicated to new players and 'mentors' so that whenever you feel lost there's someone to ask. I've come across very few nasty players, there's a huge emphasis on helping others in this community.
I absolutely adore the designs, the attention to detail - You have the ability just to change your characters expressions for close up screenshots, and the amount of detail that went into just designing faces is astonishing. Casting and fighting animations are also beautiful, so it makes fights pleasing to the eye rather than repetitive animations.
I really enjoy how the class system works - You pick a starter class, and once you reach level 10 you can then pick up any other class you want and then switch over to it. Essentially, you can have one character who switches between every available class and profession. It feels nice being able to focus on one character and maybe a few alts, rather than having to make a new character whenever you want to try a different class or profession.
My only complaints for this game are ones every MMO tend to have - there are way more DPS than there are healers or tanks so queue times can take a while.
Lastly, the cat race is really cute. All of my characters will always be cat girls.

All of them attack from improbable angles, or suddenly, or with combination of the 2, and attacks in this game hurt a lot. Additionally, its bloody dark everywhere. Learning patterns just dont seem to worth it. All of the above clearly define a winning strategy: Go in fast, smack em once, and bug off before they hit you, which makes weapons with big damage simply better then the rest. Forcing the player to act in certain way seems to be the theme with this game.
5. Only saw 2 out of 5 boss fights this far, and they both can be described simply as annoying.
PROS:
1. Exploring is fun, and level design is very cool.
2. Cool stuff with exoskeletons, implants, and such. High-tek is something pretty new for this genre.

One of the most overlooked video games, The King of Fighters XIII is the latest entry in the now 20-years old series developed by SNK.
A complete overhaul of the 12th KoF game, KoF XIII is incredibly well-balanced (with the exception of some characters having mild advantages, like Robert or Kensou), has stunning 2D hand-drawn graphics and fantastic music (this being a staple of the series, even though it is not on par with masterpieces from '99 or '00), with a generic story, something not needed in a fighting game, unless you want to dig up this game's tangled and confusing mess of a narrative. The in-game art is anime-y, but not "moe", thus managing to look pleasant to the eye. Character illustrations and cutscenes are all skillfuly drawn, reminiscent of KoF XI's in-game art.
But, since it is a competitive game, the
is the most important part:
More fast-paced than other fighting games, such as Street Fighter or Mortal Kombat, KoF XIII delivers by moving back to the series' roots, with its gameplay most reminiscent of entries like as '98, while managing to fit in complex elements from '02 and XI. All of the 30+ characters are very well balanced (though not as much as in '98), fun to use and each with unique movesets and seemingly endless combo capabilities, feat managed by the inclusion of a cancel system, which allows multiple unchainable moves to be used one after another in a combo. NEO MAX moves make an appearance, reminiscent of '02s most devastating moves. The system is fluid, the hitboxes are okay for the most part, and the roll and hop systems give the game more dynamism as opposed to its competitors. Projectiles though seem to have been buffed from XI, giving them more potential not only for zoning, but also for their offensive and hard to counter nature (for some characters, such as Robert and Kensou).
It takes a lot of time to get used and good at the system, and for newcomers to the genre I wouldn't recommend this game, but to veterans that are looking for challenge and a deep and complex game, this game might just be for you. The netcode is vastly improved compared to the console versions, but can still be unsatisfactory at times. I am still waiting for a matchmaking feature that pits players of the same rank, and a spectator mode.
Overall - 9/10

Now that I've recently returned to 100% the game, I feel that I can finally review it. (And don't worry, no spoilers.)
First off, if you've not played Bastion, you don't need to in order to play this one. They aren't connected in the least besides gameplay and artstyle/music. Of course, I'd recommend playing that game too; it's a good one. If you
played Bastion, then I'd still highly recommend playing Transistor. Though it doesn't have the multiple endings that Bastion does, the story is still quite satisfying.
Transistor is a great game, and I enjoyed it even more than I enjoyed Bastion. Its gameplay, though similar to its predecessor, feels a lot more polished and varied, with Red's many attacks having much use as you go along. What's nice is that a little ways in you get a way to attack even during your cooldowns (if you choose to use Turn()), which mixes up the fun even more. The story is just vague enough to keep you interested in its mystery (as Bastion did as well), and as minimal as it is, it works quite well. It's a really nice tale of love and loss (cheesy, I know), and the characters and world that it builds are very imaginative. It's short, it's fairly action-packed, and it's heartrending.
The theme at its core - the potential imperfections of paradise - is touched upon tastefully and openly enough for the player to form their own opinions on how such would work (if it could). The game contains a couple of anticlimaxes that are done in an intentional manner to add to the mood and storytelling, and while for a game that's generally not the best idea, I found that it made sense for the most part here. That is still, of course, a flaw, but it's a justifiable one.
As for the ending, without spoiling anything, I found it beautiful. The art, the music, the circumstances... they all blend together so well to make an impactful ending. It's amazing in its simplicity, and it is, for the most part, a logical conclusion to the story. I suppose there could maybe have been a choice as there was in Bastion (though only one choice and two options here), but that's just a very small piece of missed potential. The ending that the developers chose works, and it works well.
The art in the game is awesome, and I figured I might as well give it a brief mention. The whole game looks great, and every time you get to see full art in its glory, it really does feel like a treat. The artist is
in case you want to see more of her work. Anyway...
Finally, I get to gush about the music! I
recommend buying the soundtrack, because it is phenomenal. It has some powerful songs (especially the vocal tracks - if you've not heard Paper Boats before, please don't listen to it until the end of the game. It just adds so much to the ending.) as well as many intense or atmospheric ones. A while back I made a review for the soundtrack itself, so check that out if for some reason you're interested in my favorite tracks. Anyway, all of the songs fit the game, and they add a lot to how artsy and beautiful it is.
That's about it for this review - it turned out a little longer than I'd expected! For a rather short game, Transistor is one of the best; like any Steam game, it's in your best interest to buy it on sale, but to me it's worth the full price. Even after fully completing it I can see myself going back to it in the future.
I don't really like giving numerical scores to games in general, so I'll just say that while it isn't perfect, it's really great and most certainly worth picking up if you can.

A game about what happens when you don't make the move at the critical time when given the chance. A lesson in living in the now.

So, basically, at one point in highschool you decided to either go to the grad party or not. If you went, a girl took you aside and basically made all the romance happen for you and you didn't go for the kiss. If you decided not to go, you missed out on the above scenario even though she wanted you to go.
If you liked her from the start, you messed up before the game even began and you can't change a thing, the wheels are in motion.
If you didn't like her from the start or didn't care for a relationship, this game goes by smoothly, just helping a friend through a hard time or not depending on your level of empathy or babysitting skills.
Regardless, if you're thinking right now: "Wow, this guy/girl I'm playing as is a real wet blanket! I'd have totally gone for it when given the chance! Hindsight 20/20!" Then, huzzah! Nothing's stopping you from doing it in real life with your own crush!
Lesson learned. Live in the now. Don't fabricate a wall where there is none, you're either in or you're not. You're either the protagonist to this endless game of pitty and frustration or you're an actual living being with the capacity for change and higher cognitive function! You're able to make that difference, you're not stuck in a binary (or in this case ternary) system of absolutes! You can get the girl.

I've only been playing this game for about a week, and I'm already addicted. This game rekindled my love for MMO's that I had grown out of quite a few years ago.
It's perfect for both new players or returning ones - There are tutorials that I've found are more useful than ones I've seen in any other games. It explains dungeon roles in details so that new players won't feel lost, and there's a chat dedicated to new players and 'mentors' so that whenever you feel lost there's someone to ask. I've come across very few nasty players, there's a huge emphasis on helping others in this community.
I absolutely adore the designs, the attention to detail - You have the ability just to change your characters expressions for close up screenshots, and the amount of detail that went into just designing faces is astonishing. Casting and fighting animations are also beautiful, so it makes fights pleasing to the eye rather than repetitive animations.
I really enjoy how the class system works - You pick a starter class, and once you reach level 10 you can then pick up any other class you want and then switch over to it. Essentially, you can have one character who switches between every available class and profession. It feels nice being able to focus on one character and maybe a few alts, rather than having to make a new character whenever you want to try a different class or profession.
My only complaints for this game are ones every MMO tend to have - there are way more DPS than there are healers or tanks so queue times can take a while.
Lastly, the cat race is really cute. All of my characters will always be cat girls.

Open world games seem to have two ways to go.  You are either going to love it, or hate it with no inbetween.  It is safe to say that I am in love with this game.  The storyline alone could keep you hooked, but it is much more than that.   I have a tendency to go off on sidequest adventures to the point where I forget where I was in the main story.  Fortunately this game does not let you get that deep into sidequests as they open up while you progress the main story.   At first I was annoyed by being forced to complete missions in order to open up side quests, but in the end I appreciated the fact that I never got so into side quests that I forgot where the heck I was in the story.
What can you say about Wei Shen?  At first I thought his character was going to be this angry guy that carries a chip on his shoulder the size of China.  While he does remain pretty angry, he is a protaganist that has every reason to be as you discover in the story.  I really enjoyed the fact that he was undercover amongst the Triads and you get to see him walk that line between the law and the underworld.  I also loved the fact that you had side missions that were on both sides of the law as well.  They did a wonderful job showing Wei's struggle to do what is right over just wanting to go on his personal revenge.  Every great protaganist needs a silly sidekick, and you get that with Wei's best friend, Jackie.  If anyone watches the show Pawn Stars, Jackie's personality reminds me of Chumlee.  The voice actors were on point with their characters.  All roles were played beautifully.  Oh... Wei Shen singing karaoke is a must do in this game.  Listening to him sing Flock of Seagulls was hilarious.
The world itself is pretty big, so it took me awhile to explore every part of the map, but I have always enjoyed games where you have the ability to explore from one corner of the map to the other.  Of course it took me a few car crashes to remember that I was driving on the wrong side of the road.  After that, exploring became more enjoyable.  I went into this game blind, so I knew nothing about these random events that would pop up while you explore.  Finding some lady in a trunk of a car with lingerie on, who then proceeded to chew me out because I messed up her and her lover's fantasy, kept me quite amused.  I won't say what any of the others one are, so I don't spoil things.
Combat was okay.  I did like that you did not have to use a gun or any other weaponry for the most part.  Hand to hand combat was effective and I didn't have to curse at my screen because I had to wait while Wei reloaded.  The reason why I just say it is okay is because it was pretty simple using a mouse.  You just clicked and clicked and you could pummel some unfortunate peon into the ground.  I did play with a controller as well, and that made combat a lot more challenging when it came to getting off combos and the like.  Wei's leveling system was pretty well designed.  He had a level system as a Triad member, as a police officer, and as an ordinary helpful citizen.  Each of these level systems had some wonderful perks, so they were all worth maxing out.  The hardest one to level up for me was for the Triads.  I had to replay some missions to get a higher score, but the police and citizen track was pretty easy.. no backtracking needed.
There is so much to do in here, boredom just does not happen.  If you like open world games, you will love this one.  Regular price or sale price, it is completely worth the money.  I even enjoyed the DLC, which is not something I say very often about any DLC.

Where to begin...
The only reason I had stumbled upon this game was because of a 90% off coupon that I had received, so for around $.50 I purchased the game (because I really do enjoy this style of game). After playing 'Vault of Honor' for a couple of hours I cannot wrap my head around the fact that this game is worth $5.49 -- that's a steal! Not in the common sense of the meaning... you're being robbed, darling.
What is wrong with this game:
1. There is absolutely no sense of accomplishment with this game; there are no achievements, milestones or goals to reach.
2. The lack of a UI becomes an annoyance; there is no button to 'Pick' locks or 'Disarm' traps, instead you simply click anywhere on the screen; unlike Attack/Defend animations.
3. The most obvious problem with this game is the price; this plays similar to that of a 2004 browser game.
How to improve this game:
1. Add achievements (reach x floor, kill x monsters, x in game hours, etc); create a lore/atmosphere that is PRESENT. Give us something to think about in-game rather than having us wonder why we spent whatever we did on this game.
2. Create a UI; make the weapon/armor drops viewable at the least -- like a gallery to see what they do. It could be tied into the first improvement point if used in a */100 sense.
3. Reduce the price. If you add achievements and lower the price down to a more reasonable price of, say, $0.99 then people would definitely purchase it.

This is simply the best target-based MMO on the market. It's the only MMO I've played where I actually read the quest dialog, because it is all well written. With just a few sentences, they give a clear personality to each NPC, and the scenarios for each quest are all tied together to form cohesive, open-ended stories about the land and the people in it. While the quests generally involve "kill this" or "fetch that," I don't think they need to be anything more complicated. If you want to take on something more involved, then PvP, dungeons, and raids got you covered.
The land is a joy to traverse, with beautiful landscapes and a day-night cycle that radically changes the vibrant colors of the world. There are plenty of bells and whistles, like housing, retainers, and crafting that I haven't even begun to get into yet in the first hundred hours. Inventory space is leniant and you don't need to worry about looting every mob you kill because you loot things automatically.
Also you can play as every class with just one character. *mic drop*

If you're a Darksouls hardcore kinda player this is perfect for you. However, the bosses are insanely hard. Having beaten Darksouls 1 and 2 I can personally say the bosses in this are sadistic in comparison. While in DS bosses are complex enemies that need to be understood to be defeated, bosses in The Surge offer no such niceness. They're extremely tough, taking tremendous damage and they have no explanation as to how to damage them in any special way. From the two I encountered they take virutally no damage and virtually insta-kill on contact. While the cannonfodder combat is easier and actually more enjoyable than Dark Souls, the bosses are crueler and counter act any improvement over DS with serverely unenjoyable boss battles. If I had more than 2 hours to try the game before steam would cut off my return option I would try to delve deeper into this, but sadly that's all I'm allotted before I get stuck with a game I might not enjoy. To be clear, the exploration and grind of The Surge is terrific. However the boss battles ruin the entire experience for me, there is no explanation as to how to defeat a boss, not even hints in the gameplay. They do tremendous damage to you and seem to take none, this isn't fun it's just brutal. I presume however the typical person looking into The Surge is a Dark Souls player, most DS players are way more into slamming their head into a wall repeatedly than I am, if you are that kind of player then this is for you, hopefully you'll figure out the secret to the bosses because the rest of the game is awesome.

This was a very enjoyable game that I finished in about 2 sittings, it doesn't feel as polished and the areas aren't as nice as dark souls but I think the melee combat is alot more fun. It feels really good flying in out of combat instead of that awkward rolling on the floor, the weapons are actually well balanced with heavy ones having high stunlock and damage, while the fast ones have fast attacks that you can weave in easier. There are some really cool weapons aswell like fire shooting duel blades and an axe that shoots out energy blasts (my personal favourite).
The game works waaaaay better on a mouse and keyboard than dark souls does, I actually prefer the mouse and keyboard to the controller for this game which means alot since this is a 3rd person action game.
The story is more in your face than dark souls and it has a really well done moment with the presenter hacket later on, everything in the office area is well done actually. I don't quite get why they didn't add character creation (I myself don't really care) because alot of people really love it and the story definitely didn't need you as a set character at all.

There are two things I have to point out before being able to recommend KoF XIII fully.
The first one being technical issues: this game has issues with VSync, lack thereof, and everything surrounding game-speed. You will have to spend some time trying to set up your game so that it doesn't run too fast or too slow, but that's just a matter of combining forced VSync through your GPU's settings and fiddling with the ingame-options (fixed framerate); make sure to add "-r" (without quotes) to the launch-options for the game in Steam.
The second thing to point out is that this game is pretty difficult to play. If you wanted to compare KoF to Street Fighter, you'd probably have to say that where Street Fighter has tight links on buttons (plinking 1frame-links) but relatively simple motions, KoF has demanding motions (qcbhcfb and similar) but lenient input-windows for buttons. KoF also has 4 different types of jumps (hop, hyper-hop, jump, super-jump) and a huge roster of characters. All that said,
(general non-KOFXIII-specific KoF-tutorial).
As for the good things, the game being fairly difficult to get into means it's also very rewarding. Momentum plays a huge role, so the neutral game and knowing how to apply/escape pressure are very important. The netcode seems pretty good, from my experience thus far it's very close to playing offline with a good connection. The characters allow for a fairly varied approach to the game and building interesting teams (3 characters/team that fight 1v1 until you or your opponent run out of characters). Game-balance overall is generally considered pretty good; there are no complete duds on the roster, only some chars need to work harder to win. The training-mode offers most of the functionality you'd expect- could be better. The trials are meant to showcase shortcuts and be a challenge to experienced KOF players, if you try to learn the game by playing them (which can be done, theoretically), you're going to have a very bad time.
To get started I'd recommend watching the tutorial linked above, look up the bread-and-butter combos for the characters of your choice/interest on the
or the
or similar sites, and to maybe just jump right in and play with a fellow noob, that's always very helpful- online you'd probably get destroyed, from what I read on different forums.

As you can probably tell by my hours played, I was a huge fan of this game while it was in development. I could live with the bugs, knowing it was all an Early Access alpha, and that it was being worked on regularly. Some day, it would be finished and fun.
Except that never happened.
Tim Schaefer himself gave the order to pull the plug on development, claiming that not enough people bought the game during Early Access to fund the development. That's right, the business "plan" was to use Early Access money to fund the actual game (smacks head).
If they'd done a standard crowdfund (like Kickstarter) and said "We need X dollars to make this game", they probably would've gotten the money because, you know, Double Fine -- but, apparently, they completely misunderstood what Early Access is for (hint: it's not for funding the majority of your game's development).
Short version? Same as everyone else has been saying: the developer abandoned the project, but called it finished anyway. It's not finished. Do not buy.

TLDR: I picked up and played this game when it was at full price, it was worth it then. Now that the price is reduced it's totally worth it. Its one of the few games that can boast that they're in the same genre as Dark Souls. The combat is similarly slow and deliberate. That said, that's just the skeleton.
The game makes both successes and failures beyond that point. I'd say 90% of the gameplay decisions are interesting, unique, and fun to play. There are definitely parts of the game that creak a bit, but the core game is great. Do note that mechanically I wish they made more varied weapons with a higher weapons scaling level. The equips can only be upgraded a few times, but theoretically your stats can go up forever. So logic dictates you need a high scaling weapon... which are very limited (one or two in each of a variety of weapon types), functionally deeply restricting weaponry as the game goes on.
The primary issue that I had with the game was involvement. The plot slowly unravels in an intriguing way, but the information that it reveals is never revelatory. Of course the megacorp is making decisions that ignore the value of human life... duh. That's really the only extended revelation in all the audiologs. They do have interesting tones and personal stories, but they ultimately arent worth anything beyond the quality of the voice actor's delivery. A few of those voice actors do a real good job and a few do... less well.
I also do not recall the music at all. That may be a failing of my memory, or it was mostly just ambiance.
Summary of my experience:
I enjoyed the introduction and began learning the system, after a few stumbles got rolling along with smooth progress.
Slammed my head against being killed repeatedly by a certain hostile environment early on... I mistakenly thought I was supposed to push on like I did in DS's swamps... wasted time and effort on the dead end with minor equip.
Gained full command of the combat system and built my character up over the next few hours.
Tore apart my first few robot dogs... I'd come to get very good at that.
Made steady progress through new environs and enemies.
Slammed into a brick wall of a boss in the form of one of the hammer bros.
Tried repeatedly
Gave up and ran off to level up more
Came back and tried till giving up
Returned and immediately succeeded with patience and crystalized tactics.
Was rewarded with somewhat vague plot reveal information
Continued to push through
Something about 'nanomachines' (insert MGS meme)
Ended up stopping after just getting lost as to where to go to progress.
Didn't feel like coming back any time soon
Uninstall
... months later
Writes review and makes mental note to reinstall and finish it off.
Essentially the combat becomes repetitive, the plot banal, and while the environs are intricately connected in a manner similar to dark souls it lacks any 'weanies' (things like a castle in the distance you're making progress toward). Your movement and progress has no indication as a result. Expect areas to be connected by deeply similar jefferies tubes, loading screen subways, and hallways that end up being increasingly disorienting even for someone who has been gaming for years and has a pretty strong mental map. There are more interesting environments that are definitely memorable, but their connections are often baffling and serpentine with quick turns and multiple elevators leading to separate branches. All in a 'jeffereies tube' tileset that despirately needs more variation or large signage.
Hopefully this has been informative as to some of the mechanical aspects of this game and how they work together. If you can put up with those flaws its definitely fun and worth the reduced price. :)

Dark Souls, but in the
!
That's a simple way to describe the game.
The game isn't without its faults.  It's brutally hard at the beginning.  It takes a lot of practice to get your weapons timing down.  The game insists you stick with one weapon type through the game, because your damage is based on how much you use it.  Switching weapon types late in the game is a recipie for disaster unless you plan on spending too much time grinding.  There's only 5 bosses compared to Dark Souls 5 billion, and each has a "special" way to defeat them that gets you a fancy weapon, but the game makes no hint that defeating the bosses a certain way would give you anything special.  The maps are crazy confusing at times, with shortcuts within shortcuts, making it very easy to get lost, and the maps are mostly quite similar.
So why a positive review?  I had an absolute blast playing it.  In the beginning I was getting mopped by basic enemies, and by the end I was mopping them up.  The game punishes you hard for messing up and overcomitting like Dark Souls would, but if you're cautious you can pull through.  Every fight at first feels like a mini-boss battle.  The system of getting armor and weapons is a little weird at first, but as soon as you see a new enemy with a weapon or armor you haven't seen, your first instinct is chop off all their limbs so you can play with their toys.
Overall, I personally had a ton of fun with this, even with its brutal difficulty.  It could defenitly use more polish, more bosses, more maps, more everything.

However there are HORRIBLE problems with this game, and it doesn't seem like these SNK guys are ever going to solve these.
Problem number one, arcade mode is fine, but the bosses are as f**king hard as ever. They always use moves that freeze you solid and cannot be blocked, meaning you never get any chance to move, unless you can find a flaw in AI and keep using one move that the AI doesn't care to block.
Problem number two, the difficulty setting doesn't seem to affect versus mode. Even at highest difficulty, the CPU opponent in versus mode is still too easy.
Problem number three, online match sucks. I don't play well and lose most of the time, but won't it be better if the balance can be adjusted according to the players' stats. This system is there in versus mode, so why not online match mode? Because I always lose, I've lost all interest in online matches.
With the three problems, I don't want to play arcade mode because the boss is too hard and I can't finish the game; I don't want to play versus mode because CPU is too easy; and I don't want to play online match mode because I always lose. There's no point in playing anymore. Well there are still trials I can challenge, but that's about all.

I bought this game to replay the singleplayer portion of the game since I used to play it a lot when I had an Xbox 360 and I wanted to experience the nostalgia of playing through it once again. And I have to say, it sure delivers on that and more!
I played through Call of Duty 4 - Modern Warfare right before jumping into this one to better understand the story and of course to re-experience CoD 4 as well. During the 8 hours I spent completing the campaign of Modern Warfare 2 (MW2) on Veteran I never once got bored, this is a game filled to the brim with action all the way throughout the campaign and there's never a dull moment, this game had my adrenaline pumping and my heart beating like crazy during a big portion of the game.
I am not going to get into any details about the story here in this review since it would take too long, but the story is a story of betrayal and most of the story takes place during a war between Russia and the US. You get to play as multiple soldiers during the campaign and as such you get to play with different teams of soldiers as well.
I found this game to be a lot easier than CoD 4, I played both on Veteran but I found MW2 to be the easiest one. CoD 4 just has a lot more difficult missions and scenarios compared to MW2. That said, this game is not afraid to give you a challenge should you choose to play on the higher difficulties.
If you are thinking of buying this game for it's multiplayer alone I would stay away, the game's multiplayer has a very low player population and a lot of the players still playing are cheaters.
I found this game to be an amazing experience and I would highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys shooters but I would highly recommend that you play CoD 4 before this one, it is not required to understand the story however CoD 4 is an excellent game in it's own right and you will get to know some of the characters in MW2 during CoD 4 (MW1), that way you will already be familiar with a lot of the characters when jumping into MW2.

It's hard to see the majority of people wanting to play any other multiplayer shooter until the next CoD is released, such is the quality of what's on offer here. I enjoyed the hell out of this game.  Once I started playing I pretty much spent every free moment I had playing it until I beat my first playthrough - and now I'm gonna go ahead and start my second playthrough.
Part 1: Souls-Like!
Lot of games coming out with this label and I can only hope they're all this good.  I've played the entire souls series and I see the things I like from there in this game.  Lemme go through what you'll find here that you also found in Dark Soul.
- Deliberate, measured combat with impact.  This game actually rivals any souls game in this regard as even the lighter weapons feel like your beating someone over the head with a lead pipe.  There's no gracefulness here just brutal beat downs.  The way your character attacks feels a bit clunky, but that makes sense since you're not a warrior using weapons of war , you're a factory worker using tools.  It should be a bit awkard, but that awkwardness actually makes it more engaging as you have to work with the specific rythm of each weapon's attacks.  As far as pacing goes, they managed to get about the speed of DS3, with even more weight than DS1.
- Shortcut Porn.  This game is crazy with shortcuts and sometimes you're amazed to find yourself back at your hub at the beginning of the level when you thought you must have been miles away.  Boss shortcuts in particular are fantastic and often lead you from your hub directly to the boss with only a handful of enemies to run past.  Progress in this game is measured in shortcuts.
- Limited but powerful healing.  Just like estus, your self heals will heal a lot very quickly, but you have a limited number of them and things can get dicey when you're not really sure where you are, you don't know how soon to the next shortcut, and you just ran out of heals.  Being careful and proceeding slowly are important when exploring new areas.  You have some choices here though with the implant system: load up on heals, or get other stuff instead.
Part 2: Beyond Souls-Like.
So this game brings some new things to the game that really adds to the gamplay, or does some things better than a souls game.
- Promoting aggression.  The energy system, which is simply a bar that fill up as you hit enemies more, rewards you for fighting aggressively rather than passively.  You can use that energy to activate various attacks or self buffs that can have a big impact on the fight.
- Upgrade system.  Implants as they're known in the game provide you with a variety of options when it comes to passive buffs and active effects.  For one, Implants are where you heals ( estus ) comes from, so it's up to you just how many heals you venture out with.  Maybe instead you'd like to have a truckload of hit points?  Or maybe you'd like to be able to burn energy to do a bunch more damage?  Maybe you'd prefer healing-over-time instead of estus style burst heals?  Or maybe you'd like to use your implants to improve your core power so you can equip heavier rig armor?  There's a good amount of options here to play around with and I found myself switching out implants to deal with various situations.
- Limb Targeting.  In combat you can target specific areas of the opponent ( head, legs, arms, body )  There are two considerations her.  On the one hand, targeting areas that are unarmored will do more damage.  On the other hand, beating on armored areas makes it more likely that you can rip them off, and ripping off limbs is how you get new recipes to craft different kinds of armor, as well as the crafting materials to build and upgrade armor.  The system stayed relevant throughout my entire playthrough and it adds a few seconds to the start of every battle as you check out which areas are armored and decide if you want to go for the mats or the faster kill.
Part 3: Things I didn't like.
Won't lie this is gonna be a short list and the entries are gonna be pretty shallow.
- It crashed a few times.  Nobody likes that!
- The targeting betrayed me at one point by locking on when I didn't want to which cause my camera to do things I didn't want it to do.. but that was easily solved by turning off auto-targeting on attack.  Told you the dislike list was gonna suck.
- Some things are unexplained, like why does everyone burst into flames when they die?  The answer is: so the game would run better by not having to render defeated enemies.  An in-game lore explanation would have been nice.

Comparatively I think the Surge is somewhat lacking in actual gameplay content. It is a bit repetitive although visually very cool and well optimized. The Surge has a great story and that's what sets it apart from the other 3rd person rpg "soulslike" games out there. It's obvious the Surge isn't some half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥attempt to cash in, this game is well made and made by people who clearly wanted it to be great. The story is interesting and there are a lot of high quality visuals in the game, to the point where it carries this game.
I don't know if they patched the game but I had no problem with the difficulty increases between zones and thought it was very well paced actually, I wanted to mention this as it seems like a lot of negative reviewers seem to think the difficulty spikes are insane. I honestly didn't find this game that difficult at all, even NG+ I'm coasting through pretty easily.
The demo is a small taste of the game but it accurately represents what you'll get more of. The later levels can become extremely complex and backtracking is quite frequent if you're trying to see everything. The thing about the demo is that what you experience in it is largely unchanged in the main game. Enemy types are few and bosses even more sparse. If you want more of what the demo has to offer then you'll enjoy this game, but the thing is there isn't much more gameplay wise. It's more of the same in a new location, even choosing a weapon type will probably come down to what animations you like to watch more rather than playstyle because your playstyle depends more on what you are fighting than what you are wielding.

My only gripe is that the areas get slightly repetitive, as you would expect with the 'run down factory' theme throughout. It doesn't ruin the game, but just makes samey in some places.

The only chats you get to play out are chats with one individual: Emily, the titular character, who you're supposed to like. Unfortunately, literally the only reason you're supposed to like her is because your responses say you should. She has exactly zero interesting moments throughout the game, to the point where the characters you only know through their AIM bios are more interesting and engaging.
The choices you make in the game don't matter almost at all, and no matter what you do you're framed as a manipulator and general jerk. This whole game plays like the sad diary of a guy who got "friendzoned" in college and still hasn't gotten over it. It was a novel idea, but it could've benefited from hiring someone who knew how to write.
It's not worth playing.

text:
Ironicly, the title says all. The demon of insanity saves the world, with some friends! But not with yours.
Cthulhu Saves the World is an old school based RPG with dynamic combats and a revisited gameplay.
When you think you've seen everything in all RPGs, you're wrong. Cthulhu will show you some skills you've never seen before, and for a small, tiny, microscopic price.
In this game you can create your own party of 4 characters, choosing between around 9 to 11 characters, each with different classes and abilities, you will have to try them all out to find their best skills to beat the bosses.
In combat you can fusion with one of your party to create a unique powerful skill that can be as useful as useless, you will need to study every single detail to make the game easier.
The story is counting many dungeons and villages which all have an event (zombie apocalypse, diseases, thieves), 2 sub dungeons to farm your experience if needed. Also, there's a limited number of random battles in a dungeon for you to fully  explore it after. But don't worry, in the menu you still can choose the "Fight" selection to battle and earn experience.
The dialogues are funny and maybe for the first time in a RPG you're gonna read every single sentence.
Finally, when you end the game, bonus modes and challenges can be unlocked to extend the gameplay.
However, the "Cthulhu Angels" is the same story but with different characters (only girls.) and a different dialogue.
Also, with the graphics, I was hoping for some chiptune music but the game has a quite disturbing music that comes over and over and sometimes in an inappropriate time.
The game is a little too easy, especially on "Normal" which I did my 1st run today. The final battle wasn't so epic as in an old RPG game. I mean, a final battle should take around 10 to 30 minutes to make it. This one can be made in 3 minutes, even less. (In Normal Mode, I repeat.)
Anyway, for this price you can't refuse to play this game, if you like RPGs or not, this one is made for everyone: for beginners as for harcore gamers. When the old RPG was too epic, Cthulhu gives some insanity to make it funny and it works.

A long-time popular fighting series since the golden 16-bit era.
From the start of Fatal Fury and Art of Fighting games comes a popular hybrid now with 13 official titles.
The King of Fighters is what makes 2D fighting right. It's a shame that this game is overlooked by the PC community and lacks any local players online (coming from an Aussie standpoint).
More PC gamers should definitely check this game out, it's worth the while. If more attention could spread towards this game with the PC community then everyone can enjoy the KoF experience together.
Another downside aside the lack of online players is that the players you actually find are already experienced, and most opponents are from another country so the lag doesn't make up for its solid netcode. There are small communities who list their names down to make it easier to find local opponents, but it still proves difficult when wanting to play a ranked match - especially after a long wait until you find an opponent who's more skilled with well over 150 ping.
Aside from the internet issues and lack of community, the whole package is there. It's perfect for those hardcore and newbie fighting fans alike. If you're looking to get into fighting games then this is a MUST. Becoming skilled at this game may be complicated and scary, but the time put into it will be well worth it in the end.
And, this game is part of the professional eSports scene such as EVO. So if you're planning on becoming all MLG with fighting games then KoFXIII is definitely the way to go.
I recommend this for everyone, except those who aren't fond with the fighting game genre.
If you love games, then pick this up. Play online and let the PC community of KoFXIII grow, because it deserves a larger community for the Steam port.
It's a 2D fighting game as well, so you don't need a spec-heavy PC to play.

This review is coming from someone who played a lot of Wargame from EE to RD.
I was a little skeptical at first, I mean "Steel Division: Normandy 44"? They couldn't have come up with a longer lamer name. I don't think it would be hard to come up with a better alterative, like say "Wargame: Normandy"?
The gameplay itself is actually a lot different from Wargame, to name a few:
I like the game. I'm pleasantly surprised myself, I expected to say "oh this game has less depth I'm going back to Wargame," but Eugen has done a great job so far with the open beta. I don't have too many complaints, I'm looking forward to more maps and battlegroups. I think my ultimate opinion of the game depends on having a large array of unique units and lots of different terrain to fight on.

Went in with very high hopes for this game but was honestly really dissapointed. I played wargame red dragon a lot and enjoyed it greatly, but this game doesent feel the same at all. Im aware that it doesent have to feel the same to be a good game, but just as a strategy game it was not particularly good (I play a lot of strategy games). I know it is early access but minus some unit and map variety this is pretty representative of what the final game is going to be like. Im just gonna list a bunch of points of how I feel about it. If you disagree comment on here or add me
- The four deck commanders they have availible feel extremely linear in terms of what you can choose. You might as well click autofill and roll out because you either have an infantry focused deck or an armor deck and thats pretty much it. A few categories have more variety like planes and support but otherwise I never felt like I was sacraficing anything in order to get a unit I wanted.
- Transport system could have been done better. Transports without weapons just disapear because I guess they have no more use. Otherwise they stay and become fire support / suppressors. Going back to the deck building aspect troops pretty much just give you one or maybe 2 transport options, and ussually just one with the armor decks. Sometimes if you shoot a transport everyone instantly dies and othertimes everyone just gets out completely fine. Im guessing its because in some cases the transport was only disabled so everyone just gets out and othertimes it blows up but I dont know.
- The entire game is pretty much based around the panick level of troops. To be fair panick was extremely important in the other Wargames as well, but unit training and higher end units could handle it better and still fight. In this game as soon as your red bar fills up past half you basically turn into advanced fodder. Not only that, literally anything can panic something. Missed shots against the front of a Sherman jumbo with 21 front armor from a Panzer with an AP value of 14? Full retreat. Also since tanks cannot hide anywhere you can pretty much assure that the 81mm mortar will permenantly panick your tank while the enemy picks off your useless infantry.
- The phases system of the game does not really work that well. Phase C doesent mean you have more advanced units it essentially means spam of Phase B units. Phase A is just recon, arty, and anti tank guns.
- The frontline system is good, but does kinda of remove any sort of flanking/stealth from the game. On the map that is availible, sneaking infantry around the side of the maps is extremely hard, and even if you do if your infantry arent paratroopers they will panick when behind enemy lines.
- Ranges are weird and the scalings of stuff is annoying. Lines of trees that appear to have around 14 trees in them are literally 500m long. Infantry AT weapons are a joke. Even if you sneak into the forest and try to ambush a tank the 150-250m ranges on the AT weapon mean that unless the tank is glitched into the woods you will be out of range. So you then move your infantry out of the woods to shoot the tank, and the tank instantly panicks your troops by missing a shot with its main gun and shooting at them with an mg.
- Infantry combat feels awful. It comes down to who gets panicked faster. The fights either end instantly as one slightly more trained squad massacres another one because it panicked it, or nobody dies becasue both squads are panicked and the sound effects and tracer rounds you see and hear are just morale support. Some units have frag grenades which instantly level buildings and one shot entire infantry squads.
This is just kind of rambling at this point but to summarize: the game feels clunky and I didnt enjoy it.

Going against most of the people here, it seems, I think DF-9 should get a generally positive review.
So you know where my view comes from: I bought this game early in alpha because I had a DF coupon, but I rarely play early EA games.  Aside from a quick try in alpha, I have only played the current 1.06.  I also rarely look in the forums, so perhaps I'm less angry than some.  :)
Bottom line: if you enjoy city/base/island-building sandbox games, you will enjoy this.
I found exploring the game after a minimal tutorial enjoyable.  I had several false-starts and refined my base layout as I went.  Lost one decent early base when I learned the difference between tear down and vaporize: when removing a section of wall, vaporize removes everything including the floor.  Everybody was blown out before it could be repaired.
The graphics and animation quality are quite nice as are most of the sound effects.  The user interface is also easy to use in most cases.  It has a few issues when it comes to placing objects, especially ones that go on walls.  Even though they might be hard to see sometimes, the game does not allow you to use the south-east and -west walls interior (hidden) side for object placement.  Turrets are one of the few items that can face in any direction and it can be difficult to place the turrent as it will jump from wall to wall.  There needs to be a manual method to move the selection tile-by-tile.  It matters where the turret's cone of fire reaches.
The AI is perhaps not superb, but so far I haven't had any serious issues with it.  At least, not yet.  Pathfinding seems okay, as long as your base isn't riddled with paths because of doors everywhere.  Picking/keeping a good crew goes along way towards avoiding frustration.  You should also invest some time in keeping them happy.  It can be difficult sometimes, but all of the information you need it given in their tabs.
Sometimes, though, the AI will do something really stupid or annoying.  Like avoiding the conveniently placed fire extinguisher in the hallway and trying to stamp out the fire.  It seems as though the extinguisher must be within the room on fire.
Of course, sometimes it helps to discover or know the AI's priorities.  With builders, for example, it's rather easy to observe their work, or lack of it, and to figure out what they prioritize.  They tend to prefer building floors before walls, and walls before any indoor work, and so on.  So, if you have a room built and while waiting for it to be filled you plan on a new hallway, the builders will drop their indoor work and go add that new section of hull first.
The game's biggest flaw, by far, then is the lack of depth.  Except for the residence and pub areas, every room has only a very small number of objects that you can place in it.  Researching does not alleviate this problem as you really just get upgraded versions of an object or an upgraded replacement model.  That's not bad, but it would be nice to have a number of topics to research (maybe based on your contact with alien visitors) that would give you new objects to use in rooms or maybe even a new room type.
This lack of depth and seeming lack of forward progression after a point seem to be the primary reasons other posters give for giving the game a thumbs down.  These really impact the length of play and replayability more than they do playability, however.
If the poor description of the game that I've given sounds like a genre that you enjoy, you'll definitely have some fun playing.  For how long I think largerly depends on how much you like exploring the mechanics of the game while you learn to play.  Experimenting with various base layouts for efficiency reasons or asthetics also adds some time and depth.
Whatever the reason for DF ceasing development, it seems pretty clear that what has been delivered is a
for a game.  But, of course, they were supposed to deliver a game.  Fortunately, the platform seems to be robust and moddable and even as-is provides a good amount of fun.
Judging by DF's last announcement, I doubt we'll be seeing anything more from them.  I choose to be optimistic about the game's future, though.  The quality of what they've open sourced appears good enough that I think the mod community will add a lot to the game in time.  I wish DF hadn't dropped it, but they did and there are far worse states they could have left it in.
The game does provide some long term objectives conveniently located under the "Goals" tab of the main HUD.  They are more like milestones, however, such as getting X number of crew, surviving the Mega Fleet, or killing X number of raiders.
Finally, price:  It's definitely not worth full price given the lack of depth.  I would pay anywhere between $5 and $10 for it and feel that I got my money's worth.
If you're looking for similar games, I would certainly recommend either Startopia or Evil Genius.  Startopia doesn't let you build the base, but you fill it and manage the station.  It came out some years back so it runs great on most any machine and it's a lot of fun.  Evil Genius has you building a base in your island mountain hideout.  You get to design the whole layout, rooms and hallways, similar to base building in DF-9.  Evil Genius has a lot of depth as you take on nefarious missions or as you build booby traps into your base to catch unwitting good guys.
I hope this provides a sufficiently objective view of the game.  Keep in mind that I'm still playing and making ever larger bases, so it's possible that there are some issues I've yet to encounter because my population hasn't been large enough.

Factorio is a stellar, first-class game for simulating factory automation and production, and more importantly, a very original creation. While most games are based from the same ideas borrowed from other successful games, Factorio is developed with all original ideas from yet another group of very talented programmers in Eastern Europe.
While the graphics aren't the main attraction in this game, they are basic and functional in order to play the game. The intensity of the graphics won't interfere with performance while building a very large factory with thousands of entities. If factory automation is something you find interesting, using conveyor belts and oil pipelines to automatically deliver ammunition to your turrets to fight invading aliens, then you should check this game out.
Pros:
- Works well on Mac OS X along with Windows.
- 100% Original content, with brand new ideas to the gaming industry.
- Performance is still very good even with a very large factory.
Cons:
- While the game supports multiplayer mode, I had trouble with constant map desync. This will probably be improved upon in the future.

Having played Lords of the Fallen, I ended up liking this one more up to the point where I reached the final levels. Keep in mind, that the game itself is very well designed; the environment fits a threatening, cyberhorrific atmosphere with a complex layer of facilities and open areas used in conjunction with each other. There is no map, and you really have to explore stalwartly in order to find those juicy shortcuts and hidden items. This game does not hold hands with you, but it's not quite at a level where you should be drawing a map on paper to keep yourself on the chart.
Let's talk about combat. This is the game's forte, it's fluid, and there's a lot of weapon disparity and lengthy combo potential. You are targeting the target's limbs instead of the target in whole, which will result in some areas being weaker against attacks than others. As you target those limbs, indicated with a blue font, as opposed to a yellow one, you are able to keep the targets stunned, and build up energy used to dissect the part. This part is used in crafting, which is done quite neatly.
There is not a lot of enemy disparity, the game is filled with "Hollows" aka. humanoids, and some different drones and constructs. Nor are there a lot of bosses, and even out of them, only 4 feel like a real boss encounter, of which 3 were enjoyable to me.
The plot is quite good, even though you figure one of the twists out by yourself soon enough. The end was worthy, and in the end I do not really regret slogging through the last couple of levels. I'd say this game is worth to get when a sale strikes, and if you do not expect to fight bosses on the same pace as Dark Souls series, or even Lords of the Fallen. The good thing is that this time, there are next to no gimmick bosses.

So here we have The Surge. The second 'soulslike' effort from from developer Deck 13.
Right off the bat I can confidently say that this is a MUCH better effort than Lords Of The Fallen. There were elements of that game that were enjoyable but it was heavily marred by some infuriating combat mechanics with enemies rotating on the spot to land attacks on you even when they'd commited to their attack animations. Fortunately this has been addressed in The Surge.
That issue was by far my biggest complaint with their last game because it took it from a game of skill to a depressing exercise in tedium. As a result The Surge feels much more balanced and the combat is actually very enjoyable. The mobility is much more akin to Bloodborne and the limb chopping mechanic is a nice addition. What's really cool is some of the clever little techniques you can learn for combat to gain the upper hand on your enemies. Some enemies will have weak points like their back and they're behaviour will change depending on your attack patterns.
For example there are some big maintaince mecs that tend to try and repair themselves if you attack their legs leaving them open to attack. It adds that little extra layer of tactical thought to the combat that elevates it to being not just good but great.
World building wise it's pretty subjective. For me I really like the industrialsed sci-fi look. Gives me glimpses of Alien and Red Dwarf which is an odd mix but a good one! There's a surprising amount of atmosphere in the game too. Some of the dark environments can be quite unnerving especially when an 'infected' comes barralling out of the darkness screaming like a nutter and lashing at you with arm blades! Verges on survival horror at that point which is pretty cool.
I'm running the game at 4k with a resolution scale of 70% with settings between high and medium with motion blur turned off and get a fairly steady 60fps so I wouldn't say the game is as well optimized as it could be but it's not awful either. I'd say if you're playing at 1080 you should be okay even with meager hardware if you're conservative with the settings.
All in all this is leaps and bounds better than the Dev's previous effort and I'd legitimately like to see a franchise made out of this. Fingers crossed.
Recommended.

I'm writing this review being very close to the end of the game. So far I found it very enjoyable. It's definitely souls-like, although I'm finding it much easier than any game on the Souls series. Dark Souls 1 is probably where the authors took most of their inspiration, seeing as the level design in this game revolves around shortcuts and the combat has a similar feel (with the added fun of dismemberments).
There were some reviews that almost made me not buy this game, so I'm going to address some of the negative points on those:
1) Lack of enemy diversity.
This one is true, but it didn't bother me much. Combat is fun enough and the animations are so detailed it's underestandable why they couldn't create more enemies.
2) Lots of backtracking.
There is some backtracking built into the plot, but it felt natural to me; it's not about having to fetch some mcguffin you left three areas behind and had no way of knowing was neded later. There is also some optional backtracking required if you're a completionist (there are collectibles locked in areas you'll only be able to access after acquiring end game equipment), but it's entirely optional.
3) Lack of a map or proper direction to progress the plot.
I guess people who complained about this aren't fans of Dark Souls. Not only it didn't bother me, but I found the progression in this game almost linear. There are frequent branching paths, but they are mostly shortcuts back to the Med bay and short paths to hidden loot. I can imagine having trouble getting my bearings if I stopped playing for a while, but it shouldn't be much of an issue for someone with an average memory.
4) Regular enemies kill you in one hit.
This one had me worried the most. Some guys wrote that they ended up only using running attacks and then backing of, because enemies were so punishing; it sounded terribly boring. Fortunately I found that this can happen, but it depends mostly on the armor and implants you use: if you use light armor and don't equip a few implants that raise your health, you will get one shotted by most enemies; if you play with heavy armor and equip health impants you'll be able to survive a couple of hits from even the strongest enemies.
Finally, I just want to vent about a particular mechanic, that I think detracts from the overall game experience: weapon proficiency. Weapon proficiency boots your damage with a weapon type, is gained through using that weapon type and doesn't seem to have a cap, so it punishes using different weapon types. It's a damn shame this mechanic exists, because I tried all the different weapon types for an achievement and they were all pretty balanced and fun to use.
P.S.: I played this game with mouse and keyboard and it was fine. Unlike Dark Souls, playing with a controller is not a necessity here.
