For a game that's so heavily constructed around its plot, it's odd that the plot should be the weakest part of the game. Nevertheless, The Surge is a huge step forward for Deck 13 from their previous Soulslike, Lords of the Fallen.
A lot of Lords of the Fallen's design elements are present in The Surge, from weapon movesets to UI decisions to the general cumbersome feel of combat, but the rough edges have been sanded away at to the point where they've mostly disappeared. Instead of going for a same-y fantasy setting like LotF, The Surge goes for a same-y sci-fi setting, but fights feel more or less identical. Mooks are damage sponges. Bosses are huge rather than interesting. Weapons upskill as you use them, forcing you to funnel into a particularly build based on what was available early on, or else grind away at your subpar weapon stats to get the most out of a late-game drop.
Unlike other Soulslikes, in The Surge, you cannot increase your stats. You have one stat, Core Power, and every other bit of your statblock scales off of that. You buy up core power with scrap (the souls equivalent), and you equip items to tweak your stats. Weapons and armor are abundant, and the game's complete lack of vendors is made up for by letting you rip the limbs off of your enemies to wear on your cyborg body.
Like the railroaded path through the plot, limb-ripping is central to the game and fundamentally kind of boring. You build up combo meter, lower the enemy's lifebar, and then hold X to end the fight. The first time you do it, it feels kind of visceral, but then it promptly turns into a chore. To get every piece of armor in a set (legs, chest, hands, helmet), you have to rip each one individually off of a different enemy (since ripping is a kill, and all corpses in this setting instantly self-immolate to prevent you from scavenging further). Worse, to upgrade a piece of gear, you need to do a number of additional rips of the same limb off of equivalent-strength enemies to build up the crafting components. Combat ends up having a flow because of it, and that's nice in a Nioh/Bloodborne sort of way, but overall The Surge still feels fundamentally bland. I like a lot of complexity in my Soulslikes (Dark Souls, Salt and Sanctuary, etc), and this does not deliver in that respect.
So, after all that, you might wonder why there's a yes vote.
It's because The Surge is not actually a bad game, and it's a fundamentally solid step forward for the studio. It might even be a solid step forward for the genre, as I would love to see more scifi Soulslikes on the market.
The Surge has decent game length (decent, but not tremendous. My playtime represents a single runthrough, with me trying to be as completionist as possible and grinding occasionally for scrap), its plot has good pacing (apart from the slow start and abrupt-feeling endgame stretch), and there's a clever twist in the story that the game never completely spells out for you, in true Souls fashion (scroll down to the bottom, past the spoiler tags, for the twist.)
It's not a bad pickup on sale, especially if you love the Soulslike genre without reservations. If you're on the fence, $30 is probably a reasonable ammount to risk on it.
On the other hand, if you have very specific things you require from a Soulslike for it to be fun, it's probably best to give this one a miss.

I'm a casual gamer, with only an hour or two each evening to play games (and a few more on weekends).  As a result, I've found myself picking up and dropping several mmos, because I can't commit to that kind of constant need to sink time and effort into a game in order to keep up. Because of that, I usually solo play.
With that said, I decided to give FF14 a try. I've always loved the rich storytelling of the series, and read positive reviews about this one. It seemed quite solo friendly, with lots of instance matching to carry you through dungeons. Well. I gave it a try, and over 1000 hours later, I'm unable to put it down.
First, it's very beginner friendly.  It teaches you the basics, and the leveling speed is decent. The community is very noob friendly, and before I'd even played a half hour, I was already invited into a Free Company. If you run around without an FC tag, you'll be swarmed with invites no matter where you go.
Second - it's designed for casual players. A few hours a week is more than enough. Sure, it might take you a bit longer to catch up to current end game, but it's entirely possible.  As mentioned, the Duty Finder makes running dungeons easy, Most people complain about dps queues and derpy players, but I main healer, so my queues are short. And it's more fun when things go horribly wrong, anyway. I like a challenge.
Third - it's fun. There's lots to do. Crafting, Gathering, dungeons, raids, extreme boss primals, games and events at the Gold Saucer, and a long main quest line that gets better as it goes along. Even some of the side quests are clever and hilarious. If you like the usual boring fetch this, kill that quests, then there's plenty of that, too. Also, lots of glamour, though male glamour kind of pales in comparison to the female options. It takes real effort to dress a male healer character in something other than a dress. :(
Fourth - frequent updates. It feels like there's always something new coming out every few months.
Any cons?
Well, male glamour kind of sucks. Healer robes especially where designed with female characters in mind. So you if you like dressing up your dude in dresses, great. Otherwise, you've got less options to choose from.
Levelling dps can be a bit of a pain, but there are other options other than dungeons.
If you go hard at this game, you can burn out. It's geared towards casual players, so the same old system can grind you down. A lot of people take breaks, then return to the game.
Also, inventory space is lacking. I have three retainers to carry my junk, and even then, my own inventory is full. We need better storage systems!
Overall, if you've got $15 a month to spare, it's totally worth it. I also recommend getting Heavensward. It has the best story line so far, with Stormblood close behind.

A short, yet great nostalgia trip filled with your favorite Windows XP sounds. It is sure to keep you engaged in less than an hour. In-game IM chat seems very authentic from what you and I would type down to our friends with some emotional attachment laying down the foundation of the core experience of the game and its progression.
However, if you're looking for a game where every response drastically changes the outcome of the relationship between you, the player and Emily, this is not it. All choices lead to one ending that do not differ no matter how strong you believe your relationship to Emily is. It is a sad yet nice touch the game went towards the notion that no matter what you may say or do to keep a well-rounded relationship as a friend or lover, there are many key factors that are not within our hands to keep it afloat.
In essence, the game portrays that sometimes, you do not "get the girl". You do not triumph. You do not matter to this person as you once did some time ago. There is no "us". However, many of the choices you are given to interact with Emily do not make a significant impact on this ending. So if you had lied to someone else about Emily in-game, sure, it can come back as a dialogue option where Emily asks you if everything is alright to where you are given three options that really only amount to the same response from Emily and that is that.
With that said, it would have been a much better delivery for these to have an influence towards the last chapter. As a free short experience, it's worth downloading and playing through it. And a lot of the achievements are no challenge so that's a plus.

tl;dr:
Pro:
- Interesting and diverse ship building options, reminds me a lot of the mechwarrior games, especially the older ones.
- A lot of different ship-chassis to choose from. As you explore the galaxy, more and more ships will become available.
- Very interesting and nice storylines.
- Really big map to explore.
- A lot of options on the galaxy map that make it very easy to figure out where you want to go next.
- Completely bug-free (at least I never got to any bugs)
Con:
- No music.
- Controls might feel a bit awkward at first, if you are not used to this type of game.
It is a pretty nice game. Normally, I would expect to be charged 15 - 20 € (at the very least), and I'd be completely fine with that. There are no microtransactions or anything, so it is not one of those "for free" games. The entire game is actually completely free, you will never have to pay for any content at all.
When designing ships there are a lot of things to think about. What weapons do you want? How fast should your ship be? Should your shields recharge quickly or slowly, or do you want to go entirely without shield generator, which would mean that shields only recharge when you land on an inhabited planet? How much heat can your ship handle before shutting down due to overheating? Can you fit a generator that is big enough to satisfy all your power needs or will you have to also put in batteries and keep an eye on energy during combat? All that are the questions you will have to ask when trying to design your ship. Depending on your playstyle, it is likely that there will be even more questions that you'll have to ask yourself.
Of course you might also just try to google "good ship builds" or something, but as someone who really enjoys designing his own stuff rather than just building after some sort of blueprint, I have not tried that so I cannot really say anything about the availability of such "blueprints". If you do have some questions about certain parts, you can also try to search the steam forums and, if your question is not already anwsered in an older thread, ask the people there. To me, the community always seemed very helpful.
From the beginning, you already have the ability to choose from a few chassis in every category, assuming you have earned enough money for the chassis that you want to buy (transport, light/heavy freighter, light/medium/heavy warship, just to name the most important ones). Every chassis also comes with a pre-made loadout, so, if you don't want to (or you can't afford to), you can also just skip the whole ship-design-part entirely and simply use the ship as it is (though I would strongly recommend to start modifying your ship(s) as soon as you can, because the pre-made loadouts will probably not fit your playstyle very well). Once you have explored a little more and met some of the alien races, they also may let you buy some of their ships. Sometimes you can buy their ships as soon as you find one of their planets with a shipyard, sometimes you have to progress in their side-story a bit before their ships become available to you. However, there are also a few exceptions which will simply not allow you to buy any ships from them, no matter what you do. Sometimes the reason may be that the related side-story that would unlock the ships is not finished yet (like the navy license, for example, which is currently unobtainable), sometimes the reason is simply that it would not make sense for them to let you buy any of their ships. maybe it is because they try to keep a technological advantage or they simply do not trust anyone or similar reasons.
(no spoilers)
The story is entirely optional and nothing at all is forced. I think you can skip absolutely everything, though I have never tried this, because the main-story as well as all the side-stories are all very interesting and immersive. This, of course, might lead to you accidentally skipping the story, but so far, at least to me, it always seemed very obvious which option would prematurely abort the storyline and which wouldn't, so I'd say the risk of accidentally skipping anything is very tiny. For the most part, the game also allows you to progress at your own pace. After you have finished a story mission, you will usually get asked to meet person x at the spaceport in a few hours. At that point, you can either click on the spaceport button to immediately continue the story, or you can just lift off and do your own stuff, until you feel like doing a bit more of the story (you should probably write down the name of the planet where you can continue the story, if you plan to do other stuff for a longer period of time). This is especially handy, if you come across a story mission that seems very hard. In such a case, it is usually a good sign that you should probably do some trading or some of the random missions that are offered on every planet, until you have enough money to upgrade your equipment or buy a new ship before you continue the story.
Most of the story missions will also stay active indefinitely, so if you come across a mission that feels impossible, you can also just wait with doing the mission until you have better equipment or a better ship. However, I would recommend creating a savefile (snapshot) before you start to ignore an active story mission, because, if I remember correctly, I have come across at least one occasion where after some time of being ignored, the story mission had dissappeared (the quest marker was not blinking, which usually means that the mission has no time limit). So generally, it would be a good idea to finish what you started and at least complete every active story mission, before you do other stuff.
While there is no music ingame, it should be relatively easy to just make your own playlists. Personally, I like to listen to the Rebel Galaxy Soundtrack or the hero radio playlist on youtube, but of course it is entirely up to you what music you want or if you want any music at all.
The controls, while feeling a bit awkward at first, were fairly easy to get used to and after a few hours it was no problem for me at all. You can also customize your controls in "preferences" in the main menu, so that will also make it much easier.
So, overall, I'd give this game a
. There are a few very minor issues but I have not found any major annoyances and, as I said, I have not come across any bugs at all, which, sadly, must also be noted as an advantage over a majority of other recent games (even games that are supposedly "finished"). Normally it would be a
, but Cheeki Breeki is always a good reason for a bonus point.

Familiar with Wargame?
Interested in historical accurate RTS?
Sick of metagame and looking for a more casual, fun and fluid strategy game?
I guess this will be your choice!
(written by a former Wargame player)
Getting into the game:
The learning curve isn't as steep as in Wargame. Of course you still have to learn what commander units do or how the frontline system works, for me it took 2 or 3 matches. But you will find yourself pretty familiar with all the cover and piercing and what not for nifty shifty mechanics. Its pretty intuitive. Plus the big advantage (for me at least), if you got a certain image of a certain unit, for example the M4A1, the unit represented my expactations. Smashes infantry, kills light Tanks. Could even take the fight with a Panzer IV. But as soon as the Panther arrives on the battlefield you are - overwhelmed. With some tricky tactics you could still try and fight this guy but you are probably better of getting a 75mm gun.
Skirmishing:
What I prefer over Wargame is the fluid Frontline. The objectives do not get picked by the game. You can choose for yourself where you want to place your units and outplay your opponent. This can be a forest line or a village occupied by infantrists, supported by tanks and anti-tank guns. At any time a Panther can break through and crush your units. Or suddenly your flank falls in and you have to relocate troops etc. etc.. Basically anything you imagine could happen could happen. (no there are no Reichskangroo!)
You should watch out for your morale. Being shot at behind enemy lines basically kills your units or makes them surrender. Always have some kind of leader around. It will save you from a lot of frustration.
Anyway, enough of the basic gameplay mechanics...
Veterans of Wargame: buy!
New players: buy!
Wargame players who sucked at Wargame: BUY!!!

This game isn't Dark Souls and it really wants to be... but the designers really failed to capture the right gameplay elements to pull it off.
Armor in the game is straight up broken in a way that makes playing the game unnecessarily difficult, unintuitive, and unfun.  The Lynx armor set can probably carry you through the vast majority of the game.
Attacks occasionally have combo strings from a single button press and while I'm sure that that seemed like a cool idea, they're actually quite detrimental to gameplay.  You don't have the ability to cancel out of most attacks, so getting stuck in long combo animation means death against a lot of enemies.
Mobility in the game is pretty decent and feels good to use.
Level design is labyrinthian but not in a way that's interesting or makes sense.  Meandering around service corridors that all look the same and are also filled with toxic gas is not fun or good.
Visually the game is fine. The UI is fine.
Anyhow, The Surge sucks, don't play it, thanks for reading.

If you are a fan of the old Wizardry games or the newer Etrian Odyssey games then this is probably the game you have been missing. You slap together a team of four ragtag adventures and make your way through the dungeon.
The only difference is that it's more like a roguelike in that you are basically on a one-way trip. You don't have a town to go back to, so there's no back and forth, which is a little missed. Trying to delve as far down before being forced back for supplies was always part of the fun. In this one you're basically diving in and not looking back.
You have to manage torches like in the old Shadowgate game. They run out and you have to light up a new one, but they seem fairly plentiful. There's a hunger mechanism so you have to feed your party.
Combat is real-time so there's an emphasis on tactical movement (like dodging enemy projectiles) and positioning (for the rogue's backstab). This can be a bit difficult with the default control scheme and tile-based movement, since you use WASD like normal (A and D strafe) but Q and E turn 90 degrees on the tile. It can get a little confusing. I probably just need either more practice or to change the controls to something easier.

I have played Escape Velocity (Original one, only available for Macintosh), EV Override (Cartoonish sequel that didn't get much attention sadly), and EV Nova (The gem that Ambrosia has made).
Reason why I mentioned all of the above is that I can safely say Endless Sky expanded on the gameplay of the aforementioned titles.
I noticed that not only are there outfit space and cargo space, there is also a crew space now. Players can also choose to start with 3 different types of ships that will introduce them to different styles of gameplay compared to EV's always shuttle start.
Graphics-wise, I think EV Nova has better 2D graphics since the shades on the ships has always a relative direction (even though not relative to the star, but slightly better). But gameplay-wise Endless Sky definitely has the upper hand. The interface for merchant players have improved so much (relative resource prices, hyperspace jump fuel count, and many more I have yet to discover)
This game is the perfect game that EV fans (myself included) have been waiting for.

Movement is a nightmare. It feels both slow and incredibly loose at the same time, like you're controlling the camera rather than the character directly.
Combat is awful. It's slow, which I actually like, but it's also bad. One-on-one fights are alright for the most part, but the combat is not tight enough to support anything beyond that. Multi-part attack animations will leave you far more vulnerable than they should. Dodging sounds great until you do it and realize just how disorienting it is because of the bad camera.
The graphics are not half bad.
The implant system is interesting (but you'll probably just want to slot in +health implants because of the extremely high damage output of enemies coupled with the very poor dodge system)
It's really too bad, because under all the poor execution of such a critical part of an action game, it does seem like they had some cool ideas.
If the developer is reading this: if you're going to make a Souls-like game (which you clearly tried to) please have someone on staff actually play one rather than just reading about how it works. Combat tightness is key. If the combat doesn't feel polished, making the enemies extremely unforgiving/powerful isn't going to make it feel like a challenge, it's just going to be infuriating.

This is a great game for a souls like challenge with a fun, different atmosphere. It is easy to pick up and to understand right away. As you progress, new weapons, armor, and gadgets come available to you to keep things interesting. The gameplay and setting are both completely enjoyable and make you want to keep playing. While I do think this is a really good game, it does have some short comings. There is no map you have access to at all times, you have to rely on the rare map on the walls or somewhat vague hall signs. Unlike in the souls franchise, you only have 1 "bonfire" per level. This makes you spend much more time unlocking short cuts and can sometimes make progression feel stale. There is no "fast travel" from the "bonfires" so if you get to the final boss and realize you missed one collectible, you have to walk all the way back, hope you have all of the short cuts open, and pray that you remember how to get back to the boss. There is no option to keep playing after the final boss. As soon as you defeat them, you can only choose NG+ so if you missed out on a collectible you have to find it in the new play through, but audio log collectibles do transfer over to NG+ which is nice. There are 5 levels of weapons and armor that are color coordinated but do not change when you start NG+. You are only allowed to go up a max of 5 for each play through so the first time is 1-5, NG+ is 6-10... but the materials from your last play through carry over. So mark 1 have the same color and appearance as a mark 6 and a mark 2 looks exactly like a mark 7 which can cause some confusion. Some missions and NPCs have the potential to glitch, a main issue is the character being invisible so you can hear them talk but are unable to speak with them to move forward. The main disappointment was probably the skill level of the bosses. Once you figure out the gimmick of each boss you just keep working with it doing the same cadence of attack, dodge, drone until they fall. If you think the bosses in dark souls 3 are a little hard solo, this could be the game for you.

Pros:
- If you just want to get on and farm a bit it can be fun.
- It's fun to mess around with different farm equipment.
- You can fell a tree and watch it land on a car and receive no penalty. Then you can walk on said tree while it is resting on the car and cut off the limbs. After this you can cut it to smaller pieces and drag them over the hood of a car, again without any penalty. You can do this as many times as you want on another person's property and completely deforest land you don't own...without penalty.
Cons:
- Physics are horrible. If you cut a tree down there is a chance it could drop right through the earth. Things will start to bounce around at random and act rubbery.
- Collisions are messed up. If you are plowing a flat field you will probably be fine but the moment you start to navigate precarious equipment in tight circumstances things will start to either pass completely through other items and scenery or they will get stuck in it entirely. Light poles and railroad fences are notorious for grabbing onto my farm and forestry equipment.
- The "simulation" factor is pretty low. If you are a fan of heavy equipment and get a kick out of that aspect you will find that you can't press any buttons or interact with the equipment other than by using a few keymaps or by sliding the mouse around. If you are a fan of farm management you will be disappointed to know that instead of hiring and managing staff you just press H to hire a person to do the job you are currently doing and it "auto-drives" your tractor. Books management boils down to paying off a debt the game automatically just hands you (or collecting more debt), and you can't even have equipment or seed delivered to your farm. The store you buy pallets of seed from doesn't even have a forklift to load your seed pallets.
- The UI is terrible. Nearly everything in the game is icon based yet you can't mouse over anything to see what it is. You are just expected to know the symbol for a certain type of plant or seed.
- Menu system is not very good. Why should I have to save the game then exit to the main menu just to see the entire keymap? That should be visible in the game.
- AI vehicles and "NPC's."
- Annoying pop-ups in the game that will stop you from driving until you click them away.
- Walking near a tree with a chainswa will give you a "cut ring" maybe 1 in 10 times making it frustrating to cut down trees. (then you watching about half of them slide straight into the earth and disappear).
- Originally I had the train as a pro because I thought it was cool. That was before I tried using it to haul logs. Even if you cut the logs to length and stack them evenly so they shouldn't move they will end up bouncing all over the place like rubber. I lost every single log going 30-40kph, watching them all shoot into the air like rockets! I've never seen anything like it...
- I have encountered a bug in literally every tutorial I have done...all of them related to poor physics. After having a tree fall through the earth on the forestry tutorial I decided to abandon forestry until they patch it. I decided that maybe animals would be a good way to go. After dumping the feed into the trough my tractor did a front flip into the air and landed in the pig pin...

I was on the fence about this game cause I didn't want to get my hopes up.  To be honest the RTS catagory is dieing out a bit and most tittles from this are trash, hot trash.  This game is the perfect mix of COH2, Wargame, Assault Squad, and Paradox brain food games.  This game is in Beta and is better than tittles that have been out for years, only minor tweeking and balancing issues to fix, also I have had two random crashes in the past 30 hours of gameplay.
The battle phase of A, B, C makes your strategy even more dynamic as you have to think through and counter your enemy's units, not follow a dumb build order and do the same stuff every game.  Right now there is 4 decks and 18 to be out soon.  I can only imagine how dynamic it will become.
The feature of the line of sight button is the single best thing to ever happen to a tactical RTS.  No more guessing or blaming♥♥♥♥♥♥pathing on developers.  Its clean and stable.
The use of micro, and hot keys is a amazing blend but not crazy over whelming.  No you don't need 200 button mashes a minute to do well, but the faster and cleaner you are the better.  The hot key and unit assignment layout is smooth which rewards those who are good with it, but doesn't make it a 200 buttons a minute freak out.
Once the graphics get a little more polished I think this game is a 10/10 if your looking for a RTS ww2 game.  For $40 you should pick up this game.

This is definitely the best game about building and running a factory with a multitude of different production lines, manufacturing a lot of different goods. It works as a strategy game, and as a logic one, and there's only one big thing missing here - trade. Sure, you can get that with mods, but those don't cover all the products from your other mods and prices are not balanced at all. Trade would give another purpose to manufacture goods - to make profit, to fulfill the needs of the market, to adjust your production or else prices will drop... that's what I really expect from a factory sim. Although it's other aspects are pretty good, that is my one major complaint. It's still in the Early Access so I'd expect it to be implemented in the future.
1. A lot of different products and all the possibilities you get with the whole supply chain.
2. Moddability and easy access to mods. There are a lot of great mods for this game that really allow you to expand your factory and make some aspects like oil refining much more realistic. Built-in system will also check whether mods are compatible with your version of the game and check for updates.
3. Stability - even with a lot of mods the game hasn't crashed once and I haven't encountered any bugs which is pretty unusual these days.
4. Performance - even with a huge factory, thousands of robots, dozens of trains and countless miles of transport belts it still works like a charm. That's nothing short of amazing.
5. Enemies that react to pollution. I love the concept - it both provides some challenge needed in the end-game and also motivates you to try to be a bit more eco-friendly, which is a good lesson for us all. I even kinda feel sad for all those creatures who just want to protect their planet. If you don't want to fight them, you don't have to at all - there's a peaceful mode too.
6. You get a lot of great tools to plan your logistics right - many different types of transport belts, flying robots, and trains. Each with own strengths and weaknesses. Simply love it!
7. Reasonable asking price and a very good money-to-value ratio.
1. Trading - lack of trade is a huge disappointment for me,
And that's about it. The game is really great and worth checking out.

For the record, I've played all 3 Souls titles, the first two on PS3/PS4, and the 3rd on PC.
The Surge isn't a Souls game.  It's not "a souls-clone".  It's more than that.
The similarities are there, but if anything The Surge takes a subtly different approach to the HARPG (Hard Action Role-Playing Game).  Combat feels more streamlined, heavier, and a bit more real.  There is a definite story with a hard-set character, and there isn't much room to alter what's happening, just how you go about doing what you do in game.  The world is dystopian, but not unbelievable.
In short, where the Souls titles craft a superhuman character capable of going toe-to-toe with demigods, The Surge puts you in control of a guy who REALLY needs a break and to file for L&I.  It's grittier, bleak, and wholly solid.
I recommend this game.  It's been worth it's investment thus far, and I look forward to more from this team.

I wanted to love this game, but after over 20 hours and finishing the campaign, I almost feel cheated. This game is NOT what was sold to me. I bought an undercover cop in Hong Kong game, one where your character would have to constantly skirt the line of trying to do the right thing, while trying to no blow his cover. This is NOT the game that I got.
This is a game where there are no choices to be made, you simply follow the narrative presented to you. Yes, your character is an undercover cop, but the presentation of this concept is so unrealistic that it is in no way believable. Wei (the main character) unashamedly murders, yes, murders on more than one occassion. He participates in bloody gang wars, engages in numerous chase scenes around the city in which he fires machine guns indiscriminately at enemy vehicles even though a single stray bullet would realistically kill one of the numerous pedestrians on the street. By the end of the game, the number of people he's killed is far greater than any of the gangsters he's supposedly trying to take down. The vast majority of the game Wei's motivations, stated even to his fellow cops, is not to topple the criminal organization, but to murder so-and-so gang leader because they killed so-and-so gang member that Wei really liked.
On top of that, there is even a point where Wei tortured. Under this torture, he is cut up in numerous places, is shown to have lost so much blood any normal person would have died, his foot is smashed with a hammer and a hole is drilled into his knee. He then gets up and proceeds to do a bunch of kung fu on DOZENS of people, run all over the town, jump, shoot up places, etc. There is virtually nothing realistic, cop-like, or redeemable about the main character.
Don't get me wrong, this game could have been amazing. It should have been amazing. It had so much going for it. The combat was amazing. The game world was rendered spectacularly, probably the best done I've ever seen. The sheer variety of missions, styles of gameplay, and game modes were all very well done. As it is, this game may as well have been Grand Theft Auto. If you're a Grand Theft Auto fan, this is the game for you, it even has better writing than a GTA game... but with all that being said, if you're looking for a game about an undercover Hong Kong cop that will cause you to question what's right and what's wrong... then look somewhere else. This isn't it.

I picked this game up because it's an Open Source version of popular 2D flash games from back in the day. It plays very similarly to Flash Trek (my favorite), except with more emphasis on a galactic scale.
The gameplay itself is very simple, but so open ended that it's fantastic to play for hours and hours on end. I've put all my 12 hours on this game in the last week, which is huge for me.
My only complaint about this game is that it does not use Steam Cloud Sync. Thankfully, I have Syncthing running on most of my machines so I've been using that to sync my saves automagically. Other than that, there is nothing wrong with this game - it'll run on a single-hamster powered potato computer, the story is interesting (albeit kinda confusing how to progress, and it feels like you can't start the campaign until you have a pretty strong fleet, but that's just my opinion since the first few missions don't give you a ton of moneys.), and the game has some pretty strong feelings of progression - why stop at three freighters? Why not upgrade to a small fleet of Argosys or Mules so you can take cargo to the farthest reaches of pirate infested space without fear?
I'm in love with this game, and all I've been doing is transporting cargo from one planet to another.

To start with, this game is a class space trader/pirate/shooter open world game like Escape Velocity.  You can basically do whatever you want, there is a main quest but it's kept pretty far in the background...even finding it is relatively difficult for a first-time blind playthrough.
You start the game with a choice of three ships: a bad fighter, a bad passenger transport, and a bad freighter.  There's a small tutorial for each one to show you the basics, but then you're on your own.  From there you can trade between worlds and complete randomly generated missions with varying objectives (move cargo from one world to another, escort ships, transport passengers, kill pirate fleets, etc.) to make money.  Once you make money you can buy a new ship or upgrade your current ship however you want.  There are a ton of different ship types for different playstyles--bulky freighters that are good for moving a ton of cargo, huge warships that can take a pirate fleet by themselves, carriers that hold lots of fighter drones, small zippy escort ships, or large passenger transports that let you ferry lots of people across the galaxy.  Upgrading is relatively painless because of a loan system in place, where you can borrow a certain amount of money based on your net worth and history in paying off previous loans.
After your economy really starts rolling you can afford to buy multiple ships and start commanding a fleet centered around your flagship.  This lets you dominate space combat or haul even more freight to make better profits.  You also have to manage paying crew expenses and protecting your ships so they all arrive at their destination.  An alternative option is to fight enemy ships until they're disabled, then board them with extra crew members that commandeer the ships and put it under your control.  This is a high-risk high-reward situation until you can get a large enough fleet to protect your flagship as it's capturing enemy vessels.
The map is pretty huge, composed of linked systems that you jump between.  At each system with an outfitter you can buy a star map that will reveal the surrounding 12 systems, which allows you to make informed jumps rather than plotting out the entire map by hand.  There are also areas off the linked map for you to explore, but this is gated behind finding one specific piece of technology either through the main quest line or on your own.  Getting this tech on your own requires some extreme luck for a first time player, but once you know how to game the system you can reliably get it relatively easily.  There's a real cool sense of exploration once you get off of the grid, since you're not entirely sure what you will encounter or when you will encounter it.  I've also gotten stranded once or twice because I've misjudged how many jumps it will take to explore, which requires slowly filling your fuel gauge by hanging out near a star.  There is technology that will allow you to passively recharge your fuel gauge much quicker, and it's key for exploration jumps like this.  Since I've last played they've added quite a few new alien races, ships, and technology.  Almost all of the aliens are a complete surprise the first time you encounter them, so I won't go into anymore detail on that.
There are a few areas I feel they could improve on.  The very start of the game is pretty slow until you start building up some capital.  The way the game is structured it's almost always easier to just do ferry/freight missions until you build up enough of an economic base to buy a reliable warship, rather than starting off with the beginning fighter.  Kitting out a top-of-the-line warship will require jumping around the galaxy to find the optimal parts from each faction/race.  Gating a lot of the content behind one specific technology is a neat idea but can be a bit frustrating for players who want to know how to explore those planets, which will most likely result in a google search that could ruin parts of the game for the player.  Combat gets pretty hectic once there's more than 15-20 ships on screen, at that point there's not much the player can do to avoid damage and you rely more on your fleet and ship's shields to see you through.  There are a few times early in the game where you'll just be plastered by a giant pirate fleet and there was Nothing You Could Do.  Thankfully the game saves at each planet stop so you can reload a snapshot pretty quickly.  The main quest is hard to find if you don't know what you're looking for, and there are lots of opportunities to deny a quest and completely cancel the main quest line without any chance to restart it.  NEVER TURN DOWN A MAIN QUEST EVER.
Since the game is open source there are mods and plugins you can install to vary your game up a bit, but I don't have much experience with any of them.
All that said, I've put a lot of hours into this free game, so I'd say it's definitely worth it if you have that space trader itch to scratch.

This game is one of the best MMORPGS I ever played and emotional rollercoaster I have ever had in my life, something I had not felt before with any other game. At one point, I LIVED in the game, made countless great friends that totally replaced my real life ones, that rush of excitement defeating savage raids with my former static, and the daily occurrences with my former free company.
I have played various MMOs such as WoW, Ragnarok, Rusty Hearts, Pangya, etc in the past, but none really come close to the quality FFXIV displays. However, as many awesome stuff FFXIV provides, there are some pros/cons that go along with it:
PROS:
- Stunning graphics and visual quality
- Helpful and supportive community while you are new and leveling up
- Free Companies that make the game much more enjoyable
- Not overly complex battle system
- Tons and tons of minions to collect
- Pretty cool rare mounts
- Challenging extreme trials and savage raids
- Lots of dungeon and trials content to run through
- Fantastic soundtrack
- Glamour system
- Extremely fun playing with other friends (The social aspect of the game is great)
- Interesting and engaging main story
CONS:
- Pretty cool rare mounts with a very small drop rate that cause infighting among parties
- The wait between patches and the small amount of dungeons that get added between patches
- The toxicity of the community at endgame raids
- Drama in-game that can cause the total break-up of free companies and statics
- Playing solo may not be as fun
- The limited housing system where one player can hoard as many houses as they like
- Very time consuming
- Veteran players that may not wait or bother explaining for newbies in older content
Additional things:
While some may be my own bias, this is the most honest review I can give. While some may or may not agree, but I found the savage raids to be alot more fun with a static than what a random party finder group could give. However, as a former Free Company leader, I found FCs are able to make or break the game for anyone new. If you haven't found the right FC, I advise keep trying, it's worth it!

A great MMO, There's this great sense of richness put into each zone and town, Characters around them feel well planted into the world they were placed in, When it comes to players experience, there's a great amount of Player Fantasy. What I mean by that is that if you decide to be a Conjurer, you feel like a Conjurer, When you then decide to take a step into becoming a White Mage you really feel like you've taken this character through a Journey.
With the game making you immersed in such a way, you look at all other characters the same way.
Leveling is different, but fun.
There's a Main Story Quest Line that you will have to complete, and side quests to do in tandem.
Dungeons are really genious, If you're at max level, you can queue for a dungeon roulette that will make your level suit the randomly picked dungeon. This way new players and low level players hardly have to wait to queue for a Dungeon.
Raid like events (Trials) are amazing too. This game isn't really happy about people wanting to use DPS Meters, and thus the community doesn't really judge or inquire about it. Only Item Level.
I started playing this game a few weeks before the release of Stormblood, I was lucky enough to enjoy the Stormblood expansion with a large community, and it's the best MMO experience i've ever had.
I do want to mention that this is one of those MMO's you'd have to invest time in, The Journey of the main quest is long. If that is not your Forte. and you came in here to get the game, wanting to play with friends in higher levels. I might suggest playing as normal until you learn the basics of the class you've created before you start wondering if you want to pay to skip the main story quest and levels up to the Stormblood expansion.

Before I start with my review, I just want to give a general warning to all those who are considering purchasing this game. It is a major time sink, at least in my opinion. The game is extremely rewarding if you are the type of player who can stick with it in the long run. Rewards, such as being able to own a house, and having all classes fully levelled, are ultimately tied to total game time. The more you play, the more substantial these rewards. If you are not the type of person who can commit to 10-15 hours a week, year-long, then you may find yourself not getting value for money.
The Pros:
+ Great Graphics. It's not be next-gen, but the game can look seriously beautiful at times
+ Near infinite levels of content. I'm not kidding. Every patch brings more content to a game that has a Main Story that will take you about 250 hours to complete. If you want to level all classes, get all the best items, and do everything, I would put total time to completion at 1,500+ hours.
+ Helpful Community. I have never really experienced unusual amounts of toxicity. You might get a bit of it happening in the higher level raids, but nothing infuriating. Free Companies (Guilds) usually have veteran players who will help you clear content, advise you on how to gear up etc.
+ Excellent Music. If you have played other FF iterations, you know that the music is fantastic most of the time. Well, this is one of those times. Fairly diverse soundtrack. Not an expert, so won't comment more on it.
The Cons:
- The Subscription: If I must be honest, I don't like it. Many argue that the subscription is justified by the hard work of the devs. This is true, but the model here can be seriously frustrating. The way the game is designed, you have to keep paying the subscription if you want to retain the rewards. An example of this is housing. For many people, owning a house is the pinnacle of their RPG careers, and there is enormous satisfaction in owning one in FFXIV. The problem is, if you are not active for 45 days, the game will put your land up for auction, at which point another player will snap it up, and you will get 90% of the sale value. So, if you want to retain posession of your home, you got it; pay up. "But I don't want to be forced to pay a subscription for a game I don't play regularly" is the dilemma I am sure many players face. The subscription model limits your choices.
- Time Sink: I bought this game when I was in high school. Back then, I had enough time to play this game. I am in university now, and I don't have that kind of time anymore. This means I am always behind others who can invest that time. Now, this is a basic element of all MMORPGs, so I am sure I sound stupid. BUT, the time sink in this game is especially potent. Missing a couple patches is going to put you back 100+ hours, and playing catch-up from that point on is going to become more and more frustrating.
So, if you can wrap your head around the fact that the subscription model is somewhat prohibitive, and that the game expects you to be a frequent player, you will find one of the most fulfilling games on the market. If not, I would advise you to consider whether this is a worthwhile investment of your time and money.

Comparing this to the regular Sleeping Dogs.
PROS:
Unsightly "Free XP" & "Free Money" DLC not present.
All of the worthwhile DLC from the main game is here. Unlocks as your progress in the story, unlike before.
Subtle bugs fixed (Sifu's "WHAT WOULD YOU LIKE TO L--")
More dense population, which is more reflective of Hong Kong.
A nice, though not subtle Fog effect, which also masks the hideous DoF effect of the original.
Ridiculously lazy 'Red Envelope' DLC no longer an insult to whoever buys it.*
Clothes DLC no longer immediately appears in wardrobe, you buy it from the Market instead.
More subtle detail & breakable props added.
Ear♥♥♥♥♥♥Mission Failed sound effect is replaced with something less terrifying.
You can still throw that woman over the railing.
Camera feels way less floaty.
CONS:
Scripted sequences in missions have bugged numerous times.
Some places were clearly not designed to handle this increased population.
The menu has been arbitrarily shrunk. Maybe they think small = HD? Not really.
Some minutiae such as animated signs, have been changed for the worse.
Some textures are lower definition than in the original game. Same goes for lightmaps.
The default control scheme is totally different from the base game.**
Comparatively, the performance-loss-to-improvement ratio is unimpressive.
The game was an opportunity to redeem themselves for the horrible profile backgrounds from the original game, but they didn't take it.
*The Red Envelope collectables are now scattered across the map, instead of placed next to every parking garage.
**While the default controls of this game conform to most open world action games, they feel wrong to somebody who has played the original game for so long.
If you don't have Sleeping Dogs already, you should get this. If you already own the other version, this isn't worth it if you have the DLC for that version.

One of the more promising management games I've seen.
To me, it was like Space Colony mixed with a bit of Startopia, both games I absolutely loved.
I was very much looking forward to playing the finished game.
They never finished it.
Midway through alpha development they 'ran out of money'.  This resulted in them slapping a poor excuse for a tutorial onto the game and fixing only a handful of the hundreds of bugs the game had and releasing it.  They stuck around for 6 more patches fixing even more bugs, and the game still has dozens of bugs.
They released the source code expecting modders to finish developing the game and continued to sell it for full price.
It's still being sold, incomplete and extremely buggy.
This is the game that dragged Double Fine's reputation into the dirt, and rightfully so.
If you choose to give them money (or get it elsewhere, as it's essentially abandonware at this point), you will have a few hours of fun, especially if you loved management games of old; but play it longer than that and all you'll experience is complete frustration at the bugs and the general incompleteness of the game.  Every now and again I decide I want to play it again.. and can barely even get a colony started, let alone last more than an hour without crippling bugs breaking the entire thing.
You can pickup Space Colony HD for $2.50 (on sale) on GoG or Steam.  It's a much, much better game.  If you want something a bit different, Startopia is great too, but you'll need to get a widescreen FoV fix to play it properly on modern displays.

Eugen is back at it again, and in top form. They've created maybe their best game yet in my opinion. Steel division is a historical RTS taking place in world war two on the western front. The scale of the combat is very large compared to similar titles in the same genre. Maps are kilometers wide taking place on both land and in the air as you command tanks, planes, and men to push the enemy back. For all you WARGAME players this title will feel very similar. Visually the game has improved over past titles. A much welcome improvement being both the cleaned up interace, and your infantry's behavior, which was necessary in my opinion seeing as in contrast to some previous Eugen titles infantry are now the backbone and workhorse of your army. You still have 'decks' though they call them battlegroups. Tanks, planes, and infantry still take to the battlefield in a similar fashion. There are some notable changes though. Instead of your income 'ticking' up slowly a handful of points at a time, you will have a set income that will be granted at regular intervals. Units (while retaining expendable ammo) no longer have hitpoints. Ultimately it feels similar to WARGAME, and i would recommend it to any fans of the series. The game doesnt have too steep a learning curve, but i can already tell that it will be difficult to master.
Overall i would say 8/10. I am thoroughly satisfied, and with more content on the horizon... im absolutely excited!

So far, I'm enjoying it. I have to take it in spurts, though, because the AI is too good and the players range between brain dead baboon and fiendish mastermind. There are a number of very interesting mechanics and mixed elements that makethis game in many ways a match made in heaven. However, there are a number of issues. For now I'll ignore bugs.
Pros-
-Unique combination of RTS mechanics. There is both physical and psychological damage. Often this manifests as a unit breaking and retreating. This mechanic is similar to R.U.S.E's retreat mechanic, but it doens't only indicate damage. A tank can be supressed by a flak or HMG in the right circumstances, like in real life, because the rain of lead will scare the crew. No damage is being done to the tank, its all psychological.
There are a number of destruction mechanics, and as of now I'm not sure if they are based on a damage model or a random number generator. Infantry can be gunned down, burnt, or exploded. Vehicle crews can bail out, fuel and ammo can be exploded, and other things can cause the vehicle to become destoryed or inoperable for a time. This is a lot like the variable effects on units and vehicles in Wargame
Buildings are destructable. This is great, because it means that, eventually, constant fighitng in a town will reduce it to a point of very minor strategic value, as infantry can't use the buildings as cover. This is a lot like Company of Heroes 2.
Vegetation can be between medium and good cover, and works like both CoH2 and RUSE/Wargame in that it is a useful stealth option and a source of cover.
Near true combined arms. Infantry, variaty of ground vehicles, aircraft (fighter, fighter/bombers, bomers), artillery/towed/self-propelled guns, off map artillery. This is like RUSE/Wargame, and like older traditional RTS games.
'Decks', or 'battlegroups', based on historical divisions in the Normandy campaign can be built and customized with historically accurate equipment available to that specific unit. This is like Wargame, but the attention to detail is interesting, if only leaving the player wanting a bit more from the roster.
-Highly detailed, very large maps with lots of players.
-Generally good connection in multiplayer maps.
-Challenging AI with varioius difficulty levels for all players to enjoy and have a challenge.
-Pretty good graphics and good effects. Decent sounds.
-The frontline system. As far as I know, no RTS has had this type of system in this kind of setting. Its a fresh take on a well established formula that adds spice and makes the game feel more authenitc, as well as more dynamically engaging for the player than a simple territory system like Wargame.
-More complex than RUSE, less complex than Wargame. Take that as you will, but for meit means that the game is much more approachable and can still have some intense strategy-counter strategy moments that arent simple rush tactics.
-The phase system. It's interesting, and allows a more authentic experience while allowing you to streamline your planning more easily.
Cons-
-Limited unit roster. Quite limited. I'm not of the persuasion that the unit roster needs to be massive, but I was hoping for a bit more. I'll hold my breath until the end of the beta to see if we get a proper roster.
-Poor individual unit AI. This is part git gud and part programming error. It doesn't seem to be a bug, the units are just a bit dumb and will need more micro than you first expect from this game. You've heard "too many cooks ruin the broth," well, this is more like "too many broths ruin the cook." You've gotta be on your toes or you will lose units that where key in holding an area or making a push.
-Some balancing issues. Again, not a bug but I'll hold my breath until after the beta to really judge this. The AA is basically usless you'veprepared a trap very meticulopusly and the enemy falls for it. The tanks need a little reworking, and I think the fighter/bomberscould use a little nerf as well. Thats just me.
-Repetative tactics. I've only played a few hours but I already see the best ways to approach each of the three maps. This could be countered by a bigger unit roster, maybe dyanmic weather (with unique effects or something), and time; as players fingure out tactics to counter established map tactics.
-Deckbuilding is too game-directed and bland. This is a roster problem, but it goes deeper. The phase system is fun, but combined with the limited roster you basically can determine after a few games what the most effective design for a battlegroup is and never need to change it. This may change with more unique variaties of the same unit, even if most of them are filler, as it would at least extend the player's interest in trying all the combinations out.
Conclusion:The game has a lot of good ideas, and for the most part they're very well integrated. However, there are a number of issues, not the preformance or connection, but with the core game mechanics.

It's basically Wargame. But that's not a bad thing. The things changed this time around are enough to make it interesting enough aside from the WW2 coating.
-The frontline system is flat better than sectors from WG.
-The phase system adds varying depth of play, as time progresses you get more and more powerful units.
-Lack of reinforceable HP, combined with morale system makes even a good engagement hurt more and allows a player that fell behind to catch back up.
-Terrain changes alter engagements. Only infantry can enter bocage, forest, and buildings. Since vehicles are slower, and cannot fire on the move, they're more prone to ambushes without adequate recon. This makes infantry, much more vital.
-Artillery ranges decreased, smoke less prevalent. Long range for an artillery piece is 2400m, half the range of a tank destroyer or AT gun. Not all of them carry smoke either so generally if you need smoke, the artillery has to get up close, thus making it vulnerable.
-Planes on the whole are more effective until the opposition has amassed a large AA screen or buys a couple of fighters. On the other hand, unless you're airborne or infantry, you get a LOT less planes.
-I'm not a comp stomper, but I did play one AI match, and on medium it seemed WORLDS better than few times I've played Wargame's AI.

I played this game for an hour, but allow me to head off the people who don't think that is enough time to understand a game. If I am not enjoying my first hour of a game why would I spend more time playing it?  I am not here to suffer through a bad start for a possible later pay off.
So why don't I like it?
The developers put way too much time in making an elaborate upgrade system, and making the combat technical, instead of worrying first if it was fun.  The combat is not fun, it's a tedious chore to kill even the most basic enemy.  My character feels sluggish and uncoordinated, and I picked the agility/speed class.  This is the combat: you do your little 2-3 hit combo, wait for the bad guy to flounder about with his and either move back or block, and repeat your combo.  Eventually the bad guy dies, or you hack his arm/leg/head/robot♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off for a possible upgrade.  You beat on basic scrub enemies for minutes each, and if you don't you can't improve your "rig".
So let's talk about that for a second too, because it goes back to the crux of what's clearly wrong with this game.  So much time was put into a system letting you craft your own gear, upgrade it, and toggle around implants that may or may not matter.  All this is great yeah, but if I don't want to play your game past the first few areas it doesn't matter.  I do not want to put up with several hours of fighting boring crap to level/gear up my character just so I can hopefully fight some fun stuff in a fun way.
I get it, you want to build the plot and scale the gameplay; but you might want to add some actual plot and character building to the game so i want to see it advance.  This game starts out super generic, you roll your character's wheelchair off a train after some speech about the company changing the world.  Then you pick if you want to be a beefy tank class or an agile speed class.  You see a cutscene where they drill a bunch of techno-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t into your body and make sure it's known it's a big deal they didn't use anethesia.  You then wake up in a garbage dump and carrot-on-a-stick your way to retrieve items to advance the plot.  Some ethnic lady in glasses says things are bad, and doesn't know why.  What a plot, ladies and gentlemen.
The devs took a few things from Dark Souls, and even invite the comparison.  This was a mistake, but if they wanted it they can have it.  Dark Souls was fun from the beginning.  It had a challenge, but flowed.  I wanted to explore this strange world, and I wasn't shoved in a specific direction to do so.  Dark Souls has upgrades, but it only had a couple layers to it and the game was focused on fun gameplay.  The Surge on the otherhand dumps the fun for an upgrade system, and puts you on rails to finish a generic plot.
Hard pass on this one folks.  Especially for $30/$50 depending on when you saw it.

This is definitely the best game about building and running a factory with a multitude of different production lines, manufacturing a lot of different goods. It works as a strategy game, and as a logic one, and there's only one big thing missing here - trade. Sure, you can get that with mods, but those don't cover all the products from your other mods and prices are not balanced at all. Trade would give another purpose to manufacture goods - to make profit, to fulfill the needs of the market, to adjust your production or else prices will drop... that's what I really expect from a factory sim. Although it's other aspects are pretty good, that is my one major complaint. It's still in the Early Access so I'd expect it to be implemented in the future.
1. A lot of different products and all the possibilities you get with the whole supply chain.
2. Moddability and easy access to mods. There are a lot of great mods for this game that really allow you to expand your factory and make some aspects like oil refining much more realistic. Built-in system will also check whether mods are compatible with your version of the game and check for updates.
3. Stability - even with a lot of mods the game hasn't crashed once and I haven't encountered any bugs which is pretty unusual these days.
4. Performance - even with a huge factory, thousands of robots, dozens of trains and countless miles of transport belts it still works like a charm. That's nothing short of amazing.
5. Enemies that react to pollution. I love the concept - it both provides some challenge needed in the end-game and also motivates you to try to be a bit more eco-friendly, which is a good lesson for us all. I even kinda feel sad for all those creatures who just want to protect their planet. If you don't want to fight them, you don't have to at all - there's a peaceful mode too.
6. You get a lot of great tools to plan your logistics right - many different types of transport belts, flying robots, and trains. Each with own strengths and weaknesses. Simply love it!
7. Reasonable asking price and a very good money-to-value ratio.
1. Trading - lack of trade is a huge disappointment for me,
And that's about it. The game is really great and worth checking out.

Comparing this to the regular Sleeping Dogs.
PROS:
Unsightly "Free XP" & "Free Money" DLC not present.
All of the worthwhile DLC from the main game is here. Unlocks as your progress in the story, unlike before.
Subtle bugs fixed (Sifu's "WHAT WOULD YOU LIKE TO L--")
More dense population, which is more reflective of Hong Kong.
A nice, though not subtle Fog effect, which also masks the hideous DoF effect of the original.
Ridiculously lazy 'Red Envelope' DLC no longer an insult to whoever buys it.*
Clothes DLC no longer immediately appears in wardrobe, you buy it from the Market instead.
More subtle detail & breakable props added.
Ear♥♥♥♥♥♥Mission Failed sound effect is replaced with something less terrifying.
You can still throw that woman over the railing.
Camera feels way less floaty.
CONS:
Scripted sequences in missions have bugged numerous times.
Some places were clearly not designed to handle this increased population.
The menu has been arbitrarily shrunk. Maybe they think small = HD? Not really.
Some minutiae such as animated signs, have been changed for the worse.
Some textures are lower definition than in the original game. Same goes for lightmaps.
The default control scheme is totally different from the base game.**
Comparatively, the performance-loss-to-improvement ratio is unimpressive.
The game was an opportunity to redeem themselves for the horrible profile backgrounds from the original game, but they didn't take it.
*The Red Envelope collectables are now scattered across the map, instead of placed next to every parking garage.
**While the default controls of this game conform to most open world action games, they feel wrong to somebody who has played the original game for so long.
If you don't have Sleeping Dogs already, you should get this. If you already own the other version, this isn't worth it if you have the DLC for that version.

I am really impressed with this title. I liked the Wargame series and I liked RUSE. I also liked World in Conflict. This game is similar to these but also different. Its hard to explain but someone familiar with Wargame will feel comfortable with this game however using Wargame strategies will get you killed. This game is slower paced and more tactical than Wargame was. There is a real atmosphere of "Hedgerow Hell" as you navigate your Shermans down a small country lane only to have two of them detonate by a hidden anti tank gun.
The line of sight mechanics and the way recon dominates really floats my boat. The synergy between the units on the field works really well and as such I can happily reccommend this game to people who liked Wargame or to people looking for a slower paced and more tactical RTS.

However, in the beta there are only limited maps AND units available but it is a good preview of what is to come.
Grafics when zoomed in max could maybe be improved a bit, but atm it runs fine on max settings on my system.

I was quiet surprised to find out that Eugen / developed  the game again in the WW2 time period and I am very thankful for this.
To begin with, Steel Division is not Wargame in the second World War nor is it the successor of R.U.S.E..
One can see clearly where Steel Division is coming from, but it is different to the two named before. Since this is not the final release version, consider my explanations to the game limited, there is no campaign, there are “only” three fractions to choose from (two German divisions, one British and one American), and “only” two playable maps.
The final release version should have 15 divisions to choose from, a campaign, extra special units (an American air unit, a German Tiger unit and more to come), plenty of maps which from what I read have been carefully researched to get quiet close to the original time set, an extra modding area (so far I do not know what can be modded, the fact alone that they planed parts of the game modable is simply great) and plenty of online and offline battles, which a player can create.
First of all, it is a tactical wargame where the player controls all combat units on a small map.
The scale of the map is not exact compared for instance to modelling, but, a vehicle represents one vehicle and squads are represented in numbers, where the number represents the actual number of men in a squad.
Like in Wargame you choose a battle group from one of the three playable fractions, i.e. Germans, British or Americans and unlike R.U.S.E. you  do not have to “built” units in specific construction buildings.
And here the first difference to Wargane: You choose from a former real existing division!
You pick combat units which were available to that specific division. That also means you can be limited to what combat units may be offered to you, like specific tanks only being available to infantry kind divisions for instance. Thanks Eugen for considering something more close to reality!
So you can let the computer make the choice to pick units for you or, like in Wargame, you make the choice to create your own custom battle group. And here comes the second big difference to Wargame, you have now three timed phases where you are limited to what you can “call” into battle.
When you choose your battle group you have the three phases named as A, B and C phases, where your picking of men and material is different in quality and numbers.
In the beginning (phase A) you are pretty much limited to only a few men and vehicles and equipment. Phase B and phase C also give you different equipment and more infantrymen.
This means for instance that in the beginning you are limited to a few AT-guns, a few infantry squads, single support vehicles and only few tanks which are most of the time not the top notch battle tanks. The classification is as it is in Wargame, you have Recon units, Tanks, Infantry, Support and air Units as well as AAA and Artillery ones.
After a specific time in the actual battle (a timer indicates it in the game) you reach phase B and later on phase C. Phase B gives you access to “proper” tanks in larger quantities, Infantry in greater numbers and air units while the C phase will give you access to everything you got, also the heavy combat tanks (for the Germans for instance it is the Panther).
So careful planing is needed, to what someone wants to do when and to what a player can react!
And again as in Wargame a player cannot choose infinite units and vehicles but is limited to points in the different phases (which the choice of division you play seem to influence) which give you limited numbers of units in total.
Once you have chosen the units you like to play (or in a skirmish the enemy is using) you start the game.
The map is dome nicely and the proportions (i.e. the scale) is similar as in Wargame.
The two example maps give you either a typical Normandy landscape with loads of hedges, a few streets and plenty of room to set up defensive positions or plan offensive manoeuvres.
The second one is set in an urban surrounding with a few villages and a nice industrial complex but also a few areas with long range view. But, there are no more zones like Alpha, Beta etc. you need to control. On the map your units generate a control zone on the map measured of their combat value, indicated either in blue or red. The map control of specific percentage gives a player bonus in income, from which troops can be called into combat. And these “reserves” are limited in numbers, as you have chosen by picking your battle group. Also you have only specific routes into the map, where you can call in troops, which is similar to Wargame. All units will enter the map via those routes and, again, like in Wargame, closing this routes mean in the worst case you cannot call in units anymore!
The set up zones are opposite to each other and the area is not like in Wargame a box but you have the full length of your side of the map to deploy your troops while the enemy has his own side, the middle is “neutral” and cannot been used for deploying troops.
Here you plan your starting movement, might set points of interest and plan careful with other players, when doing multiplayers, who is going where.
I personally like the fact that you now can mark points on the map as usual “Defend here, attack there” but you now can mark a point and write a comment which stays longer so you have another tactical help on the map (like Attack Point Phase A or Arty here, etc.).
After deployment you start and here the game plays like Wargame or R.U.S.E..
Infantry now sets up in buildings if you want but also can deploy where you feel like.
Vehicles on the ground are pretty much effected by the environment,, so a tank cannot drive through huge hedges or through big buildings like factories. Lorries drive slower in cross country then on streets. And here come the improvements to Wargame:
The units now have a button where chosen you see on the map what the unit sees. The areas which are blind for the units are greyed out,  This makes ambushes lethal and gameplay mean, so once more THANKS EUGEN!
The game itself pretty much plays like Wargame or R.U.S.E., where the detail level of the single units in Steel Division is above the other two mentioned. You can zoom in and watch your men doing whatever you ordered them.
Combat is held in the same way as in Wargame or R.U.S.E., but combat effect itself is different.
Your units are effected by stress, being under enemy fire stresses them up to a point where they try to avoid being shot at or even worse, surrender to the enemy around them.
There are now new command units, which influence behaviour of units under fire and this is another improvement from Wargame or R.U.S.E.. Also your units only now need ammo supply and you do not need to keep an eye on the fuel consumption of  your units as this feature is not included.
So far the game is fun to play, plays similar to Wargame or R.U.S.E. but has lots of gameplay improvements. It is not another COH derivative, but the possibilities offered here are far more then the tactical games on the COH scale. I read a few things in the forum like positioning, realistic behaviour of units and historical correctness.  This is a game people, not a simulation! If someone thinks that specific unit behaviour is wrong, special units should not be there, I would recommend some serious researching before claiming “that kind of unit has not been there” and please respect the work the developers and the team of Eugen put into this game. They have used a lot of different sources and from what I saw the game is excellent in terms of research, The fact alone that they allow a player to control SS units is a brave step for a gaming company and I will try to support them that this is NOT a political statement but rather the correct historical commitment of names and units being at the actual historical place.

Grid Masters is a case of giving a game a second opportunity. The first time I played the game it was under the provision of a single player game. The game, after all, does include that mode. I didn't enjoy myself. The game was too simple and not deep enough for my liking. It just didn't offer enough gameplay value to me as a single player game. I was almost ready to write a scathing review about a game that simply shouldn't have been released. And while I still feel that the single player game is lacking - and not for a lack of trying from the developer and admittedly there is room for growth - it was under the advisement of a friend that I gave the game a second chance to woo me over as a multiplayer game.
This game was intentionally designed to be played as a multiplayer game either on a couch or online. If you are hoping for a deeply engrossing single player experience you'll likely be left disappointed as I was. However, as a couch game with buddies or hosting your own games via the game's online set up you've got a far greater likelihood of finding hours of entertainment and joy in the title.
Grid Masters works as a strategic action game played between factions. You need to carefully consider your position in your twelve slot grid. You are given powers that have different areas of effect and behave in different ways. Each character has their own set of powers. There are, as of writing, five characters with more to come. The game is heavily dependent upon strategy and button mashing will only work when you're playing someone who doesn't understand the game.
I'd like to see some story and character backgrounds provided because although the game can be fun I don't have a reason to care about any of them. That would be my largest request at this stage of development. I'm interested in seeing how development progresses along in this regard as well as the addition of the other characters. There is a lot of scope for improvement.  As an Early Access game there is a lot of development left in order for the game's potential to be fulfilled. However, it is in a playable state and is entertaining when played with friends.

If you're a fan of the Souls series you'll like The Surge.
Heavily inspired by Dark Souls, but by no means a cheap knock-off.
The combat is incredibly satisfying. Instead of the souls 1-2 style weapon combos, The Surge features an actual combo system. By combining vertical and horizontal attacks (equivalent to Light/Heavy attacks in DS) you can create some really cool 4 or even 5 hit combos. The tradeoff here is that there are 6 classes of weapon, and each class shares the same combos with only slight variation between weapons if any.
There's a big focus on targeting limbs and using executions to get specific gear parts for crafting, the executions are brutal and fun to watch, if you like them as much as me you can set them to be "slo-mo cinematic" every time you use them, sometimes, or rarely. If you're not into the whole finishing moves thing, you can turn that off and just let them play as a part of your combat.
I personally like the gear system, most of it looks really cool and they encourage wearing whole sets together for set bonuses. You gather schematics from enemies and craft the gear yourself, so you don't have to worry about not finding a matching set. The interface for crafting isn't particularly engaging so if gathering materials isn'y your thing you may not like it.
Don't get me wrong, the game IS difficult, but for a reason I can't place I found it easier to defeat enemies after you figure them out, very much the same way I felt about DS1. Like, the enemies will definitely whoop your♥♥♥♥♥until you really get them down, but once you have fought the same enemy enough times they literally become a non-threat, even the harder ones. I didn't really feel that way about DS2&3, there were plenty of enemies that would destroy you without careful timing and quick reflexes no matter how many times you had fought them before.
The game seems to have a decent length, I'm 22 hours in at the time of this review and I'm definitely less than a third of the way through. As of yet I can't really speak for environmental variety, but it seems fairly bland in that respect. It's hard to make unique environments when the game has such a niche theme. I don't hold it against the game personally, I think it makes up for it in other respects, but it's definitely something to consider.
I bought it on sale for 29.99, and I have seen it on sale plenty of times since, I'd say it's a definte recommend at the sale price, but for 49.99 I would say it's really only a worthy buy for hardcore fans of this genre.
