When it comes to fighting games in North America, Capcom has always been top banana. From Street Fighter to the VS series, it's usually the Capcom games that get top billing. However, they're definitely not the only developer with a rich history of making great fighting games. Enter SNK Playmore (formerly SNK), and the King of Fighters series. Building off their previous Fatal Fury and Art of Fighting series, KOF has a soon-to-be 20 year history, as it all started in '94. Does two decades of fighting game crafting experience add up to a great game, or is SNKP over the hill with their 13th entry?
Gameplay
----------
The meat and potatoes of any fighting game. While there is a story to KOF, it's generally not what keeps the public coming back for more. Rather, if you're like most players, you'll spend the majority of your time duking it out with your rivals, either sharing a couch or through an internet connection. Local multiplayer is your standard player vs player affair, with 3v3 and 1v1 modes available. 1v1 allows both players to select one character, with which they play through multiple rounds like in most standard fighting games (aka, Street Fighter mode). It's good for when you're starting out, and learning 3 new characters at once seems a little daunting. Rather, it'll allow you to focus your time into playing and mastering one character. However, 3v3 mode is the classic King of Fighters set up, allowing each player to assemble a team of 3 separate characters to battle each other with. This is also the only mode available for online play in either Ranked or Player matches. There are also several other modes, including Time Attack, Survival, and Trial Mode, which offers a series of increasingly difficult combos for players to attempt.

The game can get fast and furious, with a hefty amount of movement options available for every character. Mastering the nuances of maneuvering your character effectively may be a somewhat daunting task for newer players, but the rewards are more than evident during gameplay. Characters can walk, run, hop, hyperhop, jump, and super jump. They can also roll, which can avoid most attacks, but are vulnerable if predicted or done at poor times.

The combo system allows for a good amount of creativity and flexibility, allowing players to come up with their own combos in training mode. The Power Meter, similar to the common super meter found in other games, is used for performing EX special moves, Desperation and EX Desperation Moves, and is necessary to perform your character's devastating NeoMAX Desperation Move. You can build differing amounts of meter depending on which character you're on. Your first character can build up to 3 stocks, the 2nd 4, and your last character can build a maximum of 5 stocks of power meter to use against your opponents. On top of that, KOF XIII introduces the "Drive Cancel" mechanic, which allows you to cancel certain special moves into other special moves using your Drive Meter. Using this mechanic, one can create very damaging and brutal combos that'll quickly drain your opponent's life bar, with each Drive Cancel costing 50% of the Drive Meter. However, to add to the combo craziness, there is also the "HD Mode" mechanic, which veteran KOF players will recognize as similar to the MAX mode from KOF 2002. HD Mode allows players to utilize the Drive Cancel mechanic freely for a certain period of time, each drive cancel costing a much smaller amount of drive meter. HD Mode also allows a character to combo certain Desperation and EX Desperation moves into their NeoMAX, otherwise known as a MAX Cancel. This allows you to create absolutely devastating combos, but only if you can manage to pull them off!

On the defensive end of things, players have the "Guard Cancel Roll," or GCAB, and "Guard Cancel Blowback," or GCCD available to them in order to help them out of sticky situations. As the name states, these moves are performed when your character is guarding, or blocking an attack from your opponent. The GCAB allows your character to perform an invincible, and unpunishable roll in either direction while blocking your opponent. Used wisely, this can be used to get out of dangerous situations, or even punish an overzealous opponent who gets too predictable by rolling out of the way of their attack sequence and striking them during their recovery. GCCD, the Guard Cancel Blowback, is an invincible attack that will knock an opponent away, giving you some breathing room and a little time to reformulate your strategy. However, if it is predicted and blocked it has a lengthy recovery, and can be punished. Each of these maneuvers costs 1 power meter, so they should be utilized only when necessary.

Much has been made of the difficulty level of this game, or rather in the difficulty of executing your characters' combos. However, these things are much exaggerated. Yes, there are some fairly difficult maneuvers to pull off, but nothing that can't be ameliorated through practice. Just as there are advanced combos that only veteran players could hope to pull off, there are still a great deal of combos that beginners and intermediate players can do with a little practice. Given the game's combo system, even players with average execution skills can do serious amounts of damage. I find that fundamental skills like spacing, good defense, and not letting your opponent get away with mistakes are far more important than who can do the longest, most damaging combo. Also, don't be discouraged if you only have a gamepad and not a fancy arcade stick. I myself have used a DualShock 3, DualShock 2, and PlayStation 1 Pad in the course of playing this game, and all have served me just fine. For proof, look at the combo videos I have! However, if you have an XBox 360 pad, you may wish to find something else, given the general awfulness of that controller's d-pad.

Visuals
-------
Many fighting games in the modern era have switched to using 3D visuals, even 2D fighters like Street Fighter IV and Marvel vs Capcom 3 utilize 3D graphics in their games. While this approach does have several advantages, and certainly has its appeal, the old-fashioned 2D sprite work found in KOF XIII is absolutely beautiful in its own right. Done with painstaking efforts, with each character taking the equivalent of more than a year in man hours to produce, KOF's sprite work exudes a charm that most games today just can't match. While certain shortcuts are apparent (Hwa and Joe sharing the same body, for example), the passion of these characters' development is evident in their appearance. Besides, nobody complains about Street Fighter IV's Ryu and Ken pretty much having identical bodies, and that game is in 3D! The backgrounds are also gorgeous, or at least 99% of them (you'll know which one I mean when you see it). With strong colors and a great deal of fun details and cameos, they add flair to any fight.
Sound
-------
The PS3 and XBox versions of the game came with a soundtrack, just sayin'. The music tracks in this game are all great, catchy tunes. One stand-out example in my opinion is the theme of Team K'. Each track fits their respective teams, and works well with the action on screen. If one great soundtrack wasn't enough for you, the game also allows you to use a B soundtrack through the options menu, replacing the characters' themes with ones from King of Fighters past. Classic tracks like Esaka and Geese Howard's theme make appearances. The sound effects in the game are also very effective and add to the experience. Some games' sounds are too muted, not matching the visual flair with audio that matches the excitement on screen. KOF XIII's sound effects are fine-tuned for this game, giving each punch, kick, fireball, or giant chest laser beam an oomph that few games match. (Ryo's NeoMAX for example!)
Long story short: Get the game, it's really good. 100x better with friends.

So to the game play. The fighting system, as I stated before is very advanced. And this has translated well into the Steam version (unusual as most Japanese ports from console/aracde to PC general suck noodles). It is recommended that you get a very good joystick or joypad to enable you to pull off the specials. Also, as this is a team battle, you need to gain skills for not just one character, but three as you are involved in 3x3 battles. This adds to the learning curve if you a noob.
All-in-all, I wholeheartedly recommend this game. It's migration to the PC has been handled very well by SNK-Playmore. A welcome game on the PC that so sorely needs more fighting games. Buy it now!!!

I bought this game on a whim and it turned out to be quite awesome!
For me this game strikes the perfect balance of strategy and micro. I don't enjoy most RTS games because I want to be able to actually think about what I'm doing and where I'm moving things instead of focusing on APM. Most of these games never give me a chance to breath. Luckily Steel Division is a MUCH slower-paced game then something like say Company of Heroes, or even Men at War. It's more in line with something like Total War. I can actually enjoy the multiplayer and when I lose it feels like it's because my opponent played smarter, not because I couldn't multitask fast enough. However, you still get to have some micro-ing fun when having tank battles with your opponent, trying to outmaneuver them to get a nice side-shot on their tank for example.
The other thing that feeds into the more strategy focused gameplay is the excellent camera. I love being able to zoom way out and see the entire battle. The super-zoomed in cameras of other RTS games feels claustrophobic and makes multitasking difficult compared to Steel Division. It should also be noted that the controls are super fluid (this game is surprisingly accessible). Thank god someone finally gets that edge panning with a mouse is stupid. You move the camera around with WASD instead and it's infinitely better. I think this is probably the first RTS I've played where I don't constantly think about and fight with the camera.
I haven't even mentioned the super-cool battlegroups system for deciding what units to take into battle! This is such a slick system and probably half the fun of the game is building different decks of units. It gives me a bit of a Hearthstone/card game vibe when I try to figure out the best build.
Also, the way that you use the hedgerows/forests and other cover on the map is very intuitive and the way it is used feels totally unique. Positioning units and using this cover to block lines of sight is a large part of where the strategy and fun comes into this game.
Lastly, each type of unit feels useful to me and all of the units and factions seem to have pretty great balance. I like that each unit excels in certain situations so you always need to be on your toes and switch up unit types based on what the enemy is doing. You can't just make a huge ball of tanks and roflstomp the enemy, they will use AT guns, arty and air support to blow you to kingdom come.
Overall I can't wait for the full release so I can see all the other awesome content they will be adding! I think this is a must-buy for anyone who likes slower and more strategic RTS games, and especially a must buy for anyone who likes games like Total War or table top wargames.

Foosball: World Tour:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

This game sends me back to my childhood! I actually used to have a Foosball table in my bedroom (“Baby-Foot” in French - go figure!) and used to hold tournaments with my close friends. Boy, this was fun!
Foosball: World Tour is a casual Football game simulation where you play the world game (Football) on a specifically made table with four rods on each side of the table: 2 rods in defence, 1 rod in the middle field and one rod for the attack. The aim of the game is to score the most goals against your opponent on the other side of the table.

On the single playing mode, you will be able to play in 20 different locations around the world. Each location will have a certain level of difficulty (from easy to master), different types of table (French, Retro and more) and different type of balls.  You will have a variety of objectives; it may be the first one to reach 10 goals, or you may have 10 balls per game and whoever scores the most goals win the game.
At the end of each game you will be awarded up to three stars; accumulate as many stars as possible and you will be able to unlock trick shots, such as snake, pull, tic-toc and pin shots. You also can customize your foosmen from Mafia to Hotdogs!
It will take you a little bit of time to get used to the controls regardless of whether you are using the gamepad or the mouse and keyboard. Whatever you prefer to use, expect accidentally score plenty of own goals for your opponent, which can be a bit frustrating! The graphics are decent and you have a good soundtrack.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Fun to play
-	Unlock trick shots
-	Single and online mode
-	Good soundtrack
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Controls will take you time to master
-	No Single player tournament
-	No trading cards
Foosball: World Tour is a fun and competitive game; it will no doubt bring you some great memories!
7/10

I'm sorry but I can't recommend this game.
I think the graphics are good enough, the game options decent (career mode, quick play and online) and customisation options are nice as well (once you unlocked them by playing a few games).
What I dislike are the controls and the physics which are by far the most important aspects of the game.
Issues with controls:
Playing with a controller felt clunky and not intuitive to me so I mainly used keyboard & mouse controls. You always control all 4 of the poles at the same time which may result in unwanted shots on your own goal if you hit your own player while moving the mouse. I would like to choose which poles to move at any given time so I can position my defense while attacking with the middle and attack poles for example. Hold buttons 1 and 3 to move pole 1 and 3 or hold button 4 to move only pole 4 for example. There could be issues with keylocking keyboards but maybe there is a way to implement something like this. The expert mode kinda tries to do this but only seems to work with a controller.
*EDIT* With the latest update (v1.03) some changes addressing this issue were introduced. While I haven't gotten to test them out myself (still waiting for a demo to avoid the buy-refund-cycle), they seem to be a step in the right direction. At least the developer seems to be involved with the community and striving to improve the game.
Issues with physics:
The ball behaves weird and the hitboxes sometimes feel a bit odd. It doesn't feel like the ball is truly rolling around the playing field and it sometimes gets stuck, diverted or slows down without an obvious reason.
I really wanted to like this game and waited a long time for a game like this but this just isn't it... yet. It sure has potential and I will gladly give it another try if it gets updated and improved but for now I will have to get a refund. Asking price (at least with current 30% discount) would be fair if the game wouldn't have the issues I mentioned. Unfortunately I can't enjoy it in its current state. :/
A demo would also be nice...

probably hampered my experiance a little with Final Fantasy XIV. Well, that and the tedious grinding played a role in me having a bit of a sour taste for this game. As of this moment I have almost 100 hours of play time, have just reached level 58, and have barely started the second expansion Heavensward. You would think that with all this conent it would be a good thing right? All this while I'm playing a White Mage (healer) I can get instant ques for dungeons and raids which helped me progess a bit faster than others, but for DPS I can only imagine the wait for a que pop. I was lucky enough to of had a lot of free time within the time span of 2-3 weeks to be able to play this game so much and level up quickly, but to the ordinary Joe/Jane who have to deal with school and work or sometimes both, you're going to be stuck at the beginning stages of the game for quite some time I'm afriad. Seeing everyone run around with all the cool gear and the likes gets you really envious and hungry to reach end game content faster only to lament the fact of the snails pace you're moving at which will lead most people to dropping the game I believe.
With that cry baby rant over, there are a couple of things that stood out to me while playing that made me want to continue the grind. I've put more time into this game than I ever expected I would (currently almost 500 hours over the past year). People draw lots of parallels to Escape Velocity, but I've never played it; so I take the game on its own merits.
The entire game is you controlling a spaceship, and later on, a fleet (if you so wish). You run around the galaxy, fighting pirates (or merchants, or aliens, or the human space navy, it's up to you), or doing trade runs, or running missions for people on the various worlds. These range from transporting people from star system A to star system B, to hunting down pirates with bounties on their heads, to providing protection and escort for merchant ships.
No matter what you do, it boils down to a few different activities:
-Trading commodities
-Boarding ships (to capture or loot parts/cargo from)
-Exploration
-Deep, involving storylines
You can build up an armada of ships, and build them up however you want, within the limits of what the ships can hold. Want a sleek, fast, hit-and-run ship, or a slow, lumbering slugger? A freighter that doubles as a troop transport? A big, lumbering cargo hauler? These options, and many other goofy combinations, are readily available to you. With dozens of ships, and even more ship outfits - weapons, engines, power sources, shielding, heat management systems, all fully interchangeable - you can build your ships to be however you like.
It's worth mentioning that the game is still (and likely will always be) "in development." That doesn't mean that it's broken and unfinished, merely that the game universe - and that's pretty literal - is continuously being expanded. The game is open-source, and the community at large is encouraged to get involved in content creation. Storylines, star systems, and new races are being added at a pretty decent rate (there's a major patch a few times a year). The major central plotlines are all done by the main developer, one dude acting on his own to make great content. Side stories, new ships and outfits for the ships, and other things not central to the main plot points are constantly being added by the very active community. I personally have not yet dabbled into content creation, but I hope to someday when I have more time.
One point that I would definitely like to make is that this game is, at its core, a vessel for telling stories. The gameplay, mechanics, side stuff you can do, are all just that - things on the side of the mission chain narratives. And the storylines we have thus far are all surprisingly immersive, well-written, and polished. For a free game, I was not expecting the quality of writing (mechanical and story-wise) that we get in Endless Sky. It's all told through text, there are no cutscenes or even character portraits, but there are memorable moments and characters nonetheless.
It's 100% free, there is nothing to buy, and trying to give money to the developer is actively discouraged. I will personally exted a money-back guarantee to any dissatisfied customers!
If I could recommend it higher than "yes," I would.

Developed by Eugen Systems, creators of  R.U.S.E. and the Wargame series.
Whether or not this game is for you depends on what you want from it going in.
If you're a hardcore Wargame fan much of it will be familiar, but there are stark differences so don't expect a Wargame installment with a WWII skin. The degree of comforting familiarity or disgusting deviation will probably depend on how hardcore of a fan you are of the Wargame series.
If you're big fan of R.U.S.E., Steel Division compares to it only in time period, so don't get you're hopes up for R.U.S.E. 2. However if you're looking for more of the rock-paper-scissors unit mechanics that R.U.S.E. was based around, you won't be wholy disappointed. If Wargame wasn't exactly for you but you could see yourself getting into it someday, Steel Division could be a viable introduction to the style and mechanics, while units and their roles will be similar.
At the time of writing, a couple days into the beta, there are some contentious subjective opinions being expressed in-game. These are things to keep in mind and look up further information on if you're looking to buy.
Some people have stated, in a less tactful manner:
-They prefer the Wargame ui
-They don't like the music
-They think the graphics are bad or too "cartoony"
Be sure to have a look at the above in game footage and see if you agree or disagree with the opinions.
There are undoubtably many Youtubers and Twitch streamers showing off the game. However teh publishers, Paradox Interactive, have several time streamed the game themselves and provided commentary from both the lead publisher on Paradox's side and the creative director on Eugen's. I highly recommend you check out their videos. In addition to showing off the game itself there is a lot of helpful insight from the creative director into what their intentions for the game were and some important things gameplay wise to keep in mind, even for veteran Wargame fans, as you play the game. Previous streams can be found on Youtube from ParadoxExtra and future streams of the game can be found on Twitch from Paradoxinteractive.
My opinion and experience:
Initially, several units felt unbalanced. The thought "There's just noting you can do against X" occured a few times. After a few matches I learned ways to counter or at least force back previously seemingly invincible or uncounterable units. It's always good to keep in mind that when you can't kill a heavily armoured unit, you can always force it to fall back with a relatively heavy volume of fire or air units. For someone not experienced with Wargame: the deck of units you build is exceedingly important. Build your deck with units that make up fo reach other's weaknesses. Build decks taking into account each of tha maps and their terrain. Build deck taking into account your potential opponents and their strengths.
A very importnat thing pointed out by Alexis, Steel Division's creative director and co-founder of Eugen, ground based anti-air unist are "A shield, not a sword." this is very different to their function in R.U.S.E. and Wargame. In the aforementioned games, AAA and SAM could be expected to, single handedly in Wargame and in small group in R.U.S.E., take out an air unit thus being a "sword". Don't expect them to do that in Steel Division. AAA is primarily intended to cause a pilot a lot of stress, either forceing them to break off before they deliver their payload or to give enemy fighters less staying power in a dogfight, thus "shielding" you're own fighters. An anti-air unit scoring a kill is not unheard of, but don't expect it when developing your tactics.

Ugh. All Spacebase needed was time, and that's exactly what ran out.
This is a great concept for a game. Build and manage a space outpost with a focus on resource & personnel management and design. It has a great, fun art style, and a cheeky sense of humor.
It's also abandoned, unfinished, and now, unloved.
Double Fine mismanaged this project from the start, and the result is a "game" that has no goal, no progression, and few failure conditions. A "simulation" where there is little beyond the most basic needs management that can be solved in a few minutes, with no further complexity or depth to ever grow. A "product" that's buggier than The Temple of Doom.
If you're really curious to look at what happens when a game project gets aborted but somehow thrown at the public, stillborn, then pick this game up and watch as the first few promising minutes of fun fade into unoptimized monotony.
If not, stay away and check out either Cosmonautica for a similar "Silly Space" atmosphere, or Startopia for a better Spaceport management simulation.

Probably the best 2D fighting game I've ever played, and one that's far more deserving of popularity than any of the recent Capcom fighters. Unlike those games which have mechanics specifically engineered to rewarding losing players with easy comeback chances (Ultras in SF4, X-Factor in MvC3), KOF XIII has none of that. Instead, what it offers is an incredibly solid, fast-paced, balanced and honest fighting game where victories are always earned, and the better player is always the one who wins.
However, it should also be noted that the game is significantly less beginner friendly that any other fighting game on the market, with no easy inputs and strict timing requirements for combos. Additionally, the game only teaches the basics on the guages and on universal moves, but very little on HD and how to use it for combos. Unfortunately, you'll have to experiment in the training mode or search online to learn how to use each character. There is a character trial mode included, but the difficulty ramps up extremely quickly.
The last thing worth mentioning is the online play which, when playing in Australia at least, is largely hit-or-miss. Of the online matches I've played since its release, roughly 90% have been noticably laggy or worse, with matches typically feeling like you're playing underwater, and at its worst dropping completely. However on the rare 3-4 bar connections, the lag wasn't an issue at all. Your mileage will vary.

As someone who never game fighting games a chance in the past, who dismissed himself as 'just being bad at fighting games' and thinking they were too fiddly to get used to, I recently decided to buy a madcatz arcade stick, a proper one, too, with sanwa buttons and everything. Like a REAL FIGHTING GAME PLAYER. I picked up KOF as the first of three games I had in mind for this sale (skullgirls and street fighter IV being the other two), and I loved it immediately.
As a beginning step into fighting games (although I did spend a couple weeks on SFIV a while ago using a pad) I couldn't have picked a more daunting task, but really, I love it. I think if anyone wants to get into fighting games, make sure you've got a friend with you, compete against them, and give it a proper try. Three hours a day for a week will do, then you'll get the swing of things and it'll all come naturally.
In reality three hours a day for a week isn't enough to scratch the surface of KOF, but you'll definitely be engrossed in it, unless you'd prefer something like Skullgirls of SFIV. The characters are the pinnacle of balance, there is no ultra-low-tier, there aren't really any cheap tactics either, it's just a pure-bred competitive fighting game, and tragically despite this, it isn't the most popular one. In fact, it's one of the least popular fighting games out there. Despite its beautiful sprite graphics and animation, despite it's pretty great netcode, variety of characters and playstyles, it suffers from a smaller scene.
I don't really think this is all bad, however. It's easy to find people to play with, that's for sure, and there are tournaments, if you should care for them. Definitely get a friend interested in this today, invest in a stick (because even if you find yourself not really liking the whole fighting game thing after a while, the stick is still useful for mame - metal slug, anyone?) and give it your best shot.

Glory to Arstotzka
With limitation comes innovation, this is how Indi games have boomed this generation, and with "Papers, please" we see an inventive fresh take placing you in the seat of an immigration border inspector.
Set in the dystopian communist state of Arstotzka, after a six year war with the neighboring state of Kolechia just ending, and the borders just opened, your role is to work as border inspector controlling the flow of people entering Arstotzka.
Fortune has finally smiled on you as you finally will be able to provide for your family after winning the Oct '82 lottery, but this's no common lottery as you live in the communist state of Arstotzka, what the lottery grants you is a job in the government sector giving you a chance to provide for your wife, son, mother in law and uncle.
Every day you start your job with a great amount of pressure making you think "how much money will I bring home tonight, will my family eat or sleep hungry tonight? Will they sleep in under a working heat system or will they sleep in the cold? As you start your day you will be presented with your rule book and daily policy update that will instruct on how to do your work properly and updating almost on a daily basis with every new permanent policy.
If you ever held a desk job interacting with customers you'll probably be able to relate to the game as they have captured that feeling of holding such a desk job whether it’s from the feeling you get as a new employee to a new job meeting new people and learning step by step how things work and getting familiar with your tools, colleagues and how to do the job.
Being a border inspector your work consist of granting or denying entry into the state of Arstotzka using two stamps, this is the main gameplay idea in nut shell moreover is knowing who should be granted entry and who should be denied. With the help of your rule book and daily update of policies you inspect the documentation of all travelers looking for discrepancies; if found the traveler shall be denied.
Your salary is calculated upon the work done; how many people were processed how many were denied and how many mistakes have you done as you will be penalized after a number of mistakes. By the end of every work day you get paid and have to face an impending dilemma of a short paycheck compared to a larger need. how will you divide your pay, is according to your families need per person; will little jimmy sleep hungry or sick tonight or is it your mother in law that shall bear the hunger. It’s up to you, No easy decisions are made here making it truly impacting your state of mind.
What makes the game mechanic more interesting is the moral dilemma it bombards you with, will you take a bribe to help your family survive another day by granting entry to a drug dealer to furthermore increase your income; or help a loving wife without the proper entry documentation unite with her husband and in the process getting penalized with a decrease in your income.
The aspect of progression in “Papers, please” is well refined and not just in terms of narrative, the game rewards you with items that you can hang on your wall making the booth feel more and more like your own office as you grow attached to it. The work polices also builds up with the game progression as well some recurring characters making you memories some of them if not all, what this aspect does is make you feel even more as part of the border and this dystopian world.
The game does something few other games in the industry does, which is establishing a mechanic, building on that mechanic so well making you feel you're playing a sequel to the game.
As you progress in the thirty day work period the plot widens with many paths to delve in and choices to make with moral impact affecting you, your family members and your country at large. I have found the moral impact at time so effectively applied I found myself thinking of what choice I should take meanwhile effecting the quality of my job as an inspector, this shows how well-crafted this games is and how much thought was put in stringing many aspects making it a great and well imagined product.
Something worth noting also is the saving system which is represented as a time line, giving you the flexibility of returning to any day of the month and picking up from there, this is worth noting since the game has 20 endings depending on your choices and paths taken, making it easy for you to see all endings
If you’re looking for a game with an innovative idea, engaging, involving experience, a well written narrative, fresh and on top of it on a budget price, I cannot urge you enough to at least try this game as its wonderful experience created with great care craftsmanship.

Legend of Grimrock is a classic dungeon-diving game. You play as four criminals who have been chained together and tossed into the seemingly endless labyrinth of Grimrock. Loads of enemies, puzzles, secrets and loot await you. The game also has an interesting combat style. You move around on tiles like moving on a game board, and each of your four party members can attack individually, though they always move with each other and face the same direction. Lots of fun, definitely recommend it, especially if you like games that make you think, with lots of hidden stuff to find.

The second mmorpg I've ever played. This is not an in-depth review, just a very light overview of what to expect if you purchase the game.
In my opinion, the storyline is where this game excels in comparison to other mmorpg type games. It's easy to tell that a lot of details has been put into it, especially in the later expansions. I would also say that the storylines are well paced (the original ARR storyline is a bit slow at times, but still enjoyable), and are very emotional, being able to portray the overall atmosphere very well at times.
I won't go into too much detail, but there are 9 original classes you can start off as, with 2 being tank, 6 being dps and 1 being healer. However, there are many other classes/jobs you can unlock later on through progression (1 tank, 2 healers and 3 dps). It is also very important to note that you can change the class of your character at anytime, so you are able to level multiples classes on one character. Every class is different and unique, so it's easy to find one that you're able to enjoy. All of the classes are also very well balanced, so don't feel pressured into playing a specific job/class just because you think it might be stronger, but less enjoyable. (There are also crafting and gathering classes if you're into that kind of stuff, where you're able to make a lot of money if you have the patience to level them).
Fighting (and fights in general) feel smooth, which each boss having different mechanics, meaning that new dungeons and fights always feel fresh and exciting to play.
It's also worth mentioning that the ffxiv community is one of the nicest out there, with many people willing to help you if you simply ask, and just generally being friendly and supportive, especially to newer players (new players have a little sprout icon next to their name, so people can tell if you're new and feel more inclined to help).
It's definitely worth the monthly subscription in my opinion, and I very highly recommend it to anyone who was unsure if to buy it or not.

Regular enemies are a challenge through out most of the game, often times more so than bosses, which to me were a weaker aspect of the game.  That said, looking for the "hard" way to beat a boss and get a unique weapon does given them depth, shame there is a very small number of them to actually fight.  I enjoyed the level design, how every area only has one Ops Center (bonfire / hub point / etc) and everything wraps around to it via shortcuts and good level design.  Though the second region did look a bit samey, the other regions looked good and had enjoyable (to explore and look at) level designs.
Definitely a niche game, but leaps and bounds better than the devs previous attempt at a souls-like.  I wouldn't mind future games having multiplayer (coop / pvp invasions), but this is still a good single player experience and I look forward to what the devs come up with next, be it more content for this game or a new title with similar mechanics.

I recently finished my first playthrough of The Surge, and I’m working my way through NG+. It’s an excellent game, equal in quality to any other Souls-like experience I've had (as good as Nioh, even…in my opinion). It has several unique twists and additions to the traditional Souls-like mechanics.
The most interesting new mechanic to me is the surplus energy meter that’s included in the health/stamina HUD. The energy meter sort of operates like a combo meter, in that it builds up with successful strikes and then depletes over time. However, it causes you to constantly make mid-combat decisions between harvesting parts and “potion-free healing,” depending upon which implants you equip. In other words, when the surplus energy bar is charged enough, you have a choice between using that energy to execute a finishing move (and thereby have a chance at harvesting the enemy armor part you were targeting during combat, not to mention a guaranteed end to the skirmish) or using that energy to heal, and thereby save your limited supply of healing injectables for later. Theoretically, a good enough player could have infinite healing power just by managing surplus energy well.The surplus energy-based healing injectable mechanic feels a lot like the Ki Pulse in Nioh; it's a pretty addictive combat mechanic once you've got the rhythm down.
Another mechanic I've noticed involving surplus energy is the potential loss of souls upon death. In The Surge, you have a limited amount of time to return to the scene of your demise in order to reclaim your souls. The clock starts ticking when you exit the save/upgrade zone. However, more time gets added to the clock if you successfully execute a finishing move, so this may force you to spend healing injectables instead of surplus energy in order to give yourself more time to get back to your at-risk souls.
Movement and combat is fluid and feels natural (i.e. this game is nothing like Deck 13’s prior Souls-like attempt, and they clearly learned a lot after LOTF). The graphics are great, and the environmental ambiance is extremely well-done (albeit somewhat repetitive). I personally like the song that plays incessantly in the save/upgrade zones, but it would be nice if this could be changed up in the options or a mod (Edit: you can! There's a "songs" folder in the game files where you can upload a .WAV file of any song you like. Now the Medbay plays Zeppelin's No Quarter, and this small change had a pretty radical effect on the feeling in the game).
The one major complaint I would have about this game is the way implants are managed and used, which is really clunky. There’s no reason they couldn’t have made it easier to sort and arrange the various injectables that are available in the game, all of which have very similar icons and colors so its very hard to go through and select between them. When you do have multiple injectables equipped, they are all on the same button, so it’s difficult to cycle through and select them. Particularly so, given that you don't get a moment's peace during any single one of the combat scenarios, so this forces you to be really quick and precise when deploying consumables. They should have just used a traditional consumables selection and equipping interface.
A more minor complaint is the absence of backstory and lore. The events that led to the state of the game's world really deserve some exposition, and there were plenty of missed opportunities to provide that to us. NPCs have little dialogue or interactive value...they seem as clueless as we are about what caused all this chaos and mutation. Granted, you don't play a Souls-like for explicitly narrated storylines. But, here, Deck 13 was able to create a unique and curious sci-fi world, and even built in all the story mechanisms that would have been needed to tell the backstory (i.e. left-behind emails and journal entries from victims of the incident, and NPC dialogue options). But they didn't deliver on the story to bring it home. They could have taken some queues from Horizon Zero Dawn in this area. If they continue with this IP, I think some lore and backstory would go a long way to give the game a timeless nature (maybe even a prequel DLC for starters?).
The bosses seem pretty fair, but really most enemies in the game are hard. The enemy leveling gets more progressive on NG+ (as described a little more below), but the first playthrough isn't very forgiving. You need to focus on upgrading equipment and weapon proficiency to make it fun. That’s probably intentional, given that they have a parts harvesting mechanic that is very integral to the combat system, so farming and upgrading seems to be intended as a core player objective here.
The NG+ game is very well-thought out, and clearly reflects the developer’s intent to present a new experience for players who have beaten the game. In a very interesting twist, the game seems to have added significant defense and damage to some of the enemies, but left the others alone, so now levels feel a lot more like Bloodborne’s set of tiered enemy capabilities (and less like a game that is nothing but bosses and mini-bosses, which is how I felt throughout first several hours of playing Surge).
Overall, I’d say this is one of my favorite gaming experiences, and I’m pretty surprised that this game isn’t as popular, widely discussed, and highly rated as Nioh in the Souls fan community. I’ll close by saying that I highly, highly recommend “TotalBiscuit’s thoughts on The Surge” for a brilliant and scholarly nearly-hour-long analysis of this game.

Despite not normaly writing reviews for games, I have made an exception for this game. As you can probably see, I have quite a few hours on this game, and for good reason. It is one of the best free games I've found on Steam, especially for its likeness to EV, which is know as one of the best games of the genre. I will split my review into several parts, hers the first.
Ease of play: While others have critizised the lack of an in depth tutorial and how hard the start is, I find this to amplifiy the gameplay. You have to learn to get better at the game, and this makes it more fun. The controls are simple enough that you do not have to be a genius to play, so I give this a 9/10
Controls: The controls in ES are not hard to learn, and once you do so, it takes little keyboard skill to play.
Combat: Combat in Endless Sky may not be that of a large space sim like EVE, but the nice focus on combat allows one to have quite a bit of fun combating Pirates, aliens, and other factions. The outfit system also allows for a lot of different weapons combinations and ways of fending off adversaries.
Story: The story of ES is told thru text which will pop up when you do certain things, and these stories are well layed out and have mostly satisfying endings. I won't go any farther as to not spoil the game.
Other aspects: Enless Sky is a 2d Space Sandbox, so you can pretty much do whatever you want. Become a Trader moving cargo around the whole galaxy, help colonist make there way to new worlds, take bounties hunting pirates or become one yourself. Conquer the whole galaxy if you want.
Overall this is a really good game and I would recomend it to anyone that likes games like this. Overall Score:10/10

Steel Division: Normandy 44 is an incremental improvement of this deep strategy approach in the best tradition of the Wargame and Ruse series. Wargame is not only very realistic but also very accessable. It is easy to play but extremely difficult to master. The Gameplay Mechanics of Wargame were satisfying but contrived in some instances. This was necessary for game balance but I can think of quite a few that broke immersion like the mechanic that put command units in zones to increase game income.
However, Steel Division not only appears to be more accessable than Wargame, but also more realistic. I can give a few examples: The stress system for units, the way in which armor engagements play out, the rewards for successfully integrating combined arms, and the excellent frontline mechanic that not only reduces cheezy, unrealistic tactics, but also assist in the immersion of fighting on a front line. I have played games from 1v1 to 10v10 and it feels better and less imbalanced than Wargame.
I am sure there will be minor problems to work out and balance issues to resolve. However I am looking forward to diving in and learning all about the history of the units I will be deploying. Keep up the great work!

Cons (I know these will get ironed out - it is a beta, but they are still worth noting to make an informed decision when deciding to purchase)

-Stability issues (game crashes somewhat frequently)
-Some graphical design is pretty gross - esp the trails on the tank rounds
All in all - this is a decent game as is and will get better over time. I have high hopes for the official release and the devs have demonstrated they will continue to improve/balance/add good content over time as they did with their other titles Worth the $40 even if you've never played WG before.

Okay. So let me start off by saying that your heart was in the right place while making this game, dear creator. That being said, what the ****?
I have put (thusfar) 3.3 hours into this game since downloading it this morning. THREE POINT THREE ****ING HOURS. WHY? Because my stubborn *** refused, REFUSED, to believe that this game could amount to exactly 15 minutes, if not less, of actual gameplay, and a good half hour or so struggling through unskippable, poorly translated dialogue (I might as well have just kept it in the original language and had been arsed to learn Chinese) than feel every one of my muscles clench every time I tried to skip the dialogue with unforgettable errors (good comedy!) and overall a sense of the try-hards.
The plot is inconsistent and leaves you with a sense of something left unfinished. Hence why I took the liberty of continuing to play through this game in multiple attempts (with a new bubble each time, as well as visiting a new combo of places during the days leading up to each exam) in an effort to see if there was more to the game. My quest is still unfinished, as I have only gone through with three bubbles thusfar. Aside from the looming exam (I came to this game to forget university exams, and found questions just as hard-- and I'm an honours science student), the whole idea of returning lost items seems very thin in material. Like, I can see what you're trying to do, by making each character have some life and meaning and ultimately teaching Natari something, but it just doesn't fit. There is also no more development (as far as I've seen) between Natari and the other characters, most notably Astor and Lily.
The art is good for a quick, cute indie game (although I was freaked out by the bloodied-hands holding the doll and sewing needle during my second trip to the river setting) and could lead to a good game, given a better, longer, more consistent plot, and more material in general. As well as an apparent, proper ending (will Natari ever get the bubble of her dreams?)
Furthermore, I feel as though the game is also left unfinished after the exam takes place. The game abruptly ends. Given that the game is focused around exploring the opportunities that come with different bubbles, there is not only very little to do with your specified bubble, but nothing happens after you get your certificate. I realize that this is supposed to be only part one of the series, but perhaps reassuring the player that there will be more (assuming there is/will be) would go a long way.
Overall, while there are many problems with the game, it's relatively harmless, and full of potential. I'm interested to see where it goes from here.

All right, where are my disgruntled meglomanaical geniuses who just know that if they had the chance, they could fix humanity?
How about my militant nihilists, ready to purge the earth of the infection that is man?
* looks at sea of hands *
That's what I thought. This is your game--design a super-plague, racing against WHO teams, collaborating nations, and doctors to wipe the earth clean of humanity. If even one of those damn apes survives, you lose.
The game features a variety of different micro-organisms, from the ubiquitous bacterium to nano-viruses and necro-plagues. It also features historical simulations of various plagues from world history and a Planet of the Apes simulator, just for fun.
Symptoms, optimal conditions for survival, resistance to anti-biotics and cures, and various infection vectors can all be managed to achieve optimum infection levels. (HINT: aerosol + coughing. Also insanity + coma or systemic organ failure. Two thumbs up, would wipe out the planet again.)
Steam achievements range from funny ("Oh-no") to frightening ("STALKER's delight"), each a consequence of the rising death toll and infection rates from your plague. Governments can fall as their citizens take to the streets, and world events provide vectors for new infection. There is even an achievement for infecting astronauts before they launch from the planet.
Play can be slightly repetitive at times, as you unlock gene boosts and/or mutation additions to your basic plague. While the game is occasionally fast-paced, it is primarily strategic.
So get out there, all you mad, evil scientists, and cleanse the virtual Earth.

Did you ever see that video about the guy who "won" Sim City?
I feel like this is how Factorio expects you to be playing it, ruthlessly min-maxing every value at optimal efficiency without ever explaining to you why (or how).
This game had me in alternating sessions of loving it and hating it as I slowly figured out how things worked and how to automate the more tedious tasks I had been performing by hand. Understanding that I could feed fuel from an active coal mining facility instead of a box full of coal was exhilirating, and each such discovery unlocked a wealth of new approaches. I put 40+ hours into a single world, working as best I could towards the apparent goal of building a Rocket Silo, before I gave up. Because once had I spent hours setting up the prerequisites to research the Rocket Silo, and then likewise to build the Rocket Silo, I then encountered a brand new system of incremental 1% progress towards using the Rocket Silo to win the game. That's when I realized the game was not for me - there was a kernel of something I really liked in there, but it was never going to grow into the game I wanted to play. The design honestly feels exploitative at times, like they had rigged these tedious systems to give you incentive to purchase mobile-game-type Gems to skip these build times or resource requirements, but then forgot to ever implement them.
And I was initially glad for the options on startup to seemingly disable combat. I'm one of those gamers who likes crafting but doesn't enjoy combat, wasting an hour of resource gathering by stumbling into an enemy hive and getting annihilated. So initially I loved this aspect of Factorio, being able to ignore the military research and wall-building paths in favor of a more pacifist approach. Until, of course, the tech tree introduced a new resource only acquired from destroying enemy structures. And, of course, 20 or so hours in, these enemies had all "evolved" to be more than a match for my starting equipment, so I had to level up those withered branches anyway. I feel like a resource like this honestly goes against the spirit of the game; maybe you could automate something like this with enough combat robots, but I was left to resort to save-scumming and waiting minutes on end for my regenerating health to kick in to even stand a chance at these hives.
But I am still glad such a game exists, for those who do really get into this sort of thing. As a programmer I am forced to respect how well various systems work together with one another in countless unexpected ways; I wouldn't know how to begin setting up a platform of such complexity, so perhaps it's fair I never learned how to use each piece to its fullest. For what it's worth I would say that the trailer and other game media are misleading, because the average player will likely never reach any such layer of involvement. But for that rare percent who are able to understand and setup supply chains in full, Factorio is capable of being a game truly without equal in the crafting space. I just wish I were part of that, because otherwise this game is a frustrating, baffling mess of ever-increasing expectations, where it's your fault if you can't keep up.

I will split my review into several parts, hers the first.
Ease of play: While others have critizised the lack of an in depth tutorial and how hard the start is, I find this to amplifiy the gameplay. Combat: Combat in Endless Sky may not be that of a large space sim like EVE, but the nice focus on combat allows one to have quite a bit of fun combating Pirates, aliens, and other factions. The outfit system also allows for a lot of different weapons combinations and ways of fending off adversaries.
Story: The story of ES is told thru text which will pop up when you do certain things, and these stories are well layed out and have mostly satisfying endings. I won't go any farther as to not spoil the game.
Other aspects: Enless Sky is a 2d Space Sandbox, so you can pretty much do whatever you want. Become a Trader moving cargo around the whole galaxy, help colonist make there way to new worlds, take bounties hunting pirates or become one yourself. Conquer the whole galaxy if you want.
Overall this is a really good game and I would recomend it to anyone that likes games like this. Overall Score:10/10

Dark Souls without the soul.
On paper, The Surge should appeal to fans of the souls series. Unfortunately, that's only where the similarities exist: on paper. In execution, The Surge lacks much of the complexity and depth of the souls games.
The combat becomes stale, in part due to the lack of enemy variety. The way they look may change as the game progresses, but it all boils down to the same rinse-and-repeat tactics as you come up against yet another randomly-armoured humanoid. The weapon profiency system means you'll probably be using the same weapon for the majority of the game, as your skill with other weapon types will be so low as to essentially negate any real desire to use them. This even stretches to different weapons of the same class, as your proficiency with a particular one-handed weapon doesn't seem to benefit you when wielding another. The dismemberment system however is a satisfying mechanic, and a cool way of collecting upgrades, weapons, armour, and loot.
The boss fights are good, if a little lacklustre, and the small number of them works considering how few unique locations there actually are in the game. Bosses for the sake of them is not always wise, and given the flow of the story and the locations you visit, the number and placement works.
The sci fi grimdark aesthetic creates a sameyness in level design, which can make exploration tedious as you traipse through yet another service duct. There's a claustrophobia which, while perhaps appropriate, made me feel the levels were intentionally maze-like in an attempt to disguise just how small they actually are. The game does have a certain amount of complexity in level layout, made manifest primarily by the traditional unlocking of shortcuts back to your safehouse, but unless you consider this mechanic to be the hallmark of interesting level design you'll soon be yearning for areas with actual personality and uniqueness. Doors which you encounter but aren't yet able to open should provide a tantalising motivation to backtrack and explore previous areas, if only you could remember in which dimly lit, pipe-filled corridor you saw it...
The NPC side missions are glorified fetch quests and have little bearing on the story or your character. And, unless you want to feel like an underpowered weakling with a new weapon halfway through the game, the rewards often just take up space in your inventory.
The Surge feels like a copy of a copy, a half-heard description, a humourous Google translate error. It's the result of a too-literal interpretation of the soulsborne ethos - "make fights hard, make levels twisty, make deaths punishing" - which misses what those games
by aiming to replicate what they
.
People are asking why I've recommended this game. I recommend The Surge because, in spite of the above, it's not an inherently bad game - just be aware of the points I've made and adjust your expectations accordingly. If, like me, you're a sworn follower of the Dark Souls games, you may be left wanting, but there's surely no harm in picking up The Surge when it inevitably hits that 50% price reduction.

FS17 is the Most Casual Player Friendly farming simulator game on the market.
This time you can actually enjoy the game in tne most simple way.
Just take a mission from the field's owner and you will get all the necesary equipment for completing the job.
Do it, enjoy it and don't worry about anything else.....and you will also get paid when you have finished it.
If you don't want to spend your money on anything, you can do that. There is basically no need for you to be a farm manager owning all the fields and have a lot of thinking to do. You can just be a simple employee having fun at work.
The new Mission system which is basically identical with the Quick Job system from Euro truck Simulator 2, makes the FS17 the best experice for any casual player who only wants to drive a tractor or a harvester on a field and not think about the huge ammount of knowladge he/she needs to know about farming activities or the ammount of texts he/she needs to read in the game manual
Don't forget you can even listen to a few radio stations while you are driving,
plus with the new mods available in the Mods tab in the game you can add more realism to your gameplay like dirt densities to make the driving boucy or the wheels destroy crops. All these plus more are made directly by the Giants Software.
In the options you can also make your vehicles start engine manually or automatically when entered.
Also, you can make a sort of manual reverse by Stop and Go option which makes you press two times S for getting into reverse. Once to fully stop and once for reversing.
From all the farming simulator games on the market, including the previous titles by Giants Software, I trully recommned this Farming Simulator 17 game to all the players: new, casuals and veterans alike.
and one more thing... you can even run it on lower specs then the minimum reqs posted in the description.
If you can run Euro Truck Simulator 2 then you can run this one perfectly. To test it, you can dowload the ETS2 demo and then be sure if your PC can run Farming Simulator 17

I've noticed a trend in my reviews: I tend to only review games that I have a negative opinion of.
NOT ANY MORE!
I thought this game was very good. Not amazing, or fantastic, but very good. The puzzles can be diabolical, and the boss fight at the end can be a frustrating test of patience, but overall, Almost Human did a great job with it.
Combat is almost always fast-paced and hectic (trying to click on the right runes for a mage while trying to dodge attacks from multiple enemies is a blast), the graphics are rather impressive, the puzzles are satisfying (for the most part), and the variety of enemies is very welcome indeed.
Many games of this genre can get boring, as they are truly turn-based, and you can take your time, but not with this game. Your characters have a food (hunger) bar that continually shrinks, even when standing still. Add to that the fact that food is not by any means a common find in the dungeons, and you have a real motivation to always keep moving.
There were a few places where you could grind for food, and I wish I hadn't discovered that fact, as it took away quite a bit of the urgency of the situation. If/when you play through, I would strongly suggest you not take advantage of any grinding opportunities you come across (they won't be too easy to find anyway), as the game is fair about food, and will give you as much as you need. With my grind, by the end of the game, all my characters were slightly overburdened with food that I refused to throw away.
Character designing is a lot of fun, and trying different combos of teams adds quite a bit of replay value, although certain teams work a lot better together than others.
Puzzle solutions are always sensical, although some of them are rather esoteric. Clues on pieces of paper and random items you find are almost always relevant to puzzles, so keep your wits about you.
Overall, this game is an example of just about everything done just about perfectly. It's not an easy game, but it's not punishingly difficult either. It never asked for more than I could give, but it was always close.
Plus, indie team. Always awesome.

That's what I thought. This is your game--design a super-plague, racing against WHO teams, collaborating nations, and doctors to wipe the earth clean of humanity. If even one of those damn apes survives, you lose.

Symptoms, optimal conditions for survival, resistance to anti-biotics and cures, and various infection vectors can all be managed to achieve optimum infection levels. (HINT: aerosol + coughing. Also insanity + coma or systemic organ failure. Two thumbs up, would wipe out the planet again.)

Governments can fall as their citizens take to the streets, and world events provide vectors for new infection. There is even an achievement for infecting astronauts before they launch from the planet.
Play can be slightly repetitive at times, as you unlock gene boosts and/or mutation additions to your basic plague. While the game is occasionally fast-paced, it is primarily strategic.
So get out there, all you mad, evil scientists, and cleanse the virtual Earth.

This review is based on only the tutorial and first scenario, just so all of you who are waiting can see some comments :-)
First - no issues to complain about at all, so far.  There are some 'hints/tips' shown during load/save screens which can flash past a little quickly but as they're only there to give you something to look at I don't THINK I've missed anything important.
Gameplay :- Turn based.  a) select a protein for each of your incubators.  This is a random-draw which dictate what you'll be able to do later in the turn.  b) open the AV (doh, can't remember what it stands for!) to see which proteins you need to destroy the remaining viral hexes, c) check the store to see if there's any machine/person you wish to buy.  d) decide which of your staff and machines you wish to use this turn, e) harvest proteins and allocate them the AV f) kill those parts of the virus that your completed AV options allow, g) end turn for random events; virus spread and mutation included.  Gameplay for the first scenario is short (5 minutes) but affected by (random) mutation.  In my first playthrough I needed an additional two turns thanks to a mutation that I didn't in the second.  This second playthrough was to check replayability.  I'll leave it to you to find out what does and doesn't change, but think there's enough that you can play each scenario several times.
Graphics are as good as they need to be, but this isn't a graphics-based game.  Music wasn't annoying enough to turn off - although that's generally the first thing I do in any game - and effects-sounds are also acceptable if unremarkable (again, it just isn't that sort of game, so they don't affect gameplay).
Summary - plays as a puzzle game rather than 'hard science' because of the protein random-draw and various references to die-rolls (which are automatic).  Bear in mind that I have not yet played the later scenarios, where world-events become significant.  Knowing the makeup of the virus but having a random selection of proteins seems the wrong way around to me.  I'd have thought the choice of which proteins to incubate would be up to me, while trying to find a combination that was effective against a particular virus would be the hard part.
[Compared to Plague Inc, since that's what a lot of people seem to be asking - You are CURING the virus here and it's entirely based in your lab.  As far as I have played (which isn't very far) there isn't the same sense of progress or control here.]

A great addition to the category of games like Dark Souls, this one brings us a more cohesive and understandable plot and sci fi setting without ruining the feel of these sorts of games with the ranged weapons one would expect in a sci fi setting. The Surge's combat may seem a little slow and cumbersome to some, but having to think about when is the right time to attack and which part of your enemy you should be attacking really makes the combat feel more deliberate and thoughtful rather than rewarding button spamming. The play space's ambiance is filled with great visual and auditory design that really sets the feeling of the games locations in an excellent way, be it signage, post catastrophe graffiti, or the regular intervals of internal company propaganda videos. Level design is excellent any well thought out spaces that actually feel like places where people might actually have worked and not the usual nonsensical semi-linear spaces found in many games. Unlike Dark Souls' many bonfires in a region approach, The Surge instead gives us only one Ops Center per location, and yet still keeps the feel of do you risk pushing on with much of your limited resources spent in the hopes of finding the latest shortcut back to Ops, or turn back the way you came and try another foray out after restocking with the hopes of doing better this time. This style of level design focused on exploration from the single Ops Center per location really brings a feeling of some of the best Dark Souls I level design, but doubles down on it in a wonderful manner.
Deck13's first foray into Soulslike games (Lords of the Fallen) was a passable and fun early days entry into this emerging "genre". The Surge shows they have learned a lot from what makes Soulslike games good, but also bringing to it some of their own good elements.

However, once I forced adaptive V-sync via the Nvidia control panel I rarely had framerates drop below 55 fps. . My only real complaint in the graphics department is the lack of the adaptive V-sync option in the graphics menu, at least on my install.
Second; yes the story sucks but the combat more than makes up for it. This game however, has much more depth in my opinion with the addition of the various gear sets and the implants. You can do quite a few cool different builds if you are careful and get most of the implants as you progress. This allowed me to tune my character for certain difficult enemies and bosses which I really enjoyed. You can also have builds that allow you to return to the med center less thus gaining extra XP.
I thought the fighting mechanics and physics were flawless. The combat is crisp, sharp, and offers a lot of depth once you get the hang of it. I really liked the ability to do horizontal or vertical attacks and experimenting with different chains. I am still learning so much.   There are no telepors but if you pay attention and memorize landmarks you can actually move quite quickly between areas.

First of all, the humor is fantastic and carried all thru the game.  The names and descriptions of the creatures encountered will leave you in stitches.  The dialog between the narrartor, Cthulu, and the various party members accquired is well done and alot of HP Lovecraft references are sprinkled about in the right doses.
The music is epic and customized to the different areas and dungeons encountered during the game.  It's so good that I only listen to the game music as I'm playing it.  It's dark and dreary and fun and light hearted.
The ability to bring in swap in any party members and save the game anytime is a godsend.  Also, you can hold a button and your party will  be able to run thru the open world and dungeons, saving you alot of time.  In every dungeon , there is a fixed amount of random encounters you will  have. (unless you override this)  This making the leveling pacing and amount of grinding required down to a minimum, allowing you to solve any puzzles and gather all the items from every area without being encountered to death by monsters.
Cthulu and the party can instantly teleport back to any town they have visited.   Also, you heal all your hps and some magic points after every battle.  This sure beats having to carry a bunch of potions around.
Characters level up pretty frequently as you acquire experience and are able to accquire alot of different things such as innate abilties, stat increases, HP and MP increases and spells or techniques.  It's fun to try and decide what to get on each level up, so you could play thru the game multiple times and build the team in different ways to find out what works best for you.
The battle simple is very detailed and complex.  Every spell, technique or attack has a certain number of hits which give you combo points.  Certain abilities are called Combo Finishes and the damage dealt is multiplied the number of hits on the combo meter.  You want to get as many hits as fast as you can to use the finishers and end battles quickly.  Mastering this technique help immensely on the boss battles.
Monster A.I. is pretty good, creatures will use thier best abilities and grow in strength every round.  If you accidently encounter the wrong mix of creatures and don't or use the right counters it can easily lead to restarts or game over.
When you beat the game, you can replay it in a new mode called Cthulu's Angels.  It's a whole new storyline and your main character is one of the girls from the original game tasked by Cthulu to accquire a quarted of hot chicks to save the world.  You accquire portraits of the characters that can be saved and looked at any time.
I had a blast with this game and asked Zeboyd Games to please make a sequel with triple the amount of everything.  Do yourself a favor and play this game, it's the most fun RPG you will EVER play in your life!
Even though you may not have been consciously aware of it, you know you have always wanted to play as Cthulhu in a Legend-of-Zelda-ish RPG with turn-based combat that doesn't take itself seriously.

I'm only a few hours into the FS17 and I have to say that this is the best FS sim in the entire lineup. There's enough reviews out there to tell you what to expect in this years FS, but I want to give the FS developers a lot of praise for improving the core elements of this game. They've also provided DLC in previous FS (and I'm sure they will in FS17 as well) that actually feels like you are getting your moneys worth, and I can think of only one other sim out there that does that (Euro Truck Simulator 2). In final, if you're looking for a solid casual simulator, this is one of very few I can recommend. I hope the developers read this review because you all seriously deserve high praise for putting out another great sim….just keep doing what you’re doing, it’s great stuff!

After about 10 hours or so played, I've tried all four factions currently in the beta. As it stands, there are two for the Axis and two for the Allies.
Representing both are a single infantry-based division, and a single armored division. You can customize which units you want to have available in-game prior to the battle by filling out your battle group with "cards." Each card allows you to call a unit in at a particular phase of the game - starting at Phase A, then continuing to Phase B and C at 10 and 20 minutes in respectively. With each phase, you get new units available, and different divisions have different strengths.
The gameplay is very good in general. You control large numbers of units on a diverse battlefield. Strategy actually matters, unlike in many RTS type games (where often your ability to click quickly is all that matters). What units you decide to bring in, where you decide to deploy them, and how you react to new situations on the battlefront all play a role. The battlefields are large enough that you are forced to react to a wide front and pick multiple points to attack and defend depending on the geography and situations at hand.
Units behave as you would expect them to. Infantry are relatively cheap, and have excellent stealth capabilities. They are also the only units able to take and hold structures (obviously), which make natural strongholds and allow for easy ambushes. You can also hide them in forests however, and making use of cover is very necessarry for them as they can be easily routed or destroyed if caught by something like anti-air guns or artillery, or even ordinary machine guns.
Tanks are tanks. They are excellent at destroying lighter armored vehicles, but have poor vision. You need to use scouts to see what is going on properly, and gaining intelligence in this manner is very important to gameplay.
You also can call in various types of aircraft - fighters, bombers, anti-tank specialized attack fighters. There's artillery of all types, from mortars to large artillery pieces. Anti-aircraft guns double as mobile infantry support weapons, and later in the game are even capable of taking out ground vehicles quite well.
There is no lack of variety in units, and there is still much to be added to the game prior to the full release.
The game implements a frontline system to determine victory, as well. Pushing you units forward pushes the front line forward, and you gain points depending on your percentage controlled by your team. Battles supposedly go from 1v1s all the way up to 10v10s, but I've only gone as high as 4v4s.
The AI is quite challenging and fun to fight against.
In the end, the game is excellent in its current state, and I would recommend it to anyone who loves large-scale real time strategy games. It still needs some polish, but I highly recommend it. Check out some gameplay videos if you are unsure if you would like it.

Almost every move in every character's moveset has a use, which is testament to trimming of superfluous waste in this truly streamlined fighter. Effort was put into developing the game and it shows; most evidently in the highly balanced character roster in my opinion. Like all figting games the learning curve is steep, but because of the very technical nature of King of Fighters the execution barrier is even higher. Regardless even if one is new to the genre I can recommend it due to the extremely balanced characters, advanced mechanics and a well executed pace. As such there is a lot less frustrating nonsense that plagues many other fighters.

This game was a suprise for me.  For the record, I loved the Souls games and even really liked Lords of the Fallen for what it was.  I bought this game but didn't get to playing it right away.  I'm almost sorry I waited so long.  I didn't have huge expectations and the reviews were kind of luke warm.  Ultimately though, the game was really good from start to finish for me.  I liked the combat system, I thought it was quite excellent actually.  Similar to but not exactly like a Souls game.  I ended up really enjoying unlocking new armor, testing out sets of armor to see what their set bonus was and liked trying out differnet weapons.  The story was ultimately pretty interesting.  The one issue for me is the audio logs and everything are actually way better on the second play through.  Many speak of things and people you encounter way later in the game, but they are almost background noise till you know more about the characters.  For example, there is an audio log in the first part of the game that talks about Dr Chavez.  I had actually forgotten entirely about this by the time I met her.  But on a subsequent playthrough I found the log enjoyable because it let on that there is more to this world than what is right in front of you.  It let about a story where workers that were not you had thoughts and feelings about important events in the games story, and it felt more impactful once you actually had your own interactions with Dr Chavez.
I liked the gear upgrade and unlock system quite a bit.  I liked going for the hardcore kills of bosses to get better weapson, I like how thinking about gear upgrades actually made me consider what part of enemies to attack.  Also, in many cases I would think about whether it's woth going after the parts I needed or if my stims were in bad shape, I may just find a weak unprotected area to attack so I minimized my chances of death.  It very much as that same effect of souls games where the amount of scrap you are carrying makes you think about what exactly you want to do in a given situation.
The game is not perfect though, as you can imagine.  I disliked how confusing the maps were, which were one of the main complaints in other reviews.  I appreciate how they tried to loop everything back around to the start of each area quite thoroughly as a way to get back to the ops center.  But in the second area, which acts as something of a main hub to get to and return from other areas, becomes a confusing mess of corridors as the game progresses.  There were multiple occasions where I stumbed back into areas I had already been.  There is also some enemies in there at actually represent more annoyance than anything else.  They are some kind of repair bot that have a ridiculous amount of health.  You get no worthwhile drops from them and earlier on they can two hit you if you aren't careful.  I would be fine with them as they are except they are hostile towards you like anything else it.  It would have been way better if they had just made it so they weren't hostile unless being attacked by the player.  It would be a nice ambiance effect of the area you are in rather than a hostile, hard to kill enemy that you try to avoid at all costs because the risk/reward is very lopsided towards risk with little reward.
Overall, I think I liked the game quite a bit though.  There were some annoyances with the map and how it loops back on itself, but overall that meant very little in regards to how much I enjoyed this game.  I would have liked more than 5 bosses though, perhaps more weapons or gear to try out as well.  But what was there felt impactful and was worth considering how you wanted to build Warren around gear and implants.  Combat felt very good, very responsive and active with much to consider in many encounters.  I was a bit disappointed with NG+ only because I wish they did more to change the world on a subsequent playthrough.  Little changes and tweaks throughout the world do exist, but I would have liked to see something like enemies being in different locations and maybe some optional hard enemies thrown in a bit more.
