This game has a simple premise, collect papers, check papers for errors or discrepancies stamp the papers, return the papers, over and over again. At first, one might consider this a chore that could never be entertaining, but it is very fun and very enjoyable. The rules are always changing, so you have to remember slightly different rules every day. There are over 25 things that could make someone unable to pass the border, and YOU need to find each and every one of them. There are only several minutes to complete as many clients as possible, so time is of great concern. And since you are paid by the client, and you have a family to keep alive, time is even more pressing. This game will force you to think not only faster, but accurately, since every bad decision you make could kill your family. I would highly recommend this game... just don’t pay ten dollars for it, anything less than six is a fair price.

Never would I have thought that playing a game about a singer with no voice and a talking sword would be so compelling, riveting, and beautiful. The screenshots don't really tell you much. The game just has an atmosphere that draws you in. Its indescribable like any good piece of art.
The game features a kind of interesting Action-RPG/Tactical combat system. You can move about and use your attacks/powers freely, but you can also freeze time and plan out advanced manuevers as well. After you unfreeze time, Red will carry out your planned moves instantly. Early on tactical mode is totally optional as most enemies and situations can be resolved without it. Later however it becomes very important you master this system as many enemies are too fast or too dangerous to be engaged normally without taking a lot of damage. It is honestly a really fun and well designed fighting mechanic, and without the atmosphere and engaging story the combat system would still hold up.
Which brings me to that. This game is one of the only games that made me sit at the ending staring at the final screen not knowing what to do. I wanted more. I wanted more answers. I wanted to know everything and see everything. I finished the game in two nights and I had no idea that I'd be a different person two nights previously to me finishing it. There's a lot of unanswered questions, but I feel like that is okay in this situation. Red herself is trying to figure everything out and doesn't have all the answers either. The Transistor itself is kind of a mystery as to how it works, but that quickly became unimportant to me as to what it was going to say next, and the relationship between Red and the man in the Transistor.
And the music, oh god the music. It is fantastic. One of my favorite things about this game is the fact that the soundtrack is dynamic. If you are in combat, the music is louder. Outside of combat, it quiets down. When you engage tactical mode, the regular music fades away to just Red singing as she plans out moves and thinks about what next step to take. But there is even a button devoted to just having Red hum along to any song currently playing. Many times across this adventure I'd stop and listen to her voice (played by the talented Ashley Barrett) if there was a particular song I liked. Especially the beach song.
So look. Nothing I can write can really describe this properly. I can't give you the details you'd really need. You just need to play it. Maybe pick it up when you have a few extra bucks. Maybe buy it on sale. But get it. You'll thank me later.

WARNING: Spoilers in this review.
On the positive side, this game is well scripted and a blast of nostalgia. If you miss being frozen out by girls in the Windows XP and AIM days, this is the game for you! (Also, brush up on your knowledge of music from 2002-2006). Most of the dialogue is extremely realistic, and I love the selection of user icons, including the unlockable ones.
On the negative side, there's not much branching in the narrative. Yes, it is somewhat realisitc in the way that you can't always end up with The Girl. Still, it leaves the player unsatisfied that there is NO way to at least remain good friends with her (nevermind date her). When people call this game "Friendzone Simulator", they aren't kidding; it's literally the #NiceGuy perspective on girls not wanting to date him. Why can't the player and Emily just end up as friends? Why is it "all" (a romantic relationship, which is the only thing valuable from the game's perspective) or nothing?
So overall, it's well made, but the game gets a downvote for me. There's no replayability and no real satisfaction upon completion, since it only gives the ILLUSION of choice. You're still guided to pretty much the same ending no matter what you do, and that's not much of a game in my opinion.

I followed the production of this game back when it was first announced as True Crime Hong Kong but lost interest in buying it when it became clear that the quality of the game was not going to be up to scratch due to it being tossed around and re-built. But now in 2017 i decided to give it a shot thanks to steam's summer sale and the overwhelmingly good reviews the game has from players. I thought that it may be pretty good. But i was wrong. This game is rubbish.
First of all i am huge fan of open world games and have played dozens of them in my lifetime. But Sleeping Dogs is by far the worst i have ever played. The game feels like a steam early access game. The driving physics are simply DISGUSTING with vehicles that accelerate to FULL SPEED as soon as you press the acceleration button and a ridiculous mechanic that allows you to rapidly ram your car into other cars and BLOW THEM UP regardless of what vehicle you're using or how fast you're going. All the vehicles in this game feel weightless and floaty as if there was NO effort put into the driving physics whatsoever.
During gameplay there are SO MANY glitches, the game often feels like it is hanging on by a thread and one wrong move will cause the game to spaz out and crash, if i knew it was going to be this bad i wouldve gotten a PVR ready and recorded the greatest glitch montage of all time. NPCs get stuck running into walls, get stuck on objects, dissapear, appear out of nowhere, T-pose, spaz out, vibrate, launch into the air, stand on their cars or other objects, fail to react when you shoot someone that is standing right next to them and MORE. Your character will also often get stuck on objects and glitch out. Everything feels clunky, buggy and just cheap. Nothing flows naturally no matter how accurate you try to be.
The open world is so bleak and repetitive. Most of the map is comprised of tight roads with cloned buildings lined up on both sides. The few open areas still feel cramped with un-breakable and un-climbable fences placed all over the place. The city only looks decent when it rains, but that still doesnt change how lifeless the world feels. There just isnt a real "sandbox" here, nothing to do besides the main story, the side missions suck, and worst of all... you don't have any access to weapons during free roam! What is the point of playing an open world crime game if you don't have the option go on a shooting rampage when you're bored? its depressing.
The combat system tries to borrow from the recent Batman games but fails miserably. Having a smooth and free flowing fight is now impossible because the game makes it annoying for you to chain attacks and counter successfully. Knowing when someone is about to attack you is like trying to find a needle in a haystack because your only indication is a thin red outline around the enemy which is incredibly hard to notice when you are fighting a dense crowd of goons. Most of the time you will end up pressing the counter button at the wrong time which makes your character freeze for 2 whole seconds allowing enemies to strike you and eventually kill you.
Sometimes you are required to rapidly press the counter button 2 or 3 times to dodge a combo move, but there is no way of knowing if an enemy is about to do a combo move or a single move, so you will often rapidly press the counter button when you're not supposed to which causes you to freeze and then get hit. The environmental kills are the only good part of the combat system in this game. Shooting is alright when on foot, but when you're in a car literally all you need to do is shoot at your enemy's wheels once to INSTANTLY blow up their car. What the hell was going through the minds of the people who designed the vehicle physics in this game.
The animations are horrible, especially during gameplay where NPCs will loop the same awkward 3-second animation over and over with zero facial expression. Even during cutscenes the characters look and move around like puppets.
And the story tries to be dramatic but its just too convoluted and random. You're essentially an undercover cop that...guess what....GETS TOO INVOLVED. Wow so original. I don't really care about anything that is going on with the triads and the game gives you no reason to care anyway. Although the final mission was actually pretty fun to play.
This game should have never been released. And i think there is a major bias towards this game from people who are excited to play any game that takes place in China, because the game itself is garbage.

To clarify the martial art in this game since people think it's kungfuu, the moves are motion captured by none other than UFC welterweight champion George St. Pierre, who has a base in karate. Outside his mma (mixed martial arts) training, he is originally a 3rd dan black belt in Kyokushin karate, and a blackbelt in Shidōkan, which is basically mma with a karate base. The DLC consists of outfits that enable the Muay Thai flying knee, mma superman punch, and the armbar and kneebar Brazilian jiujitsu submissions. You can also level up to earn the double leg takedown with ground and pound. Certainly a game for martial artists with a trained eye who's tired of typical action games with tacky and fake fighting moves. The story leads Wei Shen to a dojo led by his kungfuu instructor, but really it's karate in disguise. Since it is a game that takes place in China it makes sense to have Chinese martial arts. Can't say I blame them for mislabeling.. or couldn't they have hired a kungfuu expert? Shrugs.
Aside from having the funnest fighting mechanics out of any GTA-type game, this game is also my favorite "GTA" for doing a better job at tying gameplay elements together in harmony, where everything from clothes to dating has a purpose to keep you motivated. I'd give this game an 'A' if it wasn't for the clunky issues that are commonly addressed- cars, camera controls, etc, but I'd still play Sleeping Dogs over GTA any day of the week.
Can't help but add that I cracked up when I entered a triad mission after I decided to put on a cop outfit. "Why, no of course I'm not a rat despite wearing this police uniform!". "Oh, sorry I doubted you.", LOL!
I love that I'm playing a protagonist who is essentially in the body of George St. Pierre.
Bored of GTA? Give Sleeping Dogs a definitive chance!

Note: Played through the main story, and every instance of savage raid and trials (as of patch 4.05 when this is written), however fights done before Alexander: Midas, were post-nerf minimum ilvl. With experience in raiding as a dps, healer and currently a tank (WAR, as of writing this review). A lot of this is opinion based, if you disagree - come flame me ingame, my character and server are on my profile.
Getting to the end-game is the real challenge since very little has been done to remedy the levelling grind. Where it is literally a grind. You must complete over 500 quests (estimated, many of which are boring fetch quests), to complete the base game and heavensward, this isn't counting stormblood. To level, you either grind dungeons, palace of the dead, or do fates.
Where DPS are faced with queue times of up to 30 minutes (often depending on what you are wanting to do) for dungeons. Forcing many to go through palace of the dead, which is a RNG dungeon that gets repetitive since you will be doing this for many times to level as a DPS.
...or you can pay an extra £40 to skip the story to the start of the Stormblood expansion and boost a single class to 60 (ARR + HW jobs, can only be done once per account).
It's a matter of convenience but also effects the player base where you have way more people who do not understand basic game mechanics or rotation, which they would learn by just playing from the beginning before boosting.
In terms of each Job's identity outside of the holy trinity roles (DPS/TANK/HEAL), each do have a unique identity.
For example, in regards to the caster dps;
An offputting thing though for every job, is that there is a large GCD time, this is a common complaint when people come over from different MMOs. The FFXIV default GCD is 2.5s, this is the reason is due to controller/console support, where 1.5 - 2s is incredibly fast for many users using a controller as far as I’m aware.
The solution to this is the excessive ability bloat.
Where you have baseline rotation of some actions, then a large line-up of oGCDs and cross-class skills for every job. This is more elegant for DPS since it is all damage oriented CDs that fit into the rotation. Less so for tanks and healers, since they will have more utility/role-based CDs with exceptions e.g. SCH chain stratagem (crit buff), AST buff cards.
For the actual end game itself, the current content cycle is 4 savage raids, 2 or 3 trials every major patch, and a super savage fight for the patch after the next raid tier is released. As a result, if you clear content at a hardcore pace (farming all fights since week 1 or 2), it leads to early content drought where there isn't much to do besides farm weekly raids, farm mounts, do speed kills (if you are inclined to optimise runs), or do older fights at synced ilvl, or min-ilvl. Those are examples, that come to mind personally, the point is that you will find end-game quantity to be lacking compared to how much is in something like warcraft's expansions.
It's end game instances at savage and extreme-mode trials are good, but suffer from two main problems, being heavily scripted (always the same), and more recently making the fights easier to appeal to casual players and abandoning the mechanic skip in fights, meaning you cannot push dps so hard that you are rewarded with skipping mechanics, causing the current tier (omega: deltascape savage), to be highly repetitive with no change to boss rotations. This is unlike older tiers, all fights are scripted but the added randomness to what is skipped due to raid performance allowed some interesting variety with how player rotations would need to adjust as a result.
Overall: FFXIV is a solid MMO. It has a well implemented, but flawed solution to support controller users. The end-game is excellent and quite fun for progression, but lacking in instance quantity during the farming period, and as of patch 4.05 when I’m writing this, omega savage 1 - 4, is easier than the previous tier alexander creator, which is known for being more streamlined than Midas. The jobs are fun, and each is unique however the levelling process is a mind-numbing grind overall, more so if you're levelling a DPS.

So with nearly 60 hours and level 48 I have some opinions. Opinions I'm sure people will be mad about. I kept playing because of my friends and I'll try to push for 50 and see what happens.
But lets start.
Every fight is the same. Every dungeon is the same.
This is not a good indication of the late game for me. Also I've run out of Quest to level on so it's either the boring dungeons or Fates to do. Leves quest offer some help.
So why is every fight the same? Well you can start with the first enemy and an enemy from the same level as you from 48 and it will roughly take the same amount of Ruin spells to kill.
All the fights are done 1v1 or 1v2 when you're playing normally. Because your class have no AOE capability and even if it did you wouldn't be able to tank the damage and the AOE spells are pretty weak sauce.
So it's just spamming the Ruin spell over and over because most new spells are not worth your time. Except for the Aether ones that Steal mana. It does higher damage than your Ruin spell and you got 3 charges late game.
Don't bother with Miasma or Bio until you got Fester spell at level 45 or so. Because the the Damage over time is absolutely worthless for Arcanist/Summoner.
It's just not fun to play as one. The summons themselves are pathetically weak and boring to summon. They just serve as a meat shield for you and to pull aggro. Making most fights trivial. But I'm sure late game dungeons will throw monsters that deal so much damage they kill you in one hit because "Difficulty".
So that pretty much sucks. But there are more stuff I'm bothered about.
Every enemy has the same defense value and no other defense stats. So a Fire spell would never deal more damage to a Zombie type enemy or Water spells wouldn't deal more damage to a fire enemy. Because the game has none of it.
Which mean there is no thought needed when using skills. Just spam them and call it a day.
The same goes for armor. There are no Fire armor to tank extra fire damage or no Water armor to tank extra water/ice damage. Just use the highest level gear you can buy and you'll be just fine. Except they don't do much at all. This is the weakness with progressive gears that just get a bit better and better as you level up.
I see that I have Materia slots but I'll just laugh at them because this game have ignored everything that is Final Fantasy so far so I'm without a doubt not gonna get anything good from those slots.
The game just have Final Fantasy slapped onto it and it's the only selling point it has.
Combat is nothing like any previous Final Fantasy game.
Spells are nothing like previous Final Fantasy game. Fire, Fira or Firaga are not there.
Summons are so weak and pathetic that any previous Summon from any Final Fantasy game could just slap it around.
This entire time I have never felt powerful in any kind of way. Every enemy is treated like a mini boss and specially in dungeons.
There is no reason what so ever to do low level dungeons. Like none.
There is no planning when you enter a dungeon, because you don't need to worry about gear, weapons, skills or anything else because it all works just as fine against everything.
Every dungeon demands 1 Healer, 1 Tank and 2 DPS. Stray from those numbers and you will DIE.
So if this game actually took gameplay features from previous Final Fantasy titles except their previous MMORPG one. The game could actually get a lot of fun to play. It could even add some depth to the game but with it's kiddy pool level of depth I doubt SE wants to change that.
Last thoughts, this feel like most other Korean MMORPG I've played when I was younger. I tried out plenty of them and they all feel like this. Guild Wars 2 is one of them as well.
So instead of picking this game up, pick any of the previous Final Fantasy game out there. Because they will actually let you do more than what you can do in this game. Even when they are SP games.
Oh and no Final Fantasy 6 Overworld music while riding the MagiTek Armor? Absolutely disgraceful. Just wrong.

As someone who has enjoyed Demons Souls, Dark Souls and Lords of the Fallen, I can thankfully say this game brings enough new ideas to stand above them all. Having played this for a good chunk of time, lost sleep and eagerly going on, I find myself enjoying it a great deal.
Here is where this game mechanics mainly differs from the others; classes. In a the afore mentioned titles a player would be stuck on a specifc style of fighting (heavy, fast, magic) without being able to swap unless they started a new game and made a new build. Not this game.
The surge allows you to adapt in fantastic ways to new challanges by managing what your 'rig' or base suit is capable of through interchangeable nodes. I found myself struggling with some enemies until I changed my strategy, the freedom of this change is honestly a wonderful feature and I praise Deck13 for its brilliance.
I think of The Surge as a challenging souls type game but with a great deal more thinking. Strategies need to be made per enemy, maps are more like maddening mazes, and the satisfaction piecing it all together is sweet.
People complain that there are too few bosses, I disagree. While limited every encounter feels special and the fewer bosses have allowed some very creative ideas into what they can be.
Honestly speaking, I grew bored of the Souls series as it repeats the formula but in a different labcoat with some light adjustments, and I dont expect to make friends with such a bold statement. The Surge does have a different coat, but a different formula without being unfamiliar.
--------------------------------------------------------------
If you like a fun game, this is for you.
If you dont like the Souls games, this is for you.
Try the demo and enjoy this brilliant game.
Not Dark Souls 3.

This is Wargame: WW2 Edition, which honestly would have been enough for me, but they've also added several things that are absolutely fantastic. The graphics and sound are great, the new units are fun (everybody has a couple of favourite tanks or planes from WW2), but the biggest thing for me is the Frontline system. I absolutely thought, after seeing development streams and whatnot, that this was a bad idea, and that since the line moves whether you have recon or not, it would ruin the element of stealth. What it actually does is make the entire battlefield equally valuable, so if you're up against a tough enemy dug into a fortification you don't need to fight him on his terms. You can bomb him, or surround him (being isolated in a pocket severely hurts your Morale, which is even more important than health in this game), pound him with artillery, burn him out with flamethrowers... it just opens up the battlefield and makes the entire match feel much more "organic" (as much as I hate to use that word) and natural.
There are balance issues at the moment of this writing - AA doesn't do enough damage, American half-tracks are too resistant to morale damage, etc - but with a month and a bit left to go to release I believe they'll sort it out. If you're into Wargame, WW2 or just plain strategy games this is a safe bet.

Fine, the long review. This is mostly a direct comparison to Red Dragon so wiill not make much sense without a knowledge of that game.
Sectors have been replaced with timed phases. Every Division (deck) has a set income in each of these timed phases which can go up if they are being successful taking ground - overall vastly superior to secotrs.
Route mapping by units during a fast move is far superior.
Supply now only replaces ammunition and there is no ingame repair  or infantry replacement. More realistic than RD.
Hit points for units are gone. AT weapons now have a percentage chance of hilling an opposing vehicle. Vehicles being hit without penetration suffer moral damage and "fall back" when their panic bar is full. Which results in your vehicles wandering about being shot at rather than staying in cover like they are supposed to.
Infantry are now much more vulnerable because Eugen screwed up buildings - which can now be destroyed. A single infantry unit can occpy a set of buildings. There are no longer grouped units in the game. When the building is destroyed it becomes impassable terrain to new units including infantry. Only a unit that was in the building before it was destroyed can occupy it.  This basically makes keeping infantry alive nearly impossible, as the indirect assets in the game are greater than that of red dragon. Also keeping in mind that units cannot be reinforced or amalgamated
Imagine Red Drgon where all of the artillery in the support tab is actually useable, and there is addtional even harder hitting off map artillery. Add to that the bombs from planes being much more effective with much greater AOE and you have Steel Division.
Oh, and tanks that have suffered moral damage from artillery also fall back, so that your carefully organised defensive line can be completely eliminated by some off map artillery and an air strike.
So yeah, all the air and artillery spam of Red Dragon with more fragile units moving at 2/3rds the speed - plus nazis.

For me personally it failed to capture that fun factor of the Wargame series, both graphically and gameplay-wise. The unit selection was quite sparse, I wasn't keen on the battle stage system (A,B,C) which restricts which units you can use during certain phases of each match, and the graphics/explosion effects felt underwhelming and small.
Is it a bad game? Well no probably not, but it's alot slower paced and features less content and eye candy than the Wargame series, and for those reasons I didn't like it and have requested a refund.
Summary:
Underwhelming, but may appeal to fans of slower paced, more structured tactical gameplay.

Endless Sky is a 2D, space "sim" (Sim being used very lightly in this context) where you start with a ship, and do stuff to get better ships, which allow you to do more stuff to get more ships, etc, etc.
PROS:
1. This game is completely free, and doesn't have any sort of microtransactions. At all. AAA companies, take notes.
2. There is a very active community, both here on Steam and on the Github.
3. You can sink a lot of hours into flying your ship everywhere.
4. There is a story, if you're into that sort of thing.
5. Updates, while not *too* frequent, are influenced by the community. You can post an error on Steam or the Github, and if it's valid, it'll probably get patched in an update. They also sometimes have a lot of content. Generally, unstable releases have content, stable releases patch up the new content.
6. One of, if not the, easiest games to mod. You can very easily create a flying pizza ship stuffed with nukes. That spawn more nukes  (that home in!!!). And the nukes look like Ferraris. It can get really crazy, really fast, and it only takes a few minutes to do. You just need a text editor, and a sprite for your ship.
7. The story has a few different branches, and is really well-written.
However, all games have their downsides.
CONS:
1. Updates can take FOREVER to come out. Granted, you can compile a copy from GitHub, and see the progress, but compiling can mess up your saves if you don't know what you're doing. Or a feature is removed/changed.
2. It can be very repetitive with the same types of jobs, and the story missions generally consist of A) We need to defend this planet, B) We need you to escort this ship, and C) You need to blow this ship(s) up.
3. Only 1 complete story, with another about 1/2 done.
4. After completing the stories, there isn't too much to do, except try to dominate the galaxy. Don't get me wrong, it's fun to cover Earth in an endless tsunami of gatling gun shuttles, but it gets old after your unstoppable tide of DOOM SHUTTLES!!!! have conquered the galaxy. Six times over.
5. Your life is literally in the hands of RNGesus. If you get unlucky, you'll launch from a planet and get your ship plastered in tiny bits across half the planet below from the pirate dreadnought that decided to stalk you in orbit. While the other three pirate cruisers laugh at how stupid you are while eating the rest of your fleet for brunch.
Overall rating 9/10, while it lacks some content at the end of the game, it's a long, fun journey to get there, and has a lot of replayability.

Sleeping Dogs is a third-person RPG with a linear drama plot and a dash of comedy. It revolves around martial arts and gang activity in 2012 Hong Kong. It is essentially a gory Bruce Lee / Jet Li film.
First, the narrative. In Sleeping Dogs, you play as Wei Shen, an undercover cop. Wei has strong ties to the gangs of Hong Kong but is tasked with dismantling them from the inside. I think Wei could have been better written. His personality is confusing, as he flits from kind-hearted and honorable to an enormous prick. Occasionally, Wei will make decisions that do not make sense given the situation. The game itself has a long, linear story with several arcs. While occasionally overdramatic, it is surprisingly compelling. Many of the characters are beautifully written, making them easy to love or hate. While Wei doesn’t develop much, those close to him do. By the end of the plot, I was fully captivated. I recommend playing it primarily to experience the story. The side quests are unfortunately all simple favors or have basic, uninteresting designs, save a few exceptions.
Second, combat. Fighting is primarily hand-to-hand martial arts. Wei fights with a blend of Kung fu, MMA, and street tactics. Typically, you are hopping around within a group of enemies using fast and strong strikes, blocking, parrying, riposting, and grappling. This type of combat can easily become boring, but the developers put a lot of care into avoiding that. You can utilize a wide array of combos, more of which can be unlocked through various methods. In addition, Wei is able to incorporate much of the environment in fights. As usual with brawlers, some enemy types need to be dealt with in particular ways, forcing you to adjust your strategy. Wei and his enemies can also utilize different melee weapons. These do more damage than being unarmed but eliminate the ability to combo or parry, as well as become unusable after a number of strikes. Guns are also a part of the game, but they are rare outside of story missions. There is a decent range available, from pistols to automatic shotguns. The gunplay is rather clunky, but it is a small enough part of the game that I can forgive it. Weapons are very transient in Sleeping Dogs, requiring you to obtain them from enemies and disappearing during most cutscenes. Lastly, car-to-car combat is a ton of fun. Aiming out your window at an enemy engages bullet time, allowing you to shoot tires and drivers, causing their vehicles to flip and explode. There are no stealth mechanics in sleeping dogs.
Third, map design. The game takes place in Hong Kong, with four districts connected by highways. Each district represents a different leg of the story, and the difficulty and wealth of each scales accordingly. Exploring the districts is a lot of fun, and they vary enough to keep things interesting. Different shops and activities are distributed throughout, increasing in class with the wealth of the area. You can explore the entire map from the get-go, but most of your activities will be in one particular area at any given time.
Fourth, graphics. The game is very impressive, despite its age. The game is also fairly well optimized, with a decent variety of options.
Fifth, driving. I have mixed feelings about driving mechanics in Sleeping Dogs. Some cars inexplicably turn in increments of about fifteen degrees if you are accelerating, making them frustrating to drive. Others handle smoothly. Turning in general is somewhat clunky. That said, I was fairly used to the driving after a few hours of adjustment, after which it was decent fun. Motorcycles, by contrast, are thrilling to drive and handle really well, though they verge on over-responsive. Hijacking and fighting at high speeds works really well, and its thrilling. There is a great variety of vehicles available for purchase, increasing in performance and style as you move to wealthier areas. Street racing is a large part of Sleeping Dogs. Vehicles are ranked in classes, stratifying them according to performance. Each race has a designated class and type (either motorcycle or car), and the player must choose a suitable vehicle from their garage. I found car races to be typically fun and satisfying, while motorcycle races could be frustrating. Small parts of the terrain, unpredictable civilians, and flying clutter would constantly strike my motorcycle and take me from first to last place.
Sixth, DLC. The game can no longer be purchased without the DLC, so I will review them as part of it. There numerous small quest additions and outfits, in addition to two expansions. The first expansion, Nightmare in North Point, is more comedic than the base game and involves a gang member coming back from Hell with an army of undead for revenge. The second, Year of the Snake, is more serious, involving a terrorist group striking at the Chinese New Year. In this expansion, Wei is overtly a cop. Neither adds any new locations to the world, and both can be beaten in about three hours. I did not enjoy Nightmare at North Point, as the bulk of it was fighting a new type of enemy that could only be defeated in one particular way, making combat far less interesting. Year of the Snake was a bit more fun, involving your standard enemies. I think both were far too short, involved too little new content, and had very mediocre stories with no engaging characters. They were far lower quality than the base game. The rest of them are neat additions, though I wouldn’t have paid for them prior to bundling them in.
Because of the well-fleshed-out melee combat and engaging story, I am recommending this game. Few modern crime RPGs can boast the writing of Sleeping Dogs, and the enjoyable combat is icing on the cake. I had a great deal of fun riding around Hong Kong as a cop and a triad, and I got pretty roped into the story. I wish there was more to do after the story than just tiny side quests and activities, but I suppose I got a fair amount of gametime out of it already. Don’t play the two expansions unless you are starving for more Sleeping Dogs content, as they will leave a sour taste in your mouth after the very solid ending to the base game. Taking the story at my own pace, with roaming and side activities between missions, it took me about fourty hours to finish the game and under ten more to tack on the two expansions.

I'm writing this review upon completion of the Heavensward story, so no endgame content will be reviewed here.
Gameplay: 7/10
Honestly, if you have played one tab targeting mmo you've played them all.  They key differences that FFXIV, and say, WoW have are that:
FFXIV has a 2.5 second gcd, reducible with skill speed, as opposed to wow's 1 sec gcd
FFXIV makes up for this additional time by putting a greater emphasis on abilities that are off of the global cooldown, so in effect you get a very similar gameplay pacing once you get access to your ogcd abilities
FFXIV does not have talents, so the gameplay differences between one ninja and another are going to be minimal.
FFXIV tends to have more of a focus on a rotation/priority system rather than a proc/priority system.
So what it boils down to is that the games play very similarly.  It doesn't exactly innovate anywhere in this department, but it works, and feels decently rewarding.
The crafting system is one of the best I've seen in an mmo because it is an actual system, not just a press button get items task.  Same for the gathering system.
Story: 8/10
FFXIV is an MMO with a heavy emphasis on story.  You have to complete every quest of the main story line to actually get to endgame content as opposed to other mmos where its just level locked.  However, the story is pretty decent, not amazing, but decent.  If I were to have any complaints about the story it would be that you(the warrior of light) have copious amounts of impenetrable plot armor.
Pacing: 4/10
Probably the game's weakest point, to the point that I give it its own section.  The story, gameplay, and everything do not become interesting until around level 35-40 ish.  Up until that point, the game is paced painfully slowly.  For instance, your rotation as lancer has a grand total of 2 spells until about level 26, 1 if you don't care about a mere 10 potency increase, and this problem persists over other classes.
The story sends you on a lot of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥quests up until that point as well, to the point that the game makes jokes about it.  Then once you get to to 50, you get to do about 100 quests that give you practically no experience and are just there to advance the plot, and there is a fair amount of♥♥♥♥♥♥taking in these quests as well.  Heavensward, however, was interesting start to finish, so there is that to look forward to.
The game also requires you to do dungeons while leveling.  I'm not wholly against this, but this plays into the issue of the pre 40 pacing, there is a grand total of 1 healing class pre 30 since arcanists are counted as dps, so your q times are moronically long as dps.  Doing a string of quests at your own pace just to get a quest to do a dungeon, and then having to wait 20 minutes to find a party really breaks up the immersion and feel of the game.
Music: 9/10
is final fantasy has good music, nothing new under the sun.
Visuals: 8/10
The game is rather pretty.  Not much to say here.  The only potential downside is that particle effects can be rather overbearing in fights and make it hard to tell what's going on.
Overall:
About a 7/10, but if you can get past the pacing it goes to a 8-9/10 pretty quickly.
As an aside, there are a lot of complaints that the steam version gives people troubles, so you might want to get it through square's website instead.  It is also of note that you can't refund the game if you get it on steam unless you're able to download and install the game in under 2 hours.  That said, there is a free trial you can/should try.

I've been a long-time player of MMOs, most of which you've heard of and probably a few you haven't.  I started WoW early 2006 in the original game and played every expansion since.  At one time, I was among the top 50 internationally rated Alliance Trees.  Not a rookie, as these things go.
I just recently started FF14 and in the 140 hours or so played thus far, I must say - nice!  Polished, very few bugs, if any and thus far no great horking game-breakers at *all*.  I say "if any" because I'm starting to think that some of the 'bugs' I thought I encountered were just my unfamiliarity with the game, not bugs at all.  Nice environment, atmosphere, game mechanics, players - the whole shebang.  And you can have *every* class in one character, which means, of course, that I'm levelling the lot of them in lock-step.  It will take longer to level that way, but at any point I can pick and choose what suits me best at the moment or for the day.  It's a very nice feature, that.
You can, if you wish, rush a single 'toon to max, or play along at a leisurely pace, as you wish.  There are a set of 'tests' that you must pass before you can play a dungeon in any particular role (tank/heal/dps) - they're not hard, but they ensure that if you're in a dungeon, you know the basics of dungeon/party play, which greatly reduces the chance of newb mistakes.
The crafting is comprehensive and well put together - and *useful* which is a nice thing to have in crafting.  If I had to ask for anything, I would say the ability to craft using materials that are in your retainers' packs without having to summon them and withdraw it.
The combat mechanics are interesting and nice to watch while at the same time not being onerous or overly difficult to learn or use.  That's very nice when you can literally be a healer in one moment, a rogue in the next, and a tank in the  next.  The switches aren't disorienting - you can pick up a new class/role in a minute or two even if you haven't played it in awhile.  Yet the abilities are suitably nuanced that there is a definite skill level involved - you better you know your class, the more effective you are at playing it.
Actually, having played this, I'm done with other MMOs for awhile - probably at least a few years.  This one is going to be entertaining for a *long* time, I think.  I'm glad I bought it, and I think you will be, too.  Highly recommended.

Overall, I think this really could be a breakthrough in WW2 Wargaming. However:
- I would love to see more units per card (+50 or 75% maybe). In 4vs4 map size I felt I had not enough forces to reasonably "cover" the front, and after loosing some units I found it too hard in getting my way through the battlefield.
- More balance in unit limitations. In the Normandy campaing, Allied armies had a superiority in firepower and supplies. On the other hand, German tanks and armoured vehicles were fewer in number but generally better armed.
- Terrain accidents improvement. I know this game is based on the Normandy flat valleys, but I also would love to see more diversity in terrains such as hills and dales.
- More realism (or maybe is Quality?) in audio effects: Explosions, firing, motor roaring, tracked vehicles across country, etc.
- Offload HERE option for transports as in the Wargame Series.
- Morale system improvement. Maybe using some modifiers per Division, where the elite SS Divisions have less morale penalties, since their courage was more fanatical. And the rest of the Divisions more dependant on a (bigger) Command units' aura of influence. Just a couple of ideas.
- Please give us some modding tools! It really would be too much asking for a map editor, units editor?

summary: CoD:MW2 is a sharp as hell shooter, providing a very fun, action packed single player campaign with plenty of story twist and mind blowing moments. in addition, MW2 has a very fun, alive multiplayer. this being in despite being full of hackers and players who exploit weapons and features. All of this, while looking great graphically and performing even better.
Shooter: One of the most refined shooters out there MW2's mechanics feel really smooth and easy to control with a little bit of adjustment. with this, the game never feels like you are fighting the controls, allowing you to git gud in multiplayer, enjoy the story of singleplayer or just have fun shooting bad guys.
Singleplayer: without spoiling anything, Throughout the camapign the story unfolds back and forth through the eyes of two soldiers, "Roach" and Ramirez. Ramirez is apart of a US Rangers squad and fights the public war on the frontlines. "Roach" on the other hand is apart of a British special forces group who fights the secret war, fighting towards learning the truth behind the events. both characters go to various locations throughout the world, The story has plenty of action, mind blowing twist and awesome characters, all working well with the highly bang bang shot'em up style of gameplay.
Multiplayer: MW2's multiplayer has a lot of issues, the weapons are imbalanced, hackers are a common sight, players exploit cheap methods to get kills etc but despite it all, the sharp mechanics and shooting pulls through and makes the multiplayer still a lot of fun. on top of that, the multiplayer is still alive after over 7 years of other cods being released.
Performance: MW2's performance is great, there are plenty of settings that can be toggled and the game is made really well. even back when I was running this game on Intel HD graphics and a dual core cpu, I still got 60fps on the default settings with anti aliassing turned off. with that, just about anyone can play this game.
Graphics: This games graphics are sharp and stands as one of the best looking games of the time with highly detailed models, textures and environments, complemented by the very well made and well used effects, shaders and lighting.

This game has an interesting mix of slow-paced reading and contemplation mixed with very intense encounters that come on very quickly. I think that's the biggest problem with the core mechanic: the switch is too fast. There's not enough warning when danger is around the corner. You might be peacefully transporting cargo around the galaxy for 30 minutes and then enter a low-security system and be almost immediately destroyed - and there's no way to know exactly which systems are dangerous in advance. So your death seems random and unfair. There are these two fundamentally different game experiences, so the join between them is very important to get right.
Beyond that, whether you like this game depends on whether you like the core gameplay of these kind of games. I find it very grindy and quickly boring. I don't see how it could be significantly improved without changing to a system like Star Control II (1992) where the universe is clearly dynamic and things happen regardless of what you do. That game is also an example of a good transition between the fast and slow subgames.
It has a lot of potential but at this stage there are many other 2D space games that do the same thing but better.

This is a great game, not awesome but great.
I have a few minor hold-ups--namely, I didn't like having to use doors or dancing around squares for combat, it felt like gaming the system or just abusing the engine.  And, near the end, the puzzles started to get annoying--especially the timing ones.
Those minor quibbles aside, I loved this game.  The character creation, the atmosphere, the older-style combat system.  It is a bit odd, as it seems to largely be following the Ultima Underworld / Eye of the Beholder style of game, and I was never a fan of those games back in the day.  Be that as it may, it was a refreshing step back to the games of old and it certainly shows what a modernized version of those kind of games would be like.
I love making my own party of characters.  I love the game being largely agnostic to my party, so as that I can make what I want the the role-playing takes place in my imagination.  There was enough variety of creatures, and almost perfect sense of increasing difficulty in all challenges, and just enough loot to both have you desperately never having just quite enough and yet never leaving you without what you needed to continue.  Especially the having to choose between treasures several times not only forces you to make painful choices but also rewards specialization in your party.
I highly recommend this game.

The story itself is really interesting, but it's a little short and, again, always gives you essentially the same ending, which is also infuriating.
You can't talk to other people other than Emily, even though you have a "buddy list" that shows you people you could potentially talk to, but can't... since you can only talk to Emily, ever.
The pros:
Honestly, as many cons as there are, it IS a free to play story adventure game and that is always fun. As mentioned above, the story is also fairly well put together and fun to go through on your first try.  I feel like this game has a ton of potential, and if the developers ever decide to do anything with it (like add more characters, more dialogue options, allow you to type things yourself, etc.), I feel this game would be freaking amazing and well worth it to play. As of now, though it is just... kind of depressing and sad.

I haven't been an active player for quite some time now, so I can't comment on the current expansion: Stormblood but I realized I hadn't left a review for FF14:ARR yet and it was something I meant to do. This review will not be organized and will be sheerly an off the cuff commentary from me.
Let me preface this by saying: I quit playing.
So why did I unsub? Simply put, I wasn't spending enough time on the game and did not have the $15 ish a month anymore to pay the subscription fees. When your budget gets tighter, you have to make decisions like this. It was not because FF14 is not an excellent game in it's own right.
Simply put, FF14 is everything a modern MMORPG should be. Yoshida and his team played many other MMOs, both F2P and paid, like World of Warcraft and Yoshida avidly took down notes from his experiences (while he mostly admitted he played free trial periods for paid MMOs). He also did alot of reading on forums, blogs and other sources to assess why players play these games, what they like about them and what keeps them coming back -- and then he did his very best to apply everything he learned to FF14:ARR.
And in many ways, his research and effort paid off gloriously.
FF14:ARR offers a huge and immensely impressive world. Tons of quests. Lots of distinct classes with unique flavor to them. There are more than enough dungeons, and they add more regularly. FF14 has a ton of raid content, too, and again they add more all the time.
The one thing Yoshida said alot was a demand for constant, content rich updates. And to spite the fact they admit it is a struggle at times, they soldier on and keep delivering huge content patches at a solid pace, and Yoshida has been very forthcoming many times, about what is coming and when. He knows communication is very important to making a successful game and a passionate community.
One of the most striking things about FF14 is that it has a "main story line" which starts off very slow but quickly becomes like reading an excellent book. I found myself feeling strongly about the cast of characters, from the allies that I loved to the villains I hated. Squaresoft has made their living making games that tell a story and FF14 puts this on grand display like, in my opinion, never before.
The music is also a very important feature, that again, displays Squaresoft's years and years of talent and experience. Like any other game they've ever made, there is a rich and expansive soundtrack. When you fight a boss, there is actual BOSS music that begins playing as you pull the boss, many raid bosses have their very own, unique themes .. infact, almost all of them do.
Something else that this game does that really struck me, is that in most cases (but oddly, not all), it does not ask you to GUESS when it comes to avoiding enemy attacks, AOEs, "skill shots" and randomly target'd attacks. 90% of the time you will see a VERY clear, bright orange shape appear on the ground that is telling you:  "If you stand in this, you are gonna take alot of damage, MOVE." The orange zones appear PRIOR to the attack and give you plenty of time to get clear before the spell or ability actually goes off. I really liked this over other MMORPGs that often ask you to guess and sometimes, even if you think you're out of it, you still aren't and get hit. FF14:ARR is very clear about where, when and how big, and is very precise in it's warnings which helps alot in the games very frequent and very complicated/active raids & fights late game. This makes it so that even if you are new to a fight, you can easily see where you need to move to stay safe most of the time.
FF14:ARR was also designed better than most other MMORPGs in how it teaches a new player to play. While this was not necessary for me, having spent half my life playing MMORPGs, I was impressed by how it's done. Dungeons and raids start off with simpler mechanics, and get progressively harder the higher in level you go, but they do so at a very comfortable pace. FF14:ARR also does not forgive mistakes as easily as other MMORPGs. When you mess up, you will die and sometimes, you will wipe your whole group. So as you level, you will learn this and hopefully, it will mold you into an aware and capable player by the end.
So, I've talked alot about what impresses me about this game, so let's take a look at more of the reasons why I unsubbed.
First and foremost, the subscription fee. There is NOTHING WRONG or unusual about the $15 a month charge. FF14:ARR piles on quality in excess, they have every right to charge for a game of this quality, furthermore, as Yoshida said, subs ensure constant and reliable money flow to keep the content and quality coming.
The subscription fee comes into it because I have to justify the cost in my budget, especially with my budget becoming tighter around the time I unsubbed. To justify the cost, I have to spending enough time on the game that I feel the money is worth the sacrifices to pay it.
So why wasn't I spending enough time on FF14:ARR to justify the cost?
The most important reasons here, are that simply put, I was very heavily into other games and found myself wanting to play other games more. WoW had recaptured my soul and unlike FF14, I have been playing WoW since Vanilla, so there is a much larger emotional investment in WoW than in FF14, both in the sense of accomplishment and in my commitment to my characters.
But why did FF14:ARR not just push some of these other games aside?
There were several factors at play here. Firstly, leveling is very time consuming in FF14 for the first time. (Leveling other job classes is much faster.) It felt so slow and time consuming at times, I found myself burning out and wanting to do something else. It felt like WoW back in Vanilla or TBC. If I hadn't been into other games at this time, this wouldn't have detered me but when you have other options, and something is wearing on your patience, you tend to move on instead of continuing.
So why is leveling so slow? Because, simply put, there is no way to speed it up. You MUST complete the main storyline quests, and do ALL OF THE CONTENT, even past raids and stuff, a long the way and while those experiences are all impressive in their ways, being forced into doing them all wore me down.
If I could have just spam-ran dungeons up to the level cap, I would have hit the level cap in no time. I am a dungeon and raid person, while the story was amazing, it was just "in my way" to get to what I really wanted to do, which was max level content.
If the story had been somehow optional, I have NO DOUBT I would have come back and done it inbetween doing end-game content, because I would have wanted to see how it turned out. I'm still tempted to read up on the story somewhere, and keep up even though I am not even playing.
The other issue that stopped me, is the core gameplay for classes. The game either throws too many, or too few buttons. You either have long, elaborate combos you have to repeat over and over, or you mash the same button alot. FF14:ARR feels very binary and unrewarding since it's just repeating a pattern over and over, or hitting one button, waiting for something else to happen that gives you a brief break in the boredom.
WoW has always thrived on it's push/pull give/take system where you generate resources and have procs, which you must manage and use wisely moment to moment, to maximize your performance. FF14:ARR just seems to try to make up for a lack of true complexity, by throwing a ton of buttons at you instead, and it just wasn't appealing to me.
I tried many of the classes, trying to find something that excited me and just never did.
-------------
FF14:ARR had 5million+ players a year or so ago and I'm sure it's still growing.
If you've read this far, you're really commited, or really bored. Suffice to say, FF14:ARR is free to play up to level 30. Try it for yourself, if you get to 30 and love it, you'll love it all the way.

TLDR; It's fun, don't compare it to dark souls and your good. Beware the♥♥♥♥♥♥camera.
UPDATE: After making my way through the game and reaching the second to last level and having over 20 hours logged, the game crashed and i lost my save. Now i have to start from the begining. Needless to say, i am extremely upset by this occurance.
Fair warning, I don't have loads of experience with souls style games, so this is really a first for me. I cut my teeth on the souls genre with Lord's of the fallen, after it left a bad taste in my mouth I went for the surge, it's style, setting and feel captured my attention.
Before I identify what's wrong with the game, I want to take a moment and explain a glaw I have seen with alot off the other reviews I have read. Either they praise the game and don't call out any of it's flaws or they mercilessly compare it to dark souls, the king of this genre. Neither of those perspectives are fair to the game at all. The first thing to know is that unlike dark souls, this game does not emphasize the boss fight. Rather, levels are peppered with enemies that are challenging and require good timing, skill, and a bit of tactical thinking to take down. Comparatively, bosses are just larger, spongier, and stronger versions of the same mobs you fight throughout the level. Second, it's a lot slower paced that dark souls. It rewards slow, methodic thinking and the use of unorthodox tactics. You will be rewarded often for thinking outside of the box. The game is also much smaller than dark souls. The maps are far less expansive and vast and at times that is where the challenge comes from. But considering the game takes place in an industrial center, I think it's very fitting. My point is that the game is not dark souls so comparing them is hardly worth the time.
That said, I have spent a fair amount of time with the game, and comparing it to deck13's previous attempt at this genre which, in my opinion, is damn near unplayable at times due to camera issues, overly cramped spaces, geometry problems, and a general lack of direction. The surge doesn't suffer from those issues to as great an extent as Lord's of the fallen. While I desperately wish I could say that all the aforementioned problems do not exist in this title, that is sadly not the case. While the game is good, I overall would recommend it to anyone who enjoys a challenge, rage quiting at 3am, and anyone who is a fan of the souls genre, it does have glaring issues.
Camera movement and perspective:
this is perhaps the biggest issue that I have with the game. 99% of the times that I have died I find that it's usually my fault. Either I am not prepared for an area or I made an error in battle. Unfortunately, that other 1% really sticks in my♥♥♥♥♥ I can't help but get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off when I die because of the field of view or the angle that the camera is at and I simply couldn't react. This was not particularly a problem at the beginning of the game when things are more mellow while still being challenging. During the first boss fight it became a small issue and I quickly learned that you should not lock on to the legs of the boss while attacking. During the second boss fight I had the same issue but to a larger degree as the boss is highly mobile and has multiple phases of attack. Then there is the third boss. Arguably the hardest of all 5 bosses in the game. The camera in this section is so ♥♥♥♥ED. UP. it is rediculous that testers and designers allowed this to pass inspection and test plays. The camera zooms out because of the scale of the boss, affording you presuous little sight of your character. This makes movement difficult and the entirety of the boss battle feels cheap, particularly when you die.
Combat: there is no nice way to say it. Combat gets repetitive when it works. Though rare, I have had a hand full of instances where my attacks fail to chain properly despite my repeated input for more damage with the rappid tapping of the mouse button, leaving my character to stand like an idiot and neeldessly take a hit. But I also think that this may be an issue with my mouse from time to time.
Now that I have criticized the game fairly for what it fails to deliver, I think a proper run down of what it does well is in order.
Graphics: the game looks amazing. There is plenty of fidelity to all of the models, geometry and textures look infinatly better than they did in Lord's of the fallen. The over all feel of the game is astounding and reminds me slightly of Titanfall.
Sound: the sounds are spot in my opinion. Hitting unarmored flesh sounds like the most painful thing in the world, while armor sounds sturdy and gives a solid report when hit. The sound track is also wonderful, setting the mood well and giving a since of aw. Unfortunately, this is a double edged sword as I fail to be surprised by the enemy waiting around the cordner when the music suddenly goes from being barely noticeable to in my face.
Gameplay: gameplay is, on the whole, very good. Not only are the combat systems of slicing specific limbs off of your email for their precious precious loot amazingly gruesome, but they are rewarding. The game never fails to make me feel like I am progressing. Whether it be farming parts for upgrades, trying to collect new gear, or making my way back to previous sections after gathering upgrades and abilities only to find a few new challenging enemies and a while other half of the map I didn't know existed prior. The mechanics of the game are exicuted perfectly in my opinion.
Story: okay. This one is a tuffy. I think the developers played dark souls, saw that the story was hard to access and took that as a staple of the genre. Unfortunately, their exicution on this is Rocky, but not bad. I had the story figured out pretty early on after listening to some audio logs and (I'm not as ahsamed as I probably should be for this) looking up the ending on YouTube. Turns out there are two endings that people overlook as being to similar. But what I've learned through my play through of the game is this: their story is hard to access because of how subtle they are with it. For example: both endings are pretty much the same EXCEPT for one major factor, the diolog at the end of the cutscene. Since watching the ending prematurely u have gathered an appreciation for every since gle small detail such as the music in the ops center that plays on loop for ever and ever, it's done on purpose. Listening to the lyrics and beating the game will make you slap your forehead in realization as to what details where in front of you the whole time. While their method of story telling is different is most certenly is not bad by any means. It is very well constructed and I think does an amazing job at portraying a setting that we have seen many times before.
In summation: the game has problems. Deck13 is clearly trying their damnedest at making the genre more diverse with interesting titles that expand on the possibilities. Unfortunately, innovation comes at a price and that price happens to be their♥♥♥♥♥♥camera work. Does that make the game bad? Probably. Full disclosure, I'm hooked on the story even though I know the ending and I just keep coming back. All humor aside, the game is more than playable, just occasionally frustrating. It is a compelling title with loads of potential and after spending enough time with it you might be thinking that it was wasted potential. And you would probably be right. Deck13 seems to only be able to deliver a partial package. Bethesda does the same thing and people enjoy the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of their titles though so maybe it will work for them. Only time will tell.
I personally love the game, story, and challenges it has to offer and desperately hope there is a sequel. I think that people need to stop comparing it to dark souls, allow the game to stand on its own merrits and judge it fairly so the next time we get a game from them it's perfect.

~~~Forward~~~
I don't typically do reviews, however this game having "mixed" reviews does not accurately convey the quality of this product.  Due to this, I wanted to throw in my two cents in the attempt to add my voice to the sea of criticisms to this game.
~~~ END Forward ~~~
~~~ TL;DR ~~~
The game uses similar thought processes and logic to a Soulsbourne title however, like the PS4 game Nioh, uses different mechanics to showcase the "puzzle logic" Soulsbourne titles use to make their combat engaging.  The difference with The Surge is two-fold.  The first is it follows "Lords of the Fallen" from the same developer that was a carbon copy of Dark Souls with literal poor mechanics, the second is the mechanics of "The Surge" are close enough to a Soulsbourne game (unlike Nioh) that people misinterpret their own misunderstanding of the game's mechanics with 'bad mechanics'
~~~ End TL;DR ~~~
~~~ Graphics & Performance ~~~
PROS - Stunning visuals, modern showcase of technical ability, could have been made by a AAA studio. Sound design, animations, and polish are all here to create an immersive experience.
CONS - I have engaged one bug on an exo-lift that caused me to have to restart, and some exeucte animations can cause slow-down or hangs before completing.
~~~ End Graphics & Performance ~~~
~~~ Level Design ~~~
The levels are inter-connected in a way that is reminscent of Dark Souls but not as good as that one.  Plenty of secrets, some of which will require you to come back to the zones later in the game when you have had some progression.  The over-all progression from level to level is seamless and the well made visuals align with a very cohesive exploration your first play through.
~~~ End Level Design
~~~ Combat ~~~
The combat is engaging.  You have a vertical and horizontal attack.  You can create combos by combining these attacks with each other up to a 4th attack ( Ex, RB / RT / RT / RB - 4 attacks ).  Each weapon can have different attacks - but not all do.  The dodge mechanics is engaging and the counter mechanic works as intended.
CONS - The problem with the counter/block mechanics and dodge mechanic is there are some units that have undodgeable ( no invulnerability frame ) or unblockable ( you need to dodge/jump counter ) and there is no way of knowing which attacks are undodgeable or unblockabel without being screwed by this via trial and error.  This is very frustrating for a blind playthrough.  The mechanics themselves work well though.
Also, the stats are ambiguous and you have no way of discerning what each stat actually does.  There is some intended obfuscation here which is not necessary or needed in this genre.
~~~ Story ~~~
Typical cryptic soulsbourne story with a hint of deus ex machina and cyber dystopia.   You can take it or leave it as it's pretty much completely optional
CONS - Some of the sidequests are very poor in the "work vs. reward" for the sidequests.  Also without any codex to track quests it can become easy to forget about them.
~~~ End Story ~~~
~~~ Summary ~~~
Give this game a chance.  It is well worth your time if you like the puzzle logic -style of a Soulsbourne game.  It's subtly different and the setting is engaging enough to give it a shot considering it's not the full AAA price even at full price it is worth the buy in.  It has a demo which transfers your time to the full purchase and then you can get another two hours of the game before refunding it if you dislike it.  Very good value propisition.

While this game is not ideal, if you are interested in souls-like games and sci-fi then it is worth a try. It does not do either particularly well, but it does not do either particularlly bad. Go in with low expectations; be pleasently surprised. Go in with high expectations; be dissapointed.
In terms of game play, it is a souls-like game where the main (yet, truly minor) deviation comes from the combat system. Instead of heavy and weak attacks, there is horizontal and vertical. To complement this, you can target specific parts of the body. While playing, you will not really care too much about horizontal or vertical, instead opting for specific combos. As far as the targeting system, you target the weak points. This variation is rather minor.
In terms of execution of a souls like, the game comes up bland once again. There are only 5 bosses, but you do get to learn there moves and patterns. And they are fair, for the most part. The combat pace is closer to bloodborne, and the game does require a few fights against multiple opponents. But, you soon become comfortable after you learn the moves and what to watcch out for. Overall, decent combat. Not great, not really memorable. But it fixes the souls itch for awhile.
As for the sci-fi setting, the game is rather straightforward. The only problem here is everything is just given to you, instead of dark souls which only shows you a piece of the entire picture. That is to say, do not expect to have a dark souls like intrigue with this game. On a dissapointing note, the sidequests very rarely have satisfying conclusions.
But if you want to play a souls-like game, and like sci-fi, it is worth a try.

If you love the wargame series then you will love this game. If you are a fan of RTS and WW2 then you will love this game. Can't wait for the full release, already recommending to friends so we can team play.

Having played the wargame series since it's first iteration, I have to say I like the direction the developers have taken their game. For new players, if you like your historical RTS with some realism and depth, this is the game for you.
For those who came from the Wargame series, here are some points that I have found:
Plus:
+ Frontline system feels like a natural development from the sector system. It forces you to form a coherent frontline instead of holding arbitrary sectors in the previous games.
+ The frontline system forces more coördination in teamgames. I found that its easy to leave gaps in the frontlines between teammembers that can be exploited.
+ Better looking maps, they look more natural now instead of the artificial and symmetrical maps in the previous games.
+ Better ground - air interaction. Air is more useful now since ground anti air alone isn't enough to stop planes, you actually need your own planes.
+ New deck system forces some more historical builds instead of optimized decks.
+ The slower pace means that controlling roads are more important to quickly move your units. It also forces you to plan ahead, since you can't race your units from one side of the map to the other as easy. It's also more rewarding to achieve a decisive breakthrough, since it takes longer to reinforce the frontlines.
+ The healthbars have been removed and replaced by a more in depth moral system.
+ They removed the fuel micro. Now you only need to keep an eye an ammo. In theory the fuel micro in the previous game added depth, but in practice it was just unnecessary micro that limited your playstyle too much.
+ Lot of other small quality of life improvents. Specifically the line of sight tool and the ability to give orders in the deployment phase.
Min
- Deployment phase could be a bit longer know that you have the ability to give orders in this phase.
- It's hard to make a comeback if you lose early momentum. Your opponents army will get stronger and stronger without real incentive to attack, forcing you to attack with a smaller army.
- Removed the ability to reinforce depleted squads and I haven't found the option to merge squads yet.

summary: CoD:MW2 is a sharp as hell shooter, providing a very fun, action packed single player campaign with plenty of story twist and mind blowing moments. in addition, MW2 has a very fun, alive multiplayer. this being in despite being full of hackers and players who exploit weapons and features. All of this, while looking great graphically and performing even better.
Shooter: One of the most refined shooters out there MW2's mechanics feel really smooth and easy to control with a little bit of adjustment. with this, the game never feels like you are fighting the controls, allowing you to git gud in multiplayer, enjoy the story of singleplayer or just have fun shooting bad guys.
Singleplayer: without spoiling anything, Throughout the camapign the story unfolds back and forth through the eyes of two soldiers, "Roach" and Ramirez. Ramirez is apart of a US Rangers squad and fights the public war on the frontlines. "Roach" on the other hand is apart of a British special forces group who fights the secret war, fighting towards learning the truth behind the events. both characters go to various locations throughout the world, The story has plenty of action, mind blowing twist and awesome characters, all working well with the highly bang bang shot'em up style of gameplay.
Multiplayer: MW2's multiplayer has a lot of issues, the weapons are imbalanced, hackers are a common sight, players exploit cheap methods to get kills etc but despite it all, the sharp mechanics and shooting pulls through and makes the multiplayer still a lot of fun. on top of that, the multiplayer is still alive after over 7 years of other cods being released.
Performance: MW2's performance is great, there are plenty of settings that can be toggled and the game is made really well. even back when I was running this game on Intel HD graphics and a dual core cpu, I still got 60fps on the default settings with anti aliassing turned off. with that, just about anyone can play this game.
Graphics: This games graphics are sharp and stands as one of the best looking games of the time with highly detailed models, textures and environments, complemented by the very well made and well used effects, shaders and lighting.

If this game had multiple people to talk to, or even just branching paths in the main story. Also, there are certain segments of this game between chatting sessions that you have NO control over at all. The main character makes some pretty dumb decisions, but they are not changeable since they are written into the script.
The second reason this game fails is due to the lack of caring about the characters. In the end of the game, events transpire, and you are expected to feel bad for a character. Except, there isnt really a reason to. You talk to her once a year over the course of like, 5 years. I'm sure the ending would've had a greater impact if these sequences were longer, but they aren't and thus the ending lacks the impact that was intended.
To conclude this review, I will say this: I really enjoy the concept of this game and it could succeed if it had better writing behind it, and more player freedom. I REALLY want to see more chat games in the future, as this game was a really interesting experience even if I didn't enjoy it that much.
Final Score: 4/10

TL:DR: Good game, and a solid MMO, close knit community and very welcoming to new players. Good on the PvE content end, and alright on the PvP content end. Also a bunch of RP available if that's your cup of tea.
PROS:
+ No P2W, at all.
+ Good looking NPCs and PCs, with a lot of customization.
+ Character models and animations are top quality.
+ The armor looks amazing, and the glamour and dyes systems makes everything even better.
+ Very friendly and welcoming community, not a lot of toxicity can be found.
+ High population, it being the second biggest MMO at the time!
+ Class fantasy is extremely well done. (Also you can be all classes in one character!)
+ Story is great! And the dungeons and raids are fun, with them being integrated into the story, and having unique and fun mechanics.
+ You can get a Moogle Costume! 10/10
+ 8 men and 24 men raids! 8 men trials, and 4 men dungeons! Content, content EVERYWHERE!
CONS:
- High GCD, you don't notice it at higher levels, but at lower levels it can become a pain.
- Early leveling is a bit of a mess and a pain, the game starts to pick up at around level 30, when the story gets interesting and you unlock your Job.
- Some class rotations can be straight up boring, but to be honest that's more of a personal opinion.
- Most content is gated behind MSQ (Main Story Quests) which can be quite stressing at times.
- No AddOn support.
- And lastly, it's subscription based, while for me this is a pro, because it ensures quality, and quantity of updates and content, I can see why for some it could be a problem, which is completely understandable.
Now, for the long version... Well, where do I start? Maybe by telling you how I ended up in this game to begin with.
Before FFXIV:
I've been playing World of Warcraft for about 7 to 8 years, since I was a small kid. My first game ever was Warcraft 1, my second Warcraft 2, and my third Warcraft 3, so It was no surprise that I ended up falling in love with World of Warcraft... However, I had been feeling burned out, the game is great, and still my favorite, but I was starting to notice it's age.
As mainly an MMO player, this kind of sucked, A LOT... I had given this game years of my life, and I was falling out of love with it. I was no longer a noob, and I knew everything, the sense of discovery was gone, my feeling of being a Hero banished.
Discovering FFXIV:
A friend recommended me FFXIV during this period, (I had played it at launch, but we know how that went.) However he explained to me what ARR (A Realm Reborn) had done, and how HW (Heavensward) made the game even better, and with SB(Stormblood) coming out, now was the best time to start.
I'm gonna be deadly honest, I hated this game for the first few levels, but once I reached around level 30 or so, the game started to come around, and honestly I fell in love. The sense of exploration and the feeling of being a Hero WoW had given me years before had returned. I felt at home, now it also helped that I made some very good friends and met people and a Free Company (basically a Guild) that made me on of their own as soon as I joined. I enjoyed my time.
After FFXIV:
To this day I still play WoW, but FFXIV has become my new main MMO, it's given me experiences I couldn't find anywhere else, and being the Warrior of Light is more fun than I thought. I've played countless FF games before, but had never tried my hand at their MMOs (FFXI and FFXIV), least to say, I'm glad I finally got down to playing one, because I think I've found my second home.
I know this a bit of a cheesy and a complete MESS of a review, one that isn't really that good, but I just wanted to give my Opinions and thoughts on the game, honestly, it's not for everyone, but I would at least give this game the benefit of the doubt and try it. Thanks for reading, and have fun in your adventures!

Overall, a really enjoyable game and well worth the subscription fee.

TL;DR: A bad Dark Souls addicts' last resort for a quick fix but nothing more.
Is it a good game? No. Is it a bad game? Also no.
My initial draw to this was, as for many, it being built off the Souls formula. However, it lacks the refinement of it's inspiration.
Part of me wants to love this game and another wants to hate it so I'm sitting on the edge of whetheror not to reccomend it.
For those who love the Souls formula and need more of it, have at it. This game, while I've not necessarily enjoyed it to the extent I have other games in the niche this attempts to fill, does satiate my desire for more of these types of games.
For those unfamilliar with the Souls formula, leave this game alone. The story is mediocre, the combat is okay, and the level design ranges from acceptable to awful. I would offer that the only real draw this game has for me anymore is sthe world aestheic.
Overall it feels like a game whose designers saw Dark Souls and thought "people love this super hard game, so lets make a game that is hard" without realizing what subtlety made those games work. The Souls series punish mistakes, reward observation and patience while creating a world that is deep and intuitive to explore. The Surge however, in my opinion, seems to ignore observation in favor of blind surprise, favor difficulty for the sake of frustrsarion rather than catharsis and punish exploration and curiosity for the same aforementioned favor of difficulty alone.
While the game isn't intrinsically as difficult as other games it will be compared to, it is that the application of this difficulty that is at fault. Fights in The Surge lack the fluidity and nuance that makes these struggles worthwhile, and the environments feel as if they are setting you up for failure rather than giving repercussions for poor spatial awreness. So while I applaud the effort in trying to capture the essence of what made an astounding and difficult series what it was and how hard it must be to do so, I cannot recommend it to anyone who doesn't have a feverish Souls addiction.
