Using the frontline mechanic with a progressing combat phases system and very distinct divisions in a time period where mobile warfare ruled supreme yet was still in it's infancy, Steel Division: Normandy 1944 adds a well calculated and diverse strategy game where you must move your offense wisely and supported while desperately defending against the enemy with many possible tricks up your sleeve. Shrubs, crops, buildings, roads, ammunition and fuel add variables, complications, and advantages to your strategy. The best I could describe this game in its current state is near if not already perfect. I can comftorably say that this is one of the best strategy games ever made. If you want this compared to Wargame, I'd say it hardly stands up to it.

Really enjoying this so far, even in the Beta with only 2 maps / 4 divisions released. As someone who loves but often stuggles with the pace of Wargame: Red Dragon, I'm finding Steel Division plays a little 'slower' -- in part of course due to the fact that WW2 vehicles / aircraft are a lot slower than modern military equipment. I prefer the somewhat more deliberate pace of SD'44. Units seem to survive longer; infantry seem less 'squishy' than in Wargame.
Really like the dynamic front-line and the fact that you no longer have to cap territories with Command Vehicles. Love the phased "A,B,C" development of the combat, which makes for some interesting decisions / trade offs in building your decks. And love that the decks are based on historical divisions.
Overally, Beta is very impressive and have high hopes that the full-release is going to be a fantastic game, every bit a worthy successor to the excellent Wargame series.

I really didn't expect much going into Sleeping Dogs and my expectations were very low. To my surprise however, this game is very good and I love it alot. Probably one of my favorite games of all time to be honest. In my heart I wanna give this game a 9-10/10 but I think this game deserves an 8/10 due to some issues and I think normal people would give this a 7-8 out of 10. The problems with Sleeping dogs is that the ai is really easy to kill and you aren't gonna be challenged too much. The main problem is that the story felt way to short and anticlimatic. I was really hyped for more missions but the game kinda just ended when I wanted more. Sleeping Dogs does have a lot of Pros however. First, the combat is really satifying and if you just wanna kill things, this is a good choice. Animations feel satifying and you feel as if you are getting stronger and combat gets more fun the more you play. The atmosphere and enviorment is aesthetically pleasing and venturing through hong kong street lights and crowds of people looks interesting and pretty. The radio stations, music, and catonese that people in hong kong speak also adds a lot to the experiance. You feel like you are in Hong Kong and the developers did very good job unlike other games where everyone speaks just english or whatever. I do find that the main strength of Sleeping Dogs is the characters and story. You like and get attached to some characters and hate the guts of others which creates a tear of trust for both the player and Wei Shen. I found Wei Shen to be a charming protagnist. The story is also good and the earlier mentioned tear of trust in the story causes a lot of build up in the story. The ending however doesn't really take advantage of this tension and it's anticlimatic. After finishing the game, I felt as if I wasn't finished but I feel like that in a lot of games when I finish them so interpret that as you please. I just wished the main story was longer and the ending was better, then I would give this game a 9/10 or maybe even higher. If you are into cop movies, or kung fu movies then give this a shot. I'd also wait for a sale before buying. Even though I gave the game an 8/10 I still highly recommend Sleeping Dogs.

has an interesting premise that has not been done before in a personal computer game. The ambiance is very
-esque, while the combat reminds me of parry techniques in
and
. The premise is between two forces, one good, and one evil. The knight in armor, Tom the Cat, is the main protagonist while the turkey Mealagris is the main antagonist. You go through rooms of a castle with doors that are shut on a quest to find all the key masters. After defeating the hardest enemy type, the key masters, new doors in the castle open.
However, there are two main drawbacks to this. The first drawback is there is no mini-map nor in-game map, nothing to collect and no loot. This is a survival-action game with hordes of enemies that appear out of portals with turkeys and other enemies that replicate themselves. The second major drawback is the difficulty spike. Until you make it outside the walls and underground of the castle, the game resets you from the beginning to start from permadeath. However, once you finally make it outside the castle walls, there are two checkpoints in which the game does save your progress.
The gameplay is simple. You enter waves of turkeys that track you down much like zombies along with mage ducks and the key masters. You have the opportunity to refill on ammo at blue and red pillars of stone. Ironically, there is no control scheme layout provided in-game, but by default, E is the action button to refill ammo while the left-mouse is used to parry and strike the sword. Q allows you to heal which is refilled after a certain amount of hitpoints to enemies are dealt. Healing regenerates slowly, so you will want to refill on the stunning trap which releases a trap that looks like dynamite that glows purple, best used when you can escape enemies and in all key masters within it who kneel where you can attack them more efficiently.
R releases this which also sometimes kills nearby enemies. Otherwise, go to the other stone pillar to refill on arrows, the max limit is forty arrows at once, and only twenty of the other can be held at once. You receive currency after sword fighting through the turkeys. Refilling each separate ammo type cost one thousand currency which I do not know how it is measured. Running away from groups of enemies is efficient and parrying, sword fighting works well.
Enemy variety is scarce. The primary threat is not the key masters, but the mages that respawn all enemies. The strategy I used to get to the final boss fight was I took down the key masters in the group without attacking anyone else. Then, after the key master is defeated by stunning them, immediately use your sword once the key master has knelt, then go for any mages if there are any. Finally, go for all the other turkeys since they are the weakest, so the best strategy is to go for the most formidable out of enemies to the least degree of threat. I wish there was more enemy variety. However, the mages make up for the lack of variety.

A peculiar game with absurdist humour. Which in my opinion is its main redeeming quality.
Gameplay:
You play as a cat in the turkey castle/headquarters trying to find your way around. There's very little explaining and lacks any tutorial or even a keymap setting in order to check the keys out.
Apparently it uses WASD and Q/E/R but you have to stumble on your own pressing random keys until you figure out what does what. You have your main sword attack, a ranged attack that has limited ammo and mousetraps that are even more limited. It is possible there's something else in your arsenal that I did not manage to find.
Combat in itself feels VERY clunky which is something that makes the game difficult. I do enjoy difficult games but only when said difficulty is not based on clunky controls and animations but actual gameplay difficulty.
The game feels very much rushed which is evident when you find a huge bug at the first minute of playing. Running to the corridor to the far right, from the first room you start in, makes you fall through the geometry and respawn at the start. This is 100% repeatable and you can't help but wonder how something this huge went by unnoticed?
Other than that, gameplay, once you get the hang of it, feels very repetitive.
Graphics:
Graphics-wise the game is mediocre. It is made with Unity engine and I'm pretty sure I've seen some artwork assets (eg the protagonist's armor) in several other projects. There are very few graphical settings (mainly Resolution, Fullscreen, VSync and AA toggle) and only the turkeys look very good in my opinion.
Music/Sound Design:
While music quality is decent it is also quite repetitive and gets old fast. Very fast. Sound effects are good.
Pros:
-Funny.
Neutral:
-Some artwork assets do not look original.
Cons:
-Clunky combat
-Very repetitive gameplay.
-Repetitive music.
-Very high price for what it is.
Conclusion:
I can not recommend this game at its current price of 14 Euro. Perhaps bundled or on sale for the comedy value alone.

TL;DR: It's a short, sweet and amusing homage to the JRPGs of old. You can usually grab the bundle version that also gets you Breath of Death VII for less than $1on sale. Even without a discount, these 2 games are worth the cheap price of $3.
[Graphics - average]: I love the retro graphics but sometimes it's hard to tell where things are while exploring areas with large amounts of objects.
[Music - good]: The soundtrack uses a mix of catchy rock music for battles and epic classical style music while out of combat but sometimes trade places.
[Combat - good]: It's classic, turn-based combat which is what I prefer for RPGs. Each area has enemies (except safe areas) with a battle counter. Once you've fought the set number of battles, random encounters turn off to make searching for treasure much easier. You can then use the forced encounter option to continue fighting enemies as much as you want. Each time you level up, you're given a pool of base stats, skills or skill effects to choose from which gives you a lot of freedom for each of your party members' roles.
[Characters - good]: There's a decent amount of unique/bizarre characters to fight or recruit. When even the narrator plays a part in the story, you know the fourth wall is going to be in pieces by the end.
[Length - average]: The first playthrough is only 8-10 hours long but more time gets added on when you go for the second playthrough... The cast stays the same pretty much, but their roles and the story itself change completely, giving you a brand new adventure to enjoy.
[Overall - good]: The humor is great, it's not a huge timesink and it's easy or hard enough for just about any player... AND it's dirt cheap, there's no reason not to buy this!

Right I'm going to be a little controversial here, so make yourself a cup of tea, get comfortable and I'll explain.
OK now that you spat tea all over your screen, I'll get into why this game impressed me so much. First of all, I have to say that Deck13 did an amazing job with the setting and Sci-Fi theme of the game. It's dark and gritty but oddly beautiful, which is only bettered by the graphical quality and performance of the game. Even on my somewhat low-end laptop, I was blown away by just how good it looked. The combat (which I'll get to later) is where the game really shines, it's visceral and incredibly satisfying to pull off finishing moves when it looks so good. It shows signs of improvement since Lords of the Fallen which also looked pretty good for a smaller development team.
In terms of controls and camera, The Surge feels quite fluid and combat is only occasionally clunky due to preemptively pressing combos (I think this can be canceled thanks to a recent update) or getting stunned whilst trying to attack. Your attacks consist of horizontal and vertical variants which then, depending on your weapon, form combos to apply greater damage and other additional effects. Limb-targetting is an important mechanic in the game but using the sticky-limb control feature I rarely had any problems. I must admit in the heat of battle I would often forget to target the weaker limbs but that's my bad. Locking on and switching between enemies was fast and the camera is quick but smooth to react to any changes you make.
A lot of people seem to agree that the story was really lacking or that it was just non-existent. Although I did find it to be a bit shallow that was to be expected from a Souls-like game. I won't go into detail as to not spoil the plot but essentially Warren joins CREO as they can give him the ability to walk again amongst other things. However, much like a cliched Sci-fi film, it doesn't go very well for him. The story unfolds in quite a predictable way with CREO being a big corporation with ill-intentions, but I did enjoy the lore and back-story that the game provided. Most of this is found through audio tapes and scraps of information from characters. The characters themselves though, they weren't anything special. I assume Deck13 placed 1-dimensional people in there to keep the player from feeling too isolated. Essentially the plot feels like the equivalent of a Dark Souls story, just with a Sci-Fi twist for freshness.
Enemies in this game may appear to be generic and boring at first but thanks to the limb-targetting, each encounter can be different and require an alternative approach (More so in new game+ and beyond). You mainly find yourself fighting the "zombified" workers of CREO, some more capable then others. Later on in the game, this is switched up as new enemy types are added providing additional challenge and forcing you to choose different tactics. The most notable of these would be the Smelter mini-boss units and the Tripedal security bots (Damn those guys are annoying). The further in the game you get, the more advanced and smarter the enemies become. Again trying not to spoil, but the last lot of enemies were a good challenge as they exploit limb-targetting unlike anything else. In terms of boss design, each one is unique and requires you to learn their patterns and attack them when they're weakest or recovering from an attack. The set pieces of the later bosses are fantastic and taking them down provides a lot of satisfaction. The issue with this is the empty feeling you get when you realize there's only 5 in the entire game :(
Overall, I'd say the design of every enemy/boss was decent and well-suited to the Sci-Fi theme, which is important when you see them so often.
Right now to the juicy part, severing limbs is so damn satisfying :D
The main bulk of the gameplay comes from Warren's ability to sever the limbs of his enemies and collect loot from their mutilated corpses. If that doesn't sound fun to you, you must be sane! Combat is fast, aggressive and fluid with enemies dishing out substantial damage if you mess up. More like Bloodbourne than Dark Souls, the combat requires quick reflexes and offers the player a risk/reward system based on how aggressively they play. Blocking is an option but I never found myself using it. Even high-def armor won't let you turtle for long. Essentially every humanoid enemy wears armor to protect their body, attacking armored limbs does less damage, but severing armored limbs has a chance to give you the armor schematics and components from the damaged part. The more focused damage you do to a part, the higher the chance. Alternatively you can target unarmored areas to do increased damage and sever them for faster kills. Every attack you make builds energy and this energy allows you to; A-Do finishing moves B-Use your drone to stun, knockback, damage or agro enemies (Yes you have a freaking drone) C-Use injectables which are basically items or flasks from DS.
The components and schematics allow you to craft new weapons and armor or potentially upgrade existing ones. This makes for a very fulfilling cycle of grinding and murdering then getting stronger through upgrading and murdering some more. Unlike DS this game doesn't let you upgrade yourself through levelling. Instead levelling up gives you higher core power which lets you equip more weapons, armor and mods (whilst also allowing access to other areas of the game and increasing mod effectiveness). Swapping mods is as simple as going back to a med bay for a completely free respec if you desire. Some mods known as hot-swaps can be switched on the fly too. This is an interesting take on the DS style of grinding souls then levelling as it gives much more freedom into what you want to equip. There's too many mods to list here but rest assured, you won't be limited by a lack of attributes and skill levels in The Surge. I feel I'm going on a bit so I'll just cut it short, this game may be Sci-Fi Dark Souls on the surface to most but it brings something new and exciting to the table in terms of gameplay.
Now back to the matter at hand, I thoroughly enjoyed every minute of this game despite it's shortcoming's. I found combat very satisfying and overall more fulfilling than that of other games like Dark Souls. Being able to cut my enemies up and then craft myself a set of their armor with the accompanying weapon felt good, really good. Yet at the same time this game is very punishing and somewhat lacking compared to DS. As a longtime fan of the Dark Souls series, I'm not saying they're bad (if anything they're the reason The Surge was even made) but I feel that the combat of those games has grown stale over time. The Surge provides a new and fresh take on the Souls-like genre and for this reason I found myself enjoying it much more. However, The Surge is short and with only 5 bosses, you find yourself wanting more and new game+ isn't really enough. For the price they're charging I'd actually recommend DS3 over The Surge (le gasp plot twist) but I'm writing this review assuming my fellow Dark Souls fans are here looking for a new game to try. If that's the case, get this game, see what you think. It'll tide you over until From Software release their next masterpiece :)

Personally I enjoy the arcade-like style of R.U.S.E. more than the realistic hardcore style of wargame series. This game borrows a few excellent ideas from R.U.S.E. like the 1939 (phase A), 1942 (phase B), 1945(phase C) era evolving system. The three phases make this game more like a traditional tech-hierarchy based RTS. Phase A is the most important. It decides your initiative and income for the first 10 minutes. Remember to bring enough phase A units in a pvp game.
I love the new line of sight (LOS) indicator. You may check the LOS at every spot on the map. The distance is also displayed. In Wargame you have to use the force-to-attack button to measure the LOS.
Overall, units are very hard to kill. Infantry in a building is especially hard to kill. It may take a couple of tanks and several HMGs two minutes or so to kill it. Axis tanks have heavy armors in the front. They may take 3~4 shots from the same era US tanks without retreating. With only a couple of AA you'll never kill a hit-and-evacuate bomber. So hitting the flank is probably the best strategy.
The logistics is much easier to handle with compared to Wargame. Troops do have limited ammo, but they don't consume fuels. The supply one truck can bring is more abundant than the cargo in Wargame.
The front-line mechanism is very interesting. The commanding unit plays a role of boosting the troop's morale near the front line instead of taking over a sector. The front-line is one kine of troop density indicator. For now, I don't see how to attack in a stealthy way. Probably special units that don't affect the front line will be added. Units behind the enemy line take more pressure and tend to surrender. So attacking the flank and surrounding the heavily defended area is usually more efficient.
There are just too few airplane models and too few available airplanes. No paratroopers. No heavy fighters like Me262. No heavy bombers like B-25. Even the Ju-88 feels like a light bomber. Hope Eugene has the plan of adding new airplanes and making the air fight more interesting. A heavy fighter escorted carpet bombing by B-25 is something I'd love to see. Massive paratrooping to towns and forests behind the enemy line is very exciting.
This is a problem succeeded from the Wargame. The front-line tank, infantry and mortors require a lot of micro managements. Moving mouse to the screen corner is always a hassle for me.

Alright folks, this game (as is suggested by the title) takes place 1944 Normandy and is an RTS. The developers who produced this game have a long history of producing quality wargames. I like this game, I have put more hours into it in two days than I put into personal hygiene. The combat has a cadence to it, the vehicles feel like they have weight to them and when you are actually hammering the enemy you can feel the momentum of your assault building like a wave to come crashing down and push the fronline back for miles. Its a throwback to the halcyon days of RUSE in many ways but it still keeps (and improves in my opinion) on the mechanics introduced in the Wargame Series. A point in the favor of this title is that the developers have stepped back from the frantic pace of modern combat and have captured the cat and mouse maneuvers of the Western Front. This game is not for someone who wants a "click click click oh look there is my instant gratification" style of game. You need to think about where you place your troops. How your armor will support your infantry in the next assault and trying to figure out if your IGs and ATGs have enough range to provide additional fire support. Its one of the games in recent history that have had me chapping my lower lip as I bite it and wait for an assault to be carried through. For all of the negative points you are obviously seeing here related to issues with graphics and the other BITING critical reviews (including "not fun", "why isn't the Argentina represented here?", and "Geez devs, you should have consulted me before researching and producing a title with obscene amounts of promise"). Just remember that a.) the reviews you are seeing here are from a beta (so no need to melodramatically post that you are REMOVING THE GAME FROM YOUR LIST *swoon). The game is still being tuned for a decent release so just keep your pants on. For anyone complaining about the scope of the game consider that the game is advertised as Steel Division NORMANDY (See that? See that there?) '44. If you want an eastern front experience check out Graviteam Tactics. They have the marked cornered there. Hopping off my soapbox there I can say that this game has really been a joy to play and I would suggest this to any friend of mine who wants a WWII RTS worth its salt.

Let me start off by setting the tone.
I've played since FS11 and despite the radical inclusion of forestry in FS15, which I enjoyed very much, I was still very bitter towards the GIANTS and their progress from 11 to 15. I felt their added features lacking, their improvements lacking and overall vision or direction absent. Their DLCs quite often were obvious money grabs, rather than any real addition to a player's farming strategy.
Odds are, they were a small but up and coming software development team which accomplished what they could, considering they were also creating smaller versions of the game for the Android and iOS platforms. Maybe they were spread too thin.
This year, they release FS17 with a $45 price tag, up from $27 in the past and I couldn't help but facepalm myself. I sarcastically thought, "Let me guess, we'll have MORE TRACTORS" as a way to justify the new cost.
24 literal gameplay hours into it, and I have to say, it has caught up to most of my expectations. Kudos for bringing this game up to speed and making it worth the $45. It's about time.
The game mechanics haven't changed a whole lot. It seems like midway through FS15, before they fleshed out all the bugs, they cloned it and started making FS17. This would explain a lot of the bugs that were resolved late in FS15 showing up in FS17. Currently, the "jitter bug" prevents me from doing forestry unless I use autoload trailer mods.
So what's the deal?
Missions have changed. Previously we had delivery and mowing missions. I didn't mind the delivery ones, but they were sorta boring. The mowing missions I enjoyed. They're now gone, which I don't think is right. They should come back and with more variety.
Now, we have missions where we are maintaining other farmer's fields. Thing is, you can't hire anyone to do it. You have to do it yourself. I would prefer to be able to hire, even if it meant it would cut into my profit.
There are a few more crops, 1 more live stock (pigs), chickens haven't changed and lots of tractors. There are even two useless trains. Well, useless on the Goldcrest Valley map. Two little loops around the center of the map. Regardless, it will make for great maps by the modders. Goldcrest Valley is an awful map. How is it that modders make better maps?
Despite my gripes... I'm really addicted to this game.

Started playing about a year ago, during early access. Have played the game as it developed, up until 'official release'.
The theming and art of this game is excellent. It's cute without being saccharine, the dangers of space are presented realistically, which somehow feels acceptably couched within the hand-drawn avatars and cartoon 3d models. I love it.
The game starts off viciously (excluding the tutorial), dropping your three spacefarers off in the blackness with a small pod of resources and 8 minutes of oxygen. Within those eight minutes, you have to build a small space station that can support a oxygen-producer, and an airlock.
All my astronauts suffocated before I was able to do this, and it was excellent.
The game presented me with such a challenge, I was glued, it was excellent. The first time I successfully got my guys into that little pocket of safety,
.
And thus ended the difficulty curve of Spacebase DF-9.
From that point on out, excluding game-breaking bugs (to be addressed later), the game gets easier and easier. Your first foothold allows you to establish resource collection, you invest wisely, and eventually you have a thriving base of about 40 personnel, you've run out of local resources, and are colllecting recycled resources from passing derelicts.
Some playthroughs got to be so easy, I'd just start building massive space-station shrines, or just interior hallways that stretch across space to the next resource deposit, because it was fun.
Sometimes, I'd have enough surplus to just install double-walls around my entire station, so when boarders attempted their namesake, they'd just drill a entrance into the interior bulkhead.
There are some minor issues I have with infrastructure, for instance, for oxygen, the recyclers produce oxygen that free-flows through the station, but aside from that, there's no real way to control it. Usually it's best to center the recyclers in the base, and build the other rooms off as spokes, but if you have say, a long hallway, the oxygen just ceases to flow down the hall, since it's 'range' is too far. The addition of oxygen ventilation, and power conduits, would be a much appreciate increase in control and complexity.
This game had/has such potential, if well balanced and bug-fixed, but there are powers higher-up putting an end to that. Developer Double-Fine has recently seen a round of layoffs, shorty after CEO Tim Schaffer announced that production would cease on Spacebase DF-9. While I've not gone through the process of comparing Spacebase's credits with the current Double-Fine roster, the coincidence is certainly suspiscious. Double Fine, who since Brutal Legend have been relying on Kickstarter and Early Access to fund their products, may have found that charitable funds are not an effective way to bankroll game development.
Regardless, the premature cessation of development on Spacebase has it's noticable effects. Massive, game-breaking bugs still exist, that completely ruin the expierence.
For instance, technicians are tasked with repairing damaged or worn-down equipment around the base. At it's peak, I had around 20 assigned, and I typically ignore them, as they automatically prioritize things to repair.
Instead, I'm focusing on the Marines I've send out to a derelict to clear any threats. Surprise, surprise, there's a xenomorph on this derelict, and I haven't committed enough troops to deal with it. As it chases the final doomed marine around the derelict, it's tail flicks a door, damaging it. I sigh as I watch the marine die to the monster, when I notice that there's movement elsewhere in the derelict.
A conga-line of technicians stroll through the airlock, ready to fix the broken door. As the alien rears it's head on the first, I'm frantically trying to do anything I can to get them back into the main base. But it's too late. They're all panicked, and it's not like the game has any system to give independant commands to a single unit. I lose half of my base's population to bad AI. This is not a one-off; it has ended essentially all of my long-running playthroughs.
Other bugs exist, such as the game having trouble determining what is and isn't space, which leads to things like units being sucked through an interior doorway into a bedroom, only to hover there, trapped, as if it were zero-gravity, until they starve. Or the fact that something about scientists causes them to almost immediately 'go insane' when assigned the position, causing them to run around fighting other crew, and breaking things.
Some of these bugs may have been fixed since, but they were present in the game when it went 'Final', so I am writing about them here.
I really, really like what this game could be, and maybe mods will get it there. You'll noticed I've 'Recommended' it on this review; while it's certainly one of the most ambivalent recommendations I've given for a game, it's entertaining and unique enough to definitely be worth playing.
Get it on sale, though. And don't trust Double-Fine to not release another half-baked product... definitely wait until the next title is complete before putting cash down.

I really didn't expect much going into Sleeping Dogs and my expectations were very low. To my surprise however, this game is very good and I love it alot. Probably one of my favorite games of all time to be honest. In my heart I wanna give this game a 9-10/10 but I think this game deserves an 8/10 due to some issues and I think normal people would give this a 7-8 out of 10. The problems with Sleeping dogs is that the ai is really easy to kill and you aren't gonna be challenged too much. The main problem is that the story felt way to short and anticlimatic. I was really hyped for more missions but the game kinda just ended when I wanted more. Sleeping Dogs does have a lot of Pros however. First, the combat is really satifying and if you just wanna kill things, this is a good choice. Animations feel satifying and you feel as if you are getting stronger and combat gets more fun the more you play. The atmosphere and enviorment is aesthetically pleasing and venturing through hong kong street lights and crowds of people looks interesting and pretty. The radio stations, music, and catonese that people in hong kong speak also adds a lot to the experiance. You feel like you are in Hong Kong and the developers did very good job unlike other games where everyone speaks just english or whatever. I do find that the main strength of Sleeping Dogs is the characters and story. You like and get attached to some characters and hate the guts of others which creates a tear of trust for both the player and Wei Shen. I found Wei Shen to be a charming protagnist. The story is also good and the earlier mentioned tear of trust in the story causes a lot of build up in the story. The ending however doesn't really take advantage of this tension and it's anticlimatic. After finishing the game, I felt as if I wasn't finished but I feel like that in a lot of games when I finish them so interpret that as you please. I just wished the main story was longer and the ending was better, then I would give this game a 9/10 or maybe even higher. If you are into cop movies, or kung fu movies then give this a shot. I'd also wait for a sale before buying. Even though I gave the game an 8/10 I still highly recommend Sleeping Dogs.

As someone who hasn't had much experience with MMO's in the past, this is a game to spend hours on a day. After you are done with the intense Main Scenario, you can go on to end game trying to max your characters gear. Personally, I like spending time grinding for mounts, which is also a relevant part of the game. I haven't played much of PVP mostly because the game is PVE focused, but there was a recent update regarding it so it is still relevant. After maxing your first class, grinding levels on different classes, which can be done on one character, gets very repetative and boring. Although leveling in this game isn't hard, its very boring. I wouldn't say classes are balanced the greatest. There are some classes that are easily better than others, but that doesn't stop people from playing what they like. The community in this game is unreal. You play with people who love helping you when you don't know whats going on. Although once you reach end game, you are expected to know more and if you don't, people will throw salt. If you are looking for a MMO to spend hours on, this is the one.

A super solid MMO with an enticing story and really polished engine that both looks good and runs exceedingly smooth on max settings with my GTX960. In addition, the non-time limited free trial with minimal restrictions is really generous (But make sure you look up the steam vs non-steam trials as it can screw you over when purchasing the full game on or off steam) and allows for hours of time to help get your head around the game and make an informed decision before purchasing the full game. I'm playing from Australia, and while their are no oceanic servers, there is a big community of Aus gamers on Japan servers which allows me to get <200ms which is really nice for an MMO. I haven't got to end game yet, but so far it seems as if it is pretty standard technically in the low levels, so it should be quite a nice game to start off if this is your first MMO. It even gives a really nice tutorial at ~lvl15 which instructs you on how to play your role (DPS, Tank, Healer) when in a party. Finally, the community is one of the best i've seen with no flamers in 40 hours of gameplay (Even when I screwed up a few dungeons first time round) and people always willing to help out newbs, it's really great and refreshing to see. No major complaints so far!

TL;DR - A text-based game that puts you in the shoes of a guy who's about to graduate from highschool and chats with her throughout the years. If you've got 30minutes to spare and don't know what to play, I highly recommend that you give this a try!
Who knew a half-an-hour game like this could hit me right in the feels?!?
This game is simple, easy to understand - remember back in the day when there was Windows Live Messenger? The time before Facebook took the world by storm?
Yea, you sign up with a hotmail, pick a display name, throw in a special status or description of your mood or your fav song if you want, add some friends and start chatting!
Well, gone were the days, but this game brings back all the memories!
You play as a guy, whose name and username is whatever you desire, in a period of 5years, from 2002 to 2006, chat with a girl called Emily, which takes you from senior year in highschool to college.  The game plays just like how you would in a chatbox, you read your friend's text and respond accordingly. However, since this is a game, you're given dialogue options, although they might not be your choice of response in reality if you're asked the same question, they are all quite sensible and realistic.
Albeit short, this is a great game! I applaud the developer's effort for going the extra mile to make the game feel authentic, whether it's the Windows XP boot-up soundclip, or the various Profile Pic you could use that suit the years(my fav being 2005's Batman Begins logo), it really shows the extra attention to detail the developer had when developing this 30-40minute game. Kudos!

Nothing makes Lovecraft roll in his grave more than this game. I got it, expecting it to actually be clever, but soon found myself wallowing in misery and disappointment. It's supposed to be humorous, but the humor boils down to making silly faces and putting Cthulhu into only mildly ridiculous situations. There's a bit of fourth wall humor, but it's far from adroit. In addition, his out of character reactions only left me cringing. This is a god who makes people insane just by being seen, but here we have him idly chatting with mermaids. It's not funny, it's a failure to draw comedy from an emasculated creature of pure destruction. It's saddening that the only way they could conceive of a Lovecraftian comedy was to completely change the very fabric of what the elder gods are. The only relation this game actually has to Lovecraft's works is in name alone. You could name all of the characters and places differently, it would still be the same game.
Gameply-wise, it's as bare bones as an RPG can get. There are no mechanics we haven't seen since the 80's. Every battle can be won by mashing the fight button, and there's a good chance you won't have to grind either. Some of the maps are too long, and the encounter rate will have you groaning over the tedium of having fought this same enemy fifty times in the past twenty minutes. I explored most (I say most because toward the end I just wanted to finish and be done with it) of this game's maps, and there are very few secrets to encounter. In fact, there's very little to the game besides the main quest. There's a few game modes to unlock, but I haven't bothered playing them because of how soul crushing the main game is.
If you're an appreciator of Lovecraft's work, or if you think comedy should be witty, or if you like innovative RPG mechanics, this is not the game for you. You're better off spending your money on a hamburger, at least it won't leave you starving and depressed.

I do wish Deck13 had taken the opportunity to tell a more immersive story; the minimalist style that works so well in Dark Souls falls a bit flat here.

I really had fun playing the Surge and I am looking forward to a second playthrough and the DLC. The combat is challenging, but never unfair, and progression feels rewarding. The story may not be extraordinary, but certainly interesting and well told. The last boss fight could be a little bit more challenging for "maxed out" players. If the game becomes "too difficult" at some points, there is always the possibility to grind (or to look up some tips about combat).
There are a few glitches, but nothing that spoils the fun. I did not encounter gamebreaking bugs and frequent autosaves would have prevented any progression loss.

The King of Fighters XIII: Steam Edition brings SNK Playmore's excellent 3-on-3 2D fighter to the PC via Valve's digital distribution platform. If you've rumbled with friends and foes in the version that appeared on last-generation consoles, you'll feel right at home here: the intricate combat mechanics, gorgeous graphics, and uptempo music are successfully ported over to this Steam port. Even better, The King of Fighters XIII: Steam Edition contains all the console DLC, the King of Fighters XIII: Climax arcade features, and PC-centric graphics options. In short, The King of Fighters XIII: Steam Edition is an excellent title, but a few problems keep it from KO'ing the fighting game king, Ultra Street Fighter IV.
The King of Fighters XIII: Steam Edition isn't for the faint of heart. Casual fighting game fans will enjoy executing basics and supers, but those who are willing to spend significant time in the digital dojo are the ones who will make the most of the game's complex combat system. That's true of all fighters, save for the incredibly basic Divekick, but in order to truly get good, you'll need to learn, and properly implement, cancels.
Cancels—Drive Cancels, Hyperdrive Cancels, and Super Cancels—let you quickly exit a move and input another to unleash ungodly combos and big damage. These cancels are governed by each fighter's Hyperdrive Gauge, which fills as you land, block, and take hits. Depending on the cancel needed, you'll consume between 50 percent to 100 percent of the Hyperdrive Gauge—so cancel with prejudice.
The King of Fighters XIII: Steam Edition has many defensive options that help you avoid or mitigate damage. Rolls let you quickly evade attacks. Short hops allow you to avoid footsie attacks without leaving yourself exposed to a possible anti-air attack. CD Blowback Attacks costs meter, but they let you quickly counter a move when you're in block stun. It's essential to master these excellent moves to get yourself out of sticky situations.
The King of Fighters XIII: Steam Edition's graphics impress in a manner that few modern 2D fighting games can match, as it balances silky animation with a ruggedness that fits a fighting game. Guilty Gear's visuals are beautiful, but overly polished. Ultra Street Fighter IV's polygons are lovely, but lack soul. The King of Fighters XIII: Steam Edition, on the other hand, drips in colorful, expertly shaded pixel love. Its graphics may not match Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike's insane-to-the-point-of-distraction animation, but what's there is absolutely stunning.
What isn't quite as attractive is The King of Fighters XIII: Steam Edition's netcode, which is decent at best. Lag appeared in many of my online matches, though in varying degrees. Sometimes the lag appeared for a second or so; at other times, it impacted my ability to beast an opponent. SNK Playmore's GGPO aversion baffles me.

Grimrock is a triumphant (re-)discovery of the first-person dungeon crawler genre, fused with modern sensibilities which make it all the more atmospheric and immersive.
The real-time combat encourages skillful dances around enemies (as well as careful timing of one's actions to interrupt enemies' attacks). The brain-rackingly devious puzzles are intensely challenging and rewarding. The secrets are often extremely well-hidden and reward careful exploration. Multiple playthroughs can offer very different experiences based on how you design your party members.
Never have I been so terrified of mushrooms.
I highly recommend this as a thinker's game and as an excellent sampling of the core old-school dungeon crawling experience.

I have been playing all the previous titles, and I really like what they did here.
PROS:
-I like the slowed down take on combat, which really helps the sense of realism. I always found the old games to be a bit too fast paced, and units died too quickly. Infantry in buildings should be hard to wipe out.
-The new deck system is great, I like the fact that it´s based on real divisions. Adds to the realism! It also seems a lot more fluid than previously.
-Conquest is cool with the dynamic frontline. Also much better than the static zones.
-Seems like morale and other psychological factors play a greater role. Always seemed odd to me when a single soldier kept on charging forward on in previous games even though 40 of his mates just died around him.
CONS:
-I think the graphics are good enough, but I had hoped they would be better.
All in all it feels a bit like Wargame mashed up with Close Combat. Not just because of the era, but also the dynamics. This is good, more detailed, deliberate and realistic!
UPDATED after release:
The campaign is somehow a disappointment. With Red Dragon they got real close at making something unique and extremely fascinating with the campaigns, but somehow throws all that in the bin now with just a line of serial missions. I am mostly a SP kind of guy, and this feels so much like a wasted opportunity and confirms that Eugen, at their core, are tailoring their games for MP.
Apart from that, almost all of the above still holds true. I must admit, however, that I find that the speed of gameplay is still just a bit too high, and that the game is struggling to find a place between realism and arcady gameplay. It´s a tradeoff for sure!

Plague inc takes a different look on strategy games, with its highly addictive gameplay and tonnes of replay-ability. There are still some downsides to it but I'm going to start with the pros first. The main aim is to evolve your disease, spread it and wipe out humanity.
Pros
- Its different from most strategy games on PC, and has a wide vairety of diseases to use
- There are loads of funny and gross disease based combos to be made
- The difficulties available include easy, normal, hard and brutal, each have their own challenging moments
Cons
- There is a difficulty spike in some of the diseases, particularly in the Virus disease type
- Each disease type has to be unlocked by beating the game with the previous one, this can be seen as both a negative and positive but if you get stuck with a certain disease like I did it can be discouraging
- This game is free to play on my Samsung but is £12 on steam? This seems way to overpriced, the cheapest it has ever been is £8.75 on sale
- The game is still in early access, it feels to me like it has been finished, because it has been far too long since anything new has been added in
Overall if your looking for a strategy game that requires little effort in terms of just clicking the mouse loads of times, can be too predictable through multiple playthroughs and has a wide variety of diseases to choose from then this is for you. Plague inc gets a solid 7/10, its still fun for me.

A super solid MMO with an enticing story and really polished engine that both looks good and runs exceedingly smooth on max settings with my GTX960. I haven't got to end game yet, but so far it seems as if it is pretty standard technically in the low levels, so it should be quite a nice game to start off if this is your first MMO. It even gives a really nice tutorial at ~lvl15 which instructs you on how to play your role (DPS, Tank, Healer) when in a party. Finally, the community is one of the best i've seen with no flamers in 40 hours of gameplay (Even when I screwed up a few dungeons first time round) and people always willing to help out newbs, it's really great and refreshing to see. No major complaints so far!

Good social aspects, good instance design, but incredibly immersion breaking, tedious solo quests.
There are adequate tools for grouping (dungeon finder), guilds, player housing and the works.
Since MMOs are about playing with people, the game is replete with instances, the quality of the instances is very good and the gameplay is passably interactive (rotations are reasonably complex for PvE), it's hard not to recommend this game to people who are looking to play with others.
If you like to solo in your MMO, or have to due to time constraints, I would not recommend this game, since I find the story puerile and the invisible walls that litter the game utterly immersion breaking.
Overall a more than solid alternative to WoW with arguably better PvE content.

"Alien Swarm" was made available as a free download on Steam and it absolutely rocks... not just by free game standards, either.
The game is a four-player co-op shooter in the vein of "Left 4 Dead," though you're blasting through an alien-infested space station instead of zombified towns. "Alien Swarm" also uses an overhead third-person view, which is helpful for dealing with the, uh, swarms of aliens that will attack your team.
What I really like about the game is its atmosphere borrows heavily from the best sci-fi action movie of all time, James Cameron's "Aliens." I'm talking space marines with high-tech assault rifles, shootouts in ventilation shafts, and beeping motion detectors that wrack your nerves.
Even cooler: you can use a hand torch to weld doors shut and help keep your team from being overwhelmed.

It's kind of funny. This game is a LOT more coherently built than the first AVWW, with all the parts that don't work fully excised and a better framework built around your adventuring. Heck, the turn based strategy game that acts as a framework for the action/exploration segments is actually GOOD.
And yet, due to how much more it limits what you can do, how much less varied your goals are, and how much less varied the environments are, it's a lot less fun. You're always just trying to get from one end of the level to the other. There's a handful of human minibosses that repeat themselves instead of a variety of monsters. You're stuck with a limited selection of spells instead of picking your favorites. Which biome you explore is dictated by overworld strategy concerns rather than what you actually feel like playing. Etcetera.
There's no room to enjoy the environments or the music, the exploration has been gutted since all levels are linear treks, and combat feels lifeless. It's one step forward, two steps back. I stuck with it for quite a while because I wanted to see the campaign through, but I don't think I had that much fun doing so.

Having just slaughtered the prequel of this series, I tried giving this one a little more time to impress me.
It didn't.
It does have full controller support, which is nice, but that's about the best I can say about it. Because the game still tries to do EVERYTHING in one go, and fails at so many of those that it becomes a horrible slog like its predecessor. All those ideas that went into it could have been neat on their own, and quite frankly split into maybe 3-4 different games, instead of being mashed together into one.
It's like a chef mixing many great small courses into one heap of a meal, which I'm sure is SUPPOSED to be super. But the truth is it turns out to be a desperate pile of gruesomely mixed steak with fish with marmite with foie-gras with 10 salad dressings with sweet dessert with wine, beer, milk, and orange juice on top of it. It's everything in one meal and the chef wonders why the guests aren't happy with it.
It saddens me, because I'm sure the developer's attitude is in the right place, but they seriously need to learn restraint - cut back on at least 75% of the ideas, stick with the rest, and then pretty please with sugar on top, POLISH that stuff until it shines. Because it could.
You see, genres are there for a reason - it's why The Lord of the Rings doesn't have FBI agents or astronauts in it. It's why Street Fighter 2 doesn't have City Builder and RPG elements in it. It's because it would make those pure genres indigestable if watered out too much with everything else you could think of to put into them.
For now, I wouldn't recommend this, even in a bundle.

King of Fighters is a long running series of 3v3 fighting games. Series started with KoF'94, but the real  hype started with KoF'95. This game has a history of being one of the best fighting games in years. You think Street Fighter was the most popular? Maybe so, but those who wanted more skill and execution + balanced game played KoF.
I started to really enjoy KoF series about 4 years ago, as I got PS2 and tried some older games of the series, before that I played KoF 99 on a PC, but then got my hands on Guilty Gear X2: Midnight Carnival, so I put KoF 99 aside... Reasons were obvious, it was easier, had flashy characters and great music.
In a few years I matured (lol) a bit, and I wanted something that wasn't button mashing. What shocked me was the complexity and fun provided by the series. The NESTS saga was awesome. 2001, 2002, 2002UM, XI were awesome, even if XI had many unfamiliar faces at the moment. Then there was KoF XII which was an strange game, it was like a demo of KoF XIII, but since KoF XII series started using new character art, higher quality textures(720p) and game itself became much more fluid. And speaking of sprites and art of the game, KoF games were always done using Dot Art system. This is one of the things that separates and makes this unique. So if someone is saying even Skullgirls have better visuals, it's cause of different pixel art used.
I Pre-ordered King of Fighters XIII on the first day it came out on Steam. So this should show you how hyped I am about this game. I do own  Mortal Kombat, Skullgirls, Ultra Street Fighter IV,  Street fighter X Tekken, Injustice, Guilty Gera X2, Guilty Gear Isuka, BlazBlue Calamity Trigger and BlazBlue: Continuum Shift EX on Steam, but this game just blows them up to dust. Maybe it doesn't have the additional stuff MK/ Injustice/ Continuum Shift has, and it isn't as easy to get in to, as SG, still this game blows them down in my opinion. The only modern fighting game from that I own, only Injustice and Blazblue Continuum Shift EX, can at least slightly catch up to KoF XIII. (Won't be mentioning the amazing Guilty Gear X2 cause, well it's old, no online, no additional game modes, low res.)
Now about the game itself. It has Story, Arcade, Versus and Online modes, which you'll spend most of the time. Other stuff like Practice, Gallery, Missions and etc are self explanatory. In versus you can play 1v1 if you want to. Also, if you want to play against a challenging A.I. play Arcade mode, somehow in VS and Story mode A.I. is weaker.
If you're feeling confident in both your skill and your connection, do enjoy the Online mode. But I'll tell you, if you are NOT used to fighting games with lag, don't even bother with less than 3 bar connection. I personally can barely play it even with 3 bar connection. It is bareable, but you do get frustrated from time to time. So it's probably best if you'd find people in your area to play with good connection.
Or better!!! Gather up and play it together in the same room. This is what fighting games are for!!! Online... meh. Screw it. Connect your PC to a big TV, grab some drinks and snacks, and the fun is guaranteed. Game supports many controllers, so picking up one should not be an issue.( personally got Razer Sabertooth just for this occasion)
I am very pleased with this port and I hope SNK Playmore will provide as much support as they did in the beta. And also wish them luck in putting even more of their games on Steam.

The number of factories you can build depends on the 'Resources' of the planet, so often you can make 2 Factories, then all Research. Demolish later to add banking, police and whatever else you unlock, depending on the planet's purpose. What I should have built more of were shipyards as it took 11 turns to get anything from my Home to the front lines.
Research Tree is pretty vast; it's split into 3 categories - Science, Economics, Military. Spent most of my research on Economics to get the gravy flowing, then some into Science to help later research. Military I only touched for the engines, really. But if you focus on Economics, then you should finish with them as progress will just slog while you get your weapons up to snuff.
Menus are pretty self-explainatory. You have a handshake for diplomacy, eye for intelligence, ship-with-arrow for next ship.. stuff like that. You only have to click on them once or twice to see what they do. Only issue I had with that is the Tutorial's (descriptive boxes) font is really small.
Navigational plane is 2-d, and I haven't touched on battles yet. Ships have a preset shape; the 'building' part is just placing different parts into their respective slots so kinda disappointed about that honestly.
Conclusion: Currently it's marked as 32.99 CAD and for that price.. HELLLLLLLL No. I got it on a Steam sale for a really good price so in my opinion 10.00 is the most I'd pay... but when it comes to a Steam Sale, I can still be El Cheapo :P.

The King of Fighters (usually shortened to "Tekken" by fans) finally returns in this incredible new installment. And it's one heck of a game, packed with a smattering of fan favorite characters. The gang's all here - including the mysterious Ashley Simpson, the carefree Tommy Bogart, the hot-headed Corey Yamada and the ever-popular Kai Kostanza (and his leather-loving brother, Kay Apostrophe), and even that one woman with the cartoonishly oversized breasts and crippling spine problems and groan-inducing character design that serves as a painful reminder as to how gross the game industry's (as well as the gamers themselves') attitude towards women is.
Featuring several riveting modes of play, like the spine-tingling Story Mode (in which you discover the deep and complex motivations that drive these people to punch each other in the face) or Arcade Mode (in which you punch people in the face) or Time Attack mode (in which you must attack time itself) or even Online Mode (in which pro competetive EVO players hunt down beginners and mercilessly slaughter them) you will almost certainly find something to do in this game.
KEY FEATURES:
- Poorly animated cutscenes, complete without voice acting. Discover a new style of post-modernist minimalism. Why could they not voice the scenes when the characters already have in-game voices? Like all historic artworks, this game makes you think.
- High-resolution backgrounds to look at while you're being juggled for twenty seconds by someone who enters Novice matches for fun whenever he's not competing in EVO.
- All characters come COMPLETE with graphics - not a single one is rendered invisible due to the artists forgetting to draw them. This alone makes the game far more balanced than some of its competitors. (We all remember the Stealth Sagat fiasco from Street of Fighters III)
- The game has several sound effects. Everything from "Smack" to "Whomp" and even "BWOOOoOOOOOOoooOSH". You will be amazed by the variety of sounds of people getting punched.
- It has an SNK boss.
- Make your own color palettes. This mostly seems to involve making everyone look naked by setting all their clothing colors to skintones.
FINAL SCORE:
Graphics: 8/10 Every character is completely opaque, and the menus are all in a language.
Sound: 9/10 This game has full compatibility with ALMOST ALL brands of headphones. (Speaker support not yet in, but the devs are working on it!)
Gameplay: 7/10 It might be a bit hard - by the time you've found the sixth page, it will be very difficult to avoid Slenderman for long enough to find the last two. However, it can be done with practice.
Character design: Skeezy as hell, sometimes
TOTAL SCORE: 9/10

Basically this game is another GTA clone, but the theme is set to 180°. Here you play as an undercover cop trying to cripple down the gang from the inside. This game also have high moral story, deep, serious, realistic, and much darker than any GTA. This game has decent open world, you can do what you want, like steal cars, etc. but your crime is limited and not as much fun as GTA, since this game way is too serious.
So let's break down my impression:
✔ The graphic is good, the details is great, and the post effect is great.
✔ Plenty of songs on radio in high quality
❌ But the music radio will reset to beginning of song if you exit and enter the car again, which is not cool
✔ Voice acting is great, but
❌ Face and character animation is below average, sometimes feel goofy
✔ NPC interaction to your character is great, like when you walk past people they will say something that affected by your progress, like
or when you drive too close to another car they will be mad, etc.
❌ But you can't talk to them
✔ Parkour element, and some mission is basically force your parkour skill.
❌ And for an action, open world, and parkour game, this game don't have jump button, like seriously the game won't allow you to jump at will. The only time you can jump is when you run and you face an obstacle, release the run button and hit it again so you can jump.
✔ 3 main experience progress to level up: cop, triad & face. Level up up to 10 to gain upgrades.
✔ This game has a good length for open world, about 12 hours for main story mission only, and about 20-30 hours if you do open world mission too.
❌ The story is kinda 'meh' for first few hours, which is bad for first impression and risky for kids who like to buy and refund. But,
✔ the story is begin to rise to super interesting from half way of the game, like "need more 30 minutes" but you can't stop playing for another 2 hours because the story is good.
✔ Story about best friend & betrayal is so thick, which I think is essential to a crime based game and this game is full of it.
✔ More martial arts than shooting kind of game, which is good and not a "basic" fps game.
✔ Realistic weapon carrying, you can't have 7 kind of guns and a baseball bat all the time, instead you can carry one pistol plus one of any other weapon than that including knife and riffles if you found one that can't be carried all the time, and must be dropped at some points.
7/10 - If this game allow me to do anything I want, especially jump, and kill peds. But this game is about a police story.

As much fun as I've had with SD44, I can't in good conscience recommend it.  There are some lingering issues that make the game a bit too frustrating at times:
1. Pathfinding ... routes generated don't seem to have any goal at times, i.e., not shortest, fastest nor safest.  Backtracking over the same path is not unusual, sometimes 400m or more.  Units, especially retreating ones, sometimes get caught on terrain features or the map edge.  Although flames are certain death for most units, they will not automatically divert around them and will even fall back into them.  (The worst I've seen is a couple of trucks stop their advance despite only minor suppression when some napalm dropped *behind* them, back into the fire and explode.)
2. Dropped players ... although vastly better than at release, players still get dropped (not surrender) regularly.  By watching the ping meters prior to start, it's even easy to predict who will likely drop.  Yet there are no pre-enforced minimums on the dedicated servers.
3. AI ...  except on the easy settings, the AI tends to play a rather aggressive game, even in destruction mode.  Early game can be interesting, but later game turns into a player steamroll.  In multiplayer games, a dropped player is a kill feeder for the opposition.  Although the AI does adapt to your moves in real-time (even ones it can't see), it doesn't learn nor seem to have much randomness in it's moves, i.e., a set series of moves by the player will result in the same set of moves by the AI.
4. Solo campaigns ... the campaigns are of set difficulty.  I found the assigned difficulty levels to be fairly meaningless, with difficulty depening more on withheld or, in one instance I recall in the German campaign, even misleading information.  Once you solve them, they become trivial, i.e., no replay value.
5. LOS ... once is a while I've run into situation where LOS is clear is one direction, but not for the return path.  It's not a huge issue, as it's reasonably rare.  More my beef is with the LOS tool that works well for woods and buildings, but was never updated for elevation.
6. Player population ... several months in and the player population is still so low that finding multiplayer pickup games is frequently an excercise in patience.
I do have some positives to mention:
1. Phases ... I like this mechanic of funneling units not just based on point value, but also by type.  One can imagine lead elements making contact before the bulk of the forces roll in.
2. Balance ... unlike many of the forum comments, I find the balance for conquest mode to be decent, albeit with many ahistorical elements.  (Destruction mode is another matter.  My past experience has been that the Axis unit mix is favored, but I haven't played enough destruction post-patches to offer an opinion currently.)

First and foremost, the game is a lot of fun! It's nice to see the designers innovate and move the RTS formula forward without breaking the key mechanics that define the genre. They've walked a nice line here in both design and complexity. Their
mechanic for example is a clever way of rolling unit health, moral & suppression into a single metric and works very well.
The pre-game customized army/deck building and initial deployment is a nice alternative to the the traditional RTS base building. It's easy to examine the stats/abilities of the different units and fun to agonize over which ones will suite your tactics the best. Deployment feels like an additional 4th "phase" of the game in addition to the well defined (10 mins apart) A (early), B (mid) and C (late) game phases.
The scale of the game seems particularly well suited to Eugen's game engine. With
, you're playing on a very small scale that requires unrealistically short weapon ranges. Similarly modern titles (perhaps like
) with long range missles, etc. can suffer a similar problem where the map is just too small for realistic engagement distances. However, the more limited WW2 era technology is well matched to the scale of the maps (made from real WW2 recon photography) which just adds the feeling of authenticity.
While the pace is less frantic than some other RTS titles, you stay busy - just concentrating on different things. Rather than flash decisions and CPM, you have more time to spend scouting, planning and angling to maximize line of sight for example. While the staple rock, paper, scissors mechanic is still there, N44 feels more like a game of cat and mouse and that is another welcome change.
Even after such a short introduction, I'm very comfortable recommending it and really looking forward to learning about the rest of the divisions/maps and developing tactics. I'm also looking forward to the single player campaigns. I usually skip them for RTS games and stick to multiplayer. But, I could see this pace/style being much more suited to it.
EDIT: One more thing that is worth mentioning is the visible front line mechanic as there seems to be quite a bit of controversy with some loving it and some hating it. I'm loving it! It is a great gamified way to visually portray the flow of battle that you might get from listening or tips from local resistance for example. It's also very WW2-esque which adds to the flavour. For those wondering: Yes, it can be turned off; and yes, there are units which don't influence it and can "hide" behind enemy lines. IMHO, it's another welcome innovation from Eugen.

For the sequel, it seems the devs wanted to change everything for the sake of change and experimentation.  And it is decidedly much less enjoyable.  Perhaps if I hadn't played the original at all, but no... this game is too much of a mess.
It appears to want to be a more straight up platformer and has a control scheme to match, encouraging you to use a gamepad over KB and mouse as in the original.  In doing so, I can't help but feel that most of the gameplay and mechanics that made the original fun have been removed or extremely stripped down.
For example, via spells and enchants, there was a significant amount of character customization you could do in the original.  Granted, I've had only a brief look, but being able to use only one item at a time in the sequel really limits things.
I'm guessing here, but I think that the devs, or perhaps too many players, found the original *too* complex and daunting and that explains the more limited gameplay.  Personally, I much prefer the complexity.  Yes, even the unusual "graph" based dungeon map that they needed to take a couple of help pages to explain.  It worked, and it was a good idea on their part.
So, skip this game unless you find it on a really steep sale price.  The original is worth your time regardless of sale price.  It's looks dated, but it runs great even on old machines, and is a lot more fun.

AVWW2 is a turn based post-apocolytpic land/resource management game wrapping a 2d Platformer. You move troops around the map to farm, build buildings, etc. to fight the evil head honcho who can show up and wreak havoc. Monsters spawn every so many turns.
There's a number of little nuanced details about the turn-based aspect which feels like much ado about nothing. The game, like its predecessor, beats you over the head with tutorial text for the management aspects of the game (although the platforming aspect does seem to carry a little less of the complexity baggage from the first game).
The platforming here is pretty uninspired. Moving feels sluggish; I was amazed that holding down shift actually slowed down my already slow character who can jump 4 stories high.
The game warns you about using mouse+keyboard (and actively makes it a chore to set what should be default) due to it being "overpowered for the game design". Okay, so fix your game design. Playing a platformer with 2 hands on the keyboard feels like junk. Trying to play this game with a controller only feels like junk. Trying to do a hybrid of those 2 feels like junk.
The music here is much better than the first, but that's not saying much. The graphics still feel lackluster for 2013. A SNES-era retro look would probably serve the game better than what it has which carries an air of mediocrity.
Unfortunately, the whole thing feels uninspired and boring in the most insipid way possible. Technically, it possesses the aspects and features a game should have, but so many things are either poorly implemented or not implemented in a way that makes them synergistic or relevant. On the scale of quality, this game lies in that precarious spot where many things sound good on paper, but it all fails to add up to something engaging. It's like the developer had a checklist of features that they think every game should have, and they checked them all off as development progressed, but they failed to take a cohesive look at the sub par results. The game takes no risk with unique gameplay aspects. I suspect the developers felt that the genre-blending would be that unique offering, but it feels like 2 poorly developed games smashed together.
4/10. There are far better turn-based strategy games and far better platform shooters. This game is neither a jack nor a master of either trade. Save your money for something with far more polish and presentation.

UPDATED REVIEW: At first, I couldn't figure out how to access the story. It's buried, so much so that without looking up a guide a new player can very easily opt out of it without knowing the difference. It's a poorly cobbled triggering system and I actually had to go in and edit my save files so that I could trigger it again. When you do get story missions, don't try to have any fun, roleplay, or explore any of the "choices" you are given. Pick the most obvious answers, or you'll be locked out of the story.
Upon getting a taste of the story, I've gotta say... meh. It's average for a video game, nowhere near that of a good sci-fi novel. The writing is wordy and amateurish, and the characters are unremarkable. Nothing notably bad about it, but nothing particularly good either.
The gameplay, though, is terrible. Making money, pretty much the core of the game, is a speed bump rather than a challenge. Pick a mission, press J till you get to your destination, and repeat ad infinitum. Do that, and you're a millionaire in a couple of hours. The trading system... exists. That's all that can be said about it. Things sell for higher prices on some planets than they do on others. Buy low, sell high. That's literally all there is to it. The profits you'll make aren't worth the time it takes to stock up, so the system can pretty much be ignored despite its simplicity.
There are space pirates. They can more or less be ignored. Just press J and you'll warp to the next system before they can deal any real damage. I completed an escort mission that involved constant bombardment by pirates. Didn't bother firing a single bullet. Just pressed J. Mission complete.
It's probably for the best because this is some of the worst space combat I've ever seen. In principle, it behaves like Asteroids. Turn your ship, fight inertia, pew pew. However, the ships are as slow as molasses, which makes maneuvering frustrating, and the weapons auto-aim. So, the developer managed to ruin the two things that make this kind of system fun. There's no point in aiming, no way to dodge, not tactics, no strategy, and no skill. You just spray and pray, and hope your ship has bigger numbers than the other ship.
This is branded as an "exploration" game. It's not. There's nothing to explore. The systems have different names, but it's all the same no matter what side of the galaxy you're on. There's nothing to find, and nothing to do.
As for the actual story missions... those follow the theme of being pretty bad. Most of the story missions involved... pressing J. Over and over again. The dev decided to throw in the mother of all difficulty spikes though, with a mission that was so frustratingly difficult, I altered my save file to skip it. It's just bad game design all around.
And here's the kicker. I know I didn't finish the whole story. I've looked at guides and seen that there's many more missions. However, the story characters were just like "bye," and left me to go do mundane nonsense. I've looked up how to access the rest of the story. It involves randomly clicking one planets until the story feels like showing up. And even then, you have to do MORE mundane point A to point B missions that are special cause you got them from the spaceport and not the job board. Sorry. That's where I draw the line.
I give Endless Sky a 2/10. Not worth trying, even if it's free.

I've played and beat the entire Souls saga(Demon's Souls, DS1, DS2, DS3, Bloodbourne) and watched this game from it's early development to release. Without a doubt I really enjoyed it's Sci-Fi twist on a genre of games I enjoy. Here's where I thought The Surge worked and didn't work:
Worked:
- Limb targeting makes deciding to kill enemies for souls or items easy and quick
- Executions look cool
- Game has a cool design and atmosphere which often reminded me of Alien and Souls.
- Weapon Patterns are easy to learn
- Implants add for vast and cool effects
- Characters and Story were interesting, Quests were engaging
- Exploration and world was very fun to explore, interwoven
What I'm Iffy About:
- Weapon Proficency was strange in this game. I often would grind because I enjoyed the combat but found the need for proficiency with weapon types to be tedious.
- I wish the Weapons had more, for lack of a better term, variety. The weapons you initially game are awesome, once getting to the security weapons and armor there's again a lot of suprise but I was disappointed to see two weapon models which are virtual reskins
- The game has five bosses which actually shocked me once I beat the game. Coming from DS tradition (Not so much DeS but more DS1 & 2) I expected the CREO facility to have more bosses in it. I know this was abused in Dark Souls 2, but I felt there could be a nice balance struck. Big Sister was my favorite boss of this game for being a mix of a puzzle and a fight
and I thought it could be interesting to meet many other bosses with their own quirks. While, certainly, I don't want the game's bosses to come at the player in a structured  and formulaic fashion ala Demon's Souls I wish the game had atleast 10 rather than 5 bosses.
What Didn't Work:
- While I praise the story I disliked how the game implements the alternate ending this is because of me feeling fooled, which I will go into. Dark Souls (imo the most plot heavy game of the series) gives the player a forked path; the literal followers of Gwyn's words, or the reading between the lines of their words and some leads. Getting the Lord of Hollows ending in DS1 can be figured out with some guessing work. By comparison The Surge has mulitple parts which imply an ending path. For example I thought the player, in a nod to DS1, could follow the Project Utopia doctor or the Project Resolve and was sorely mistaken. This is how I initially got the vanilla ending of the game but may beat in and a NG+ cycle. However this is where I want to point something out: my expectation of vastness was defeated by the fact the story is very isoteric, you have to piece it together and even though it's not DS it's still extremely vague and dystopian even if in a different manner.
- This game also has a bit of a learning curve to it's systems that initially seems jarring to souls vets, this is far more so than Bloodbourne. The game lacks or reworks several defense mechanics to be very different from DS and (I hear) LOTF but it becomes a mess to learn and will take excessive trial and error before grasping. Here's the issue however: the game lacks both real Parrying and Blocking (like with a shield and movement) and implements a type of "counter-poise" which replaces armor and most defense stats. These are two stats: You weapon and your Stability stat. in The Surge you can block but will be static. If your counter-poise is high enough you can immediately counter attack or dodge (ill advised to tank hits, you will quickly lose stamina).
-I realized that to even utilize defense stats minus implants your stability needs to be high to utilize defense. If a CERBERUS or RHINO set this meant I could block the attacks of most enemies besides end game security and any mech enemies but still do a counter attack (which replaces parrying but is far less effective). I disliked how much bs I had to go through to learn this system
-The game maintains backstabs but they are less rewarding for guaranteeing you receive no item but instantly kill most exosuit enemies, however they are far less practical to do in situations with multiple enemies and less helpful.
- The Surge implements a Jump/Duck mechanic that other reviewers touch on, though I suggest this game I want to honestly say these two things bothered me the most for the reason of being mostly unuseable. Most enemies in the game can not be ducked under with the exception of about two Jumping is similar and take a lot of practice to get good at though I think you can use it against a boss. The two techniques are like a parry for mechanical enemies but most mech enemies are far too strong and aggressive (specifically the mech hounds) that you will never want to try these defensive maneuvers first against such enemies. The stun is rewarding but the risk is often too great to try unlike parrying in DS which just takes a small degree of practice
- Last but not least this game is allergic to i-frames. I have no idea why but it makes fighting multiple enemies a complete pain especially in NG+ so far. Dodging depends entirely on if you physically moved away from an enemy attack rather than an i-frame cushion to account for multiple enemies. It also makes certain moves extremely risky like prolonged combos with 2h or similar weapons that will only result in stagger unless blocked and even then transitioning to block doesn't break a combo.
tl;dr fun twist on the souls formula which, while short, feels original and posseses enough potential to be a series of it's own. Get the game on sale for maximum enjoyment
