One of the best games in the genre. While everyone compares it to Dark Souls games it has its own presence in the niche group of games it belongs in. It's unlike anything you'll ever play. Personally, I think I actually prefer this sci-fi Dark Souls approach moreso than Dark Souls games themselves. It just seems more "real" personally. It's also not so big on itself as to have you needing to read 10 different wikis to understand wtf kind of story the game is trying to convey.

A quick rundown of things the game does very well:
Combat= OFF THE HOOK. It is done so well. It's meaty, it has OOMPH and it is spectacular to behold once you nail it. With multiple classes, tons of different combinations of armors and weapons and upgrades you'll find yourself in a dizzy just trying to figure out what to move forward with and what is your favorite. Just like Dark Souls you'll find yourself coming back again and again to figure out move sets, weapon combos and those special hits that make ending an enemy a very deep satisfaction.
Graphics= Again, very well done. Everything from the environmnets to the little tubes and wires coming out of your rig actually seem like they belong in this world. This isn't Dark Souls muddy, washed out textures. This is on point, scientifically based sci fi graphics. Everything seems like it actually has a purpose or had a purpose. Enemy armors and weapons will surprise you with their graphical effects and procs. Fog effects and smoke are done wonderfully in game. My personal favorites so far are building and upgrading my rig and weapons. Everything, and I mean everything, looks so amazing and detailed you'll actually forget it's even just a game. The immersion factor is off the hook. The different areas ALL have a look that is detailed per what their purpose is and it all looks like it actually belongs there. Some areas are so vast and huge that it will take you HOURS to figure out all the ins and outs of the area to best serve you and you'll discover so many wonderful bits to look at along the way that make it seem so real.
Sound= What's not to like? Man, I could spend days on the sound alone. Weapons hits, armor grating, procs, the sizzle of nuclear waste, the rotation and maneuvering of robot arms, it is ALL so well done. This game deserves that 5.1 or 7.1 surround system you've been really DYING to use for a proper game. This has so many awesome sound effects and musical cues and wonderfully arranged sound bits it's a disgace to play this game on anything except a full surround kit.
A short list of gripes= First and foremost, this is included because the game is NOT perfect. It's close but not quite there yet. Things that slighlty annoy me and may annoy you. That country music tune that plays EVERY SINGLE SAFE AREA. You'll tire of that quickly. However, there is a nice explanation in the GUIDE forum that tells you how to use your OWN music. A saving grace honestly. That country music loop is good for one or two listenings. Then it sucks.
Exploding boxes and cargo crates. Yeah, they crumble to your touch and weapon hit but do so haphazardly and can sometimes obscure a fight you're going into. Annoying but not game breaking.
Enemy AI can be wonky around tight areas. Yeah, sometimes you'll see a robot or enemy NPC hop up on a rail or side stair and get stuck in their loop sometimes. Very rare but has happened. Easy kills ensue most times. Most times, but still be cautious.
While I'm the LAST person to complain about an in-game map, the maps located throughout the areas are not well done and leave a LOT open for interpretation. While some may like this, the fact that the devs included them in the game means they don't want you to spend literally hours getting lost. Which, btw, is quite easily done if not paying attention to the NPC conversations you'll be in. Slightly better detailing for these maps would have been appreciated. I don't need a map, but if you're making one in game on the walls, just make it better next time. You know?
Pertaining to those NPC convos, there is a lack of an in-game "journal" so to speak. If you need reminded of what you're to do better go backtrack to that NPC and have another chit-chat. Otherwise, the game doesn't keep tabs on your missions.  While I, personally, don't need my hand held in a game like this I do like to know what I'm supposed to do without either guessing or backtracking. Sometimes you get so caught up in the pursuit of upgrading that you forget your mission. Minor annoyance at best.
All in all, a wonderful  game by Deck 13. If you didn't know there was a favorite little title of mine they did years ago called Venetica. Over the years, and their games, you can really tell they were fine tuning their craft for a game like this. Their previous title, Lords of the Fallen was a mixed bag in Steam reviews but actually one of my favorite games of the past few years. It wasn't perfect but it was meaty and the combat was on point most times. If you like games in this genre you deserve to play The Surge. It's a giant game meant to take you 40 hours or longer. Well worth the price tag if you ask me.

The problem with games that follow the lead of unfinished freeware games with incredibly good ideas is that when the original lacks a definitive purpose, the derivatives tend to as well. As the name suggests, Spacebase DF-9 is derivative of Dwarf Fortress, a city-building ASCII title that has absolutely no purpose outside of building your base and keeping it afloat until that sudden, inevitable downward spiral that brings your civilization to ruins.
It's a decent idea, for sure. I picked this game up as soon as it was available because I'd tried the Amnesia Fortnight prototype and desperately wished that it would be expanded into something great. The premise has a lot of potential, after all, with space being as vast as it is. Unfortunately, DF-9 left Early Access far less than what I'm sure a lot of people hoped it would be.
Spacebase DF-9 is a fairly simplistic base-builder sim. You pick a spot on a big galactic map and then build your fortune on it. Starting with only three people and some meager resources, it's your job to thrive in your little sector, mine up asteroids for more building material, and balance out the health and well-being of all the space grifters you pick up along the way. Sometimes you're attacked by bandits, or a bit of wrecked ship will float by for the taking. Sometimes you'll come across a particularly pushy visitor who insists on joining your roster. Sometimes you'll be stricken by a space disease and need to research the cure before it kills off your crew. That's about it.
The problem I've noticed is that there is really nothing in the way of depth. It's fine to be tossed into the wilds and learn the ways of the land by yourself, but once you've built one of everything you're pretty much done.  The happiness graphs and space social networking tabs might promise more to the individual psychological needs of your people, but there seems to be little to no chance of even the most dour, reclusive person on your base succumbing to space madness and striking out in a hilariously deadly rage. So that's one of my secret space fantasies rendered undoable.
If you want to build a space-base with a little more depth, I'd recommend Startopia. If you want to Dwarf Fortress, just play Dwarf Fortress. Unfortunately, Spacebase DF-9 is relegated to the Horrors of Early Access bin, which is a shame considering all that potential.

Before you rage at me, yes there are loads of bugs, and yes the development is "finished". I know this, so either take note of my review or shut up.
For those who actually want to read my review, I say in short this game is good if you like base management, but buy it on a ridiculous sale.
The last game I played that could be compared to this is Prison Architect, so I'll compare to that. This game has its ups and downs, but I found that Prison Architect became a bit stale after a while; build fast at the start, expand for new prisoners, work on efficiency. Rinse and Repeat. Not that it wasn't good, but that's the gist of it.
Spacebase Df-9 on the other hand, was a somewhat evolving base management, and a bit of tower defence thrown in when raiders visit too. Once you get the hang of it, you need to constantly adapt your base to make room for new people, keep up with the component decay and so on. One of the hardest bits (albeit interesting) I found was defending against multiple raiders. If you can manage to defeat the raiders, you're then left with a depressed crew (that don't want to work) that needs to repair the remains of the station and hold out until more people show up... or more raiders.
I honestly haven't seen any game breaking bugs yet (touch wood!). Bodies stick around for ages, but with enough doctors they get moved over time. Components decay rapidly, but with the right balance you can keep them in check until you research better things. And yes, research takes ages too, but it's helpful if you're around long enough to finish it.
All in all, it can be problematic, and there are plenty of issues people have talked about, but with patience and taking the time to learn the game, it can be pretty fun. Maybe a 7/10 from me, buy it on a very good sale.

Spacebase does well enough for what it is - an alpha build rushed to release - but it lacks the strategic depth that a simulation needs in order to keep the player's interest. It doesn't even have enough pretty distractions to make up for the spartan gameplay. This is the kernel of a game that could have been great, but unfortunately that game will never be completed.
On the plus side, Spacebase remarkably stable. I experienced no bugs, glitches, or crashes.
A tip for those frustrated by raiders: build at least one turret in every room and leave them deactivated when not needed. When raiders attack, simply activate the necessary turrets and seal the doors. No muss, no fuss. Don't bother claiming derelicts; they are difficult to defend. Rather, explore them to acquire new crew members or loot and then let them disappear.
In its current and final state, Spacebase is definitely not worth $20; I would not recommend this game at any price other than "free" (I got a complimentary copy with my Hack 'n' Slash purchase).

Hoo boy.
The original
struck me as about the quality of a particularly impressive bit of shareware in the late 90s: horribly dated by modern standards and without 1980s retro charm (though maybe that just means it came a decade early), but at the very least technically competent. Animations were smooth (though obviously based on some simple figure rendering program like Poser), the control scheme worked, the story didn't make much sense but a lot of 90s shareware didn't so I could at least poke around with it and be vaguely amused.
You will note that I only have 19 minutes on record with
.
I'm going to hold off on explaining why for just a moment. This sequel--if it can really be called that, since the whole
"broken reality" thing never made much narrative sense to begin with, and apparently intentionally so--has you running a rebellion against a big bad. Unlike the original
, where you had followers who you would make go away for so many minutes to go gather firewood or whatever while you ran around the infinitely side-scrolling (well, infinitely transitioning, at least) map, this actually has a strategic map for you to tell your followers to go to places and do things and fight baddies. It's a nice touch, adding some level of strategic force movement rather than simply "Bob has a 57% chance of getting a carrot with a 99% risk of dying because Bob is a loser."
Well, I lie. It would've been a nice touch. If it worked.
If anything worked.
If
has the quality of decent 90s shareware,
has the quality of
90s shareware, the kind that I have spent a good decade and a half trying to forget that I grew up on. The characters have gone from smoothly-animated pre-rendered 3D geometry sprites to poorly MS Paint'd cartoons that move as though they're suffing grand mal seizures. In
, everything was made of pre-rendered sprites so it all fit together visually. Random elements in
are pre-rendered, some are drawn, others are painted, and they're all mashed together in incoherent tilesets so it's actually extremely distracting. The control system went from a simple but effective "keyboard to move, mouse to aim" system in
to a clunky and incoherent keyboard-only system. For a comparative example, let's say you want to shoot your magical ball-o'-death at some critter at an angle:
, point and click.
, hold the right and up and fire keys at the same time and pray to whatever gods you have that you timed that perfect 45° angle shot just right because 45° angles are all you're going to be doing and also if you don't do the fire button at the right time then you're just going to jerkily leap your character up and into the target in a valiant but utterly stupid attempt to smash the enemy with her face. That's how
worked back in the late 80s. It's as though the
was coded for a particularly archaic D-pad setup. Everything about it is completely retrograde from the original.
It's completely unforgivable, since these people were able to make something competent, if not particularly impressive before. However, it's also unimaginably hilarious. It is so bad you just have to stop and laugh at everything.
And then just stop, since there's absolutely no point to go on any further with it.
There's certainly no point in actually spending money on the experience.

Pros:
- Fixes some of Wargame's issues
--- No longer able to view win ratio from lobby
--- Front line system opens up the entire map for play instead of always focusing on the command sector
- Historical authenticity (lots of influence from the Close Combat series)
--- Accurate infantry loadouts and vehicles
--- Inaccurate weapons AT & tank weapons
--- Morale/surrender system
- Simpler gameplay mechanics (similar to how Civilization V was on release compared to Civilization IV) to appeal to wider/more casual audience, and hopefully increase longevity
Cons:
- Persistent perceived issues from Wargame series
--- Still no matchmaking so unless you're playing 1v1, you're often going against a coordinated premade group [Update: This has since been implemented since first reviewed but queuing for more than 1v1 can take a long time depending on how many players are online]
--- Still no persistent multiplayer campaign - without this in the series I think longevity and holding players' interest is inevitably going to suffer and will rely on the generation and release of new content to keep it going
- Introduced perceived issues
--- No way to resupply artillery observers (would prefer a cooldown system than a finite amount of uses)
--- No way to repair critical damage to tanks, even with supply trucks
--- No way to replace infantry casualties despite there still being a destruction mode
- As a result of fundamental design changes, and a much more constrained time period, unit variety and tactical gameplay are lessened compared to the latest in the Wargame series (mostly affects the hardcore Wargame: Red Dragon players who stuck around much longer than 99% of people who bought the game)
--- Less player choice when making decks/battlegroups
--- Less variety of tactical strategies
--- Less variety in units
In conclusion, I think there's a good balance of catering to the hardcore Wargame players, as well as making the series more accessible and approachable to more casual gamers. As a result of fundamental design changes, gameplay has gone to the simplest version of what it can be. I assume this is so that the developers can fully understand the effects of the changes - rather than changing fundamental design and keeping a high amount of complexity which would likely lead to a development nightmare for a number of reasons like balancing.
Ultimately this is going to hurt the hardcore players but makes sense, and it provides an opportunity for the series to build back up the complexity iteratively through patches, DLC, expansions, and sequels towards the amount of complexity the hardcore players want (compare Civilization V on release to Civilization V post-expansions).
The worst case scenario here is that the game becomes too mainstream and doesn't cater enough to the hardcore Wargame players - which just opens up an opportunity for new developers to create a product that fills that niche of having a high learning curve, high mastery curve, and more tactical depth.

First off I would like to say that I recommend Steel Division even at this Open Beta state. So there you have it go and get it! To further explain why, I will review this game in 4 categories with each category getting a score out of 100.
Gameplay: Steel Division shines at this department. The gameplay is neither too historical nor too arcadey. The developers have found the perfect balance of these two critical elements for a world war 2 game. The new Frontline mechanic emulates the historical situation but still gives the player tactical as well as strategical input. This system also has gameplay effects such as morale which is critical to the survival and manouvre of units. In addition in the conquest mode a point accumulation system dependant on the map control percentage slowly ticks you towards victory.
The battles in the game are seperated in to three phases. The first phase is the "Recon" phase where the lighest units can be brought in. The second phase is the "Skirmish" where combat slightly intensifies and the overall battle starts shaping. Last but not least the third is the "Battle" phase. Not constricted by time but the points accumulated this is the heaviest of all phases in terms of combat and units brought in.
There are a lot of units in SD. Right now with the 4 divisions available you can get quite the varying experience through creating unique battlegroup decks selecting which units you want within that division. Each phase has different units you can call in which means that you have to pick some sort of a sub strategy within the unique division you choose. The divisions themselves have different attributes and requisition points per phase making them unique.
90/100
Graphics: One really has to mention that this is the greatest scaleable rts engine out there. You can have 10v10 multiplayer battles and zoom to a building to building fight then suddenly zoom out and watch a 10km frontline being fought over fiercely. The visuals are quiet good. They are of course not the greatest compared to other games but that is beside the point. Even when you zoom in you can see your units quiet detailed.
The visuals also have a certain retro style that adds to the world war 2 feel to it. Optimization wise the beta performs alright. At max the frames may dip down a little but issues like these are generally taken care of by release. Especially when specific drivers and further optimization updates come out. The Graphics options menu is quite detailed and offers a huge variety of extra selection to adjust your visuals.
85/100
Audio: The Audio in Steel Division is good but nothing special. The best part about it I would say is the voice overs that units provide. Battlefield effects sometimes sound a little muffled and indistinguishable but they provide for a certain atmosphere without breaking immersion. You notice some sounds could be better if you stand still and just concentrate on the audio. That being said the music is pretty good but might be a little too powerful or at the forefront for such an intense gameplay. The audio options are somewhat limited in the beta so we hope there will be more options by release.
80/100
Value: The game is set to a Pre-Order value of 39.99 in most countries. Which seems to be a fair price for the amount of content and replayability this game is and will be offering. 3 Unique Singleplayer Campaigns, 16 Divisions and 15 Maps will provide for a lot of gameplay time. Add in the multiplayer in the mix and most fans of RTS games are looking around 100 hours of gameplay here. As of now at the BETA the price might seem a little high since most of the content is not present but one thing is certain there is nothing like Steel Division out there and if you want to get your ww2 strategy itch scratched this is the Pre-Order BETA to buy in to!
85/100

I played the game a lot as a kid (in German at the time, though it was an EXCELLENT localisation) and it's been a pleasure to rediscover it now and discover that it's just as good as I remember.
Very brief description: you control up to six different characters at a time (depending on plot progression and mission), each with unique abilities, and have to make use of them to complete the map with various objectives, usually eliminating or otherwise taking out most enemies in the process.
The plot is fairly interesting, but not the focus. Gameplay is the main pleasure. The controls are extremely intuitive and the design is full of little details that you sometimes have to discover by yourself regarding how best to eliminate the enemies. Often using elaborate lure and distraction tactics. There is usually an easier and more elegant way (involving a specific ability) to get past big obstacles in the game (for example, a gang of bandits showing up to besiege the tower you're trying to kidnap their leader from), but raw persistence and shoot-outs will also eventually solve the problem. AI is pretty good and includes a lot of potential complications for you - mooks tend to band together, send underlings to explore suspicious noises, call for help, etc. Sometimes, but not always, they'll be adept at spotting things out of the ordinary (such as a missing patrol partner or a horse wandering around by itself) and might even raise the alarm just because of that. Enemies tend to be just as good at shooting as the protagonists. Quicksaving and reloading often demonstrates that enemies sometimes take slightly different approaches even to identical situations, so there's a good degree of unpredicability. Quite often, difficult situations arise spontaneously, such as an enemy spotting you when you hadn't realised he was there, or your desperados being held at gunpoint when they were safe just a moment ago. It makes for fairly unpredictable, adrenaline-filled strategising, and these situations can be extremely thrilling. By occasonionally switching up the combination of characters available to you, the game also does a good job forcing you to adapt your tactics and come up with new things. Combat is fairly realistic - shooting lethality and accuracy decreases dramatically with distance, but guns are almost invariably instantly lethal at short range. Most of the characters have a firearm as the primary weapon, but each has a slightly different one - for example a revolver, a rifle, a small handgun, a shotgun, and a long-barrelled Colt that can be converted into a sort of sniper rifle. They all have different attributes in terms of reach, loudness of the shot, reload speed and magazine size, so are best suited for different situations. Care must be taken when shooting if the weapons begin to overheat. The same level of detail and variety applies to the environment, with some elements having different effects on how far sound carries, for example. In short, some very nice gameplay design, thoughtful and detailed without being overcomplicated or ceasing to be intuitive.
Cons: I can't trully come up with negative points for this game except that maybe the story and characters might be a bit too simplistic for some tastes. (Personally, I think it works the same way often simple characterisation for adventure movies works.) In this and other ways, the game is a little bit dated, having come out in 2001. Though I think the graphics, even the 3D movies, actually withstood the test of time very well, it's obviously not on the level of modern games. In terms of characterisation, the overuse of Mexican stereotypes (and Chinese ones, to an extent) would rightfully be seen as too crude today. Though on the flip side, not every game made in 2001 had a multiracial cast that was also one third female, so that deserves some points. On the gameplay side, there were some moments when I felt that the quickest, simplest way through a level relied too much on weaknesses of AI (for example, running towards gunshot sounds into a pile of corpses where you'd hidden a snake in the shadows without a second thought). (Sam's rattlesnake was borderline gamebreaking at points for the body count it had, but it was balanced by how quickly enemies would kill it if they spotted it in advance, and by how few spots were actually suitable for it.)
I recommend this game if you like Commandos-style gameplay coated in a layer of pleasantly familiar Wild West cliches. ;)

After playing for several hours, all I can conclude about this game is that it's
First off, the tutorial lacks a lot of important information.  No mention that you have to build aesthetic stuff all over to keep up morale, no proper explanation of what most of the structures/objects do or why you should care about them.  I lost three bases to everyone flipping out on each other before I pulled up the (terribly-made) wiki and a starter's guide said to scatter cosmetic stuff everywhere to keep people happy.
The interface, while thematically good at first, gets very old very fast.  Every UI element is oversized, and everything flickers like an old TV set with every interaction, and everything has horizontal lines through it like an old computer monitor.  It gets grating and hard on the eyes rather quickly.  Event warnings on the right side of the screen can be minimized (usually), but not dismissed, even for minor alerts, or ones that no longer apply.
You have no direct control over the citizens of your station, which is fine, but it means that when they're all ignoring your orders - which happens fairly often - you can't do anything about it.  The closest you can get to controlling anyone is setting people to the "security" job and setting a beacon  - they'll jog over and stand near the beacon, but that's all you can do.  You can't prioritize commands, or set a "do this first" type thing on anything, so if you need a room built NOW, you have to go across the entire map and cancel every other build/dismantle task.  If things fall into disrepair, technicians take FOREVER to fix them - each time they work on something, they only improve it by a few percentage points, and then wander off again.  You also can't set anyone to do more than one task - a guy can build things, or repair things, but not both unless you constantly toggle his settings in the roster screen.
Raiders and derelict ships spawn far too often and too regularly - it's not at all random.  If you don't get "security" to respond in time to raiders, your citizens will just wander through and drop one by one.  Seriously, multiple times I've lost almost my entire station's population to single raiders because nobody has the sense to run away when they're being shot at, or security gets there one at a time and just drops.
A known bug (I'd say it's a bug, anyway) with derelict ships is that sometimes they'll just "drift away" with your people still on-board.  What this means is that the derelict despawns - taking your people with it.  This means you have to very quickly "claim" every part of the derelict to prevent that, at which point it's treated like part of your base - including constant alerts that it's not connected to the power grid, and citizens will wander over to it and just hang about, making it impossible to safely dismantle.  This also includes warnings about rooms on the ship not being tended to properly, even if you've already flagged everything to be dismantled for materials.  Heaven forbid you don't tend the garden on that ship you plan to scrap (by the way, it mentions this only in passing in the tutorial, but you NEED a garden - it provides food that doesn't eat through your resources like the food-dispenser does.  And you need a bar with full facilities to serve/store that food properly - also only hinted at).
Researching new technologies/illnesses isn't discussed at all in the tutorial, nor does it say how gardens work, or what to do with incapacitated-but-alive raiders.  It doesn't talk about building a brig, or whether you can ever do anything with these raiders - you only find out on third-party guides that EVENTUALLY these raiders can convert to citizens if they're confined long enough.  And your own citizens will freely wander through the brig, even if occupied, and get injured/killed by captured raiders.
"Passing ships" also happen like clockwork, and get spammy.  The sense of humor in all the dialogue is great and everything, but it wears thin after the 200th ship in a 2-hour session, especially since most of the somewhat-limited encounter types seem to play out the exact same way every single time - either they give you more citizens, or they send raiders.  If you tell them to go away, they either go away, send citizens anyway, or send raiders anyway.  And you almost always know exactly what it'll be the moment it pops up.  Passing ships also turn off timelapse - you'll be going along at 4x speed to get something built, then it pops back to 1x so you can tell some guy to bugger off because you have no more room for more people.  And he may still send more citizens, in which case you have to quickly build beds/rooms for them to stay in or they'll start throwing tantrums and send station morale into the toilet.
I'm sure there are other issues I've forgotten to mention, but I think this gives a decent idea of how obnoxious this game is to play in general.

The game starts out seemingly good enough, if a bit basic. I played Freelancer for many years and I love games with ships and customization, and add in the ability to take ships too? Sounds good to me.
This game unfortunately plays poorly. The biggest problem is combat and how the ships control. It's just not fun. You will likely pick a basic transport style ship to start with, maybe with a gun or two. You'll run some trade routes, do some jobs, the money will start coming in. You'll soon pay off your starter ship and now start looking at the next upgrade. You finally get something at least capable of a fight instead of having to flee everything. You get some decent weapons, considering the game shows you all the ones you can get and besides a few really expensive ones - this is the best you're going to get, bigger ships just get more of the same gun with more HP and shields.
As soon as you try to fight a pirate, unless it's a tiny baby ship you'll quickly get destroyed. You can't dodge their attacks, the aiming is literally a la Asteroids. You can't reverse, so combat is painful if you get going too fast in one direction and try to turn as you're always turning against your previous momentum. Go too slow and they just slaughter you. This momentum based flight can work in 3D space combat games, but for this 2D plane game it's awful. Most enemies use lasers and they hone on you like an aimbot. You will not avoid them. Your shields will rapidly deplete and before you know it your ship is disabled and then it's dead.
I had enough money I just went all out on a combat loadout, even snagged some much more powerful weapons off an enemy ship that the AI disabled and made it work on my ship. Nope, the guns are decent but your ship is just paper. You cannot do ANYTHING to stop the onslaught from enemy ships. And it's rarely just one, usually 2 or 3. And sometimes a far more powerful one warps in with torpedoes or something and then you're disabled in almost one hit. Sometimes you leave a planet and a powerful ship is just waiting outside the planet and hits you before you can even move.
Maybe if you suffer through trade run after trade run, job after job for hours and hours you might be able to afford a ship that doesn't just crumble. But the combat at its core just is not fun. Even beating up on the small ships just feels like a game of who does more DPS, the skill involved is absolutely minimal. And trying to have a fleet is a real cluster, it just controls poorly and it's difficult to get them not to destroy a ship that you want to loot or board.
I tried to like this game, but even for free this is just not good. As a game, it's really not fun unless you want to run from every ship that tries to shoot you and do nothing but trade runs for 30+ hours. So many mechanics are just shoddily implemented. There are better and more enjoyable space games out there, save yourself the grind and skip this one.

Old school RTS veteran here, love CoH, love ALB/RD, love WWII.  Played 6 hours of the game last night, and wow man, I am blown away.
Two HUGE design points for me that makes this the best WWII RTS game that I've ever played.  No joke.
One of the things that I enjoy the most from the game right now is how map control is now free from set VP points.  This allows the player to make flanks and thrusts in different areas of the map to apply pressure, and allows a player to be creative and exploitative rather than focus into areas of the map where battle is always contested.  This inadvertently mediates one of the most difficult challenges for RTS developers and that is map design.  The battlefield is now photo-realistic, and with this change in how VPs are collected, maps can be asymmetrical and somehow still work in an RTS.  There is no real one way to play, which in turn expands on the player choices as your unit make-up can be completely different based on location alone.  Overall, this also plays remarkably well with the theme of the genre, where there is a very real feel to the tides of war as the game progresses.  You know, both mentally and visually when you're gaining or losing ground, and when you're about to be surrounded.  This achieves a empathetic connection with the player to the game situation.  Often times when designing games, the "feel" of pressure being applied by the opponent is portrayed in an arbitrary and superficial way:  Units die, or they blow up, so what?  When the entire map turns red around your army after your opponent makes a masterful thrust through an area that you deemed safe, you actually feel dread because you are now cut-off.  This is a vibrant and most-welcomed change to static VP points where the scale of battle centers around those areas and everywhere else is a skirmish.  This is an absolute brilliant way to not only make the battles themselves more realistic, but is a masterstroke in RTS design that I haven't seen in years.
Another thing that I love about the game is the divisions and how it fits with the overall economy design of the game separated by different phases.  Not only do the different divisions come with their own unique flavor because of the unit choices, availability, and veterancy, but they also receive income differently depending on what division they are.  This means the certain divisions can be deliberately stronger than others in earlier phases of the game, but they lose steam as the game progresses because their later game units are not as powerful.  The same could be said about other divisions where they start out weaker, but become powerhouses later on due to their enhanced economy and more powerful units.  This subtly adds additional flavor to the division design and even portrays a sense of story-telling where even when the situation seems dire in the early phases of the game, all is not lost.  At the same time, this concept should also reinforce a particular division's strengths, and players should be wary of that and exploit their opponents' weaknesses not only in unit composition, but also during phases where they are weak.  All-together, this is simply wonderful design:  Not only does this add true identity to the game's different "factions", but it also adds another layer of strategy that otherwise wouldn't exist around the economy system.

So I have about 50 mins/ 1 hour on this game right now and I have to say that I absolutely love what I see so far.
For those of you who have played Eugen's Wargame series (I LOVE Wargame and have 100+ hours in) will relish this game. It's very similar to Wargame but they made some excellent improvements to the strategy genera. Battles are fought in different phases like on a real battlefield. For instance phase A is essentially light infantry, tanks/recon. You are essentially feeling out the enemy, prodding him here and there, seeing where he is weak... light contact. Phase B is an escalation, medium tanks, better infantry..etc. are now available as the light prodding turns into an all brawl with tanks pushing into villages, infantry clawing for every inch of every wood and treeline, artillery starts pounding fighting positions into dust. Phase C is an even higher escalation which supports your phase A and B troops.
I haven't played multiplayer yet but with "10 v 10" brawls you can gleefully guarantee that it'll be real chaos!
My real only gripe that I have is that there are some rough edges here and there with animation/graphics. I'm not too worried about it because I've owned each wargame in their Beta versions and they started out very similarly. By the end of Beta they polished each game up perfectly....I have no doubt this will be much the same.
I really look forward to seeing where Eugen takes this series (I'm hoping and praying for some action on the Eastern Front as well as in the Pacific!)
All in all, well played Eugen...well played!

In my opinion this game is currently (2011) the most enjoyable first person shooter on the market. If your computer can handle the graphics (they're intense) than you will not be disappointed. Although some may prefer the mindless fast-paced killing that exists in the Call of Duty Modern Warfare franchise, I find that this game provides a much more fulfilling experience. It requires more skill and foresight to fully enjoy, but if you are willing to put the time and effort (it takes patience - not running and gunning) into learning how to play you will appreciate the difference in gameplay and style. Although there is a single-player campaign, this game is primarily a multiplayer game. The single player campaign is mediocre but enjoyable (nothing like COD's excitement) but the multiplayer is where the game really shines. The fully destructible environments create an experience where every match can be different and you can surprise your opponents at the flip of a coin. 10/10 stars.

A highly entertaining western strategy game with a variety of characters and unique abilites, which makes a large number of possible strategies and outcomes. A game I have always come back to over the years and have always enjoyed. Unfortunately, there are many problems with this version of the game: many people experience extreme lag on anything above Windows 8 (so I'm told), which doesn't affect me since I fortunately have a computer that runs Windows 7, but even then, the game will freeze every 20-30 minutes, which can make playing this game very frustrating. If I was new to this game when I purchased the Steam version, I would have given up after about the 2nd level. Needs to be fixed, but this doesn't seem likely to happen anytime soon.

In all honesty, this is one of the best games ever made. BUT it's unplayable on anything newer than Windows 8, which is incredibly sad. Sure, there is some thingy that will make it run with more than 7 fps, but the developer should do something about it.
That being sad, if you have an old PC or Laptop, with that I mean something with an OS that's Win7 or older - install Steam there and play this jewel of a game. This game got it all: some of the most athmospheric western music, absolutely badass characters, great and creative level design, superb voice-acting (I'm playing the German version, so I can't say anything about the English one) and some of the smartest AI I've ever seen: enemies will group up and investigate together, they will get suspicious if one of their friends is suddenly gone and will investigate, and they will even do things like kicking dynamite-sticks you throw at them right back in your face if your not careful.
My rating of this game would be:
Sound: 9/10 High quality, some gunsounds (Sam's Winchester for example) sound a bit weird
Music: 10/10 Absolutely amazing
Graphics: 10/10 It's an old game, yes, but it looks colourful, alive and detailed
Story: 8/10 A western through and through, but with a surprising twist in the end.
Characters: 10/10 You WILL love band of misfits you're playing as
Challenge and Leveldesign: 10/10 Some missions are easy, and some are REALLY DANG HARD. There is one mission where you're not allowed to get spotted in a certain area of the map, which is a little sucky, but it makes sense story wise and can easily sneak around that area, so it's simply a little extra challenge.
Overall: 10/10
It's simply amazing, especially for how old it is. For me personally, it is one my very first games ever, and it's still fun and feels fresh today. It's right up there in my top 5 games, together with games like Metal Gear Solid 3 and Civilization IV.

Buyers guide to Transistor (as unbiased as possible).
What you'll get from buying this game:
-Story:
An elaborated story that places the focus on the protagonist (and her talking ironing board/weapon/partner). The fully voiced narration is a mix of on-the-spot quips and exposition. Additionally to the narration you'll get text documents from the weapons menu and in-game billboards. You'll understand the setting and story as you progress through the game (warning: the text documents are in advanced English, which might be difficult for non-native English speakers).
-Gameplay (action/puzzles):
-Action: In this action/rpg you'll be progressing through several locations in which you'll have several encounters with a group of enemies. There's no running away from or avoiding encounters. As you progress though the game you'll aquire several moves (called functions) which can be used as an active move, a booster to an active move or/and as a status booster. This system encourages you to experiment with all the moves to see which playstyle suits you best. During an encounter you can choose to fight directly (click-to-attack) or in a sequence of pre-planned moves (called a Turn). After a Turn, your weapon needs some time to recharge, during which you can't perform any moves (just run around to avoid damage). It's possible your Turn won't have the desired effect because the enemies are moving, are protected or because your aim was wrong. It's possible to artificially make encounters harder by activating boosters for enemies (called limiters). Activating limiters yields more EXP.
- Puzzles: the main campaign barely contains any puzzles. Yet similar to Supergiant Games Bastion there are locations which have nothing to do with the main campaign (called Backdoors) in which you'll find challenges. Some of these challenges are puzzles.
-Graphics:
The lay-out is hand drawn, the menus are all neon-like and there are many filters to add to the atmosphere of this game. Animation is fluid if your computer is strong enough.
-Soundtrack:
As far as I can place music in a genre, I would say it's a mix of Jazz and Alternative music. Some tracks are sung by Ash Barett, who also performed in the game Bastion. Most of time during the campaign, you can make your protagonist hum to the soundtrack with the voice of Ash Barett.
-Unlockables (in-game/ additional to game):
-In-game: (See chapter Gameplay/action). While experimenting with your moves, you'll unlock the text documents which explain the setting of the story. As you progress through the game, the Backdoors will give you more challenges to complete. By completing these challenges, you'll unlock soundtracks which can be only heard in these Backdoors.
- Additional: After completing the game you'll unlock New-Game Plus (called Recursion). In Recursion, you keep your moves you previously have unlocked and the enemies are harder.
-Tips for purchasing
- Check out other reviews (I personally always follow Zero Punctuation's Yahtzee's reviews because he points out the bad things in a game. Link to his review of Transistor :

- Check out the OST and the Extended OST on YouTube before you purchase. If you like it, then buy the bundle which includes the OST (most of the time it's cheaper this way).
- Check out reviews of Bastion. Transistor is similar to Bastion and is from the same creators. Steam might bundle those games together with the soundtrack which can save you some money.
- Wait until SuperGiant Games Pyres release for the same reasons stated above.
-Personal opinion (for what it's worth):
I liked this game in general for it's atmosphere, gameplay, story, setting, soundtrack, in-game unlockables and encouragement of experimentation.
Yet I disliked the imbalance of puzzles and action, its hard English (I'm not a native English-speaker) and the limited additional-to-game unlockables.

I'd been looking in to the possibility of running through this games since the days of release on Xbox 360.....then again on the Definitive Edition release for PS4/XBOX One. It wasn't until I joined the PC "Master Race" and saw the game on sale for £4 that I thought "sod it, why not".......and I'm glad I did!
As a huge fan of GTA5 (and the series in general, plus similar open world games), I half expected this game to be a massive dissapointment in comparison. If anything, it's clear this game had some positive influence towards GTA5 (yes of course, Sleeping Dogs is a blatant GTA series copy, albeit set in Hong Kong) in regards to the huge amount of side quests/tasks and general things to do to keep you entertained outside of the main quest. Everything from gambling,♥♥♥♥♥♥fights and races to drug busts and criminal investigations are present. Not to mention the dating aspect of the game, if that's your thing. For me, this is better than GTA4 but not overall as good as GTA 5.
The combat is awesome - best in any game I remember. The driving is solid. The world is huge but feels busy and alive (this was one of my biggest gripes with Watch Dogs. The world felt dead). The shooting is spot on. Worst case, everything in this game works well, best case it's awesome.
On to the main quest....again, amazing. Not hugely long (15 hours or so for me, at a reasonable pace), which I quite like as it doesn't drag out, but very well thought out, with unexpected twists and turns alongside interesting and very likeable (plus hateable where they're supposed to be) characters. You feel genuine emotion towards allies that become close to Wei, with genuine sadness when things don't always end well. As far as being loyal to police, or siding with the triads - this becomes more confusing (in a good way) due to the corruption involved, particularly on 'the correct side of the law' side.
My only real issues with this game came from either optimisation, or niggles with my own hardware. I found at times the game would turn on and everything seemed in turbo mode, albeit fine after a reboot. Other times, my fps would for no obvious reason drop as low as 30-40 fps with an i5 6600k @ 4.4ghz, 16gb DDR4 2,400mhz RAM and a GTX 970. I have no issues with much newer, more graphically demanding games. Seems to be a problem across the internet in trying to find advice on some forums....
Overall, a great game and well worth it - particularly if you can pick it up on sale.

I don’t recommend playing this game on bigger size of galaxy when vs AI – the map is big enough anyway and tbh size differences in the galaxy settings are very small increments. The only reason I’d choose the bigger galaxy sizes is if I have all 8 factions in play, and most crucially playing it in multiplayer. The distance between systems vs the speed of the ships is really far and AI has an awful tendency to snatch the best planets from under your nose making all the empire borders look as a checkered patchwork of planets on the bigger maps.
Good:
+ Has multiplayer (every 4X tbs should imo) including LAN
+ You can scan planets to find out their bonuses (but this at times feels like a waste of time)
+ During exploration you find special debris that works as a special encounter
+ You can give speeches for glory-hole points
+ The type of government your empire has depends on your policies
+ I like the in-game music
+ You can do diplomacy with pirate clans - even use them to harass your enemies (AI factions will make sure they harass you anyway)
+ Different factions to play (8 total) – tech tree and buildings seem identical while govt type, faction bonuses, preferred planets and ship models differ
+ Trading cards
+ Diplomacy
+ Trade routes
+ Random events
+ Turn based battles on hex battlefield
Bad:
- Multiplayer is human only. The game won’t let you add AI factions to play with you and your friends when you play multiplayer
- Only two types (shapes) of galaxy to choose from disc or circle
- Four main galaxy ambient backgrounds, nice bluish ones or an ugly muddy mustard ones
- Reloading saved games is very bugged often creating weird things and most importantly – loading the next turn instead the one you saved the game at.
- No sound in intro movies for me (have to watch them straight from the game folder in explorer to just get the vibe)
- Alt-tab doesn’t work
- No schematic view for ship designs you’ve already created makes it hard to remember what design had what module
- Cycling between planets is bugged, if you go left then right… it will take you to the wrong planet, so basically you can cycle them just one way at a time
- Game does feel empty at times, so I recommend you play it with good buddies to actually make up for less actual content
Ugly:
- AI cheats, especially during colonization phase. AI factions have colony ships spawn out of nowhere right next to the planet you were on the way to colonize flying there over 10 turns. And in fact, if you load a save 3 turns earlier or so, their colony ship might spawn even sooner and it’s kind of like random which AI faction will it be, including those far far away from the colony you’re aiming for
- AI cheats and gets at least 8 warships at the start of the game when they couldn’t possibly make them so fast (every AI faction gets it, not just the more industrious ones)
- When you load the game your ships will all be crippled to 5AU speed instead of full speed, which further compounds the planet stealing by AI or outmaneuvering you since you won’t even be able to reach the target planet even if you adjust your planning with reloading the save
- You can put more than 1 type of weapon on a ship design, but during a battle you can shoot only 1 weapon type at once per ship, while in practice this might make sense for you to say use missiles if enemy is away then beam/plasma when close, in practice you start the battle very close so firing long range loses the benefit and the limited number of hulls available in the game (4) makes it practically pointless to mix weapon types
- There’s no experience on the ships, so fighting AI (pirates or other factions) is a chore, even on easy difficulty because they keep getting tons of new ships out of nowhere, while you need to keep sending your own at them over and over eventually running out of cash unless you have a very strong economy already. The good thing is that other than pirates AI factions tend to be rather peaceful so I’m not saying it’s impossible to beat them, it’s just far more frustrating and time consuming experience you would want
The game also has a “total war” option which puts all AI factions at war with each other since the beginning of the game, which theoretically might be better (haven’t tried it myself) but I worry it might make things worse and with the level of AI cheating they would simply all gang up on you from the start which is not fun at all.
I must be the lucky one because so far the game hasn’t crashed for me even once.
Bottom line is, it’s an overpriced, often frustrating 4X game with bluntly cheating AI. I still probably recommend it if you want to play it in multiplayer (just remember, no AI factions in multi) but mostly because I love space 4X games so that is my bias.

Concept: a band of four prisoners is taken to the dungeon of Grimrock for their crimes, where none thus far have ever escaped.
Gameplay: despite its appearance, it is NOT turn-based. It's realtime, although most enemies' movements have LONG delays. You navigate on a strict grid and cannot cut diagonals. The combat consists of clicking weapons and hoping for special attacks, or clicking magic and casting your own damn spell. Not that the rune system really helps you.
Graphics: look closely and you'll notice that the texture on the face of every wall is exactly the same. The graphics, even aside from the walls, are pretty lazy, although the monsters are fine. However, the headbobbing of moving around is a wonderful way to get sick.
Audio: no music. Just generic, boring ambience and a single audio effect for each monster that you get to hear 20 times a minute.
Difficulty: dungeon crawler. It has difficulty settings, although I have only played one difficulty thus far, so I've no idea what the difficulty affects.
Synopsis: hardly worth $15(but I got it cheaper) unless you're really into dungeon crawlers.

Full Review:
Big discussions arose about the Early Access programm and kickstarted games. Leaving that aside I wanna focus purely on the game, that I got bundled in a Humble Bundle when it was still Alpha and played several times until its current version.
The premise and style of the game seemed enticing to me: Build and manage a space station with room for crew and their needs. I like space and sci-fi settings, plus the whole base-management had a Theme Hospital-like feel to it, which was also a great and creative game.
So I started out in space and began building. The game doesn’t offer a campaign, you basically free-build and manage your base from scratch. After a few basic rooms for living quarters, refining asteroids and oxygen supply your base begins to take shape. An intercom window pops up: other space drifters saw my station and want to join my effort. Randomized events like this keep things interesting and challenging. Not all encounters are friendly and you need to be ready for intruders - or pay the costs.
The building and managing is fun and keeps me entertained: There are some fun ideas in Spacebase DF-9 that I really like. Your base-dwellers for example post about their wants and needs in their social media “Spaceface”, where you can read how they feel and if they are happy with their occupation. The rooms and objects have good ideas that tie into each other: Plants can not only produce food but also oxygen. The food you produce can be brought into the pub for cooking. When fire breaks out you can not only use fire extinguishers but you can also cut off the oxygen supply to a room - though this usually takes longer and damages your equipment.
All these ideas and concept sound fun - on paper. In the game however they can get buggy and very frustrating. The power management for example can get very messy as the only data I have is a bunch of colorful lines across your base. I don’t see how much reach a generator has and how much power is being drawn. New derelicts appear out of nowhere that are so close to my base that my building plans are screwed. And several times my crewmembers kill themselves by simply staying in space until their oxygen runs out or not fleeing a empty vessel that runs out of oxygen. This is very frustrating and something that doesn’t feel like its the players fault. The build-queue is also not very clear as my crew builds rooms but just doesn’t make time to build the door that would connect them - ordering them useless.
All in all Spacebase DF-9 is a game that had great promise but will never live up to it because bugs ruin the experience. I tried, I spent the time to build a big base and train my crew to fight back an alien invasion - but when the same men later just suffocate by standing in an room without oxygen, I just feel like its not my fault, its the games. And I don’t want to play it any more.

Listen.  I love this game.  It's one of a kind.  If you like metroidvania type games you should definitely check it out especially when it's only 2.99 right now on sale.  What makes it so unique compared to other games of the kind is that every level is a tile on the turn based strategy game portion, and what level you will want to do is going to be decided by what you need to be happening strategically.
What makes the game such a fun challenge is that each tile has a difficulty percentage that can vary widely depending on different factors including what is happening in the strategy portion.  So, you might really need to open up a section of a map that's blocked by a tile with %500 difficulty level, but have fun with those crazy fast enemies and projectiles that knock off a third of your health, but hey, you gotta do what you gotta do.  Or, what if you can't make it through?  Time to rethink your strategy,  work on earning enough coins to hire mercenaries to open it up for you, tweak your character to go for speed over health, or or whatever else you can think of.  The world has it's own rules and mysteries and a lot of the fun is these things slowly becoming apparent to you as you play.
What I love about the game is all the variety in the side scrolling action and it's effect in making your strategy come together to win the game.  I think personally this game is tied with Red Faction Guerilla for most underrated, but this probably even more for all the hate it gets from people that can't look past its subpar graphics to see the amazing gameplay and feeling of being in a coherent world with its own inherent logic all coming together in a challenging and satisfying experience.  Just like other Arcen games there are lots of difficulty settings, I suggest you crank it up a bit.

Buyers guide to Transistor (as unbiased as possible).
What you'll get from buying this game:
-Story:
An elaborated story that places the focus on the protagonist (and her talking ironing board/weapon/partner). The fully voiced narration is a mix of on-the-spot quips and exposition. Additionally to the narration you'll get text documents from the weapons menu and in-game billboards. You'll understand the setting and story as you progress through the game (warning: the text documents are in advanced English, which might be difficult for non-native English speakers).
-Gameplay (action/puzzles):
-Action: In this action/rpg you'll be progressing through several locations in which you'll have several encounters with a group of enemies. There's no running away from or avoiding encounters. As you progress though the game you'll aquire several moves (called functions) which can be used as an active move, a booster to an active move or/and as a status booster. This system encourages you to experiment with all the moves to see which playstyle suits you best. During an encounter you can choose to fight directly (click-to-attack) or in a sequence of pre-planned moves (called a Turn). After a Turn, your weapon needs some time to recharge, during which you can't perform any moves (just run around to avoid damage). It's possible your Turn won't have the desired effect because the enemies are moving, are protected or because your aim was wrong. It's possible to artificially make encounters harder by activating boosters for enemies (called limiters). Activating limiters yields more EXP.
- Puzzles: the main campaign barely contains any puzzles. Yet similar to Supergiant Games Bastion there are locations which have nothing to do with the main campaign (called Backdoors) in which you'll find challenges. Some of these challenges are puzzles.
-Graphics:
The lay-out is hand drawn, the menus are all neon-like and there are many filters to add to the atmosphere of this game. Animation is fluid if your computer is strong enough.
-Soundtrack:
As far as I can place music in a genre, I would say it's a mix of Jazz and Alternative music. Some tracks are sung by Ash Barett, who also performed in the game Bastion. Most of time during the campaign, you can make your protagonist hum to the soundtrack with the voice of Ash Barett.
-Unlockables (in-game/ additional to game):
-In-game: (See chapter Gameplay/action). While experimenting with your moves, you'll unlock the text documents which explain the setting of the story. As you progress through the game, the Backdoors will give you more challenges to complete. By completing these challenges, you'll unlock soundtracks which can be only heard in these Backdoors.
- Additional: After completing the game you'll unlock New-Game Plus (called Recursion). In Recursion, you keep your moves you previously have unlocked and the enemies are harder.
-Tips for purchasing
- Check out other reviews (I personally always follow Zero Punctuation's Yahtzee's reviews because he points out the bad things in a game. Link to his review of Transistor :

- Check out the OST and the Extended OST on YouTube before you purchase. If you like it, then buy the bundle which includes the OST (most of the time it's cheaper this way).
- Check out reviews of Bastion. Transistor is similar to Bastion and is from the same creators. Steam might bundle those games together with the soundtrack which can save you some money.
- Wait until SuperGiant Games Pyres release for the same reasons stated above.
-Personal opinion (for what it's worth):
I liked this game in general for it's atmosphere, gameplay, story, setting, soundtrack, in-game unlockables and encouragement of experimentation.
Yet I disliked the imbalance of puzzles and action, its hard English (I'm not a native English-speaker) and the limited additional-to-game unlockables.
Amazing soundtrack, great game play, interesting story. What else can one want?
Simply amazing.

This game is legit the best MMORPG I've ever played, and let me tell you why:
1. CLASSES: Every class there is in the game (And there are a lot), you can play on the same character. No need to restart the game every time you wanna try a new class. You just perform an instantaneous class change to the class you want, almost whenever you want.
2. BALANCE: The classes are also very balanced. Yes, like all games, some stand out from the rest, but at the same time there is no obsolete class, you can play the game under any role you want and still have an excellent performance. Also, there are constant updates which aim to balance the classes, so if something gets too OP/UP, its gonna be sensibly nerfed/buffed sooner or later.
3. CONTENT: The amount of content in the game is astounding. I've played 500+ hours and I've barely scratched the surface. Dungeons, Trials, Raids, PVP, Side Quests, you really can't count all the things you can do in this game. And it all gets frequently updated, so the amount of content grows even larger every patch.
4. GRAPHICS: For an MMORPG, this game has astounding graphics, and beautiful scenery to go with it. It doesn't even require that much computer power to run at high settings. Often were the times when I switched my Class to Fisherman and admired the scenery while I waited for the fish to bite. I'd be surprised to find an MMORPG with better graphics.
5. COMMUNITY: The people in this game are marvelous. Generally, if you manage to screw something up in a dungeon, rare are the times where people get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at you. What often happens instead is that your party members stop for you and explain what you did wrong and help you make your life easier with helpful tips. It's also very easy to be accepted into a Free Company (Guilds in this game), making the social aspect of the game very easy to approach. And for those of you who don't like interacting with other players, the game accomodates you by implementing a system that pairs you up with other random people if you don't have a party of your own.
6. STORY: When was the last time you ever played an MMO with a good story? Because let me tell you, they ain't easy to find. This game is one rare example of that. Aside a few obvious exceptions, the characters are all likeable and have a satisfying amount of depth to them, and the plot itself is surprisingly well written. Now, its not why I play the game at all, but for those of you who require a good story to play a game, this one won't let you down.
All in all, this game is the source of many fond memories of mine, and I'm sure most fans of the genre will have a marvelous time with it as well. I hope this review helped someone join, an if it did, I hope to see y'all online!

It is highly intriguing and elicits quite a few time-sensitive questions on a relevant topic today... for everyone. Whether you are concerned about Contagion, Plagues, last-days scenarios, or bio-terrorism; Plague, Inc. is there.
It doesn't take too many play-throughs to realize that not all diseases are created equal. But, the game does draw you to multiple play-throughs, as you spin out each scenario, captivated by the results of minor changes in your strategy. The game starts with a basic menu of disease types in the main-game portion: Bacteria, Virus, Fungus, Parasite, Prion, Nano-Virus, Neurax Worm, Bio-Weapon, and finally Necroa (Zombies) and the Simian Flu for those who want to turn Earth into the Planet of the Apes.
The game is overflowing with feature-rich side scenarios; from real diseases past and present like The Black Death and Smallpox, to the fantasy diseases like Pirate Plague and spreading Christmas Joy, and myriads of others. And, if that weren't enough to keep you busy with the 142 achievements, they have included a workshop, so you can download community made scenarios and/or create and share your own.
The premise is simple enough. You create a new disease and your goal is to watch it spread around the world. Naturally, since it is a game, you can't win by simply covering continents. You must wipe out humanity for a victory. You are able to name your disease, and choose the genetic traits, as well as the symptoms and the transmission traits for spreading the disease, whether it is something that spreads from insects, birds, by air, or sea... etc. Then, as humanity fights for a cure, you try to stop the cure before you've covered the planet.
I originally reviewed the game in early access. The game has gone through many updates, and since then I was able to participate in the alpha and beta testing phases for multiplayer, which was added to the game along with the full release. So, I've updated this review to reflect all changes.
The game has given me more than 150 hours of fun in early release, and now with over 300 hours in-game, I am still exploring all the fun and challenging levels. When I first started exploring this fascinating game, I found I was able to beat the Virus and Bacteria easily; finishing off both in one play-through each. But, I found the Fungus Disease and the Black Death scenario both to be very difficult to spread before they were cured by Scientists. But, they all are accomplished with time. The game definitely contributes to obsessive personality traits, like repeated hand-washing, and 12 hour gaming sessions.
I managed to turn the Earth into a 'Planet of the Apes' with my own Simian Flu on the 2nd try. The first time, I had tried to develop the rampage gene. It didn't spread far before the humans managed to develop a cure. Too aggressive! So, I slowed it down a bit, and worked on the Simian side of the coin; developing colonies of apes, and making it spread among them, while increasing their intelligence. When the Earth was covered, I added deadly symptoms to finish it off with one quarter of the ape population surviving the human drone attacks, which were colossal-scale.
The game is imaginative and rich in story, not-surprisingly since plague is the story of civilization. The main game plays out on a world map. If you watch the news bits, and little popups, you see that some countries begin to execute and/or bomb whole cities of the infected, out of hysteria and fear. The disease spreads in real-time, as you are making changes in the control panel to try to counter-balance the reactions of the humans to your disease. But, there are speed and pause buttons for those who want to control the action. Also, in the single-player, opening up map and disease screens automatically pauses the game so you can get back to bursting dna bubbles when you are finished making changes.
I've already decided that Greenland is the place to go in the case of world contageon. They are so isolated that many games are lost simply because Greenland closes their ports to prevent the plague spreading.
The graphics are first-rate; utilizing a variety of color and fx cues to help you monitor the situation as it develops. The different countries are covered with the color of your disease, and then turn to black as the humans there all die. The control windows are amply stocked with a variety of graphs and charts to analyze your disease's progress, and at game's end, to analyze why you won or lost. The music is intense and dramatic. Different sound bits include children singling "Ring Aaround the Roses" which was a children's song from the Middle ages about the Bubonic Plague.
You can choose games with friends, random matches, co-op or versus mode. Leader boards let you know how your opponent ranks. The multiplayer community is already spreading and many more are dying for a chance to win the co-op brutal achievement. These achievements, though easy to obtain if you have a good working partnership, would probably be more difficult if you don't chat or talk to the other player to coordinate. You can't play "by the seat of your pants" here. It takes team-work.
*High Strategy and realistic simulation gaming at it's finest
*Multiplayer Vs. & Co-op
*Extreme Replay Factor
*High level of control-The element of choice makes you feel like a Superman in game. When you make small changes, big things happen.
*Friendship forming- You will develop close partnerships in the multiplayer co-op, because you won't win otherwise.
*You will not finish this game in under 100 hours. My testing buddy 100% it in under 200 hours, even with all the beta testing hours. I'm not finished yet.
*Though guides are certainly helpful, having a list of steps won't guarantee success because your timing and decisions effect results.

On to the one pro I've found so far for the game... the hex-based, turn-based space combat is actually a quite interesting addition to the 4x space genre, and one that I quite like. Admittedly, it can turn into a bit of a chore once the participants have large fleets, if you can get to that stage... but I do like the idea.
However... the game is plagued with a multitude of crashes, which makes any sort of progress, especially in multiplayer, very frustrating. Even when you're lucky enough to not encounter a Crash to Desktop, the gameplay itself is not quite up to scratch. The tech tree and units are somewhat disappointing, and there are many better games out there if you want to customise your own space ships as part of your plans for galactic domination - which brings me to my next point - the galactic maps are pretty sub-par. It doesn't look nice, the travel is boring (there are no restrictions or wormholes or gravity wells or any other mechanic) between systems. There is an arbitrary limit on which systems you can travel though, in an expanding circle, but I have not been able to figure out how that works, but apart from that, you can travel to any system without any changes.
And the economic and diplomatic options are both also disappointing. This combos with the 8 "different races" you can play as or against - they don't look or feel different, and the bonuses and "unique generals" aren't very noticeable. In combination with the lack of options, and a lack of descriptions of the various pre-game setup options... it just doesn't make for a compelling experience.
Especially for the asking price, you can do so much better if you are after a 4x space strategy game.

I'd been looking in to the possibility of running through this games since the days of release on Xbox 360.....then again on the Definitive Edition release for PS4/XBOX One. It wasn't until I joined the PC "Master Race" and saw the game on sale for £4 that I thought "sod it, why not".......and I'm glad I did!
As a huge fan of GTA5 (and the series in general, plus similar open world games), I half expected this game to be a massive dissapointment in comparison. If anything, it's clear this game had some positive influence towards GTA5 (yes of course, Sleeping Dogs is a blatant GTA series copy, albeit set in Hong Kong) in regards to the huge amount of side quests/tasks and general things to do to keep you entertained outside of the main quest. Everything from gambling,♥♥♥♥♥♥fights and races to drug busts and criminal investigations are present. Not to mention the dating aspect of the game, if that's your thing. For me, this is better than GTA4 but not overall as good as GTA 5.
The combat is awesome - best in any game I remember. The driving is solid. The world is huge but feels busy and alive (this was one of my biggest gripes with Watch Dogs. The world felt dead). The shooting is spot on. Worst case, everything in this game works well, best case it's awesome.
On to the main quest....again, amazing. Not hugely long (15 hours or so for me, at a reasonable pace), which I quite like as it doesn't drag out, but very well thought out, with unexpected twists and turns alongside interesting and very likeable (plus hateable where they're supposed to be) characters. You feel genuine emotion towards allies that become close to Wei, with genuine sadness when things don't always end well. As far as being loyal to police, or siding with the triads - this becomes more confusing (in a good way) due to the corruption involved, particularly on 'the correct side of the law' side.
My only real issues with this game came from either optimisation, or niggles with my own hardware. I found at times the game would turn on and everything seemed in turbo mode, albeit fine after a reboot. Other times, my fps would for no obvious reason drop as low as 30-40 fps with an i5 6600k @ 4.4ghz, 16gb DDR4 2,400mhz RAM and a GTX 970. I have no issues with much newer, more graphically demanding games. Seems to be a problem across the internet in trying to find advice on some forums....
Overall, a great game and well worth it - particularly if you can pick it up on sale.

Endless sky [v 0.9.6] should rather be called Mindless sky because You will be pushing buttons and the game will do the rest for You. Sure, You push buttons in every computer game, but this game... well, it feels like working on an assembly line.
Before automation!
Example? To get from one planet to the next, which is 3 jumps away, You select the target on the map using your mouse and after that you can turn off your brain. Because you simply have to push a button, your ship will allign itself automatically with the target system and jump there. You repeat that twice and you should be in range for your target planet. How do you land? Well, just push a different button and your ship will land for you.
And the combat is not so different since your ship will allign with its target when it is in range and you push the fire button.
As a trader it took me 'round about 1.5h to pay off the loan from the bank. Then it would take another 2h to be able to buy the next ship. And I maxed out my freight capacity. Yeah, you can modify your ship. But the modules available leave me with a wish for more. So either the price for the next possible ship should be lowered or maybe some modules should be added, which are more expensive but UPgrade your ship.
The game has a tutorial (which help you to get started) and it appears to have a story (something about a civil war), which starts after the loan has been repaid, but I didn't had the nerves to try that.
Don't get me wrong. Endless Sky has potential. The movement in space is realistic. You can not fly around like in other space games. If you move into a direction and turn your ship, you will stille be flying into that direction. You have a huge variety of earning money. From transportation to bounty hunting, it's there.
Endless Sky has potential but there is work to be done.

This game is very similar to the Escape Velocity series. For those unfamiliar with these games, they centered around going to different planets and star systems to trade goods and make deliveries to earn money and buy a bigger ship to trade more goods and make larger deliveries to earn even more money. There is also combat and piracy in a top-down 2D space setting.
Endless Sky is very similar in format to this; you are a pilot who has just started out with a bottom-tier ship and just enough money to get by. You can basically do whatever you want: explore the distant reaches of space, do piracy and steal from other ships to earn money, join a militia and save the universe, etc. The storylines are well-done and interesting to read. The world is expansive and continues to grow with new updates. Despite the game technically being unfinished at this time, there is more than enough content to keep any player satisfied for countless hours.
Plus, it's free.
The only problem really is the fact that it is still in an incomplete state. Some storylines have not been implemented yet and one is being released in segments with each update. This can be frustrating at times due to the long periods between updates. Other than that, there aren't many if any major gameplay bugs or much that affects the overall quality of the game.

A real challenger to the Call of Duty series. Bringing a totally different gameplay style to the FPS community. Combine vehicle combat and infantry tactics to build large scale battles. Not only does it take skill but it takes tactics as well to win any battle.
I truly enjoyed the combat in this game. Rush was my all-time favorite game mode. Requiring teams to work together to destroy MCOM stations. Coordinating vehicles and squads was a big part of Rush to be succesful. Or, having an opposing team that only uses sniper rifles.
The so called 'realism' of the game immerses the player into the battlefield and makes large scale battles feel so much more engaging. Though it's still possible to cross-map snipe someone using an SMG, pistol, or shotgun slugs, it just adds to the 'Only in Battlefield' feeling.
Because it is testing platform for the Battlefield series, it isn't a full Battlefield series as we know it, such as Battlefield 2, but rather a mini-series and to show what's to come in Battlefield 3.
Right now I would not suggest buying BC2 but rather wait for B3, but if you really want a great FPS to play I would highly recommend this game.
