King of Fighters XIII Steam Edition is PC ported version of Beloved The King of Fighters XIII(TM) released in Console (PS3 / Xbox 360) with additional improvement such as minor bug fixes and balance patch and significantly improved net code.
As a Fighting game, Contrary to many belief and rumor, King of Fighter is one easiest fighting game to start jump in playing without 'input assist' on the market. Thanks to versatile and powerful movement option and clean game play, players can easily start the game without thinking concept such as linking or set up.
Combo is mostly direct and there is many combo that can be done with What You See Is What You Get without complex timing issue. With systemic assist such as button holding, short cuts, and longer registration -early input- kicking in even you don't realize they're helping you to remove pesky timing errors in combos you can perform.
While it is KOF XIII's Trial mode is indeed considered as hardest trial mode in all fighting game and that's true - But never be afraid, you don't need them, and with Drive / Hyper drive cancel system you can enjoy making your own combo in practice and use them actively.
If you're just in to enjoy playing fighting game with small group, or single and practice mode. You're in for treat. If you're in competitive play, KOF XIII will provide you with honest choice of any character being able to dominate opponent regardless what character they have picked.
Netcode wise, KOF XIII Steam Edition relies heavily on player's computer spec, meaning lacking certain capability in processor, etc can actually actively effect net code and slow down both player from playing it. However, there is usually good chance to find someone you can play or teach you as fan bases of KOF series are very dedicated to this game.
If you're a fighting game fan, don't wait to pick this up. Even you're not, you might check it out when there is discount going around. With multiple innovative, unique and lovable characters and fascinating move, great sound track that captivated Asian Game Communities since 1994. You will find something you will like.

Lets leave aside the fact that the game isn't finished, shall we? Double fine decided its done, so lets look at this as a finished product
Spacebase DF-9 is The Sims, but in space. I know what youre thinking, I was hyped too. You can assign different jobs to different citizens and theyll like it a certain amount. Your citizens will scurry around and converse with each other about inane things like space mudcrabs. You can select asteroids to be mined, which works kinda. You can get other people to come by and ask to join your space-hovel, and supposedly they might even try to do other things, but that never happened in my playthrough. You can send you citizens to go and explore derelict ships, and they will find things. You can build rooms, and put things in those rooms, and your citizen will use them. You can give those rooms different named functions, and your citizen will use them for those functions. Spacebase DF-9 is The Sims, but in space.
Pros:
-Aesthetic: If you can count on Double Fine for anything, its that their stuff always looks good. The semi-retro looks of the interface and the hand drawn aliens look nice and stylized. Sending your citizens off to investigate a derelict ship is always a harrowing affair, as the ship is completely dark, with red warning lights flashing ominously through the hallways. Even if you have no idea whats coming, the atmosphere of the ship makes you anticipate losing a few citizens. One fult is that the play space looks very flat, even though your citizens, while in space suits, can go under your space-hovel, which was very confusing the first few times.
-Sound: The soundtrack is short but nice. Ambient trance music has a soft spot in my ear canal, but I found the music very nice, even though it will be seen as repetitive to some. If you dont like, it, you can always mute it and play Eminem, or what have you.
-Core gameplay: The game mechanics I described above are very good, and makes the base of a great sim game. I'll elaborate more on this in the negatives.
-Fun alien designs: I like the designs of the aliens. I didnt see two aliens who looked exactly alike in my playthrough, besides the two humans I started with. Reminds me of Star Wars!
Negatives:
-It isn't Psychonauts. Lets all face facts, the main reason we all buy Double Fine games is in hopes of another wacky, fun game like Psychonauts. It doesnt need to be a Psychonauts game, it just needs to have the same spirit (Although, I'm still holding out hope that if I keep buying DF games, they'll eventually make Psychonauts 2). The plain fact of the matter is that this has none of that spirit. Spacebase DF-9 is as sterile a gaming experience as there is to be found. The most funny thing I did was purposefully suffocate my citizens in the bar. Forshame, Double Fine.
-The gameplay is completely flat. As in grossly, sadly, boringly flat. If you have played 30 minutes of DF-9, you have played 30 hours of DF-9. With the exeption of the rare derlict ships, I spent most of my game watching netflix on the other monitor. Even the derelict ships suck in a way, since even with their mystery, it takes too much time and resource to explore and kill the monsters inside for it to be worth it, since all your citizens will be terrible at fighting. In other games, like the Sims 4, this could be remedied with patches and DLC, but Double Fine has no intention to patch or make DLC for this game, and so were tuck with the husk of a potentially great game.
Ending score: 4/10. A passable game that works just fine but because of its pedigree should be a while lot better than it is. If you really need your fix of a Space Station simulation game, try Space Colony on GOG, if you need a Sims-esque game, just go back to the Sims. If you want a fun Double Fine game, just play Psychonauts or Brutal Legend again.

Be advised, I'm not a Dark Souls person. If you want a review from somebody who likes Dark Souls, I won't be able to provide that for you. Sorry.
The Good:
-The high level concept was great. Defeat your opponents, use their stuff to progress.
-Every enemy is a serious challenge
-I honestly enjoyed running around exploring
The Okay:
-The combat system is... okay. When I started the blocking option didn't work, and more often than not I was winning by luck more than anything.
The Bad:
-Too few enemy types/exoframes. There are around six of them, which is dissipointing.
-Weapons are designed in a fashion which rewards you with extra damage for using them. Which takes away any desire to swap to different weapons. Why would I switch to a new weapon which does significantly less damage? I used the weapon from the first boss until the end of the game.
-I hated the bosses. I never found them fun, and without a guide I just got my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me. Honestly they felt like a punishing roadblock to the only part of the game I liked, exploring.
-The story.... oh god.... I know people rave about the style of storytelling in the Dark Souls series. Where you have to learn what's going on by reading absolutly everything and you never get any real answers to everything.
For some people this is immersive, and realistic.
For me? I found it lazy and forgettable.
Upon the start of the game you know only that something went wrong, everybody seems to be completely insane (except the security?), and that you need to get to the main boardroom where all the answers will be revealed.
After you get to that point the only person who regularly talks to you... stops. You're given no answers, and bizzarely you're expected to continue on to trying to stop a rocket launch but nobody bothers to tell you why.
The secret experiments they're doing are barely hinted at, nobody botheres to explain what happened (in fact everybody asked says "I don't know what happened." Everybody!)
So why am I ripping on the story so heavily?
Well, without anything else to hold onto this game isn't really good.
A  good solid story could have elevated this to something memorable.
And I'm not even saying that they had to tell me everything, but they needed to get me engaged. A story that encapsulates the main character's attempts as survival would have been fine.
But the main character barely speaks, has no character to speak of. You can save around four to five people, of which almost all will be dead by the end of the story with little impact. You won't know why you're going forward beyond "A woman told me to" and the end of the game really feels like a slap in the face with either of the endings not really showing any impact from your efforts.
Is it a bad game? No.
But it's not a good game either. It's long, and without a good story it's boring.
I could see this engine being used to make a better game.
But my suggestion is: If you want it? Wait for a sale.

The Surge is often reffered to as a souls-like game, as it should be. Although I believe that only judging this game based on how it steps up to the soulsborne series is a detriment to what this game offers that the soulsborne games dont really do as well in my own opinion and thats boss and world design. I belive that the boss and world design of this game is its biggest strength, the game looks great not only graphically but also design wise, all the weapons and enemies bleed sci fi feel and all feel really great to fight against. I believe I'm about halfway through at this point but i cannot be certain although I feel i can already say what really made me enjoy this more than dark souls and I realized it during the fight with Big Sister "SPOILERS" Big Sister is a boss that is unique to me as someone who plays a TON of role playing games, I do not remember a single time when the boss is also the arena in which you fight, that design really sank in the rest of this games strength as it seemed to show them all off.
1. The combat is more dependant on movement, placement and dodging than powering through enemies.
2. The dismemberment system makes the game much more interesting, think of the last time you played a soulsborne game and saw an enemy carrying a weapon and thought "man I'd really like to have that weapon", this game allows you to use targeted strikes against a specific part of the enemy to gain energy and eventually finish them with a chance of dismembering them and removing that limb, thus gaining the weapon if you target an arm holding a weapon and/or the components and blueprint required to craft the armor they are wearing
3. Boss fights that actually require thought. The bosses in this game aren't simply going to stand there swing a few times and dodge while you widdle them down and run around them, these bosses are going to relentlessly attack you and unless you use your head and think of their weaknesses or ways to keep them from striking you, you are going to be hit and you will lose the fight, as an example. "BOSS FIGHT SPOILERS DO NOT READ IF YOU DONT WANT THE FIRST BOSS SPOILED" when battling PAX the first boss of the game he is going to attack you for a time while you simply swing at his legs, eventually he will enter a different combat pattern in which he will jump jet away from you and launch missiles at you. I'm sure you can imagine what to do, you need to stand under him so he attacks himself leaving him open to damaging blows.
In the end these are just my top 3 reasons to pick up this game I'm sure I could think up more but this is just for a review. I really think that if you enjoy role playing games and you enjoy the soulsborne games that you should give this game a shot, it might surprise you. 9.5/10

TL:DR-

Combat 10/10
Story 6/10
Visual/Auditory Appeal 8/10
Optimization 8/10

Viewpoint Quality (Camera Angle Adjustments) 9/10
As a dark souls Veteran, it's hard not to compare elements of this game to the series, but it is important to remember that although people consider this game a souls-like, it still has it's own aspects that make it a good game without comparing it to what has already been done. Nevertheless, enemies and bosses in this game were amazing fights for me, there is more than one way to defeat a boss, usually with the harder way giving you some sort of a bonus item, enemies have variety in moveset and design, although the majority of enemies are humanoid.
Combat in this game is near flawless, it is fully fleshed out and there are many mechanics at play that make it just feel fantastic to execute.
As far as the story goes, it's not bad. It is not the greatest game story you've ever played, but it is not a terrible one, it's a simple arc and there are limited choices to be made which overall do not impact the end, even so, I still found myself immersed on what was going on, although at first it may be difficult to discern what is happening, I cannot stress how important it was to my experience by playing the game with no outside aid or any explanations until the end.
Auditorally and Visually the game is greatly appealing, there are quite a few effects used perfectly to give depth and make scenarios seem more dynamic.
The game is optimized well, running a pretty poor setup currently and only had occasional frame drops below 60 when users would watch my broadcast.
I've never had any bugs besides it crashing twice.
EDIT: Free DLC=Yes from me.
I loved this game, and I hope that you do not miss out on a chance to purchase it.

STEAM AWARDS:
I’d say, nominate this for the ”No Apologies” award. The game isn’t perfect, but is all in all absolutely fantastic.
REVIEW:
First of all, Endless Sky is a masterpiece. I consider this and The Witcher 3 to be the best games in my entire library of over 50 games.
This game is both open source and absolutely free. That means that rather than reading through these reviews you should actually just download the game and try it out for yourself. I will instead write down some tips which should make the early-game more manageable.
When first beginning a new playthrough you are forced to choose a starting ship which, while not being significant after the first few hours, will determine how you are introduced to the game. The choice is between a freighter, a shuttle, and an interceptor.
Playing the shuttle you primarily make money through working as a taxi, moving around tourists in the galaxy. This is not very fun and is not something I recommend to anyone.
The light freighter, called the "Star Barge", is similar. You trade different commodities and take on contracts for moving cargo around. This is not particularly interesting either although while it does make you more money through "Large Rush Deliveries".
The interceptor is the starting ship which requires the least grind and is the ship that I recommend. You make money from three major ways: Mining asteroids, escorting freighters and looting pirates. (Don't bother picking up pirating yourself, that is ultra-hardcore mode)
I would recommend mining asteroids in the beginning. This lets you avoid the grind of the others starters, explore the galaxy and is much safer than the anything involving actual combat.
First when starting new playthroughs is it a good idea to start the game another way.
The early game stretches between starting and having enough credits to buy a heavy warship. I'll avoid spoiling anything, but here are my tips for it.
Sparrow -> Fury -> Argosy -> Mule -> Bactrian
This doesn't make much sense at the moment, but these ships are my recommendations. Outfit these as you want, that challenge is up to you.
Your first priority is to pay off your mortgage. Do that through mining asteroids you come across while exploring the galaxy. Meaning, depart from a planet, jump to a new system, mine any mineable asteroid, land to sell the ore. Repeat. Don't forget to buy a "Local Map" if the planet in question has an outfitter.
After you've upgraded to a bigger and better ship, consider switching to escorting freighters. Or maybe not, because you have found a system with particularly profitable platinum or uranium, who knows? The choice is yours.
A more extensive guide provided by the main developer:
Last thing, play through the entire tutorial and read everything in it! It takes very little time, and explains many of the core mechanics.
This should be enough to enjoy the game to its fullest. Good luck!

Really amazing game.  From both a single player, and co-op perspective.  Hands down one of the most fun games that still holds up even today in 2017.  With over 100 hours in - there is still an abundence of content I have yet to explore.
Pros
• Story is decent length, but not too long.
• Well thought out side quests.
• Good humor, although this is subjective to individual perspective like always.
• Fleshed out NPC's, I guarentee there will be at least one of them you will absolutely love.
• Fantastic game for Co-Op.  Get a few IRL friends on board, and it will be a blast.
• Decent soundtrack.
• Very high replay value. (Each character is unique in terms of gameplay, and multiple types of "new game +")
• Great sense of progression with the loot, and leveling system.
• Easter eggs for dayz!!!
• Visually pleasing
• Challenging difficulty (which may be interpreted as a pro, or con depending on individual perspective)
• Butt stallion, and badonkadonks
Cons
• Early game may seem kinda slow as skills builds don't really begin to shine until mid, and late game.
• Difficulty could be a perecieved as a negative thing for some players.
• High replay value may make some of the unskippable story narrative moments feel repetitive after a few runs through.
• Slightly old game so it won't receive any more DLC, or much more updates.
Tips
• Look online for Shift codes.  There is a chest in Sanctuary that uses keys acquired from these codes that give decent weapons up to your level.
• Some named enemies/bosses drop unique items.  If you defeat one and they don't drop it then you can simply save and exit then re-enter the game for them to respawn (you may have to retraverse back to their location however).
• Don't stress about skillpoint mistakes.  There is a cheap, and easy way to respect when you get access to Sanctuary.
• Explore each character to see which one you like the most before completely devoting to your adventure.
• Co-op is insanely fun.  Find, or invite a few friends!

Fool me once, shame on me. Fool me twice, damn it Arcen Games!
Valley without Wind was terrible - with clashing graphics and horrible animations.
Valley without Wind 2 is just the same. It's creative, but not fun. Arcen Games is amazing when it comes to creating game systems, but they need somebody to sit down with them and work on visuals, a good user interface, and make the game systems work together flawlessly.

It feels more like a step back from the original.  The graphics have improved slightly, but not nearly enough to cover the poor play control and reduced customization options.  More of an action game than the RPG that was the first one and not interesting enough to warrant a recommendation.

There's some interesting ideas here, and it's a multiplayer game in the strictest sense of the word, but at the end of the day when you cross genres you want to blend them rather than keep them in their own awkward boxes.  This game has an art style that will be off-putting to many, but I found it charming in an odd way.  The different powers are interesting, but could be a little more imaginative and balance between them is basically non-existant.  For the most part, the powers don't make good use of the movement- and neither do the randomly generated maps that generally end up being narrow tunnels to fall down and strange ceilings.  The boss fights are slightly better by being a little more open, but overall it's very static and repetitive.
The game has a metric ton of good ideas, but the implementation and integration is so poor that everything steps on each other's toes.  In addition the game uses strange terminology and despite explaning itself is still pretty difficult to puzzle out.  Figuring it out is kind of fun, but once you unlock the puzzle you realize that it's a lot simpler than it lets on in a bad way and it's more about getting lucky early on with a co-operative starting area than anything else.  Speaking of Co-op, it is barely functional and requires a great deal of patience.  Still, it's nice to have the option to be able to suffer together.
To it's credit, I can't say I didn't have any fun, but bad platforming, dissonant storyline, confusing mechanics and characters and luck-based play (a decent beginning can trivialize the hardest difficulty but a bad one makes all but the easiest one impossible) as well as terrible implementation of platforming means I'm not going to be missing it.

The premise is good, but the approach and subsequent developments are not - at least not from a wargaming perspective.
Gameplay experience and patches are all based on competative RTS balancing, not historical realism. Opposing forces are modelled to be balanced not realistic. There is nothing wrong with an attempt to bring in balance in multiplayer scenatios - under certain conditions - you can achieve that by the cost of units while maintaining realistic modeling. However that's unfortunately not the way it is being done in SDN44. Sure there is some cost model involved, but the main balancing mechanism is on the unit level - by adjusting fighting power.
So SDN44 ends up as a failure if judged as a wargame, but a success as a competative RTS with a historical flavor, it ends up being the BF1 of wargames.
Recommended as a RTS, but not really if you are into wargames.

I'm pretty torn with this one. On one side, the game is fun...to WATCH. But the gameplay itself is uninteresting, repetitive and requires grinding. This game is currently in early access (at the time of writing) however I feel that there is enough content here to justify an official review. Overall, I reccomend the game IF FOUND ON SALE.
The game itself involves creating a plague (you choose the name) and then watching it infect the world. The only control you have is upgrading the plague to make it more infectious, severre and also lethal. The strategy element is rather light in the game and sometimes you are impacted by good old RNG (random number generator) which can screw you over at the last minute which can get frustrating if you are desperately trying to win a level which you get close to, only to get RNG screw you over and making you lose. I honestly had more fun with going online and looking up the guides on winning the levels instead of figuring it out myself, because I honestly found some of the levels annoying and the rewards for completing all of the levels on the hardest difficulty are amazing.
The reason the game requires a lot of grinding is because some levels are a struggle without certain upgrades which you obtain after completing the game on any difficulty with any plague. The problem is you only get one unlock at a time and the unlock you get is completely random. Meaning to unlock all of them, you will have to play through the main game 20 times, and since there are about 9 different plagues with most of them being difficult to complete, it can become a chore.
The real fun in the game comes from watching the plague infect and destroy the world. Our world. The actual game itself...is boring and repetitive. If this game was to take place on an alien planet instead of the world and we were to destroy aliens, that would make the game worthless. I still reccomend this game because the fun that is there from watching your plague that you have mutated yourself go is good fun, and also is more fun than watching someone on YouTube do it. I would reccomend the game if you purchase it on sale.
+Fun to watch
+Fairly realistic
+Creepy to watch Earth get completely destroyed
+Solid atmosphere
-Strategy elements are weak
-Requires a lot of grinding
-Bad luck can screw you over
-More fun to watch than actually strategize and play.

But...I just can't get into the combat system.  You can combat enemies in real-time (think Diablo) or pause and set up actions and then unpause and have your actions play out.  You can't edit actions you've planned out, though.  And you have "functions", named with () after their names to make them seem like a program (ugh - I never liked hardcore programming).  Those are your weapons and you're supposed to combine them to make stronger combinations.  Or something.  I never got that going.  That's probably why I can't recommend this game.  When you lose a battle, you temporarily lose access to one of your functions.  So that reduces your ability to experiment, which you're encouraged to do (experiment, that is).
Ultimately I just didn't enjoy the combat, at all.  Unfortunately, the combat is the only part that requires any thought.  There aren't any other choices to be made in the game. HEY YOU! DO YOU LIKE GUNS? HOW MANY GUNS DO YOU WANT? DOESN'T MATTER, THIS GAME HAS MORE! DO YOU LIKE CELL SHADED GRAPHICS? THIS GAME HAS BLOODY CELL SHADING, AND I'M NOT AN ENGLISHMAN! DO YOU LIKE BEING A TANK IN RPG'S, BUT THINK IT'S BULLSH*T THAT YOU CAN'T BLOW THINGS THE F*CK UP? YOU CAN DO BOTH HERE! YOU EVEN HAVE OPTIONS FOR HOW YOU WANT TO TANK ALL THAT DAMAGE! DO YOU LIKE KILLING PEOPLE IN ONE SHOT EVERY TIME? YOU CAN! HOW ABOUT SLICING MOTHERF**KERS TO PIECES WHILE INVISIBLE AND LITERALLY FLYING TO KILL A HELICOPTER WITH A F**KING SWORD? YOU CAN DO THAT WITH THE SAME GUY AS THE LAST THING! DO YOU ENJOY SITTING BACK AND LAUGHING MANIACALLY WHILE AN AI KILLS EVERYTHING IN A MILE RADIUS? YOU CAN! HOW ABOUT PICKING UP A MOTHERF**KER AND ENSURING HIS DEATH IS FULL OF PAIN AND FEAR? YOU F**KING CAN! DO YOU LIKE LAUGHING? YOU F**KING BETTER, SINCE THIS GAME IS SO HILARIOUS IT'LL MAKE A FEMINIST LAUGH AT THE OFF-COLOR JOKES!
In all seriousness, though, this game is amazing. I love it so much I bought it on steam even though I already own a copy on xbox360. It even fixes a lot of the issues with the previous game(such as lack of fun without multiple players). Not to mention one of the funniest villains in video game history. Not to say the game is perfect.
There are glitches, however they are rare and inconsequntial most of the time(notable exception being the badass rank loss glitch on release, but that got patched a long time ago), and I've never come across one that wasn't a graphical error that you could expect from any game ever(physics glitches with corpses, opening screen features your character with sometimes glitchy weapons).
Some enemies are also outright broken in the game(at least if you're playing alone, which I do most often).The only two examples I can think of are Terramorphous and badass threshers, the former because he was designed to be INCREDIBLY tough to beat, and the latter because of(what I'd assume) lack of playtesting the mechanics(they cause an elemental explosion upon exiting the ground, which they do often, and the explosion damage is ridiculous).
Barring those few things, everything about this game is amazingly well thought out. For example, even though loot is based on RNG, any time you open a loot chest in the game, it takes into account the weapons you're holding out when you open it, and gives you good odds of finding something at least better than what you have equipped. I have done extensive testing on this(over 150 hours worth), and know it's true.
But hey, if you don't believe me, just try it out for yourself. You won't reret it.

The fields have better textures and a a small amount of 3d effects to make it look more realistic. The game has new mechanics that make the game harder, which it really needed since i thought FSA 15 was too easy. Some changes they made that i really like are: Seeds are no longer infinite spot in your farm, you now have to buy seed pallets that makes having a front loader more valuable not to mention you can now move your seed stocks around using a trailer so no longer having to drive all the way to your farm to load your seeder.  Finally straps, now you can strap your bales or logs to their trailers, so no more just falling off.  And something nobody has mentioned, 4K support, this game looks so good in 4K and the UI automatically scales which is a HUGE plus for me.  and another major change i really like is the mission system, now you work for other farmers and gain reputation with them that makes it cheaper to buy fields. Plague Inc: Evolved
What can I say about this game. It is weirdly cathartic to annihilate the population of earth.
Essentially this game is the reverse of the popular board game Pandemic with several differences.
You are the pathogen -  Bacteria, Virus, Fungus, Neurax Worm, Parasite, Prion, Nano Virus and Bio Weapon. Along with the current DLC - Simian Flu.
There are multiple ways that you can advance your pathogen.
- Transmission (do birds spread it?, is it airborne?)
- Symptoms  (do they cough? sneeze? have a rash?)
- Abilities (does it resist cold, warm, drugs, is it hard to get a cure?)
The idea of the game is annihilate the worlds population before the cure is found and distributed.
The game is very easy to play but it does become harder at higher levels. It is great for a quick game when you have 10 minutes or so.
I highly recommend this game.
There is only a few cons I have found.
You will need the extra gene options that you unlock for the pathogens to win at higher levels. It is easy for them to be obtained though. The problem is it is does artificially inflate the play time.
Frustration can be very high when you think you win only to loose. Remember in this game to save often and the different game settings do have other things switched on or off in them. They are not all the same.

The game is addicting and provides a challenge later in the game when you have to look out for forgeries, false info, smugglers, international criminals, etc. It has a great soundtrack as well. The player can make decisions that can end the game in 1 of 20 different endings. Quite different from the original and in all the wrong ways, whereas the original was not a particularly good game (ugly graphics, difficult control scheme, minimal to no mechanics explanations, etc.) the sequel does away with any endearing elements of the first game in favor of...an entirely different set of gameplay mechanics? The new art is, surprisingly, less attractive than the original and many monsters seem to have been glued in from different artists, with different styles, and the various types of 'classes' are really a matter of what type of colors you'd like to hit enemies with.
The overworld aspect is interesting and would've been better with more depth but as is its very shallow and the game's instructions even treat the two halves like separate games prompting one to ask: why aren't they? Both ends have been drastically over simplified and there isn't any real feel of progression or transference from one half to the other. Getting better at the combat doesn't influence the overworld and vice versa. Plus the tacked on timer, rushing you to try to understand its clunky interfaces as soon as possible and penalizing early mistakes sharply composes the sprinkles on this inedible cake of a game.
Is it playable? Yes.
Is it fun? Half of it (depending on what type of gamer you are)
Would I be better off just buying a TBS game and an indie action platformer instead of Valley of the Wind 2? Absolutely.
Or just play the first game if you find yourself wishing the combat half of the game was bigger, better, and more expansive.
If you search for a soulless mix of cardboard strategy game and sidescroll action, dont't care about story or decent character progression, A Valley Without Wind 2 is a good choice for you.

Endless Sky is a free-to-play single player game and it took me around 45 hours or so to get to the end of the Free Worlds campaign.  I didn't check to see if it had controller support, but I found keyboard and mouse worked just fine, with me just sticking to plain keyboard most of the time.
It's the early 31st century and like any bright-eyed youth on your backwater planet, you want to leave home and see the stars.  You apply for a bank loan and drop the cash on your very first craft...and now that you're out in space, you need to figure out how you're gonna pay off that loan before the interest gets outta control.  There are plenty of options out there for the enterprising captain, and some of them aren't legal.  Decisions, decisions.
I never played Escape Velocity, but Endless Sky is something of a homage to it made by one guy in his free time with the help of users and fans' contributed content.  I wound up playing this since my last foray into scratching that "gotta do space" itch fell apart, and I'm honestly impressed with what I found.  Here, space is a 2D ocean seen from the 'top' sorta like in SPAZ, but everything is on its own invisible layer/plane when asteroids and other ships are taken into account.  This goes out the window when weapons are involved.  You can't ram ships but trying to down a target with missiles doesn't work too well when you're in the middle of an asteroid field.
Controls were kinda different and this was one time I didn't change anything.  Arrow keys control thrust and turning (no strafing) and turning your ship around 180 degrees for reverse.  From there, the keys are kinda weird because instead of them being in something resembling an array or shortcuts, they correspond to the action you want.  So you hit L to Land on a planet, you hit J to Jump between systems, you hit F to have your fleet Focus fire on your current target, you hit B to Board a disabled ship, etc.  Kinda intuitive too, I thought.  You can use the mouse to click on things but I didn't do that too often except where the autopilot picked poor options for things I wanted to board or so on.
There is a small variety of missions.  You have your standard "deliver X amount of Y resource to Z system," you have the same but with passengers, then you have those with time limits.  When you jump between systems, the game's calendar advances a day, you pay crew salaries as well as the current payment on any ongoing loans, and your ship uses up some hyperspace fuel.  Landing on most planets refills your fuel and repairs your ships, but also advances the calendar when you leave, so there is some strategy in planning routes to your destination.  You are able to hail ships to request repairs or fuel, but it's not something I'd rely on, especially with several ships in your fleet.  There are also "escort ship to X system" missions where you need to help another captain get their ship to whichever system without the pirates you'll undoubtedly face blowing them up first.  And once you've won yourself some fights, you'll get bounty missions where you're to search nearby systems for a ship or a small fleet and destroy them for the bounty.
But those are just the sandboxy missions.  There are currently two longer quest chains that have characters and actual choices and there is a major branch in the Free Worlds storyline too.  The story missions are still kinda structured the same, but having actual interaction with characters makes it feel less samey as the random missions you get otherwise.  Free Worlds deals with a terrorist attack and an investigation into the real culprit, while war with the Republic gradually becomes a reality.  Or you can just ignore it all, but apart from explicitly timed missions, you lose nothing by putting things off for a few years.  One minor gripe is that some story missions are unlocked by visiting random Space Ports on planets and hoping you trigger something to advance.
For those who want to do trading to get by, the interface is extremely easy to understand.  Pick your destination system in the maps screen and look at the Ports submenu, and it'll show you the price difference for each commodity between the two systems.  While prices fluctuate a little as you travel, I didn't see anything drastic like a 250cr profit per good dropping to -10 or something before I even got there.  An early strategy I used was to find a nearby system with several quests I could complete at the same time and I filled up the rest of my cargo with the most profitable commodity to get a bunch of cash for one run.
Space combat is a little overwhelming when you first start out because all three of the starter ships aren't great at all and apart from friendlies in the system, you're on your own.  There's an option to have the game automatically turn your ship to face your target so your forward-facing guns stay on target, and I'd suggest using that.  You can later buy ships that have a turret slot and turrets fire independently of your ship's orientation, a massive help.  When you have more ships under your command, they generally follow a 'seek and destroy' behavior, but you can have them either focus their attacks on a single ship, swarm around you, or hold position at a fixed point/current position.  Your ships stop attacking (but fired projectiles keep going!) when an enemy ship suffers enough hull damage to shut down, and you're able to board the ship at that point.  You can either take the ship's equipment like their thrusters or weapons, or you can try to take it over altogether with your crew fighting the other ship's crew to the death.  It's kinda funny that you can get a lot of money by playing pirate against the actual pirates.
Customization in this game is pretty deep.  Each model of ship has its own stats like hull integrity, mass, and a default loadout of engines and other systems as well as weapons sometimes, and there's a comprehensive stat screen for each ship that shows this as well as other information like how many degrees a second it can turn and how much heat total it can generate before it overheats.  On planets with Outfitters, you're able to install different hardware on each ship in your fleet, provided you respect the limits placed on you.  Every piece of equipment takes up Outfit Space, weapons take up both Outfit Space and Weapon Space, and engines take both Outfit Space and Engine Space.  You also have only a set number of Gun and Turret Slots, and you also also have to mind the power generation and heat generation that comes from operating each ship.  A lot of limits but there's still quite a lot of play with how you set things up.
I didn't really dislike much about the game.  I would've liked an option to slow down combat since trying to give individual orders (hey you, nearly-dead ship--get outta here!) kinda didn't work, but you can click on the ship's icon on the bottom-left to sorta target it for commanding.  I'd sometimes reload just because I lost a ship I liked.  I mentioned the thing with the random nature of starting story missions and that kinda sucks.  I really only had lag when I had a ton of ships on the screen fighting each other, even if everything's only 2D images.  And shuffling parts between ships is a little bad because you have to sell the part to an Outfitter and then buy it back (at no net loss, thankfully) with the other ship selected to install it there.
It doesn't have much variety but I still got nearly 60 hours out of it.  There's a lot of space for personal challenges, like "I want to have every node on the map unlocked" or "I want to amass a billion credits any way I can" or "I want to conquer Earth", but completing the Free Worlds story is really only part of the game and there's always more storylines to come someday.  And if you like the game, you can contribute with plugins or new ships or outfits or entire quest chains if you want!

I’ve just started my sixth playthrough of Sleeping Dogs - twice on PS3, three times on PS4 and now PC.  It is easily one of the best open-world action games out there.   What could have so easily been a cheap GTA knock-off is instead a joy, and a great example of making everything work so well in a game.

For me, the main reasons why you should be playing this game if you haven’t already (and if you have, will remind you why it’s fantastic):

Combat:  The main thing you’ll hear everyone rave about is the fighting.  IT’S SO MUCH FUN.  Yes, it basically takes all the best ideas for melee combat from every game in the last five years, but does it all with such style you’ll be hard pushed not to have a massive grin while playing.  Fighting feels so smooth and tactile, with a great physicality, the satisfaction after a particularly well-executed brawl is immense.  You know melee combat is doing something right when you find you’re actually disappointed to be given a gun. Beating a horde of grunts with your bare fists never - EVER - gets old.

Plot:  Often overlooked in these types of game, the plot here is absolutely superb, and surprisingly deep.  Although very familiar territory for anyone into Hong Kong cinema (the plot is a beat-for-beat ripoff of Infernal Affairs), it does everything with such aplomb it’s easy to overlook.  A memorable cast of skeevy characters, some genuinely surprising and shocking moments and a great sense of place all build the story into something you’ll be happy to revisit.

World:  I’ve never been to Hong Kong, so I have no idea how accurate a depiction the game is.  But SD seems to take the Rockstar approach to world-building - take a place, and make it feel right.  SD’s Hong Kong feels like a living, breathing world.  This genre always runs the risk of making the world you inhabit feel like a playground, but SD is superb at making it all feel alive and bustling.  Gently roaming the bustling streets on your off-hours, taking in the feel of the place, is an absolute joy.

Obviously SD certainly isn’t perfect.  As I mentioned, gunplay is a low-point, at best sloppy and at worst an outright hindrance.  Driving maybe falls on the wrong side of arcade-y for some.  Many of the side activities are simple, irritating fetch quests.  Voice acting can be pretty stilted (which in itself is kind of impressive given how oddly stellar the cast is).  Some minigames stray far from being the fun addition they should be by being shoehorned into the main quest (looking at you, karaoke).

But if these all seem nitpicking, that’s because they are.  The game is just so much fun its very easy to overlook the minor flaws it has.  All in all, I’d have to put Sleeping Dogs as one of the finest games in the sandbox genre, and one you will not regret taking the time for.  Seriously, in a Steam Sale this a steal.

Review for Mac Users, but does cover general issues:
This is one of the best running open world games on Mac I've yet to find. Sleeping Dogs itself is a great game. It's story is nothing unique, if you've heard any Hong Kong cop story, the twist is obvious but still satisfying, but as a whole has some moments which made me feel genuine feelings, a rare occurance in this day and age.
Gameplay wise, this game is nothing special. It's melee combat is an easy to learn mish-mosh of blocks, counters, and combos, that feels satisfying to progress. Gunplay is basic, nothing you haven't seen in a cover based shooter before, but the addition of bullet time adds a bit of a twist. Driving is very arcadey, but works well, and unlike other open world games running on Mac, doesn't slowdown the game at all.
Graphically, this game looks as good as someone can hope for running on Mac, the moments where it rises to a higher framerate are beautiful, but are rare and far between. Rain doesn't slow down the game, a welcome exception to a rule, nor due the moments with many enemies on screen.
Overall as a game, 8/10.
As a game you can play on a Mac, 9/10, it makes a great alternative to other open world games if you play on mac, and is easily a game you could spend extensive hours playing.

The game is addicting and provides a challenge later in the game when you have to look out for forgeries, false info, smugglers, international criminals, etc. It has a great soundtrack as well. The player can make decisions that can end the game in 1 of 20 different endings. It's also really interesting to be able to decide if you want to help someone even if it's against what you're supposed to do as an immigration inspector.
Overall, this is a genuinely enjoyable game! I wasn't sure if I would like it at first, but it has plenty of content and is very unique.

Put simply, Lords of the Black Sun is a mechanically sound game (i.e. all the pieces, although not flashy, work and serve their purpose) that fails to blend together to create a harmonious whole. The game often feels disjointed, lacks real depth or innovation, and is mediocre even in what it tries to do differently from others (i.e. espionage, empire-wide management).
While it might be worth a few hours of gameplay, Lords of the Black Sun lacks the fine detail and substance that make players return to games over and over again. This will likely be played once  by most and then gather proverbial dust in the Steam library, especially fans of the genre who have come to expect much more from 4X titles.
Lords of the Black Sun has some positives, but they don’t come close to outweighing the negatives. The limited graphics, lack of flavor (races, diplomacy, planets) and unfinished edges make for an experience I have no interest in repeating again. The current price tag is exorbitant for a game that could easily be mistaken for a title designed for a browser or mobile platform.

I've picked up Final Fantasy XIV on and off a few times, but everytime I've stopped playing it was because all my friends were playing WoW instead, this is no longer a problem I face today which has caused me to invest more time into it. In my time I've tried a few MMOs, including having spent over a year of my life (in hours) playing WoW. That's a huge investment and coming from that game, Blade and Soul, Wildstar and many other MMOs the first thing I can say is that I feel the game is mildly clunky in comparison. It doesn't really do favour to itself in terms of how it introduces the classes at first, things will seem monotonous and simple. This is potentially the reason the average person at first might stop playing it. For most classes I've experienced this changes dramatically and mechanics turn considerably more complicated than that of any WoW equivalent (in a good way). The main problem is that this change happens very late in the game, post level 50 in fact.
That about sums up the primary con of the game that me and a few friends personally struggled with. If you can bear that and reach the "end-game" you'll find a gem of a game that has so much more to do than your average MMO, including WoW. It has amazing aesthetics, music, memorable story and interesting boss fights. Until this game I never really felt invested in MMO NPCs, at least not to a greater extent but Final Fantasy XIV might be the first MMO to make me feel strongly for certain NPCs.
That's just touching top of the mountain of things you can do in Final Fantasy XIV. I can't speak for all of them, as I haven't tried them all. But I know the game has pet battles, card games, gambling (not with real currency, of course), chocobo racing, gathering professions, crafting professions (with their own mechanics), PvP, housing that you can customize in a similar fashion to Wildstar, raids, dungeons, hard modes and so forth.
I honestly feel like I can't say enough to give the game credit where its due, but I'll attempt to highlight a few things I've enjoyed personally.
- The PvP is interesting and features both Arena and Battleground combat. Arena is 4v4 Ranked or 8v8 Unranked where you compete for medals in a similar fashion to Kill Confirmed in the Call of Duty series, for those of you familiar with that. Except the more medals you are carrying the more you are worth to the enemy team and the more damage you take. Frontline PvP, also comparable to battlegrounds in WoW is a three-way battlefield featuring 72 players, 24 on each side. It's the mainstay of my own PvP experience but suffers from botting players, which is unfortunate. That hasn't really ruined my own experience yet at least, but it happens. I believe the PvP was recently changed in Stormblood, thus its newfound quality.
- The game has wonderful customization, spell effects and animations. I struggled a bit creating a character that wasn't conventionally considered an anime character but ultimately it's not impossible. If you like putting a lot of detail into your character you could potentially spend an hour or two doing so. If characters with spiky or zany hair are your thing, well it has you covered as well. Spell effects in the game are quite frankly unrivalled, as are the intensity of the spells (one of the classes can literally summon a supernova that destroys opposition or a meteor from the sky). Animations are also of high quality, with a plethora of emotes that your character will do as well as different standing and sitting poses. In combat, the voices of the character's can feel a bit repetitive though, especially if you're a melee class.
- The lore of the game world is deep. I know this doesn't interest everyone, but it lends itself to the story. The scars of various eras, the lore of the magic and classes in the world and much more is quite frankly great. The unique culture of the races and how it doesn't shy away from exotic concepts is also wonderful. Compared to another MMO, Final Fantasy XIV will knock it out of the water. Compared to more story driven games, I can't say it's better, but it isn't much worse. The story feels a bit slow to me in ARR (A Realm Reborn) but picks up into a thunderous pace towards the end of ARR and maintains this pace all the way to Stormblood. As of writing this review, I'm yet to experience Stormblood so I have nothing to say about the new expansion besides the changes I've seen to PvP.

A Valley Without Wind 2 is an attempt to refine the basic ideas presented by the first game and like its prequel it's a mixed success. Where as the original was a procedurally generated metroidvania with little strategy and plot, this games has a lot more of the latter two and is lacking in the first. If you've played the first one, you'll immediately notice the improvements in the overworld strategic parts. You control several soldiers that you must keep alive while running away from monsters and an undefeatable demonic overlord. The strategy part of this, is actually very well done, and the map is littered with special structures that you can task to produce resources or other special effects.  The plot is impressively coherent for a procedurally generated game, and actually rather interesting. My main complaints with the game, lie in the fact that I'd argue that the platforming is a step down from the original. It no longer has the fluid speed of the first game, which makes it far less enjoyable to play. The controls have also been changed to make the combat more keyboard centric and calculated with certain moves blocking certain enemy attacks. Frankly, I didn't enjoy it as much. I believe the could have found a better balance between the rapid fire spamming from the first and this messy system in the second. There are more RPG elements added on in this game than it's prequel, but unfortunately their implementation is lack luster as well. Most equipable items have a limited amount of uses and generally only last for one map. Other than perks, and new classes, there's really nothing else to unlock, so content feels a little scarce. Over all it's a better designed game than it's prequel, with a stronger sense of progression and better story, but I found the gameplay a lot less enjoyable and at times hard to slog through.

Review for Mac Users, but does cover general issues:
This is one of the best running open world games on Mac I've yet to find. Sleeping Dogs itself is a great game. It's story is nothing unique, if you've heard any Hong Kong cop story, the twist is obvious but still satisfying, but as a whole has some moments which made me feel genuine feelings, a rare occurance in this day and age.
Gameplay wise, this game is nothing special. It's melee combat is an easy to learn mish-mosh of blocks, counters, and combos, that feels satisfying to progress. Gunplay is basic, nothing you haven't seen in a cover based shooter before, but the addition of bullet time adds a bit of a twist. Driving is very arcadey, but works well, and unlike other open world games running on Mac, doesn't slowdown the game at all.
Graphically, this game looks as good as someone can hope for running on Mac, the moments where it rises to a higher framerate are beautiful, but are rare and far between. Rain doesn't slow down the game, a welcome exception to a rule, nor due the moments with many enemies on screen.
Overall as a game, 8/10.
As a game you can play on a Mac, 9/10, it makes a great alternative to other open world games if you play on mac, and is easily a game you could spend extensive hours playing.

Did you like Lords of the Fallen?  If you did, this is basically a sci-fi "Elysium"-ish follow-up.  If you didn't like LotF, what the @#$%! is wrong with you?  Seriously, gameplay is very similar to LotF, with a unique and unusual progression system.  What you have here is a Dark Souls-ish action RPG set in a dystopian future where characters wear "rigs" bolted into their bodies like the one Matt Damon had in the film "Elysium".  Destroy body parts of enemies and craft new rig parts based on schematics found on their parts.  Don't like crafting in games?  Me, too... I hate it.  But this game makes it simple and easy with minimal farming.  This isn't an MMORPG thank goodness.
Graphics are excellent, and if you get "blue flashing lights", update your drivers to resolve it.  The landscape is basically industrial with a lot of trash and debris, which unfortunately gets a little busy and same-y for my taste.  Enemy designs are interesting.  Music is dark and electronic, but sparsely used which is unfortunate.  LotF had a great soundtrack which was well-utilized.  Story is told through logs and holographic messages.
In all, a worthy sci-fi "sequel" to LotF, but not quite as good in some ways.  B-
UPDATE:
Much like LotF, this game gets far more difficult right near the end.  The second to last boss can be extremely infuriating, so be warned.

I've been a Steam community member for a number of years now, and in that much time, I've only been to compelled to review only a couple of games. I just started playing this game a few hours ago and it's already one of them. Yes, it's that great. I'll skip any kind of general summary, since others have already provided it. Instead, I'll discuss a couple of important features that I think a lot of reviewers here seem to be missing. (TL;DR at the bottom)
: arguably the most important aspect of any gaming experience, no doubt. From a design standpoint, this game is absolutely brilliant--not to mention brave! In this day and age, it takes courage and intelligence to create a game that doesn't rest on the laurels of its graphics or cinematic qualities to make the experience come alive, doesn't it?
Like most conventional games, Papers, Please has a linear framework in which the objectives become more complex and difficult to complete as each "day" or level progresses. What's extraordinary about this game, though, is that
. Skill and relative difficulty are, of course, subjective and vary from person to person, but for as for me, I found that as
as I had just about mastered the tools and pitfalls of each new situation, they ended abruptly and were immediately further built upon in the next round. It's almost clinical in its effectiveness. Did they run tests to measure the exact optimimum amount of time to give the player so that they feel productive and yet uncomfortable at the same time? They must have, because it's really working here. It pins you right to that intersection between things you can do and the things you can't yet do; in psychological literature, this is known as the
, and it is evident that the makers of this game know how to effectively implement this concept.
: another reviewer on here mentioned that this game creates "tension", and I agree with this on a couple of levels. The general flow and structure of the game, as I mentioned above, gives you a sense of urgency and frustration at your own occasional ineptitude. However, it also creates a kind of cognitive tension for the player by introducing elements which are story/plot related and not
game-changing. There is a sense of mystery, of dynamic forces at play which propels you to keep going and uncover more of the game. It starts out simply enough, but things start to change rather quickly, and sometimes require split-second decisions. In other words,
(which do not directly affect their chance of success in that moment)
. As the player, you have to juggle your own wandering thoughts along with your own precision, dexterity, and attention to the task at hand.
This is made all the more visceral with the minimalistically but superbly crafted communist aesthetic. How the creators managed to impart even a shard of the fractured and desperate moral landscape historically imposed by the failures of communism with such little at their disposal is beyond me. Indeed, the creators demonstrate their design acumen again by showcasing familiarity with yet another fundamental (yet often poorly executed) concept:
. Everything you see in this game is put to good use (even the title screen!) (I suppose this really just an extension of the design commentary, but I digress). At the end of each level, one can't help but feel frustrated and disappointed. "I worked so hard for THIS? I did so well, how am I so close to losing everything?" It's immersive and it makes you want to play more.
: I think it's worth mentioning that these things only add to the level of bravery that went into the making of this game. Some people don't even like to make JOKES (much less video games) about communism, especially if they refer to the tangible products of many communist regimes--oppression, surveillance, poverty, violence, etc.--because they lived through those things and they were horrible. I'm no such survivor, but I can tell from the level of attention and care that went into this game that they have done such people a service, by offering a glimpse (if not an ultimately entertaining one) into the world they endured. The fact that we have ourselves here a beautiful and challenging game about communism that doesn't incude spastically convulsing your trigger finger and shouting obscenities into your mic at teenage boys on the internet is really something, in my (long-winded) opinion.
The one sort of meaningful criticism I have of this game is that it doesn't seem to have much replay value. When you lose a level, you're allowed to start right back from the beginning of that level. This sounds great in theory, but if you happened to let a terrorist slip through by accident near the end of the day, going through the same process again from open until close can seem like a chore. You know what's going to happen, what choices you'll be asked to make, and more or less who you'll see. However, the briefness of each level really makes this a non-issue, and for the price, you could always just watch your friend play it for almost equal enjoyment.
- Phenomenal design - unique, interesting concept - skillful and tactful allusion to sensitive social and historical subjects. For the price, especially if on sale, you really ought to buy this game, especially if you're into smart (read, thoughtful), quality gaming. Definitely among my favorite purchases all year. Highly recommend.

IT'S A WARGAME, IT'S JUNE 6TH, IT'S SAUSAGE TIME!
*Beta Review and tips*
Thankfully Steel Division is not just "Wargame with a WW2 skin". It's far, far better than that. It has one hell of a lot of meat on it's bones. I simply can't imagine how juicy this game will be with all the planned divisions. For even the £50ish quid I spent on the bells and whistles version of the game I forsee myself playing this for 100s of hours.
I was in the VIP Beta  and at the time I couldn't get my head round it. Everything kept blowing up. My infantry kept getting massacred. I didn't like the Wargame titles and prefer things like Graviteam Tactics though I've never managed to put the time in to that title or read the manual (when I'm not playing EUIV). Steel Division hits the tactical strategy sweet spot for me.
Now I've played the beta a bit more I'm getting better and the game is starting to feel awesome now I've got more my teeth into it.
Tips
Put the speed down a notch to slow. This will give you time to react and queue up orders...
Shift to queue orders. C to see lines of sight.
I'll admit there is a steep learning curve but after a couple of games and playing with battle groups I'm getting the hang of it. 2v2 is by far the best mode even against ai. 1v1 the battlefield is too large and too much to micro. Putting the game speed down a notch helped.
Battle group composition is key. As glorious as it is to use a load of Panthers in B/C how are you going to afford them? Wouldn't a cheaper, experienced, crack shot Pz IV that's to arrive in B be a better choice?
Infantry are very vulnerable. Defence only. I can't seem to get my flamethrower chaps close enough to use them. If you have to attack with inf, smoke, smoke, smoke.
German AT guns rock. Buy loads in A, plonk them in a tree lines with a bit of supporting inf and watch the shermans explode. If you can set up a crossfire all the better!
Don't forget your ammo trucks! (It's nice to have a bit of logistics in the game)
I really like that the otherwise useless trucks disappear as soon as the troops dismount saving a lot of pointless non combat vehicle mamagement. Expendable combat transports are really useful for doing a tactical feint or just suppressing a location while your inf moves up.
Oh and recon, recon, recon.
It's a bit of a shame it's not on the Eastern Front tbh with longer lines of sight and a bit more flow to the battles. Kursk would be amazing. I could easily imagine this systems portraying Operation Market Garden or Wacht am Rhein (The Bulge). Fingers crossed for a fruitful series.
In short, this is WARGAME, but for grown-ups!

First impression is of a very good looking game, with instantly likeable toons that are very well animated indeed. The entire feel of the start of the game is a sort of relaxed Hobbiton, and indeed the music seems to have had all of two notes changed from the film. Graphics are very good, and attention to detail is pretty remarkable, with the greatest number of character emotes I have seen in any game.
If you are worried about an anime connection, don't be, it's minimal. Although there are Neko  characters (humans with some cat features) , they don't even really look very anime style. There are very few connections even to Japan and if anything more a traditional element than anime.
All in all the game seems good on the old PC. It barely manages to warm my PC up yet maintains a constant fast fluid motion at all times.

Aiming is the tab system, which I have to confess that I really don't like, but a lot of people do, so I won't mention that again. All I can say is that it just takes a little while to get used to. My one real frustration with the controls in this game is that you have to hold a key down all the time to get mouse-look. There really should be the option to reverse that ( so that you can have mouse-look all the time and you have to press a key to engage the cursor pointer ).  Other than a few issues the controls are remarkably good and most important, they work! Unlike a game like BDO for example, in which they are pretty badly designed and have issues all over the place.
The game is very easy to pick up, albeit the map takes a little getting used to. The mini map is pretty useless and I seem to have the main map open all the time, but even so the map is less than clear at times. That tends to be a common issue with the game ~ that it could be more clear for new users. It's just a little too complicated at times. It is often difficult to find out to perform basic operations like buying, selling and gathering. These should be really simple tasks, but they aren't.  It's not that the game shouldn't have depth and complexity, just this game has those things in the wrong places at times.  It is also CRITICAL that you join a social group as early as you can becuase there are many ways you can progress through the game and you need to know what they are.
Combat is surprisingly good. Not least because the developers cleverly limited rate at which you can cast skills which no doubt limits the stress on the servers, but more to the point you are unlikely to notice the addition of a little lag here and there when skills are well spaced apart. I play on the US servers so my ping won't be less than 100ms and yet I never notice any lag. During and between casts you can dance about as much as you like which gives the game a real feeling of speed even if there isn't any! And you know this really is where this game stands head and shoulders above some others, it's been very well thought out.
Combat is a mixture of non-marked and more damaging marked attacks ( the enemy clearly indicates where it is going to attack ). That may sound like a bad thing, and it sure is unrealistic, but personally I find it makes this type of game much more playable, and that too sums up the entire game, it's a good balance between realistic and playable.
Crafting is pretty clever really. To gather and craft you have to change clothes, and that effectively makes you in to a new character that has to be trained and equipped. Each major crafting and gathering branch has different skills and equipment, so it really is like you have many different characters all rolled in to one toon. As you go through the game, though, you can learn other classes, so eventually your class is determined by the weapon you carry. That reminds me of Warframe.
Gathering and crafting are pretty painful to level. Part of the problem is that the market prices are not controlled so they tend to be ridiculously expensive. Any materials you need for crafting, well, you really have to source gather or craft yourself, which means that you need to level ALL of the crafting skills at the same time, unless you have millions in the bank to throw away. That's a serious grind. This is one game where I think the market is disfunctional and should have prices limited. Greed is stopping the market performing well.
The number of quests is staggering. They just keep popping up all the time and the developer input to the game must have been huge because there are so many cut-scenes it's almost unbelievable. There are main quests, side quests, this quests and that quests, as well as a myriad of crafting roles you can take on. Of all the games I have played, this game has by far and away the most content.
The community seems very friendly. Becuase the game doesn't highlight who does well and who doesn't in the dungeons, there doesn't seem to be the elitism, that dominates some other games. I think that's really important if you want good team-play.
One of the few things I don't like about the game is the way that the class you have chosen takes on secondary skills ( called a job )  later on ~ and you get no choice in the matter. Archer, for example, becomes a  Bard later in the game. Death by song, if you can believe that. It's a support role rather than a DPS role. Importantly above level 50 your job becomes more powerful than your main class so it's important. Luckily each toon can learn dfifferent classes so it's not the end of the world if you don't like your job, you can always develop another class skills. Anyway, the one thing I would recommend is to research the classes and their jobs before you start the game to make sure you are going to be happy with your choice once you get to level 60 or so.
The Trial or Starter from Steam will give you play up to level 50, then you need to buy the Online Complete Edition, which is discounted if you already bought the starter. All in all its very difficult to fault the game.
The geme is subscription, but the shop is also really cheap. As litle as 1/10th of the cost of some other games to buy outfits, rides and bonuses. I have to say that I usually buy all the extras in a game because I believe in supporting the developers, and to my mind it is far better if everyone pays their share rather than charging crazy prices in the shop to make up for those who don't pay anything. Shame on you people!
I still have some way to go, but so far this is definitely one of the best games of it's type I have played, so it gets two thumbs up!

CONS

NEUTRAL
-Questing:  Time Investment = Money.  The larger the field you work for a neighbor the more you'll make doing it, but you'll spend a greater amount of time doing it too.  For instance, I spent 40 minutes plowing Goldcrest Field 20, (second largest field on map) Not game minutes.  Real, live human minutes.  Of course, the dollar yeild on this was about $100,000. *This review is of the beta build*
Steel Division: Normandy 44 is a great spin off of the Wargame series! The game has the same back and forth attack/defend gameplay Wargame fans know and love. But now the emphasis is on precise unit placement and preparation. In order to suceed in Steel Division, you need to have a keen knowledge of the battlefield surroundings as well as the positioning of your units within that environment. Lines of sight for AT guns, building positions of infantry, and tank formations win games!
There are a few problems I have with this game however. One is that there seems to be a bug when playing against the AI on total destruction where the AI will not send out their remain 1% of units (game will stalemate if no timer is set meaning you cannot win). There also seems to be a few balancing issues that could easily be tweaked for launch. None of this stuff ruins Steel Division for me, and I know Eugen will fix any bugs in the near future.
Things are a bit slim content wise currently as we are in the beta stage. There is no campaign, only 2 maps for skirmish solo against AIso, and the multiplayer is limited to 2 game modes on those two maps. More content should release as the May launch date approaches!
TLDR: Should you buy this game? Yes, but you might wish to consider waiting for launch as the content is bare bones. However, the combat engaments alone make this worth the 39.99 USD asking price!

I don't like this game.  I know I'm in the minority on this one.  The first game, I loved and beat with every character at least once.  This one?  Not so much.  I spent well over 100 hours playing this one, trying to give it every chance that I could.  But it always just felt off.
I'll start with the subjective parts.  Obviously this doesn't apply to most people who have reviewed the game, as the majority have loved it.  But here goes.  The first one nailed the atmosphere perfectly for me.  Bleak apacolyptic wasteland punctuated with bits of humor.  It was awesome.  I also felt the humor was better in the first.  The second one is just jampacked with goofy over-the-top jokes.  There's so many jokes that it sometimes feels contrived.  I wasn't interested in a lot of the characters, whereas in BL1 I liked all of them.  Knoxx was a blast to listen to!  There's also random sentimental bits.  Why should I suddenly care about Mordecai's bird companion?
On to mechanics.  The loot just seems to be sorely lacking... something.  You will spend far too much time sifting through boatloads of useless greens, blues, purples, oranges, etc.  In BL1, the rarer weapons were usually always useful in some way.  Not much use in vendors here either.
There's a new element introduced, Slag, where no matter what character you are, you will need a slag weapon if you want to wreck stuff.  Not something I'm a fan of.
This game almost feels sort of MMOish, which if you like MMO's you'll enjoy.  I'm not a fan of those either.  Playing solo is HARD.  You usually need a team composition of some sorts for the harder bosses, and you will spend quite a while whittling down their health (reminding me of an MMO).  For me this only introduced a level of tedium that I did not enjoy.
"WELL WHAT DO YOU LIKE ABOUT IT!?"- The graphics.  This game came out in PhysX's hayday, and they really made interesting use of it.  I was blown away by the awesome explosions and liquid mechanics.  That's something that will always stand out in my memory of this game.  I built a gaming PC right when this game came out.  Me and a couple of friends had the same monitors, so we hooked them all up to my gaming rig and played this game.  It really blew us away with triple monitors.  It was definitely a huge highlight for me.  Despite the awesome level of awe from the triple monitors and gorgeous graphics, sadly this novelty was something that eventually wore off.  It was beautiful, but this didn't fix the gameplay.
TL;DR- I'm simply not a fan.  Most people disagree, I understand that.  It is what it is.
Cons-  Jokes, jokes, jokes.  You can't make them ALL good.
-Characters are either lame or they try to make you care about ones that are little known.
-Poor loot system.
-Slag, needed for every character no matter the class or playstyle.
-Tedius boss battles- whittling health down for a long time
Pros-  Graphics.  Amazing use of the PhysX technology.
