This review is the result of all the negative Brazilian and Russian reviews that have occurred recently (skip to bottom for more on this).
Final Fantasy XIV is one of, if not the best subscription based MMOs on the market today.  With constantly regular content updates (every three months) and an actual coherent storyline, with a main storyline brought in self contained chapters with every expansion, and sub-plots and side quest storylines continued via the quarterly content updates.
Thats right, each expansion is an expansion in itself, no cliffhangers to make you stay subscribed just to see "how it all ends."  What FFXIV relies on to get you to say is all the extra content they push out, and not a denial of completion cliffhanger, with a lifelong grind in between.
Furthermore, unlike other MMOs on the market, if you want to try other classes or jobs along the way, you can switch to any class and any job, on one single character at any time, just by changing your weapon.  So for the one low subscription cost you get it all, no need to build rep multiple times, no need to regear every character (well of the same job type - cloth armor vs. heavy armor etc) or transfer gil (gold) via an account bank or mail system.  Nope, all there on one character.
The world itself is beautiful, one of the most beautiful MMOs out there, with lots of perks for players to take screenshots and capture their memories.  They even have a tuneable screenshot system (other than the quick standard screen shot) that allows you to capture special moves, add filters, convert to black and white, add frames etc.  The world is smaller than a few other MMOs but its growing with every expansion, and the constant steady growth, I personally am willing to wait for, as no zone feels incomplete or rushed.
Battles in the game can be a bit tedious at times, but with the newest expansion Square Enix has added a lot of new innovative ways of making it interesting.  The addition of Active Time Events and non-combatative elements to some battles is refreshing if not completely original.  But honestly, Ive died to some moves/events I wasnt expecting with a smile on my face.  They're trying to make the dungeons more fun, and for the most part they have achieved this goal.
The older dungeons do have some of that old grindy feel, but it passes as you go along.
One other negative often brought up, is how the story is hard to get into, and the game is slow.  Unlike most MMO's and games, FFXIV doesnt give you a 20 minute tutorial where they're telling you what to do, and hope you learn everything you need to play.  Basicallly you need to think of the first 30 levels as a tutorial.  Not demanding or preachy, the game just introduces new aspects of its gameplay slowly and naturually through the story progression.  At about level 20, the story takes a turn from the "you" and turns to the "world."  Less about your character and more about whats going on, and needs to be corrected.  One nice thing about this, unlike most MMOs where you're an adventurer helping great people do great things and watching as your "king" or "great hero" rises with your help, in FFXIV, YOU are the hero.  this is YOUR rise to become that great hero, and the world and NPCs refinforce this, they're your helpers, and respect you.  Thats a nice ego boost!
Another great almost untouchable aspect is the music.  The music is outstanding and especially with the new Stormblood release each zone's music sets the feel of the area and is both memorable as they are beautiful.  Not to take anything away from all the previous versions, each expansion, each zone and boss fight has been unique, especially the games big battles (Trials) with musical arrangements varying from choral epic to metal to electronic/trance themes.  For examples, you can look up Yanxia Theme (Day), Azim Steppe Theme (Day), Titan Theme, Shiva Theme. (warning as all these will almost definitely have spoilers).
All in all, I've played FFXIV from the failed version 1.0.  When I played ARR I enjoyed it a lot, but still had fond memories of previous MMOs, and held FFXIV a close 2nd or 3rd in my esteem.  After Heavensward and Stormblood (Note: Buying Stormblood - Includes the previous expansion Heavensward) FFXIV, has skyrocketed to my most recommended choice when recommending an MMO, overall the main story is nothing short of amazing.  I enjoy that an MMO makes me actually FEEL for the story and characters and not just make me worry about gear, or grinding or that vanity pet I may have to buy.
The development team is committed and helpful and cares about its players, as of this writing, Im sure you'll probably see something really special if you bought the game now (late August) during the games anniversary month September.  To put some perspective on it, the dev team has stated their goal is that at anytime you wish to start playing the game you will be paying about the same price, no matter when you join, as they want to set it up you'll always only have to buy the base game A Realm Reborn and the most current expansion (which will include the previous expansions) to play.  WoW has done this constantly in the past, but have to my knowledge never commented on it, they just push "new xpac is coming back, try this free preview and get a free copy of the previous expansion for trying.  Both games do it right though, I cant and wont take that away from Blizzard, just FFXIV vocally stated their commitment which is pretty ballsy.
Now the reason for the negative reviews from Brazil and Russian players:
To re-emphasize how much the development team and square enix cares about their player base:  In response to changing the price for Brazilian and Russian players, Square Enix has issued an apology to them, given all players affected 30 free days of time to their accounts, retroverted their pricing for 60 days to allow completion of the expansion and main story should players wish to complete it and then cancel (to get their moneys worth).
Note: all the comments on % of price increase mean very little.  The goal of the price increase even if drastic when put in percentage form, equals the balancing of subscriptions to the rate of 12.99 USD (roughly).  Square Enix is not gouging certain groups, but rather normalizing the costs across the board so no matter what country or region a person plays with everyone is paying the same cost, which is also @ 3 USD less than most MMOs on the market.   This wasnt an increase off the norm, but rather an increase to the norm.  Again Square Enix has publically posted their apology and corrective action.  In my opinion all the negative reviews for this reason are invalid.  (I understand the point of view and agree there's definitely room for players in those regions to be upset for paying more, but the negative reviews at this point are unwarranted).
In anycase, Ive played almost every MMO on the market since say 2001, I've enjoyed a lot, seen a lot, but havent had a better time in an MMO, as I have in FFXIV.  I highly recommend this game, at least trying the free trial that allows play to level 35, to experience Eorzea.  Watching FFXIV grow from horrible ver 1.0 to great ARR and now the amazing Stormblood, gives me great hope for the future of this game, and if you do try it, I hope you see it to!

Price: 50€
Duration: less than 20 hours (hardly more than 15 hours, if you don't count all the falling in holes, running in circles for nothing or being forced to grind items)
That already speaks for itself.
But the game is lacking content in any regard. The game has a thin story with few NPCs that are not memorable. The graphics look all the same and there are only 6 small areas to explore with only 5 bosses and less than 10 different types of enemies.
Just judging by quantity, the 50€ price tag feels like an insult to the players. There are many other games out there that offer more (and better) entertainment for less.
But let's also look at the quality of the content instead of just quantity:
Graphics: 6/10
Looks great and runs great and smooth on first look. But soon it becomes clear that there are very few different graphics and levels and everything looks the same. Worse, the lighting effects, which play an important part in the game's dark tunnels, are hideous and unfunctional. It only lights exactly the cone of the lamp and the light doesn't reflect of other surfaces. Add to that, that the lamps always point to the floor while walking, it makes it almost impossible to see anything in the dark areas and result in the player constantly falling into dark holes.
The animations are also all extremely similar.
Then there are a lot of physics bugs - or rather the lack of physics - causing weird lumped up objects to float around the game.
So behind the nice graphics are serious issues and just plain lazy (or rather penny-pinching) design.
Story: 2/10
Plot is interesting, but the way it's told couldn't be more boring and obvious.
Setting is very subjective. Main issue is the lack of ranged weapons in a setting that obviously screams for them. Also setting is too close to modern day life and for that it's not nearly realistic enough like for example GTA.
There are hardly any NPCs in the game. The few NPCs are unengaging and one-dimensional and most of all redundant fellows. Without them, the game wouldn't have changed a bit.
The main character has the personality of a brick wall - yet there is no character customization...
There is hardly any storytelling and the ubiquitous audio logs are just a lazy way of trying to add some mystery and saving making extra NPCs. Often you don't even get to listen to the audio logs because they are either not interesting or the game already continues while you are supposed to listen.
All in all, the game has almost no story and it often is unclear where the player is supposed to go.
Sound: 5/10
Not much to say. Almost no music, not memorable at all. Soundeffects are fitting, but badly mixed.
Gameplay: 4/10
Too much to write here, so I just talk about the main issues in no particular order:
1. Level Design
Small, cramped, confusing, repetitive. Kind of fits melee only, but still a nightmare to navigate, especially with the little to no direction from the game. Too many dark holes that are hardly visible. Too many places the player accidentally falls off to while fighting. Too many places that look like the player can go there but instead dies.
2. Limb Targetting
Nice in theory, but in practice just a choice between more damage or more loot. It doesn't even matter much which limb you target as it doesn't change anything but the armor values which are either too much to stagger the enemy or not enough to stop you from spamming the enemy to death.
It also makes no sense to only get the stuff you cut off while the rest just... burns?
Why does the game even have multiple armor parts? It's just pointless grind and the set bonus makes it so that nobody will ever want to mix...
Most of all, the limb targetting takes forever and forces the player to scroll through limbs for every enemy - especially annoying if said enemies stand up again or if the player has to try and switch targets while fighting.
All in all, the limb targetting is redundant and a chore.
3. Horizontal / Vertical Swings
Supposedly that's for hitting the targetted limbs. In reality the player will use the same attack the whole time, regardless of what he is targetting.
Worse, every weapon has those attacks, so the all feel like the same weapon with different speed.
4. Difficulty and balancing
All in all, the game is way too easy.
Most deaths come from falling in holes. 2nd most come from gettin one shotted or insta-comboed by enemies. Never died because I actually ran out of health packs.
Health packs are instant and super casual to use.
Enemy placement is boring - 10 samey enemies in a row.
Enemy placement is unfair - often hidden and then onehitting the player from behind or while in combat.
Holes are hard to see.
Yet the game features no actual death traps - just bad level design.
Enemies easily combo the player, without being able to retaliate.
Yet enemies have a hard time hitting the player at all because of the ridiculous player mobility and the extremely low endurance cost of evasion and the extremely high amount of possible endurance.
Finishers are not only extremely annoying to watch, interrupting the gameplay, promoting grinding, but also make things even more easy as you can easily just skip the last 25% of combat by pressing E.
Armor is almost useless.
Damage calculations make no sense.
Enemy humanoids have moves the player doesn't.
The list is endless and I can't be bothered to continue anymore, also apparently there is a limit to reviews here.
5. Backtracking
The backtracking is just a really, really bad idea. Nobody wants to go back to the first level to pick up some pointless item he doesn't need to finish the game. Why not make it available the moment the player sees it? The mechanic itself is already bad, since all that stops the player from getting is is some weird button with a number on it - it's neither fun nor engaging and mostly just a chore.
6. RPG System / Character Development
There is almost no character development. Core power is just a number to open stuff and forcing backtracking. Implants are not permanent but yet almost predetermined since you will want to use health and endurance implants that fill most of the slots anyway - so the player doesn't really have a choice.
Overall, there is no sense of character development whatsoever.
7. weapon combos
Use a combination of different vertical and horizontal swings to do a different animation. Doesn't do more damage and locks the player in the animation for longer.... pointless and actually detrimental since just spamming the same attack does more damage and faster.
8. weapon types
5 weapon types. Heavy duty and single rigged feel almost the same. The rest is samey because of the vertical / horizontal swings. The weapon proficiency scaling makes it almost impossible to switch weapon unless you want to grind 5 hours extra...
9. general combat
The combat basically boils down to either staggering and spamming the enemy to death or the enemy having too much armor and forcing the player to jump --> attack --> jump away --> repeat. That goes for every enemy in the game. Also there is nothing else to do in the game. Just the same boring combat the whole time. It doesn't even feature ranged combat - what a joke.
10. camera
Camera in a 3rd person game should be easy right? Keep the player char always centered right in the middle and maybe move the cam upwards at a wall right?
Not in the Surge!
Here the camera often just floats around randomly, changing angles and interrupting the game.
Worst part is that in the 3rd boss fight, suddenly, out of nowhere, the camera intendedly zooms out so far that it's almost impossible to see the player character anymore, killing the player for sure.
Overall: 4/10

A rip off of Dark Souls? Yes, and for me, that's a great thing. "More Dark Souls is always welcome, if not, is revolutionary." -Yahtzee (Zero Punctuation)
I've only made it to the second area but I am loving it already, it's different enough from Dark Souls that it has more than just its own Sci Fi skin to it. For me, this setting is more interesting. While it would be blasphemy to claim that this game has more beautifully themed areas with scenic views, I do enjoy the world more. There seems to be much more of a story in this game. The main character, Warren, was a new employee in a futuristic tech industry called "Creo" and when he was receiving his tech implants, something went horribly wrong, and he wakes up outside the company's fascility with no knowledge of what has happened. Unlike Dark Souls, this story seems to have a suspense factor to it. I'm only four hours in but unlike Dark Souls I have that suspense factor driving me forward, because of the urge to find out what has happened, why all these armored monsters have appeared and what went wrong enough to cause all the helper robots to go rogue.
Unlike Dark Souls, which could boast of gameplay that was almost completely absent of RNG, this game actually is. Instead of the mindless grind to farm certain items and equipment that you would innevitably have to endure at some point in Dark Souls, this game lets you deliberately target certain body parts on an enemy to get the equipment that you see on them. (i.e. attack his right arm if that weapon looks like it's for you :D) in order to receive it you have to perform the right hit combos so as not to kill him and generate enough energy (which is different from stamina) so that you can perform the right finisher attack, then bam, the weapon is yours.
Like Dark Souls, each weapon has a dozen differerent ways to attack and combine moves, making this very dynamic and engaging gameplay. The boss of the tutorial area was much more challenging than the Asylum Demon, for me. There was a certain pattern you had to follow in order to even damage it, I hope for more extremely aggressive puzzle bosses, they are the best!
Note: There's a complete lack of multiplayer mechanics in this game, so that might be a real turn off for you jolly-cooperation fans, but I didn't care. I always enjoyed Dark Souls for the single player experience, and The Surge is just more of that.
Gameplay 10/10
-Everything that made Dark Souls good and more, I love the new targetting mechanics they've added, and on top of that there's plenty of crafting, equipment management, aggressive enemies, puzzle bosses, catwalks, jump scares, shortcuts, and probably plenty of secrets I haven't discovered yet.
Level Design 8/10
-Maybe the level design is better, but I innevitably have to compare it to Dark Souls and I would give Dark Souls level design an 11/10, the areas are brilliantly and artistically layed out and connected to eachother, and one should never expect a game to ever do that so well as Dark Souls did, but this game comes reasonably close.
Atmosphere 8/10
-I know people say Dark Souls has better atmosphere with its lack of music, but I will always disagree, and my same complaint applies here. The immersion could be enhanced and each area had its own themed, ethereal and ambiant noises. The pop song that plays in the Medbay/Bonfire is pretty lit but that's it. Still, the dystopian future feel is just as strong with this game as the Dark Fantasy feel was with Dark Souls. It's good fun to run around getting chased by bloodthirsty rogue-bots while the Creo lady reminds you over intercom "Safety at work is our highest priority."
Story 7/10
-You would never say this game has a great story, it's just not the reason to play it, but I really enjoy the suspense factor this game has in contrast with Dark Souls. For a game with focus on gameplay, it's a nice added feature that is driving me to keep playing.
Polish
-Hardcore gameplay like this is ruinned by glitches, and I've encountered a few annoying ones that temporarily hindered my progress, due to the inability to save, like Dark Souls. Still, none of them were game breaking, but certainly annoying.
The areas just aren't as masterpieceful as Dark Souls, and while the dynamics are there, wielding some piece of sci-fi junk just isn't the same as a classic Dark Fantasy adventurer with a halberd and platemail. No, it's not as good as Dark Souls, expecting anything to be would be unreasonable and pretty much gaurantee your disapppointment, but it's good, really good, and better than Dark Souls in certain ways. I certainly hope we keep getting Dark Souls rip-offs like this.
8.5/10 (might get higher if later areas impress me more)

Well, the surge is basically dark souls 1 in a futuristic environement.
Besides the obvious similar gameplay due to demon souls inspiring a hole videogame genre, both games share the same characteristics:
+ Huge interconected world with a lot of shortcuts
+ Punishing yet rewarding game experience
+ A very very high skill cap
+ Gear is important but won't carry you through the game
+ Both games don't hold your hand and tell you what is happening and where you have to go. You must figure it out yourself!
Even if they are similiar, some differences can also be noted between dark souls 1 and the surge:
=> Environement variation: Dark Souls had way more environement diversity than the Surge, although it isn't that bad in the latter
=> Looting: The Surge looting system is much more rewarding, as loot depends on your capacity to cut down parts of the enemies
=> Crafting and character customisation: The Surge feels way more in deep that Dark Souls one's, with implants and different armor configuration that matters for other things than just poise and protection
=> Weapon diversity: Dark Souls 1 has a massive advantage over The Surge, although weapons from the latter seems to have much more diverse moveset. Also it seems to me that The Surge has way less useless weapons that Dark Souls.
If you are a souls-like fan you should go for the Surge without hesitation!

VWOW2 gets some negative feedback from reviewers, and the main complaint is usually that it's not the Castlevania-style game people expect. I feel this is unfair to the developers. The sidescrolling levels and strategic map work together well. Each tile on the world map can be played in sidescrolling mode, and depending on what's around it, it'll be a different type/difficulty of level, have different rewards etc. I found that this system gave more meaning to the levels, since they were each part of my greater strategy. There are some light RPG elements, but it basically comes down to switching movesets once in awhile and choosing attack or health bonuses. Nice, but not too deep.
The production values are surprising for such a budget game, featuring nice backgrounds, tons of menu options/difficulty settings/etc, and a memorable soundtrack that even has a vocal theme song. The one downside is that the sprites are kind of crappily-animated, though you get used to it after an hour or two. Netplay has been smooth for me with 3 players... For some reason, it supports (in theory) hundreds. It wouldn't make any sense to do, but could be quite funny.
There is a story, but it feels more like justification for the gameplay than a real setting to invest yourself in. You fight robots and dinosaurs in the future with magic... Just go with it.
Overall, VWOW2 was a really nice surprise, and I'd definitely recommend it despite what others say. As far as things to improve, I'd say Arcen should get a different team to do the sprite work, make less predictable/more complex enemy AIs, and either refine or ditch the half-baked equipment system. I can't fault them too much for throwing it into a game with already-robust features, but it seemed pretty unnecessary.

Finally some important changes to make the experience more realistic! Especially vehicle sounds and driving physics are much better than in the previous Farming Simulator. No bugs or crashes so far.
If you like simulator games, this one is highly recommended!

PROS
-The Texture and lighting improvements are much improved over 15
-new game mechanics such as multiple ways to fertilize crops
-Customization of farm equipment
-Manual engine start (its an immersion thing)
-New crops and the overhauled quest system make for some fresh gameplay
-The new tutorials are a god send for new players as these do a good job of simplifying gameplay that seems complicated
-The new map is lovely and I love the access to the trains for large amounts of product along with the highway that goes straight through the middle of the map, making transport relativly uncomplicated.
-So relaxing.  Easy to play even when I have to get up early the next day.  No complicated thinking required.
CONS
-Wonky Physics.  There's been a time or two where a trailer did not go where it was supposed to or wobbled uncontrollably.
NEUTRAL
-Questing:  Time Investment = Money.  The larger the field you work for a neighbor the more you'll make doing it, but you'll spend a greater amount of time doing it too.  For instance, I spent 40 minutes plowing Goldcrest Field 20, (second largest field on map) Not game minutes.  Real, live human minutes.  Of course, the dollar yeild on this was about $100,000.  Compared to say, field 16, same map.  It's much smaller and only net me a couple thousand each quest, but the time chunk was much more digestable at about 10-15 minutes.

But it really was the gameplay style that hooked me completely!
The single character action-pause strategy rpg is already a somewhat rare breed, but combined with the skill combination and effect combo system, it reaches an incredible and unexpected depth and flexibility!
It lets you choose the play-style that suits you best (more fast paced shooting, more chess-board chain explosion calculating, etc).
Yet at the same time you are forced to gradually adapt the strategy for each battle and keep exploring and thinkering to overcome these challenges each step of the way.
The game also has great replay value, with an also innovating implementation of hardness control (you can activate and deactivate special effects to make battles harder in order to gain more XP.
Everything just makes *perfect* sense together! Its a masterpiece!

Mission 13: I give up, this is just too frustrating. Horrible ♥♥♥♥ing game, almost nothing works as it should (and everything happens slooooooooooooooooowly), the game mechanics are downright broken. No wonder Spellbound went under.
There's only one thing I don't understand: the good reviews at the time. Has any reviewer even completed half of this game? The first few levels are charming but then the flaws start coming out more and more to the point where the whole thing becomes a barely playable mess.
Let's take the supposedly 3D environment that would let you take advantage of the height differences. The idea is great, hell, it's even more realistic than what you have in Commandos... but the developers just forgot to program it 75% of the time. You're crouched behind a small wall? Doesn't matter if it's not programmed to make you hidden, guards will just spot you even on a night mission.
To make things worse the game is just full of great ideas that simply doesn't work as they should. It was awesome to see that Sam can take control of gatling guns... then I got the chance to use one in mission 9 to find out that it's absolutely useless.
Dynamite? Have fun spending half a minute with getting it to the right position with the trajectory display before you throw it instead of you know, having it work in the obvious way (you click on a spot that's in range, you throw it there and it explodes but nope, that would have been too "casual" I guess, too logical for a game like this).
Sleeping gas? Again the idea is great but the Doc can't throw it above a ♥♥♥♥ing wall. The first time I managed to make myself go to sleep instead of an enemy I laughed by the 5th time I was furious. The worst part of this is that it just makes reactive gameplay non-functional, you can't just lure a group of enemies to a corner and throw some sleeping gas at them because it's just too slow and the trajectory is too random (sometimes you can throw it well enough, sometimes you can't and the 2D graphics makes it hard to judge without waiting for the trajectory to be displayed - why isn't that instant btw?). Also it's sleeping gas you know: a guard shouldn't just kick a gassed collegue out of it, it's a chemical substance that makes you sleep.
The 2D graphics btw? They get in the way too much. You know why Commandos very rarely made you do things outside of your field of view? Because that's bad game design. I shouldn't do stuff blindly, ever.
The worst thing however? This game simply doesn't let you make even the smallest mistakes which is again horrendous game design. I should be able to make a mistake and correct it by reacting accordingly (you know, like in Commandos) but here? Nope, you make a mistake, get shot in the face and it's time to reaload.
Horrendous, just horrendous.

Steel Division is a successor of the Wargame titles but this time set in WWII (my favorite time period). It plays at a somewhat slower pace than Wargame Airland Battle and Red Dragon and you also have to take into account that most tanks do not fire on the move, so you have to get used to it.
A very good feature is that you can give commands while your units are still in the deployment phase and also the units retreat automatically when their stress level is too high (reducing somewhat the micromanagement). I also very much like the moving front line. This is much more realistic than capturing zones with a command vehcile (like in their previous Wargame). Very clever indeed.
Furthermore I very much like the Commander units. They really make your infantry much harder to beat. There is also much attention to detail, eg. you can see all the soldiers sitting in the (open) trucks when transported and some unit replies remind us of famous WWII movies or series (A Bridge Too Far, Band Of Brothers,...).
Hint: you can also jump to the area of the last warning message by pressing the "space" bar (not described in the manual or under key bindings).
Another splendid feature is the replay mode where you can review the heroic feats of your units (this was also already present in Wargame).
Hint: in order to follow a unit you must not only select it but also keep your mouse pointer on the unit while you zoom in. Then the camera will 'stick' to that unit.
I've played 100+ hours now and the more I play this game the more I like it. I even had a good time loosing a battle and that's always a good sign.
Although it's designed as a multiplayer game the skirmish mode against the AI is very decent.
The only disadvantage I see is that the solo campaign is not a strategic map where the player decides on the next move (like in Wargame Airland Battle and Red Dragon) but is a sequenced story driven campaign where you have to finish one mission before going to the next (which I think is very old school). Of course this is a personal preference.The advantage of those old school campaigns is that the briefings an naratives can be made more detailed and fancy (as the next map is decided by the designers and not by the player) but the disadvantage is the lack of replayability.
Nevertheless I can still advise to buy this game. In my opinion it's the best realtime WWII battlefield simulator around.

Wargame but in in World War II.
The game portrays battles fought in Normandy in 1944. For those unfamiliar with Wargame, this game uses a deck system or as they coin it now battlegroups. What this means is that the player builds how they want their army to be while falling into a specialization. This goes even more depth with the new phase system. Have three phases with the first two phases lasting 10 minutes each. If you want to be an Airborne battlegroup then you will have the advantage in Phase A as you can bring in cheap elite infantry. Phase C on the other hand favors Armoured battlegroups, which up this point have not really been able to bring in any heavy tanks or fully bring their amount of armoured vehicles to bear.
For those that have played Wargame in the past, this will take some getting used to with little nuances here and there to relearn.
For those that have not played Wargame, go ahead and jump right in if you are a fan of RTS games and WW2. The amount of depth and player control is simply amazing.

First things first - "Lords of the Black Sun" is a space-based 4X game, where you attempt to conquer the universe,
-style.  You build installations on planets, create colony ships, build pre-defined military vessels, and can even create custom units.  Units stack, and space battles take place in a sort of
cut-out battle scene.
All of this sounds like a strategy gamer's dream, so why do I sound so against it?
First, the interface is horrible, and I'm not merely talking about the presentation, though that's pretty awful.  The UI isn't optimized for a player's experience; it's hard to see even a neophyte developer looking at the UI and thinking, 'the players are going to
.'  Most of the menuing takes more actions than is really necessary.
Second, the game itself feels utterly
It feels like someone started by taking a look at
, then proceeded to put it
, but instead of hiring a writer, gave it to someone's nephew.  The result is an experience that doesn't capture the wonder of interstellar colonization, or galactic politics, but is rather an experience that it's hard to care about for even a single session.
Mechanically, the game is sound - as stated above, it's the sort of thing strategy gamers claim to
.  The execution is so terrible, especially given the
, which is entirely too much for what you're getting.  Firaxis Games, these guys ain't.

This is one of those cases where I give a very positive overall view on a game despite some fairly serious problems. Let's get those problems out of the way first.
1) It's fairly short. My NG completion time was around 19h30m, which is very short indeed for a Soulslike. On the other hand, it's not bad in general terms for a game (particularly as there seems to be a lot of value in NG+) and it is generally a good thing if a game leaves me wanting more.
2) It doesn't match the look or the lore of the Souls/Borne series. Most of the areas have the same dark-industrial look. The few sections that have a different look are fairly short. The plot is mostly a generic pile of sci-fi wibble. It attempts to mimic the Souls/Borne storytelling technique, but still comes over as heavy-handed.
3) Clipping bugs. Not frequent, but serious. Took a couple of very irritating deaths to them.
Those problems aside - and yes, they are big problems - this is a pretty fantastic game. In both level design and combat, it recaptures a lot of what was great about the original Dark Souls.
The level design is really notable. At the core of the game is Central Production B, a huge, intricate, three-dimensional labyrinth riddled with short-cuts and cross-overs. It serves as a hub for much of the game, with other areas spanning off from it. Over the course of multiple visits, you unlock new sections of the area, while the enemies and environmental hazards evolve in line with plot developments. It's an amazing area. Some of the other areas are damned decent in their own right, though none match the scale of Central Production B. What I really like is the way that the area's two boss fights are at its highest and lowest points respectively; a lovely little nod back to the first half of Dark Souls.
And the combat is also amazing. Compared to Bloodborne and Dark Souls 3, The Surge makes very limited uses of invulnerability-frames (i-frames). They are there, but there are very few of them and enemy combo sequences are not timed to match them. What this means is that unlike in the aforementioned games, you do not have an effective "turn invincible" button you can mash whenever things get hairy. You need to think much more about positioning and there is much more risk involved in over-committing to an attack. A dodge might get you out of the way of a single attack, but you still need to think in positioning (or countering) terms about how you are going to get yourself out of harm's way properly. It brings back the tension from the combat in Demon's Souls, Dark Souls and Dark Souls 2, which got a little bit lost from later From Software games.
The bosses are also notable. There are not many of them; only a handful in the entire game, although there are a couple of unique-enemies who are harder than normal trash mobs and don't respawn. But each of those bosses is unique and memorable (and very, very hard). There's none of the boss-spam that characterised the second and third Dark Souls games, with interminable "big dude in armour" or "slow moving giant" bosses who blur into one and can often be one-shot by a veteran player. I'm a Souls/Borne veteran (platinums on Bloodborne and Dark Souls 3) and none of those Surge bosses went down in under 10 attempts, with some taking a good bit more.
In short, the improvement this demonstrates over Lords of the Fallen is massive. It lacks the sheer genius of the original Dark Souls, the generosity of content of Scholar of the First Sin or the atmosphere of Bloodborne. But it is frankly better than Demon's Souls or Dark Souls 3 and there are actually lessons that From Software could learn from it.

A post-apocalyptic steampunk fantasy sci-fi turn-based strategy RPG platformer. With landsharks.
Weird mash-up of different genres. Plays really well, both in the world map's strategy mode and in the platformer mode you go into when exploring tiles of the map. The art style and graphics are... interesting, but very low quality.
The objective of the game is simply to survive in the Valley, until you're strong enough to beat the evil boss, Demonaica. Survival is pretty damn hard at times, as Demonaica's stronghold regularly spawns nasty creatures to try and kill your survivor buddies.
On the world map, you get to move around survivors you've rescued, construct buildings that increase resource generation on specific tiles, heal nearby survivors, etc. The interesting bit is that because the game spawns monsters regularly, you need to keep your survivors mobile, while still balancing the resource generation with losses taken in battle.
The platformer sections remind me of Terraria's combat system: you run and jump around in randomly generated levels while monsters try to eat your face. Every class has 4 spells, usually one long-range spell, two short-range spell and a unique, extremely powerful special spell.
The objective in the platformer sections is to find wind generators and destroy them, allowing your survivors to move to the tiles you've 'purified'. Certain tiles also have perk tokens and other things for customizing your character, usually found in dangerous caves.
There's some weird time travel stuff going on in the platformer sections, as different tiles represent different time periods: you can explore the ruins of a modern city, with skyscrapers and stuff, and next turn find yourself in a steampunk city, or perhaps the ruins of an ancient, Egyptian style civilization. The level art is quite diverse, but as I said, the assets are pretty damn low quality.
Fun game, and very much worth the low price if you'd like to try a platformer with a strategy game element. AVWW2 does both damn well.

Very similar yet very different than its predecessor, AVWW2 is a unique and fun game. The platforming and weapon/equipment systems from the first game have been streamlined and polished up, but the overworld has been transformed into a sort of turn-based strategy game. The mix between these two modes keeps it moving along throughout each "world". It's a little hard to fully grasp all the concepts at first, but once you get a feel for it, it all falls into place. There was a lot of initial forum hate upon release, which was pretty unfounded IMO, but quickly addressed by the awesome developers, understandably begrudgingly.

AVWW2 is a blending of strategy and platforming genres into one 2D game experience. The gameplay alternates between two different modes: turn-based strategy and side-scrolling platforming action. Your basic goal is to ensure that your Resistance survives long enough for you to gain enough power to defeat Demonaica. In order to do so, you'll need to level up in power, acquire higher level mage classes, find feats that give you special abilities and customize your character with perks. There are different mage classes which change the type of spells you can use. Everything from water to decay-based abilities. Feats allow you to gain special abilities necessary to progress through the game. Perks are items that let you fine-tune your character.
A Valley Without Wind 2 is a well polished sequel that takes some of the ideas of the previous game and polishes them up. The combat is more engaging with its variety of spells, different classes and different monsters. It's not the same game AVWW1 was and that's for better or for worse depending on your point of view. It's not the same open-world game like its predecessor. Instead, it focuses on a direct evil threat that you get to know throughout the course of the game. The linear nature of the side-scrolling areas and the combat do eventually become more frustrating later on as the challenge really starts to spike at the end to the point of unfairness.
The combat is definitely more engaging and rewarding than the original game. You only have four spells you can use and I think they worked. You have a fast primary attack, a slower but stronger secondary attack, a special attack which varies depending on your class and ammo spells which are more powerful spells that you can only use in limited amounts. For the most part, the spells felt balanced to their own strengths although some were a little too situational for my tastes. The combat system is about you finding the ideal place to throw your spells while dodging the spells being thrown at you. Taken as a whole, the side-scrolling element is nicely designed. I had a lot of fun with it until the mid-late to late end of the main campaign.
That's when I begin to notice a few problems with the combat. I was starting to die a lot more. Sure, the combat should be more challenging towards the later end of the game, but it felt like a constant battle of attrition. I would simply run out of health before I could get to the end of the level from all the little cuts of damage I would take. It got too frustrating at times. The floaty nature of the jumping and the large hitbox of your character feels at odd with the bullet-hell and precision that the game demands. You have so many spells being cast at you and traps to avoid that it's nearly impossible to avoid taking a lot of damage in the course of the level. Taking on the tougher monsters becomes a bad idea as you'll likely take a ton of damage for very little reward. Your better off just avoiding them altogether. Combine that with the difficulty of regenerating health and you can end up dying a lot.
This was definitely the highlight of the game for me. The strategy element of the game is fairly simple and straightforward, once you figure it out. As I’ve mentioned before, the main goal is to keep the members of the Resistance alive long enough for your mage to grow strong enough to overthrow Demonaica. You have to salvage food and scrap, constantly recruit new members, destroy obstacles and capture/construct new buildings. Moving your resistance members around, planning out how to tackle new areas of the map all while dodging Demonaica and his forces really worked well and I had a blast with it.
AVWW2 comes with all of the PC settings you'll want/need and I can't think of anything missing. It's built on the same engine that all Arcen Games have been. You can adjust the resolution, rebind all the keys and a lot of other settings you might find interesting. It also supports modding via texture packs which you can find in Arcen's forums. As for the controls, well, that's a bit complicated.
AVWW2's design was focused for controller and keyboard only. While it does allow for mouse aiming in the game, I don't recommend using it. It was put in after the game was released due to a lot of complaints made about the lack of mouse control. I personally don't agree with their decision to put it in the game but I can understand why since they did. Keyboard works but it's not as enjoyable to use as the controller.
A Valley Without Wind 2 is a different kind of platforming/strategy experience. Unlike it's open-world predecessor with city-building & light strategy elements, AVWW2 is a more laser focused, linear side-scrolling/strategy game. It does remove a lot of the open-world aspects that the original had. However, I think it works out for the better. You should treat both AVWW1 & AVWW2 as unique games sharing the same universe. Also, keep in mind that while the game is worth experiencing, there are some aspects that may turn you away due to its more experimental nature.
This game is a curious mix of 2D RPG Platformer, and Turn Based Strategy. It is very good at both of these things, and given its low price point it's definitely worth considering.

A fantastic game for those who love old school JRPGs, and even something for those who do not.
Cthulu saves the world is a game that wears its heart on its sleeve. You are Cthulu who has just risen from the depths of the sea to rip the world asunder... only to be smacked down by a evil(?) wizard who drains Cthulu of his power and leaves him on a beach. By eavesdropping on the Narrator, Cthulu finds out that if he becomes a hero, he can regain his powers. So, with a sword, tunic, and the ability to break the forth wall, Cthulu sets out to regain his power by becoming a hero... so he can destroy the world. Along the way he is joined by a cheerful girl who has a crush on him, a necromancer, a man who may or may not be Santa Claus, a mutant cat, and many other silly creatures. The dialouge is silly and full of meta humor, every enemy has some funny quality to them and every bookcase, shelf, drawers, and tombstone has a unique message to go with it.
The humor is easily the strong point of the game, but the gameplay is fairly strong too.
You move around the world in a party of four and engage in turn based battles and level up before moving along to the next area. While turn based combat may be a draw back for some, CStW has a pretty clever way of dealing with it. All areas including the world map has a set number of encounters that you can fight (15-50 for dungeons, 200 for the world map) that you can see on your party menu. After the number expires, you can freely move around the dungeon unhindered, OR, chose the "FIGHT" command in your party menu to instantly go into a battle to level grind your characters or run out the timer early.
The battles themselves are fairly fast paced thanks to the combo system in which every attack on your enemy adds to a counter which powers up finisher moves. On top of that is a branching level up system in which you choose between two "Level up bonuses" which include which states are raised (Do you take 30+ strength or 15+ magic and agility) or two versions of an ability (A spell that hits one enemy for increased damage, or one that hits all enemies for less.) This leads to some nice expirementation with the characters (although two characters felt significantly less useful than others).
The game is pretty linear (aside from a few optional dungeons that contain special equipment and silly enemies) and pretty much tells you where you have to go next, but considering you really want to progress the story just to see the next bit of dialouge, this ends up working in the game's favor.
The game also comes with Breath of Death 7 the Beginning a similar, if smaller game featuring an undead skeleton swordsman, and Cthulu's Angels, an even sillier sidestory unlocked after you beat the main game that I personally am still working on.
For $2.99 this a steal and definitely worth the money.
If you have a fondness for retro JRPGs and 4th wall breaking humor, pick this game up.

Cthulhu Saves the World is an RPG with a slice of humor. Whether the humor is your cup of tea or not, though, can potentially make or break the game. Although, I won't really b reviewing that.
Gameplay-wise, combat has some unique implementations. First of all, each dungeon has a set amount of encounters. If you meet this, random encoutners turn off. However, you can also hit the Fight command in the menu to start a fight before or after you've run this out. This allows you to choose to progress with random encounters as normal, or camp near a save point to recharge your MP and grind out encounters so that you can explore freely.
Combat is also designed to be fast-paced and end quickly so as to not sepnd a huge amount of time in combat should you do that grind. One way this is done is through minimal animations. Another is that combat itself is designed to be fast. Your enemies gain attack power after every turn, and you have a combo meter which lets you unleash really powerful attacks if done right, which is meant to balance out your opponent's getting stronger.
I won't pretend this game is perfect though. Having run the numbers, magic abilities are frequently useless compared to their physical counterparts. In some cases you might be better off ditching the combo system entirely, and there's some minor nitpicks I have with the spread of abilities. That said, the Normal difficult is easy enough you can design your team very poorly, like I did my first time, and still beat the game, albeit it could be really hard. If you feel like Min-Maxiing, I recommend Insane mode. You're going to need to Min-Max to get through it. One downside to fast-paced combat is that the later bosses feel rather anti-climatic due to having to, in some respectes, keep up with a barely slower pace than regular battles.
Still though, I recommend you try it out if you're tired of RPGs having several second animations to do one attack. The lightning pace is very obvious.

I have been playing MMO's since 2005. As a 12 year old, my first-ever MMO was Runescape. After that was GPotato's FlyFF.
Let me tell you, it's not every day I come across something unique and special. That's exactly what this game is. Its quest system follows the same system as WoW: kill X or deliver Y. That's always going to be a 'thing' with this sub-genre of MMO. However, its class system is unique in that you can change classes on the fly. Let's say you're a level 50 Gladiator and you're tired of that playstyle. Lo and behold, if you get the proper training you can also become a Thaumaturge. You'll start all over again, though -- a level 0 Thaumaturge.
What I also found unique was its dynamic weather system. You must bear in mind that you're playing in a game world. Just like in the real world, different continents have different weather patterns, time zones and climates. This game takes that into account. You can check the weather of certain parts of the in-game globe. Although it's raining for you in one town, for your buddy in the other part of the world, the skies are perfectly clear.
Lastly, its lore is very immersive for me personally. The Final Fantasy series are unique in that each iteration takes place in a completely different universe with completely different characters in a storyline that's unrelated to any other Final Fantasies. The only things that are constant are certain objects or things (such as Chocobos). One final fantasy can take place in the future with hovercrafts, bullet trains and an industrial atmosphere. Another final fantasy can take place in the medieval times with blades, magic and other fantasy elements. As you can see, it's never the same. This specific iteration takes place in the latter: the medieval times.
The game DOES require a subscription. $12.99 CAD if you only want one character per server or $14.99 CAD if you want eight. I personally think this is a ripoff and to split the option of an already costly subscription is beyond me.
What this game lacks in comparison to an MMO such as Elder Scrolls Online is the PvP. There is no realm vs realm battles. There is no megaserver where all characters are in a server. From what I understand, this game has plenty of players; equal to that of the players on ESO. I did a little further research and found that the demographic for this game is mostly anime lovers/female gamers. I guess the 'cute' graphics appeal to them?
I give this MMO a 7/10 - a few unique features tossed in there, but not enough for it to truly set itself apart from other MMO's. It's still a grindfest but then again, what MMO isn't?

I could have saved roughly $30 playing this game instead of Void Expanse or Space Rangers 2 HD.  This game is well made for what it is, a free game.  If you are wondering wheter or not you want to play this game, I would submit to you this: If you found yourself looking at Space Rangers 2 HD or Void Expanse and thought to yourself, "that looks kind of cool, I guess."  Then you should play this game first.  If you cannot get behind this, you just saved yourself 20-40 bucks by not bothering with paid content that isn't much better than this game.  Now the technicals:
You start in a small ship and have to run errands and trade for a bit before moving up to a higher tier and running more lucrative missions / story.  The story is not all that long, more like a handful of events in a sandbox, and the ships look like star wars and battlestar galactica knockoffs.  The game is also difficult for beginners, as you start off relatively weak and need to know your place, learn where the right place at the right time is.  There is lots of fighting in this game.  Combat is very common, as pirates are everywhere and very opportunistic.  You can travel to a safe system deep in protected space, land on an earth world, trade, and once you take off, find yourself in a massive free for all with an alliance of trade ships and police vessels battling frantically against an armada of pirates.  I suggest running away until you know the tactical capabilities of yours and theirs, additionally, know you have a clear shot at winning and a clear path of escape.
When you start scouring the web for super weapons and the ultimate ship, well, you probably got too advanced and the game has now become a grind stone.  Anyways, there is a lot of travel and deals to be had before you reach that point.  I wanted to find the various secrets the game had to offer, but got bogged down with life and other games that took priority over this.  However, if you find yourself looking at this review, just play the game.  You only have time to lose, and you will invest time in it.

Deck13 doesn't appear to have learned much of anything from Lords of the Fallen.
The Surge has a competently designed world and story. Exploring and learning what's going on in the game is engaging and entertaining. Most of the environments nail the interconnected, shortcut littered style that Dark Souls fans enjoy. Some of them are a bit samey and mazelike in construction, which can make exploring a chore, but overall I liked them.
The combat is another story. Most enemies have unreasonable amounts of poise, and most encounters are single humanoid enemies at a time. You will do your forward dodge attack, then dodge back, repeatedly, to kill most enemies.  Enemy attacks typically have too much horizontal tracking, ambiguous hurtboxes, and low startup to do much of anything else. The forward dodge attack for most weapon types does significant damage, has a fast startup, and a fast recovery. Many enemies utilize the same kinds of weapons and attacks, including some bosses, making combat pretty samey overall throughout the game, with a few exceptions.
Compounding this, there are only five weapon types in the game. Though there are many weapons of each individual type, they're more or less just superior or inferior versions of one-another. Due to the way damage scaling occurs, you're disincentivized from trying different weapon types, because your proficiency will be low and require grinding to get back up to par.
The armor selection is pretty varied, but most pieces offer little additional protection in exchange for significantly hampering your character. There are some locations where the Liquidator (basically a biohazard suit) set is helpful to negate environmental damage, but otherwise I saw no reason to use anything other than Lynx for the majority of the experience, aside from swapping out the arm pieces for parts of a better set towards the end of the game.
Overall I had fun with The Surge, but my time with the game was marred by several frustrating moments, including an instance where my progress was not saved upon exiting the game from the menu. I was ready for it to be done when I killed the final boss.
If it goes on sale for less than twenty dollars, I'd encourage Souls fans looking for something to do to pick it up. Otherwise, pass.

I'm surprised by how much I've enjoyed this game. I don't actually like the Dark Souls series, so seeing everyone say it was Souls-like (to put it politely) almost put me off. I'm glad it didn't.
+ Neat futuristic, sci-fi setting
+ Looks great and runs even better
+ Addictive, weighty gameplay
+ A good challenge without being too difficult
+ I like the upgrade systems
+ Limb-focused combat is cool
+ The risk/reward nature or staying away from base for too long, and feeling very isolated and at risk when venturing away from it for the first few times on each level
+ Can progress at your own pace, and there's always the fall-back option of grinding slightly better stats or gear if you're struggling with an area (usually a boss)
= Levels can feel quite maze-like at first and it's possible to get lost, but you gradually memorise them
= The bosses aren't the highlight I was hoping/expecting them to be after hearing all the Souls comparisons
- It does become repetitive towards the end for two key reasons: 1) enemy variety is quite limited, and 2) you have to revisit one of the levels (and you do so not once but twice)
- Dis-incentivised to trying out new weapons (you level up your gear class so once you commit to a certain class of gear you're unlikely to ever try out the alternatives in that playthrough)
- Sometimes you may get stuck not knowing where to go or what to do next. I ended up clearing levels entirely of enemies a couple of times, trying to work out what to do next, before resorting to a guide that told me exactly where I needed to go
So I'd definitely recommend it, but ironically probably not to Souls fans, who seem as likely to rip into this as being inferior as they are to say they enjoy it because of the similarities. It stands really well in its own right and I'm glad I decided to give it a shot.

This is a style of play I have not played before.  I was expecting it to be more of a fighting game.   There is fighting, but it definitely takes patience.  The enemies respawn every time you visit the medical center.  You die, a lot.  If you die, all the collected material you were carrying lies back at the spot you died.  You have a few minutes to go get it, but if you die while trying to get back to it, it is all gone.
Not a gripe, just a frustrating part of the game.  It reminds me of Doom, but instead of weapons that shoot, now you have a mech suit and it is hand to hand combat.
I find playing this with a mouse and keyboard to be satisfying.  I have not tried the controller yet.
The map is very interesting - there are many ways to get back to the starting point by unlocking doors as you proceed.
There are implants and armor - things you can upgrade.  You can customize your load out as you see fit.
It is a game of trial and error.  Lots of error.  Every time you are killed or go back to the med bay, all the enemies have spawned again.  There are shortcuts and ways around them, but an enemy you dispatched quickly in the last round my not go so easily the next time you see them.  It is a combination of finding the right implants along with the right weapon for your fighting style.  Do you want to fight with a big, slow, heavy weapon that deals maximum damage per hit, or do you want a quick light weapon that will require more skill in dodging and blocking?  Do you want to have max health or max power?  Do you want to replenish your health via health injections or use the power gained from putting your enemy down?  You get farther and farther along, only to turn a corner and be ambushed and put down with two hits.  Then, you have to start from the beginning of the level ... again.
My way of playing this is to start out fresh and see how far I can get, getting killed multiple times, learning the layout of the level and unlocking all the doors I can, collecting all the secrets.  Once it becomes a grind, I'll exit the game - it will be waiting for me later.
This is a game where you may find yourself playing multiple sessions to try to perfect the right strategy.  If you rush, you will die.  No matter where you are at in the level, if you die, it is like starting over each time you die or visit the med lab.  Each level requires you to be able to maneuver it with a "do not die once" strategy in order to proceed to the next level.  I have also come across machines that I cannot kill yet or shortcuts I cannot unlock without a significant portion of grinding to level up.  It's a trade off between banking your collected resources and starting again, or pushing it a bit further each time.
Made it to the third level after 40 hours of playing.  Finally getting past the second level boss was a challenge.  I find energy management to be my weakest part of my strategy.   You gain energy from attacks, but it drains quickly.  Right now it makes more sense for me to focus on my stamina and health because energy just drops so quickly if you do not use it.

Borderlands 2 isn’t a game to be played alone. While it’s a perfectly competent single-player experience, to make the most out of this ludicrous role-playing-game♥♥♥♥♥shoot-‘em-up then enlisting an additional three gun-toting maniacs is a fundamental necessity.
It’s rare for a co-op mode to feel anything other than a throwaway supplement, but Borderlands 2 integrates it in such a way that it’s near essential. Alongside obvious advantages when it comes to completing missions and tackling enemies, crucially extra players increase the amount of loot dropped. It doesn’t sound like much incentive, but Borderlands 2’s compulsive design entices players to battle onward with the alluring promise of richer rewards – more money, more ammo and, yes, many more guns.
Regrettably the story fails to compel players forward in quite the same gripping manner. Set some five years after the end of its predecessor, Pandora is now governed by charismatic despot Handsome Jack, who has claimed ownership of the Vault and its contents. It’s a rather paper-thin premise that remains borderline arid, until some second act twists accelerate the story in the latter hours of the game. Jack himself proves a laudable, formidable antagonist, goading the player on frequent basis over comms, which does much to paper over the cracks in pacing.
Pandora itself is a hugely inviting location. Imposing at an initial glance, you’ll soon be driving around the dusty plains, icy peaks and picking up quests in hub-town Sanctory. It’s populated with a likewise assorted mix of enemy types, but there’s some dubious logic to their AI – certain enemies leave few defensive options, forcing an over-reliance on luck to survive.
It’s a minor niggle however when you consider the wealth of content available, and the best of which only becomes available once you’ve finished the game. Unlocked upon completion, the True Vault Hunter mode introduces new enemies and better guns to an arsenal that already ought to make Call of Duty blush. Needless to say, it’s a game that requires a serious investment, but one that also pays dividends in return. Just make sure you invite a few friends to reap the benefits.

Question the graphical choices all you want.  This game is the ActRaiser successor I never realized I wanted until I played.  It's a strategy board game tightly integrated with run and gun action.  The regular threats to my units and structures provided by Demonaica and summoned monsters along the way kept me alert.  You need those units and those units need at least some of those structures.  While I won on the default settings, know that this is a game that allows you to lose after hours and hours of investment.
The duration might be the only real gripe I have.  I could be biased by my analysis paralysis and the time it took to learn my first game.  However, the promise of another procedurally generated map to conquer loses some of its charm for me when it takes double digit hours to finish.  I realize that's probably not uncommon for the strategy genre, but I have to too many games in my Steam library to bother.
As a bonus, the game also comes with the prequel.  Some may enjoy the more freeform exploration, but the branching pathways contain a lot of empty, useless space.  It's big for the sake of being big.  I much prefer the sequel's selection of more linear playfields.  The prequel also allows players to gather much more loot and micromanage their inventory.  Though I may whine when my equipment breaks, I much prefer the sequel's limit of a single, temporary piece of loot that disappears when replaced.  With the collection of perks, feats and mage classes tied so closely to one's progress, there's enough to gather and worry about as it is.  In short, the sequel cuts out a lot of the cruft and is a better game for it.
Finally, forum complaints can largely be ignored.  Mouse control has been added.  It allegedly makes the game too easy at the moment so I'd suggest gamepad or keyboard controls for now.  Either way, it shows that Arcen listens.  I'd personally also like to see more animation detail and a final sendoff when the game ends.  However, it's worth playing as it is.
I recommend you buy a different game.

THIS GAME IS AMAZING.
I read reviews months ago and was turned off by some of the things people said. I forgot about it, but then it stood out to me when I saw the overwhelmingly negative recent reviews on Steam. This actually made me want to give the game a try for myself, haha... and oh my god, I can't believe I've missed out on this world for so long. The story is deep and meaningful, the characters well written and fleshed out, the fights/dungeons/bosses are awesome, the classes are so fun to try and the community on my server is wonderful.
I've played over 170 hours in the few weeks since I've started this, and my partner is now hooked too. Having played ESO and WOW and enjoying them, I have to say that FFXIV is a unique MMO experience to me. You can stick with one character and try out all classes, and the character customization is gorgeous. You can buy a few things on Mog Station, but I love that this is not a pay-to-win game. I also love how dungeons are such a big part of the story - it was nerve wracking at first, but it feels amazing to finish off a boss with a great team of people around (and if the people suck, it can make for a funny story). The usual stuff like guilds (called FCs) and housing and crafting are here, but they're great. There feels like SO much to do... for example, I just recently unlocked flying and have been running around hunting down currents and vistas and mounts in this vast, gorgeous world. This game might not be for everyone but as a huge JRPG fan and someone who never felt quite welcome in WOW or ESO, FFXIV is just what I've been waiting for.
Anyway, I'm half way through Heavensward and so excited to reach Stormblood and level 70 and endgame content... but it's about the journey, not the destination, right? So far, the journey has been incredible and I can't recommend this game enough.

I'm one of those MMO players that prefer to go it solo. It's not the multiplayer that attracts me to MMORPG's but the ever evolving, open and often unpredictable world they offer. This combined with the progression make MMORPG's my favourite genre.
When I found out FF14 forced you to group tp progress through the story I decided to give it a miss. Despite hearing nothing but good things about the game I continued to ignore it. Instead spending my time with games like GW2 or ESO or Black Desert Online (all fantastic games).
When It was on Sale recently I decided to give it a go. I've never looked back. Turns out the forced grouping is so easy and painless it's not an issue at all. Nor does it require a large time investment. It is actually very enjoyable.
FF14 is a fantastic MMORPG. The world, the community, the story, the class/job system, the graphics and the sound..... all wonderful.
My only gripe is the combat. It's not bad at all but I personally just prefer the more active style offered by games like GW2 or Black Desert Online. It's still enjoyable.

TL;DR for those in a hurry:
Is the game worth buying despite the 'Mostly Negative' verdict on the most recent?
YES IT IS
Wanna know why? Read below
-------------------------------------------------
Bet you're looking at that 'Mostly Negative' huh?
Well, honestly? That's a load of crap. Sure, brazil and Russia got F'd over, but that's not the company's fault. Their currency exchange plummited and in order for Square to get their just due they had to raise the price to match the equivelant of the $US. That's just common economics.
Believe me Russia/Brazil, there are countries out there with WAY more ♥♥♥♥♥♥ deals than you, trust me.
So in all honesty? If you DON'T live in Brazil or Russia, or if you do live there, but are willing to pay twice as much as everyone else to play? Read on. Otherwise, just stop here and move on.
Now if people could please stop spamming the reviews with negative verdicts over the same exact bogus excuse over and over again when there's a perfectly logical and economically sound explanation for it? That'd be great. Your salty attitude isn't gonna change how the world works, guys, sorry to throw a stick in your wheel.
NOW, on to the review...
Gameplay:
Nothing really exemplary here. How the game runs in terms of UI, HUD, etc. is pretty much all exactly the same as every other MMO out there, quite literally.
...But...How classes work? Completely unique.
Instead of picking a class early in the game, and being that class for the rest of the game...your character can be EVERY class...If you put the time and effort into unlocking each and every one and leveling them all to 70? Your character can essentially be everything, and switch around classes depending on the situation you're in. This might sound OP, but it's actually really damned useful! It doesn't break the game in any way, and each class has its strengths and weaknesses.
This also eliminates the risk of literally deserting the lower level zones forever once all the questers etc. have swept through like a tornado. You know in other MMOs like WoW where a new expansion comes out, and the first month is SUPER HIGH activity in the newly released zones/dungeons? Well, how do you think the original level 30 areas are holding up? They literally go for months without a single person running through there to level! No such problem here. Every zone has people in it, all the time, non-stop. You simply can't go into a zone in FFXIV and have it to yourself. It doesn't happen.
If I literally went through EVERYTHING you can do in this game right here right now, it'd be a long, boring, drawn-out review that'd have everyone quit reading 200 words in. So let me boil it down to this: If you want an MMO where there's tons of stuff to do? This is the one for you.
Graphics:
Mediocre, at best. If you're looking for eye candy? I suggest Black Desert Online for that. This game is by no means pretty at a stellar level. Is it adequate? Oh yes, you still have the dynamic SSAO and Sun Shafts and the simply stunning night sky etc. You have all of that, but it's not gonna make you have sparkly bits in your eyes like an overzealous anime character. The graphics are rather out dated, and any modern computer with ~GTX 950, or even a relatively good deal older than that, will be running this game at max settings with few to no issues of any kind.
The beauty of it? The difference in performance from lowest to highest possible settings is nothing short of VAST. Meaning even people with a really bad, outdated, slow PC that can't even run Team Fortress 2 without sending you a suicide note? This game will most likely run for you on the lowest settings.
Subscription:
Now, this is not WoW...So you're not stuck with two ways to pay for your monthly subscription: In-game purchased gametime, or Pay Per Month with a credit card. If you buy the game through Steam, you can also use your Steam Wallet to pay! Meaning if your mommy has cut you off cause you lost too many good boy points? You can sell one of your australiums on the failing TF2 market on Steam and have enough money to pay for your sub for a year or more. You can pay for as many months as you like and they'll stack up for you.
Servers:
Almost all servers are heavily populated, and those that are not have some pretty damned good incentives to bring people in to populate them...300% experience boost to all new characters for the next month anyone!?
Cool things you can do:
Type /gpose in the chat log and you get put into an interactive 'screenshot' scene where you can edit how your character behaves and thus take some pretty darned neat screenshots. It even features a freeze time feature so you don't have to sit and watch the same animation again and again until you get the PERFECT screenshot.....after flooding your screenshot folder with 100+ identical pics that all need to be deleted now...
Sit on everything, everywhere, at any time.
Unlock new dances, emotes, etc. through simple questing.
Turn your mount into a companion that you can level up alongside you, as either a tank, DPS, or healer.
Transmog(aka change the appearance of your best gear, to look like gear that might be worse, but looks better on you) is alive and well in this game.
Level your character from 1 to 70 without ever attacking anything. You can level up by crafting/gathering alone!
Standard PvP/Raiding system, except it's actually done right...Like Vanilla WoW.
Super intense RP community. Each race comes with 2 sub-races, and each sub race looks a little different than the other. There are even pre-decided 'culture' and 'naming style' for each and every sub race of each and every race! Don't believe me? Try looking up 'FFXIV naming conventions'. You'll be amazed.
RP in this game is nothing short of awesome.
Events are fun, but not overwhelmingly time consuming. They're sweet and to the point.
Healers get to DPS too. It's not a suggestion, it's a requirement, healers DPS too.
Classes have their own unique 'class quests', meaning the only way to get the whole experience out of your class is to do the class quests every 5 levels.
You can be a skimpily clad catgirl and no one will complain about it.

Oh god. SPIDERS!
♥♥♥♥ing Spiders every time I turn a corner. I hate those ♥♥♥♥ers. They move way too fast and then murder your face off.
Ok, so genre-wise it's pretty much Might and Magic. But there hasn't been a new Might and Magic game (not the Heroes one, the main series) in quite some time. Also, they were confusing as hell. This one is much more straight forward. The magic system is a little obtuse, but the rest of the game plays out very fluidly.
I honestly don't know if there's more of a story than "get out of the mountain" and "scare the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the player," but that's enough for this one. It's played for the puzzles. It only helps that the combat is not unwieldy. I don't know if I would particularly call the combat fun, but once you get into a rhythm it's almost soothing. Like a music simulator video game. Step, turn, hit. Step, turn, hit. Open the gate, hit, close the gate. Unless they're the ♥♥♥♥ing spiders. They move and attack way too god damn fast. But then again, they aren't that strong, and that's part of the challenge. Balancing tanking with movement and hitting. That's an old school first person RPG for you. Tile based and Fighter friendly. I wonder how a team of 4 fighters would have done...
Anyways. This game is really fun. It's an interesting play on old school RPGs with lots of new school polish. I'm actually really surprised that this one was an indie. But it definitely is a good one.
Also, with the level editor added into the game now, I'm looking to see what new adventures await. Perhaps a cow level?
