First things first - this is a Souls-like game, meaning that it will have slow and challenging combat with focus on dodging and blocking. Can I reccomend The Surge? Yes, but only when it's on sale. Don't get me wrong - the game is fun and I love it, but quite frequently it makes you want to pull you hair out. These moments are rare in the first area, but in every single other one (except 4th), you will die in the most unfair ways imaginable, so let's discuss all the problems this game has (I am pretty passionate about this game and reviews, so strap yourselves in boys - we are going for a ride):
Insta-death problem: There are some areas that have poor lights, so you won't see botomless pits before you fall into one. Second and third areas are just filled with them - narrow stairways or paths that don't have barriers to protect you from falling, other stairways have a tiny gap between stairs and floor, where you can fall in the botomless pit if you try to attack an enemy that's standing three steps away (if the enemy charges first in this situation, he can also fall - seen that happen once or twice). Horrible flashlights also don't help in these situations (I've seen just 1 armor set with a flashlight that lights up the area around you pretty well).
Difficulty spikes: This game has such difficulty spikes that I've never seen in any other modern game. You feel that game becomes easier when nearing the end of each area - upgraded armor and weapons give you this sense of increasing power, but chances are - when you enter the next area, first enemy you meet will wipe the floor with you, unless you're very careful. This can be dealt with in two ways - either grinding to get better gear by farming NPCs or trying to slowly progress and dying a lot while doing so. I tried both and I can absolutely say that farming NPCs is way more effective and less frustrating (though tedious). In the last stages of the game farming doesn't help much, because enemies do a lot of damage and despite wearing upgraded medium armor, some of their attacks just 1 hit kill you, which makes a difficult game a bit more frustrating when you have to back-track every 10 or 15 minutes in mazes without a mini map.
Navigation: This game has some of the worst navigation mechanics since Morrowind  perhaps. There is no objective marker (which is okay - I don't need a game to point me mindlessly in one direction), but there's also no map you can carry or a minimap and the levels are big. Very big. You can get comfortable within a level after you've spent few hours in it, yes, but having no map in mazes and labyrinths isn't helpful and makes you spend more time in levels than you'd like to.
Missed oppurtunities: I was excited about this game since I saw the first trailer for it. I'm a big Warhammer 40k fan myself, so I love the idea of big power armor made from scraps. I think this game missed a lot of interesting and unique twists by forcing you to wear gear sets. In trailers they showed you how you build your armor piece by piece and you can mix it up to make unique combinations. Well - you can do that technically, but it's not viable. I wish the developers took their time to make a game where you can actually build your own armor combination that fits your play-style - not just choose an overpowered set bonus and play with it half of the game (yes, I'm looking at you, Gorgon armor with 100% stamina regen speed increase).
Speaking of playing with something half of the game - How do you like the idea of a game that has a couple of dozens of weapons with unique attack combos from several weapon types with unique play styles? Sounds awesome, doesn't it? Now how do you like the idea that you get one of the top 5 or so best weapons in the game in the first level? Sounds nice? No, because it kills the need of weapon variety - chances are you will be using that Single-rigged heavy hitter until the last level (you may switch it out for something more fast in boss battles). Thus despite the fact that there are several dozens of weapons, most (absolute majority) of them are obsolete even when upgraded. They are just bad - they don't scale well with levels - that is the most important weapon stat, which dictates how much damage a weapon will do when you have high weapon proficiency - only few weapons have high or very high level scaling and they are usually from Boss fights. Weapons that you get from side quests or in secret areas are absolute junk that you can't even scrap. Yet another missed oppurtunity....
Yet - there are many good this about this game, like its story - it's dark and miserable. You have to go looking for it, because there aren't many cutscenes, but I'm telling you - listening to all the audiologs is worth it.
I also liked varied and fair boss fights (even though there's just a handful of them). I like most of the enemy NPCs, because they are tough, but not unbeatable if you're smart. Though some of them aren't fair, but many things aren't in this game. Gotta take the good things with the bad. I like the audio and visual design. Love the idea of improvised weapons and armor, yet there were some oppurtunities missed as I've stated before.
Combat in this game is good. Very good. Animations are crisp and organic, finishing moves are brutal, yet they get samey. Attack combinations offer unique combat styles, because some of the weapons have flamethrower attacks or several 360 degree spins to deal pretty massive damage. Blocking isn't very useful, because it drains much more stamina than dodge, so I suggest you become good at dodging.
So - my verdict. It's a flawed gem, like most of the good games, yet this is gem is so flawed that it will make a lot of people overlook it - even the best gems don't shine very bright in a pile of mud. Don't get fooled by all that dirt though, because somewhere in there is a very fun game with some brilliant ideas and great mechanics, even though it sometimes punches you in a stomach.

After 300+ hours of FS15 I 'ummed' and 'aaahhed' over buying this for a good couple of weeks before deciding to take the plunge. And TLDR; I'm glad I did. There are many major improvements - not least for me being simply able to set up a steering wheel quickly and easily (a pain in FS15).  I'm only a few hours into this one, but so far, so very good. Certainly worth getting if you liked any of the earlier incarnations.

At a quick glance, it may seem like FS15.  Only after playing the game for a bit do you notice all the improvements.
It begins immediately when you enter a tractor.  You have to start it manually.  As soon as you start to drive, you notice the sound is infinitely better.  The tractors sound better, engine RPM isn't linear with speed as it was in the past.  The dirt crunches like in real life when you drive on dirt roads.  When you exit your tractor, the lights stay on.
Those little things are just a small example of the many things they have improved.  The game is also deeper with mandatory plowing every few years and more fertilizing to make it realistic.  The storage on the farm is limited an you need to buy more silos to store more crops.  You must also buy seed and fertilizer in pallets from the store, there isn't a magical endless supply on your farm. They also have more equipment and vehicles released than FS15+all DLC.
There I go listing more improvements again. Did they make any huge improvements like in FS15?  No. In FS15, if you take forestry or the physics away from the list of improvements from FS13, it would not have been a good game.  For FS17, remove any one change, heck even any 5 changes, and it is still a great improvement from FS15.  The improvements are probably most noticeable when you go back and try to play FS15 again.  FS15 just isn't fun anymore.

Even though it was a mere 6 hours long, my time with Transistor was likely one of the best experiences I've had in gaming thus far. Transistor boasts a rather large amount of depth in its gameplay, this depth is offered through the sheer variety of  unique permutations you can create with the games' abilities. In typical ARPG fashion you're only given 4 active slots to work with as well as 4 passive slots, each of these slots comes with an extra 2 slots of their own. These extra slots allow you to modify abilities with other abilities. Every ability in the game has some effect on all the others both as a passive and as an active, this mechanic alone trumps the efforts of many other AAA titles that have tried to create depth in their gameplay, this system allows the player to fully customise their experience and find a build that both suits their playstyle and the challenges presented to them by the game. Much like its predecessor 'Bastion', Transistor offers a variety of modifiers that make the game harder, ranging from increasing enemy HP to losing 2 abilities upon death. Transistor also has reasonably intelligent AI that constantly poses a threat to the player thorughout the game and pushes you towards further customising your build and going outside of your comfort zone. This game forces you to experiment with your builds and I don't feel as if enough modern ARPGs do this well enough, it's easy to find a build you like and are comfortable with but when you're put into a situation where you have no choice but to change it and re-think your strategy you very well may come out having more fun than you'd expected. This game has a lot of depth and it forces you to explore its mechanics as much as you can, that is something I can truly admire.
The art in this game is another thing I greatly appreciate. Jen Zee managed to create a bright, colourful and clean Cyberpunk world. Keyword in that sentence being 'clean'. It's very rare that you see an interpretation of cyberpunk that isn't grimey or edgy, the fact that Jen Zee managed to capture the optimism of the city she was painting while maintaining the cyberpunk motif is a feat on its own but the fact that she managed to do so while giving the art an ominous feeling to it as well is nothing short of phenomenal. The same could be said for the OST that I've been listening to for the past 2 years. When you put the gameplay together with, the OST, the art and the great story I'd say you have a near perfect game. Supergiant did a wonderful job with Transistor and I wholeheartedly reccomend it to you!
BUY THIS GAME

This game is not bad, just mediocre. It is unpolished, but not bad looking. It is a 4x space game, but without the depth. I'll break it down.
The good:
- Loads at the beginning but minimal loading afterwards.
- Graphics are crisp but still run on older hardware decently.
- Not overly complex (If you're not looking for complex).
- Accessible for players newer to 4X games.
The bad:
- Grammatical errors to the point where I noticed and it bothered me enough to mention.
- Underwhelming UI.
- Combat is boring.
- Research is boring.
- Production is boring.
- Bland AI and diplomacy.
- Economy that lacks balance. (Or I need a better tutorial for it)
- Too easy for expereinced players.
- Speech system is unbalanced.
I might not have played it enough to see the depth here, but the economy seems to be very simple and not very easy to deal with. If you get it going early and get lucky with the random exploration treasures (and not just have your scout destroyed without a fight) then you can be dominant pretty quickly. If you get set back by a random event (which rarely cost less than 1000 BC) or hit up for protection money too often there's not much you can do to come back. If you lose a planet and suddenly have -12 BC per turn and only around 120 BC in the bank you have literally nothing you can do to come back aside from hoping that you have enough Glory to give the +5000 BC speech. Oh and you earn that glory by winning battles, so if you're behind in military now good luck getting there on that one. The speech system overall seems to just be covering for sloppy design OR this game is specifically trying to be a short playing 4X game, which is kind of a weird concept to me. Case in point. In my last game before I wrote this, I was dominating the galaxy for most of the game with diplomacy and science before a few bad events and one AI deciding to finally attack me left me with only 1 planet left (not my homeworld). So I just pulled up the tech tree and selected the "You win" tech (which always seemed to take 28 turns to complete no matter how much science I had) and hit the "Your current research finishes next turn" speech to instant win even though I was clearly outmatched otherwise. I did not feel like I was snatching victory from the jaws of defeat, I just felt like I cheated better than the dumb AI did. Also, you need to have an "Army ship" stationed at a planet in order for it to be defended at all when attacked, otherwise they just stroll in and take the planet without a fight. This is a conscious design decision I'm sure, but it's not one that I find fun.
I do not recommend this game over other games in the genre. It's not a strictly bad game, and I'm glad developers and publishers are coming out with more games of this type. This one is just not for me.

Desperados is a squad-oriented stealth/action game following the footsteps of Commandos, but with a Western setting. It may be a copycat, but a copycat with great levels, good mechanics, and memorable characters, easily earning its rightful place among all real-time tactical game fans.
Desperados: Wanted Dead or Alive is the proof that you can create a copycat that can be on par with the original. In our case, it is a clone of
: a series of WWII real-time squad-based tactical/strategy games, where you control a group of highly trained specialist through a set of mostly stealth-oriented levels.
The core mechanics are the same: your task is to clear each level from enemy guards and bandits to reach your current mission mark. To do so, you take control of a colourful cast of Western stereotypes, all with their unique abilities. They are maybe a little too unique, as even mundane tasks as tying a knot or saddling a horse need their own specialists.
Another similarity is that diversion tactics are the bread and butter of gameplay. This is where Desperados outdid Commandos: you can pre-record a set of commands for all characters to execute a complex plan with the push of a button. Thanks to the devilish enemy placements, this feature is almost essential after a while.
The setting makes one big difference though: we cannot have a Western without some shoot-outs, so Desperados puts a smaller emphasis on sneaking to give way for some old-fashioned gunplay instead.
The story is built from spaghetti Western tropes: a mysterious bandit leader pulls a few high-profile robberies, which attracts the attention of a veteran bounty hunter, who then collects a few outlaw buddies to get to the bottom of the events. After this, the plot runs into a few dead ends on purpose, which may be a little tiresome, but eventually it reaches its typical adventure-oriented Western movie conclusion.

TL;DR for those in a hurry:
Is the game worth buying despite the 'Mostly Negative' verdict on the most recent?
YES IT IS

-------------------------------------------------
Bet you're looking at that 'Mostly Negative' huh?
Well, honestly? That's a load of crap. Sure, brazil and Russia got F'd over, but that's not the company's fault. Their currency exchange plummited and in order for Square to get their just due they had to raise the price to match the equivelant of the $US. That's just common economics.
Believe me Russia/Brazil, there are countries out there with WAY more ♥♥♥♥♥♥ deals than you, trust me.
So in all honesty? If you DON'T live in Brazil or Russia, or if you do live there, but are willing to pay twice as much as everyone else to play? Read on. Otherwise, just stop here and move on.
Now if people could please stop spamming the reviews with negative verdicts over the same exact bogus excuse over and over again when there's a perfectly logical and economically sound explanation for it? That'd be great. Your salty attitude isn't gonna change how the world works, guys, sorry to throw a stick in your wheel.
NOW, on to the review...
Gameplay:
Nothing really exemplary here. How the game runs in terms of UI, HUD, etc. is pretty much all exactly the same as every other MMO out there, quite literally.
...But...How classes work? Completely unique.
Instead of picking a class early in the game, and being that class for the rest of the game...your character can be EVERY class...If you put the time and effort into unlocking each and every one and leveling them all to 70? Your character can essentially be everything, and switch around classes depending on the situation you're in. This might sound OP, but it's actually really damned useful! It doesn't break the game in any way, and each class has its strengths and weaknesses.
This also eliminates the risk of literally deserting the lower level zones forever once all the questers etc. have swept through like a tornado. You know in other MMOs like WoW where a new expansion comes out, and the first month is SUPER HIGH activity in the newly released zones/dungeons? Well, how do you think the original level 30 areas are holding up? They literally go for months without a single person running through there to level! No such problem here. Every zone has people in it, all the time, non-stop. You simply can't go into a zone in FFXIV and have it to yourself. It doesn't happen.
If I literally went through EVERYTHING you can do in this game right here right now, it'd be a long, boring, drawn-out review that'd have everyone quit reading 200 words in. So let me boil it down to this: If you want an MMO where there's tons of stuff to do? This is the one for you.
Graphics:
Mediocre, at best. If you're looking for eye candy? I suggest Black Desert Online for that. This game is by no means pretty at a stellar level. Is it adequate? Oh yes, you still have the dynamic SSAO and Sun Shafts and the simply stunning night sky etc. You have all of that, but it's not gonna make you have sparkly bits in your eyes like an overzealous anime character. The graphics are rather out dated, and any modern computer with ~GTX 950, or even a relatively good deal older than that, will be running this game at max settings with few to no issues of any kind.
The beauty of it? The difference in performance from lowest to highest possible settings is nothing short of VAST. Meaning even people with a really bad, outdated, slow PC that can't even run Team Fortress 2 without sending you a suicide note? This game will most likely run for you on the lowest settings.
Subscription:
Now, this is not WoW...So you're not stuck with two ways to pay for your monthly subscription: In-game purchased gametime, or Pay Per Month with a credit card. If you buy the game through Steam, you can also use your Steam Wallet to pay! Meaning if your mommy has cut you off cause you lost too many good boy points? You can sell one of your australiums on the failing TF2 market on Steam and have enough money to pay for your sub for a year or more. You can pay for as many months as you like and they'll stack up for you.
Servers:
Almost all servers are heavily populated, and those that are not have some pretty damned good incentives to bring people in to populate them...300% experience boost to all new characters for the next month anyone!?
Cool things you can do:
Type /gpose in the chat log and you get put into an interactive 'screenshot' scene where you can edit how your character behaves and thus take some pretty darned neat screenshots. It even features a freeze time feature so you don't have to sit and watch the same animation again and again until you get the PERFECT screenshot.....after flooding your screenshot folder with 100+ identical pics that all need to be deleted now...
Sit on everything, everywhere, at any time.
Unlock new dances, emotes, etc. through simple questing.
Turn your mount into a companion that you can level up alongside you, as either a tank, DPS, or healer.
Transmog(aka change the appearance of your best gear, to look like gear that might be worse, but looks better on you) is alive and well in this game.
Level your character from 1 to 70 without ever attacking anything. You can level up by crafting/gathering alone!
Standard PvP/Raiding system, except it's actually done right...Like Vanilla WoW.
Super intense RP community. Each race comes with 2 sub-races, and each sub race looks a little different than the other. There are even pre-decided 'culture' and 'naming style' for each and every sub race of each and every race! Don't believe me? Try looking up 'FFXIV naming conventions'. You'll be amazed.
RP in this game is nothing short of awesome.
Events are fun, but not overwhelmingly time consuming. They're sweet and to the point.
Healers get to DPS too. It's not a suggestion, it's a requirement, healers DPS too.
Classes have their own unique 'class quests', meaning the only way to get the whole experience out of your class is to do the class quests every 5 levels.
You can be a skimpily clad catgirl and no one will complain about it.

*SPOILER FREE REVIEW*
This is one of the first games I've bought in a while that had JUST come out (I typically wait for a steam sale or whatever), and I did so despite some super negative reviews that I read and decided were just salty people who couldn't handle the difficulty. I'm SO thrilled with this game, it is absolutely awesome and delivers on every level as advertised.
I found it to be very difficult but definitely not quite Dark Souls' level of throw-your-controller-wtf-is-going-on. You aren't going to get lost going the wrong way for hours or end up somewhere without a crucial item that you need as long as you explore everywhere you go thoroughly. It was a very nice challenge, and I was able to complete my run-through without looking up anything at all - never got lost very badly, the bosses are all intuitive to fight (and amazing in design!). The gear system is quite brilliant, with how you dismember enemies for their blueprints and then parts to make the armors you see in the world - it too is quite intuitive. Its also worth mentioning that this gear collection system removes the classic sort of "rolling for your loot each time you kill this guy and then respawning him like a billion times to try to get lucky" RNG bullcrap that has permeated action RPGs for too long now. Also, you see a guy, you think his armor is cool? You can go take it. No BS armor sets or weapons that you can't get for yourself or are "badguy only".
I read some reviews that claimed that there was no story - that must be a joke! I mean even if you weren't meticulously exploring everything 100% to get all the audio logs (which pretty clearly spell out what's going on) the environment you are in and the main progression through the game shows and tells the story brilliantly. The settings are beautiful and not dull at all - yes for part of it you are in a factory, but it's huge and awesome and complex! Take some time to look around as you play through and you will find a lot of interesting tidbits, i.e. things scrawled on walls, etc. The story is frankly one of the coolest and most interesting plotlines I've gotten to play through in a long time!
Overall the game is quite fun, due to the layout of the areas you will definitely feel like you are making progress and when you make a mistake and die you are never too far away from your "Tech Scrap" to make it back to pick it up. Once you get in the groove with the combat system you will find yourself flying around fighting multiple enemies at the same time. Again from bad reviews I've read that the combat is "clunky"... well let me be clear, it is NOT clunky at ALL! All the moves are a bit like a fighting game, you need some timing and you might get animation locked if you mash a button too many times but each different weapon has a completely different set of moves, speed and animation so really you just need to find one that fits your playstyle groove. Maybe some fast dagger like weapons, or maybe a big heavy hammer are your style? It won't be too far into the game that you can find what you prefer and get into the deeper combos with your favorite weapon.
Just a really great game. Challenging and hard, but not really quite "WTF IS GOING ON" Dark Souls at any point, you definitely have just enough of an idea of where to go or what to do, but it definitely doesn't baby you or hand hold. The combat and crafting/gear systems are really tight and intuitive and fun. The bosses are incredible. I can't recommend this game hard enough  - give it a try, it's amazing!

I want to love this game. I'm a huge Souls fan and when I saw this gameplay, I was excited to get more gameplay that follows the souls formula. The start of the game was a blast, the story was actually interesting, and it LOOKED really nice. The combat was also exciting and VERY rewarding, and the cut/loot system is fresh and well done.
But oh boy does this game lack polish. The rocket assembly boss is horrendously bugged. It is challenging, and the idea is well implemented, but the execution is awful. Once your target reticle switches to the upper torso, you'll more than likely shoot up and clip into his center torso, making that block/attack trade worthless as you won't do any damage. If you choose to NOT lock him, you'll clip into his legs and have 100 damage done every ~second until you die. And when you DO get him to fall forward for the attack phase, more likely than not, he'll be facing the wall and you won't be able to attack the proper areas to do any damage.
Like I said, I want to love this game. It's a new story that uses a proven combat system with several innovations of its own, and it's great to look at. But don't buy it until you see reviews saying it is completely fixed. Not "runs fine for me" but "yeah, they patched that, doesn't happen anymore"
A testament to the risks of Early Access. Never assume a game will be any better than its current state, regardless of the developer's pedigree.

After 300+ hours of FS15 I 'ummed' and 'aaahhed' over buying this for a good couple of weeks before deciding to take the plunge. And TLDR; I'm glad I did. There are many major improvements - not least for me being simply able to set up a steering wheel quickly and easily (a pain in FS15).  I'm only a few hours into this one, but so far, so very good. Certainly worth getting if you liked any of the earlier incarnations.

At a quick glance, it may seem like FS15.  Only after playing the game for a bit do you notice all the improvements.
It begins immediately when you enter a tractor.  You have to start it manually.  As soon as you start to drive, you notice the sound is infinitely better.  The tractors sound better, engine RPM isn't linear with speed as it was in the past.  The dirt crunches like in real life when you drive on dirt roads.  When you exit your tractor, the lights stay on.
Those little things are just a small example of the many things they have improved.  The game is also deeper with mandatory plowing every few years and more fertilizing to make it realistic.  The storage on the farm is limited an you need to buy more silos to store more crops.  You must also buy seed and fertilizer in pallets from the store, there isn't a magical endless supply on your farm. They also have more equipment and vehicles released than FS15+all DLC.
There I go listing more improvements again. Did they make any huge improvements like in FS15?  No. In FS15, if you take forestry or the physics away from the list of improvements from FS13, it would not have been a good game.  For FS17, remove any one change, heck even any 5 changes, and it is still a great improvement from FS15.  The improvements are probably most noticeable when you go back and try to play FS15 again.  FS15 just isn't fun anymore.

The most interesting mechanic for me is the pseudo-strategic aspect behind combat. This aspect certainly grew more interesting with a diversity of Function combinations. I'd only really play the game once, however, as several playthroughs did not communicate anything new about the mechanics for me. Enemies and Functions grow all too familiar.
Visually, I'm pretty enthralled. Supergiant is not anything if not capable of style. I could never really find a word for that Western/Eastern blend, but if someone could find it for me, I'd be pretty happy. There's a detail to everything that well fits the idea of a city run entirely by technology but expanded upon by the people. It bears elegance without warmth, which I feel fits the thematic purpose.
As for the music and sound, I felt that they were amazing and purposeful, respectively. I tend to be more concerned with the artistic cohesion of these aspects, and they fit the storytelling and setting very well. Atmospheric music is somewhat reminiscent of hiphop and techno, borrowing dirtier soundwork and largely focusing on bass and beat. The more organic music, particularly singing, sort of takes on this soul-ish, blues-ey vibe like that of the cabaret. I think this contrast really brings out a somewhat anti-mechanical theme, which I find somewhat interesting.
There's something both vibrant and desolate behind the concept of a slowly devolving city comprised of programs. While the story itself is a pretty simple revenge story, that setting adds a few themes regarding a resistance to mechanization in the urban. I never got the impression that it implied a resistance to all matters of urbanization, rather a criticism of the formulaity of these settings. Come up with your own interpretation of everything. Either way, it's fun.

This is a game that has a lot of variety, so I cannot speak for every role. But I'll tell you what I do with it.
Space Trucker Simulator. Now I know the immediate thought for a lot of people must be, "Well that sounds dreadfully boring." And sure, it's not usually a very action-packed job. I don't get filthy rich, I don't purchase fleets of dreadnoughts and battle for control over planets. I don't side with factions and fight space wars, or hunt down pirates and slay them for bounties.
I load up on food on one of the many agricultural worlds, then haul it to one of the larger tourist destinations, or a heavy industrial planet, or a mining rock where they can't produce their own. Every planet you go to is unique, with it's own description and flavor. It's nothing big or ridiculously in-depth, but it's tasty and immersive. You can travel from major, bustling starports like Earth, where millions of ships arrive each week to deliver goods from all over the known galaxy, and then you can fly straight to a backwater world that doesn't even have a starport, just land on a pad in the middle of a field where all the country yokels come out to gawk at the spaceship while you load up grain to deliver somewhere else.
It's a lovely, realistic place that I enjoy traveling around when Im tired and want something simple. I've conquered so many galaxies, it's nice to settle down, haul some space cows, and ferry a young family away from the busy industrial planet they lived on to go start their new lives as farmers.

Pixel Space is a very simple yet fun indie game for all your spacey-shooter needs. It is games like this that stood out the most among all the others with its simplistic and clean style.
The game relies on standard WASD and mouse, alongside with 1-5 to control the spacecraft. Unfortunately, there isn’t an option to switch up the hotkeys provided within the game for those who aren’t comfortable with the initial setup.
Right off the bat, Pixel Space welcomes the player with a small pop up tutorial message that the player could choose to skip over. Once you’re officially in the game, a small list of missions is available on the left side for you to choose:
There is a small “warp” key under the selected mission, which enables the player to fast travel to the specified location in matter of seconds. Although after following the missions a couple of times, it could prove to be quite repetitive, the option to fast travel really makes it up for it by being conveniently accessible.
A game gets old if it doesn’t offer customizable weapons and whatnots, Pixel Space offers the player a chance to change it up via the store with several color options for your spacecraft and laser beams (it would be great, however, if there is an option to change the model of the ship as well). You can also find different weapons to help you shoot down your enemies (I suppose the enemies would be much better with more diversities and different formations as well to surprise the player).
In regards to combat, it is rather easy to play with the “shoot and dodge” method. With the asteroids floating around, my first thought was to avoid them, but when I realized my space ship is fine crashing into them, I wanted to use them as shields against the enemies. Unfortunately, the floating rocks didn’t seem to be able to block the enemies’ laser beams (I must add, it would be really cool if they could block the incoming fire and be able to explode into pieces), so I could only try to dodge the beams as if I was playing
.
All in all, this game is quite fun if you’re looking for a casual game to play and I definitely recommend this for those who’re interested.

Cthulhu Saves The World is a 16-bit old school traditional console style role playing game.  The game has been dated by over 20 years, but still is fun for those who appreciate the older generation style.  The game's battle system is intuitive and encourages magic point management.  The story is linear, and took me about 8 hours with in depth exploration on my first run.  I do encourage playing it on the hardest setting for the most fun, and because the normal setting is a bit easy for the seasoned adventurer.  The replay value is low, as the story is a bit bland for a linear game.  Overall, it was a fun old school romp with a bit of humor and micromanagement, but I'm not going to pick it up again anytime soon.  If you enjoy it, make sure to play Breath Of Death VII, written by the same designer.

Borderlands 2 is one of the best co-op shooters out there, and a great sequel to a good game. It's also a good game on single player, but it's way better when played with someone. Also, make sure you get at least the Game of the Year edition, because you get an additional amount of content at least as big as the base game for just a little more, especially on sale. The game itself is an FPS with heavy RPG mechanics, for better and worse. There's a lot of weapons and supportive items, however getting the best ones can be tedious. There's 6 distinct classes (in the GOTY) and you'll want to try them out at least once. My favorite was the Gunzerker, just shooting my way through the game with 2 guns at once. And each character has different builds, depending on the skills and items you choose. There's a lot of depth, without being overwhelming. The gameplay is great and varied, depending on your class and build. This sequel has a great story with one of the best villains in videogame history, and plenty of great NPC's, both new and returning. And lots of memes, humor and references. Plus, this time there's more variety in the maps, so the game doesn't feel as recycled and lazy as the original. That was a huge plus for me. The music is also better. It's a true, great sequel.
But the DLC practices are polarizing. The game has a lot of overpriced DLC's, but also has 4 story true expansions that are way, way better, especially the last one, Tiny Tina's Assault On Dragon Keep. This last expansion puts you in a classic fantasy world, which works wonders. The GOTY version adds all these expansions, 2 classes and smaller DLC packs, however it doesn't include all content. Besides some customizations items, the GOTY doesn't include 5 short stories and more importantly, lots of end game content. I know that this content was released after the GOTY edition, but the GOTY should've been updated with all this content, creating a definitive edition. But no, you need to buy that content separately. I'm focusing on this because i really enjoyed this game, both the main campaign and the DLC, and like i wrote before, i highly suggest you to get at least the GOTY version. This game is also highly replayable and will waste many hours of your life, but they’ll be good hours wasted.

So what can i say about this game. I First started out playing this MMO back in 1.0 on, and did not like it. As the game progressed and became A Realm Reborn, I started to play it again. As time passed, I made plenty of friends, and started getting more and more addicted to this game. Fast foreward to this day, and this mmorpg has taken the most of my time out've every game i've playn outside of consoles. Yes, it'll have it's infuriating moments, and as with all mmorpgs, theres always gunna be people whom will irritate you, but if you're willing to work at it, even casually; even you can get to the point where you'll be able to run raids with friends and be successful.
The games learning curve isn't to high, though honestly a lot of classes/jobs do require a bit more of an active role in learning them. Each job has it's own sort've "specialty" to them that makes them different from all the otheres within the same roles. The battle system does take some time to get used to, but the devs are constantly trying to improve each job so they're "easy to learn, difficult to master."
As someone whom frequents mmorpgs quiet often, i find often times that the biggest problems i have when starting a new mmo is when you're trying to do a dungeon only to find that no one is around to party up, and you can't possibly do it on your own. This is not the case with this game, as party of the daily quests is to do what is called "roulettes" where higher leveled players will be placed in random dungeons, and will have their jobs forcibly leveled down to match a "max level" for that dgn. they will recieve exp proportionate to their level, and special currency used to buy higher tier gear while helping lower level players with their dungeons, thereby making it very newbie friendly!
The story is pretty decent once you get to the heavensward story, as it starts to get a bit more darker. A Realm Reborn (ARR) story for the first part of the game is alright, but i found it to be very long and overly tedious (with over 200+ quests, often times making you go back and forth between places.) However, once you get passed the ARR stories, and assuming you bought the DLC's (which i HIGHLY reccomend) the story picks up and gets better and better.
The music is the typical epic music you'd expect from final fantasy, and i promise you'll find a theme here or there that you'll absolutely adore (personally, it's the theme for sophia).
The raiding in game is pretty newbie friendly as well, as they always introduce an easier "normal/hard" mode to give you some basic knowledge on how to do said raid, and they introduce more mechanics as you go into the "extreme" and "savage" raids.
The UI is pretty decent and very customizable, i've found it takes a bit of time to figure out how to navigate some of the options to customize the game, but they offer you many different kinds of customizations from hot bar shapes and placements, to moving all of the ui's, size adjustments, etc.
biggest thing i can really say is a negative is the subscription fee. I won't beat around the bush, the subscription fee isn't very cheap, and it requires you to go onto their mogstation website to get more time... but at the end of the day, it's up to you if you're willing to pay for it; i would like to note that if you buy the game for the first time, you will recieve a 1 month "free" subscription so that will cover you for a bit atleast, and it is very possible to hit max level and raid with people before the month is up.
Finally, biggest thing to note: if you ever decide to play this game and wish to meet me; I play on the primal data center on Brynhildr, and my character name is Remi Aschente. If you ever need assitance or just friendly advice, help with getting dungeons done or anything; feel free to come by and say hi!

I'm a fan of open world games in general. Sleeping Dogs may be a little dated at this point, but the city is interesting to me and so far I've had a great time.

If you like Grand Theft Auto, you'll probably love Sleeping Dogs. The setting is more interesting, the story more engaging, and the combat a million times more complex and enjoyable. It's similar to an old-school arcade beat-em-up, and yet it still has fast-paced and challenging driving sections. Rather than merely having punches and guns, there's a whole skill-attack learning system which depends on timing and button combos. There's a lot of fun to be had committing crimes, exploring Hong Kong, dressing up your character, meeting many interesting faces, and you can even play as an officer of the law. In many ways, it surpasses Grand Theft Auto, though some may be disappointed with the size of its world, or the limited amount of vehicles (that is, there's no airplanes, tanks, or boats).

Personally, I hate to say this. I don't like this game. It gets really repetitive really fast. But you're not reading this to hear me whine. So here's pros and cons instead.
Pros: Level design is something to behold. The areas are beautiful and expansive, for the most part. The enemies are hard to, but that's what makes it fun. It'll keep you on your toes and keep your wits sharp. The scenes are fantastic and the combat is... interesting. Selecting body parts for weak points is a neat concept. Cons: Gameplay gets repetitive along with combat. There is no clear indication of what to do. While that is sort of what these types of games are about, I feel at the very least there should be a map so the player could at least figure out where they are. Difficulty will spike randomly without warning. While that could be fun, it's mostly VERY annoying. The first boss could either be very easy, or extremely hard to figure out. Hit boxes are off, you could get hit by a weapon landing a foot away from you (however, that could just be my game or lag)
Overall, I could go on, but I would not recommend this game. While it has it's good moments, be it that they're far and few between, there are too many bad moments or just really long, drawn out moments where I'm trying to figure out what to do next. I could just be incompetent though. But whatever. Do what you want, I'm not your mother.

Transistor has a fantastic story, eye catching visuals, and unique gameplay.  However, what sets this game apart from many others is the soundtrack.  It is absolutely the best part of this game.

The most interesting mechanic for me is the pseudo-strategic aspect behind combat. This aspect certainly grew more interesting with a diversity of Function combinations. I'd only really play the game once, however, as several playthroughs did not communicate anything new about the mechanics for me. Enemies and Functions grow all too familiar.
Visually, I'm pretty enthralled. Supergiant is not anything if not capable of style. I could never really find a word for that Western/Eastern blend, but if someone could find it for me, I'd be pretty happy. There's a detail to everything that well fits the idea of a city run entirely by technology but expanded upon by the people. It bears elegance without warmth, which I feel fits the thematic purpose.
As for the music and sound, I felt that they were amazing and purposeful, respectively. I tend to be more concerned with the artistic cohesion of these aspects, and they fit the storytelling and setting very well. Atmospheric music is somewhat reminiscent of hiphop and techno, borrowing dirtier soundwork and largely focusing on bass and beat. The more organic music, particularly singing, sort of takes on this soul-ish, blues-ey vibe like that of the cabaret. I think this contrast really brings out a somewhat anti-mechanical theme, which I find somewhat interesting.
There's something both vibrant and desolate behind the concept of a slowly devolving city comprised of programs. While the story itself is a pretty simple revenge story, that setting adds a few themes regarding a resistance to mechanization in the urban. I never got the impression that it implied a resistance to all matters of urbanization, rather a criticism of the formulaity of these settings. Come up with your own interpretation of everything. Either way, it's fun.

You know how many reviewrs like to divide games into parts like visuals, soundtrack, gameplay, interface and so on? I like that to, and I was going to do it here, but... Well it ain't that easy with this one.
Some things are just greater then the sum of their parts. And Transistor is surely one of the best examples for such things. So standard review forms don't apply, which is only appropriate, because Transistor is anything but standard.
For me this game redefined the term "story driven".
There are many games, where story plays an important role, but Transistor goes much further. In some sense Transistor is nothing BUT story, because it seems like every other game element was designed around it and provides support and focus for the story.
Unfortunetly that concept puts strict limits on what one can do besides following the story.
Exploration is almost nonexistent: there are no side quests and secret lore waiting for you in rarely visited corners of the world.
It's tiny: only about 4 hours start to finish.
Combat system has just enough depth so it doesn't bore you and fights, while intense, are short and not very frequent.
So if you play Transistor to take your sweet time gradually exploring the world, powering up and beating the hell out of monsters and mechanics, like we often do in RPGs, you probably will be dissapointed, because this game has nothing special to offer here.
What it offers though is one of the most beautifull, tightly paced and focused stories I ever saw, heard or read. Transistor is a masterpiece that still brings tears to my eyes even after more than two years passed since I played it. So I encourage you to set everything aside for a day and enjoy the expierence while it lasts.
10/10.
P. S. I don't comment on art and soundtrack here because I don't thik it's really necessary. All it takes to realise both are gorgeous is pair of eyes and ears.

---Borderlands Characters---
1. Maya
Pros:
Best healing abilities in the game. Sweet Release and Elated are unmatched when it comes to providing health, and Life Tap makes you completely immortal.
Best co-op partner in the game. Res is the best co-op skill, and PL's CC is key to keeping mobs managed. Her healing abilities are also very respectable even during raids.
Definitely one of the most powerful mobbers in the game, coming in behind only Zer0 and Sal.
Cons: Very PL dependent. Almost all of her good skills are only active if you can PL something, and that can fall off during boss fights or if you can't PL something in general.
Poor damage dealer in raids. Beehawking is nearly mandatory for her to provide damage. Granted, she's probably the only character that can use it as a legitimate strategy with the Cat COM, but still.
Slightly weak damage capabilities. Maya is a little more reliant that the other characters on good equipment, since she doesn't have as many skills that increase her damage. The few skills she does have are extremely powerful, however.
Best played as: CC/support. You can definitely play a more aggressive role if you build her right.
Zer0
Pros:
Extremely powerful damage. Zer0 ranks only behind Sal when it comes to overall damage output, and both of his strongest builds are capable of some downright obscene kills.
Arguably the second tankiest character in the game if you play melee. Zer0 basically can't die as long as you're in melee range of an enemy.
Zer0's gear requirements are very light. Due to the nature of Critical Ascension, some very basic snipers will be enough to tear through mobs given enough stacks. The two most important weapons in the melee build are very easy quests, and everything else can be obtained in vending machines if you're really desperate.
Cons: Highest skill ceiling in the game. He is not an easy character to play, and an even harder one to master. Be prepared to read up and practice a lot if you want to achieve some of the things he's capable of.
Adding on to the previous point, Zer0 requires that you can aim well. Sniping obviously demands excellent precision, and melee requires some very precise maneuvers and actions to be potent.
Fairly weak when it comes to actually surviving if you're not playing the melee style. You'll either need to take cover a lot, have a way of recovering health, or dodge very well.
Best played as: Main damage dealer or supporting other players with damage and Kunai.
Axton
Pros:
Simplest character by far. His skills don't do anything fancy--they just read "increase damage" or "shield good". His action skill is obviously uncomplicated and straightforward, and his playstyle is very reminiscent of your standard FPS hero: your only job is to click on enemies repeatedly until they die.
Extremely powerful explosive damage. Axton is capable of killing some raid bosses faster than Sal if you utilize his explosive damage to the fullest, and when you take into account the fact that Torgue weapons benefit from both gun and grenade damage, he becomes an absolute powerhouse.
Excellent shield abilities. If it weren't for the fact that Gaige has a skill that reads "your shields never go down ever", Axton would be the best character when it comes to managing your shields. This makes him the second best character when it comes to using the Bee.
Cons:
Even with his plethora of gun damage abilities, Axton's damage can be lacking compared to what some of the other characters can put out. This naturally lends him to have the second strictest gear requirements and excellent DM (though not as much as Zer0) to be able to match the other Vault Hunters in some of their more impressive feats.
In exchange for his simple but efficient playstyle, Axton sacrifices diversity. There aren't as many ways to build him, and his playstyle might become boring at the higher levels. Being a jack of all trades means that he is also a master of none.
Best played as: Axton can play a lot of roles, but I like playing him as a support/general damage dealer.
Gaige
Pros:
Anarchy is one of the most powerful skills in the game. I don't like it, but I will not let that change the fact that Anarchy is simply absurd and can allow Gaige to keep up and even surpass some of the damage from the other characters.
Best shield abilities in the game. Axton used to take this spot for me, but after playing with Gaige, I've come to the realization that Blood-Soaked Shields is downright absurd. Your shield will basically never be down.
Lightest gear requirements. Anarchy, and to a lesser extent slag, can bring even mediore guns to the damage-dealing capabilities of some legendaries. Her best gear is all received as quest rewards or are very easily farmable.
Cons: Probably even more boring than Axton. You'll spend half of your time shooting at the ground, and there's not a lot of crazy aiming involved.
Anarchy is a fickle skill. If you're using it to boost your weak guns, dying will mean that you are now stuck with a character that has no other good damage boosts. Survival becomes hyper-important.
Deathtrap has a host of bugs and issues, and is slightly unreliable as a combat partner. Granted, you don't need him to still be able to absolutely destroy mobs, but it's something to consider.
Best Played as:  I'm still inexperienced with Gaige, so I can't pinpoint a role for her yet. I'd just use her as a general nuker--spam the battlefield with homing ricochet bullets and let Deathtrap or your teammates play clean up.
Krieg
Pros:
I was wrong about Gaige: I think Krieg has the lightest gear requirements, as there are plenty of videos of him going through UVHM without any gear whatsoever.
Arguably the most powerful skill tree abilities in the game. Release the Beast is even stronger than MMF in some cases, Bloodsplosion alone can clear entire rooms with a single kill, and Raving Retribution is almost never bad even though it's only fire element.
Cons:
His playstyle is the most unique in Borderlands, and can definitely take some time to get used to. It's not difficult like Zer0's is, just strange and might be a little counterintuitive at first.
I haven't played Krieg a lot either.
Best played as: Definitely a main damage dealer. I really can't wait to take Krieg into the higher levels to make use of his insane survival and damaging skill tree.
Sal
Pros:
Everything. Sal is broken.
Cons:
If you don't like your video games to be an exercise in pressing your forward movement key and holding down your two mouse buttons, then Sal is not the character for you. Sal is broken.
best played as: Team carry/god-tier damage dealer/kill everything, what are teammates.

What can I say about the surge so far? I like it. I'll be making some comparisons to both Dark Souls and Lords of the Fallen here (The devlopers previous game)
First off let's talk about what they improved over Lords of the Fallen (The developers first push forward in to souls-lke territory) they improved pretty much everything over the community dubbed 'Clunky Souls'. It's no longer clunky that's for sure, combat and just movement in general is smooth and quite fast paced.
Combat has some interesting mechanics. You can't parry like you can in dark souls and you can't move while blocking like you can in Dark Souls and LoTF. When you block you are stationary BUT they did add in a neat little counter mechanic in the form of ducking and jumping. While blocking you can duck under an enemy attack and then counter or you can jump over the enemy attack and counter that way. It still requires the same sort of timing as say a parry in the DS series. Not being able to move while blocking would usually annoy the hell out of me but with those little added mechanics I can deffinately give it a pass.
Rather than rolling like DS/LoTF you have a Bloodborne style of dodging which again, is a wonderful addition and helps combat feel a lot faster (You'll be using this dodging a lot) You can combine these dodges with attacks too that create good combat openers that effectively stagger your enemy, allowing you to get a good couple of hits off before you back away.
Combat is smooth, it's fluid and such a HUGE improvement over their previous entry. It's also pretty damn difficult too. Unlike LoTF, the enemies in 'The Surge' do not screw around and will severely punish you if you make a mistake (This isn't a negative, this is exactly what us souls-like fans want) and that's just the regular enemies, the bosses are tough as nails. In LoTF 90% of the bosses were a joke to be honest but in 'The Surge' the two bosses I have fought so far have given me some real challenge.
For somebody like me who has put a ridiculous amount of hours in to the soulsborne series it's easy to get to grips with the mechanics, you go in to a boss fight knowing what you should look for, what you should pay attention to and such since you're so used to fighting bosses in a souls-like game but even then for me it was still a challenge, I imagine for those not used to souls-like games it would be an even bigger challenge.
The way gear is handled in this game in my opinion is a HUGE improvement over not only LoTF but the souls games as well (Yes that's right, I said it) In the Souls games you can kill up to 50 maybe a little less of the same enemy and cross every part of your body to just -hope- you get an armour or weapon drop, it becomes tedious and crushes your soul (No pun intended)
In The Surge however with the way you can target enemy limbs you are 100% promised at the very least a schamtic to craft that portion of armour and once you have that schematic you can cut off that same limb of the same enemy in order to get the componants to craft/upgrade said piece. Now it is not lost on me how grindy that feels and I don't really like grinding but it is still less of a grind that farming armour/weapon drops in the souls series. It's not based off pure luck in The Surge and you -always- know what you have to work toward.
So how about the world design? It stacks up to the souls series of games in layout but not in design. It's all inter-conected, full of shortcuts to unlock, secrets to find, hidden weapons and implants to find etc.. like you'd expect of any souls-like game but the world doesn't tell a story in design the way that the souls games do. To their credit they gave it one hell of a try and while the world and story elements, NPC that you meet etc.. are quite interesting, it doesn't grip me the way Lordran/Drangleic/Lothric did.
That's not really a bad thing, those are hard world designs to beat.
People have been calling this game a "Cheap Dark Souls" or a "Ripoff" or a "Cash in" but it's really none of those. It takes the souls formula but then does enough of its own thing to make it stand out from the rest in new and interesting ways which is what game design is all about really, improving ideas and concepts for others to then improve in the future and improve our quality of entertainment overall.
This game also runs flawlessly. I have yet to encounter any graphical glitches, any FPS slowdowns or any crashes. It's a very stable game on my system at least.
Now that the praise is out of the way however, I will talk about the issues the game does seem to have. Firstly it does have a few bugs such as not being able to talk to NPC's which will require you to restart the game, not being able to pick up items which again, requires a restart of the game and also buggy enemy AI that sometimes (Although rarely) notices you WAY before the point they should notice you, we're talking through walls and up stairwells here, that's not acceptable.
There was a certain point where I was fighting an enemy at the top of a stairwell, killed him, started walking down the stairwell only to be greeted by five enemies at the bottom all trying to get up the stairs (We're talking a stairwell that goes down six levels here) so I manage to pull agro from five enemies while being six levels above them, that's not acceptable ever.
One other downer is the lack of a fast travel system. Now usually I don't require fast travel, more often than not in my souls runs I will not bother with fast travel but this game severely  needs it. It's really difficult to find your way to past areas, often you have to jump through a♥♥♥♥♥♥load of hoops and if you want to get to a specific area you'll find yourself having to manually travel to and through the previous areas in order to get to where you actually want to be and then when you're done? You have to go back through all the areas you just came. It's very tedious and one of the worst flaws the game has.
All in all though I'd give the game a solid thumbs up. I'm really enjoying it so far and I can see myself enjoying it for a while to come yet. Highly reccomend you pick this up whether you're a fan of souls-like games or just a fan of action/RPG type games in general.

This might come as an odd surprise to some people, but I actually like Emily is Away. I really liked it.
No, I'm not kidding. I really enjoyed it.
Emily is Away focuses purely on two characters, the invisible "you" and the invisible "Emily", and the relationship you two share. The game is detailed enough in the story that transpires between the passing years and vague enough on the specific details of what "Emily" represents or means to "you", so that you're left to make your own interpretations. I really see Emily is Away as an art game. It is short, but it's value is just as high as games like Loneliness or Majesty of Colors.
The simple dialouge between you and Emily (which is an interesting nostalgic trip to old Windows chatting, along with a statement on their disconnected relationship), really makes you want to see it through that you end up with Emily, but ultimately fail. And that's one of the key points of Emily is Away. Is the ending ultimately good for you, or bad for you? You do have some choice, but the actual in-game "you" will actually type sentences and edit them. You're more or less a  participate in the in-game "you"s decision-making process. And how the two type and message each other really speaks volumes on what they're obviously thinking.
Emily is Away is one of the better games of 2015. It's not as big as Undertale is, but if you like art games or very emotional free games, Emily is Away delivers a unique perspective on video game narrative, that's a joy (and a pain) to play.

Soooo, Lords of the Black Sun. I was remotely involved with some part of this game (localization) and was somewhat looking forward to it, but I feared the worst. I won't call this game a really bad game, and I have only played about 1 hour, but this is what I think nevertheless:
I have played Galactic Civ 2, Endless Space and others. I found none of them extremely satisfying and perfect. Good games in some areas, lacking in others. Lords of the Black Sun I think is not doing anything better than those games and that in my eyes makes it an immediate failure.
The empire management is tread of the mill. Manage gold, health, reputation blabla. Low health on a planet? Build a health center, build a police station vs crime. Build a factory to produce faster, build a tech lab to research faster, build colony ships, colonize planets, rinse & repeat the same meaningless "choices"...You have a few building slots, but if you can only choose between 5 or 6 buildings, all of which fulfill exactly one role, this is pretty boring.
Economy: Visit planets and establish trade routes...yea. There are some interesting concepts like immigration and laws you can establish, but again, those seem shallow I'm afraid...90% of the population want free speech, better give it to them before they rebel and take away your planet.
The map and moving units is ok I guess, but you get easily lost, because at max zoom icons are no longer displayed. Graphics are neither very pretty nor extremely bad for such a game. Ship models look like♥♥♥♥♥♥on the galaxy map though.
Diplomacy? Nothing new here, either. 10 minutes after meeting the first race they already demand a fifth or your total gold in tribute...cmon that is the easy AI. I already loathed that in Civ games.
You can also hire ministers and generals...ok. Those cost money and improve your empire in one way or the other...oook
Ship design...design...yea. You seem to have 4 different hulls at your disposal from the very beginning. The game wouldn't bother telling you that unless you click on the ship design icon (otherwise you only have a scout, an army ship and a colony ship). You can then proceed to build a light, medium, heavy or capital hull. The stronger hulls can of course take more punishment. You can then outfit those hulls with meaningless weapons (beam, plasma and missiles) as well as an engine, some armor and shields and 1 module. Your capital ship has 1 engine, 1 module, 2 armor and 4 weapon slots. No way to customize those slots I think? It does not matter where I would put my weapons, only the range and damage are affected by the weapon type, so generally build lots of ships with rockets and position your heavies with lots of armor and beam or plasma before them...research stronger weapons, replace them...nooooooo cmooooon. That is so boring. "Oh, I now have plasma weapons II...yay". Time to replace all my ship designs with the new weapons (I think, otherwise why would there be obsolete designs?).
Research is a chore. My 2nd tier research already took 50 months (Maybe I wasn't building enough colony ships and research centers, but on the other hand you are not supposed to colonize at will, because it will stretch your resources and your defensive capabilities thin, and because colonization is boring. The research trees are pretty linear and nothing interesting either. They don't offer much, but every tier takes long to research. You have the usual stuff in there.
There are barely any options in the game at all, which is another gripe of mine. Also the fonts are ♥♥♥♥ing small in 1920x1080 and you apparently can't make them bigger.
So, you basically build meaningless buildings, meaningless ships and research meaningless things and then you have your scout fly through a meaningless universe that looks all so very tidy and you discover your AI partners and yadda yadda yadda. In the one hour I was able to play this game all I did was basically "End turn", because there is just nothing meaningful to do. Maybe later on you will have to micro manage more, but it just all seems so generic and bland.
Last bit, combat: Who the ♥♥♥♥ thought of that? It is a hex and turn based combat system with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ graphics and animations and no great depth to it either. It's playing Heroes of Might and Magic in space with only a hand ful of units. And there is just no weight behind the combat. You fire a beam weapon and you barely register it. Missiles have at least a little bit of impact, but with only 3 different weapon types (all available from the beginning), this is bound to get boring after 2-3 battles.
I know I should have played longer to offer a good review, so please don't take my word for it, but I just couldn't bring myself to do it. It all seemed so pointless :( Endless space (despite the silly auto combat) and Galactic Civ seem way better than this, so why bother? Also, the game has like 15 achievements and I unlocked half of them within 1 hour. Is this maybe indicative of the game content? There is only Single Player and Multi Player, no scenarios, no campaign apparently. I just cannot recommend it.

I am a enthusiastic player of all 4X games, sank lots of hours into the Civ Series, into GalCiv2 and also played Master of Orion 2. And if you expect something of similar quality here, I have to disappoint you:
-The Mechanics: One of the Game Defining Mechanics is how the production works. It works on a global level. Meaning each planet generates global production. If you colonize a second planet the production from the main planet will therefore sink as it's not the only "receiver" anymore. In addition you speed up the production massively with each factory you build. It's almost like reducing the time by half with each factory, which makes no sense. This way you spent a couple of turns building factories, then you design your combat ship, create a couple of them, and kill one "very hard" opponent after the other. Your hardest opponent will be pirates. Balance is completely broken and make all mechanics besides of production and military obsolete. The Global mechanics also kill the feeling of having "special planets". Each planet is just contributing a bit to the "geater good". But that doesn't feel good.
While the game features tactical combat it's not planned out well and as the AI does not focus fire on your ships it will always lose when having troops with even strength.
-The Interface: It works. But it isn't good. Instead of mouseover tooltips you have to click on stuff to get the information, right mousebutton is closing windows. The production windows are tiny, creating a minimum of overview. You also cannot re-arrange your production queue or edit your ship-designs.
-Stability: The game tends to crash after you solved a combat. Within 90 Minutes of the release version the game crashed twice.
-The Music: Is really good, but of course doesn't save the game
Considering that in terms of balancing and game mechanics I didn't see much of a change since I played one of the first alphas I'd say that the chances of getting fixes in the near future is very low. The game has some potential, but in the current state (Release Version / September 2014) I recommend to not buy this game and take a look at the Galactic Civilization 3 Beta instead.

FINAL FANTASY XIV Online has been a game under my radar for quite some while and as a MMORPG requiring a monthly subscription, I was a little bit sceptic. I picked this game up during a sale and with your first purchase as a new account, they give you 30 days free of subscription so you can decide whether you like the game or not. Now, I've played most of the popular MMORPG, WoW, BDO, Rift, TERA, MS and the list goes on.
This game has absolutely stunning graphics. The gameplay is fun and almost everything is customizeable such as your HUD and UI which is a lifesaver. The community is great, not as toxic as most games and since it's cross platform it seems to be more friendly. Now, some may wonder if this follows a certain story and lore and yes it might be more appealing if you're familiar with the world but I feel as it is not required. The cutscenes however of the main story does not come with full audio support. DO NOTE.
The job system in this game is great, tons of jobs to choose from and instead of having to make tons of characters, 1 character can essentially turn into any job.
The character customization might not be super advanced as different MMORPG's such as BDO (most complex character customization) but it suffice as a great MMORPG nonetheless.
The questing in this game is as any but it's great to know that there is no looting in this game. Looting as in you have to manually go and pick up your things from a slain mob or boss, it's automatic and you start with maximum amounts of backpack space which is great.
Also, to everyone else wondering why this game has so many reviews, it's due to unfortunate butthurt players from South America and Russia complaining about prices. As I've noted, Russia and South America were paying a much lower price than ROW and since then Square Enix have now decided to change the price to the NORMAL pricing. Yes, NORMAL pricing and not underpricing it for those two nations. This is a just change and the game itself does not deserve negative reviews due to this.
I might not have over 500 hours into this game and not understand the entire game but as someone who has tested tons of different MMORPG's that just haven't stuck on to me, FFXIV is one of those games that actually did it. My journey continues.

Don't listen to the recent reviews by Russians and Brazilians. Both of these communities are generally a cancer upon MMORPG's, and all Square Enix did was adjust the prices to the proper levels, as previously they were paying much less than other countries. They're just salty - ignore them.
The game's outstanding, and one of the most polished RPG's I've ever played. The story, gameplay, and depth offered are unmatched by any other game on the market. If you have ever enjoyed an MMORPG, or would like to get into the genre, this is the game for you. You won't regret it.

I got Sleeping Dogs simply expecting a decent open world action game to entertain me for a while but to my surprise it was much more than that and was quite the unique game. First off this is much more than Chinese GTA which is what I went in expecting.
+The game is centered around hand to hand combat similar to the Batman games. Its doesn't have the variety of difficulty that the Arkham games have and its never that challenging but its still quite fun and the environmental takedowns are great.
+The voice acting is excellent. The voice cast features actors like Will Yun Lee, Kelly Hu, Emma Stone (though briefly) and even Tom Wilkinson himself. There is a lot of cheesy dialogue here but its done purposely and has a lot of charm to it.
+The story plays out like a classic hong kong action film and its a great and entertaining ride all the way through. I was never bored or wanted the game to end.
+The side activities here are actually quite fun and I didn't mind doing them.
+Visually the game holds up incredibly well and the lighting especially is simply beautiful.
+The game is very well optimized and I achieved 144fps the entire time without any drops at all.
-The vehicles are not too fun to drive and just feel rather dull to me. Driving on the small crowded Hong Kong streets certainly doesn't help this either.
-After time the fighting can become repetitive as despite unlocking more combos you don't unlock many new ways of tackling a fight and there aren't many new enemies either.
-The guns while fun for slow motion aren't anything to write home about. Since they aren't in the game much however this is a very small gripe.
-The two main DLC packs I played Nightmare In North Point and Year of the Snake are both very mediocre and short and do not provide any meaningful continuation to the main games story. I do not hold this against the game at all however as they come free with this version anyway.
If you have any desire to play an awesome Hong Kong action game with a great open world and a lot of things to do I highly recommend this. The story and characters are excellent and I would love for us to get a sequel.

Alright, I think it's time for a review. After playing this game for 45 hours, and now completely beating it 100%, I just have to say that I really enjoy this game. It's fun, action-packed, you go driving around their little Hong Kong, etc. I loved a lot about this game, but of course, it has its flaws.
What I liked;
+The combat. The combat system in this game is great. While sometimes wonky on counters, I found this combat system to be great, fast, and not difficult to master.
+The story. While it went very fast, I liked every mission. None were too long, repetitive, or just plain boring. It showed that the characters have emotions and you cared for Wei a lot of the time. Of course made you hate certain people too (won't spoil anything).
+The outfits. There are a bunch of outfits. I've always loved games that let you customize your character. Even if I can't change his appearance, I can still change his style. If fun and the preset outfits are badass. Especially the Square Enix specified ones.
+The pull to make you play more. This game kept making come back to completely finish it. You know it's a good game when they have you be occupied the whole time. Sure I took breaks. You can't keep doing the same game all the time. Unless... you do.
+Races. The races who fun and a bit easy. I never had a real tough time with races. I always had the better car really. They were fast and sometimes slow, but really fun. There's quite a bit too!
+Upgrades. The upgrades just make you unstoppable. You learn new moves and they kick♥♥♥♥♥ You also get some perks as well. Like stealing a car without the alarm going off for instance.
+Gaining stats. There is a certain achievement where you need 30 silver medals and 30 gold medals. That was a doozy to get. You gain most just from playing. At least the majority you do. Others you can really just farm for them.
+The ideas behind the DLCs. They are great and are fun to play. The Nightmare in North Point one was great, while the Year of the Snake was ok.
What I Didn't Like;
+The cars. While the car themselves looked awesome, the turn radius on these supercars is just awful. You can't even make a sharp turn nor turn fast in some of these fast cars. Pressing space (or whatever your drift button is) just makes you drift which slows you down.
+Drifting. When you drift, you basically stop. While you'd do that in real life, most games just have you still move. Also, it's very wild. You can't predict where you're going except a wall or railing.
+The DLCs themselves. While they were fun, they were so quick. You get each one done in about an hour or two. It's way too quick compared to the main game.
+Dates. While they help out with finding lockboxes, health shrines, and jade statues, there is no point. You see that they hang out, you do the date and that's it. No continuum, nothing.
+Use of weapons. You don't use weapons that often besides in the missions. Even when you do, guns are the only things that last a bit longer than the melee weapons. The melee weapons literally just wear off.
+Roland's and Tang's jobs. They are just time-consuming and suck really. Tang's does give you a looooot of money though.
All in all, I loved this game. It was amazing and I would totally recommend you buy it!

Definitely a great game for those looking to have a Dark Souls/Bloodborne experience. Wonderful environment, good story so far. Combat seems a little clunky but that might just be because I'm using heavy armor and heavy weapons. Despite the Soulsborne feel, it has its own unique brand of panic-inducing rage.

I hate to say the old "This+This=This", but it really is a great representation of the Dark Souls formula. With Maze like exploration, bonfire-like safe places called Operations/OPS, losing Tech Scrap (souls) when you die, and having to retrieve said scraps, you can easily see the resemblances...BUT NOW YOU HAVE AN EXO SUIT!
Obviously a difficult game, but it does it well. You can only take a handful of hits (maybe less) before you need to inject yourself with some drugs. Par for the course with these types of games. Seemingly more shortcuts back to safety than Darksouls' bonfires, but with less safe places overall, means you can learn the layout of each area pretty easily. Being away from OPS for about 20 minutes and losing your way, only to find a door that leads you right back, is an awesome feeling.
The Combat/Gameplay is great. Trying to dismember body parts to get blueprints or crafting materials is a great way to give more control to the player. Want the weapon or armor this guy has? Focus attacks on these body parts until you can cut it off with a slowmotion, bloody, cinematic camera. Just don't forget to block or dodge enemy attacks, they tend to hurt.
It looks and feels incredible! You can't understand just by looking at screenshots or watching videos, you have to experience it.
Oh! Once you've beaten the game, you can restart with NG+ all the way up to NG+++...I think. 4(?) playthroughs total really adds to the replayability; Or you can just start over from scratch again...and again...and again...
Probably my favorite game of the last few years. If you are on the fence about getting it, and are a fan of Dark Souls, or difficult games in general, do it up.
