is a rather interesting addition into the "BRPG" (Brutal RPG) genre.   "Souls-like" is too limiting a term for this new style of ARPG created and made famous by FROM Software's "Souls" series.   While
has some familiar mechanics (stamina based combat, no map, a central hub for saving, and a single currency for leveling both your character and gear), it goes beyond with a more subtle combat system which allows for specific targeting and more in depth dodging.
I have bought this game twice... on Steam and for the PS4, and have achieved 100% trophies on both.   This speaks volumes for how fun the combat actually is.   Were this game yet another random RPG doing the same-old, same-old... I would not have finished it now... 9 times?
Your character's gear is completely fluid... meaning that you may choose any type of armor your wish to wear, and specializing in any type of weapon you choose.   You have the ability to install "Implants" which grant you various abilities , such as increased health, health injections (think health pot, or estus flask), health on brutality, increased energy, treasure sense, toxic gas immunity, GF, etc etc etc.   Any weapon you find can be leveled up, along with armor.
The setting is a Sci-Fi industrial dystopia... the industrial theme is prevalent throughout as you are working your way through the heart of a multi-national corporation's scientific and technical launch facility.
You play Warren, and Warren is anything you wish he or she to be.  I, personally, like to think of my Warren as a STUNNING AND BRAVE transwoman who is also transracial while being hadicapable.   So, you want to play as a beautiful woman?  Warren identifies as a beautiful woman.   You want to play as a wise cracking, 1940's
detective?  Warren can identify as such.   Warren is the
of your imagination.

Cthulhu Saves the World is an old-school JRPG, and by old school, I mean they ditch all modern innovations, ideas and sensibilities the have accumulated over the years. Which is the point, sure, but it just doesn't add up to much these days, unfortunately. The quirky humour occasionally hits its mark and the characters are, at first, a bit more interesting than the usual JRPG trope characters. However, there doesn't seem to be any more to them except the very superficial quirkiness.
Gameplay is the usual old-school JRPG stuff. That is grind. Lots of monotonous grind. In the most baffling design decision I've encountered in a while, your party is completely healed after a won battle, but your mana is not restored. It might not sound so bad, until you realise that without Techs and Magics, your party is consistently and constantly getting beaten. So now you either:
A) have to backtrack to a place where you can restore your mana or
B) win fights without using mana. Which is not happening, not after the first area or so.
Granted, the ability to save anywhere and start random fights almost anytime from the party meny are appreciated, but in the end you still feel like you are wasting your time. The jokes, characters and settings are interesting enough to hold your interest for an hour or two, but eventually the monotony of the gameplay and the frustration of the difficulty curve eat away at your enjoyment.
Old school fun.

If I were to explain this game in one line I'd say, "Emily Is Away is a text-based chat simulation between you and a sometimes-generic, angsty teenage girl who, despite your best attempts, is seemingly never happy with your attempts at communication."
I will say that the writing in this game is very believably written and some moments struck close to home, but a portion of it felt generic and frustrating. There are some places where you have no idea what your character is going to say and he goes off on a tangent about something seemingly random. There are other moments where you try to be sensitive and even though your character is delicate with his wording, "Emily" gets ticked with you regardless.
The game has a certain level of polish to it. The game is totally replayable, maybe up to 3 times, and is has certain features added to the UI that add to your immersion. For example you can change your text colour, background colour, display photo and even open up a friends list which includes some people from your Steam friends list which you can open up and read past conversations of. You can use your real name to add to the immersion. The simple UI fits really well due to the fact that game is based throughout the years 2002-2006 when chat programs were particularly straightforward.
The audio in this game suits the theme but that is about it. There is no music, (allowing you to listen to your own music as if you were actually chatting,) chat noises, and typing noises. As I said, the audio fits the theme but they aren't particularly special.
Whilst the game wasn't exactly right up my alley, at the same time I totally finished it and it kept me interested to the bitter end. I can appreciate the amount of effort that went into this game and it is obvious that this was a passion project for the team that created it. A lot of features that could've easily been left out were added and to a level of polish they should be proud of.
I do recommend this game to anyone looking for something to think about. It was, despite some generic moments, an intriguing experience. It is also free and approximately 30 mintues long assuming you play through it once. What have you got to lose?

As of 14 Sept 2014 -
This game is not terrible - just very very bland.
You will not find anything really new in here - all of it exists in other, better made games such as Distant Worlds or GalCiv2.
There are still some major bugs that have not been taken out - I can't even open the trade menu without a crash to desktop.
Ship design is weak - from the start, you get 4 hulls that go from tiny to small - with only no improvements available to increase what you can fit in them. The techs for ships don't provide any options - the missiles, beams and lasers are essentially the same. There are no fighters or bases.
Tactical fights are available but not terribly exciting - nor does it provide any depth as all weapons are in essence identical.
Many of the "management tools" are absent or in very basic form - you can't rearrange build queues, set up rally points, understand how much science, industry, or trade any particular action is going to generate. It's weird how you have to close an empire menu before opening the next one rather than switching between them.
The tech tree is pretty minimal - maybe 50-60 items in total. It gets boring in the 2nd part where you get solid lines of 3-4 consecutive "industry +1" or "research +1". It rarely opens up new abilities, just improves your starting ones.
Minor races have no interaction, except for pirates. You can send a trade ship there, tho with the game maxing out at 4 trade lines, it's not clear why you should bother.
What is working in this game is relatively fine. It just seems like they ran out of time to fine-tune and tweak the content in fun and interesting ways. Perhaps updates wil improve this solid, but it is currently an extremely bland X4 experience.
Verdict - unless you are scrapping the bottom of the barrel for x4 games, skip until a few updates.

This game is actually pretty good for a MMO.
...Unless you live in Brazil. I've got two strong points to show you why (Although I can say both good and bad things about this game itself, my review will focus only on the player experience from my country, so others from here can know what they are getting into).
Point 1: The monthly fee. Payment through Steam was rearranged from 28,99 BRL to 41,99 BRL just recently. The price, although actually equivalent to the dollar price, is really high to the average brazillian consumer. To make a comparison, here's WoW's monthly sub price: 23,90 BRL (And WoW actually has a BR server! But I'll touch more on that soon). Unfortunately, there aren't many other comparable MMOs to use here.
Point 2: Server lag. Although the game had a pretty high ping already for anyone living here (unless you paid extra for a VPN), recent server changes made the ping even higher for us. +200ms ping is a common thing. In a game with many server-side checks, playing the game properly becomes an extra challenge for brazillian users. Make sure you dodge things almost half a second before the attack actually hits, and time that stun with precise foresight since it will take extra time for the servers to register your inputs.
Honestly, I think this is a good game, despite some things that irk me personally (microtransation-exclusive items in a paid game, with monthly subscription, and paid expansions every one-and-a-half year...). But, for a brazillian player, the experience doesn't feel good anymore. Play if you have a good amount of money to spend in a good experience (high sub price + VPN). But why not spend that money in something worthier of it? Well, it's up to you.

This game is amazing. It's kind of like Dark Souls, but it has way more differences than similarities. I'd actually say it's more like Bloodborne, but without the gunplay and armor actually provides useful bonuses.
The combat is fun and has an interesting twist. Humanoid enemies all have 6 targetable zones. Both arms, both legs, torso, and head. Where you target will determine how quickly the enemy gets stunned and how much damage you do. It also determines what the enemy drops. Bosses, drones, and robots have different targetable zones as well.
This is pretty much the only game where 90% of the weapons and armor the enemies have are dropped 90% of the time, if you kill them the right way. Chop off an arm, get their weapon. Chop off their head, get their helmet schematics. Armor always drops as schematics (blueprints) and weapons drop or are found as the whole piece. The parts needed to build and upgrade armor and weapons are farmed the same way the weapons and schematics are.
The bosses are all pretty unique to eachother. It's mostly knowing where to stand and when to dodge or attack. They aren't necessarily hard, but they can and often will kill you if you don't move fast enough. Every boss drops a weapon, and an upgraded version of that weapon if you kill them in a certain way.
This game doesn't have the usual attributes, such as strength or agility. Instead, your armor will give you certain bonuses to fit certain playstyles. There are 5 weapon types and each one is leveled separately. Every weapon has a modifier that determines how much damage each level will add to the weapon.
Killing enemies provides tech scrap, which is used to level up the rig and build/upgrade all of your gear. If you die, they will drop and you get 2.5 mintues to get back to where you died to pick them up. You can gamble and keep your tech scrap to get a multiplier, or you can store it to use later.

It's filled to the brim with conspiracies, political intrigue, war, depression, and even occasional bouts of happiness and comedy. The overall atmosphere is dark and overbearing, but the simplistic gameplay and story along with random events that can happen while  you go about your day lend to it's addictive nature. I recommend this game to basically everybody, with it's pick-up-and-playability it can be enjoyed in short bursts or for hours on end.

Hacktag is what I would call an "old-school" asymmetric cooperation game. You have one hacker and one infiltrated agent.
Here, you do not need an ally to pull that lever at the same time, push that box or simply help you defeat a boss. An AI can do that. No, you NEED your ally to progress in the level by distracting the right guard while you pass behind him, disabling a scanner so you can infiltrate the network in a sneaky way, opening the right door or slamming said door in the face of the guard who caught you.
In short, if you like cooperative games and you have a partner to play with (or you can find some on the Discord server of the game), this game is pretty fun. Go for it, especially if you can have 2 for the price of 1 (like during the autumn sales).
Hacktag est ce que j'appellerai un jeu de coopération asymétrique "old-school". Vous êtes soit le hacker, soit l'agent infiltré.
Ici, votre allié(e) ne vous sert pas simplement à tirer un levier en même temps, pousser une caisse ou servir d’appât durant un combat de boss. Vous avez BESOIN de votre allié(e) pour progresser, que ce soit en distrayant le bon garde pendant que vous passez derrière, désactiver le scanner pour pouvoir infiltrer le réseau, ouvrir la bonne porte ou claquer la dite porte au nez du garde qui vous a repéré.
En résumé, si vous aimez les jeux coopératifs et que vous avez un partenaire pour jouer avec vous (ou que vous ne trouvez sur le Discord du jeu), Hacktag est vraiment fun. N'hésitez pas à l'acheter, surtout si vous pouvez en avoir 2 copies pour le prix d'1 (avec les soldes d'automne par exemple).

Let us get this out of the way: if you're not a fan of dark souls-esque gameplay this isnt for you.
That said: this game is built for a unique style.  Definitely not for everyone.  Its generally difficult/punishing.  There is backtracking.  There is farming.  But it is a treat to play through.
Story: This is definitely a case of lore vs story.  Theres plenty to pick up on from environmental clues to audio tapes that paint a picture of what exactly happened here, but this is not the focus of the game.  The focus is the gameplay, and having just enough general context to push forward from here to there.
Graphics: Not amazing but definitely good enough looking.  I personally am having some weird issues with refresh rate and resolution scaling (up to 120%) actually BOOSTING frames, but hopefully this gets fixed with an update.   Overally, optimized well enough and looks pleasing enough.
Controls: This is another area you can consider "genre specific".  Weapon movesets and animations are a huge part of the gameplay, and you need to plan out your attacks lest yee get caught in a combo because you clicked a hundred times and now youre stuck going through all the attack animations.  The controls are nice and tight, just dont realize the kind of game you're playing and dont get trigger happy.  It wont pay off here.
Sound: Does its job.  The music is sparce but good enough, and the weapon/impact sounds are very nice.  I find myself cranking the volume on my headset to hear the extremely satisfying crashes as metal smashes into metal, and it definitely helps with the "weighty" feel of the game.
Overall: I am still going through the game, I am on boss 3 out of 5, but it seems on track for a roughly 35 hour single player experience.  I always suggest waiting for a sale for everything, but given this is a relatively small genre (soulsbourne-esque), I couldnt wait and needed to scratch that itch.  I am not disappointed in paying full price, and am likely to buy any substantial DLC they release for this game.  Deck 13 has learned alot from Lords of the Fallen, and while sticking close to the formula, this game provides a quality experience for those looking for more of their Dark Souls fix.

As soon as I watched the first trailers about this game, I knew this was a game I wanted to play. Sci-fi is my jam and powered exoskeletons are one of my favourite pieces of sci-fi gear; plus, I had always wanted to play a "tactical melee" game in such a setting (never felt attracted to the Dark Souls series due to it having a fantasy setting). Gave it some more time and eventually preordered it shortly before launch day.
Oh boy, was it a good buy.
As a piece of software, it's greatly optimized. My laptop is not powerful enough for the maximum settings, but I can run it on high settings at 1920x1080 (fullscreen) with perfect framerate. The settings screen is incredibly detailed in all aspects, and that feels great: you can rest assured you will make it work for you no matter your computer or gaming preferences. Compared to the sadly large amunt of modern games with limited settings, the developers of The Surge show they know the full extent and importance of the term "player experience".
Gameplay-wise, it is a very solid game with many unique features. Combat is fluid and very dynamic, and very varied as well, depeding on your gear, weapon type, drone module and implants. You will have to learn how to master all your available actions and abilities in order to make progress, especially from mid-game onwards and the boss fights. Make no mistake: it is a hard game and you will die countless times until you finally master how to defeat this new, apparently unkillable enemy that seems to throw everything you know about combat through the window. Do not mistake common enemies for easy fodder: each of them will be a challenge on itself, and some of them will even be (or at least feel like) minibosses on their own. Bosses themselves will require all your skills and wit to defeat. In both cases, don't expect to tank much damage: I'll say it again, you will die a lot until you learn, and even then mistakes will be paid dearly.
Being able to get materials, blueprints and weapons from your enemies is just awesome. It gives a lot of incentive to keep looking forward to see what's next, and to come back to defeat specific enemies just to get their loot. Exploration is also a core part of The Surge: levels are large, very intrincate and filled with shortcuts to Operations (your respawn, loot saving and upgrades base), and also filled with secrets, like loot, audio records (vital for the story), collectibles and even unique versions of common weapons (sidegrades): the incentive for exploration is definitively there. About gear and weapons, consider them to be all sidegrades: even though boss weapons tend to be better, generally you can stick to any particular armor or weapon you fall in love with just by upgrading it.
There's also the possibility to play New Game + and even ++ (and maybe even more), where you get to keep your previous gear and upgrades while the game gets MUCH harder with new enemies and other stuff I haven't seen yet (just started to play NG+).
The story is... serviceable. It is definitively a good one, although not a surprise for fans of the genre. That said, the way it's told -mainly through audio-records and some NPC interactions- keeps you in the point of view of a poor unlucky guy that just started his first day of work right when everything goes haywire, which is quite good in the sense of inmersion. There's also conversations to be had, side quests and some decisions to take, which is nice. A word of caution: careful with accidentaly killing your friendly NPCs.
In addition, the devs recently released the first patch of the game, including many fixes and features that the players had been posting on the forums, and have showed their will of keeping adding content to it in one way or another. These devs have not only made a good game mixing their own ideas with already working formulae from the genre: they are also showing they care for their product after release and will keep supporting it.
In summary: I highly recommend this game!

Papers, Please is a game where you play as an inspector at the border of Arstotzka, a fictional fascist dictatorship. You have to check and approve (or deny) the papers of people hoping to transit through, work in, or immigrate to your country. All while trying to earn enough money to keep you and your family healthy, fed and warm. It's filled to the brim with conspiracies, political intrigue, war, depression, and even occasional bouts of happiness and comedy. The overall atmosphere is dark and overbearing, but the simplistic gameplay and story along with random events that can happen while  you go about your day lend to it's addictive nature. I recommend this game to basically everybody, with it's pick-up-and-playability it can be enjoyed in short bursts or for hours on end.

Playing this game will only frustrate you. This is a management game that is set up in a way that should minimize micro-management of your denizens and let you concentrate on the bigger picture. The citizens of your base are expected to be able to make decisions on their own using their AI. Unfortunately, their AI is nowhere near complete enough to make this feasible. Quite often your entire base will spiral out of control because of events that are set in motion by something a citizen did or did not do because of poor AI.
Because the game was apprently intended to lean away from micro-managing each citizen, you are powerless to make a citizen do something they are neglecting to do and you cannot stop them from doing something you don't want them doing. There just are no means to give individual commands, which causes too many problems to make this a fun game. Far too often your base will die off for reasons completely out of your control because one person was hell-bent on doing something wrong.
: I've had a base sent into a depression spiral because my doctor kept deciding that she would rather lift weights for hours instead of pick up dead bodies that were accumulating from repeated raider attacks. The numerous bodies around the base put everyone into foul moods causing them to constantly fight one another, eventually thinning their own ranks so much that I could no longer defend against raider attacks. All of this could have been avoided had I been able to force my doctor to pick up bodies. Instead, all I could do was watch her and hope that she stops lifting weights long enough to pick up a body or two on her own.
: I've had a base where a small fire killed every single crew member because each and every one of them insisted on attempting to stomp the fire out with their feet instead of using the fire extinguisher posted right beside the door to the room.

Incredible improvement from FS15. I too was doubtful and worried about the fact that FS17 was using the same old engine, but oh boy was I wrong. Almost everything has been upgraded - lighting, model quality, game mechanics - and it somehow manages to run smoother than FS15 ever did for me, with a minimal amount of fidgeting with graphics settings. There are a few minor issues I have - the game has released with about 15 high quality mods "built in" to the game (as in there is a menu where you can install them easily for free) but some of these I would rather have seen be in the game from the get go, without any separate installation required. Another thing which has been improved since 15 but is still a problem for me is controls sensitivity. There are finally sliders for this, and they do change the sensitivity but let's say I wanted it my steering sensitivity for my game controller down to 50%, it reduces the sensitivity but it also halves the turning radius of the tires, which is extremely annoying and makes no sense to me. Likewise, if you were to modify to sensitivity for the gas (which is right trigger by default) down to 50%, it halves your top speed. I wish it wasn't so difficult, but it's honestly something I can forget just due to how beautiful this game is. The tractors no longer look like plastic, the lighting isn't free SDK quality anymore.... Completely satisfied with my purchase and can't wait for more hours with this game. Would definitely recommend to anyone who has enjoyed a Farming Simulator game in the past, and anyone who can appreciate the concept of waiting for grass to grow in a video game.

TLDR: This game takes the Souls formula and throws in a chunk of late stage capitalism, a twisted version of a silicon valley startup, and of course really satisfying limb chopping. It does these things well and is worth a buy to any fan of Souls-like games.
Overall, I'm extremely impressed with this game. With lords of the fallen, Deck 13 showed that they could emulate bits of the souls formula, but not really put it all together in a way that was polished or completely interesting. With The Surge, not only does Deck 13 make a game that emulates the souls formula well, but also adds its own pretty awesome twists to it along the way.
Let's first talk about the combat. It feels weighty and responsive in the way the souls games do. It is also increadibly punishing. I've read a lot of reviews and commentary on the game in fact stating that the game may be too punishing in an ill way, in that almost every enemy in the game can one shot or two shot you. This will be true if you do not care for your armor upgrades/health upgrades along the way. But even if you do, you are usually 3-5 hits away from death. Your character can hit enemies hard, but they can also hit you REALLY hard back.
I think in the game world, that makes a lot of sense. You start out as just a normal dude getting a factory job with average supplies and no combat training/proficency. If you're going to pit yourself against other people with the same/better equipment, I think it makes sense that you will die at a similar speed as your enemies do. I personally liked Deck 13's approach to enemy damage, but there was more than a few times I felt salty about an enemy that did JUST ENOUGH damage to kill me and force me to make a 5 minute treck back to my leftover scrap (souls). Overall I like that the difficulty is mostly due to enemies hitting hard and sometimes having strange hit patterns, but if that doesn't sound fun to you, that's fine. I would just not play this game.
One more thing to mention about the combat: it differs from the souls formula in that you can target individual limbs. While locked on to an enemy, you use the rights stick to cycle your lock on from the legs, to the body, to the arms, and the head. If you are locked on to a part of the body, you will get a prompt to attempt to cut it off after a few hits. IF the prompt is successful you will be able to salvage the gear you cut off the enemy and use it to form a blue print to recreate the gear with a 3D printer.
That is how almost all gear/weapons are collected in the game, and I love it. If you see an enemy with awesome armor, it means that you can have that armor, but you will be putting yourself at a significant disadvantage during the fight. Hitting unarmoured limbs kills an enemy faster, but will result in no loot. It's a really clever risk/reward system that ends in a slow motion limb cutting animation and then a few minutes later, your character 3D printing that exact piece of armor. It is also worth noting that you get the crafting materials you need for the armor by cutting of the same limbs on other enemies so building a set of armor becomes kind of a lengthy process. But luckily the combat is fun enought that I almost never minded grinding to get an armor set (with the exception of one set froma paticularly difficult enemy).
As far as armor/weapons go, it is also worth noting that you can level up every weapon/armor piece you find, just like in the souls games. I love this because it allows you to get really attached to a weapon and carry it through the whole game. You also get proficency leveling for using a specific weapon type more and more, which is a system I have mixed feelings about. On the one hand, it allowed me to get really good with my favorite weapon and constantly improve the damage I do with it. On the other hand it kind of locks you into a weapon type early in the game if you want to get the most out of this leveling system. Overall though, I love the way loot is handeled in this game as not only does it rewoard the player well and often, but also adds to the moment to moment desicion making in a fight.
Finally, I want to talk a bit about the story and world of this game. This game has cutscenes, dialouge, and a story that is far more obvious than the ones in the Souls games. These elements are done pretty well, with one character in paticular having an interesting story arch (only if you bother finding them though), but mostly the story is just good enough to not detract from the game.
The world building on the other hand is actually very well executed. Audio logs are always worth picking up, it is usually interesting to see what is playing on the T.V.s around the world, and this world feels oppresive in a way that is almost required for a Souls-Like game. The world you inhabit just sucks in a way that sets the tone really well for the rest of your actions because the fighting is just as brutal as everything else around you. In this portion it is also worth noting the level design which can visually get a bit repetative (it also looks totally rad in parts), but is laid out in a very satisfying maze like way, kind of like how dark souls one did it.
I loved this game. It is not as good as the Dark Souls games (AKA: some of the best games ever), but this game satisfies the hunger I have for the souls formula in a way that is fullfiling and suprisinlgly unique. Overall very worth the purchase.

Fantastic little RPG! It's packed full of fun characters and environments, with an enjoyable battle system and level-up system to boot! Its presentation is great too with appealing graphics and some great SNES-era style music. In addition to all this, the game has great replay value with various difficulty levels and game modes, and some other neat features such as character bromides, a bestiary and a full developer commentary.
Finally, I'd be remiss if I didn't mention the exceptional writing in this game. Most RPGs fall flat on their face when attempting humour. Cthulu Saves the World is one of the only RPGs I've played that succeeds at being funny, even hilarious at times, with well-written dialogue and great comedic timing.
For only £1.99 or less (I got it for 50p in a sale) there's really no reason not to own this game. I really can't recommend this one enough. Pick up Breath of Death while you're at it.

The first time I came across this game was somewhere around 2001. I got a copy of the demo on CD from a cereal box. I was instantly hooked on the game although it was very challenging. Sometime after that a friend of mine had received the full version of the game. We spent countless hours with the darn thing and we couldn't get past level four. But at that time, fooling around with the game was enough for me, so we started over many times and took turns playing. It wasn't about victory at all.
And now, more than ten years after the first glimpse, the game has landed on Steam, and I am eager to buy it. I got the game and I was instantly fulfilled with memories from the past. This is such a great game, there is no other like it. Commandos 2 and Robin Hood are close relatives, but there's something very special about this piece of art. The game features absolutely gorgeous graphics even with today's standards and the voice acting sounds more than professional.
If there's one thing they could have altered with the re-released version, it's the aspect ratio. There is no native widescreen support for the game, so you're stuck with 4:3 ratio. This however, isn't as big of a problem as one could think. Since it's an isometric game the gameplay doesn't look too bad at all even though it's stretched out. But just a fair warning...

This game sounds good, but even in the Early Acess and room to grow - I don't see it compare with the scope it wants to attain.
-/- the major races are restrictive, and doesn't include any customization option at the start up.
-/+ instead there is a slight reimagining of "Domestic Polocies" that can further define and charactarize your empire, you can change them during the game and alter some aspects slightly - but there are pros and cons to them and often a particular race will just prefer a certain setup.
-/- the universe is limited, with little options outside colonizing a few planets you can take, and attack or occupy others. There isn't much interaction with the universe as a whole outside it being a static generation from the start. Perhaps I was spoiled with Space Empire's abiolities to drastically reform the universe even while in the game, but here its marginal.
-/- even with another strike against it is the "neutral" races or "pirates" which are just a bit more than just target practice and nuciances occupying a planet you want.
-/- the diplomacy feels shallow. I am sorry, its just not as in depth as I have seen others - it can be altered to get there sure, but as it stands I don't see it shifting to that. Many of the diplomacy options require facility constructions that will limit your options on the planets you own, and some options won't happen unless you or the other race have room to invest, further limiting who is really benefitting.
-/- the tactical turn based combat is restrictive as hell. You only get to do so much per turn, and each ship is further limited by its loadout. Multiple loadout designs with different weapon types or perks limits the ship's ability to function as you can only do one per turn, making the combat really limited in scope to the design and swarming of a few cheap ship creations of a doubled weapon or three.
-/- this further falls under the ship construction as there are limited sizes and options for what can be loaded on which ship. It limits design and role choices heavily.
+/- the genreals are a cool idea that develop as you use them, but the risk and reward are staggering comparisions. Due to the combat being so restrictive there isn't much for strategic desings possible and the random generation of the generals is flawed at times - they may have an attack power, but without a type given so it doesn't work. The development of them can be cool, and it directly affects their strengths, however the combat risk can easily leave them out on a limb and you'll loose all your progress.
-/+ the unrest aspect is interesting, but difficult to cause and easy to avoid, making it a moot issue that rarely surfaces unless you let or make it.
-/+ further deplomacy aspects sound cool as well, but the AI is fineky on its choices making its fulfuilment in many regards challenging, or just a question of finaces. A good economy can basically buy allies in most cases wtih a bit of espionage fixing.
-/- the AI cheats. I'm sorry, it does. It doesn't do something its not confident it can win, making it more hesitant and dulling the gameplay. Set up safe enough even with cheap ships and you'll never be threatened as you grow until you amass that army to just wipe everything out.
Sounds good, can be interesting - but I've seen other 4x games pull off similarities better, so its not really worth it for most.

I dont recomend playing this game unless micro-management of a few dozen things at once sounds like a great time to you.
The first time I played I loaded up on as many AI opponents as I could and a huge galaxy. I made one attack on a pirate faction and then every race hated me and started going to war with me. I was also experiencing some learning curve set-backs, so I quit out of that game and started a new one.
Round 2 I went with just 2 alien AI opponents, in a small galaxy, and tried just making nice with them. We claimed our planets, established trade routes, built stuff.... 5 hours later nothing had happened. I was basically just making the same colony ships over and over, going to new planets, building the same buildings... My population was happy, my enemies were all happy, I had more money than I knew what to do with. The game kind of just devolved into a management of the empires finances and construction.
This game is really lacking from random events that spice up your experience. They attempted by puting in 'disasters' which is basically just a simple: 'pay money and keep people happy' or 'Tell your people you wont help them and♥♥♥♥♥♥everyone off'. Its a pretty shallow wildcard system.
The interface is clean, but is also very lacking. For example, when looking at what buildings are on a planet, only the 'build menu' has the names of the buildings and what they do. The buildings you already have in place do not have names, and you cannot click on them to see if they are being effective in any way. So you have to do a cross reference on what the buildings look like to even know what you have built...
And on the subject of building, its super boring. I'm sure I would eventually get to more advanced structures down the tech tree, but in the 5-8 hours I played Puting the same combination of 5-10 buildings on 20 different planets was about as much fun as organizing a deck of cards. Also it seems when you do unlock better versions of buildings, you need to go BACK to all of those planets, destroy a building, and put in the upgrade. Its not automatic.
So when you are 20 hours down the line in this game and you wonder why every race has a better economy than you, it might be because you forgot to upgrade 5 of your 40 planets to better factories... better go check them all... one... by... one....
While I cant recomend this game I hope that the developers learn from this one and make a sequel with the holes filled in. It's a great idea, It just relies WAY too much on the player to micro manage all of their systems.

Amazing game with a classic Hong Kong style mafia-themed storyline. One of the things I love about this game is its tribute to Hong Kong culture and its language. I always get a kick out of everyone speaking understandable (not broken) Cantonese.
While the story was decent, what made it work was the incredible voice actors. Wei sounds so badass when he's threatening other people: it's a treat listening to his voice in action. The next best thing was the gameplay. The fighting system felt so rewarding with every punch and kick. You can feel the pain when you see Wei break someone's arms or legs. Sometimes, when I get bored of playing the storyline, I can just go out on the street and create havoc over HK.
Speaking of HK, I loved the dynamic of the different areas where you can see the contrast of the rich and poor areas of HK. Although not real places, it felt really genuine.
I highly recommend this to people who like GTA style games but perhaps want a different style and theme from American culture.

Very fun game.The deign feels great and it runs smooth. WAY TOO MANY ALIEN SPECIES/FACTIONS THAT ARE'NT RELEVANT. The entire Coalition, accessible only using the special jumpdrive and is almost as large as the Republic, has no spaceports, outfitters, or special missions from the spaceports. An incredible amount of work must have gone into designing all those systems, but there's simply no reason to visit any of them. Same with the wanderers. Also, for all the hype that the characters in the game make about the alphas, they barely show up once or twice and are hardly a threat. The other major complaint I have is the outfits system. It's too confusing and would work better if there was, for instance, a drag and drop system for equipping things onto the ship that you want. Also there needs to be a better loan system rather than based on the last month's income. At some point, i had been following the story(which is great by the way) and was low on money paying for crew salaries every jump, but I could take out almost no money at all despite my owning five ships. In addition, some of the more difficult missions need better payouts, because in order to complete them, I had to build a huge fleet which cost more in crew salaries by the time I was done than the payout for the mission, not to mention the cost of replacing even one sparrow that inevitably gets lost. Overall though, it is an incredible concept and worth many hours of entertainment.

This game has gotten a bad rap for being "not Dark Souls". If we rated every game based on being "not Dark Souls", nothing would be good enough to play.
It's tough but fair, and chopping off limbs really doesn't ever get old. The game revolves a lot around fighting basic enemies, but they are tough and can hurt you badly if you are careless. You won't run into large mobs (3 or more) often, nor are there a lot of boss fights, it's about these solo fights and comboing your attacks in ways to avoid getting hit.
The level design is excellent, with a lot of shortcuts that loop you back to the bonfire/base. The maps are really interconnected well. Story is a rather bland sci-fi, I mean it's an interesting world and all but it just doesn't really deliver on atmosphere, which isn't helped by the fact the entire game starts to look the same since it takes place inside a facility.
Took me roughtly 20 hours to complete with minimal revisiting of old areas, although I did explore a lot (but the game isn't very open, it's pretty single-tracked).

Pro's:
Combat is smooth
Framerate is consistently good
Finishing moves feel great
Gear and weapon progression system is cool (targetting specific body parts to get that specific part of an armor set)
Shortcut system works well
Challenging.
Con's:
Levels can be sort of samey (Alot of sci-fi factory, lab stuff obviously).
Enemies are not very varied (mostly humanoids in mech-gear)
Level design near the end of the game can be frustrating (alot of lifts)
Some enemies simply do too much damage again even the most armored players (2 or 3 hit you) which can be annoying
All in all I enjoyed my time with The Surge. Sometimes the game threw some cheap shots (alot of ambushes) which got annoying after a while but the challenge of the game itself is appreciated.

When first playing the game, the best aspect makes it's appearence quickly: The humor.
Cthulhu is a real anti-hero who grumpily tries to save the world and he has a lot of funny dialogue throughout the game. The fact that he looks so uninviting also leads to a lot of awkward situations amongst the townsfolk, resulting in a lot of clever jokes. Along the way, he will also make allies who contribute in their own way, such as his obsessed groupie that sees him as the most charming person ever while he couldn't care less.
During the combat, every monster has their own description with some funny line added to it. Townsfolk will usually react to whoever you chose to bring along. The dialogue between the characters are also my kind of tea, with lots of arguing and misunderstandings.
The sprites in the game are for the most part well done. They can get somewhat repeatetive in the dungeons, making it a bit hard to remember exactly where you are. The rooms can look way too samey at times, so I have gotten lost in many dungeons, unable to find my way back to the outside.
I thought the music was very good. It has the right atmosphere for each and every part they take in. I especially liked the male choir chanting inside the dungeons, adding a mysterious atmosphere to them. The town music is very calming and relaxing to listen to.
I like that the dungeon chests actually contains good items. In other games, you literally risk your life for a potion that doesn't even restore half of what you lost to get to it. Here, you can get impressive upgrades and lots of money. It made treasure hunting worthwile and fun.
The armor and weapon menus could definately have been polished. Comparing items is quite clunky, with you being unable to compare stats side by side. Anytime you buy an armor or weapon, the shopkeeper says "Thanks!" and throws you back to the option whether you want to buy or sell. It would have been better to be able to stay on the page you just purchased something.
There is one huge flaw with this game unfortunately. And it is the combat system.
Anytime the party has taken a turn, whether damaging the enemy or healing themselves, the monsters gets an increased percentage of damage. This number is quite high, around 10%, which builds up extremely fast. This forces you to use your strongest and fastest abilities, as otherwise you are going to end up in an endless die/revive loop where the monsters will get stronger while you can't keep up reviving your party members that gets slayed within one or two turns.
It also leads to making many spells and abilities useless, since you don't have time to use them. One of my characters has so many spells that she never gets time to use. And it's not just one or two, she has about 6 different spells which basically spells "Game over" for me if I even concider using them. Their damage output is just too weak to compete with the monster damage output. So each and every fight, I am constantly casting the same powerful spell.
It unfortunately leads to a lot of scrolling in the menu, as usually these spells are learned much later. So you have lots of useless abilities and spells clogging your menu, which you have to scroll through each and every time you want to use an ability or spell. I haven't found any way to sort the abilities and spells, which would have been greatly needed.
As the combat is completely text based, there is also a huge lack of action on the screen. The monsters will just implode on themselves when they die and there's not even a picture of your members on the combat screen. Only when you make the choice to attack do you see their faces. Then the monsters just flashes when they take damage. The combats are very boring to watch, though thankfully you can scroll through the combat text quite quickly, ending some battles in seconds.
After playing this, I understand why they have a system which fills your characters HP to max afte every encounter - otherwise they would never survive in this game! The game really shows you no remorse once the monsters have taken a couple of turns.   Forget being tactical, you simply don't have the time to waste. Forget about wanting to use a different spell than the fire one. If fire does 200 more damage than ice, you have to stick to fire. Each and every encounter.
To me, the combat system feels like a filler into a very short game. I love the humor, I love advancing through the story and reading the dialogue. But at the eight hour mark, thinking about combat makes me groan. Same old spells over and over. No thanks.
After eight hours of the game, I only enjoy it due to the humor and dialogue. But at this point, the combat system is so offputting that I am literally forcing myself to finish the game. So I honestly wouldn't recommend this to anyone. It all boils down whether I would recommend the game based on the story and seeing as the dialogue only happens after encounters, then it will be a no.

This is an odd title, to say the least.  It's a solid game...  But seems to exist less as a game than as a parody of a game.
Cthulhu Saves the World is very reminiscent of the old Final Fantasy games.  Similar gameplay mechanics.  Similar character and storyline tropes.  Except...  You aren't actually playing as a hero out to save the world from an ancient evil.  You're playing as an ancient evil out to destroy the world.
The graphics are delightfully nostalgic.  Simple 2D sprites that immediately brought me back to the old Dragon Quest and Final Fantasy games.
The combat mechanics, also, hearken back to those classic games.
But the humor is delightfully fresh.  Lots of fun being poked at the CRPG genre.  Lots of self-aware humor.
It's a simple, fun game.  And cheap.  But I'm not sure if it'd hold my attention long enough to actually play through to the end.

Cthulhu Saves the World(CStW) Review
Cthulhu Saves the World is a game starring everybody's favorite Lovecraftian abomination, Cthulhu. Stripped of his powers by a mysterious spellcaster upon yonder cliff, Cthulhu must set out on a quest in order to become a true hero so he can regain his powers and destroy the world after he saves it. Sounds crazy, right? Well, if you're interested in the premise, then it is well assured that the rest of the game is even better. I'm here to analyze the game and give my personal opinion on it, so if you're looking for a serious review, you've come to the right place. Let's start by looking over the story.
Story:I'm going to just give you the Cliff's Notes version of the story: Cthulhu rises from R'lyeh to destroy reality. Sorceror robs him of his powers. Narrator tips off Cthulhu that he has to become a hero to destroy the world. Cthulhu begins quest to save then destroy world. After that, Cthulhu goes from town to town saving the populace from stuff, such as Nyarlathotep-controlled zombies or a demon-dragon in a volcano. While the title says that Cthulhu saves the world, he never really does so until the final dungeon, making the game more like The Adventures of Cthulhu the Hero and Friends. CStW's story has nothing connecting the various events that occur together, but since this game is a parody of JRPGs, it's just enough for a person to not question it.
Characters:While the story of Cthulhu Saves the World may be a loose string of events that barely constitute as a plot, the characters can kinda make up for this. As per Zeboyd Games standard, the characters are rather creative. In the party you're stuck with throughout the game's course, there's the hero himself, Cthulhu, who is on a quest to restore his powers; The resident Red Mage, Umi, who has a crush on Cthulhu after he saves her from two slime monsters; Sharpe the living sword, who is only there because Cthulhu wants a huge sword like every other hero; The angsty Black Mage and gothic necromancer, October; Cthulhu's old alien cat friend, Paws; The senile White Mage on the brink of madness, Dacre; And the reformed demon-dragon, Ember. They're all wacky and provide the game with most of the humorous dialogue, but are the ones given most of the characterization, since they appear more than once in the game. Besides them, there's those three hero guys who only pop up twice and the chapter bosses who, besides Ember, who joins your party, only appear once. It's kinda unfortunate that nobody else gets any real characterization besides being a stereotypical NPC. However, the characters that do get some focus make the game much more enjoyable.
Gameplay:Cthulhu Saves the world's gameplay is a refined version of Breath of Death VII:The Beginning's gameplay. You can choose to battle at any time and there are a set amount of encounters in each area of the game, like in Breath of Death. When you engage an enemy, you can attack normally, use magic or physical skills, use a Unite skill with another party member, or defend/dodge. As each turn goes by, enemies grow 10%, giving you a psuedo-time limit. When you win a battle, your health is fully restored and you get some magic points back. Despite sounding so simple, it's a welcome departure from the battle mechanics of other RPGs and makes for a fun, albeit repetitive, experience.
Music:CStW's music is really good. Each track fits the feel of the situation it plays in, from the relaxing town themes to the action-packed boss themes, Cthulhu Saves the World's music is certainly notable among other RPGs.
Graphics:Cthulhu Saves the World's graphic are an homage to the graphics style of early 16-bit era JRPGs like Final Fantasy IV and other games like that. However, they still manage to be well-detailed to the point where enemy recolors always have something besides palette that sets them apart from the opponents that came before them.
All-in-all, Cthulhu Saves the World is not for everybody, but it provides hours of fun with its various references, fun gameplay, and unique charm overall. If I had to point out any major flaws, however, I'd have to criticize the lack of coherent and fluid story in addition to lack of characterization for non-party members. However, if you like classic JRPGs like Final Fantasy, Dragon Quest, Breath of Fire, etc. then Cthulhu Saves the World will not disappoint.
Score:7/10 - Good
Cthuhu's Angels Extra Mode Kinda Review
Cthulhu's Angels is an extra mode of Cthulhu Saves the World added in for the PC release of the game. It features October as she goes on Cthulhu's quest for him with three other (female) party members because... Hey, octopus/dragon/demon gods are generally lazy. Now, before anyone asks, I call this a "kinda review" because I'm not giving it a score, but I am going to go over the altered story and added characters while giving my opinion. That being said, let's get on with it.
Story:In Cthulhu's Angels, October the super-angsty necromancer has fled to that place where Cthulhu washed up in CStW because everybody in her hometown mocked her for studying the arcane art of necromancy. There, she finds a holographic projecter that Cthulhu contacts her with,telling her that he was stripped of his powers and needs her and three other ladies to become heroes for him because he's off doing who-knows-what in who-knows-where. Along the way, the Narrator keeps messing with the party, doing things like bringing a bridge to life as the boss that replaces Star Terror, the second boss of CStW. And, yes, I said "replaces". This is because the story is a rehash of CStW's, and a poor one at that. But hey, this is a parody game. Keep that in mind throughout the whole thing.
Characters:Now, Cthulhu's Angels adds some new characters to the party. First, Elona/Elonalina from those random hero group replaces Umi as the first party member, and is a rehash of Dacre gameplay-wise. Then, Umi replaces Sharpe as the second party member and is a direct clone of him in terms of gameplay. And by the way, this isn't the Umi you all know and love, this is her silvery-haired evil side brought upon by her trying to wield Sharpe, who is now her weapon, and a cursed sword. Kinda like what happened to the Masamune in Chrono Cross, the "sequel" to Chrono Trigger. The third and final party member, Molly the Were-Zompire, joins where October would've, and is a replica of Paws in terms of gameplay. She's from one of Zeboyd's other works. Now, in terms of other major characters, Cthulhu becomes mission control, the Narrator just messes with the party, Ember doesn't do any fighting and is just there as a means of flight, October is left unchanged, Paws is killed right after he says one sentence, and Dacre... I won't spoil what he does.
My Opinion:Cthulhu's Angels feels like a poorly-done ROM hack of CStW, with characters being replaced left and right. It follows the exact same path as CStW, and just feels like a boring rehash. However, the ending was one of the most insane twist endings in any video game I've played, so there's some redemption to be had there. But in all seriousness, this extra mode left a somewhat bitter taste in my mouth, with only one dungeon changed, all the bosses altered in some way, and if it isn't already blatant enough that Zeboyd just took CStW and changed it slightly, I dare you to try entering the first bonus dungeon before visiting the first town. See what Umi, who isn't even in your party at the time, has to say. All-in-all, I felt like I was just playing an amatuer's attempt at a ROM hack. But please, don't let my opinion on an extra mode keep you from buying this game. The main game itself is well made, and this mode is just an extra unlocked after you beat CStW. So if you don't think this mode seems interesting, don't play it. You've still got a bunch of other modes to mess with besides this one.

I understand buildings having only 1 or 2 varieties but I shouldn’t see things like the same rock and tree over and over so easily which can usually be dealt with but just rotating an object. Ruby Sea feels like a huge empty zone given the water doesn’t add much actual gameplay either. If you’re going to add a mostly water zone you should at the very least add some type of gimmick rather than having it be nothing more than a barren land of emptiness and copy pasted rocks and kelp that you swim through. In general some zones just didn’t feel like they reached their full potential such as the Lochs and Yanxia (seeing ‘Doma’ on the map just to go to the area and find out it was 80% water was disappointing) while others like Azim Steppe were really well done. The zones still feel dead in general when compared to WoW’s where you’ll see NPC’s actually doing things such as bears hunting fish or predators hunting prey and in general FF14 zone design seems to be nothing more than ‘this is the bear area and over there’s the wolf area and this final area is the bird area and the mobs are just all walking back and forth in their little zone’.
My main issue with SB right now is that once you hit 70 the game is the same exact game as HW. You do the same 3 dungeons over and over (with high DPS queues) to grind out tomes and in general are doing nothing at all actually new unlike how Legion added Mythic+, artifact weapons, and the world quest system (an improvement of the old dailies system). And of course with Omega they are continuing the convoluted ♥♥♥♥♥♥ gearing system from Alexander. Square is once again relegating any new systems to patches and we have to hope these new systems are well developed unlike Lord of Verminion and Diadem and even things like the eventual beast tribes may just be the same ol’ 3 daily quests. I’m iffy on this thing Square does where they release a ‘skeleton’ expansion and how they instead put new systems into patches I’m holding out hope that they surprise me with the upcoming patches though given Square has been nothing but predictable with FF14 so I’m not getting my hopes too high.
In the end if Blizzard released Legion with only 3 max level dungeons, no mythic+, no artifacts, no world quest system, and a 4 boss raid they’d have been destroyed by the gaming media and players especially if that was the same exact stuff the last expansion launched with.

Great MMO with quality mechanics and far more pros than cons.
Pros:
+Responsive MMO combat (standard auto attack with skills combat system)
+Level one character and change your class at a single button press
+Friendly and helpful community
+Effective graphics
+Various ways to level characters
+No crafting or gathering skill limits
+Fun and mechanically complex dungeons and bosses
+Large diverse world
+Cooperation friendly loot and experince rules. No "mob tapping" and instanced resource nodes means you never compete with other players for loot, kills or resources
+Never slog through low level areas with no mounts again
+XP bonus' when you level alternative classes
+Easy fast and cheap teleport system
+A few hundred inventory slots
Neutral:
>Hilariously bad story loaded with contrived plot points and anime tropes. It suffers from the "You're the one" storyline where you and thousands of other players are somehow "the single person who can save the world" dispite hudnreds of main story quests requiring you to group up with other "chosen ones". You will also come across atleast a dozen instances of a more powerful foe that can literally kill you in a single attack opting not to kill you but give you a speach about how they will defeat you next time you meet, allowing you to gather a group to take him down. It shatters your suspension of disbelief and for me it never recovered.
Cons:
-Horrific content gating. Most instances are locked behind a main story which is annoying but not too bad, but both expansions are locked behind hours of questing. Getting to heavensward will take 20+ hours after you finish the base main story, with Stormblood taking 4-6 hours. They of course sell items on the website that bypass this making it glaringly obvious the only reason it takes so long to unlock is to push the sale of bypass items. This is my single biggest complaint with the game and the only reason this is remotly acceptable is you only have to do this once. If each character was locked to a single class this would be a dealbreaker.
-TONS of missing QOL things. For example, areas are instanced in two ways, each zone is its own independent instance and each zone has up to three different versions depending on population, if you need to go to a specific version of a zone (for instance a world boss) you need to physically enter the zone by running into it to get the instance choice pop up. This could be fixed by simply allowing you to pick an instance upon teleporting into the zone. There are dozens of examples of small QOL issues that dont make that serve to detract from the overall experience.
The game has it's flaws for sure and it is by no means a perfect game but this is the single best MMO I have played since vanilla wow. It feels like the developers looked at their competition and pulled bits and pieces of a dozen different games and combined all the best mechanics into one game. Its been over a decade since an MMO has sucked me in like this, and the whole level every class with one character thing is right up my "I want to play every class" mentality with these kinds of games.
If you love MMOs there is a solid chance this game may scratch that itch so many other games fail to reach. Download the trial and ignore side quests till around level 10, the beginning of the game is paced VERY poorly but quickly picks up steam and gets better and better as more content is unlocked. If you hit 35 and are still not sure, switch classes and try a different role, the game encourages you to level as many classes as you want.

Transistor is probably one of my favourite games of all time, for a variety of reasons, which includes things such as masterfully crafted artwork and aesthetics, an amazing soundtrack by Darren Korb, and an incredible world-setting, characters and lore. This is, of course, a non-exhaustive list, and it has a surprising amount of replayability value for both the completionist and the non-completionist.
Just like Bastion, it's a story-rich game that leaves a lot of the world to the player's interpretation and imagination, with only one constant voice to accompany you through the game: the Transistor's. The optional rooms found within the Backdoors are challenging but non-intensive and fun, and there's a certain charm in exploring all of the areas to find all of the interactive objects to hear the Transistor/narrator expound upon the world.
The cons of this game would include things such as the combat system, which can be difficult to get used to at first (or be frustrating if you decide to use limiters), and the lack of obvious direction in-game (as you might end up progressing before you mean to), though these would only be a problem if you're a completionist. Luckily enough, you can go through this games as many times as you want in the NG+ mode, which basically eliminates these issues.
It's definitely worth the full price, but grabbing this game during a sale only makes the entire experience better. ; )
EDIT: Even playing it years after it's been made, and the experience is still just as novel and as breathtaking as the first time I've played it. The voice acting and music is absolutely phenomenal.

Eventhough I do understand that lots of effort was put into the creation of Borderlands 2 and it having lots of content, I do not agree with the overwhelmingly positive reviews since it feels like an extremely grindy and boring shooting game to me.
After playing the linear progression campaign, I felt completely exhausted since it is very grindy. It is all about finding quests that require you to locate an item or to assassinate a person and returning in order to claim your reward. I find myself constantly moving back and forth between levels in order to progress. There are basically no side activities and there is no social sense either since there is no global chat - being in a group of players makes sense only if you have similar levels.
My biggest complaint is the lacking combat system:
- There is no stealth so you always have to engage against enemies because ignoring them is not an option either.
- Melee is just a simple strike - you cannot block incoming attacks or use a variety of slashes. You cannot even have different melee weapons.
- Fighting enemies is all about numbers since there is no balance at all, skill does not matter. The higher your level, the more health you have and the more damage you deal.
- You walk, sprint, or crouch. Well, you can jump. But this is it, there are no other evasive or aggressive maneuvers to perform which often makes you feel clunky since you cannot take cover appropriately or use the environment to attack tactically.
Five years after its release it is still very buggy with a GUI that breaks frequently and bad AI enemies. I do not feel any immersive gameplay and I rarely feel like playing it.
Borderlands 2 is a silly game with a generic storyline. Its stylised graphics are mildly irritating in some combat scenarios. This game may be exactly what you are looking for but I would not recommend a purchase for its full price.

Well what can i say about Farming Simulator 2017, amazing..simple amazing. After spending about 1800 hours in fs15 i can  say ive seen alot of interesting stuff, the great equipment, the modding, and the great community. the moment i loaded up fs17 i noticed the vast improvement on graphic options, the ability to use Track Ir, and the Automatic setup and detection of gamepads and steering wheels.
Loading into the game was incredibly fast, and there it was Goldcrest in all its glory, i spent about 45 minutes just driving around and taking in the sights, and driving the trains.
As i started my career i noticed big improvment on drive quality of the vehicles,the environmental lighting and road noise.....road noise from the transition of hard pavement to the gravel dirt roads. Every sound is different, from the combine reving high...to the moment you begin to combine your crops and you hear the revs go deeper as you begin to swath. all little details that make Fs17 great to begin with.
From inspecting fields and seeing that you can work to improve relationship with farmers that own fields and do work for then to bring the price down, so its cheaper for you to buy later on. I spent a good ten minutes looking for a spot to fill my seeder when i realize i had to buy seed and purchase extra pallets of fertilizer, something that was left out of fs15 (except in Modding) this all adds to the overall experience of the game. I have still alot to explore, and found that buying livestock you no longer have to click to buy animals but rather buy and transport them to your farm. Fs17 has made leaps and bound in the Farming simulation catagory, I cant wait to see what else is in store for the future. Great Job Giants Keep up the great work.

I have seen many reviews compare Sleeping Dogs to GTA V, but personally I tend to see the game a little differently.
Unarmed fighting
The unarmed fighting in this game is one of the highlights and it really needs to be since this will be your primary form of taking out those who get in your way.  While it is not as detailed a hand to hand fighter as a 3D fighting game is I would say it compares favorably to the fighting system in Sega's Yakuza series.  You get a one button counter and all of your various attacks come from the 4 primary butons (run, attack, grab, and counter).  There a few moves that also rely upon having a lockon on your target but for the most part the primary 4 actions comprise the input for 90% of the main characters attacks in various combos and strings of presses.  From this relatively simple setup you can make a fairly cinimatic Kung Fu fight scene and are bound to do so at least once while playing it.  Even when facing opponets with knives, tire irons, meat cleavers, ect. the hero never feels like his hand to hand skills put him at a disadvantage and the feeling of becoming a Kung Fu movie action hero only grows as his array of skills grow over the course of the game.
Gun play
The team who made the game did not wish for guns to become the focus of combat through out the game and made all weapons more along the line of powerups to be obtained and then discarded.   This shows in the combat sections with weapons.  The scripted events where you get a gun and are expected to use it are well designed and hide the major flaws in the gun combat.  The fact the hero gets a bullet time like ability when he does something movie like (action doge over a barrier, a disarm, jumping on to a car, shooting out a tire, and other) does a good job in making the very deadly gun combat more manageable.  If you are shooting from a vehicle and are trying to stop persuers then the second one gets next to you or ahead of you it is probably better to just reset since high speed precice aim is not this game's strong suite.  The few non scripted, non vehicle gun combat areas are not the best parts of the game and half the battle is finding a good place to hide, not get shot at from 6 places at once and die in 30 seconds.
Driving
The cars handle fine and the roads are a lot more interesting then most open world games you drive in.  There are city races and once you have to go at highspeed you quickly realize that even if you wanted to be a good driver and not damage other cars/property or kill innocent bystandards, this game makes this really really really hard not to become the largest mass murderer on the road.  Cars will swerve in to your path if you try and pass at high speed.  Pedestrians are every where ready to make one slightly missed turn into a 6 person murder scene.  Also for those not used to it (Americans) the right side of the road is incomming trafic... not the left.  Be prepared to kill more people then you intend to while driving in this game.
Story
If you are a fan of old school and new(ish) Kung Fu action movies then this game has it all for you.  There is even an island of death.  If you are a fan of gritty crime dramas then this game will give you a look at a vibrant society with criminal undercurrent that should replace generic cop drama 32 that is on this season.  The story is really good and even if you are not a fan of the gameplay this is a story that can keep you playing just to see what is next.
Missions/side quests
The main missions are all interesting for story reasons and the "boss" fights are great.  The side missions vary from repetetive things you do to get the rewards (exp, items, cash) to some of the most interesting things this game has to offer.  One side quest (zodiac tournement) is really a small self contained story dlc and great fun.  The 2 other main DLC expansions are stand alone and also good and interesting content.
Over all I would definetly recomend giving this game a chance.

Papers, please? More like depression, please.

**scroll to bottom for TLDR review**
... I woke up in my usual spot on the floor of the OPS center, huddled near the Medbay.  The gentle hum of electronic equipment always helped me fall asleep after a hard day of exo-salvaging.  No, I'm not that work-aholic who sleeps in the office.  Circumstances had been less than ordinary for the past... I don't know, days?  Weeks?  Suffice to say, things have been happening.
Before passing out from exhaustion the previous night, I had made a few interesting discoveries while exploring the factory.   I decided to buzz Sally on the communication terminal to see if she had any interesting observations. She gave me her usual carping about distress beacons, and I continued to wonder if she might be an AI of some kind.  All joking aside, the slight pang of attraction I had felt upon first meeting her made me feel uneasy - could someone be manipulating me?  I always had a hard time saying "no" to women.
... I also had a streak of paranoia that could be described as... "not insignificant."  At any rate, I felt hopelessly ignorant of my situation here, and she was the only person that had helped me move forward at all.  What "forward" meant, exactly, remained to be seen.  I couldn't even remember the details of why I currently "enjoyed" the use of a military-grade exoskeleton.  I remembered accepting a manufacturing position at CREO (they were quite literally the only company hiring these days), and going through an orientation process, after which I woke up amid flaming wreckage somehwere inside the compound.
Like I said, things have been happening.  Nevertheless, I gave the weird guy, Warren a "please-don't-stop-me-right-now" nod, walked past Davey without acknowledgement (sometimes I regretted rescuing that worm), and "forward" I went, into the factory.
"Look out for your fellow workers.  They look out for you," the creepy female computer voice droned as I walked out the door.  Sensible words for a manufacturing environment, but lately they had taken on a new meaning.
I decided the logical thing to do would be to pick up where I had left off.  I had recently found the entrance to Toxic Waste Disposal and had been... reclaiming some equipment.  I made my way back down there, giving co-workers the usual high fives and fist bumps along the way.
Finally I made it to Toxic Waste.  I saw a new co-worker, equipped with a few pieces of Liquidator anti-exposure gear, which I had been collecting.  I jogged up behind him, did a mechanically-assisted baseball slide, and simultaneously brought my katana-length Vibro-Sawzall down in a sideways hacking motion, directed at the back of his knees.  Not how I would usually introduce myself to a co-worker.  Again, things have been happening.
The guy seemed barely conscious like the rest of them.  Almost feral even.  He grunted, stumbled to a knee from the impact, and I raised my weapon for the coup de grace.
"THWONG!!!"  The impact caught me beneath the jaw, only partially absorbed by my Sentinal class headgear.  The scab had taken advantage of my over-confidence and landed an uppercut with several hundred pounds of force behind it.  That was unexpected, which only made it hurt more.  This guy might wander around like a drunken zombie, but his exosuit was still capable of viscious speed.  Never let your guard down in exo-combat.
I shook it off just in time to raise my left arm and deflect the next attack, causing him to recoil back on his heels a bit.  Or, technically speaking, destabilizing the gyros of his suit just enough to make it take a step backwards.  But I wasn't going to allow that.  While my left hand was still following through from the deflection, I swept the Sawzall in my right hand down with an arc, aiming once again for the knees, as if harvesting wheat.  His Operator class stilts did little this time to protect the fleshy bits from the force my suit was applying.  There was a sickening metallic/organic crunch as the Liquidator leg gear (free leg included!) tore free and came to rest on the floor about a foot away from... the rest of the equipment.
"Sorry, I guess."  I shrugged and picked up the gear, excited to have completed the set.
It was all over in a few seconds.  I didn't have confirmation, but I was beginning to wonder if the neural implants driving my exosuit came along with some sort of "frame-jacking" ability that allowed me to experience time at a much faster subjective rate.  It was a strange sensation that I couldn't fully describe if pressed.  It just seemed like I was a bit more... precise than before.  Especially when my adrenaline was pumping and my fight or flight instinct was engaged.
Wow, not to mention, my mind seemed to be constantly wandering and multi-tasking, like a computer with ADD.  I continued through Toxic Waste and found a Power Terminal, with the number "10" brightly contrasted in red and green on an LED screen.  I used the power core of my suit to bypass the terminal's PSU, overloading the terminal.  The terminal sparked like ball-lightning and a large set of steel doors nearby slid open, disappearing into the walls.
Upon closer inspection, I realized the doors led to an elevator.  With anticipation, I stepped on and waited for the pressure-sensitive subfloor to register my weight, engaging the magnetic drive.
"Ha, love it when that happens," I said as the elevator doors opened and I found myself back at the main level, just around the corner from OPS.  I ran into OPS to craft my newly acquired Liquidator gear and try on the completed set.  Along with protecting against exposure to toxic radiation, fire, electricity, etc., the Liquidator set reduced stamina cost from dodging, and was by far the coolest looking I had seen yet.  The drawback was it had less armor, and wasn't as stable against heavy impacts.  Hey, "you look good, you play good," right?  I decided to keep it, uh, installed.
Vital injections refilled, sweet looking new suit with a sick green light, I set off once again.  This time, taking the new elevator shortcut back down to Toxic Waste.  I had seen the words "Hazardous Bla Bla" stenciled on a wall and wanted to use my new hazmat exosuit for some exploring.
"HAZARDOUS WASTE STORAGE"  I noticed the marking again as I made my way down the corridor.  I couldn't help but notice there appeared to be a major problem "storing" the "hazardous waste," because there was toxic material literally all over the place.  I was glad to be wearing the full set of Liquidator gear because it was hard to step anywhere without at least some exposure.  It even looked like it might have been growing.
"Things have definitely been happening," I mused as I walked through a large holographic door into a room large enough to be used as an aircraft hangar.
A loud computerized female voice said "CONTAMINATION DETECTED.  LOCKDOWN IN OPERATION.  INITIATING DISPOSAL MEASURES."  The holographic door behind me turned red.
Upon entering, I hadn't noticed the truck-sized, round, multi-legged robot hovering in a dimly lit corner, which was now approaching me menacingly.  There was a problem with hazardous waste indeed, and apparently the problem was ME.
"PLEASE REMAIN STATIONARY DURING CLEANUP PROCEDURE."
Don't think I'll be doing that, thanks. Come get some, you spindly son-of-a-
