The Surge is a game based around the Soulslike premise as seen in Dark Souls, Demon Souls and Bloodborne. The game has resources, tech scraps which you use to level up and upgrade gear that you drop on death, but that can be collected from the place you died on respawning.
I'll break down my review into several categories
COMBAT:
The combat in The Surge is a lot smoother than in Dark Souls, it focusses more around dodging than blocking, a skill I barely used in the game, but still retains that heaviness that Soulslike games tend to have.
You lock on to enemies to focus your attacks on, but you can select what parts to attack. This is used so you can see what parts are armoured or unarmoured so you can kill them faster or try to loot their gear. The enemy variety is a bit limited, but I didn't find myself getting bored of it. The enemies are fairly strong, but they broadcast most of their attacks so it doesn't feel too unfair when you die. As the game progresses the enemies change their equipment and attack patterns, so you need to adjust how you fight them accordingly.
ENEMIES:
Enemy variety is a bit limited, its humans with different armour and weapons mostly with a few robots and other weirder things a bit later on. The different types behave fairly similar so you can notice patterns consistently and fight around it.
PROGRESSION:
Progression is done by levelling up your Power Core with Tech Scrap. You get Tech Scrap from killing enemies as well as item drops. The higher your Power Core, the more power you have to play with. You use power to equip weapons, armour and implants. Weapons and armour are fairly self explanitory but the implants is as close to character customisation as this game comes. You can only change your equipment in a safe room called the OPS Centre, but you can swap them out as and when you want inside there, essentially respeccing your character as many times as you want. The OPS Centre works like the Bonfire at Dark Souls, using the Med Bay to heal yourself and restore your injectables resets all of the enemies in the current area. One thing I did like is the ability to bank scrap at the OPS Centre for later use. This mitigates one issue I had with Dark Souls where I had a lot of souls, but not enough to level up which ended up with me losing more than I needed. Thankfully this game gets around this.
Different types of armour are aquired by cutting them off enemies and rebuilding them. This is really satisfying as you hack bits off enemies and rebuild them for yourself. The weapons are either dropped by enemies or found around the map.
BOSSES:
The bosses were a mixed bag. There are only 5 and they varied wildly in how good they felt. The first boss was really satisfying with strong attacks broadcast well so you could learn to avoid them and counter it. The second broadcast its attacks well but I had a few issues with the hitbox being a bit off, making this harder than it could be. The third boss looked intimidating but was a fairly simplistic stage based boss. The fourth one was a mix of the first boss and basic enemies you encounter later in the game, being hard but fair. The last boss was a bit of a letdown, the first half was interesting but quickly lost tempo in the second stage.
STORIES/PLOT:
The game does the typical Soulslike thing of drip feeding the backstory to you. This is done through audio logs found throughout the game, messages at terminals throughout the game, NPC dialogue and finally the promotional videos found throughout the game. The audio logs piece together to build the main story slowly as well as have a few smaller stories that help to give a feeling to the human cost of the plot. The voice acting is a mixed bag, going from good to utterly terrible. The plot starts fairly bland but becomes quite interesting towards the end.
The promotional ads steal the show as they are light hearted but insightful, they require some reading between the lines to get the most out of.
LEVEL DESIGN:
The levels are fairly similar aesthetically, but this fits the lore of the game. The levels tend to have a single ops centre in, but this is essential as it gives the player an incentive to explore as there are plenty of shortcuts back to OPS. Given you only have a fixed amount of health top ups, this makes a longer run feel riskier knowing you could find a shortcut and level up or die and lose your progress. There are hidden areas as well as places locked off for later on in the game, meaning backtracking to get everything is required.
FAIRNESS:
Soulslike games are renowned for their difficulty and this game is no exception. The difficulty curve is....interesting. The first few areas of the game will kill you for making minor mistakes as you try to level up. You'll reach a point where you can just walk through areas effortlessly once you've learned what is ahead and how to fight them. This continues until later in the game, with the difficulty spiking, levelling out, spiking and levelling out. Towards the end of the game you will have to be pretty damn good to survive the enemies thrown at you.
Some of the enemies have issues of poorly broadcast attacks. This ranges from stuns that break combos, some one shot kills or a lot of damage over time attacks. This was my one issue. Sometimes i'd be fighting at full health and something would just tap me and kill me in one hit.
CONCLUSION:
Would I recommend The Surge? Yeah. I struggled initially but after a while it really gripped me.

This is a game by the developers of that dark souls ripoff game "Lords of the Fallen".
You don't even have to see my negative review on that to find out so many bad things about that game.
The combat was horrible, slow and unresponsive.
Basically they tried to mimic Dark soul's lockon combat system but failed miserably as the weapons forced slow tanky playstyles.
Anyway, that being said
.
I'm only one hour in and i can already see so much improvement.
There's a more unique combat system this time around, allowing you to target enemy's body parts.
You can choose to hit parts with lower or no armor to take out an enemy quick and stagger him, or you can focus on a certain limb in an attempt to dismember it and salvage it's parts.
Basically this involves some more thinking to the combat, but also to the salvaging/crafting.
The story and graphics are both very good and interesting.
Like i said i'm only 1 hour in but i'm usually very quickly bored or annoyed by the genericness of a game's plot.
This one's not the case so far.
Customisation is cool so far, allowing me to recover parts from enemy's limbs, or salvage broken ones to create new ones.
Basically you level by upgrading your "power core".
The higher your power core; the more (powerful) equipment you can equip.
This forced me to pick between which armor and weapon i wanted to use before expanding on.
As for combat you can dash to dodge, jump over swings, duck under some and genuinely move from A to B to C while dodging hits very easily as long as you keep a slight sense of stamina consumption. It's very agile and fast, but so are your enemies.
As for attacking you can do horizontal swings and vertical swings. Both of those can be charged or chained in a combo.
Right now i don't see much of a difference in using the two as they both feel the same for me now, but i reckon they'll vary with later weapons in the game (i'm using one of the starting weapons).
Let's just say the game is well worth it money so far.
I only write reviews if i'm either very dissapointed/annoyed or when i'm genuinely impressed and latched to a game.
I bought this expecting to refund it especially after the sour taste Lords of the Fallen left for me, but this game is blowing me away so far.

What a pleasant surprise The Surge is !
Made by the same devs that did the sad and truly forgetable Lords of the Fallen, this is a souls game worth playing.
The first three areas definately reminded me of Dark Souls 1, with SOLID combat, a large choice of weapons and armour and a leveling system that is complex but makes sense. Having only one MedStation per area initially seemed a bit rough but finding a shortcut back to said area was as gratifying as finding a new bonfire with a bucket load of souls and only one estus flask left.
Further into the game I thought the kills became a bit cheap. There are minor enemies that CAN and DO one shot you. It became a bit frustrating, almost infuriating. However, after learning the attack patterns (which you really have to do) and coming up with good counters, I overcame this difficulty spike. I had as good as a journey that is had in a Dark Souls experience.
The boss fights are ordinary, not memorable. There is one that reminded me so much of the shocker that is The Bed of Chaos. However, the best gameplay is had in the main areas. As I said, the combat is solid, responsive and gratifying...once you learn how to do it.
It is a little bit clunky but not very.
Lords of the Fallen was a mis step, The Surge is a great leap forward.
If you like Dark Souls or souls-like games, I would definately recommend The Surge.

Great MMO with quality mechanics and far more pros than cons.
Pros:
+Responsive MMO combat (standard auto attack with skills combat system)
+Level one character and change your class at a single button press
+Friendly and helpful community
+Effective graphics
+Various ways to level characters
+No crafting or gathering skill limits
+Fun and mechanically complex dungeons and bosses
+Large diverse world
+Cooperation friendly loot and experince rules. No "mob tapping" and instanced resource nodes means you never compete with other players for loot, kills or resources
+Never slog through low level areas with no mounts again
+XP bonus' when you level alternative classes
+Easy fast and cheap teleport system
+A few hundred inventory slots
Neutral:
>Hilariously bad story loaded with contrived plot points and anime tropes. It suffers from the "You're the one" storyline where you and thousands of other players are somehow "the single person who can save the world" dispite hudnreds of main story quests requiring you to group up with other "chosen ones". You will also come across atleast a dozen instances of a more powerful foe that can literally kill you in a single attack opting not to kill you but give you a speach about how they will defeat you next time you meet, allowing you to gather a group to take him down. It shatters your suspension of disbelief and for me it never recovered.
Cons:
-Horrific content gating. Most instances are locked behind a main story which is annoying but not too bad, but both expansions are locked behind hours of questing. Getting to heavensward will take 20+ hours after you finish the base main story, with Stormblood taking 4-6 hours. They of course sell items on the website that bypass this making it glaringly obvious the only reason it takes so long to unlock is to push the sale of bypass items. This is my single biggest complaint with the game and the only reason this is remotly acceptable is you only have to do this once. If each character was locked to a single class this would be a dealbreaker.
-TONS of missing QOL things. For example, areas are instanced in two ways, each zone is its own independent instance and each zone has up to three different versions depending on population, if you need to go to a specific version of a zone (for instance a world boss) you need to physically enter the zone by running into it to get the instance choice pop up. This could be fixed by simply allowing you to pick an instance upon teleporting into the zone. There are dozens of examples of small QOL issues that dont make that serve to detract from the overall experience.
The game has it's flaws for sure and it is by no means a perfect game but this is the single best MMO I have played since vanilla wow. It feels like the developers looked at their competition and pulled bits and pieces of a dozen different games and combined all the best mechanics into one game. Its been over a decade since an MMO has sucked me in like this, and the whole level every class with one character thing is right up my "I want to play every class" mentality with these kinds of games.
If you love MMOs there is a solid chance this game may scratch that itch so many other games fail to reach. Download the trial and ignore side quests till around level 10, the beginning of the game is paced VERY poorly but quickly picks up steam and gets better and better as more content is unlocked. If you hit 35 and are still not sure, switch classes and try a different role, the game encourages you to level as many classes as you want.

Cthulhu Saves the World is a parody RPG where you get to play as Cthulhu and drive your enemies insane.
If that and the cheap price tag weren't enough to convince you to buy and play this now, keep reading:
The gameplay of Cthulhu Saves the World is based on classic JRPG mechanics such as random encounters and turn based battles. However this is mixed with more modern design elements to proved an improved, compact, experience. Battles can move very fast with minimal time wasted on attack animation and a very quick and responsive interface. There is also the combo system to add an extra layer of depth to your decisions in combat. Plus each area in the game limits the total number of random encounters, so you won't be stuck in an easy area forever if you have bad luck (There is also includes an option to force encounters in case you feel the need to grind past the limit).
This parody RPG is filled with humor in its dialogue and enemy/monster description which will keep you entertained between battles. The game will only be around 5-7 hours for a normal play through, so if you want a classic JRPG type experience but don't have the 50-100+ hours to spend on a more traditional game, this is a great alternative. However, if you want to keep playing there are several alternate modes such as the score attack mode to test your skill, or the Highlander and Cthulhu's Angels modes to provide different experiences.
If you liked Breath of Death VII you'll probably love this, and even if you didn't, you may still enjoy Cthulhu Saves the World due to its improvements in mechanics and visuals.

This is a recommend-in-lieu-of-an-on-the-fence-option review.  Factorio is a 'living machine'-styled game that's fun to play with, but I don't really cherish my time with it.  If anything I'm just kind of sad it took me so long to recognize what I would ultimately not like about it and that it mars my opinion of it so heavily.  For the record, you could probably mod the game in such a way as to address my complaints, but I have neither the time nor the inclination to do so and since most people mod the game to be more difficult, I'm in the minority anyways.  Nonethless, that flaw is the focus of this review and should be what you consider before purchasing.
There is a sudden, jarring increase in complexity.  Up until you start dealing with oils, the game relies on five basic resources, converyor belts, assemblers and an assortment of helper devices.  You use them to build logic trains to produce goods of increasing complexity.  However, this slow increase in design and production takes a violent upshot once you start dealing with oils.  Not only are they somewhat infuriating because, unlike conveyors, you have to build mostly with underground pipes to have these production areas even be navigable, but also because the infrastructure you need to start exploiting them is nearly equal to everything you've likely built up until this point.  Once you unlock oil, you basically have to build an entire other base to even -begin- to make use of them.  They have some other quirks that make oil an even more obnoxious resource but even though I tried to get a handle on them I never found it to be as enjoyable as working with the converyor belts.
But there's another hit that comes with it.  Most of what you need to 'survive' is built pre-oil.  It's odd, but a lot of the stuff you can build with oil is just automating the the things you did before oil.  I dunno, it's a nice thing to have but it also kind of leaves me always thinking, is this it?  All this work so I could automate what little I'm doing at this point?  It's a wierd feeling.
So, because Steam doesn't have a 'middle' option for reviewing, it would be disingenuous for me to not recommend it.  I do like parts of it and I've certainly gotten my money's worth of playtime.  I really would love to see this area of the game be improved though, because the oil gameplay is just not as satisfying as what comes before it and since it's the gatekeeper to the rest of the game, well.  It is what it is, consider before buying.

In a way this is a tycoon-style game with some Minecraft/Terraria influences.
After crashlanding on a planet you start small, crafting primitive tools and doing things by yourself. But before long you are placing machines, interconnecting them with a webway of conveyor belts, trying to create a self-sustainable mechanism. Resources run out and you have to expand using robots to transport things short distances and a railroad to get things from afar.
As you expand you wreck the nature around you, pollute air causing indigenous lifeforms to attack your factories again and again. As your machine empire evolves so do they, resulting in stronger enemies and bigger damage, Fortunately there's a variety of ways to defend what's yours. In the end you build a rocket to leave the dangerous place.
Apart from freeplay there are also several tutorial campaigns available, explaining game mechanics as you go from mission to mission. The game also supports cooperative play and there's a large modding scene available, even at this stage of the development, adding more tools, resources, machines, enemies and weapons.
The biggest strength of Factorio, much like with other tycoons, is when everything clicks into place and you see a huge, complex mechanism work without much of your input.

I have seen many reviews compare Sleeping Dogs to GTA V, but personally I tend to see the game a little differently.
Unarmed fighting
The unarmed fighting in this game is one of the highlights and it really needs to be since this will be your primary form of taking out those who get in your way.  While it is not as detailed a hand to hand fighter as a 3D fighting game is I would say it compares favorably to the fighting system in Sega's Yakuza series.  You get a one button counter and all of your various attacks come from the 4 primary butons (run, attack, grab, and counter).  There a few moves that also rely upon having a lockon on your target but for the most part the primary 4 actions comprise the input for 90% of the main characters attacks in various combos and strings of presses.  From this relatively simple setup you can make a fairly cinimatic Kung Fu fight scene and are bound to do so at least once while playing it.  Even when facing opponets with knives, tire irons, meat cleavers, ect. the hero never feels like his hand to hand skills put him at a disadvantage and the feeling of becoming a Kung Fu movie action hero only grows as his array of skills grow over the course of the game.
Gun play
The team who made the game did not wish for guns to become the focus of combat through out the game and made all weapons more along the line of powerups to be obtained and then discarded.   This shows in the combat sections with weapons.  The scripted events where you get a gun and are expected to use it are well designed and hide the major flaws in the gun combat.  The fact the hero gets a bullet time like ability when he does something movie like (action doge over a barrier, a disarm, jumping on to a car, shooting out a tire, and other) does a good job in making the very deadly gun combat more manageable.  If you are shooting from a vehicle and are trying to stop persuers then the second one gets next to you or ahead of you it is probably better to just reset since high speed precice aim is not this game's strong suite.  The few non scripted, non vehicle gun combat areas are not the best parts of the game and half the battle is finding a good place to hide, not get shot at from 6 places at once and die in 30 seconds.
Driving
The cars handle fine and the roads are a lot more interesting then most open world games you drive in.  There are city races and once you have to go at highspeed you quickly realize that even if you wanted to be a good driver and not damage other cars/property or kill innocent bystandards, this game makes this really really really hard not to become the largest mass murderer on the road.  Cars will swerve in to your path if you try and pass at high speed.  Pedestrians are every where ready to make one slightly missed turn into a 6 person murder scene.  Also for those not used to it (Americans) the right side of the road is incomming trafic... not the left.  Be prepared to kill more people then you intend to while driving in this game.
Story
If you are a fan of old school and new(ish) Kung Fu action movies then this game has it all for you.  There is even an island of death.  If you are a fan of gritty crime dramas then this game will give you a look at a vibrant society with criminal undercurrent that should replace generic cop drama 32 that is on this season.  The story is really good and even if you are not a fan of the gameplay this is a story that can keep you playing just to see what is next.
Missions/side quests
The main missions are all interesting for story reasons and the "boss" fights are great.  The side missions vary from repetetive things you do to get the rewards (exp, items, cash) to some of the most interesting things this game has to offer.  One side quest (zodiac tournement) is really a small self contained story dlc and great fun.  The 2 other main DLC expansions are stand alone and also good and interesting content.
Over all I would definetly recomend giving this game a chance.

Right off the bat, let me say, if you want a space game that isn't entirely aimed towards space battles 24/7 then this is the game for you, I easily give it a 10/10. An amazing game for free. Let me give you a simple rundown, and further down a more descriptive review. I would easily pay $20 for this game, yeah, it's that good. This is one of the first space games that has allowed you to either be a trader, a pirate, or an escort ship, and actually do it well enough that it doesn't seem like they're all basically the same. It has a really great UI, so it's easy to figure things out like, where to go, how far you can go before refueling, what cargo sells better and worse, what systems are likely to have bad guys, and where your next mission is. It also has a small aspect of exploring, but nothing serious.
Now, for the more descriptive review:
The game does a great job of telling you how far you'll be able to go on the map by highlighting your path, and turning it red when you won't be able to go further without refueling, it also tell you what planets will be friendly, hostile, empty, or if you just aren't allowed to land there.
At the very beginning of the game, you get out a loan of 480,000 Credits, which seems like a lot, but you'll pay it back pretty fast. And you have a choice of three different ships. The Shuttle, which is a very lightweight, medium speed ship, which can carry a sizable amount of passengers, and a little bit of cargo. Good for bringing passengers around. Then, you have the Star Barge, a small freighter, a small amount of passenger space, but a sizable amount of cargo space, good for doing transport missions and doing personal trading. And finally you have the Sparrow, a light interceptor, a fighting ship, it has weapons to start off with unlike the other two options. Medium speed but very little in the way of passenger and cargo space, technically useful for killing things and being a pirate, although it's so weak it's basically worthless to start with. Once you choose your ship you get to name it (Yay!) and then you are given a choice, you can do the tutorial, or not. If you do it, you get a bit of a little story, it teaches you how to do the simple mechanics and you get some easy cash early on as well as reveal the map a bit, if you choose not to, you are instantly free to do as you wish.
The game centers around 3 main pillars for making money, you can buy and sell cargo, you can do missions, or you can destroy ships and sell their cargo. I will go into detail on these three in a moment. And there are different ships which allow you to do each of these at varying levels of success.
The first way of making money, is the most basic, you do missions, they are given to you at planets, they send you to other planets, you are sometimes timed, when you reach the other planet, you get money, simple as that.
The second way is still pretty simple, which is trading goods, you simply land on a planet, go the the trading tab, press m to open your map, and click on a planet nearby, or far away depending on if you are already headed somewhere, check the prices of the left and buy the item with the highest price at the other planet, then, travel to that planet, and sell it.
The third is a way I haven't even tried, but is extremely dangerous, killing other ships. For this, you will need a ship with cargo space, and weapons, go out, kill an enemy ship, pick up it's cargo, and go sell it. Seems simple, but can get you in a lot of trouble really fast.
I highly reccomend this game to anyone looking to have a nice easy to learn space game, where you can trade, protect, or destroy. And not to mention it's free, so even if you decide it's not for you, uninstall, and you're done.

First Playthrough Review... (3/5) ... Recommended only at sale price
The game is rather short, taking me almost exactly 20 hours for a first playthrough conflated by exploring and mentally mapping out every area.  It does have NG+ and the like, but I would think you could storm through a campaign in under 5 hours once you understand the layout.  I'm just going to go over the three most important categories for me...
BOSSES: (2/5)
The game definitely starts much better than it finishes.  There are only 5 bosses, which I wasn't put off by (though I will note there are more areas than bosses so I did notice the shortage while playing through), but none are particularly difficult, honestly.  And that was the saving grace of having 5 bosses, if they are all difficult, it would be much more enjoyable than 8 easy bosses and 2 challenging ones...
First playthoughs being as they are, there is a learning curve, but the last 3 bosses took me less than 5 tries each, and the final boss went down on a second go.  That may be a result of becoming more comfortable with a weapon class and learning its exploits, but it was nevertheless incredibly disappointing.  It seems to be a result of the lack of variation and randomness in their movesets.  You can sort of 'bait' a boss into an attack pattern simply based on your distance and placement.. I think I noticed maybe 9 distinct moves during the final boss and only one or two had any variations (extra hit, identical pre-strike motion) and even then you could bait that down to just one or two distinct moves.
LAYOUT (4/5)
I quite enjoyed the general layout of the game.  There are a lot of repeated textures, but it feels correct based on the story and the facility and all that.  The paths are seemingly intentionally labrynth-like which was generally entertaining.  This is all save the last area of the game which is utterly painful to explore and map out.  It took more time than any other area of the game to properly understand and navigate and it became more frustrating to explore than enjoyable.
There are a lot of re-used areas and required backtracking, but the area updates as well so it feels like a new experience (though this will chip at the enjoyment of NG+ for me)
OVERALL DIFFICULTY (2/5)
Again, it starts better than it ends.  The game felt quite difficult through the first three-ish areas.  Maybe it was because I switched to staves around that point and felt more comfortable, I'm not sure.  But after that point I could think of ways to make the game more difficult (I could have stopped levelling, used less efficient implants, or forced myself to use different weapons), but I don't think I should have to force difficulty on a first playthrough.  Most times you face an enemy, it is just one at a time... while this picks up near the games end, by then you have quick takedown combos you can use that trivialize the 2 enemies coming your way.  Then again, adding greater density of enemies would have taken away from the style of the game.  Really, the same problem for bosses seems to reach the regular enemies; it is far too easy to bait attacks and counter and there is a noticeable lack of variability, diversity, and spontaneity in the standard enemy movesets.
OVERALL (3/5)
Predictability breeds redundancy, and that definitely took the shine out of the game by the halfway point.  It really leads to a shockingly disappointing experience by the end when the last boss feels like the most trivial moment in the game.

Don't believe the recent string of Negative Reviews unless you're reading them thoroughly. There's a lot of them downvoting right now simply because they recently lost a loophole to pay for the game cheaply (Russsian and Brazillian Players), and they're abusing the Recommend system to try and send SE a message.
Onto the actual game:
This is a GCD Based Action Bar MMO based on the Final Fantasy series. Like all flagship titles, this game takes place in a unique world, though unlike the rest, this one is heavily referencing previous games in ways not normal to the series. This is a Final Fantasy MMO for fans of Final Fantasy. The enemies are an emire of Magitek Armor weilding, Esper (Primal) hating dudes obsessed with gaining the power of Magic, something your side of the equation uses with ease. To get it, they are willing to subjergate and put down the rest of the world.
All is not lost though. YOU take the role of the Protagonist in this adventure, unlike previous FF games where the main character is a pregenerated personality, your avatar represents the true hero (and your amazing friends, who are totally the heroes of their own story, but who cares right?) The NPCs talk to you directly, the tell the story centered around your character and it's your actions that change the world. An excellent choice for the narrative.
The gameplay is fun and exciting, a little slow, but the emphasis of the game is on strategy and planning over reflexive actions. Leveling includes a robust storyline in which you save the world time and time again, freeing nations from the heel of the Garlean Empire.
Don't take my word for it though, SE provides a free, unlimited time demo of the game which lets you play all base classes up to level 35.
See you in Eorzea!

I started with the free trial to play with a friend. The game is ok but while it does look and sound for the most part like a final fantasy game it kind of feels like its missing something to be a real final fantasy game. combat i found to be kind of boring after a while. for most classes it seems to be a repeating pattern of move 1, move 2, then maybe move a/b.  with move a/b being temp buffs or hey all monster next to me hit me. which i guess is about normal for a lot of mmo. the problem I have with it is some people say it get way better in end game but I find that hard to believe because looking at the skill trees for most of the class there is not a lot there with in some case it looking like you are just adding a move 3 in to the pattern and few more temp buffs leaving you going 1,2,3 over and over as you wait to use those short small temp buffs. Back then you could get a sub class which allowed you to mix in some abilities from other classes. Now they don’t do that in favor of trying to simplify the task bars. So this is my first review ever on steam, but I feel like this game deserves some thought of consideration. There are many reasons why the ratings for this game are currently "Mixed" at the time of writing this review. (At the time - very important part)
So here goes...
If you are going to be trying this game, and the expansions, let me share my experience with this game.
It starts like all other MMOS, questing and character creation. Its overall a pretty game, and a good shot at an MMO by JRPG guys, but its not quite the MMO they want it too be, and somewhat falls short as an RPG. This is what happens when you mix the two I guess. It has content, similar to WoW, the Raids, PvP, Dungeons, Story Questlines, with challenges like gear (getting best gear means more content/harder content is available) and challenges to overcome different game content. You earn your place by leveling, doing class quests, doing dungeons, doing the story, at a very lenghty level.
I am going to spread the pros and cons of this game, from my opinion, and explain them afterwards.
Graphics:
Its a pretty game and it runs well on high end rigs. Idk about a potatoe PC performance though...
Music:
Great! Awesome soundtracks! Unique tunes everywhere you go. Even mount music and battle music! But same battle music gets boring after a while and drives you up the wall. (Drove me listening to it on repeat) Will end up turning off music after you hear new zones tunes, but the Raid Boss Music is AMAZING. Like really good.
Combat:
Its slow. I know others might tell you that its BS, but its slow combat. The GCD (Global Cool Down - time it takes between abilities) is 2.5 sec. For WoW its 1.0 and less on some classes with stats like Haste. 2.5 is a long time. As you level in combat you get spells and abilities you can cast in between your general abilities, so while you do play around the GCD of 2.5 sec you do throw spells in the mix to keep it interesting....but thats towards end game levels. The Combat slows down early questing, early dungeons, early level zones, and makes the game feel sluggish depending on the class you play. (Don't pick arcanist/summoner if you want fast gameplay) The combat is what turns me off. Some classes are fun, but general questing with slow combat makes you fall asleep sometimes, so pack an energy drink. If you are someone who enjoys the pretty graphics and music, or has something happening on the other monitor then you will like the slow-paced combat of this game.
Questing:
One thing I dislike about the game indefinitely. Its like vanilla wow questing (which was awesome and rewarding) but only tad slower and less exciting. Quests are simple, fetch and collect, kill this and that, but some quests are cool, like /emote quests where you have to /emote at NPCs to complete quests. Some quests are story, with in-gamecinematics and dialogue, others are simple fast xp quests. But you also have a lot of annoying quests, like where they tell you run to the edge of the map, talk to a dude, then run all the way back. The questing ends up backtracking to zones you have already been through after level 30, so it doesn't feel linear, which is nice, but it also lacks the feeling of progression. WoW does it by making you move to new zones and experience new environments, but this game takes you back to your back yard more than once. I didn't like this at all.
Story:
NO SPOILERS. Now this is where so many people rave, the story of the game. The best part of the game perhaps? I didn't like it. Its a lot like other FF story, where there is some evil empire, and some evil bag guys, but after defeating them you discover there is an even bigger bad guy hiding behind a curtain, at the same time the princes gets preggo with a demon child, while one kid discoveres he is some remnant of an old god and must summon his power, but to do that he must first undertake a trial by combat against a powerful old god, who hides in the castle under the black rook mountain, which is actually at the center of the world, so the heroes must sacrifice their bodies to venture using spirit streams, which are actually controlled by a 2nd villain, who is also disguised as a princes of a warring kingdom and is set to disbalance political quams....  (All fiction, not related to the game, just a plot of some bad anime combined togher into fiction)
If this got your interest then this is a game for you. I didn't like it. Its not quite Game of Thrones. Its not quite Tell Tale in the story. Its mediocre, or half baked at best imo, but you might enjoy it.
Expansions:
They don't let you play other expacts until you finish the story. This part sucks, because I spent 5 hours doing vanilla end game story stuff at level 50 and I still wasnt even close to doing stuff in heavensward, let alone stormblood.
Money:
To skip said long story its $18 for up-to Heavensward skip, and $25  to skip up to Stormblood. Most general MMO's want to get you into the action with a new xpac as soon as possible. Its a game, you play it to have fun, not a life story to live like a second life, but this game you HAVE to either go through 5+ hours of story quests before hitting up new expansions, or pay up. I paid up. I got into Heavensward and had a whole new mess of things to deal with.
I am questing 50-60 so I have to quest through Heavensward. 2 Ways of doing this. Palace of the Dead (Scenario with its own gear and combat, que as any class and run this fast level scenario, get xp for your class if you don't wipe at the end), Dungeons (que in, DPS wait 25-30 mins to get in, and kill few bosses for some XP, Daily Content (run old dungeons and scenarios for XP to help leveling players) or Quest.
Palace is the fastest method, but if your group dies at the end then its 20-30 mins wasted, no XP or any rewards. Gets repetitive and really boring very quickly, but its a ton of XP (not a lot, but the biggest chunk you could get in 20-30 mins)
Dungeons are alright, but Damage Dealing Classes wait forever to get in. Tanks and healers wait less. Kinda low XP gain.
Daily content is cool, but its the same old dungeons and scenarios you would have done if you leveled to 50 or so, so its repetitive. Less XP than dungeons.
Questing. Its the same exact questing, good and bad of it, as what I wrote earlier in the review. Same "Run to Vietnam and Back" quests, same long kill and collect quests, same of all of it, but you get to hang out in the world, so thats cool. (or not if you don't like this type of thing)
Last thing...the animations.
If you are a fan of Michael Bay movies then you will love how colorful and flashy the combat animations are. But when you see them for hours, and see many people performing variety of flashy animations at the same time, it really starts to hurt your eyes. Like, this alone could probably cause seizures in people that never had these types of issues. My eyes need a rest after a while of seeing combat animations molesting my screen. Its definitely something weird to get used to. You either like it or not.
Also, many people I know who defected from WoW decided to pick this game up, and they kinda started white-knighting it. They aren't big on people criticizing the game, and feel that its perfect, and any quams are the fault of the person having faults with it. Lots of guilt tripping, but maybe thats the types of people I met, and might be the only one here. But with enough of those people you get an idea of what kind of community it creates and harvests.
Overall, if you like convenience and popular MMO practices then this game some that somewhat ok, but if you need some hand-holding and directions then forget about it. OK game, but found so many issues to dislike in today's gaming/mmo market options.

I fail to see the appeal of the game.
There is nothing to master, nothing to learn and nothing to get better at. There are no tactics, no planning, no need for any strategy or quick decision making skills. No cover to hide behind, no creative eliminations, no interesting weapons or unique combinations, also, no useful enemy weakpoints or exploits, it's just run and gun. Enemy variety and moveset is incredibly small and weapons are all variations of three or four weapon types and the only determining factor of a weapon's quality is whether it has more green arrows than the weapon you are currently holding.
You might as well be an AI character, since all you do is run around and shoot everything that moves, until your shield breacks, at which point you run back where you came from and wait a few minutes, until the shield recharges and get back shooting at the same few enemies with gigantic healthbars for hours and hours. Occasionally, there is a special ability, but it's so rare, that its use hardly matters. After the fight, you loot every box for useless garbage and get an okay story bit, which unfortunately doesn't justify the tedious gunplay. All you do is wait for numbers to get bigger. All in all, gameplay feels like something from 2004.
If you like looking at stats like "Your reload speed increased by 0.3%", than I guess this is the game for you. The only other redeeming factor is the coop, but frankly, anything can be fun in coop.

A fantastic game.  I enjoyed everything from the gameplay, aesthetics, to the combat and even the story. You should pick up this game if....
- you like Dark Souls (or souls-like) games
- you like a BIG challenges and learning from your mistakes and can learn to be patient!
- you like single player.... no multi player ;(
- you do not want your hand held. you learn as you go!! you don't get anything spoon fed to you except for the very basics
- you like dystopian futuristic settings
- you like cutting off limbs in brutal fashion, and using said limbs to craft gear for your awesome character
- you don't have hundreds of hours to play videogames (the game is relatively short, but that's a good thing in my book)
You may not like this game if.....
- you are all about story  (i personally like the story, but its one of those things you have to go searching for...and even then it doesn't make the most sense) It's ok, not the best.
- you are looking for a 'chill' game. You HAVE to pay attention in this game or you will Die....A LOT.
- you are looking for multiplayer or PVP.....none here
- you hate dark souls or souls-like games

After 45 hours of gameplay and beating it twice I got to say this game is solid. All doubts I had were gone in less than 10 minutes of gameplay, though. I love the Souls games but, call me crazy, I do like to be able to actually pause the game should I choose--something this game allows you to do.
There's a Souls type of grind with the risk/reward system but at it's core this game doesn't have an extreme Souls feel. Lot brighter, for one.
My biggest issue with games like this are that the developers PURPOSELY make your character probably one of the worst fighters in games. You know what I'm talking about... slow (and I mean SLOW) swings, a stamina gauge that doesn't even help until you're 20 hours into the game, dying in one hit and insanely goofy button-mappings that certainly don't help in combat (I mean, serously, why is B always the healing button?)
But this game fixes a lot of that. Combat is very skill based from the jump and unlike other Souls-type games you won't be literally running away from the first batch of easy enemies once you figure out the mechanics.
All in all I'd recommend this game to anyone--not just fans of this genre.
My only complaint is probably the New Game + options. Most of the difficulty comes from not knowing where to go at first but by the time you push the grind and beat the game you will have been to all the locations more than once and, if you're like me, will have finished the game with a power core level of over 100. Starting a new game with all your cranked stats puts you with a severe advantage over EVERY enemy. Sure they make them harder but it took me over 30 hours to beat the game the first time whereas New Game + took me about 5 hours.
COME ON DLC!!!
Last thing: Could've used ranged weapons of some kind, too. I mean, it's the future, for God's sake. There's no one anywhere who has at least a pistol?
Game's great. Worth the price tag, also.

Ignore my time-record -- I actually have closer to 11 hours on this game, because I played it on console.
There's nothing not to love about this game. The characters, the world, the art, the combat mechanics, and the MUSIC. Everything about it is beautiful and tremendously endearing, from the juvenile names that Red and the Transistor give to the enemy types  (eg. "Jerk"), to the beautiful and tragic story of the man trapped inside of a CPU-turned-sword, wielded by a famous singer who has had her voice stolen. Btw, the ending will make you cry.
The combat is a mix of turn-based and real-time, where you can fight in real-time or use a mechanism to freeze time and plan out your attack, which then is executed in super-speed. It is genuinely challenging because of its uniqueness, especially because if you lose all your health, you lose one of your spells, until eventually you are force to carry on with only a single option of attack (until you reach a checkpoint).
You don't have spells, but "functions" of the Transistor (your weapon). These functions can be used alone, or stacked in such a way that makes one function the Primary and the next a Secondary. The Secondary function changes the way the first function looks and acts. Combining spells to make a new spell, essentially, allowing for limitless attacks and playstyles.
All said and done, this game is my favourite Indie title. It's immensely beautiful, and the atmosphere will pull you in an unforgettable embrace.

I bought maybe 5 or 6 six games at the same time as installing this game.
Guess which is the only one among them I've installed and played till now.
This game is really that addictive.
Some points about the game:
- Probably the best money earning system I've seen in any game. You have to balance your cargo space among trade items and mission items while having enough space to store equipment looted from pirates you have shot down. Being able to loot said equipment requires you to have enough crew members to board pirate ships. Crew members require salary. You can take loans to buy that big freighter, knowing that the extra cargo space will let you pay off that loan quickly.
- Ships are customizable as hell. Each ship has a specific amount of equipment space, weapon capacity and engine capacity. Equipment for the same role may have their own pros and cons, say low cost, high space taken up, high energy output vs high cost, slightly lower energy output but a fraction of the space required etc. The same ship can be outfitted to be primarily a freighter focused on higher cargo space trading off defensive capabilities or it can be turned into a decked out escort ship that will tear apart any hostile that ventures close. And there are a huge number of unique ships.
- Disabled enemy ships can be boarded and taken over. This is a really great way to bolster your fleet or earn money. Bigger ships are more difficult to capture, requiring more crew members as well as specialized equipment, but you can always steal systems from a disabled ship. However these systems take up cargo space on your ship so you need to measure the value to be gained against the value of cargo you may need to discard to make space. (Note that selling value of equipment will depreciate over time)
- The inertial physics mechanic (your ship needs counter thrust to stop its motion) is really interesting and definitely adds to the planning that goes into equipment choice.
- When you think you have optimized your ship(s) to extract the last drop of juice out of the available outfit space, you discover some new equipment that is even more optimized (but may have a tradeoff). Alien equipment mostly always falls under this category.
- Storyline is interesting. Sometimes what you think are sidequests interlock with the main storyline. Storyline is non-intrusive with the regular free gameplay (at least till now for me).
- Easily modifiable!
I have only one complaint: the developers don't have a donation link anywhere I can see. A free game is never this polished. Devs are always adding some new feature or the other. (Removal of death benefits introduced in the recent update has made the game more interesting) I'd gladly pay a few bucks to encourage the devs to keep going! Thank you for the great game and many hours of fun!

I HAVE UPDATED THIS REVIEW AS I HAVE BEEN PLAYING.
This game is fun. I say that first because I want to make it clear that I do enjoy the game play to a point. Why then, you ask am I giving this game a thumbs down? Let's go over the Pros and Cons
PROS
1) Crafting/gathering system is great. Starting with gathering, this game spawns individual gathering points, so looking for materials to gather is not a competition for who can get there first. There are typically multiple items in each spawn and you can choose which one you are after rather than be randomly given whatever might be there. Gathering skills (or jobs) also have their own abilities which do everything from increase your chance to gather (based on %) to giving you extra attempts. The GP (Gathering point or energy level for gathering abilities) is a bit high, but not to the point of the skills being unusable. Crafting is also a skills based job, where you can craft gear by using abilities to enhance progress (toward completion) or increase the likely hood of getting a high quality item. Be sure to watch the item durability, if it hits 0 before you complete the progress bar, you lose the mats and don't get the item.
2) Plenty of spawns for missions. Missions are easily completed because when they do send you out to kill something, there are always plenty of them around. If the mission is for a specific spawn, you will have to activate a location node when you get there for it to appear, that way you're not waiting for hours for a rare spawn to complete a mission. There are also fate missions around the maps that allow anyone to run in and join, and the rewards for these are xp, money, and at a later point, grand company marks which you can use for promotions, and gear or materials.
3) Teleport function. the ability is unlocked early and allows you to easily move over great distances very quickly so getting from one city to another (while costing gil) is as fast as hitting a button and waiting for a loading screen.
CONS
1) Lack of class customization: You can change classes whenever you want (aside from in combat) but doing so does very little for you beyond simply being a different class. All Gladiators are EXACTLY the same (beyond gear and the role abilities of which you get 10 over the levels and can choose 5). This is the same problem with all classes. If you're fine being just another gingerbread man pressed out from the same cookie cutter as all the other gingerbread men, you can disregard this as a con. I like choices as I level, and this game gives you none. To me, this tells me that this is NOT Final Fantasy in any aspect other than name.
2) Story line starts out good, but turns to crap. At about level 30, after you've already done quite a bit, you're told by NPC's that you're an unproven whelp and they will not help you in your story quest unless you prove yourself. I won't say how they tell you to do this, but it is utterly ridiculous. I nearly screamed at my computer screen over the way they were acting.
3) Artificial game lengthening. This is strong in this game. From needing to run back and forth to locations repeatedly when they could have simply told you "Hey, while you're over there grab this for me too." to literally telling you to walk 20 feet that way, talk to that person, then come back and tell me what they said. Also at one point you are given a device that allows you to communicate with a person over long distances, AND IT IS ONLY USED TO TELL YOU TO RUN BACK TO THEM SO THEY CAN TALK TO YOU. The amount of time wasted running to locations in this game is WAY too high. and it is far worse early on given that you are not able to get your first mount until level 20.
4) Huge favoritism toward specific class types: This game has two base glass types, Disciples of War (Gladiator, Marauder, Rogue, Archer, and Lancer) and Disciples of Magic (Conjuror, Thaumaturge, and Arcanist). there are points in the main story line quest where ONLY disciples of war will be given gear rewards, which (unless you put in the time to craft your own gear) leaves disciples of magic with outdated gear. Also as a general rule, drops in dungeons are heavily weighted toward disciples of war as well. The first 6 dungeons I went into, with about four drops in each only dropped a total of 2 items for disciples of magic. Leaving the drop rate in this instance at 8.33% for disciples of magic.
5) Requires groups for main story missions. Yes, they have a program in place that allows you to group with other players for the dungeons, so finding a group isn't as big a pain as it could be. Problem being that if you are a new player, and end up in a group with the guys who have been playing a while who only want to rush through to get the xp, you'll miss a lot. You'll complete the mission, but you'll feel rushed and may miss some loot drops. And on top of this, at times they will not allow you to remain in a group for certain main story quests. It forces you to go in alone against bad odds on multiple occasions.
6) Spam bots: I know this is not the fault of the game, but of greedy people who don't care if they ruin your game. You can't go into a city's market district without seeing at least one spammer yelling about going to their web site and buying gil for real money. They are easy to report, and you can easily blacklist the individual, but they are almost instantly replaced with another one. This could be solved if they remove the free trial system, but that effort would be double edged.
Too long, didn't read: Not Final Fantasy, big cookie cutter, story turns to garbage, but has a great crafting system.

Having played Grand Theft Auto SA, IV, and V, Mafia 2, and Saint's Row 3 all to completion (some multiple times) I have to say that Sleeping Dogs, in my opinion get's the most right, and was the most joyous to play.
The game's premise of an undercover cop going headfirst into the underworld is not an overdone idea - most games of this style just put you in the chair of a street thug and off you go. This allows for not only 'routine' crime-based missions, but a lot of side jobs reminiscint of what was available in L.A. Noire. Bank Robberies, Car Chases, and Hostage Situations all required your attention as a badge-wearing enforcer - when you aren't running drugs or other favors to dig up information on the crime lords.
The visuals and the sound are superb, I don't know Hong Kong Personally, but I feel that this faithfully recreates the famous city with much justice. The only downfall, is that there aren't immersive vehicle interiors - a feature I loved in GTA V.
The focus on martial arts is a refreshing change from 'run to cover, shoot, repeat.' And forces you to use some strategy in your fights - and a staggering 'cooldown' on your attack counter keeps you from spamming the counter button. A variety of melee weapons make appearances, along with the obvious prescence of firearms. The firearms are pretty routine, no-iron sights (yet another feature I miss from GTA), and in my opinion, they could be better. The shotguns are useless beyond 10 feet, the SMGs have intense spread, even in short controlled bursts, and the pistols are seemingly no stronger than your fists, but it all gets the job done.
Sleeping Dogs is a new favorite of mine, and I love the new things it brings to the table.

Fun, old-school dungeon crawl in the style of Eye of the Beholder.  Despite the fact that it gives you options to play on 'Normal' or 'Hard', I'm finding that 'Normal' is quite challenging enough!
For difficult encounters, I suggest kiting. In LoG, that means running away while throwing stuff (including spells). Torches can be thrown if you run out of more pointy things.
Rest often. Food seems to be pretty plentiful, and it seems that actions (like fighting and exploring) make you more hungry than resting.

When we were young we all had a dream girl (or boy, inflatable doll, sheep... I don't judge other people's tastes). Now imagine to meet her at adult age. What effect would you? To me, playfully talking, it happened this year with "Legend of Grimrock". LoG is in fact what I have always wanted to be an old style RPG but that I have never managed to find: brainy puzzles, deadly traps, extremely strong enemies and in clear superiority, tactical combats where the key is not to crush random keys, but the careful study of each move. In short: a dungeon crawler in a pure state, which leaves no stone unturned and capable of bonding to the screen for days with the motto "just another room and then I turn off the computer".

Grimrock: A dungeon-delving exploration game with puzzles and combat (sometimes at the same time!). It features grid-based movement and real-time combat.
The puzzles themselves are difficult enough, and very satisfying to solve.
Combat is sufficiently varied throughout the game, so that it never became boring. A matter of clicking the attack button for each character in your party, or reciting the correct rune pattern for spellcasting.
My one major complaint with the game is the interface. With a lack of hotkeys, (and no auto-attack option) there is far too much clicking in combat for my liking. It becomes very repettive and tedious. Simple hotkeys and/or an attack toggle would be nice.
That aside, It is a great game, and worth the asking price. A-

If you like conquering dungeon crawlers with puzzle elements, then this is for you. If you prefer roguelikes or story-driven RPGs, on the other hand, then you might be disappointed.
It's definitely worth picking up when it goes on sale, which I've seen it do frequently.

Plays like a early final fantasy RPG, I think. One might say that the characters are one dimensional and not illustrated well, that gameplay is grindy and that every area is a freaking maze. CStW certainly gives a bang for your buck; at a mere $3 when not on sale, I can easily recommend it for it's humor (and if you so desire - challenge). You play as Cthulhu, stripped of his dark powers by a mysterious foe. The only way to regain them? Perform great heroic deeds. So begins the misadventures of Cthulhu and his colorful band of misfits you pick up (or groupies as I took to calling them).
The game itself is not demanding on your hardware, as one might expect from a retro RPG.
The combat is fluid, simple, and rewards your choices - on higher difficulties it can be utterly unforgiving, reminiscent of much older games.
And as I’ve said, the game has a great sense of humor about itself. Personally, I found myself compelled to continue playing solely to see what the next joke may be.
Grade: B.
A solid game that will last you anywhere from 5 to 9 hours on the first campaign, with a few extras to boot. Humor and Combat are it's strong points; the plot is a parody more than anything.

A retro-style parody RPG developed by Zeboyd Games, based on a series of cosmic horror novels "Cthulhu Mythos" mainly written by H. P. Lovecraft.
Its blasphemous and unnamable plot (Cthulhu the evil god saves the world!?) implies that the developers' SAN (Sanity Points) is below zero!
With improved engine and graphic, its gameplay is now much smoother and more fun than the previous title.
In addition to previous title's unique and sophisticated systems, this time players can teleport to towns they've ever been whenever they want (even while they're inside dungeon!), and increased casts allow players to form their own party with favorite members.
Finishing the main story unlocks 3 hidden game modes including "Cthulhu's Angels", a remix of the main story with different bosses and dialogues, and playable characters are all female.
it'll take about 13 hours to see the ending of the main story.
Dungeon's too large and complicated as the previous title, which is the only flaw I find.
Now sold as double pack which contains the developer's previous title "Breath of Death VII", get this during Steam sale for less than 1 dollar!
Play this game after you finished the previous title "Breath of Death VII" as there are some surprises for those who've played it.
I'd recommend the 2nd hardest difficulty as the hardest one is too much annoying and others are too easy.

Update: All the negative reviews I read for this game were before the November 14 1.06 update, which fixed a lot of the bugs that these reviewers were discussing. I played the game for the first time after this update had already occurred.
Raiders, space debris, nosy passenger ships, quiet derelict vessels, deadly diseases, and parasites that jump out of an empty husk which used to be one of your citizens. That's what you face when you become the Administrator of Spacebase DF-9. You will truly feel like the manager of a tiny oasis, alone in the vastness of a harsh galaxy.
To get a summary of what it's like to play this game, combine the play styles of a small-scope RTS like Age of Mythology with The Sims. Not only do you have to build, maintain, and defend a space station, but you must also make sure you're tending to the needs of your citizens.
Frustrations abound. Just when you have finally constructed a small, functional base, complete with power and air, your citizens will have the gall to ask for a place to sleep. Then, they'll want something to eat. Then they'll need a doctor. Then they'll want someplace to hang out with friends. Then your base needs a maintenance technician, but no one wants the job. Now they want a gym, but you're still trying to build the infirmary because two citizens died in the last Raider attack. But now there aren't enough power reactors! So you've zoned the construction to build a bigger power room, but then some Raider blew holes in your airlock in a firefight and now the whole thing is useless. But hey, at least he suffocated. Pompous jerk. Anyway, you've got to refit another room as an emergency airlock, to fix the airlock, so you can build the next reactor, to build the infirmary, and then ultimately build a gym, but darn it all, your Builder's feeling overworked so they went to bed! And NO, I do NOT want to answer your request to come aboard, random passenger ship!
In many ways, I find this game to be a very realistic depiction of what it would probably be like to lead your own vessel out in space. You have to fight constantly against the threatening, invasive, hostile environment, while not letting your crew's own loneliness overcome them. Think about it. Suppose you were one of your citizens: one of a group of ten people stranded out in, truly, the middle of nowhere, with no chance of ever seeing Earth again. No wonder my overworked builder is having trouble staying motivated, and no wonder most of my crew spends their free time in the pub. We all might want to think that living in space would be cool, but Spacebase DF-9 reminds us of the human element.
Yes, there are still minor graphical bugs, and sometimes your Miner will asphyxiate because they were too stupid to get back inside before their eight minutes of oxygen was up. However, no technical glitch any worse than this has happened to me in the time I've been playing; most of the frustrations are caused by realistic depiction of the situation. But like in Kerbal Space Program or any other pleasantly challenging game, when you overcome the trials of the moment, you will feel an immense sense of reward watching your citizens live the lives you have given them among the stars.

While I do agree with the negative reviews in that the execution of the ideas that could have resulted (and still can result) in a gem of a game is mediocre at best, I still cautiously recommend it.
Below, I list the bad and the good aspects of the game based on my very short experience playing it (one hour is normally enough for me to make my decision, but I leave it up to you to decide whether it is enough to trust my review).
The bad:
- The AI of your colonists is not the best, but is getting better.
- The game becomes repetitive really soon (for me, it has after the first hour playing it)--there is just no hierarchy, almost no gradual development (save the research), and frankly not much to do as of now.
- There is no balance. I am pretty sure the developers got their inspiration in the Dwarf Fortress (where "dying in fun" TM), but I am able to play a game of Dwarf Fortress for days, but here my colonists die horribly within 15-20 minutes (raiders, fire or what not).
The good:
- The graphics are pretty good. I liked them a lot.
- The atmosphere of the game is its best selling point, IMO. Save the frustration of loosing each game I play pretty quickly, I like how the game feels. The colonists have their own characters, interact with each other and the environment, make friends and enemies--and all of this creates a feeling of a growing community in space, which is unfortunately quickly sent to oblivion, heh (see the balance).
- Enabling the support of mods is the best of the developers' decisions, which I think has the potential to save this game. There are mods already that address the balancing issues, and I am sure there will be mods fixing the AI, adding more things to do, and generally, adding depth to the game.
Despite all the drawbacks of the game, I still recommend it for one particular reason: it (still) has an enormous potential to grow into a fantastic game.
I understand the reasons for the negative reviews, but I also know that these reviews can eventually bring the development of the game to a halt. And this would be the most unfortunate turn of events, as the game, as I said, has the potential to become a fantastic game that offers its players countless hours of fun (and not frustration as it is now =) playing experience.
As for now, the price of the game is somewhat high for what it offers, so I suggest you buy this game on sale, and try it (with mods). I also hope more mods will be made for the game to enhance/improve it.

However, I can't even get started on the soundtrack. It holds up against people who devote their careers to music, and I find myself listening to "We All Become" and "Paper Boats" over and over again. Just the Hummed versions of the normal music is just amazing.

I'm currently over 80 hours into playing Endless Sky. I have loved this game all the way through, but I never wrote a review for it until now. And now, I can really sum up how I feel about this entire game.
I greatly recommend Endless Sky. I remember launching it for the first time early last year; I don't remember how I found it, but I think it was searching through every single game with the tag "space simulator." This little game stood out to me: a self-made RPG space sim that had just come out, still with many bugs and unfinished work, but definitely containing a whole world of hard work and creativity.
From the first moment of "why can't I get off this dang screen and how do I move" (And learning the hard way not to choose the Sparrow as your first ship) to the mid moments of "wow, that Sheild Beetle took way too long to get, I should name that ship TookMeWayTooLongToGetThis" to the more recent moments of "AAAAAAA NEW ALIENS HECK YES", this game has been a rollercoaster of cliffhangers, suspence, adventure, and excitement, along with the obvious confusion here and there.
Many say that the game is simply long, agonizing stretches of trading, but you don't need to get money that way. Just remember all the paths you can take in this game, like combat or solo exploring, in addition to the numerous story lines. There is so much in-game lore that I melt whenever I find it, and indeed, it is quite hard to find, but it is numerous.
I'm currently leading a fleet of 6 Summer Leaves (Leafs?) and I can take out anything in human space, but obviously, I'm nowhere near finished yet. I know what you're thinking: ">80 hours and you haven't beaten the game yet??" Well, I tend to do that with games, and I've found that with this one, it is so rewarding to travel the timeline and to find every little adventure that you can.
I know this game has a lot more distance to go, and that's part of the reason I'm still so excited. This little bitty 40 MB game (probably more now, but that was what it was when I first downloaded it) has so much to offer and so much to look forwards to. Honestly, the feeling of it being such a small game is one of the things that makes it so great for me; It isn't popular by any standards, and the feeling that I could be one of the few people seeing a certain bit of lore so far makes my heartbeat rise tremendously. I know it won't be the game for everyone, but I know many who adore this game since I've shown it to them, and I think that the makers are really onto something here.

Graphics- Actually very good, only a handful of MMO's can compete.
Audio - Equally good, the OST provides the right oomph at the right times and usually does well at setting the mood.  Though some tracks can get a little repetitive.
Gameplay - Standard MMO faire, though due to the prevelance of enemy AOE attacks, usually telegraphed through zones on the ground, encourages movement and proper positioning in fights even in dungeons.
Story - An in-depth and engrossing story pretty in line with the single player Final Fantasy games in terms of general content and quality, and everything that entails.  If you're a fan of final fantasy, you're definitely going to like the story here, especially some of the more mature themes in it.  If you're testing the waters, it's a good place to start as it's self contained and good quality, mostly doled out in bite-sized chunks so it's easy to process for a casual player.

So, due a bug in the steam store/wallet's conversion rates Brazilian and Russian users were getting a vastly discounted paymention option than everywhere else in the world.  This was wildly abused to mass-purchase microtransactions and to set up bot accounts, along with simply being taken advantage of for a subscription for standard play.  In all, the actual users of this accounted for a fairly small portion of the playerbase.  Square Enix recently realized this and corrected the conversion rates to account for the economic value of the Ruble and the Real.  This, of course, caused the overall price to raise up and match everyone else due to the poor economy of these countries and needing to pay more to match the standard.
THAT is due to there being no official servers for Brazil and Russia, so most of those players ended up playing on US and UK servers respectively.  Which meant their currency was being converted to USD and Euro, and both are matched lower then those and thus had to pay more to even it out.  The ones who were taking advantage of the huge discount until this bug was fixed came to complain.  I specify those because any who had accounts and subscriptions via the Mogstation were always paying the correct conversion rates.
The only thing wrong Square Enix remotely did was not have enough transparency to explain this in an announcement, to my knowledge.  But then again, it's the equivilant of patching a bug so I wouldn't say it's entirely required and it's also on the fault of Steam and it's buggy conversion rate calculator to begin with.  These reviews should instead be sent as direct feedback to Square Enix instead of being spammed on the steam store, where it's a malicious attempt to misguide newcomers.
I also saw some complaints about how heavensward is bundled now and how you should feel ripped off if you purchased heavensward previously.  I don't see the problem, considering the amount of content you got for heavensward and the continued support and regularly added content.  Where most games stagnant and don't add future content until an expansion, FFXIV instead continues to provide more content even late into an expansion's life, similar to WoW's modern model.  So you're basically getting so much content you're paying for a full fledged game, it being bundled later on is just an ease of use thing for newcomers.

Update: It's been a few months since I wrote my first review on this game, I am adding this at the start while not changing my original review. My opinion has not changed much since I wrote my first review, but what bit it did change was simply to like the game more. I now have 355 hours on Steam, and over 20 days of total playtime, and I have now advanced to Stormblood content. My opinion is that the game is amazing for ARR content, mediocre and repetitive between ARR and Heavensward, and Heavensward and onward are all as good if not better than ARR in my personal opinion. My rating has gone up to a 95/100, mostly because I have advanced story to be able to get to Stormblood content, and I quite enjoy it, but I cannot give it any better of a rating because of the content between ARR and Heavensward.
A few things before I start. My opinion is based mostly on pre-Stormblood content. Steam says I have 59 hours, but my actual playtime is far more than that, I played on PS3 before support was dicontinued. If you do not like MMORPGs, you might still enjoy this, it depends on you.
Let's look at what makes the game possibly my favourite game to play. The game has beautiful visuals even with lower graphical settings. Controller support if that's your thing. Great community, even with the occasional bad egg. Fun mechanics, numerous classes/jobs, the ability to play any and every job/class on a single character. Multi-platform+cross-platform play is supported. Catgirls. Dragon girls. Elf girls. Bard.
Now let's look at some negatives. Long DPS queues. Squeenix not giving prior notice to price changes. People complaining about it being too hard, even though story content is typically pretty easy.
My conclusion is that this game deserves about a 94/100. I am no games critic, but I have played too many games for me to count, so I know a good game when I see one. Bard best job.

Extreme humor and no 4th wall to speak of, Cthulhu Saves The World, along with Breath Of Death VII, are some of the most FUN RPGs available on Steam right now. I mean it. Cthulhu, the embodiement of evil, rises from the sea after aeons of slumber to finally destroy the world... only to find out someone was already expecting him, and loses all of his mythical powers. He wants to destroy the world, but to do it, he must first recover his powers... by saving the world!
Aesthetics of old, with a modern twist. Story is as great as it's absurd, it manages to improve on the classic gameplay. You'll really wish they had these simple - yet effective - features back then: they managed to COMPLEMENT the experience without disrupting it, not even a tiny bit. Oh, this also applies to Breath of Death VII.
Comes with a bonus campaign (unlocked after you finish the normal game) with an entirely different take on the original story, "Cthulhu's Angels": what happens when the main character already knows the story (since you finished the game with him) and is just too lazy to go through it again? Everything derails into a fight for control over their own DESTINY.
Definitely recommend. But play Breath Of Death VII first.

The first impression of Sleeping Dogs is great. The city of Hong Kong is a new and exotic setting not often featured in games. Crowd density is impressive, and it is exciting to dive into the world of the Chinese triads. However, very soon all this is revealed to be a thin façade masking a lacking experience.
The city is a hollow husk and nowhere near of being a living, breathing place. The people forming the crowds just are there, doing nothing but walking and driving from nowhere to nowhere, existing only to briefly react to the player character if one gets too close to them. The city is large enough, but has only a few types of different activities, and nothing to discover - almost everything is clearly marked on a map where a destination can be selected to get a guiding HUD to follow. There are some random events that spontaneously occur when traveling around the city, but these are few and far between, and so structured and gamified that they fail to improve the immersion of the game world. Instead of stumbling upon a drunk person causing trouble to shop keeper by happenstance, you get displayed a yellow exclamation point, and a notification telling you to drag the drunk patron away, and a warning message if you wander too far away from the event. When the exact same event then occurs a few other times, it becomes clear it's not the city being a place with people living in it, but the game being a game packed with busywork.
The gameplay is divided into a few distinct types of activities. There's beating people up, driving fast, shooting or occasionally driving while shooting. The activities are compartmentalised into missions so that different things to do aren't mixed up with one another. The player is able to pick what they like and focus on missions they find entertaining. Missions are picked from a map screen, that displays what and where is currently available, differentiating between different types of missions. After selecting a mission, completing it is a matter of traveling to the location and performing the given strictly defined activity. Then it's a time to pick another mission, possibly after viewing a cutscene that thrusts the story forward. This fundamental structure makes the game feel like a checklist of chores - open the map screen, pick what you want to do next, and go do it. There's not much else to the game. The clear division of missions into different types of activities makes the missions predictable and repetitive. There are too few surprises and dynamically evolving scenarios.
The game is made competently enough, the setting is interesting, the controls adequate, all the basic construction blocks are in place for a good game to be built from them - only the shooting is numb and could use some work. The problem is that after getting used to and gaining understanding of the mission structure, the game is very monotonous and feels more like a chore than entertainment. It's not outright bad, and could perhaps pass for a mindless activity to kill time, but it's a tough sell when there are so many actually good games one can spend the time on instead.
