It's a Sci-Fi dark souls that fails in combining it's multiple aspects well. I wouldn't recomment buying it unless you're a huge souls fan. If not then get it on sale. 50 dollars is honestly too much for this game.
There are multiple good parts of this game that i'll list.
-Good graphics and well optimized
-Large array of menu options
-First area was amazing
-Combat mechanics are amazing on their own that could have an entire review writen about them
-You can cut off enemy body parts in an execution and use it yourself
-Has a lot of unique ideas, most notable ones being the implant system that works as your stats and items with some increasing health and some giving you an extra heal, and how the enemies are more like minibosses with only 5 bosses in the game (although i've heard 1 is repeated)
-Probably a few more small ones that i've missed
Cons on the otherhand
-The game gets worse area after area. The first one was amazing but afterwards it got too cramped and maze-like
-The combat mechanics that are amazing are hardly ever used properly by anything in this game
-You feel stagnant compared to how fast the enemies progress
-The very similar levels along with a massive amount of back tracking and confusing cramped layouts and shortcuts in these decently small areas makes it boring and tedious to go through and sometimes gives you a feeling of no real progression
-The enemeis go from fun to fight yet still being difficult. to just leaping out at you, all easily taking out a good chunk of your health with no issues (I am using full heavy armor with 2 health upgrades and 6 different heals) taking the miniboss aspect to an obnoxious level when added with the other features in this game
-One example of a shortcut in the 3rd level that really made me decide how I felt about the game was one where not only is it hard to reach, but on both sides of you there are enemeis waiting to gank you, the direction you want to go in has 2-3, the other direction has 1 enemy but you have to fight like 2 more enemies, and you don't really avoid fighting multiple enemies either. This shortcut is also surrounded by poison. Some of the enemies that gank you are very difficult to fight alone, with hardly any openings as their constant jump attacks go too far to attack them afterwards and attacking them when they face you, no matter what, will hurt you as they jump back to do their follow up which is the forwards leap that's difficult to punish and sometimes hard to just dodge. It's a terrible level
-Executions used to steal enemy parts are an animation that moves you around. So if you're attacking an enemy next to a hole in the ground or a cliff, you have a good chance of falling. Not to mention that there are multiple examples of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t holes in the ground.
-The weapon progression system doesn't encourage using multiple weapon types with your damage in certain weapon types going up the more you use the specific weapon, this makes weapon types you never use early on way too difficult to ever use later on.
-Other smaller issues I probably missed
Overall this game isn't bad. But it definitely isn't good. It has too many issues with it's level design to it's enemies. All of these issues ruin the otherwise great game that could of been made. I'd love a sequel to this game honestly, one that delivers a better story with better voice actors with better level design and more variety in how it's played. It felt too difficult with the best (and arguably only) way to progress is by running through levels. If you get good enough you can kill every enemy but, just run though. You'll be weaker, but you will also enjoy it more. ♥♥♥♥ the enemies in this game. They ruin it along with the level design. You really cannot trust a general review of this game, aka most of the positive ones. It's a good idea on paper that was poorly executed and most of them talk how it looks like on paper. Like they never really played it. It almost feels like payed reviews with how simple and optimistic they are. Do what you want but be warned about how little the good reviews mean about the issues of this game. As the issues cancel out a lot of the good parts.

Hi everyone, here it is my quick review of good and bad points of this game.
First of all you have to know i've played all dark souls (a lot of hours) and also played LoTF (only 1 time, the game was bad imo, to slow...)
Good points of the Surge :
+ Environments (area's are beautifull and according well with the universe, you really feel the industry robotic atmosphere all the time)
+ Executions sytem (you can finish enemies with an execution when they are low hp, and those executions are cool and violent)
+ Looting/upgrading system (you can dismember your opponents by executions and loot the part you need to upgrade your gear. You got 7 parts of armor that you can upgrade while killing ennemies)
+ Money/souls system (you earn "souls" each time you kill an enemy or exploring the world. You can upgrade your level (core) while spending souls at 'bonfire' (safe zone here).
+ Respawning mobs (they only respawn when you go again in safe zone so you can farm some items and souls if needed)
+ Quick fight (each fight is pretty quick and your character is fast when he move/dodge)
+ You can choose to attack diffrents parts of the ennemies (non armored = ennemy die quickly but you will not loot item, armored = ennemy more resistant but you can loot and upgrade your gear :))
And now the cons :
- Combat sytem is a little to simple. Only vertical and horizontal attack, block is useless so you will spend all your time to dodge
- Music are not that much good
- Sometimes the camera is pretty obvious, especially when there is lot of ennemies/big ennemies
- The lock system is slow and not really optimized (you need to push R then push LT and switch with your pad yo switch ennemy..While dodging /moving camera it becomes hard to do all things at a time)
- Upgrade system is decent but you cant spend "points" in vitality, stamina, dmg etc...Only your core lvl change all of this. Upgrading armor/weapons is also decent but not efficient as it needs to be imo.
- no coop ? :D
So globally The Surge is a very good game. The unique futurist style of this game make him good and the "dark souls like" is still present. A great game for player that likes difficulty. I will do the game 3 times i think.
PS : the game is not that hard (DS is harded imo)

A few days into the game and I got the top tier shuttle (Star Queen).
This game is actually very unique and engaging, you take the role of a merchant trying to pay off a loan from the bank. But your story could go anywhere. I'm currently helping a rebellion make public terraformers. This is a fun game about money and fuel management. You want to make sire that all of your ships in your fleet can make the same amount of jumps. Run out of fuel? You are gonna have to wait for one of the AI ships to help. Pirates are hilariously OP, however landing on a planet will make them leave. I especially love that you can make a huge fleet out of the ships you buy, and they are all customizeable. Below are some tips to getting that CA$H:
Make sure ALL of your ships can do 5-6 jumps.
Only do the highest paying jobs and Large Rush Deliveries. While risky, these usually give you tons of money.
Click on spaceport every time you land on a planet. Sometimes you can get an extra job, these pay handsomely. If you decline you can't do them ever again so don't.
NEVER run out of fuel in an abandoned system. You'll have to reload a save or wait for the AI.
Buy the local star maps from outer planets if you haven't already. They automatically explore about 12 more planets, saving you time.
Buy lots of freighters and shuttles, but also get protection. I have a fleet of two freighters and a shuttle, which I defend using two fighters. They all can do about 5 jumps.
And that's it! Also, you will unlock more ships and quests by playing. What you see is sometimes not all that you get!
Have fun!

In Plague Inc., you are literally a disease. Control your spreading, evolve your symptoms, evade the research for a cure and exterminate or subjugate the whole population on Earth through a world map interface.
PROS
+The mechanics are rather interesting: you are tasked with leading a plague to infect the whole world (and generally kill all mankind in some gruesome way), you choose your starting point and then use points to buy "perks" that adapt your plague to various biomes and situations (i.e. giving it more resilience to medications or allowing birds or else to spread it), develop various symptoms and resist to the inevitable research for a cure that will eventually start. It's cool, and well thought out.
+There are multiple plagues that require different playstyles. Some are generic, some mutate on their own or travel slowly, others require being very fast in order not to accidentally kill all the infected before going worldwide, and so on. Necroa virus and the Planet of the Apes plague are particularly awesome and different from the standard plague, but Neurax Worm is also fun because of its double ending.
+Achievement hunt is fun and satisfying, though it may require a guide to unlock some rather random events that lead to an achievement. Completing the plagues at the highest difficulty available is also a great challenge that increase the title's longevity for whoever likes its gameplay.
+Workshop community is active enough and brings to the table many new interesting plague scenarios that further improve this game's appeal and variety.
+Interface is simple but clean and enjoyable to look at.
CONS
-It can become rather repetitive after some time. After all, it's one mechanic, a brilliant one sure, but one only. Once you get used to infect the world and develop symptoms and other thingies, doing it again and again can get exhausting, also because a single playthrough may take quite some time to kick in. As said before, higher difficulty levels and custom scenarios by both developers and steam modders increase this game's longevity, but only to a certain extent for non-hyperfans.
-At some moments, it can be rather boring to play, especially in earlier stages when you slowly start infecting some people and gain points veeeeeeeery slowly. Sometimes i just stared at the screen doing nothing for like 45 seconds, which may not seem much but when there's nothing interesting going on there it's quite some time.
-Once the plague has been discovered and a cure research has started, mostly all the (expensive, point-speaking) things that a plague can do to defend itself are either lackluster (like barely reducing the research completion percentage) or seemingly completely worthless. It's rather frustrating when you invest some precious early points to "slow down future research", and then it still goes lightning-fast (like 1% per second, which is a lot, trust me) when it fully cranks up. Stealth playthroughs, in which you first infect the whole world then develop all the deadliest symptoms at once, are the more viable option, but they're also slow, boring and somewhat unrealistic (seriously, it doesn't matter if it has barely any symptoms, if something infects the whole world a cure should start ANYWAY).
Plague Inc. is an atypical "strategy" game (it was born on cellphones, for the record) with simple but addicting mechanics and a good amount of gameplay variations, as much as its limited interface and its unique but one-dimensional playstyle allow. If you like what this game has to offer you'll play it for quite a while.

AHHHHHHHHH

In addition to all of this, Transistor tells a touching and rather heartbreaking story that I won't ruin here as that would be a disservice to anyone that plans to pick up this masterpiece and play it for themselves. All I will say is I've never empathized so strongly with a sword before.
Transistor is well worth the full price being asked of it and if it's ever on sale, you have no excuse for not playing such a memorable and gorgeous game. You won't regret it.

The Surge is a
action RPG that focuses on
dodging every enemy attack possible and
slowly fighting them one at a time. The level design in this game is
rather repeditive and by repeditive i mean they re-use the same level literally 3 times over and just change the enemy placement/loot locations. Ontop of this as you progress further and further into the level it becomes more evident that instead of creating challenging enemies the developers instead just made them unfair. Enemies can, for example be in the same gear as you, with the same weapon, and 2  or 1 hit you. Enemies later on in the game just outright end your existance before you can even get an attack off.
Character progression is another area in which The Surge fails. Unlike a true souls like game dying while holding a heap of 'scrap' doesn't really matter that much since your core power doesn't equate to anything other than slightly more health/stamina or more injectables. Not to mention you can just bank it if you don't currently have anything to upgrade. All your characters power will come from his gear and his proficiency with your preffered weapon type. Which is a huge game design flaw since it forces you to stick with a single weapon type throughout your gameplay. So good luck when you kill that boss you have been trying to kill for the past 2 hours and get a weapon that is drastically worse than the one you got from the starting zone. All because you never used staves.
Most of the issues with this game could be adressed with balance changes, and bug fixes. The developers could give players a reason to upgrade their core level outside of what doing so already offers. Like better scaling on injectables, base weapon damage increases, and perhaps armor increases. They could also balance some of the later game enemies and completly remove the proficiency scaling and just bake those stat increases into upgrading core power level.
In its current state I would say don't purchase this game. You will be better off waiting for the developers to patch and balance their game. Then pick it up in a sale.
For speedrunning (which is what I personally spent most of my time doing in this game) it isn't a bad game to try. This is mainly based on my experience with the un-patched version of the game where the devs left in some tools you can abuse to get strange things to happen. Simple tech that is easy to learn/use makes it a beginner friendly speedrun game.

Loved this game from start to finish. Being a fan of all four Souls games, I felt right at home with the fast and difficult combat. Gear and implant progression is simple, but satisfying. And with no stats to worry about, you can change your playstyle relatively simply.
I see a lot of reviews complaining that the game becomes "unfair" towards the end, and I can honestly say they're absolutely full of it. I hate to be the guy to say they need to "git gud".. but it's true. I recall three points in the game were I thought it was becoming too difficult to continue. But rather than quit and write a negative review, I took another look at my gear and implants. Each time I modified my playstyle to be a little better, my loadout to be a little more cohesive. The end result was my character could tear through opposition, with some careful planning and tactics.
All that being said, there are a few cons. The story, while mildly engaging, wasn't ground breaking. Some dialogue is downright bad. There's also a quirk where you can't cancel an attack combo, which can be very frustrating in the wrong situation. (my weapon launches into a 3 hit, 3 second long combo after tapping the mouse button twice, if something goes wrong mid combo I was basically dead with no way to react) Also there's some crystal enemies towards the end, which are beatable, but arent fun to fight (with very little pay off in regards to tech scrap gained) There are only about 5 bosses, and no online play.
All that being said, fantastic game.

I'm a huge fan of the "Souls" games. I've played them all. I really liked Lords of the Fallen, and I was so looking forward to The Surge. But I am so unbelievable disappointed in this game. I am to the third area, but have stopped playing. And here's why.
1. No purpose in life: "Souls" games aren't heavy on clear stories, but The Surge has taken vagueness to a whole new level. You're an employee of a company where something has went wrong. Then a hologram tells you to go into the factory. That's the story so far threw 2 areas. You'll have no idea of why you're doing what you're doing, where you're going, or why you should even go there if you did.
2. The body part targting system: Great in theory, but horrible in practice. We you have two or more enemies on you, you don't have time to target a specifc spot. You just want them gone. But you have to fiddle around with targeting while just tring to survive.
3. Some enemy attacks just can't be dodged. There are these four legged machines (don't know what they are called) that have an attack that just can't be dodged (at least I haven't figured out how). They leap from some ways away, but no matter when or how far you move, you can't get out of their way. This wouldn't be so bad if it didn't cause massive amounts of damage, and the fact that they can take a beating. So you'll get in close, then jump back to dodge a close attack. Then here comes the leap.
4. Attacking: This is another thing that is great in theory, but horrible in practice. You can either choose to attack slowly vertically or horizontally. That's it. Even the fast attack weapons are quite slow compaired to other games. The light/heavy attack offence wasn't broken, so why replace it with something subpar Deck 13?
I wanted so desperatly to like this game because I was craving a new "Souls" game. But Deck 13 missed the mark with this one. I hope some of the things are resolved with patches, but the fundementals of the game are just flawed.

Like a polished sci-fi Lords of the Fallen, The Surge surprised me to no end by being fun and relatively bug free. It has a few quirks, sure, and a few leftover mechanics from LotF that made a comeback, but overall I can actually recommend this game without sarcasm. Good job, Deck13.

This gem revisits the classic Dungeon Crawl made famous by games such as Wizardry. With great 3D graphics, an indescribable ambience and plenty of mind-bending puzzles, this is a must for any low fantasy fans.

A nod back to the earlier days of dungeon RPGs, this game will have you thinking of Captive and Lands of Lore.
The developers have added some fresh ideas in here, like the spell casting, which is done by combining 9 different "elements" (laid out in a numpad style) in a specific pattern, all by memory (or cheating with pen and paper).
Thoroughly recommended for those who are nostalgic for those old school dungeon crawlers

Legend of Grimrock is an classic dungeon crawl RPG. If you have played and liked "Eye of the Beholder", "Lands of Lore", or anything of the sort, Grimrock is for you - be prepared to lose a few teeth on its challenges!
Fantastic blend of combat and puzzles in an old-fashioned first-person perspective. It reminded me a lot of Stonekeep to play through, which as far as I'm concerned is extremely high praise.

A throwback to the oldest-of-schools of dungeon crawling, Grimrock is a solid game full of secrets, tricks, traps, and rewarding gameplay if you want to solve puzzles, hack skeletons into bony dust, and loot the treasures of a mountain dungeon from the top down.
Here is an easy way to tell if you'll like this: do you long for something akin to Eye of the Beholder or Dungeon Master randomly? This'll be the game you want to scratch that itch! "Old-School Mode" (where the automap is turned off and you have to make your own with graph paper) is included and delicious.

Transistor has a deep and genuinely fun combat system that allows you to rip through battles at breakneck speeds or take your time and plan out every attack. The shear variety of abilities available to you because of it's combination system is almost overwhelming. With the addition of a New Game+ option, the game is near infinitely replayable.
In addition to all of this, Transistor tells a touching and rather heartbreaking story that I won't ruin here as that would be a disservice to anyone that plans to pick up this masterpiece and play it for themselves. All I will say is I've never empathized so strongly with a sword before.
Transistor is well worth the full price being asked of it and if it's ever on sale, you have no excuse for not playing such a memorable and gorgeous game. You won't regret it.

Not a bad souls-like, I haven't beaten the game yet but all I'll say is, this game is way better than Lords of the Fallen if you're looking at how non-FromSoftware souls games turn out. The game is a sci-fi Bloodborne with good combat, great juking and a reinvented targeting system.
What I liked:
-Great new enviroment
-Innovative way to get items
-"That" reveal
-Bosses are fun and feel like the good ol' days
-Shortcuts Dark Souls could be proud of
What I don't like:
-Hits still don't have that feel to it
-Most weapons are boring to use
-Enemies get repetitive
TL;DR: Buy it if you want to have a fun souls-like experience and you're ready for a challenge. The only problem that might be a turn off to you, if you enjoy Souls-Like games, is I don't feel it when I hit people in this game like i did in any Souls game.

Honestly, this game has no right being as good as it is. There are quite a few faults, as it's not perfect, of course, but it's a really great attempt at taking the Souls/BB formula and adding on to it while taking it to a SciFi setting. Combat is faster than Bloodborne, believe it or not, and there are actually way more animations and combos per weapon than in any of the Souls games. The animations are mostly fluid and some weapons are ridiculously awesome. There are plenty of new mechanics to make it stand out, such as cutting off body parts of enemies for weapons and armor pieces, and how the more tech scrap (this games version of souls/blood echoes) you carry around the higher a multiplier you get to earn more from kills. I've only fought two bosses so far but damn they were good fights that were completely different from each other and really required me to put some thought into them.
I know that the devs made Lords of the Fallen, which I never played because I heard mostly bad things, but this game is definitely up to par with FROM's games in my book. I can't recommend this more as this is the kind of design that I want to encourage.

To me this game is really amazingly fun.
This game is genre-wise compared to the Dark Souls series and indeed this game gives me the same awesome feeling of wonder, achievement and progress as the Souls series did. Only this time its set in a very cool sci-fi setting which I was not sure about if I'd like it at first. But turns out the setting fits the game and it's style very well.
I loved the feeling of being in this gigantic, seemingly endless industrial complex with all the deadly enemies around. You can find side characters with little side quest if you look for them, else you can completely miss them. A great way to encourage you to explore, despite the risks and dangers that come with it. Along with that there are many shortcuts and secrets to find.
The combat worked really well too. The combat system offers five different types of weapons which play very different. Along with that you have the facette of being able to target specific body parts of most enemies, either to do more damage by targeting unarmored parts or the head, or to damage a certain part of the enemy and cut it of and salvage it for yourself. IMO this added a nice tactical component to the game.
By the time I write this review I already played through the game and instantly started a NG+ run. They even place new special enemies throughout NG+, of which some carry new weapons.
When I first played the first Dark Souls game (which was about on and a half year ago) I was so amazed by how the game plays and how different it was to other games I played until that point. After I blasted through it I immediately bought the second one, devoured it and when I got my hands on the third Dark Souls I played through it three times in a row. The Surge gives me the same feeling of amazement but it sets itself apart enough with its setting and its added mechanics to be more than a blant clone. It does stand very well on itself and I probably like it at least as much as the Souls games.
The sound design is very well done too, with a mostly subtle soundtrack which lets you hear the mad and distorted sounds of the enemies, but increases in intensety from time to time when it suits the situation.
The graphics and especially animations leave less to be desired; light and shadow play really well together in The Surge to create a great atmosphere.
By this point you can probably tell I recommend the game...
The Surge ofcourse too, got some minor flaws of which for me the most noticeable was a certain level where I just thought the enemies where not that interesting. Allthough by the end of the level a new type was introduced which was far more interesting and the enviroment in that level (flammable gas, I died a thousand deaths) offered a lot of extra challenge (for clunky me at least).

I've never played any "old school dungeon crawlers", but that didn't stop me from enjoying this game. The combat system is unique to say the least. But it's satisfying when you finally get the hang of it. The idea is there are 4 of you, and maybe a couple dozen of them per level. But there are a finite number of hostiles per level, so you can easilly kill all the mobs then solve the puzzles. Rather than be forced to solve them under pressure. Puzzles, secrets, fantastic rpg, I heartilly reccomend it.

A healthy, refreshing dose of challenge, intrigue, puzzles, clever combat tactics, and a reminder of where good dungeon crawlers were born.  There's something curiously, immensely satisfying about finding a secret, or figuring out how to crack open the lucrative iron door'd treasure rooms, or deciphering a cryptic riddle scroll.  The combat seems simpistic and uninventive at first blush, but the game never backs down in throwing a difficult fight at you, forcing you to think and act on your toes.  To top it all off, it wraps you in the black of a dark dungeon with noises and cryptic scrawls on walls to keep the tensions thick.
Overall, what seems like a callback to an oldschool genre and style of gaming pulls through with enough modern twists and applications that it stands on its own as not only a classic, but a great modern gaming experience.  Just don't expect Grimrock to play nice or hold your hand, because it'd rather kill you and leave you blind in the dark first.

When I started Grimrock, I was expecting a simple dungeon crawler with good graphics. This game ended up being so much more than that. This game has incredible puzzles requiring speed, wit, cunning, and an attention to detail. The battles are a constant struggle between life and death, and require fancy footwork to survive. The pacing and discovery are superb. The story is told through items, scrolls, and dreams, and immerses you in the mystery of Grimrock.
I never thought I'd be able to fall back in love with such an old-school concept as a 3D dungeon crawler, but Grimrock not only does everything right, but does it with so many surprises that you'll constantly enjoy your adventure into the unknown.

The title implies three things about this game: That it is legendary, that it is grim, and that there may possibly be rocks in it somewhere.  On these 3 implications, it does not disappoint.
LOG is a 1st-person ARPG, in which the player controls 4 adventurers accused of crimes and sentenced to trial by giant, mountain-dungeon. They are flung hell for breakfast into the dungeon, and must escape.
The game is an homage to old dungeon crawlers of yore, and has some game design to intentionally reflect this, you can only move in one of the cardinal directions at any given time, and a lot of combat is frantically strafing out of opponent's attacks while fumbling with the spell system or attempting to drink a potion.
While the intentional complications can be irritating at times, the game is still quite enjoyable, brimming with traps, secrets, and monsters.
If you like a good old fashioned dungeon crawl, LOG is the game for you.

[Spoiler-Free Review]
The spiritual successor to Breath of Death VII, Cthulhu Saves the World turns it's parodial focus to Lovecraft's ultimate evil-doer and dares you to pull it's finger.
In addition to the much improved engine which brings the series more in line with it's 16-bit forefathers (bridges are now beautifully rendered), Cthulhu features a fleshed out campaign with an all-new cast of characters and plenty of post game bonus content for completionists everywhere. There's even a second quest with an all-new storyline once you've completed the first.
I'll admit I'm not very well-versed in Cthulhuian lore and felt the humour was a bit too forced and goofy at times as a result. Where Breath of Death was sharp and witty, Cthulhu was brazen, outlandish and downright silly. Like a teenager trying to impress his friends with useless and mundane "skills".
The music is still unconventionally memorable (hard rock cave music?) and nods to Zeboyd's history are strewn throughout the game. As with the first game, the optional developer's commentary is enlightening and entertaining and fits perfectly within a game unafraid to break the fourth wall.
Cthulhu Saves the World is a bit of an enigma however, while I enjoyed it less than Breath of Death VII, I'm willing to admit it's probably more to do with my lack of understanding of the source material. I ended up playing this game nearly two times longer than I did Breath of Death VII and enjoyed most of it. Chances are if you've played the first game, you'll want to help Cthulhu Save the World too.

As the obvious direct spiritual successor to Breath of Death VII, this is what you'd expect -- another old console JRPG-style game that's still more a parody than anything, but this one's a touch more serious, at least design-wise.  The graphics, especially in-battle, have been upped from feeling like a late NES game to an early SNES game, the music is a touch higher in quality, the gameplay is made slightly more interesting with the Insanity system (basically a way to make enemies die faster but also hurt you more), more characters to choose from, a more robust Unite system and many other improvements.  Add the comic-style cutscenes and overall larger game and you SHOULD have an overall superior experience, right?
Unfortunately, the killing blow for this game is the massive, abhorrently mazelike dungeons.   They are far too large and far too numerous, and are bad from the very beginning.  This one element makes the game far less enjoyable than it could have been, but it's still okay.

You can be a humble merchant, trading and hauling for steady pay. There's also passenger courier work which require the safe-keeping of those aboard to arrive at their destination. Escort duties involves distracting and attacking pirates then escaping before your objective gets destroyed. Bounty-hunting requires combat reputation, so getting a bigger, stronger ship and going pirate hunting will build up your rep to be given those high paying contracts. Or even do some of each just to make end's-met.
2. When starting out, even if you want to get a feel for the game on your own: TAKE THE TUTORIAL!!! It pays, it gets you going in a definative path, and you can buy some local maps (which it's highly recommended to just buy maps early on). Once you open up the sky with areas you have explored, do some jobs for a while within them. There are two time markers early in that you can use as reference points to gauge off of. If you manage to pay off your loan before Rememberance Day, you did awesome. If you pay it off before the Civil War, great. If you can't pay it off until after then, you may need to rethink your career choice.
3. Don't worry about goofing off and exploring or anything until AFTER you pay off your first debt (like I said before, buy some maps so you don't go stumbling about early on). If you are having problem with the Pirates, stick to the middle and 'north-west' part of the map and do trading. If you are in the mood for salvaging or capturing ships, aim for the 'south-west' area around Aldhibain (five jumps 'south south-west of Rutilicus/home-planet) since there is both a strong merchant & local milita and Pirate raids. Also, the planet within the Aldhibain has both an Outfitter & Shipyard along with the trader, so you can not only sell the parts you get, you can sell any captured ships, equipt any modules you aquire or buy new ones when you get the money for them.
4. Lastly, once you upgrade your ship (anything over $million should do) go explore and visit each unexplored spot. Can't reach there? No worries, you will soon enough. If you prefer a more peaceful venture (aside from Pirates) visit the 'north north-east' area. Want to fight some tough enemies? Visist the 'east' area and say 'hello' to the new-comers (with several salvos of cannons). Once you unlock advanced flight, throw yourself to the far corners of the galaxy and discover all there is to this game.
5. ...then finally, once you do everything this game has to offer: quit it. Yes, quit... for a few months, go play something else,  do real-life things.
6. Then come back and find new contents has updated... then you can start a new save and play through the whole thing in record time.
7. See 5, 6 & 7 for further instructions.

Could this be fun? Sure, again if you like repeatedly dying in the name of a .01 progression rate this is totally for you.  I wouldn't recommend paying full price for this.

A very satisfying and challenging old-school style dungeon crawler that works very intelligently around the developer's likely limited resources; delivering a simple, yet captivating narrative for a game that truly tests your endurance and intelligence.
My only major complaint is that many of the puzzles go a little too far in the old-school direction; requiring working around obtusely vague hints or deliberate brute force to solve. Several times I was forced to ask for help after banging my head against a specific puzzle for more than a half-hour or so, only to find out that the solution was almost impossible to solve without overly excessive poking and prodding.
Still, the rest of the puzzles do a great job of making you feel smart after completing them. The game does enough hand-holding to get you off the ground, but lets you off the leash quickly enough to allow you to struggle against the tricks and traps of a very enjoyable game; barring some inevitably frustrating moments.

This is a post-release review.  Previously I had recommended it while it was in early Alpha.  In early Alpha, I did recommend it because it showed great promise and looked like it was going to be improved greatly as development continued.  As it was Double Fine - I had high hopes.  Admittedly, I probably shouldn't have gotten my hopes up for any game that is early access.  I highly encourage you to buyer beware for any early access games you may wish to fund in the future.
A note on the current status of Spacebase DF-9: It is considered, by the developers, to be complete enough for a full release.  Currently they're bug squashing and finishing some other small details on their development list.  That's it.  They're done after that.  There will be no future development done to this game for the foreseeable future, according to the developers.  They may not get back to it for at least 2 years, at minimum.  Buyer beware.
On to the review:
I have only played it for about 2 hours since it's official release.  While it still retains the charm and brutal difficulty as most games of this genre (ala Dwarf Fortress), there hasn't been that much added since the last builds of the early access Alpha.
The graphics are passable, the sounds are passable, the text and artwork definitely has the Double Fine touch that many love and enjoy.  The actual game play and game design is a hollow shell, crying for more.  Should you survive for at least an hour to hour and a half, you will have built everything that is needed.  The rest of the game is simply adding more space for more crew members, taking care of their needs, fighting off the occasional raider/parasite, researching the lack-luster tech tree, and preparing for the “end game” fight with the raider mega-fleet (which also completes the game; I believe).  I'm unsure if the raider mega-fleet actually ends the game or just scores you as I simply got too bored waiting for the mega-fleet to show up.  I built everything I wanted, I raided derelicts for tasty materials, and I threw the troublemakers in my station in a brig or two.  Not to mention dealt with some of my own bugs that are still hanging around since the Alpha builds.
Amongst some of the issues with the game: No varied save slots for more than one base at a time, vague tutorial, unrealized or fully implemented concepts, inability to clean up blood stains (at least no way I have found out), questionable fairness (random spikes in difficulty or events that have no lead up; bad things just happen and they're absolutely devastating), and AI having no way to prioritize important tasks (so they just stand around building the room while they suffocate instead of building the single oxygen recycler they need to survive).
Elaborating on the unrealized/fully implemented concepts: There are a great deal of the beginnings of production chains, rooms, etc. - But they're just lacking.  All those things you would normally build in other games to fully flesh-out a production chain just aren't there.  You just build a room and get the end product immediately.  For example, instead of building a whole bunch of different machines and making an actual factory that takes raw ore, crushes it, purifies it, refines it, and then makes it into usable construction components – You just get a single shot “matter” resource that you use for everything.  The developers didn't want the game to be too bogged down in these systems, but you never need more than one type of room with their setup.  There's not enough décor for the rest of your base, so you're just stuck with single blocked out rooms at a minimum size to hold just what you want and that's it.  It just leads to boring designs and an uninteresting base to look at.  It's visually boring.
If you're dying for another Dwarf Fortress game, set in space – I highly recommend checking out Rimworld or even looking into Gnomoria for your Dwarf Fortress needs.  Let this derelict game drift away.

Burstfire is a poor man's Rainbow 6 Siege. (Which might not be that accurate since siege isn't out yet and Ubisoft's track record hasn't been the best as of late) The basic game formula is the exact same. During the 1st stage one team prepares defences and another scouts with little robots. During the second stage the attacking team tries to assault the defending team's defences. You win by either eliminating everyone on the opposing team (permadeath) or completing your objective. While the actual gameplay offers a decent amount of strategic depth the small map pool and equipment selection leaves much to be desired. That being said this game is in early access so I expect with time this game will eventually have a decent amount of content and be better optimized.
However despite all the praise I have given this game there is one huge caveat. The game currently has a very small playerbase (matchmaking for 10 people took like 5 minutes) that I expect will only worsen as time goes on. This is just the sad truth for these small indie multiplayer games. Without proper advertising or a very original idea (look at rocket league and guns of icarus online) these days multiplayer only indie games are doomed to fail.
I also really like the menu soundtrack.

I will write a more in-depth review in the future, however as of now I will give a quick warning. If you do not like waiting for a bit to get into a game, you may want to either purchase the game to enrich the servers, or wait till other people flock to the concept.
Burstfire in a nutshell is a multi player online only game which consists of two teams who follow swat sort of tactics to rid of the opposing team. The first stage consists of choosing equipment. The second stage has a planning stage (and a observation stage for the other team) then finally the execution where the actual game takes place. So far, stuff is OK. but this game is nothing above mediocre at the moment. There is no single player unfortunately for someone looking for a Sierra SWAT 3 or 4 reboot. The game feels alright and the concept is interesting, but I hope more game modes come out including a single player campaign consisting of obedient and non-obedient AI.
The game itself feels like a cross between CS and Payday 2 movement/gameplay. There are no crosshairs available at the moment (unless you aim down the sights in which I'm okay with).
****Update Dec 2015****
Would not recommend buying it. Servers are essentially dead. It will take you possibly an hour before you find a game, then you get reset into a new server and have to again look for players.

A strategy game in which you control various types of plagues in an effort to destroy humanity. Plague types include viruses, fungus, brain worms, zombie infection, bio-weapons, and even one that grants apes super intelligence (inspired by the planet of the apes). Custom user made scenarios allow for even more plague types to be played with.
10-12 hours (Main game)
8/10
2015-05-10 (Early Access)

(PEI) is a follow up to the game
, which was originally released on mobile devices. I didn’t play the original game, so I’m not able to compare the two games, so I’ll just point out that this one has all the content from the original game, plus quite a bit more. And since the game is in early access still, there should be more content released in the future.
But onto the game itself, in PEI you control different types of plagues, evolving them so that they can wipe out humanity. You pick a country to begin your plague in, and from there it begins to infect people, spreading across the globe. As it infects more and more people you earn DNA, which you use to evolve your plague. There a few different ways to evolve your plague, such as the how it’s able to transmit itself to other hosts, the symptoms that carriers experience, different plague abilities, such as being able to withstand more extreme temperatures and medicinal drugs, as well as plague unique abilities (more on those later).
The strategy element of the game comes in how you evolve your plague. If you’re plague isn’t spreading to island countries, then you can evolve it to transmit more effectively via boat. You can evolve it so that birds act as carriers, increasing land based transmissions.
As your disease begins to evolve symptoms, doctors will notice its existence, and will begin working on a cure. As the plague becomes more severe, countries around the world will begin funneling more money into cure research. Once the cure is complete, it will be administered worldwide, eradicating your plague. Obviously, this is counter-productive to annihilating the human race, which is why you’ll want to evolve symptoms and abilities that slow cure research. Another option is to not evolve, and even devolve symptoms until the entire world is infected, and then evolve highly lethal symptoms to kill off humanity before they can cure themselves.
There are random events that can occur, such as planes using advanced sterilization filters, preventing your plague from spreading via air travel, unless you evolve your plague to overcome that setback.
How you evolve your plague will depend on not only these random events and how your plague is spreading (or struggling to spread), but also on your plague type, forcing you to adapt your strategy accordingly.
When you begin the game you’ll only have one plague type available to you, the humble bacteria. Once you manage to use it to eliminate humanity on normal difficulty or higher you’ll unlock your next plague type, the virus. The more you destroy humanity, the more plague types will become available to your disposal (and subsequently the disposal of humanity). Different plague types have different unique traits and abilities; bacteria for example are fairly straight forward, but allow you to evolve special renitences to the environs. Viruses evolve symptoms rapidly, forcing you to accommodate your playstyle to accommodate. Fungal plagues have greater difficulty spreading, and must evolve spores to spread more effectively.
Some of the more interesting plague types including the neurax worm, which is a type of brain worm that allows you control over the hosts. This allows you to influence their behaviour, either putting off cure research, engaging in dangerous activities to oneself, endangering the lives of themselves and others (even up to suicide), and even causing them to travel to countries of your choice to further spread the disease.
There’s of course the necroa virus, which turns dead people into zombies, reanimating them. From here you can control their movement, cause them to attack those still alive, both killing and infecting them.
There’s even a virus inspired by
, called the Simian Flu (which you being with, since it’s a bonus plague type). It’s quite an interesting plague, since not only does it infect humans, afflicting them with symptoms, some of which are lethal, but when apes contract the same disease they become more intelligent. From here you can evolve the disease to spread more effectively amongst humans, or among apes, or you can even evolve cross-species transmission. You can evolve symptoms to ail humanity, or abilities to strengthen ape-kind. These abilities include combat abilities, letting apes free captive apes used for scientific experiments designed to find a cure. Travel abilities that allow the apes to travel across land, and even build rafts to traverse the ocean. Apes can evolve to build communities, which give you additional DNA to use for evolving your plague.
When selecting your plague, you can also insert different genes into your plague to bolster its abilities. These are chosen before you begin a game with a plague, and you unlock a new gene every time you complete a game with any plague. Some gene types are universal, and some are specific to certain plague types. Genes help in different ways, such as giving you bonus DNA, increasing transmission efficiency by certain means, or altering costs for evolving/devolving your plague.
While that comprises the bulk of the gameplay, there are also different scenarios that you can play. These feature a special condition, such as people being able to teleport to other countries with the use of a portal gun (yes, from the game
). Others feature special plague types, which are slight alterations to the main plague types in the game. Depending on the scenario, you may be able to choose your plague type and gene loadout, or it may be preselected.
There are also user created scenarios, which allow for even more ways to destroy humanity. I haven’t delved too far into the user created scenarios yet, but so far I’ve managed to play one that features demon possession, and another that is based on John Carpenter’s
(one of my favourite movies). There’s of course the option to build your own custom scenarios, but I haven’t yet played with this.
A typical game varies in length, generally about 15-30 minutes, depending on a variety of factors. It took me somewhere between 1-3 hours before I first successfully destroyed humanity, and my times from there varied by plague type. All in all, it took me between 10-12 hours to win a game on normal with each plague type at least once; and I’ve put in a total of 18 hours into the game so far, trying out different strategies and higher difficulties for the plagues, and having fun with the scenarios. I expect I’ll sink in quite a few more hours into the game.
The main criticism I have is that the game is sometimes a bit unclear on what different plague traits do, though one could argue that this testing and experimentation is part of the appeal. Other than that, the game lacks a tutorial at this point, which while I understand that the game is in early access still and isn’t complete, that’s something you think would be included already.
On the plus side, the game has keyboard shortcuts for any of the actions you need to take in game, minimizing how much you need to use the mouse. On top of that it allows you to remap all the controls as you see fit (though I find the default to work without issue).
In the end,
is an engrossing strategy game where you help bring about humanity’s end. It has a lot more content than I expected in it, and it’s certainly worth the $15 price tag.

Note: As of this review, the cost of multiplayer + the Russian, French, British, German & Ottoman campaigns is 34,94€, in case you're woundering, although it could change later.
TL;DR: A fun, but flawed RTS without base-building.
Wall of text below:
Like Men of War, but with gas:
The game plays similarily to the Men of War franchise, but focused much more on large-scale infantry movements & the use of artillery. Automatic weapons & vehicles exist in this game, but are of limited quantity. To put things into perspective; there can be 2000 riflemen in a mission, but only 10 machineguns & maybe a tank. There are also artillery, rifle-grenades, mortars & flamethrowers in limited quantities, whom are essential at both attacking & defending entrenched positions.
RNG Fire-fights:
The game can be a unfair at times with it's shooting-mechanics. You mostly have riflemen, whom have a slow rate of fire, but typically kill in 1-2 shots. All infantry aim at enemy infantry individually & all have their own accuracy & chances to hit or miss for every shot, which mean that cover will only increase your chances of success, but far from guarantee it. At rare occasions you can lose fire-fights where you had both better cover & more men, which can be frustrating. You can however drastically shift the odds into your favour by spreading your units, creating kill-zones with barbed wire & building sand-bags & placing machine-guns, mortars, etc at key locations. That being said, I would not want any other system to be honest, as this feels authentic, whilst being fair most of the time.
Melee:
This game, like all other games that use the GEM engine, have a bad melee system, which doesn't fit a WWI game very well. People only melee if either they're given explicit orders to do so, or if they're so close to an enemy that they cannot fire their weapon because that person blocks them. It doesn't help that there's no "mass melee" order, so that you must order each individual soldier to melee a specific target, which is bonkers if you want to order 100 people to melee. However, due to the AI never issuing melee orders, you can ignore this poorly though-out feature in all missions except stealth missions, where you typically only have 1-5 soldiers.
Destruction:
The destruction in the GEM engine is amazing, it's been ever since S:HoWW2. You can destroy nearly everything you see, trees, buildings, vehicles, parts of buildings, parts of vehicles, bridges, the ground, nearly everything. Although breaking vehicles part by part is not as important in this game as in other GEM games, the system is still here. If you want to capture a vehicle you can shoot the driver (assuming it's physically possible), or you do things like destroy their tires/threads & then plant explosives next to it when it's stuck.
Graphics:
Outdated. As long as you don't zoom-in it looks OK, but once you zoom in it starts getting increasingly more gnarly. It's not puke-inducing, and can even be pretty at times, but generally suffer from poor poly-gon counts & a lack of detail in textures.
Sound:
Servicable. Some sounds are a bit bad, others OK, nothing exceptional. Same goes with voice acting.
Historical Authenticity:
I was never thaught anything about WWI throughout my 13 years of studying, except that there was one & people used gas. However, with the limited studying I've done myself it seems that the game is fairly historically accurrate, with a few things being out of order, like finding a MP-18 when the french are still using their red & blue uniforms. They do use things that people used during the war however, so you're not going to find entire companies equipped with SMGs & LMGs like in BF1, SMGs & LMGs are in fact pretty rare in this game.
Gas für alle:
Gas exist in this game, which is devestating if you ignore it. However, if you run away from it, you likely also run away from entrenched positions. There are gas masks however, which you are given in some missions.
Horses:
Are kinda broken. They can litterally run with artillery pieces attached to them & no one understands the concept of horse-back fighting.
Missions:
They vary drastically in every aspect. Some are great, some are bad, some have a lot of units, some have few, some have tanks, some don't, some you attack, some you defend, some you do both, etc. The missions are enjoyable overall, just make sure to play on NCO or Real-War difficulties, because difficulty doesn't scale well past the 2 "balanced" settings.
Multiplayer:
HOST! HOST! HOST! or get friends to play with, as there's a lot of salty losers who rage-quit the moment they get into a disadvantage, taking down the entire game with them. About half the multiplayer games I've played either the host rage-quitted or a large amount of players on one team rage-quitted. When people don't rage-quit it's a lot of fun though.
Scale:
The scale is amazing in some missions, with thusands of soldiers on each side, every single one having it's own AI, it's own inventory, it's own proffeciency with weapons, stealth, melee, etc. Having your men fire their rifles & machine-guns non-stop as hundreds of enemies charge your positions under artillery fire (or you under fire) is quite a spectacle. This is even cool in the missions you get to set up your own defenses & then recover between attacking waves & even have to counter-attack to re-take lost ground.
Variety:
There's as much as you can get in a WWI setting. Pistols, revolvers, bolt-action rifles, semi-automatic rifles, sub-machine-guns, machine-guns, anti-tank rifles, rifle-grenades, grenades, dynamite, airplanes (only call-in support), tanks, armored cars, trucks, boats, horses, field guns, mortars & gas. There's also several factions, all of which have their own equipment & uniforms, like Britain, Ottoman Empire, Germany, France, Russia, Austria-Hungary & Bulgaria.
There's a lot you can say about this game, it's got a lot going both for & against it, so if you're into tactical RTSes without base-building & no cheap nonsensical "powers", this might be for you.

While initially fun and full of promise, this base-building game quickly turns into a frustrating mess.  As a fan of the genre, I'm generally willing to look over minor flaws in base-building games, and when I first fired up Spacebase DF-9, I'll admit I let the excitement of building a space-station get the better of me.  Now, countless hours in, I find myself pinching the bridge of my nose in frustration and dissappointment everytime I boot the game up.
The game begins by mousing over an imaginary galaxy to find an area to establish a new space-base.  While I dreamed of building my own Deep Space 9 or Babylon 5 at an optimal location, I found that I needed to spend 5 full minutes dragging my mouse around the galaxy map looking for an ideal location.  Rather than allowing the player to set start parameters, the designers force you to hunt the 2D galaxy map for 4 varying starting conditions, consisiting of generally unclear parameters.  Sure, levels of mining materials, a threat level, and a proximity to a warp gate seemed to make sense since I was a sci-fi fan, but through different playthoughs, they had only small differences.  The final and fourth parameter, Magnetic Interference, remains unclear.  This is because none of these parameters are ever explained, even during the tutorial.
Once the game begins, regardless of the parameters selected, the player has but a few minutes to build a basic base before the three astronuats supplied run out of air to breath.  They must be assigned tasks, which, at first are dictated by necessity, and later by NPC prefence, which is shown via an assignment screen using varying degrees of happy and sad faces.
The problem with building a basic base is that your resources are so low, no matter what world parameters you set, that you need to be near absolute barebones.  There is very little room for error.  Of course, once basic resources, like air, food and the ability to create building material are met, a player can always expand, and sometimes with ease.  But, this is where bugs, even in version 1.03 begin to appear.
I've had my start point pressed up against materials which have made it extremely difficult to start a base.  I've had one of my 3 vital NPCs get caught on what little terrain there is at the start.  NPCs get caught inside fully constructed rooms until you place a door, which usually isn't bad, unless you go pet your cat for 30 seconds and then look up to find everyone dead.
Or, in my last three games in a row, which inspired this review, have NPC's get stuck in terrain that was under construction, rendering the game a death sentence.  Since there is only one save, this requires a new base, which in turn requires mousing over the 2D galaxy for 5 minutes to find starting parameters...
Once a player has a basic base up and running, the game begins to punish it much too soon.  Incoming asteroids, disease, incoming asteroids, raiders, incoming asteroids, and NPC incompatibilty all appear just a 4 or 5 rooms into the base.  Did I mention that incoming asteroids will hit your base and ALWAYS target vital systems?
Once a base is established, NPCs start getting sad, angry or upset.  They all have demands.  Nobody knows how to please those demands.  I even doubt the developers know.  I have never found a correlation between the limited items I can place and NPC happiness.  I try to supply them with, say, Monitors.  What do Monitors do?  I have no idea.  Are Monitors cosmetic?  Do they increase Happiness?  Do they decrease stress?  No one knows.
In summation:  The game works.  It does some basic stuff.  But, I get so frustrated everytime I bring myself to give the game a 8th or 9th chance than I'd rather watch watch seconds tick by.  Furthermore, I'd like to say that my faith in Double Fine is rattled - a company that once did no wrong has now done wrong.

I recommend this game only if you have literally nothing better to do, either because you have WAY too much time on your hands AND you don't have enough money to buy an actual game. Assuming most people don't meet both conditions, I can't recommend this game. At least it's free, so only my time has been wasted on this game, and at least I have a decent chunk of time to waste right now. Otherwise I would have stopped at 2 hours.
If you're the kind of person who doesn't want to binge this game, I just say don't get it. You probably don't even need to read this rant. But if you do, maybe you'll get a few ideas on how to make a better game than this. It's not that hard and you could probably justify charging money for it - these guys certainly wouldn't get my penny for this one if they did.
- The graphics are terrible, underwhelming. Free game, so easily forgivable. Stock footage images in the places where you land and each one doesn't feel alien or outer-spacey at all. Annoying, but again, it's free. Just proceed with that in mind. I'd like to think more effort on the devs' part would have produced better results, but it's free, so perhaps the one critique I have that can be addressed properly.
- This game is absolutely HORRIBLE at telling you things. How does the game work? There's no guides. Did my escort get disabled? No idea, just spam shift+N until you find the right one. Aside from the retired guy you taxi around early on, nobody teaches you anything. I'm not saying this game needs a tutorial, but come on! In the wide universe, there are almost no resources to explain how equipment, much of which has been heavily used for CENTURIES, works? There's no owner's manual that comes with my 1-million credit ship, not even a downloadable PDF? Okay, so there's this "scram drive" that I can use instead of my standard hyperdrive. It activates at a higher max speed, at the cost of fuel. How much fuel???
I recognize there are wiki resources online but those frequently ruin the experience. It feels like cheating, and sometimes when spoilers are unwittingly given in their zeal to inform the public, it is.
- Ship controls are terrible. Maybe, just maybe, it's forgivable if they're trying to copy+paste the old series they claim to be paying homage to. But I think the control system is terrible. There aren't any inertial dampeners!? There aren't any forward-facing thrusters!? Come on! Your ship has to turn 180 degrees and use its main thrusters just to slow down!! And you can't strafe either! Dogfighting is a pain in anything other than a tiny fighter that can't even hyperdrive to other sectors, seriously, and doubly so if your ship can't turn quickly. Copy off a classic or not, it sucks - humanity could probably do better a hundred years from now, let alone a thousand years from now when the game takes place!
- I sort of appreciate the devs' efforts to throw in something innovative - financing. Sure, it had me in a hurry to pay off my loan at first ASAP, but at the same time balance payments between saving my earnings to get a good ship. They get points for that. I sense some people might also want to make use of the credit score and take out a loan at some point to help boost their progress. I actually liked the mechanic.
But... refer to my next point about capturing ships.
- Life's hard if you're not a spaceliner captain or tramp hauler. For combat ships, there are only two ways to make money if your fleet's worth less than 2 million credits. You can perform "escort missions", which don't pay so badly at first and pay quite nicely as the game progresses. You can also board disabled pirate ships and either strip them of parts, or board them and capture the ship as a prize.
Now here come the problems: The devs did a terrible job of the enemies who appear on escort missions. Far too often do I barely enter orbit as I leave a planet when I get swarmed with three pirate ships with some sort of high-tier lasers that shred my light warship in barely a second. I don't have any time to react. I can't deal enough damage to any of them to buy myself more time, let alone fight my way out. This brutal cycle continues for a few more loads until I get lucky and local law enforcement shows up in time, I somehow manage to get enough asteroids between me and the banhammers to escape, or the game miraculously sends me one lone pirate who is ridiculously weak and far too easy to kill. Never a fair fight, be it one way or (usually) the other. What's more, the pay doesn't usually increase. It's all based on the ship you're flying, which isn't directly proportional to the pay you get.
Okay, so the other method: disabling pirates and looting them. Ahahahaha. That's even worse. 4 out of 10 times, your hyper-aggressive law enforcement will brutally annihilate any pirates around. Out of the remaining 7 times, they will, one way or another, attack the vessel again after it's been disabled, destroying it, almost every time. Adding insult to injury, they wait for you to fly towards the target, then they shoot at it, killing it. Result? Only very rarely do you reach a ship to board it. Once you've boarded it, you can either strip what you can carry, or you can attempt a capture. Great stuff. You should expect to lose a crewman or two, but you can sell a captured ship for a lot (that's what let me get rid of the starter fighter, and also what paid off my starting loan) or put it to use carrying cargo and making your fleet look menacing. Not that the AI's that great at fighting.
So I captured a nice interceptor. Lost one or two guys doing it. WITHOUT TELLING ME, the game applied a 550k "death benefits" charge. For some reason, it started charging me 10k credits a day, and when I finally made it to a bank, I was given a nasty surprise. Remember that financing? Yeah, you have to pay interest on the exorbitant death fees too, and what's more, you have to pay it off in 60 days. I had to work my♥♥♥♥♥off to pay it off in time - the fact that I was losing 10k a day to a big black hole. So I'm gonna think twice before capturing ships from now on. Nobody's worth 700k in principal and interest. My entire spaceship and its equipment almost cost that much!
I don't know about the rest of the playerbase, but I got this game to have fun by blasting stuff. Not by being a galactic door-to-door salesman or glorified bus driver. The way it works for the first several hours of the game, it seems the devs want to discourage that.
- This game's supposed to be really moddable. It really should be, looking at how basic it is, the fact that its source is on GitHub or something. I really wish this had Steam Workshop, but my gut tells me it won't happen. There's no central source for mods, so the chances of you finding a good one - or even a variety of them - are kinda slim. I could also be completely mistaken and there are virtually no mods for this game. The site the devs link you to has only like six mods, and too many "ship mods" are just pictures of ships. I don't have time to code their implementation because of the time I absolutely need to put into the game if I'm playing it due to aforementioned reasons.
So yeah. I don't really like this game but I have nothing better to do. I'm in that bad a situation hahahahaha. Someone save me

I want to like this game but the flaws of the Surge far outweigh it's good bits and it becomes more apparent the further you venture through the game.
It starts of quite well, easing into the brutal combat system and game mechanics with a tutorial built into the level, a mix of open spaces and tight corridors, and a brilliant level design that opens up numerous short cuts back to the single OPS room in each level (the equivelent of Dark Soul's bonfire).
However the game suffers from several bad design decisions - regular enemies hit incrediably hard and can kill you in two quick hits. There is a blocking function but it's quite useless and doesn't seem to offer much more than to lock you in place so the enemies can knock off another huge chunk of your health (enemies can be found in narrow corridors that your only defense is to dodge backwards and hope you don't get trapped - there is literary an instance in one level where you take a lift up to a narrow corridor with a fast, hard enemy a few steps away that you have no way of avoiding at all).
Dodging is a far safer tactic although due to level design there have been a few times when my character has lept to his death beacuse some enemies have been placed on bridges and platforms with parts that have no railings or have an opening in the floor to make way from some scenery.  It may sound picky but when your running back to the spot you died previously and have to confront a quick, deadly enemy on a narrow bridge that is very difficult to run past, it starts to feel a cheap tactic on the developers part to make the game "hardcore".
The camera struggles with combat in tight spaces and the locking on system can sometimes get unresponsive if trying to disengage or switch enemies.  Coupled with the sheer deadliness of the regular enemies, encounters become frustrating with the player dying often in a split second and having to fight their way back through the level to pick up the scrap currency they dropped on death.
Also of note the plot is non existant, the world lore and characters not terribly interesting or engaging.  Except for a couple of parts the art of the levels are uninspiring factories and futuraristic labs that all look the same and on several occassions have left me lost because it all looks the same.  The character the player plays as is middle age white guy number #2 with forgetable voice acting and personality, and the only one unique feature is revealed at the intro of the game and is then completely moot once you get strapped into the exoskeleton.

The Surge is an enjoyable RPG, taking influence from the Souls series of games but providing enough unique mechanics and structure to make it stand well on its own. You don't have to have played the Souls series of games to have fun in this one! It brings a unique aesthetic to this kind of melee-based gameplay of repurposed industrial tools and mechanical exoskeletons, alongside a kind of junkyard transhumanism as you swap different bits in and out.
Pros:
+ The keyboard and mouse controls actually work quite well, so while there is controller support, you don't have to use it
+ While the game can initially be punishing, learning the moveset and tells of the different enemy types can allow you to beat them reliably
+ Improving your character by upgrading armor, weapons, core power (essentially your character level) and implants (healing items and stat boosts) actually ramps up your capability nicely
+ Weapons can be favorited, and favorited weapons can be swapped between on the fly (G-key by default). You can essentially mark your entire listing and swap to the best tool for the current job.
+ changing the stats of your character is achieved through swappable implants, or what pieces of armor you wear- you never really need to respec to rebuild your character, just reequip yourself.
+ better weapon and armor upgrade items drop from later-game opponents, allowing you to freely upgrade pretty much everything if you're willing to farm their bits.
+ Scrap (the game's XP) can be banked at each level's central base location, preventing you from losing it on death if you're farming it up.
+ The areas of the game are a rat's warren of shortcuts and backpaths, where a significant part of progressing is unlocking shortcuts back to the central base. Finding and unlocking each of these can be quite satisfying, especially when it allows you to bypass areas you had trouble with on the way through initially.
+ the humanoid opponents are fun to outmaneuver and pick apart, and the finishing moves allow you to literally take them to pieces! Getting good against a subtype that used to give you trouble absolutely feels like sweet, sweet revenge, like a fly that has learned to pull legs off a spider.
Cons:
- Bosses can be killed only once. Once beaten, you won't see that boss again until NG+.
- Every boss drops a boss weapon, but you have to kill them in a special way to get a more powerful version- the game mentions this in exactly one loading hint, but gives no clues as to how to determine what that 'special method' will be for any of the bosses.
- The game doesn't do a good job telling you about many of the background mechanics. For example, sometimes you'll get extra healing items out of the blue, or recover a bit of health, with no real explanation as to why. There is a root mechanic around this based on your current core power and how much scrap you've picked up since the last time you visited the central base, or the total currently carried on your person.
- The player is a fixed character, a man named Warren, but he has little initial background or character development.
- There will be difficulty ramps in certain areas that you'll mostly overcome by grinding.
- There's a LOT of grind if you want to upgrade yourself, your kit, and your weapons as much as possible.
- In addition to dropping your carried 'scrap' when you die, you have 2:30 to get it back once you leave the base/respawn area. Killing enemies can add a little time back, but you have to be quick or you'll spend more time than you get from doing it. If you die while such a pile is on the ground, regardless of remaining time, it's gone for good as in the souls games.
-Some of the robotic enemies have absurd levels of armor and hit like a truck, making fights against them long, slow, and exceedingly dangerous.
I like the elements at play here. It's recognizable as being influenced by the Souls series, much like Torchlight was recognizably influenced by Diablo, but it brings enough unique elements that it is unquestionably its own thing. Combat feels meaty, and the finishing moves you can pull off on wounded enemies are satisfyingly brutal. The mechanics around targeting individual limbs to determine what loot you want from the kill, or to hit weak points, makes for interesting tactical decisions in the heat of a fight. Most importantly, the base combat (at least against the humanoid opponents) is just fun, making the grinding you do actually enjoyable: It provides the perfect excuse to keep bludgeoning foes into submission! Though I admit, there were a few rage-quits here and there, my general experience is that it's hard to convince myself to stop playing!
TL:DR- Take the bones of a Dark Souls game, put some Dead Space on it, throw in a little System Shock and Deus Ex, and you've got something like The Surge!

Short review: This game is crack cocaine. Play, but only if you have the time or willpower.
Full review: Remember when ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Facebook games were all the rage and the ability to block obnoxious Farmville requests was lifesaving? And Zynga hired a team of psychologists to figure out how the game could dose out dopamine to best optimize playtime and microtransactions? Factorio's cracklike appeal is similar, except you're the one who chooses whatever task you feel will be most important, and after finishing it, you get a feeling of true accomplishment rather than of being manipulated.
There's always something to improve, something new to automate-and it's always fun. But when you've completed whatever task you've set for yourself, you can see the literal improvement. Your factory runs more smoothly, or generates new useful products. It's never just more of the same. Your neurological satisfaction is earned.
This scales up over multiple playthroughs. My first factory had completely haphazard organization, so I abandoned it and laid out a new one with a centralized artery of key resources. But then that one became a Gordian knot, with veins of belts and inserters scrambling intermediate production chaotically. So, I rebuilt a third time with a more modular, organized design. And still, I have several ideas in mind already for my next iteration.
It is quite stable and a smooth experience, but there are clear signs why it is early access. There are four or five main concepts to figure out, and the learning curve for each feels very difficult at first, though after experimenting, it actually smooths out quickly. You do have to be motivated to try new features when you've mastered an earlier one, because there's not much of a push to do so. In order, I'd recommend setting out playtime to specifically experiment with the following over multiple factory iterations:
- Basic production and automation
- Liquid handling
- Railroad construction
- Logistics network use
- Circuit network use
Try a game or two with the aliens attacking just to see what it's like, but then turn on peaceful mode while you learnto avoid distractions before jumping into the full game.
All in all, what impressed me was not just the sense of in game accomplishment, but that I discovered and continuously learned design and supply chain principles throughout. I literally walk down the street with a new eye for infrastructure, and a much deeper appreciation that our system of roads and powerlines isn't an incomprehensible first grader's shoelace knot of discord. No joke, I've signed up for an EdX course on supply chains after being inspired to think about why we've organized our infrastructure this way.
So all in all, it's fun and addictive, but earns this trait, something even great games like Stardew Valley don't quite hit on the head (replayability and iteration sorely lacking). Seriously: don't play if you're looking to pop in and out for short spurts; it's designed to pull you in and not let go. But it does so compellingly.

Ever wonder what would happen if China made a game similar to the Thomas Crown affair but with magicians, mazes, and wacky guards? That’s Catch Me in a nutshell. This two-faceted game has you invading other players’ mazes to steal their money while building up your own fortress to safeguard your ill-gotten gains.
On the attack, your goal is to loot every safe with the option of collecting coins scattered about the level along the way. Successful raids and defenses yield roses, a flexible unit that can be shifted to any of three attributes before the start of every mission. Over time you will collect enough money to upgrade your (maze) level and gain access to better guards and additional safes.
Gameplay in Catch Me is very resource-dependent, with your character limited to a maximum of three different tools (out of a selection of six total) each having its own weight and MP cost. Carrying too much into one mission can slow you down and carrying too little won’t allow you to complete your objectives. Managing your MP is equally critical as you don’t have much of it, even at higher rose levels due to diminishing returns. Fog is another important element of the game since a lot of enemies don’t reveal their positions to you at the start of the mission and you must spend money and MP via flares to find them.
For the first six or seven levels of mazes this game is actually really fun and you get to experiment with all sorts of different strategies to outsmart each player’s defenses. After that, it becomes impossible to finish a round without expending every single bit of MP in addition to using cost-saving tricks like deliberately getting caught in snares to lure guards or allowing explosive guards to attack you, “tanking” the damage. Parrot guards become especially annoying as they can be placed outside of the playable area and you will have to peek into a player’s maze, spend loads of money on flares, and then leave and re-enter the maze with their positions memorized so you can re-flare them for your actual playthrough in order to succeed. This gets really tedious and downright unrewarding, especially since the payout for high level invasions can actually be lower than that of low level players since it is dependent on the amount of money they have in storage.
Is Catch Me worth picking up? As of November 2016, the developer posted a message saying that development would not continue, meaning that updates are a foregone conclusion. This game is still really addictive at lower levels for at least 12+ hours so I’ll give this advice: “Rob the developer and pick this game up on sale, it’ll be a real steal”.
