Battlefield: Bad Company 2--in contrast to its predecessor--adopts a more rough and gritty tack to storytelling in its single-player adventure. I am very sad to see this because of the slapstick, absurdist charm of the first game which saw its blundering protagonists looking for gold in  "Eastern-Europistan," accidentally overthrowing dictators, and destroying the internet among other fanciful objectives.
While environmental destruction is still as fun and joyous as ever, the levels feel much shorter and the difficulty ratcheted down a few notches. The lack of vehicle selection in the sprawling environments was also a shocking and unwelcome surprise compared to the large (if gratuitous, in some cases) arsenal of armor in the first.
Some levels are a chore for even my quad-core gaming PC to run due to what I assume are inelegant threading issues. I will run into awkward hiccoughs and stutters in gameplay on any graphics setting though the game isn't a graphical behemoth to begin with.

This game has basically everything I want out of a multiplayer shooter. Well, everything but accessability. You start the game with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ weapons and no options, but by the same token, holding your own at a low level is intensely satisfying. Tanks are immune to things like small arms fire and WALLS, but  have serious blindness issues. There is no sweeter feeling than watching the C4 you planted tear apart the tank from the inside, except maybe popping all the rivets out with a drill while the damn thing is in motion.

I'm going to focus on the AI aspect here.
In the beginning, there was Early Access. In its Alpha build, DF9 AI was rudamentary. It made bad, often comically bad decisions, and it was like watching a child grow and interact with a world we knew it would adapt to. Like parents, we told our friends the marginally interesting tales of how the children stopped to chit-chat about Moonbeef and whatever while oxygen recyclers caught fire and firefights happened around them. And it was funny because we assumed that it would improve with time, development, and attention.
Then DF noticed. They thought this is where the charm of the game came from, and they pulled the plug. Our AI children stopped growing, and were now going to stay stupid. "You enjoyed the stupid AI", they say, "and now that's where we decided to leave it."
We enjoyed the AI because it was temporary and had some amusing quirks in its broken state. Being forced to deal with the game in the shape that it's in is not fun. Building a base for inhabitants who don't know how to live in it is not a sim, it's an exercise in futility.

I really wanted this game to succeed.  It is a shame that Double Fine pulled the plug on this title.  But as it stands the game is not worth buying in its current condition.  No future development on the horizon means a DO NOT BUY from me.

To start off, i'm more neutral towards the gameplay factor, but i have to give this a negative rating for the fact that DF just abandoned the game when they saw it progressed to slow.
But here's the gameplay review, if you're still wondering if you should buy it or not :
The game's idea is wonderfull imo : build a base in space, maintain it and welcome new colonists into it while fending off raiders and managing the jobs the citizens do. The way they did it was not bad at all, simple drag-build controlls and assigning the different areas by a simple click of a button and design the interior as you like with various props. Easy. Simple.
But the thing that made the game bad is the fact that it's unbalanced, buggy and just unfinished.
The A.I is pretty bad in prioritizing their tasks, and with the new mood system there is just no way of keeping them happy, even if you furnish every room and give them their favourite jobs. they all eventualy get depressed and start fighting over nothing, which screws up the whole base and delays tasks as they recover in the sickbay.
The gameplay is refined for an Alpha at the time, but there was no change in it whatsoever when it went to V1.0 .
I wouldn't recomend the game to someone who disliked game-breaking bugs and dumb A.I , but if you just like building a base and dont mind using mods to fix all of the vanilla game's problems, it is worth buying whenever it gets on sale.
But otherwise, i sadly can'r recommend it, sorry Double Fine, but ya kinda screwed it up here.

This game was made by an interesting company called Double Fine. The game it self has left early alpha and has became a full game already, now i will emit this game could of been worked on alot more then it currently is. When double fine released this into full game, they had said it wasn't to the level they wanted, they wanted to do so much more with this game but they wasn't able to do it. So instead of just scrapping the game entire like some people believe they've done. Many games have been made alot better thanks to the modding community, games that have had more things than this one even. As for actually gameplay, the game runs fairly smooth and there use to be many annoying things that happened in the game. But the game does have random generation, so you wont have the same game twice. one game you could have an entirely peacefull game, never running into Raiders, or Aliens let alone other things. while one game you could get hit near the begining and get slaughtered, Which this is slightly factored by your chosen start location, for some has more likely hood of one thing than another would. Example: One section has tons of asteriods and rare encounters, while another has medium asteriods and very common encounters.
all in all, i actually believe it's a good Space Station Building simulation game, that many people wouldn't of thought to make, the only real bad thing of this game is the Ai i will emit mainy on the builders, if you want to remove spot in a room or anything be prepared for massive pausing and quick selection, for they will try to kill them selves at times, though i have never had to unbuild anything, because i never seen a reason to do so unless i was doubling a room, which was easy to save my builders. If You think when placing security markers that something is wrong and your security isn't going to the location, it's because either 1. their asleep. (you can't wake them up you gotta let them sleep for as long as they wish). 2. you actually don't have any (pay attention to the jobs you assign) or 3. There is no phyiscal way for them to reach the location.
I will emit this is the first time i've done a review for any game, but i believed i needed to after seeing so many negative reviews that was for reasons that in my opinion didn't fit as a good full on review of the game. This game is still a nice game to play on the side, and in my opinion once the modding community actually starts making mods and more if they haven't already, this game could become even more interesting just like Double Fine is trusting us to do.
i personally would rate the game, but i'm not good at picking right numbers to what i feel it should be, it's not a game you'll want to just spend hours apon hours playing, though sometimes when you start you'll get a bit addicted.. untill your space station is killed and you rage. but you can't live forever.

This game is the reason why I started preferring indie games over triple A titles. The premise is simple, you are a frontier guard in charge of passport control in what seems to be an eastern European country during the soviet regime. Your job is to check every immigrant's papers and allow or deny their entrance.
I really like this being random although there are certain key events that always play the same way. These tell the story of rebellion against the local government, a terrorist organization, corruption and some other mature themes.
The art does seem dated but the game need no fancy graphics to be entertaining. It keeps getting more and more complicated as new laws are passed to further increase border control and you may choose to play it safe, ally with the rebel or benefit you and your family from helping catching spies. It is a cold war drama that resembles reality quite interestingly.
I really recommend this game for anyone who likes cold war stories, finding the differences kind of games, or just a very well executed idea.

Plague Inc.: Evolved; let me first start out by saying, this is exactly how the Early Access model should be done. This game is an absolute treat to play.
The main idea behind the game, if you don't already know (I’d be surprised if you didn't to be honest), is to develop, mutated and transmit your very own disease. You can choose which symptoms you would like your diseases to have, how you would like it to be transmitted around the world and many other different options. There are a number of different kinds of diseases you can choose, my favourite has to be the zombie plague; each of the different modes offers different symptoms, abilities and ways to transmit your creation as well.
The graphics are essentially a 2D world map; you don't need anything else for this game, the UI and HUD are very nicely put together and you can get all of the information you require within a key press.
Each of the different modes have been carefully crafted so that no game ever feels the same; this game really makes you think, would this symptom thrive in these conditions? How can I get my plague to travel to the other side of the world when all of the airports are closed? The possibilities are endless.
The game can also vary in difficulty; each different mode has 4 stages of difficulty; and boy oh boy does it get hard in the brutal stages. You are best of cracking out a guide if you want to tackle some of the harder stages.
I have played about ten hours so far; this has enabled me to complete all the different types of diseases and modes on offer, done a couple on Brutal difficulty and worked on a few achievements. There are still roughly 100 more achievements to collect along with the scenario modes to play; and given that they game is still in early access, I fully expect there to be more content added soon too.
I can 100% guarantee that anyone will enjoy this game; it’s a perfect pick up and play game but you can also get mind numbingly deep into the inner workings of diseases and plagues without having to do six years in medical school.

This game has an interesting formula that is rarely seen independently. It reminds me of a mobile game I spent a good amount of time on: King of Thieves. It's the concept and game mechanic of building and raiding bases that intrigues me intesely. There is, however, a few flaws that must be addressed.
For instance - I noticed early on that players learn the value of 'overguarding'. This is to stick all of your gold and sentry/guards in one corner. This defense, though simple, is pretty much 100% unbeatable. In a way, this is good, but early on in the game, it ruins the cohesion of the tutorial and the multiplayer formula.
It's a simple fix, but a small adjustment in the ability to place certain sentries could cure the issue until a permanent fix is decided.
Other than that, the game is great. I haven't played much, but I enjoy what I've seen. There is a decent mix of customization and development put into the total build that is pretty exciting.
To the developers, I would suggest working on the English a little bit. Here and there I get confused by what's being said sometimes. I don't know if it's just a miscommunication thing, or what, but I would suggest take a couple double looks here and there just to make sure everything's in shape. Great job, though. Keep up the good work! I look forward to future updates! :D

If you enjoyed escape velocity as a kid you'll enjoy Endless Sky. It's a 2d game yet i became very immersed in its lore. I always stop to read the descriptions of every planet/station I land on.
It has all the usual EV gameplay with some quality of life improvements like autopilot for certain actions like landing boarding and jump drive travel. It brings new gameplay to boarding, instead of a % chance to capture a ship based on your ship and combat rating it now uses crew members from the players ship as the boarding party vs the enemies crew.  You can hire more crew to increase success rate or install bunkbeds for even more additional crew if you really want it that badly.
You are no longer stuck in your main ship if you have escorts with you. You can pilot whatever ship is in your fleet by using an outfitter or shipyard by simply dragging that ship infront of the line in the upper right. Unwanted escorts can be sold off for profit.
I was enjoying this game allot but the new outfit mechanics started to irritate me. I think the game tries too hard to ballance loadouts with its new sub outfit catagories.
Ships have:
Cargo space ( only cargo goes here and does not overlap into other catagories)
Outfitspace ( every piece of equipment on your ship will take up outfit space )
weapon space ( takes up outfit and weapon space)
Engine space ( takes up outfit and engine space)
This overlap is where i think the game goes wrong in trying too hard to ballance its loadouts.
My heavy warship has 6 turret hardpoints and 8 fixed gun hardpoints but can I fit 6 heavy turrets and 8 heavy guns on it after buying a bunch of mass expansions? NO! I CANT!
Just downgrade to smaller turrets right? Well you see there is one problem with that. I am using a heavy alien warship that far outclasses any human ship. If I were to fit the max amount of smaller guns onto my hardpoints i would indeed have all the weapons i can fit but the damage output would be subpar for a ship of that class.
Weapon space should only take up weapon space. Engine should only take up engine space.
Every thing else goes in outfit space. The game has heat and power mechanics that could be put to better use than they are now to, ughh "ballance" out the changes, i hate that word, such a dirty word to me, "ballance". Effective firepower is fun, ballance is not.
I amassed a powerful fleet and became unstoppable then i became bored. I didn't manage to find a main quest line after 60 hours of play which is either my fail or the developers fail.
It would have kept me playing but I am bored of it now.
Whats that smell? Smells like over-ballance burning in the engine room! Time to launch the escape pod. Farewell Endless Sky.

At first I really didn't expect much of this game, gave it a try since it's free and it's on my personal recommendation list. There's also 2 things that sort of gave me a feeling that I might want to give it up, which are 1) I was hit with wall-of-texts after wall-of-texts with non-choices, and 2) that I was stuck because I don't know how to find missions that advance the plots.
But after somehow overcome these 2 early difficulties, I somehow ended up with more than 200 hours into the game.
To me the wall-of-text narrative was sort of unexpected, but then I realized the fact the writing quality is actually rather good, and the plot directions actually is kind of interesting. At least it kept my curiousity going to the end of the main campaign (The Free Worlds one) the game currently has. And after investing tens of hours into it, only then I realized how big the background setting really is for the game: various political entities, mysterious aliens and intertwined histories among all of them.
After I finished the final mission of the main campaign, it also really gave me the feeling of tremendous progression -- from an insignificant shuttle pilot to a huge battle fleet augmented with alien technologies that the galaxy has to reckon with, and also the "event density" is rather high, I suspect due to the fact that I haven't really played any space opera games not bogged-down by cinematic cutscenes in the recent years. So a return to pure-text for narrative advancements was rather refreshing.
But of course the non-choice part can definitely be improved IMHO. There's only a handful meaningful choices in the dialogue in the game right now and it's a pity.
The game's UI is also very good but it's hard to notice at a glance -- like (L) for landing, but when there are multiple landing spots in a system, you will automatically land on the nearest one or the one where you have missions to do. And press (L) twice or more to cycle through landing spots. There are many small details like this in game that really adds up. The game's UI give you a deceivingly primitive look, while actually it's mostly very very handy.
All the options of ship outfitting and fleet building have their narrative purposes as well, the system itself is also surprisingly deep -- the only shame is that the game content now currently don't reflect well to this system. The economic is easily manipulated and broken (by plundering and pirating ships), and also past a point your fleet is just simply invincible so all the choices don't matter anymore (even to some of the most powerful, seemingly unbeatable alien creatures). But I see this as room to change and improve upon, not really a decisive flaw, since the game is still evolving at this date.
The trade and mission system is simplistic, while I would love to see more depth in this regard, it doesn't hinder the gameplay experience too much.
Finally one thing I want to add is that the modding of the game is surprisingly well designed. It's simple, elegent and effective to gather all the community helps in improving the game. Though if you are not a modder this really doesn't concern you too much, but from a technical point of view I still want to give kudos to this aspect.
Recommended.

For me The Surge happened to strike a chord better than Dark Souls. To be precise - I enjoy it more than any Dark Souls game I have ever played and a lot more than I expected I would.
The biggest points for me are lethal enemies (in Dark Souls you can "outlevel" them and once you do game losses a lot of its charm. In The Surge they always remain relevant to a degree due to how deadly they can be and that's the kind of combat challenge that I happen to like in this and other games), viscreal combat system (you can cut off limbs, each hit feels like it has a significant weight behind it, etc.) and the sc-fi setting (a really good idea to allow player use something that's basically a power armor suit with melee combat system mixed into it).
Playing with mouse and keyboard is really smooth, unlike Dark Souls that had numerous issues with its PC port. This really surprised me in a positive way. I guess it's just From Software who's hopeless when it comes to doing games on PC (remember "For Dark Souls II we are developing on PC from the beginning" that proved to be wrong in the end?).
Shortcuts feel fairly well placed for the most part, although I think they could've done a better job at adding more signs/writting on the wall (graffiti, you can find some of them in the starting area)/NPCs giving directions to help navigate the areas better.
There are some "maps" here and there, but I find them largely useless because of lack of cardinal directions (no compass). This did cause me to wander around a few times for an hour or so before my brain managed to "map the area" on its own, which allowed me to find the right path. Overall I think Dark Souls was a bit better in this regard (because of NPCs giving you hints and map kind of "showing" where you might want to go next).
The story seems to be OK. Not great, somewhat typical, but not boring. One thing I don't like is lack of motivation to "go into the factory", other than a player wanting to play the game. The very first NPC really fails at making her point or being convincing and the player-character fails at noticing her lapse of logic. The PR-guy, audio logs and "environmental information" are the better part and do help to cover up for that to a degree.
The visuals are very good and game is running for me without an issue on highest possible details. Quick loading times.
I really like what weapons bring to combat. Armors I didn't figure out entirely yet (stability/impact thing). Implants are really nice when it comes to tailoring your playstyle - you aren't really locked to a single build because of that. Except for farming for parts. This can get kinda grindy when you need to upgrade/craft other armor and feels like enemies should drop more parts to speed up the process a bit.
Overall I will say the game is really good, but this might be because it happened to do everything the way I like and the points it didn't I don't mind all that much.

i have far from beaten this, but the amount of time i spent playing it gave me quite an impression of how things go, i'd say.
even tho it is clearly influenced by the souls series i'm not gonna compare it too much to those games. it has enough new ideas and mechanics and a completely different setting, that i think it's a beast of it's own.
surely the sci-fi setting is the biggest difference and it changes the atmosphere quite a lot. it is ominous and oppressing but in a different way. in souls you still had some depressing kind of hope to the world and most npcs still were encouraging you to go and succeed (except in that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child that DS2 was). here everything went to♥♥♥♥♥♥and you don't really know why or how.
besides that, the game gives you a few more hints where to go or what to do, but still: no real hand holding.
the fighting mechanics initially seem like souls, but only at first glance. sure, there is a stamina meter and punishing melee combat, but that's all it has in common. having played souls games will help you nontheless, since it feels familiar.
but in the surge you can specifically target limbs to chop them offf (for weapons, schematics and materials). that makes combat a tad more tactical, because you can chose to target weak points -to dispose of the enemy quickly- or take the risk of having a longer fight but maybe get valueable stuff doing a finishing move in the end. risk and reward.
in addition to live and stamina you also have to take care of your energy-bar. you build up energy during fighting and it can help you with using injectables, drones or other upgrades to your exo-skeleton; or rather your implants to it.
these implants are comparable to rings from souls and can give you health, stamina boosts, help you salvage more tech etc etc. you get the gist. they take up a certain amount of energy on your rig so you have to manage what you (can) use.
tech is basically the currency and xp in this game (if you want you can compare it to souls). you need it to craft things, upgrade your exo-rig or equipment. should you die -which you probably will do a lot- you have about 2 1/2 half minutes to get your tech back; it being dropped where you died. of course the enemies will be back, but defeating an enemy adds a few precious extra seconds to your timer. if you don't make it in time the tech is gone. so no pressure at all, right? the good thing: you can "bank" your tech in your 'base'. so if you don't have enough to level up just yet, you can explore a bit more relaxed without risking a huge amount or tech doing so.
the levels are very interconnected and cramped full of cut backs, secrets and shortcuts. you want to explore and find stuff. some of the areas are sealed off and can only be opened once you reach a certain (energy-)level. unlocking them is essential for progress and if not i pays off most of the time anyways. since all the areas of the game are industrial based in their design, there is a lot of weird ways to have plattforms and tunnels and so on to connect and tie together areas. thus they are more compact and complex and not quite as sprawling in since.
tl;dr: if you are into tactical 3rd person action adventures and are fond of scifi as well, then you will probably love it.

I've played the souls games for 100s of hours. I also played the developers previous games Lords of the fallen.
I like it. It has a lot of what makes the souls games good and a few fresh ideas.
Good:
- DS1 style level design, compact with shortcuts, consistent theme.
-Combat is fluid and well done. It has a backstabs which rewards good positioning.
- The limb cutting for resources is a good idea well executed.
- The implant and rig system is a quite nice allowing more customization than is normally available in a souls game.
Not so good:
- While the soundtrack is fine I find the use of songs annoying, there aren't very many and the country song playing in ops is driving me nuts. I'd pay money for a DLC disabling it.
- I find some of the mobs a little unfair. Many of them have leap or combo attacks that come out super fast which will 1 shot you with little chance to dodge. Also I think a few of the mobs have a little too much HP. I don't mind lethality but damage sink design is bad in my opinion.
- Your guy does not seem to have much in the way of iframes during dodging meaning that you'll often have to dodge away from enemies. This leads to drawn out fights which is a little boring but necessary since enemies are so lethal and hard to stunlock. I prefer the souls games in this area.
- Emphasis on thrash mobs over bosses. It's alright, but I like boss fights more. The ones i've seen so far have been OK though.
- Weapon/armor variety. I'd like a little more diversity in styles, but I guess the implant system sort of makes up for it.
Overall I like it quite a bit, it's better than Lords of the Fallen. It still does not rank among the souls games but it's getting closer.

Plague Inc: Evolved is an upgraded version of a tablet game named Plague Inc, which basically means it has scenarios included.
It is a quick game (20 min on highest speed, which is easy to play on, just use space bar to pause).  It is unique because it focuses 100% on strategy.  While most strategy games include some elements of tactics, here you make choices for your disease and everything else in simulated.
Your goal is to spread your disease and wipe humanity from the earth.  The game gives you DNA points as your disease spreads and also through random events.  You spend your DNA points to upgrade the disease.  A simple game progresses like this: (1) spread the disease quickly without being noticed (2) after it is noticed, make it spread faster without scaring the world into thinking a cure is necessary (3) start killing people and race to kill everyone before a cure is found.
The game is not reality simulator.  In real life, diseases don't mutate unilaterally in all 7 billion infected people and disease research does not progress to completion in weeks or months.
As an early access game, there is a lot of content.  You progress through the game by unlocking new diseases and disease traits, which keep throwing strategy change-ups to keep it freesh.  Likewise, there are many scenarios.  I read some guides and it is clear the game has been modified/tweaked as of late for difficulty.  So the game seems pretty much finished, but needs some balancing.  There are achievements that are impossible to get, such as killing the world with zombie virus without creating zombies.  It is impossible to make the pre-zombie virus lethal enough to out-race the cure even if you get the world 100% infected first.  Also, cold weather is overpowered.  To spread disease to Greenland and Iceland, cold weather I & II is mandatory.  I have to build every strategy around infected Greenland, which saps a little fun out of it.
I enjoy this game and it may might be slightly too hard in its current incarnation, maybe that's for you, maybe it isn't.  Nonetheless, the play is "infectious" and each game is fast.

This is an excellent game which has been lovingly put together with a mind to history. It's also a rare item, as it deals with WWI company sized tactics and rarer still that it is available for Mac. I have played the French, Russsian, and a bit of the British campaign as well as trying out the tank campaign, and I have to say the game is highly enjoyable, especially if you know much about World War I history. The French actually begin the campaign in bright uniforms whih are historically accurate and so you really get a feel for how surreal the battles must have looked at the start of the war, with combatants dressed in near Napoleonic attire. As the French campaign progresses, your change uniforms to the "ciel blue" variety that we are more used to seeing, (not that it was much better as far as camoflauge went) and the campaigns introduce new realities of war like trenches (which are well done) and new technologies for slaughtering your enemy. I look forward to playing all of the campaigns eventually.
The game offers a "real war" mode which I recommend, in which most injuries will kill your men, and if you turn on the blood and limbs option, you may get a good sense of what the horrific battlefields were like, with heroic troops being blown to bits with their equipment (your troops can salvage enemy medical kits, ammo, and equipment... you can even steal their hats for souvenirs).
All in all, a really solid effort and it seems the developers are always trying to add more. Highly recommend if you want to play the campaigns. I haven't really played the multiplayer but the game is stable and has an active community of map makers. Well worth checking out especially if you like the time period (who doesn't find WWI era tanks kinda cool)?

Bad Company 2 was the definitive modern combat fps at the time of release.  It beats the pants off Call of Duty in every possible way, and even has a decent single player campaign.  While it has since been eclipsed by Battlefield 3 and 4, it still holds up very well.  Looking back at Bad Company 2 now that Battlefield 3 and 4 are out, I can't help but miss some aspects of it.
First of all is the single player campaign.  DICE seems to be too focused on copying Call of Duty in this department these days, which is the absolute worst thing they could do.  Bad Company 2 is well written and doesn't have too much hand-holding so you still feel in control.
Second is the multiplayer maps.  Bad Company 2 had some fantastic maps and while most of Battlefield 3's maps were pretty good as well, Battlefield 4's maps are largely disappointing and making me want some of the Bad Company 2 maps back.  It would be great to see some of these maps updated and brought into the new game, but DICE seems to be focusing on Battlefield 2 and 3 maps for that.
As for the PC version, it's good though lacking in some options.  FOV must be changed in the config files and unfortunately single player cutscenes (which there are a fair amount of) will reset the FOV to default.  The interface was very mouse-friendly, and I still find it more usable than either or the newer games' interfaces, though this game doesn't have as much customization.
The game's still fun and doesn't require Origin or Battlelog to play, though I couldn't tell you how many people still play it.  There's also the Vietnam expansion available, which is something I haven't seen a competing release for in a long time.

Howdy! So I've played nearly 6 hours of this game, and I've got to say, I have had fun with it. I'm not too good at boring, regular reviews, so I'll do a Pro/Con list.
-Big map, plenty of places to go.
-The exploration is pretty fun. While it isn't super-depth like some games such as No Man's Sky, exploring the galaxy, discovering new areas, and other things are quite fun.
-The economy seems real and working. When you go to a planet, it tells gives you the description of said planet. Then, in the Port where you can buy & sell things, while the prices constantly change a little bit (like in real life), everything is in the price range that the description of the planet says it is. For example, I forget the name of this planet, (It might have been New Greenland, but I'm pretty sure it wasn't...), but the description says that pretty much the only occupation you can have on the planet is making warm, fur coats, which all of the inhabitants do. It also says that they often run out of food (or something similar). Thus, when you go to the Port, clothing prices to buy and sell are low, because everyone makes so many (Capitalism at it's finest), and food prices are high (because they don't want to sell their precious food, and will pay high amounts of money to get more).
-Has nice history and lore.
-Missions are all-around good. There are so many randomly-generated missions to choose from, most of which pay pretty well while not making the game a cake-walk. Then the scripted missions are well-thought out, have some comic relief, and are slightly challenging but pay well for your efforts.
-Very fast loading times.
-Feels like a living, breathing galaxy.
-6 hours in, and I'm not seeing much of the main storyline, except for
-Pirates are too common. When there are this many, it doesn't seem real. Luckily the game saves every time after leaving a planet, so that helps. Also, while some games have looong death/game over screens, then take forever to load, that's quite the opposite with Endless Sky. Once you die, you hit Esc, then once you're at the main-menu, can jump right back into the game. It doesn't take long and is very fast. Heh, I've said so many good things in this "Con" it's almost a Pro. :p
-The game doesn't tell you too much, mainly about controls, and how to do stuff, though this isn't really a problem after about an hour of playing. To save you new guys some grief, press Tab to fire your main weapon, Q to fire your secondary weapon, and just visit a planet to refuel your hyperdrive for free. It also happens automatically, so you don't need to worry.
Well, I'm glad you read this far. Hopefully this is an influence to making the right choice for you; buying this game or not.

It's basically what it claims to be: A barebones version of a 2D space combat game.
It's very reminiscent of Mount and Blade, in the sense that it rips off all the gameplay elements except the part where there's a challenge. And also unit training. None of that in this game, you just collect units at any spaceports and then you offload those units into the next ship you steal for a free brand new ship that is just as good as buying it off the market. A ship that is customizable. Well, not really. Ships come with a set of guns, engines, batteries, shields and battery chargers. Those things can be changed, but the ship itself will never have the room to upgrade it, unless you downgrade another aspect of it. Wether it be gun emplacements, gun "room" or ship "room", you'll never get anything better than the default unless you loot the ultra rare engines. By offloading your units into a ship you stole. You can try to take over the world, but like in Warband, it's an insane difficulty leap that doesn't do much for you.
There's only interest for the first hour of gameplay, where you don't instantly obliterate everything you come across and you try to steal a ship without a merchant fleet obliterating it. And it's free, so enjoy that free 1 hour of entertainement.
Oh yeah, also it has that old-timey logic of making the buttons match the first letter of the word rather than the standard keyboard layout. So Jump is J, turning is AWSD, firing is Shift or something, that one doesn't make sense, Land is L, Board is B.

A very viable attempt to create a sci-fi variant of Dark Souls. Many mechanics and overall gameplay seem stripped right out of the Dark Souls series, but with a few unique twists added. The loot mechanic where the player has to cut off body parts to receive that part of the armor set or the used weapon is especially gratifying and rewarding.
There's a nice variety of weapons and armor sets to be collected, but player skill remains the most important resource. There is hardly any "trash mob" in the game - all enemies can kill you with a few hits. Learning how to dodge their attacks and recognize their patterns is more important than the latest armor upgrade or unlocking a new implant slot. Maybe that's also the reason why there are only five bosses in the game - since the regular enemies remain challenging for quite a while, there is little need for more challenging boss fights inbetween.
There are a few shortcomings: It's not the longest game in the world and will take you about 15-30 hours to beat. Still decent, but it's no Witcher 3. You also gotta be careful with weapon combos, because they might take longer than anticipated and it's difficult to cancel an ongoing combo, often leaving you vulnerable to get stunned by the enemy. The level design also takes some getting used to - it's easy to get lost in some of the levels and you might stumble across an unexpected hole in the floor and plummet to your death. Does not happen often, though... just be careful where you walk or jump to.
It does not feel as rich as the original Dark Souls, with the levels and gameplay a bit more streamlined and the world feeling more compartmentalized into discrete levels, sabotaging the open world aspect a bit. The story never quite unleashes its full potential and will hardly leave a lasting impression on you - although there are quite a few neat ideas and moments, especially in the last few acts.
Nevertheless a good game. The combat is satisfying and new enemy types and variants pop up very regularly, keeping you on your toes all the time. It's hard, but rarely unfair, if you're careful enough and not push your luck too far. If you're a fan of "Dark Souls", then this should be quite entertaining. Maybe it's too short for a full-price purchase, but then maybe just wait for a good sale!?

I RECOMMEND THIS WITH A CAVEAT!!!
If you enjoy a game that gets extremely challenging, this is definately your game.
However you need to keep in mind the level of challenge between the beginning/middle of the game and the end game is exponentially different, and i dont know if this is on purpose or not. And some of the environment's falling will get you killed more than the enemy, but that just requires you to be careful and not accidently fall off a ledge or into poison gas.
But this game does a few things very well, and beautifully. The combat system is amazing! Very fun, and the bosses first group of bosses were a solid challenge, and pretty enjoyable. The combos and weapons are very easy to get used to and the executions are very enjoyable to watch. The farm system was good until end game (more on that soon), but of my 24 some odd hours played, i can honestly say i enjoyed almost all the game.
The bad part is the end game: This is where it divides those looking for an enjoyable challenge, to the extreme hard core that demand to conquer the near impossible. As you reach the end of the game, near everything can kill you in 1 - 3 hits, on top of the fact that 80% of enemies in the end game are faster than you, and have means of ensuring you dont get a full combo. due note that they are still beatable. The problem is it makes fighting a group of enemies extremely challenging and a major resource drain if you survive. The damage you take is increased the point where there is no point of farming for better gear because it feels like a waste of time.
I have every intention on completing the game 100% but the huge spike in challenge is borderline game breaking, and now im playing because of pride, not actual enjoyment. If you consider yourself a casual gamer, i would stay away from this game. If you are looking for a something very challenging and dont mind a game that needs just a little bit more polish, look no further because this game will treat you well.

Big fan of the Souls games, which so many people compare this one to. However, the biggest difference between this game and a Souls game is the deaths. Every - or at least most - death[s] in a Souls game feels deserved to some extent: dodging the wrong way, dodging into an attack, not managing your stamina, so on. In The Surge, deaths are about as unpredictable as the AIs detection range. For example, in just the second sector of the game, the heavy enemies can quite easily catch you with a poorly telegraphed attack that will do 2/3rds of your health. Mind you, stamina preservation is EXTREMELY difficult in this game, and you will rarely stagger an enemy with the inconsistent (and seemingly AI biased) "poise" system the game has. The areas are complex in a really messy way, the gameplay has actually gotten stale within about an hour of playing, and the customization really feels unimpactful. Additionally, if you don't like the main character's stoic and milquetoast personality, tough♥♥♥♥♥♥
In summary: The game's combat is self-limiting and uninteresting, difficulty curve is needlessly/defeatingly steep (think NG+7 Dark Souls, but less fun), and, maybe most importantly, the environment is TOO. DAMN. DARK.
Would strongly advise not to buy.

After Lords of the Fallen you would think the developers would learn and create a richer experience? Nope, this is not the case with The Surge. With only around 3 hours in, my view might change down the road if I were to put more hours, unfortunately a number of things simply prevent me from mustering the desire to play further:
a. Gated progression
Instead of having the ability to go anywhere you please from the get-go, you have to grind and dump points into your suit to open up areas/shortcuts. While this could of turned out great, it seems as if I'm wasting points by not dumping them into crafting gear. The implants do rely on core power yet the ones I obtained did not feel like they were making a difference (except for STARTING ones such as the "Estus Flask" one or the enemy HP bar display).
b. Weapon proficiency
Supposedly higher weapon proficiency grants faster weapon strikes. At level 8 (after a lot of grinding) I'm still hitting slow as hell with a one-hander. So I guess that's a good thing as it would allow me to forgo the mechanic and use another weapon without it? If that's the case why have it in the first place...
c. Combat
While the combat in general is fine, I have to say performing backstabs is a hit or miss (pun intended). Sometimes they work and sometimes they do not when I'm standing behind the enemy. Quick kills become essential when you simply want scraps or progression. This is especially evident as the devs decided to put more "trash" type enemies blocking your path and lowering the boss count.
d. Level design
Level design felt uninspired and claustrophobic for the most part. I was hoping to traverse a larger world with multiple med bays. Instead what I experienced was a tight area with a lot of shortcuts pointing back to a single safe zone.
e. Med Bay
Normally I wouldn't mention this but whose idea was to use that god awful music... It just feels so out of place.
f. Build Variety
The game was built with melee in mind. There are no ranged attacks that I know of/was able to use, significantly limiting gameplay.
g. Story
I guess the devs got lazy and went the full souls route in exposition. The problem here is that while the Souls series did not stand up on its story, its gameplay made up for it. With The Surge you have both that have fallen flat on their face.
In conclusion, I wish Nioh would get ported onto PC...

Plague Inc: Evolved is an upgraded version of a tablet game named Plague Inc, which basically means it has scenarios included.
It is a quick game (20 min on highest speed, which is easy to play on, just use space bar to pause).  It is unique because it focuses 100% on strategy.  While most strategy games include some elements of tactics, here you make choices for your disease and everything else in simulated.
Your goal is to spread your disease and wipe humanity from the earth.  The game gives you DNA points as your disease spreads and also through random events.  You spend your DNA points to upgrade the disease.  A simple game progresses like this: (1) spread the disease quickly without being noticed (2) after it is noticed, make it spread faster without scaring the world into thinking a cure is necessary (3) start killing people and race to kill everyone before a cure is found.
The game is not reality simulator.  In real life, diseases don't mutate unilaterally in all 7 billion infected people and disease research does not progress to completion in weeks or months.
As an early access game, there is a lot of content.  You progress through the game by unlocking new diseases and disease traits, which keep throwing strategy change-ups to keep it freesh.  Likewise, there are many scenarios.  I read some guides and it is clear the game has been modified/tweaked as of late for difficulty.  So the game seems pretty much finished, but needs some balancing.  There are achievements that are impossible to get, such as killing the world with zombie virus without creating zombies.  It is impossible to make the pre-zombie virus lethal enough to out-race the cure even if you get the world 100% infected first.  Also, cold weather is overpowered.  To spread disease to Greenland and Iceland, cold weather I & II is mandatory.  I have to build every strategy around infected Greenland, which saps a little fun out of it.
I enjoy this game and it may might be slightly too hard in its current incarnation, maybe that's for you, maybe it isn't.  Nonetheless, the play is "infectious" and each game is fast.

When I first installed this game, I was expecting not to love it. Less than two weeks later, I've logged 68 hours in it. While there is a learning curve and the game kind of just drops you into the middle of a vast universe in the beginning, if you can make it past the opening hours, then you're gold. There is an insane amount of hidden content just waiting to be discovered in the game's vast, open world.
If you're a lore junkie like me you'll be happy to know that there is flavor text for every planet you can explore and every ship, weapon, or modification you can purchase. The world is deceptively huge and expands exponentially as you progress through the story which is must more robust and well-written than I could ever have expected from a free, open-source game.
In fact, the fact that the game is open-source is its greatest strength. A lot of the content that exists right now was created by and for community members, and more of just the same content is on its way. Development is a constant process that anyone and everyone can become involved in, and I find that very beautiful.

The Surge is a good entry into the Soulsborne genre, but have quite some flaws. It is just a shame that the developers should think more about "Is this a fun mechanic?" or "Is this enemy type fair?". More about that later.
It looks reaaaally good, runs smooth on my I7, 1070 setup. It has controller issues where the camera and controls suddenly feel like they are stuck in cirup. To fix this I have to reconnect my controller. You can see the issue when this suddenly starts happening in a hectic fight.
Story is pretty meh. NPC's are pretty meh (except Irina, she is awesome and the only one that had some screentime).
I looove the combat. It feels rewarding, and the targeting system is a nice touch. It is heavy, and every blow counts. The various weapon types are very different from each other, but each weapon type have the same moves regardless if it the first weapon in the game or the last one.
Now, what I reaaaally dont like.
It is unfair. Sooooooo unfair.
You like enemies following you 360 degrees with their heavy attacks? Here you go!
You like stunattacks that can hit trough walls and containers? Sure!
How about instant kill attacks from miles away from enemies in the last area? No problemo!
Seriously, I loved the game UP TILL the last area. This area takes away everything you have learned about combat, and throws it out the window. AT that point, this was a solid 8/10 title from me. This area alone is NO fun, and you are better off just running past the enemies.
7/10 if you like Soulsborne games.
6/10 if this is your first entry into the genre.

This is an interesting one ... a rollercoaster of emotions so far. When I started out I was amazed. I was aware I wouldn't really like the environment much because the tech-production-warehouse setting has been dead to me since Doom (the original one, mind you ;-) Knowing that I came for the combat (and hopefully, the story). So I was surprised to see what effort went into building the levels. I still find the setting boring, but it has been created by a very competent team.
Difficulty level was fine for the first area. Entering the second area it started ramping up until I hit a brick wall somewhere in the middle of it. Coming up from a shortcut into an area covered in toxic waste with two leaping, sting-tailed robodogs and a guard was something I think I couldn't handle, because I was dead so quickly without time to learn anything about the enemy. The other option was to slog through the initial path, wasting minutes and minutes to end up like 30 meters from that other point, but in a much better place (from a tactical point of view). Only to be killed 10 seconds later.
As frustration built up, I had to decide to either drop the game or change my playstyle. I chose the latter. Went after some gear, tried different weapons and most of all, juggled around with implants (that basically define your character). And I found a combination that worked for me.
It's been like this ever since. Progress, hit wall, find new combination (though it's getting easier, of course), profit. You can turn your character into something completely different, there is not much holding you back. Sure, you need to grind enemies for blueprints and materials, but you get what you go for - if you need a piece of armor an enemy wears, target it and rip it off. The other thing holding you back is more serious, and I totally don't like it: weapon proficiency. It's basically an Elder Scrolls 'level-up-by-use' stat for a weapon class that increases as you fight with a weapon of that type; it factors into the damage you deal with said weapon class. This, of course, counters the ease with which you can change your whole character setup, as raising weapon proficiency is a very slow process. That's a design choice I can't really understand. Weapons scale differently with proficiency, but that does not mitigate the problem much as the low-scaling weapons don't necessarily do good (base) damage ...
Anyway, this game really pushes the player's ability to adapt, a lot more than the Souls series, I have to say. While Souls focuses on bosses mostly, almost every enemy in The Surge has miniboss-like qualities. You can't really question that design choice, but in my opinion Souls had the better idea. The problem is that after a death in The Surge, in most cases you'll have to fight every enemy again up to the point where you died, to get your 'scrap' back. Where in Souls you could try to sneak and run by, this is rarely an option here, not only because it's difficult, but also because you usually
to kill mobs on the way. Those kills give you extra time to reach your destination, as there is a timer ticking down once you start your recovery run. So unless you're lucky and died close to a shortcut, you'll be playing
the same stuff twice ... or many more times. Which can be really annoying. On the plus side you can bank your 'scrap' like in Lords of the Fallen, which is a godsend should you get stuck somewhere in dire need of a levelup to equip just one more health implant or whatever: bank your stuff, make a short farming run, rinse & repeat. It's boring, but it works.
The game engine is far superior to the Souls engine. It has very precise collision detection - if you dodge and the enemy's weapon intersects your path, you get hit. No cheesy i-frames (some players say there
i-frames - well, they might be there, but I don't feel them). It's scary, but it's also fantastic. I wish Dark Souls could have had it. (Or not ... felt fine enough, cheesy or not - at least it made soloing well posiible.)
Combat in later areas requires new tactics, but somehow I felt I was being pushed into hit-and-run (well, dodge-hit-dodge, to be precise). Unfortunately, the game has a tendency to squeeze you into tight corridors that don't really suit this kind of fighting system. Exchanging blows does not seem to be an option. I admit that I didn't really try the heaviest armor with all but health implants, because I like nimble movement in games, but I'd be surprised if you can really build an effective, long-lasting tank in this game. (Let me know if you do.)
Like in the Souls series, combat has you see your animations through till the bitter end. You can't stop what you have begun. That in itself is not a bad thing, but I felt like many of the animations are longer than you'd think they are. You'll be surprised how long your attack really lasts when you're desperately mashing your dodge or 'heal' button :) Additionally, while there's a good number of combos you can use, it's difficult
to use them if you don't want them, because some of them are quite long and leave you wide open. That, for example, soured my love for staves when I swapped out the first one, a simple pipe (that basically has no combo, you can just hack on as long as your stamina allows) for a 'better' one with a very different moveset.
Also I felt that the weapon sounds were kind of weak. You'll probably laugh about that when you watch a trailer, but playing it I didn't really feel the 'oomph' of those giant pieces of metal clashing at each other or the enemy's armor. Neither 5.1 home cinema sound nor headphones delivered the gut punches I was waiting for. I actually played the game for hours without any sound at all, and it worked just as well except for the occasional cheap ambush.
Talking about cheap, yes, there are sections in the game that feel really cheap, just like in the Souls series. I used to think we had put sudden death in gaming behind us decades ago, but it was ressurrected years ago and is still thriving. It's just something you have to live with, at least if you aren't clairvoyant or don't have superhuman reflexes. You'll know what to expect on your next corpse run ... still, it's lame and a waste of time.
I didn't talk about the story here, and I'm afraid it's not the high point of the game (which is especially sad to me, because that's the prime thing I want from games - to tell me a story), but frankly, I wasn't really expecing it and so I won't really judge it for that. It does have a story, but don't buy it in the hope of clinging to your seat in suspense. It's a combat game, really.
All in all it's easy to put the Surge off as 'just another Souls clone', but I think it has enough character and ideas to stand on its own. It will be measured up against Soulsborne, of course, but in my opinion it's refined and original enough not to be labeled a clone.
Seeing the progress from Lords of the Fallen (which I quite liked, but obviously wasn't everybody's darling) to The Surge I can say I'm really looking forward to Deck 13's next project. And that's it, ladies and gentlemen - I need to go back to playing :)

I... Can't in good conscious recommend this as a 'good' game. Now if you want a fairly difficult game, that gets stale but ramps up in difficulty all the way through, have fun.
It tries to borrow from Darksouls, it gets the short cuts and everything right, but a big part of it is how well you can memorize the map of crampt sci-fi complexes in your head. Lot's of hidden items all over the place, but most of them are similar to the 'soul' items from darksouls.
There's no where near the ammount of weapon variety, and your 'drone' abilities are as close as you get to magic and are pretty subpar, to the point where I only really used it on bosses because I had nothing else to spend the building energy on.
You get mods, based on capacity kind of like in Warframe, and the cap is based on your core level (soul level). Honestly I was just going through the whole game with  HP up, and Regen for exploring, swapping it out to instant heals when fighting bosses. All their effects seem pretty eh save for the one I did fall in love with which was cutting dodge stamina in half, essentially letting you dodge like light load in darksouls. Sadly, I got this near the end of the game.
Dodging feels sketchy, it works, but it takes up tons of stamina and it doesn't feel as good as a roll. The block is mostly worthless in the long run the moment you realise enemies can poise right through your counter attack and hit you back by the time your animation finishes. You're better off dodging, then doing a single hit, rinse repeat.
Speaking of, heavy armor seems largely useless, because enemies have the same ammount of health as you, when you're at their level, and do the same if not more damage than you. I realised this way later into the game, when I shed my heavy armor in favor of a nimbler set, and only then was I able to proceed. Granted, after this point, most enemies encounters were either a win, or a death by 1-2 shots.
The story itself wasn't bad, the characters were pretty cool, and I felt bad for ONE character in specific, if you do their quest line. I didn't like the ending, I know there are two, but still sucked. And I rather enjoyed the darksoul endings.
Final part, the game is pretty grindy. The game had open slots for the 3rd exo suit with the most ammount of mod slots, capping at 110. I beat the game at lv 70, for the record, and this of course might explain why I kept getting one shot for the most part. But the game just isn't fun enough to grind on.
There seems to be a new game plus, but I'm just not really interested.
One bonus, I did like the fact that the main character was innitially stuck in a wheel chair. Don't see it too often.
I give it a 6 out of 10, I suppose.

The Surge is a more recent Dark Souls clone, and while that may seem like a bad thing, it most certainly is not. One the outset, you play as Warren, a paraplygic man who joins the mega-corporation CREA to heal him of his injury. Things don't go as planned and after a rather twisted operation where they graft an exoskeleton onto you, you're dumped onto the ouskirts of the city to seemingly fend for yourself.
The rest of the game is typical of these types of sci-fi stories; figure out whats going on, meet random survivors along the way, and kill everything and anything that tries to kill you. While that is not a bad thing, anyone expecting some kind of sci-fi epic will be sorely mistaken.
Gameplay is very Dark Souls-y. You have your two attacks, vertical and horizontal, a dodge, a block, and medpacks for healing. Combat is satisfying however, as Warren is inside this exoskeleton, his strength is vastly increased. Every attack has weight behind it, and slamming an enemy into the air as you defeat him really never gets old.
However, there is one tweak to this formula, the ability to target enemy limbs. Most enemies, not all, have various body parts that can be targeted. Majoraly the enemies in the game are humanoid, so you can target legs, arms, heads, torsos so on and so on. This comes into play not only to deal damage, enemy limbs can be armored or not, but also to get new gear. Like what that bad guy is wearing, well attack him enough and you can tear his arm off to get it. Like his weapon too? Well why not rip it from his corpse?
This limb targeting is very satisfying. Seeing new enemies, looking at thier gear, and eventually getting it after defeating them really is enjoyable. This also ties into the crafting system of the game. Inside of the operations center, the games equivalant of the bonfires, you'll find your crafting station. You need materials, and you get them from defeating and tearing limbs off of bad guys who are wearing the stuff you are. Its pretty clevar, actually, and gives incentive to continue to attempt to gather more gear from enemies, increasing your own prowess as you go.
This same cannot be sad for the environments. While initially they seem pretty cool, as the sci-fi setting allows, near the end you'll grow weary of the same old industial catwalks, metal doors, hallways, corridors, and random vent shafts. The game does lackluster job of explaining where you are in the world. This may be my inability to best guess where I am, or simply the environments just look too similar. But in Dark Souls fashion, the game does impliment shortcuts. This makes every area much easier to traverse, especially if you are defeated (and you will be) by the bosses.
Dark Souls always had a penchant for giving you massive beasts of bosses, and The Surge is no different. Most foes tower over Warren and easily kill him in 2-3 hits. But, just like its inspiration, there are patterns to be learned here, and once you give it a few goes, any boss can be bested. The boss design range from a typical Mech to interesting Waste Disposal bots.
While The Surge may never meet the inspirations lofty ambitions, it is fun. The combat is good and gory and give meaning to its limb targetting system. The bosses are great, and hard. Oh, the game is hard. Really hard. So you may want to get ready for that. It is unforgiving at times. But ya know what. I wouldn't want it any other way

I am going to reccomend this game, but, AT THE MOMENT, I'd not get it at full price.
As it stands, it's a bit painful to see it has the potential to be the next Company of Heores, but it falls short due to technicalities like bugs and a not optimized interface.
There are good and bad thigns about this game: for starters, is obvious that a lot of love went to make this game, which is great, this is definitely the best WW1 strategy game I've played and there is a LOT of tactical potential in this game.
For example, IT FEELS GREAT when you're trying to assault a position and you grab two or three guys of your squad and send them to flank, the squad micromanagment feels great and authentic, which is a very important aspect of any RTS.
The units, the models are all good, even tho there are still some balance issues (like one of the small tanks by the allies being waay too overpowered by the time it gets out, while the germans struggle a bit to put a counter on the field) - I mean, things are doable, but whereas it feels fgreat to micromanage a single unit, said micromanagement becomes a mess on the larger scale.
Here are some issues that are very annoying without (IMO) being a deal breaker, I hope the developer takes notice and improves on them, for this game SHOULD be great and played by a lot of people, at as it stands, it feels still like a beta.
- when you put units into buildings, the roof completely blocks your view, making almost impossible to position your soldiers on the windows you want.
- when summoned, machinegun and artillery and moratr crews start on the "ready" position, meaning you ahve ot manually click the "walk" position and then click on where they want to go, this is annoying because sometimes they just stay at the spawn point.
- the CTRL key is permanently bound to the "contorl mode", AND IT CAND BE CHANGED. which interferes with push to talk programs like discord, teamspeak or mumble... so basically when you talk, your units completely STOP doing what they were doing, which is annoying because
- there is no clickeable minimap, which means you ahve to travel manually all the way back in order to order stuff to your troops, which you ahve to do a lot because
- the ai needs improvement, right now is pasable, but given the fact there are so many options aviable for them to do, they just sometimes fall short on doing the appropiate stuf (for example, anti tank units ambuhing a tank and failing to throw AT grenades on their own)
- some bugs, like machinegun crews not able to climb some staris or you having A LOT of troops on a control point without being able to sieze it.
- the inability to put MG crews inside buildings
- the interface could be a lot smoother, like with the addition on mouseover tooltips and an easier and smoother way to grab/transfer equipment
THEN AGAIN, this list MIGHT SEEM too much, BUT THE GAME IS ACTUALLY ENJOYABLE SN GOOD once you get used to live with those issues, this is a good and lovely game on its idea, but at the moment (Dec 29, 2016) falls short of being 100% recommendable.
If you see it ON A SALE, by all means buy it, if you see it on full price and are in the mood for a WW1 strategy game, I'd reccomend it a 63 outta 100.
This game kinda deserves to be supported, for it has great potential. And I hope the developers get on fixing the annoyances.

Hexcells Infinite is the final Hexcells game and boasts a random puzzle generator along with its own set of hand-crafted puzzles. But how good is it? This is what I think of Hexcells Infinite.
Very good, in fact. As you would expect with a third entry it is the most feature complete and the best experience, in my opinion. It strikes a nice balance between the last two games in terms of difficulty and with it's random generator, you can play this game indefinitely. Everything you have come to expect from Hexcells is here, and it's brilliant.
Like before, your task remains the same; clear the board by colouring or deleting hexes, using the set rules of the game. You know the drill, troops. I think this title does a better job of mixing in all kinds of puzzles in terms of difficulty. For instance, I really struggled with one but afterward I didn't have any problems with the one after that. In Hexcells Plus it would have bludgeoned you to death daring you to take it on with your logic. My logic sucks. So no surprises I enjoyed this one more. There are fiendishly difficult puzzles though, don't worry about that.
The real reason why I love this one the most though is the random generator. This thing is awesome. It uses an eight digit seed to randomly assign you new puzzles at the click of a mouse. You could even feasibly play just one every day using the different dates as the seed. Simple but brilliant. I often log in and play five or so at a time, listening to music and just relaxing. The random puzzles aren't as hard as the hand-crafted ones, or as unique, but you occasionally get one that keeps you on your toes, just to make sure you're paying attention. Love it.
Other cool little features include in-level saving. I never realized this was needed until it was there. Now you can exit a puzzle anytime and pick up when you play again. Simple and effective. Also, the area of effect hexes(as I like to call them,) now have a toggle so the area that appears is outlined by a black line. This makes it much easier to see hexes in the zone without squinting. Excellent.
Overall, this is the best Hexcells experience. With 36 puzzle of its own, and with its random generator, there is enough here to keep you occupied for some time. I have no doubt this will remain my favourite puzzles game, and I'm a little sad there is no more Hexcells. In the meantime, however, I'll continue solving random puzzles and having a blast. Do yourself a favour and pick this one up. You won't regret it.

As Clash of Clans is to strategy and King of Thieves is to platformers, Catch Me is to stealth games (which is to say, "steal other players' resources for yourself" PvP). No pay-to-win here, though! It starts off pretty childishly simple but by levels 2 and 3 you'll have to start weighing how much you're willing to spend on infiltrations versus potential payoff. It feels incredibly like a port of a mobile game despite... not having a mobile version, but that doesn't particularly detract from the experience. If you don't like the tap to move mechanic there's also a WASD control scheme. It's easy to learn, hard to master, and probably the biggest problem is a fairly small playerbase. At least it's just a $5 barrier to entry.
As a tip to those starting out, certain guards (i.e. clowns) are clumsy and will reveal not only themselves on the map, but even stealthier units (i.e. dogs) that are in range. Some torches on the walls will also reveal units. Making sure some of your guards are still hidden by the fog when setting up your maze is the best way to catch people with their pants down.

Words cannot describe how powerful and emotionally moving this game is. In point of fact, I would say that 3D Ultra Minigolf Adventures sets a new standard not only for the videogame industry, but also for all art in any medium. The work of William Shakespeare wilts in comparison to the raw energy that radiates from this majestic creation.
Fools might say that 3D Ultra Minigolf Adventures is "glitchy", "broken", or worse yet "borderline unplayable". Those people are unwashed heathens whose puny minds simply cannot comprehend the intricacies of high art. Academics are able to correctly see Wanako Games' mind-bending piece illustrates the simple truth that, since human beings are inherently flawed creatures, all things that they create will in turn be inherently flawed. Take, for example, the "Outer Space" courses. Whenever I attempt to play on any of these courses, my computer begins to dry heave like a bloated walrus attempting to give birth to a tractor-trailer. Fools might see this as a flaw, but those academics who can understand what Wanako Games is attempting to achieve here can begin to appreciate the majesty of such a feature. Space is often called the final frontier, and by making the game near impossible to play on any of the Outer Space courses, Wanako underscores human limitations. When the you attempt to push the limits of humanity Wanako breaks your computer and forces you to confront the fact that there are certain things human beings cannot do. Thus, Wanako furthers the theme of the inherent failings of humanity. While another game might seek to blindly empower the player, 3D Ultra Minigolf Adventures is far more intentioned and careful in its gameplay.
Wanako Games is also pushing the boundaries of gaming, art, and science in its character design. Wanako illustrates this pioneering in the character of Rosie. While many other characters bear a semblance of humanity, Rosie's painfully contorted spine can lead many players to the correct assumption that she is actually a snake person from the planet Tsaalormandorian IV. This is all told not through lengthy and boring pages of text, but rather through the richness of her character design. When playing Rosie, the player immediately knows the background of her character, the playing experience gains that much more depth. Once the player has collected eleven of the Blackheart Soul Stones from the “Old West” courses, they learn that Tsaalormandorian IV lacks the necessary resources to provide food. From this, players can infer that Rosie is playing mini golf in an attempt to harvest mole people to bring back to her home planet and feed to her family. This level of storytelling and world building is not simply impressive because of its depth and emotional weight, but because of how much of it Wanako games is able to communicate with Rosie's character design alone. And this is only one character!

Overall, I give 3D Ultra Minigolf Adventures a 10/10 and declare it a must play for any connoisseur of games.

If you played and enjoyed any of the Escape Velocity (EV) games you should definitely try this game out. What do you have to lose (except a few minutes if you hate it, which you won't).
Now, this is not a finished game, but there is already quite a bit of content to enjoy. It's the same concept as EV, so you fly around in your crappy little spaceship, doing missions/trading etc. until you can afford a better ship - rinse and repeat. What makes this enjoyable is the variety of available playstyles that stems from a substantial number of ships and upgrades you can choose from. There are a lot of carrots dangling in front of you.
There are some issues with the game that could possible be improved upon, mostly balancing, Please note that this will be affected by personal taste and, to some extent, skill. There are a few combinations of ships and outfits that work really well together, others are borderline useless (or I didn't figure out how to cerrectly adapt my playstyle). You can still customize your ships to a large extent (prioritizing speed, shields, armor, damage, ...) and since you don't lose any money when changing outfits experimenting is definitely encouraged. It's just that in the end you will most likely end up with a certain large ship that offers by far the best options, not counting story-related ships.
Overal progression is a little slow at start, but that's to be expected. Once you can more or less safely disable and board the first small ships, things speed up.
I really liked the approach of attaching a heavy financial toll to capturing ships (you have to pay benefits for your fallen soldiers). Smart. Overall there are a couple of this neat little ideas that gave me the feeling that some thought and care went into making this.
Can't wait to see this game progress further, as replay value at the moment is rather limited (only one faction-storyline included)
So the tl;dr
+Great Value! (thanks Captain Obvious...)
+enjoyable ride with a lot of care put into outfit descriptions, planet descriptions etc.
+lots of ways to play
-a little grindy at the start
-lack of content for replayability at the moment
Would happily pay for this, even the unfinished product. At no cost an easy 10/10.

I just want to clear something up.  There's a few reviews out there saying the combat is unfair, enemies are cheap, blocking is bad, etc.  None of that is true.  The combat is extremely fair, probably moreso than Dark Souls as there's no backstab fishing or cheap parry spamming.  Your stamina management matters, knowing when to block, dodge, jump, or duck attacks matters, and properly executing a plan in combat pays off.  R1 spammers will not find any joy here, if you go in with the mentality that this is just a Dark Souls knockoff with scifi pants on, you're going to get destroyed.
This is closer to Bloodborne than it is to Dark Souls, it's faster paced and has a serious emphasis on learning movesets, even for standard enemies.  If you're not prepared to get a bit of grind on for better gear and to really learn your weapon and how the enemies have to be approached, you'll end up refunding the game thinking it's not good.
It's fine, it's just different.
If you put Bioshock, Soma, Nier,  Dark Souls into a blender, you get The Surge.
