Another game where I wished there was more than just an arbitrary "thumbs up" or "thumbs down" option when placing a review. Skip to the final paragraph for the tl;dr of this all.
First off, I think this game is very fairly priced for what it provides and there's a huge amount I'm happy with in regards to it. At the same measure this game has a lot of flaws that can quickly become frustrating and would turn many off of the game, so let's get to it.
The game is set in the future where Earth's atmosphere is degrading and Project Resolve is started to reseed the atmosphere and save humanity. You play as Warren, a new employee at the CREO facility at the start of the game where you're outfited with the all important EXO-rig. Shortly after, things get royally messed up and it's up to you to save everything from getting worse.
I've heard it called a Souls-Like game and that's not entirely untrue, there's a lot there for Souls fans to enjoy, as well as some familiar mechanics with some changes.
Visually I will say it's above average. I've seen some texture glitches and enemies popping-in at a distance but nothing fundamentally bad. The locations look good and some of the enemies are pretty decent, the main mob you'll be fighting are essentially brain-fried humans wearing mechanical exoskeletons. Zombies wearing murderbots is a farily disturbing concept and they did a good job bringing that to life.
You pick from a selection of weapons that are either dual-wielded, one-handed, staves, one-handed heavy or two handed. Which range from fast, medium and slow in terms of attatck speed. You also pick between light, medium or heavy armor which all give certain benefits from wearing a full set, as well as a loadout of implants which affect everything from health, stamina to enemy health readouts.
Combat takes some getting used to, as you can target specific bodyparts of an enemy to cut them off and reap crafting components to upgrade your weapons and armor. Similarly, you can attack unarmored bodyparts to kill an enemy faster, but get less or no loot in return. This can make for excellent strategy against tougher enemies as you cycle between attatcking armored and unarmored parts to kill them faster, and get the parts you need, but more on that later...
Combat is quick paced, but can feel stiff early on. Like most Souls games, once you attack you're commited to that action and can't do anything else until the attack animation is complete. This unfortunately means you can open yourself up to a counterattack from the enemy if you're trying to chain together a combo.
In terms of defense, you have a very tight and responsive dodge that reminds me of Bloodborne in its efficiency in avoiding attacks.
There's also a blocking and a manuever you can perform for defense by ducking or jumping to avoid an attack to follow up with a counter that can briefly stun some enemies, but this is where things fall apart.
Enemies deal an incredible amount of damage regardless of how heavy or well upgraded your armor is, most able to kill you in two hits, even some of the earlier enemiens. This makes the high-risk, high-reward system of dodge-countering completely unreliable since if you mess it up once, you'll almost certainly need to heal.
In fact, the damage some enemies deal to you makes it difficult to fight two enemies at once, and nearly impossible fighting three. The camera doesn't have as wide a view as I would like, making it hard to see what the enemy beside you is doing while you focus on the one in front, and while this can make for some harrowing combat, it also makes for some frustrating deaths going from full health to zero as you're hit from the side once, staggared, then hit once from the front.
This frustration is apparent in later levels as well, enemies become increasingly difficult to stagger, while you can be knocked backwards or even off your feet by almost every strike, meaning you could soon have to choose between trying to attack an armored area of the body that you need. You could cycle between armored and unarmored parts, but unless you deal an unspecified amount of damage to that bodypart, it might not be cut off for your finishing move. This lack of late game staggering also makes combo attacks fairly useless against fully armored enemies, and I resorted to a strategy of dashing forwards, striking, and dashing back repeatedly.
This sort of combat structure soon meant my Health was soon a tertiary consideration behind Stamina (which is the determination of how much you can dodge or attack), and energy (Which allows you to perform finishing moves, summon your drone, or if you have the right implants, heal). The main aim ultimately became to avoid getting hit, with the block button becoming completely underused.
Weapons are fairly unbalanced as well, staves are the best weapons, having good speed, stagger most enemies decently, and have a powerful and fast lunge attack. While heavy weapons might hit hard, but they're so dangerously slow that if you hit an enemy with them and they don't stagger, you are almost certainly going to be hit with a counterattack.
I ultimately only ever used the dual-wield weapons or the staves.
With that out of the way, I did enjoy the level design. Each level only has one checkpoint/hub where you can store your tech scraps (the games equivilent of EXP, which is dropped on death and needs to be retrieved on a time limit), level up, and upgrade your gear.
This leads to levels that all have several shortcuts that can lead back to the central area, and during particularly harrowing parts make you start trying to calculate just how far you've gone and if you'll be able to double back soon. I would say the levels have a sort of spiderweb pattern to them, several paths starting out from a central spot that all lead back to it once you follow them long enough.
However this does lead to a few 'Metroidvania' style backtracking as you'll see locked doors or containers you can't access until you've sufficiently leveled or aquired specific gear.
It has flaws. A lot of them. But it also has potential for improvement and has a combat system that only needs some balancing issues to be tweaked to really make it shine. I have seen comments from the developers in some forums saying they will address the issues of the amount of damage enemies deal, and if this is the case I assume other aspects of game rebalancing will also occur.
The game isn't quite a diamond-in-the-rough yet, but maybe some work from the devs will bring out the gleam that's hidden under there.
I recommend waiting for this game to recieve further patches, but if you're a Souls fan definitely grab it if it's on sale. Until then, and unless you really need a Souls-like fix, I wouldn't recommend this game.

Hexcells Infinite is yet another standalone expansion to Hexcells, and like Hexcells Plus, just adds a whole new set of puzzles without really improving the game in any way. All of the same shortcomings are still present and accounted for: menu icons are still unintuitive and lack any sort of tooltip to explain what they do; completed levels still do not track how many mistakes were made; the soundtrack is still the same one track on a loop; and there is still no "maybe" marker for bigger, tougher puzzles. The menu just felt broken in general, with clipped text and overlapping elements. Difficulty-wise, Infinite is on par with Plus - much tougher than the original game, but unlike previous games, there was at least one puzzle that required a 50-50 guess to complete. I looked at the last couple of unopened cells every which way and there were simply not enough clues to deduce where the blue cells hide, which is disappointing in a puzzle game. The only real addition is a random puzzle generator, and it is rather underwhelming. All of the puzzles I generated were pretty much identical blobs of cells that were far too easy to solve and got repetitive very fast. It is a nice addition for those who can’t get enough of these puzzles, but it would be much more valuable if the generator could come up with a greater variation of tougher patterns. All in all, though, the core gameplay of Hexcells Infinite is still just as good as its predecessors and is still definitely worth buying.

The Cthulhu series from H.P. Lovecraft hasn’t seen much love in the form of games, but indie developers Zeboyd picked it up and turned it into a whimsical/parody 8 bit RPG and it’s done very well. You play as Cthulhu and pick up many party members along the way, but the whole point of the game is the great dungeon crawling that harkens back to the 80′s. You can attack like any RPG, but you have Tech attacks which are more powerful, magic, and then you can Unite with other members to combine devastating attacks. There are a ton of different attacks you learn when you level up, and you get a choice between two different things to level up with either stats or an attack, so by the end of the game each member has a huge arsenal to use.
The game is very close to the mythology with bosses that are from the story, towns named after the exact towns from the stories, plus the art style matches. The music is amazing with sweeping orchestral scores (in 8-bit midi audio mind you) that really moves you and sounds great. The story is hilarious with Cthulhu trying to redeem himself and become a true hero to raise his city of R’lyeh, but his interaction with characters in the world is really funny. Of course the game wouldn’t be complete without a huge over map to explore that has some secret dungeons, plus the environments and dungeons vary with lots of loot and chests to find.
However, the game’s biggest flaw is the extreme difficulty later on in the game, as well as the constant random battles which really drag the experience down. The devs tried toning this down by disabling random battles after you do 25 of them, but you will probably go through a dungeon before you hit that number. I also didn’t like how if you don’t level up high enough the end boss is impossible to beat, but each dungeon just really racks up the difficulty and requires you to grind a bit to get through the dungeon. I also didn’t like how you don’t really need a strategy to beat the enemies because you can just use the same one over and over through several dungeons. This causes the feeling of repetition to set in and makes you want the game just to end a little faster.
While the visuals are nice and give you a feeling of nostalgia they don’t look good in HD and the lack of battle animations, and everything that goes along with 8-bit graphics grates on your eyes after awhile. However, the Cthulhu license is rarely explored so any game to do so is welcomed, but this game is probably for hardcore RPG fans.
--Score: 8/10

Take an old-school RPG like Final Fantasy or something. Now, take the frustrating elements (save points, grinding, random battles, stocking up on HP and mana potions at every town, etc) and throw them away/make them bearable. Ladies and gentlemen, I give you Cthulhu Saves the World. If you're at all a retro RPG fan, you need to play this game.
If you're not a retro RPG fan, you still need to play this game for the funniness of the dialogue and the soundtrack.
If you're still not convinced, the price is really low for such a good RPG.
If you're STILL not convinced... Well, there's always the next CoD title.

This game is very interesting but, there is a lot wrong with it and it needs some of these issues fixed before it becomes fair and fun. I will say right now that you should not buy this game until it gets fixed. And I also want to add, I don’t want to get a refund for this game, I want it to be improved in the areas that it needs it; I want it to work in order to be fun and fair when you play. In this list of complaints I will not list the DLC as I personally don’t have a problem with it, and in my personal experience with the DLC it enriches and extends the single player which is something that I like, I didn’t buy this game for multiplayer … but I would like to see something for American campaign in the future …
First: friendly AI
one of the key parts of this game is totally broken, your troops are very stupid and can't do anything without you being there to hold their hand through everything; they won't fight, they won't take cover, they won't put on their gas masks, they will do anything in their power to ruin your day as a commander, and that is the WORST thing to have in a strategy game especially when you decide to try and copy enemy tactics and get slaughtered to something that the enemy AI does and usually come out of the situation with most of their men or even using some other tactic that just ends in a mess
Second: enemy AI
the enemy is exactly opposite of your guys, they know what they're doing, which is good it's nice to have an enemy that establishes a challenge ... it's another thing when they're too smart and are basically over powered, when it comes to just standard infantry they aren't too bad they'd be way batter if they had the same level of intelligence as the friendly AI, other than that the enemy infantry feels somewhat at home, but on the other hand with enemy weapon emplacement and artillery, way to mess up the game flow with nearly impassible sections of enemy guns, and tanks sure as hell don't help at all against the pin point accuracy of field artillery or mobile artillery like mortars and 37mm cannons, it's amazing when I can't finish a mission because of some damn field gun that I can't reach with either friendly armor or friendly infantry, or even the enemy machine gun emplacement that are almost impossible to get behind, but that's to be expected ... except when the thing can turn a full 360 degrees, and to add insult to injury ... when the game puts you behind the gun but your braindead friendly AI can't do a damn thing making me fail a mission
Third: the lack of the ability to call in my own reinforcements whenever I need
"War isn't fair but, a game should be..." ~ Brothers in Arms
the game of Brothers in Arms is a very moving one, it near perfectly replicates that landings at Normandy in June 1944 and Operation Market Garden in September 1944, it’s a game that realizes that its own gameplay can become way too hard and will offer to fully restore your health and revive all of your squad mates that might've died along the way unless they were scripted deaths, they realized that a game should be fun and challenging, not hard and punishing
what I'm try to get at is, give me the ability to call in reinforcements when I truly need them, yeah I know some of the missions do allow me to do that but, even those missions will royally screw with you but taking away your ability to do that, are you kidding me ? I, as a player of your game and being put in the position of a commander, need the ability to call in anything I may need; mortars, heavy MGs, field artillery, tanks (depending on the date), supply and armored trucks,   or infantry, if i don't have that ability its shoots up the difficulty to some extremely unfair state, if I can't make mistakes to learn from my own screw ups how am I going to learn at all, and basic training isn't an excuse to learn better tactics, Men of War: assault squad from what I remember has no training sequence to it but it gave me full control of reinforcing my men which made me learn from trial and error, the training that Battle of Empires teaches you is how to operate one soldier first and everything else second, no tactics, nothing, welcome to hell (First Fight isn't a training mission by the way, I learned nothing from it, and the AI prevented me from beating it)
Fourth: long unnecessary cut scenes that won’t take you back to the area of the map you were just at
this one is more personal than anything, in a game it can be nice to understand what is happening so far in the story/time era that we’re being presented with … it’s another thing when you’re forced to sit through unnecessary and long bits of dialogue that don’t provide anything, Men of War knew this and gave you the option to skip anything you didn’t want to sit through, especially when you can just look at your objectives menu and get the same information that was just given to you in a few short sentences
and as for the camera not taking you back to the area of the map you were just looking at, thanks, I love losing my troops to something I have no power over, which will most likely force me to restart a mission and get them to stay in a new position so I don’t lose as many
Fifth: where the hell am I supposed to go
this one seems like irony after just complaining about the other topic, but it isn’t and here’s why, in the game you are provided with a mini map which shows the location of enemies and the location of friendly troops, it even gives shows some parts of the map where there’s something that isn’t even interfering with the objective but you can still scroll over and check it out, maybe a downed German plane or a town that might come into play later, what it won’t show you is the objective … why do that? It doesn’t give me an unfair advantage, it just shows me where I need my guys to go, is that really such a big deal? Apparently so because, the developers have decided to give you a red arrow, no map placement of any kind, so are you close to the mission objective? Who knows, hey how about we abandon our braindead soldiers for a second and see, hopefully they can do something right for a cha- and mission failed, awesome, amazing, great job
Sixth: taking away friendly troops that are under your command for no reason
Game, “so you’re commanding a tank and a squad of soldiers, one of which is using a flamethrower, and we gave you these troops about a minute ago, is that correct?”
Me ,” yes that is correct, and I thank you for giving me the tools to at least stand a chance against these French MG impalements and mortars, without at least the tank I don’t think I’d be able to stand a chance”
Game,” here have these four troops, two have MP-18s and the others have Gewehr 98s”
Me,” but the friendly AI are brain dead, if I can’t control at least the tank then I won’t be able to win.”
Game,” and?”
Me,” well … will you at least be aiding me in the attack?”
Game,” nope, welcome to hell”
Mission failed,” the operation was a failure, maybe next time you’ll figure out how to keep your soldiers alive long enough to at least get passed the first objective.”
There are a lot more problems with the game, but I think I’ve ripped on it enough for today, I don’t hate this game and there are some fun missions, but that isn’t the point of this post, the point of this post is to reach the developers and try to get some of these main issues fixed, I know some of them come through these reviews so hopefully this one catches their attention.

As of writing this, I'm just over two hours into Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition, and I'm finding myself constantly impressed.  This has to be one of the most underrated open-world urban crime games I've ever played.  It is a phenomenally well-crafted and tightly packaged experience.  It's perfect for those who feel dirty playing GTA 5, who find it tries too hard to offend...and on the other extreme, those who want a slightly more immersive experience than the madhouse irreverance of Saints Row the Third.  Join the deadly Wei Shen, an undercover cop returning to his native Hong Kong from a long stay in the US, as he attempts to infiltrate and destroy one of the notorious underworld gangs running the brightly-lit city.  Drive anywhere, level up, and fight hard to enhance your reputation with both the Hong Kong PD and the ruthless Triad.  Take a breather by buying luxury items to improve your apartment, or by shopping for clothes to outfit Wei Shen in style.  Don't forget to use stylish martial arts combos and help people that need it - these things enhance your charisma and give you access to better clothes, equipment, and bonuses.
And the soundtrack is absolutely fantastic.
But don't think it'll be a cakewalk.  Saints Row the Third - one of my very favorite games - made me a clumsy driver who thought nothing of knocking down phone booths and roadside obstacles.  In Sleeping Dogs, this will cost you cop XP, so exercise discipline and be careful!  I'd come to the game hoping for a playable female protagonist and was disappointed - Wei Shen is the star of this story, and he's very male.  But don't worry.  This game isn't as chauvinistic and sexist (not to mention homophobic, transphobic, and just plain ugly) as GTA 5. Sleeping Dogs tells a serious story about real life for an imperfect cop seeking revenge in a dangerous city, and it proves that you don't need to be a jerk to create a truly masculine protagonist.
Sleeping Dogs is well-crafted, full of swag to purchase and earn, and loads of class, not to mention A-list voice talent from movie stars you'll be surprised to hear.  Hong Kong comes alive on your screen in all its splendor and danger, and it's been one crazy ride for me.  It's absolutely worth owning - and I strongly, strongly recommend it if you find it on a great sale.  I found it for 80% off on a Steam sale and I'm still wondering how I got so lucky.
Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition is one of the most solid titles I've purchased in a long time.

Legend of Grimrock is an enjoyable dungeon-crawler with great visuals, fluent movement and control, interesting lore, and offers several hours of gameplay without becoming dull. The enemies offer a decent challenge that requires your focus, and the multitude of puzzles and secrets are difficult to unravel and overcome. The biggest weakness is the lack of diversity in combat, as even with numerous weapons and three character classes, most foes can be overcome simply by circling around in a 2x2 grid and avoiding combat with more than one or two enemies. Well worth the price, but it becomes tedious and frustrating to do things over, and many later foes require too many hits to defeat given their complete lack of strategy and skills.

Exploration

I've just finished The Surge, so these thoughts are fresh off the top off my head. For clarity's sake, I've been playing this game off and on since release (6 days), and part of the reason it took so long to beat is that I quit from frustration a few times. This is a difficult game, and while it tries to be 'Dark Souls' hard, I think that a lot of the difficulty is what I'd call artificial. To make things worse, the difficulty is very spiky and nonsensical in many ways. The start is very hard, the second and third areas get a little easier, the next is a nightmare, the next is a little easier, then a nightmare, then a cakewalk... It's not very consistent, and that hurts it a lot as well.
Due to how difficult many of the 'trash mob' encounters are, I can only assume the developers intended for sort of the antithesis of Dark Souls. What I mean is that I think they wanted the monsters to be more difficult than the bosses, rather than Dark Souls' trash that you learn to clear efficiently followed by a very difficult boss. In most cases this stays a theme throughout the game, sans the third boss which is fairly challenging and the fourth which is (in my opinion) outright cheap. There are five bosses, and the fifth is a cakewalk - especially after the crazy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that is the fourth.
By now you're probably wondering if I clicked the wrong option on 'Do you recommend this game?'! I do recommend it, despite these and more flaws, because I do actually look back on my time with it fondly. While encounters can feel (and be) a little ridiculous, there is always a way to puzzle out a victory. While the difficulty can be really spiky, I still slogged through the nightmarish parts and then finally enjoyed feeling like a badass during the ending cakewalk. I think that The Surge's biggest weakness, more than any of the aforementioned problems, is that it tries too hard to be Dark Souls.
It goes for the vague plot that you have to puzzle out yourself, but reveals too much in too many words and just winds up a weird jumble of barely understandable plot hooks in the end. Similarly, it goes for the Souls-esque 'quest' system where you meet NPCs along the way and learn their stories while also helping them out. I think it fails there as well, mostly in offering little to no actual reward for them (I paid someone 25,000 Scrap just to have them kill an NPC I liked with no explanation and give me a crappy weapon) and just feeling... Out of place. Like they were just put in because, "Dark Souls does it, so why don't we?" I feel that they could have focused the effort they put into these Souls-esque tidbits into something innovative instead, and maybe something that the writers were a little better at.
Let me go into what I liked, before this becomes too negative, though! I really like the aesthetic. I've heard complaints that it's all just steel corridors, but I found the level design varied enough that I was never particularly bored with how things looked. Speaking of design, I also really love the armor and weapons! Some of them kind of strain to make sense within the setting (why is this guy beating me up with what is described as a medical tool?), but everything looks
and that's the thing I care about most. The animations are great, I believe motion captured, and everything feels weighty and awesome. I love it!
I really like the combat! Go figure, given I spent most of the game beating up dudes. The limb-targeting system is really cool, and I especially think that having to saw off enemy parts to make your own armor was a really cool design decision. Not only do the executions feel great to pull off, the parts they provide you with are valuable and tuned well enough so that grinding or farming never feels like much of a chore. I wound up using heavy armor, the Cerberus set to be specific, but I've also heard that lighter armor is just as fun. There are a lot of weapons in the game, though separated into only five categories - and those five categories all have very similar movesets... I didn't change my chosen weapon type ever, and stuck with one-handed all the way through the game. In a sort of unfortunate decision, you level weapon proficiencies as you use a weapon type more, and damage scales off of that. That means whatever you choose to use first and most at the start will probably always be the best type for you, unless you want to grind another up.
The implant system is another thing I liked; in favor of a traditional leveling system where you gain stats, you instead gain Core Power which lets you equip more powerful Implants that you find in the world. Certain thresholds of Core Power will let you equip more Implants, and you can also increase your Implant slots by finding new RIGs (though there are only 2). There are some no-brainer Implants like extra HP and your Healing Injections, but it was customizable enough that I swapped a lot of things in and out throughout the whole game regardless of those pseudo-necessary ones.
As for the story, I can't really say whether I liked or disliked it. It was there? I was vaguely engaged throughout most of the game, though the payoff near the end was lackluster to say the least. It wasn't enough of a let down to make me stop playing, or anything, but it sort of just made me go, "Oh. Alright." These types of games aren't known for having an impressive story to drive you forward, though! Even the Dark Souls games typically only have 'kill all the bosses and do the thing because destiny and stuff' as their motivation. You can look deeper into the lore and find a way more intricate story, mind! In the case of The Surge, though, I don't really think it's there.
In closing, The Surge is a fairly frustrating game that has its flaws, but I can still look back and go, "Yeah. I liked that." It has a great aesthetic and a wonderful combat system, but falls a little short in making some encounters mind-numbingly difficult (or just annoying) sometimes. The difficulty is spiky, though you will certainly feel like you've earned the easy jog of a one-man death machine at the end, and while the final boss was rather easy... I still liked it. And I'd recommend it! Maybe on sale, if you wanna play it safe.

If you were born and lived between the second half of the 80' and the first half of the 90', then you probably know that those times were the golden era for a videogame genre called "dungeon crawl". During that period there were games like "Dungeon Master" (1987), "Eye of the Beholder" (1991), "Ultima Underworld" (1992), "Lands of Lore" (1993), "Stonekeep" (1995), "Anvil of Dawn" (1995), among others, that represented that genre. Unfortunately, this videogame genre fell in decadence in the last years of the 90', until 2012, when Almost Human launched "Legend of Grimrock" that recover all the old school essence of those games that were just awesome for those times. I played those old games and I just complete this new one and I can say that the developers has done a really good job. Get ready to get lost in the dungeons, avoid mortal traps, find secrets, solve really hard puzzles, fight against different enemies, and after all, try to survive like in the old times!
Very classic playstyle game.  Dungeon crawling, secret finding and puzzle solving make this game very playable and fun for such a simple concept.

Early Access Watcher Reviews Catch Me
Update Version: 0.01.09
Disclosure: The game copy was bought by the reviewer.
Gameplay example:
Niche titles are beginning to surface more frequently on the Early Access market and ZuoBuLai Game's new project is no exception. Taking the role of a magician/thief, you are expected to organize heists with the help of other magicians and secure your own vaults from rivals. Over time the targets begin to get desperate and security measures are increased, meaning your tactics will have to evolve as well. It is a game of strategy, timing, pacing and above all else, magic. Is this enough to warrant a purchase or will the magic ware off before the appeal sets in?
The one stand out feature for this little title is the retro-style aesthetic. The general vibe is something between a circus performance and a noir Victorian production with everything from the character movements to the skill animations looking spectacular. Menus are clean cut and get their intended job done. Maps used for the mazes are rather barren, but given the objective of the game it can be overlooked. The music, however, is rather limited with just a couple of tracks ranging from smooth jazz rifts to an obnoxious disk swipe. Voice acting has some audio issues in terms of volume mixing, but for the most part it functions.
Gameplay reverts more into the standard puzzle game more so than the stealth them up genre. You will have to transverse mazes filled with guards and get rich by stealing from the safes scattered throughout. You can easily get through the first couple of levels just utilizing the sneak function, but the higher the level, the tougher the security types. To compensated for your lack of firepower, you will have access to skills that will hypnotize guards, disguises to sneak past tight spots and the use of exploding pigeons to distract robot dogs. They are limited use though, due to the mana bar, so you have to usually use them as a last resort.
Mazes are comprised of two types: NPC and Player arranged. Both function in the same way, but you only get one shot at the player mazes. Once you attempt a player maze, you can leave feedback to instruct how they can improve, taunt them if you feel like it, or just ignore it completely. Other players have the same ability and it can be generally useful to watch the replays that are provided to safeguard your own wealth. With each finished maze, you receive gold to upgrade your own personal maze and roses that unlock new skills, upgrade your stats and new thieves (currently three total) with their own special features. Everything is based off a timer so expect to wait around for a good thirty minutes or longer once you complete a simple maze. It feels like a cheap game lengthening gimmick or even worse, a free to play feature.
Catch Me is well optimized for the most part and I have yet to encounter any real issues. This is probably the first time I can say this out of the plethora of Early Access games I have reviewed over the past couple of months. I personally find the gameplay to be repetitive and rather stale, but I can see the charm it provides as well as the sharp difficulty that can be attributed to the multiple guard types. At the moment, I give Catch Me a recommendation for being a rather polished experience with just a few quality of life issues. I look forward to seeing what kind of new tricks this game will come up with over the course of the next six months.
Pros
- Simple, but effective gameplay
- Lovely visual aesthetic
- Challenging gameplay
- Optimized well for current state
Cons
- Timers feel like a game lengthening gimmick
- Music could use some more variety
Side-note: I have noticed grammatical issues with text and the voice acting, but I did not include it in the final result. If the issue persists, I will include it later down the line.

This was a good game, even if it feels unfinished. The interface is clever and gives you a stronger vibe of talking to a real person than SmarterChild or CleverBot, even if Emily's dialogue has no real AI behind it. My only real problem is the plot; as I said, this game feels unfinished, as it's over incredibly fast and every play through feels the same in spite of making different choices. My hope is that this game is a starting point, and that an expanded version comes out later with far more choices (that have more noteworthy consequences) and that chronicles more than just a couple of years. I'd like to see this game follow Emily and the player through several decades of their lives -- or, perhaps, keep it limited to the college timespan, but allow for more interactions to give the player's choices more opportunities to change their relationship.
One other thing: The game never really announces before you play it that you're a guy that's pining away for Emily, so figuring that out while playing was a little jarring to me, as I'd been playing as a female friend. I'd either make this clearer at the onset so the player can enter with the right frame of mind, expand the conversation options so it's not trying so hard to steer the player in that direciton, or broaden the game entirely and allow the player to decide from the start who and what they are to Emily. This game is primarily about a relationship, and that can still be examined whether we assume the role of this one specific guy or not.
In any case, none of these qualms were enough to make me not play. The game is free, so give it a peek and experience it for yourself. You can literally get through the game in about 10 minutes, so anyone and everyone can find an opportunity to give it a try. It's a nice little gaming experiment.

Strongly recommend to any Souls fan.
This game does a very good job of capturing much of the charm of the earlier Souls games.
- The level design is amazing; One enormous maze filled with shortcuts and hidden loot.
- Enemy design does a great job of keeping the game challenging the entire time. Anytime you start getting comfortable with one enemy type, a new one is introduced who will wipe the floor with you.
- Build variety is also excellent. Two people can approach combat in completely different ways thanks to all the implants and armor set bonuses.
Much like Souls games, there is a ton of gear you can completely miss if you don't take the time to explore, or if you don't do quests for NPCs. The spacing between shortcuts is perfect, making you nervous at the prospect of losing all your Scrap if you die, and right when you're about to break down, there it is.
Dismembering enemies never got old for me, especially after I changed the special camera option to only play when acquiring new gear.
8/10 : Very solid game. 9/10 if you are really craving a new Souls-like experience.

Pros:
- Meaty, visceral combat
- Limb-targeting system; target unarmored points for more damage or armored limbs for mats and gear
- Weapon types are varied and fun to experiment with
- Exploration is rewarded with gear, lore tidbits, and shortcuts
- NG+ adds new, tough enemies and lets you upgrade you gear past MK. V
- PC port runs well and has a lot of options; multiple gamepad faces supported natively
Neutral:
- Level design is sometimes confusing
- Promising story takes a backseat after the first area
Cons:
- Ugly gear
- MG Gorgon set bonus outpaces almost every other set fairly easily
- Some enemy placements are cramped or ganky
- Queued combos can leave you out of place if you're not careful

What is it?
A story-driven action adventure set in a gorgeously recreated Hong Kong setting (a mix of various Hong Kong sectors fairly accurately recreated). The game is based on real events (though names have been changed). You are Wei Shen, and you lead a double life as a Triad gang member and an undercover cop - so you will be playing both sides of the story. It is Wei's job to bring down the Sun On Yee gang (a tweaked name of the real-life 'Sun Yee On') from the inside, and so he must find a way in, and get people to trust him. Soon, Wei starts to feel divided loyalties as he gets in deeper and deeper. The main storyline is linear but the plot is fast-paced and entertaining. There are masses of side missions that fit in with the plot very well and you can choose when and if to play these.
Sleeping Dogs contains all the usual open-world elements we love: a gorgeously atmospheric and thriving city densely populated with people and traffic, great ambience (especially the night market), vehicles to unlock and drive (or simply steal), USEFUL collectibles that either upgrade your health and strength, or your bank balance!
Is it easy to play?
Very. The driving and parkour elements are simple and responsive and the martial arts moves are only taught gradually and are not overly complex, though you might find yourself scribbling down a few moves as there are ultimately 12 to remember! The game's tuition system spreads your learnt moves gradually through the game using a novel system of returning to Wei's former Kung Fu school. For exchange of each school's missing trophies, you will be taught a new move and given some non-aggressive adversaries to practise it on. It works very well. As for weapons combat, I personally found it easier to switch to mouse for aiming, but the game switches seamlessly between controllers while playing. The only negative aspect is the sometimes-uncontrollable camera angles after reversing a vehicle. The camera is too slow to face forward, meaning you often start driving blindly. Other than this, everything is great.
Requirements
Regarding game requirements, you really will need to pay attention to those because this is a heavy game graphically. There is some stutter in the cut-scenes regardless of GPU but the cut-scenes are only occasional. You will benefit greatly from a gamepad. This is not the sort of game for people who have a 'delicate' audience in the room as there is a lot of 'colourful' language and such. If you're a female gamer, you'll probably cringe at some of the lines spoken by some women (some are really bad!) - but not enough to kill enjoyment of the game.
Is it worth upgrading from the original?
If you enjoyed the game enough that you'd likely play it through again, then I'd say yes. It looked great before but there are a plethora of improvements: denser NPCs and traffic, heaps more variety in shop signs, lots more lit signs, beautiful environment effects, super-realistic road and building textures and improved controls. A few bugs in the original game have been fixed, and all the cars, outfits, apartments and cash DLC is no longer automatically awarded to you at the beginning of the game (a problem with the original version, leaving players with nothing further to play for). The only caution is that, if your PC struggled a bit with the original, it will struggle more with this version given that it is a much heavier game for your GPU.

Sleeping Dogs is a fun game. Some might even call it underrated, I'm not even sure myself if it got the attention it deserved. It's not trying to innovate anything, but it has an interesting story that inspires itself from gangster movies from the asian cinema, and it has really good gameplay, with a great fighting system reminiscent of the Batman Arkham games.

Owned this game on both PS4 and PC (so I've got even more hours than listed), so you'd be right in assuming I reccomend this. The story isn't too great, cliche and servicable at best, but the enviroment is amazing, and definitely feels different and unique. It was nice to see a change of pace from pretty much every other openworld game being L.A. or NYC. The combat system is what's king. Probably the best hand to hand system out there (for an open world game). The driving is a little awkward at first, but you'll get it. The side activities even though they weren't super story rich, felt nessecary enough and like they had purpose. So I never got the Ubisoft "go here, pick up rock for arbitrary reason, repeat 100 times" feeling that ruins side activities. Overal the tone and the enviroment are really what set the game, they make Hong Kong a city that you want to hangout and explore in (aside from the constant muder, gang violence, etc..). I was a huge fan of True Crime: Streets of L.A. when it came out (this is the spiritual successor). Although I still prefer that game, this was the closest thing we've had to that game in years.

I promised I wouldn't leave a review until it was finished, as leaving negative feedback on an early access game is just unfair.  I loved this game, and with every patch it got better and better.
So why don't I recommend it?
It's simple.  It's far too unpolished for a finished game.
Missing text, UI errors, and dodgy AI prioritisation.  The AI is good most times, but it has glareing holes where it puts things like "stomping out fire on the other side of the raiders" above "the raiders are shooting at me, run away" and you end up with "look a fire behind those raiders that they just set that doesn't affect anyone, let’s get every civilian to run over to the raiders and stomp out a fire while they shoot us all"
My personal favourite is "the oxygen recyclers are breaking?  No, don't fix them, lets panic for two hours while the oxygen slowly runs out"
Now you can put most people down to blind panic in situations like those, but out of a crew of 64, 52 of them went to stomp out the fire (they ran all the way from a safe section of the base, past security and into the raiders, most of which were assigned to security and tasked with killing the raiders.  You just wouldn't get a situation like that in real life.
I understand the reasons behind it, and the bug fixing is ongoing.  However in its current state it is still very very difficult to play smoothly, and I don't mean that the game is hard, I mean the game visibly holds you back when you want to play it and a single bug can be a game breaker.
If you like the look of this game, feel free to get it, back up your saves MANUALY on a regular basis, and don't be surprised if a sudden bug/glitch wrecks your experience.  However please don't buy this game if you are thinking it will be epic.  It's epic until a bug kills it.
As major bugs are patched I will update this review, but it’s looking like the "patches" will either not continue or be few and far in-between.  There is currently a comminity unofficial patch in the works so I will be interested to see how/if that pans out.
Over two years later and still no official patches.
Happily there is now a small unofficial team creating patches.  I've not tested it myself but the reviews for it are good.  It took almost two years for this to happen and although I will explore SpacebaseDF9 again sometime, for now there are plenty of other games to play that work out of the box.

If you ever wanted to know what it's like to have to sit in a booth and experience a gamified version of the banality of being a customs officer (and have it be fun), here's your chance. "Papers, Please" is a sometimes maddening game of "What Doesn't Belong" with some additional story elements of intrigue along with the joy of trying to survive as an underpaid, underappreciated border control agent. Once you get things down, the game changes them on you. In addition to some of the story elements, there's also a lightweight management element (personal money, time, family), and penalties (in the form of citations, which can cost you money, or game ends, which can send you to prison and other places).
The game becomes cathartic after you get into the rhythm of it, but you have to have an eye for catching differences and details, otherwise you'll find yourself prone to losing credits. Overall, a really fun game which manages to make something that nobody would think is fun into something fun.
Likes
+ Matching/Puzzling under pressure
+ Lightweight storylines
+ Lightweight personal management
Dislikes
+ Wish there was an endless mode without constrains ("catharsis mode" -- play endlessly to relax; no time limits, no points penalties, no instant death on failure. Still receive citations and have a score of number correct v. number incorrect)
+ Wish some story lines could be opted-out of.

Though a greatly thought provoking and engaging experience, 'Papers, Please' presents itself as about as boring of a game premise that one can imagine. You are a lowly border admissions officer of fictional communist state Arstotzka; checking documentation, denying entry to Kolechian scum, getting threatened by your boss for any mistake, and being paid pennies to do so while under constant threat of ending up in a windowless cell. If you do your job well, you may be able to earn enough money to both heat your home and feed your family. This aspect of the game is at most times tedious and a bit nerve-wracking.
Where 'Papers, Please' truly shines is the story, moved forward through decisions you are faced with. A woman is missing a new piece of documentation and pleads for entry to see her son? Jorji comes in with his crayon-drawn passport yet again? A person pleads for you to deny entry though all their documents are in order? Based on how you act in these situations will unfurl a wonderful series of stories, though you never leave that guard booth. The impacts of each decision is often felt both immediately and through later game events.
Each playthrough is generally brief, lasting only 20-30 minutes, but if you enjoy the game there are a variety of different endings to achieve.
In short, I feel 'Papers, Please' is worth a purchase for the experience at the very least. I've played few games which have been so thought provoking and unique.

This was a good game, even if it feels unfinished. The interface is clever and gives you a stronger vibe of talking to a real person than SmarterChild or CleverBot, even if Emily's dialogue has no real AI behind it. My only real problem is the plot; as I said, this game feels unfinished, as it's over incredibly fast and every play through feels the same in spite of making different choices. My hope is that this game is a starting point, and that an expanded version comes out later with far more choices (that have more noteworthy consequences) and that chronicles more than just a couple of years. I'd like to see this game follow Emily and the player through several decades of their lives -- or, perhaps, keep it limited to the college timespan, but allow for more interactions to give the player's choices more opportunities to change their relationship.
One other thing: The game never really announces before you play it that you're a guy that's pining away for Emily, so figuring that out while playing was a little jarring to me, as I'd been playing as a female friend. I'd either make this clearer at the onset so the player can enter with the right frame of mind, expand the conversation options so it's not trying so hard to steer the player in that direciton, or broaden the game entirely and allow the player to decide from the start who and what they are to Emily. This game is primarily about a relationship, and that can still be examined whether we assume the role of this one specific guy or not.
In any case, none of these qualms were enough to make me not play. The game is free, so give it a peek and experience it for yourself. You can literally get through the game in about 10 minutes, so anyone and everyone can find an opportunity to give it a try. It's a nice little gaming experiment.

Given the experience the developers should have obtained from making a Dark Souls clone like Lords of the Fallen, I expected The Surge to bring new, interesting and fun things to the table. Well, I was very, very wrong.
They tried to incorporate elements from LOTF like the XP multiplier based on how long you're holding "souls" aka tech scrap aka experience points, and bring in new mechanics like the dismemberment thing, where you acquire new parts by dropping a blueprint from dismembered chunks from enemies, but that's about it. The progression in the game is so strongly gated, there's absolutely no real feeling of progression. Even though the dismemberment mechanic is interesting, it also limits the gear you acquire based on the segment of the game you are in. Even upgrades to already owned parts come from scraps with varying quality that is also based on where you are in the game, limiting options even more. "Leveling up" is a joke, as the player can only level up their "core", which doesn't really do anything besides ocasionally increasing the capacity for heavier parts or making so called "implants", which are very minor customizations you can make to your character(like slightly more hp, healing packs, etc), scale a bit better. The combat is messy, slow and confusing. Heavy weapons take WAY too long to connect and leave your character vulnerable, while lighter, faster weapons don't stagger enemies nearly as much and their combo system makes the player feel just as little in control, with neither dealing considerable damage, especially when compared to how much damage the enemies deal and how fast and unfair they are to fight against.
I don't recommend this game to anyone looking for a new twist on the still so very popular soulslike games, as it doesn't have one, and is, in fact, one of the worse and less compelling ones, and don't even recommend it if you're just looking for an interesting, fun and challenging action game. I might even take a risk by saying it manages to be a downgrade in terms of fun and progression when compared to Deck13's previous uninspired attempt at a Dark Souls game, Lords of the Fallen.

I can't recommend this game. DS was hard, but at least combat was fair. The Surge is suppost to be an action game with challenging combat. The combat is anything but challenging to me it is completely unfair.

Gameplay:
The combat emphasizes aggression, making the game a bit more like Bloodborne than Dark Souls. As you get further in the game you'll handle battles with limited tactics: hit & run, pure aggro, and block/counter. Overall, the combat is fun, but the damage types could have been more exaggerated and the vertical/horizontal attacks don't make much of a difference (I plowed through NG+ barely using vertical strike).
The bosses are a mixed bag... The first one is fairly basic, another is hectic, and a couple are just slogs. Interestingly, you can earn improved weapons from beating bosses in special ways.
NG+:
Unfortunately, this was a weak implementation of NG+. Some new enemies are placed into the game (just existing enemy types with mismatched armor). The new enemies seem to have improved combat tactics, but they're a fleeting experience. NG+ was easier than the first run, with the exception of the last boss. Granted, some of this is due to learned tactics, but the gear scaling isn't quite on par (you scale a little too well).
The level design is good, but very linear. Thankfully, it doesn't feel completely linear, as the levels are built as a series of connected loops.
Story:
The main plot of the game is pretty weak, it's typical sci-fi tropes. The biggest weakness in the storytelling is that the game feeds you too much information, leaving little space for imagination. It starts off strong though, leaving you wondering wth is going on... but as you progress the game force feeds you too much information.
The strongest storytelling in the game is environmental. Everywhere you look is some tiny story about how others handled the events taking place. There's bits of information about how people lived before the incident as well... There's just a lot of character in the environments.
Audio:
Not much to say here, it's good overall. There's a few music transitions between areas that could have been better and a few audio glitches with executions (button press sounds).
Graphics:
It looks good and runs well on my old PC. I never noticed any frame rate problems while I played the game.

Yo thought i would write a little review for FFXIV:ARR keeping it short and sweet.
After playing World of Warcraft since release up to current content, i found the game depleted, no thought process into the customisation of gear and the way it looks. If your on the fence and debating whether to buy FFXIV (Especially if your a wow head like me) i would bite the bullet and buy FFXIV and i promise you wont look back. I have been after another MMORPG for a while, playing Black Desert, Elder Scrolls the list goes on. I know all about FFXIV and im fully aware of the franchise thats been advertised, but i didnt realise there was an "online" version. Since purchasing the game it really gives that nostalgic feel for how "wow" used to be socially, challenging quests, and freedom. There are no trolls that i have come accross as of yet and right off the bat i joined a free company or guild in typical MMO terms. The guys are friendly helped me out when i needed it.
The combat doesnt do the game justice at first, it some how feels slow compared to the typical or newest MMOs but i can assure you that as you progress the combat becomes better and better. putting combos into place then reaping the rewards. The gear designs in the game are absolutley stunning and again gives you that sense of pride in the character you create. I cant help but feel as i have progressed through the ARR expansion there are certain aspects that wow legion have copied into there expansion, and found it quite comical or cheeky.
Im a PvPer at heart and the PvP isnt bad at all scaling everyone right down to the same underwear, PvE is what makes this game. - Dont be put off by thinking damn do i need the expansion to keep up with others because that answer is NO.
- All instance are lvl synced meaning all content is relevant. Not forgotten.

Here is my review for Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition (SPOILER ALERT):
First off, I'll start with the main game.
Story: You play as Wei Shen, undercover cop. This makes for a good story, although it builds up to a choice between Triad and Cop, but that never pans out, and this makes the ending a bit anti-climactic. 8/10 story
Gameplay: Wei Shen is pretty good at Kung Fu and the hand to hand combat is really good. You also start using guns after some time with the game and the gun mechanics are decent. 9/10 gameplay
Driving: The driving is quite bad. If you hit an immovable object, your car can act weird. I had this incident where I hit a fence and it bounced me back quite a bit. The driving itself isn't too bad until you start racing, and this is where it becomes awkward, especially with motorbikes. 5/10 driving
Characters: The characters are fairly interesting, although the dating aspect seems like a ploy to make the collectibles appear on your map, making the dates not important to the story. You run into some pretty boring characters like Pendrew, the stereotypical corrupt cop. All in all a big mix of interesting characters, 9/10
Bugs: Oh boy, there are quite a few bugs in this game. Most of the bugs I encountered have to do with the driving. The bugs aren't too bad until you play the DLC, but I'll get to that later.
Graphics: Sleeping Dogs came out in 2012 and for 2012, the graphics are fine, but Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition came out in 2014 and for 2014, the graphics aren't all that good. 4/10 graphics
All in all, the main game itself is great, and I think this game is an absolute must-buy, maybe not for the full price, but you should definitely get it at a discount.
Nightmare in North Point
This is one of the two big DLC-packs to this game. Hong Kong becomes overrun with Jiang Shi, which is essentially the chinese equivalent of zombies. This makes for a great and interesting story where you learn some stuff about chinese mythology. There aren't that many bugs, but the story is short, which drags my final score of this DLC down to 8/10
Year of the Snake
This is the other big DLC-pack. In this DLC you play as Wei Shen, full time police officer and you need to stop evil cultists from blowing up Hong Kong, this makes for a decent story, but the side missions are extremely boring and unrewarding. The dlc is also fairly short, 6/10
Wheels of Fury
In this mini-DLC, you help Dr Tang test out the DZS-90, which is a super car with guns, emp and improved ramming. The missions themselves are fun and the car is great, but the car is also extremely buggy. I had one incident where it flew across Central, crashing into the hospital, killing me. This car also makes the Class A races a guaranteed win as its EMP device disables the other racers cars, due to the various bugs and glitches on this DLC, I give it a 4/10
The Zodiac Tournament
This is a fun little mini-DLC where you go to Zodiac Island in a 70s style kung fu movie and you kick a whole lot of♥♥♥♥♥ I think this DLC is extremely fun and the 70s setting really makes it great. I absolutely love this DLC, 10/10
FINAL SCORE AND SUMMARY
All in all, Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition is an absolute underrated gem and it's a must-buy for anyone who enjoys GTA-style games. I have the platinum trophy for this game on PS4 aswell as all the achievements for it on Steam and it's great fun, 8/10 game.

This game is a burglary game, most similar in style to games like Monaco. You play a magician, out to steal riches owned by evil people, and have a set of 'props', or tricks, to distract guards with.
The game is designed to be asynchronous multiplayer, like some other recent games: You go out and steal stuff from either the computer or from other players, and the other player can watch a replay of your attempts to steal their loot. They even let you leave notes behind for players to give your thoughts on their maze, leave tips, or taunt them if you so desire.
Currently, the game has 3 different characters, each with their own strengths, weaknesses, and special abilities.
The developer is incredibly present, and always does his best to answer concerns and make changes. For instance, some people were getting tired of hearing their magician's quips, and asked for an option to mute voices on the forum, and within a very short period of time, the option was added to the options menu.
The only real issues right now are grammatical in nature. Since the developer is not a native English speaker, some voice clips and text lines don't really make that much sense. However, this is relatively minor, and the actual gameplay relies very little on the text, so you can play for a while without really noticing.
All in all, this game rocks my socks, and I'd recommend getting it now. It's completely playable, and is not missing any major features, which is more than I can say for a lot of early access games.

Though a greatly thought provoking and engaging experience, 'Papers, Please' presents itself as about as boring of a game premise that one can imagine. You are a lowly border admissions officer of fictional communist state Arstotzka; checking documentation, denying entry to Kolechian scum, getting threatened by your boss for any mistake, and being paid pennies to do so while under constant threat of ending up in a windowless cell. If you do your job well, you may be able to earn enough money to both heat your home and feed your family. This aspect of the game is at most times tedious and a bit nerve-wracking.
Where 'Papers, Please' truly shines is the story, moved forward through decisions you are faced with. A woman is missing a new piece of documentation and pleads for entry to see her son? Jorji comes in with his crayon-drawn passport yet again? A person pleads for you to deny entry though all their documents are in order? Based on how you act in these situations will unfurl a wonderful series of stories, though you never leave that guard booth. The impacts of each decision is often felt both immediately and through later game events.
Each playthrough is generally brief, lasting only 20-30 minutes, but if you enjoy the game there are a variety of different endings to achieve.
In short, I feel 'Papers, Please' is worth a purchase for the experience at the very least. I've played few games which have been so thought provoking and unique.

This game makes me feel like I'm part of Daft Punk
You scoot around in your sleek new robo-booty through freshly apocolyzed settings, listen to heavy synth beats as you groove through industrial, laboratory, executive, and sci-fi horror landscapes, and are constantly collecting "samples" from your groove-less foes in order to mix them into a kick♥♥♥♥♥new album.
Seriously though, this game is a glorious mixed bag of spectacular aaaaand less than great things. Please don't make the mistake that this is a "souls-clone". It takes gameplay elements from that glorious franchise, but it does not imitate. It improves and twists the formula. I won't be comparing this the DS in my meanderings.
The Combat is ON POINT. It places a heavy emphasis targeting specific points on enemies to either hit weak spots OR collect new gear from your enemies. Each weapon type has it's own very specific moveset and rather deep combo set. For instance, the twin-rigged (dual-wield) has your character balancing pin-point strikes to vital areas, while using a flurry of blows to quickly stagger or escape from a sticky situation, Where as the heavy-duty weapons focus on the concept of "one hit" where the slow moveset is tactically balanced between high dmg, stagger, and increased stability to incoming blows on your end. The Combat system is deep enough that a perceptive player can easily switch to any class of weapon and ultimately feel at home with it.
The combat system is paired with the concept of collecting gear from enemies by damaging their limbs, and executing them in a "finisher" move. This keeps combat on a constant "risk vs reward" system where you'll always be thinking " I can easily defeat this robo-zombie by hitting his unguarded head, buuuuut I really want his Jordans". The armors themselves all carry passive bonuses from wearing a full set ( i.e. increased attack speed, passive healing buff, badass-soundtrack). Sadly, this does not encourage being fashionable (which is the endgame of all games).
The environments are all predicated on the concept of "this is a high-tec future corporation". That being said, you will be scooting around incredibly awe-inspiring massive construction platforms one minute, and navigating increasingly claustrophobic and maze-like conduit tunnels the next. The almost rapid transition between the two will keep you on your toes and constantly give you the feeling of paranoia and gritted determination. Let me tell you, if there is a concept of "shortcut-porn", this game has mastered it. You will be finding small holes, access panels hidden from the light, caved-in entries, and other random routes that all miraculously lead you back to your hipster-fueled Ops center ( save point).
A few of my gripes with the game are:
1. That the enemies can sometimes be laughable, or ungodly difficult. There are no trash mobs in this game, every enemy is essentially a mini-boss and can wreck you if you don't respect them. The late game areas become LITTERED with heavy armored, proton-axe wielding psychos and ulti-death eldritch abominations. That's par-for the course, I suppose.
2. The environment can get too-maze like at times. Sometimes, I would just have to sit down and think of where the fuq i was, just because i couldn't find that ONE DOOR that i opened literally minutes ago. Once all the shortcuts are opened, getting to anywhere in the level is quick and easy....but until then, good luck.
3. Lack of character. I like the premise, I like the setting, I like the interactions with the auxilliary character, but maaaan being stuck with Warren is kind of a bummer. It very much limits your RP options to Vanilla warren,♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off Warren, Warren on holiday, Tom-Cruise, or Ripley in a Power-loader, or maybe DAFT PUNK.

The Surge is Deck13's recovery from Lords of the Fallen. This time around, combat is fast and tight a la Bloodborne. This game is wholly deserving of the "Souls-like" label and is worthy to stand beside Bloodborne itself, the greatest Souls game of them all.
Disclosure: I bought the game for full price ($50) on launch day. I have completed the campaign once and am at the beginning of NG+.
Opinion on cost: $50 is a steep price for any game. For Souls enthusiasts, the asking price is fair in my opinion. I will likely replay this multiple times on NG and NG+. For newcomers, this game's difficulty coupled with a steep pricetag is likely to cause some frustration. If you have never played a Dark souls game before, or if you are just "meh" about the genre, wait for this game to go on sale, or look to cheaper entries in the Souls series (with the exception of Dark Souls 2) to get you started.
The Pros:
+ Fluid combat, tight controls. The most important ingredients in a Souls game!
+Graphics options are robust, only missing a few key features. Depth of Field is oddly absent.
+ NG+ adds much harder enemy placements and increases the upgrade cap on gear so you actually scale up into NG+ stats in a satisfying way rather than beasting on it with NG gear.
+ Bosses are excellent. Most Dark Souls games flood the game with mediocre bosses and a few gems here and there. The Surge has a dramatically lower boss count, but each is far more memorable, challenging, and mechanically interesting. Many of the bosses in The Surge demand that players have full knowledge of the main character's moveset, which is something that Souls games typically gloss over in boss design.
+ Difficulty is crushingly hard (yes, this is a pro in Souls-land). The Surge is arguably harder than the entirety of FromSoft's work, but it isn't unfair. Bloodstains are timed, so you need to rush to pick them up, but killing enemies refills the timer (retrieving souls is a more stressful matter now, but skill and precision are rewarded). Attacking works differently overall. Weapon types have different amounts of Impact and armor has certain Stability ratings, which affect hitstun strength and recovery time. Enemies usually do damage to you even when you're stringing attacks on them because their ability to attack through your hitstun gives them enough time to hit you. This seems weird at first for Souls veterans, but it ultimately makes combat a lot more intertesting because you rarely can get an easy rushdown kill on an enemy. Encounters are fewer and far between, but there are no "weak" enemies and they are all capable of killing you quickly.
The Cons:
- Depth of Field and Monitor Target settings are oddly absent, meaning console config users need to make Big Picture alter their main monitor target by overriding Windows controls to get the game over to the TV instead of having it pop up on their primary monitor.
-No MAP. In other Souls games this isn't necessary because there are so many bonfires and you can easily fast-travel. Levels are also more iconic and open in Souls games. The Surge has a lot of same-y looking areas, and lots of small corridors looping around each area. A 3D map like Metroid Prime features would have made keeping track of exploration immensely less confusing, and it would even make sense in the game's context as a sci-fi Souls.
-Sidequests don't matter. In Bloodborne, there was a host of sidequests that you could either complete or miss, and they would award you with useful gear or upgrades. They were fun to complete and added to the world. The Surge attempts a similar format in which you discover quest-givers and you can miss them by progressing the game. However, none of them give any real reward beyond a Steam Achievement. This is a huge bummer and totally unrewarding, expecially when you consider that Bloodborne and Dark Souls 3 Have entire areas that are optional to complete, including bosses. The core experience of The Surge is very refined, but the extra stuff feels very rushed.
-Balance is weighted for low-defense, high-aggression armor sets. Technically this could be considered a pro, because the best way to play the game is high-aggression, but it also means there is really only one good playstyle in the game, whereas Dark Souls 3 and Bloodborne have a host of great builds and different viable weapons. I listed this as a con because it makes a large amount of gear you can get in the game completely worthless. Literally don't ever build a piece of Goliath or Sentinel class armor. You will be a little more tanky but so much less capable of killing enemies and dodging attacks.
Ultimately I hope we see a "Surge 2" or something of that sort. The core gameplay here is excellent, but we need a game with more sidequests (good ones!), some optional areas with cool bosses and rewards, and more freedom in customization. A few games-worth of revisions to the core model of The Surge would genuinely rival the Souls francise, and could even surpass it. It is good to see games like this delivering such a satisfying combat and difficulty experience in the absence of new Dark souls or Bloodborne entries.

Now that the Early Access and broken promises are over, it's time to review this game as what it is. Forget about the development plans for now, and just focus on what was delivered.
Spacebase DF-9 is definitely playable and can keep your attention for a few hours, as you struggle with a not too clever AI to survive the problems the game throws at you.
You start out with next to nothing and your first priority is to build and airlock, a room around the seed pod for power, and a life support room for oxygen generation. From then on you will be constantly trying to expand as new crewmembers arrive all the time, and you will face problems like boarders, raiders, alien parasites, base breaches, and crewmen going crazy and causing damage.
There is no real goal to this game other than survive. Eventually you will figure out how to create a base capable of sustaining 50 people, and the game will have reached the end: there will be nothing left to do except wait for people to die and be replaced.
The game has an unfinished feel about it and that is the main reason I cannot possibly recommend this at full price, but if you can get it at a good discount and do not look at the scrapped plans for the full version, you will probably have at least some fun with it.

Coming from a background in Escape Velocity, I was pointed to Endless Sky by a friend, and I was estatic. I thought this genre was DEAD (and who am I kidding, it really is!). And I was not disappointed. Endless Sky is a top-down, space ship sandbox played in a make your own fortune or destiny style, with story and details passed along in plain text. I'll run through this review by comparing this game to its predecessors, so here we go.
So, a nice change of pace right off the start. Instead of restricting you to the measly shuttlecraft right off the bat, which was  a classic groan from all the previous games, Endless Sky starts off with you taking out a loan to buy your first ship, in which you are given three choices, which accurately depict the three different playstyles of the game: The shuttlecraft, for the completion of offered missions for money, the hauler, for hauling cargo for profit, and the fighter, for carving your way through the galaxy with a laser. They're the simplest and lowest tier of their respective paths, but they're all a start.
Now, I did say you were taking out a loan, and that's something else that Endless Sky brings to the table: The Bank. Ever present in every system, they loan and collect money. And now, you have a loan to pay off. Think of it as a means of kicking your♥♥♥♥♥♥into gear into the galaxy at large. The Bank can be a blessing or a curse. You can take out future loans to grab the ships that are just out of your pocket change's reach, orrrr you can end up paying the death benefits to the families of the crew you lost, which will be discussed more later.
For now, as soon as you walk out with your brand new ship, you get your tutorial, which shows you around. If I'm remembering right, this was first introduced in EVN (Escape Velocity Nova, 3rd and final in the series). And you're shown the galaxy at large, which like in previous games is linked by a series of hyperspace routes, which is the direction you engage your FTL in to zip off to the next system at the price of a bit of fuel. Pretty straight forward.
Ship movement and combat has hardly changed at all, though I do note that Endless Sky added a much needed feature: Intelligent targeting. It used to be, if you were targeting a ship, firing, and another ship flew in front of you? Your weapons would hit them, possibly with severe consquences. Now, however, your weapons can and will pass through ships that are untargeted. Thank goodess!
As has been a standard since EV, there are shipyards and outfitters on select worlds for customizing your ship, or just flat buying a new one. There's also the market for goods, and the bar for either a bit of flavor text about the planet, or, sometimes, special missions or even the main storyline of the game. It's all very recognizable to veterans. What's new is how the space is allocated on your ship. Endless Sky allows you to swap around the engines on your ship (which I cannot recall if this is new or not: EVN would have been the one to do it if not) but this means that outfit space on your ship is divided into 3 catergories: Weapons, outfits, and engine space. An interesting quirk.
Now, one small, but very signfigant change from the previous iterations of this genre is this: you do not automatically sell off your last ship when you buy a new one. Your old ship becomes part of your fleet, and you pay the crew salaries for it. It keeps all of your upgrades that you changed on it
The factions are predictable enough. Your semi-corrupt, militant mainworlders, your down on their luck colony worlds, pirates, and even some aliens if you go looking.
The story is also predictable, but by no means unenjoyable. Just a fair bit of warning from me: The combat heats up very, very quickly, and with no regards to what you may be flying or how small your fleet is. Things got very hairy for me in my first run through, as I was thrown into fleet combat with my lowly star liner. Oops!
Everything's quite nice, really, there's only two points I have to nitpick. One is the graphics, which for reasons I do not know (perhaps done for aesthetic choices or limitations of the engines), are more on par with EVO (Escape Velocity Overide, second in the series) than with EVN. It's a minor detail in a great game, but it irks me sometimes. ((Edit: This has been explained as an intentional choice, as 2D graphics are easy to implement and easy on people's machines. Thanks Wrzlprnft!)) The second is that if you go via the laser cutter route of life, you will find that enemy vessels will eagerly blow away any ships that you have successfully captured, leaving you with the death benefits to pay off, which I mentioned earlier.
Oh, and just on a personal note? Avoid the discussion boards. We all know that the steam forums have a reputation for caustic communities, but this one has made particularly poor decisions in appointing moderators.
But you know what really tops all of this off? It's free. Honestly, how can you beat that? Go try it out.

It amazes me how much false information is being reported by reviewers so I feel like I should point out a few common misconceptions.
This is a blatant exaggeration. In the early sections of the game many of the enemies charge attacks will adjust course if you dodge too early. The adjustment, however, is pretty minimal and the window for properly avoiding enemies is quite large. This prepares you for a later boss who has similar mechanics but a much more punishing dodge window.
I love this one in particular because someone came up with this "hyper" term that makes it pretty obvious people are parroting this idea. Yes, enemies tend to recover quickly especially in the early game. This seems like a clear design choice that enemies would not be bound by the same rules as the player as that would trivialize the game. While I struggled with this early in the game as well there are several mechanics that solve this problem. 1) Armored and unarmored areas result in different rates of stagger. Additionally, certain body parts have a higher stagger rate. For example, hitting an enemy in the head regardless of whether it is armored has a higher chance of staggering than hitting them in the chest. 2) There is no combo animation that is excessively long. If you misread a stagger and overcommit to additional attacks then you are going to get punished for it. The game requires not only that you understand the enemy attack patterns but also that you understand your own weapon combo chains. 3) Mid to late game armor and weapons with impact result in much more staggering including staggering through armor.
False, this is only relatively accurate at the start of the game while the difference between light and heavy sets is minimal. As the game progresses heavy armor takes significantly reduced damage.
This is true only in that leveling up the core does not DIRECTLY improve your stats. Improvement comes from the addition of implants enabled by leveling up the core. Not tanky enough? Add health boosting implants. Need more stamina? Add stamina implants. This system allows you to adjust your build stats on the fly. By the end of the game I had over 500 health and triple stamina. At that point you can tank even the strongest enemies hits with ease. I can only imagine that the majority of people complaining about how enemies 1-2 shot them never installed a vital boost and are sitting at the starting 100 hp.
