This game is goddamned excellent. Bosses are thrilling, but there are only five of them. Combat is tense and exciting throughout. Grinding, leveling and building are ingenious. And the story hit me with two themes surprisingly effectively.
There are only 5 bosses in this game. However, this game makes the absolute most of those 5 encounters. The first boss is your warm-up. It's your introduction to the game. It punishes you if you're bad, though. So, as a beginner, it feels good when you defeat it.
The next four bosses are absolute monsters. Every one of them is O&S or Nameless-King difficult, and each for its own unique reason. Their movesets are very complex, so it's hard to learn their patterns quickly. They also have varied abilities to trap you, meaning they have a move or two that, if they start up while you're in the wrong position, you're toast. And they hit like trucks. Very, very fun boss fights in this game.
First things first: this game is goddamned hard. By now, in this sort of game, we're used to "trash mobs." These are groups of enemies that merely stand between you and a boss. They're usually dumb and easy unless you lose your patience and do something stupid. However, even a normal enemy standing by himself is a challenge in The Surge. This means there's no such thing as a trash mob. There are mobs from which you try desperately to pull one enemy at a time. Just looking at certain mob makeups will make you♥♥♥♥♥♥your pants with fear and rage.
Anyway.
You're a man wearing an exosuit with ability-altering armor welded to it. When you fight, you feel like a man wearing an exosuit with ability-altering armor welded to it. Attacks are really heavy and slow if you're using heavy weapons. They're really bursty and light if you're using the quick weapons.
Defense is suitably complicated. Your dodge is god-tier, no matter your build. You leap whole meters to either side, front or back, and i-frames protect you on your way. If you time your dodge correctly, time will slow down for just a bit. If you attack during the slowdown, you get bonus damage. That's as tasty as it sounds.
You can block, as well. Initiating the block drains a chunk of stamina, then holding the block continuously drains the rest. So, you can't abuse it. If you block at just the right time, then you've parried. Follow it up with attacks for the good damage.
This game has an addition to defense that will give Souls veterans challenge, as well. While blocking, you can press up or down on the right analog stick to either jump or duck for a second. Jump over low attacks, duck under high attacks. Attacking afterward stuns the enemy and amplifies the damage of your next attack. If you're really good, you can use these techniques to burn through enemies really quickly.
Later, you get a drone for ranged attacks. These ranged attacks consume energy, which you build during a fight.
Energy also lets you use injectables (like a special healing item) and execute enemies.
Speaking of executing enemies, let's talk about grinding/leveling/building.
To me, this is a slog in most games. Build a strength character by committing point after point to the strength attribute. Regret your strength build? Look for a respec item, find the respec NPC, and respec.
The Surge makes me love it. Its method is ingenious.
The four components of grinding/leveling/building are gear, proficiency, implants and power core level.
Gear is obvious--it's what you wear. Each piece of a set has its own perks (defense, stability, stam reduction/increase, damage reduction/increase, etc.). When you're wearing every piece in a set, you get a full-set bonus. One set's bonus, for example, is the Chloranthy ring--stamina regens much, much faster. Another gives you health regen. Yet another grants you lots of bonus damage when you're at full energy. This is the most basic way to determine your character's build.
You get gear by executing enemies in the right way. While fighting, you can target specific body parts with your strikes--head, arm, leg, torso. If you focus your attacks on one before you execute, the execution will tear the body part away from the body. When that happens, the gear held or worn by that body part falls to the ground, and you can pick it up. You obtain weapons straight away. You get armor blueprints, which you use to craft the piece of armor back at the med bay. You also get upgrade materials from the part you chop, which can be used to craft and upgrade armor of the type collected or weapons.
Proficiency takes the place of weapon scaling attributes--strength and dex, as many of us would know them. Use a weapon type, and each kill earns you proficiency. The proficiency level of a type determines how much bonus damage you get from "high-scaling" weapons of that type. What I love about this is that you don't need to redesign your whole character just to switch from "strength" to "dex." Just use the new weapon.
Implants are how you optimize your base build--how you conform the build to your playstyle. Some can be hot-swapped in the field. Others can only be swapped out or in at the med bay. They add health, add stamina, add energy, determine how you regain health, buff your damage in certain contexts, make certain actions drain less stamina, allow you to breathe toxic gas, and on and on. Mixing and matching implants to get the most our of your build is how you build your character in The Surge. No planning necessary. I rebuilt myself entirely for the purpose of one boss fight. Then, I changed my armor and implants back to what they were, afterward, and continued on my way. It's genius. No more anxiety at the start of a game as we decide where to put our points. Those of us who built for faith in DS2 know all too well what that anxiety feels like.
This brings us to build constraints, which brings us to the power core, which brings us to tech scrap. Tech Scrap is your currency. It's what you drop when you die. It's Souls.
With tech scrap, you upgrade your power core at each zone's med bay (your bonfire). You're building only one stat in the Surge point-by-point, and this is that stat. Power Core level determines which doors you can open, how many implant slots you can use, and which implants and gear you can equip. Each implant and piece of gear carries with it a power consumption value. Total value of all equipped gear and implants must be fewer than your power core level.
You're a guy named Warren at his first day on the job. He's starting with Creo, a technology conglomerate. At your work site, they're developing a program called "Resolve." What is it? There's your story, right there.
Shortly after you're given your exosuit, you pass out and wake up in the dumpster. Your power core is busted, so the drones were about to "disassemble" you to recycle your exosuit. Other manual laborers in exosuits are nearby, but they're homicidal monsters. What happened? There's your story, right there.
The story, by its conclusion, hit me pretty hard with two themes. The first is the feeling of powerlessness as a blue-collar laborer at a massive tech company. I found myself resenting the absolute hell out of management and feeling very anxious about the lack of information they were giving me about what was going on.
The second is environmentalism. This story, however, conveys that theme through a lens of desparation that I find very frightening. The Earth is on the verge of inability to sustain human life. How do humans react to that? Scary stuff.
Buy this game and play it. Unless you're afraid of really goddamned hard games. Combat finds a way to be challenging even to a Dark Souls veteran. Grinding/building/leveling is all the reward with none of the hours of filler and prayer to RNGesus. And the story conveys some themes that are worth considering.
So do it. Do it now.

Papers, Please is a game that when first looked at, sounds like the worst concept of a game. "Play as an immigration officer that checks the legal documents of travelers." The beautiful part of Papers, Please is that that statement is true, and yet it plays as an engaging, nuanced game that has most of what good games should have. However, the games mechanics and narrative are niche, and if you find yourself not liking this game, there are valid reasons.
The game is simple to pick up as you learn the basics of what you need to do, checking to make sure all the information is correct, according to the guidelines the game gives you. The difficulty ramps up as more documents are added and sometimes made obsolete. You must process more and more people through the checkpoint in order to make more money to provide for your family, which while you don't have to keep alive to "win", you will find yourself working harder to make sure your family is warm, as you have a vested emotional interest.
This pressure to perform at max efficiency will gnaw at you to be faster and faster, which causes you to make mistakes, and the more mistakes you make you will lose money. So Papers, Please is a game about being an obsessive fact checker, making sure every detail is in order, and if you do a good job you can buy upgrades that make you even more efficient, and things to make your family even happier and safer.
The story of Papers, Please is linked to the people going through your booth, and I won't give any spoilers, because you will want to experience these stories first hand. You will listen to the stories these people have of needing to cross the border, but they don't have the right papers. You have to decide, "WIll I risk my family going without food for a night, to let this man avoid being shot?" And keep in mind, do you even know why he might be shot? This isn't a game of right and wrong, black and white morality so much as it is one of having to choose between two desperately needed options of people trying to survive, but you have to choose how much you can trust and hope when you need to make sure you are safe as well.
Alongside this depressing story is a setting and soundtrack that forces you into an emotionally tired mindset. The theme is engrossing in it's exhausted proudness: its a song you will hear at the start of the game, almost like the national anthem of Arstotzka, the nation you play in. You, as a citizen, must be fiercely loyal each day, despite being worn down by lack of money, hope, and options. The colors are muted and broken by the occasional bright blue or yellow in the form of awards and story options. These drive you to act because you just want to see what a glimmer of salvation is like in this  Commmunist Satellite State aesthetic.
And while all of that is amazing, there is a few things you should keep in mind. I'm loathe to use the phrase "not for everyone", but it certainly applies here. The game is stylized to make something traditionally boring into an engaging experience, but if you are someone who prefers a game that doesn't need to be artsy to be fun, Papers, Please may be too pretentious for you. Note, that does not make you simple or someone who doesn't appreciate theme driven mechanics, but I think we can all agree that some games don't click, just as a popular movie or book may not.
Furthermore, when I have introduced friends to this game, they find it too "untraditional" in that it isn't your typical game. The theme, objective, and narrative are all against what well known games are notable for. I largely agree with this, and if you find youself as a casual gamer in the sense that you play games for fun, rather than a hobby, only with friends, or to see how it evolves as a form of media, then this game also may not be for you.
This game should run on your computer with no problems due to it's clean but simple pixel graphics. No framerate issues, random crashes, save glitches, corruption problems. Whether you like the game or not, it will run smooth.
In conclusion, this game will be hit or miss for you, and thats ok. You'll find yourself getting into the character, role playing how you have to provide for you family, serve as a loyal citizen of Arstotzka, check papers faster and faster, and deal with a wide variety of story options that change how you think each day. Or, you'll find yourself looking at a game that, while interesting in concept, accomplishes it too well, and is a boring task too similar to work for you to enjoy.
In any case, I highly suggest giving Papers, Please a chance. This purchase could open the door for many other similar games that you'll fall in love with, or will tell you that those games aren't your cup of tea.

This is a review from a new player's perspecitve. I started playing during the Steam Summer Sale. This game doesn't discount very well btw: $4-$6 is as much as you can expect to save on the base game The expansion, which you'll "need", if you decide to start playing comes with both expansions for $40. So the upfront cost is fairly expensive, but at least it comes with 30 days of game time.
So first I found myself playing the trial for a whopping 60 hours. I decided to level all the classes as high as the trial would allow before deciding to buy the base game. I really enjoyed this time spent acclimating to a new MMO. The players and community were great. Seriously there is positivity here that is lacking in other MMO's. Even in random dungeon finder groups THERE IS CONVERSATION. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥people talk. Tons of emotes.
There is so much diversity in this game. So far, I've leveled 7 combat classes to 55. Thats realistically maybe 1/2 way to 70 (level cap). The reason I mention 'combat' classes, is that there are crafting and gathering classes as well. You know how in other MMO's your crafting expertise is just tacked onto your character? In FFIV you actually switch to an entirely new class for each profession, your hot-bars will change into profession based skill-moves. Honestly, I'm the kind of player who avoids any type of crafting, just feels like work; but this game probably has one of the best approaches I've seen. The quality of what you craft improves based the skills you choose to forge them.
What I can speak to, having leveled so many combat classes, is the class diversity in this game. I remember when I quit WoW pre-Mists, I was specifially frustrated with the design of classes. They gutted our talent trees into 0 meaningful choices. Essentially it was go cookie-cutter build, or go home. On top of this: every role started degrading into the same base gameplay. I'm happy to say that here, there is plenty of role diversity. My melee Monk gameplay flows differently from my combo-based Samurai. My red mage plays wildly differently than my summoner. One of my healing classes, Scholar, uses a pet to heal, while my White-Mage relies on more classic big heal spells. One of my favorite classes, the Bard, plays melodies that enhance my teammates while I shoot arrows from afar. There are just so many different play styles here.
I can't speak to end-game, HOWEVER, I did decide I wanted to do all the old level 50 raids before I progressed to the Heavensword expansion. I'm enjoying myself and decided I might take my time and go through the old content. I was absolutely tickled to see that I could que up for the old raids, and a group actually formed! It took awhile to fill out; but I was just delighted to see people were running the old raids at all. I've completed The Crystal Tower, the first set of 3 raids in the base game, and was impressed with these early boss enounters. Lots of mechanics flying around the room to pay attention to, the fights feel intense. I can't wait to find out what waits ahead.
Take a dip in the trial first to see if you want to take the plunge. Also everybody is going to tell you to play a Lalafell... /pet these players and move along.

This is quite possibly the worst strategy I've ever played. I've given it the benefit of the doubt, but I can't go any further in the game without wanting to take a sledgehammer to my PC.
The AI in this game is abysmal. Want to throw a knife at someone but slightly out of range (and no way of telling your range without taking direct control)? Better not move closer, let's pull out our gun and shoot them, alert everyone.
Getting shot at in the trenches and need to move? We're men, lets go over the top instead!
Ah my greatest nemesis, a fence, let's all jump over it in the same position, except for the last two people who teleport behind the fence so you have to deselect the group, select those two and make them go over the fence.
Square barbed wire traps on the ground near the trenches, don't run around them, don't crawl under them, run through them - take damage! We must secretly be German, because we're sure making it easy for them to kill us!
Of course, the enemy AI is better. I can aim 10 mortars at places and not hit anything, but as soon as they are aware of my presence, they pull out their laser designators and hit me from satellites that I can't do anything about. Yes, even on Private.
And my soldiers often have the aim of the guy on my team in CoD that goes 1-39. If the enemy is in a house, then it's pretty much easier to bomb it with artillery otherwise the war would be over by the time my soldiers actually hit the enemy.
Ok, so enough about AI, what about the rest of the game.
I'll give it bonus points for the campaign choice (well, if you shell out for the DLC of course). You get the Russians, French, Germans, British, and Tanks. Haven't tried the tanks yet, I rage quit on the British when the developers asked me to take somewhere with a timer, then do it again, and then do it again - except this time the enemy has the entire German artillery at its disposal and I can't get close enough in time.
The graphics aren't really anything special, but they function. The destruction of buildings is nice.
The sound design is awful. Specifically the voice acting. On the Russian campaign you have Russians who sound uninterested, and constantly mispronounce everything (saying reckon-ai-sance instead of reckoni-sance and 'barber wire'), not to mention loads of misspellings. I probably have some in the review, but I'm not selling my review. It makes it look extremely unprofessional.
The French campaign reminded me of Assassin's Creed Unity in the sense that everyone was British.
The German campaign made me think of how the officers spoke in the Galactic Empire in Star Wars. Overly British and overly evil. Then the Turkish came into play with an American voice actor who sounded really chipper. Like 'OH BOY OH BOY I'M IN A GAME', completely disregarding WW1. The same guy voiced the Russians.
The British campaign had English people, a decent Scottish actor and I'm not sure about the Irish actor. However, this wouldn't be Battle of Empires if it were perfect - the Australians are also British. One voice actor tried to put an Australian accent on, but it wasn't really convincing.
I've had numerous crashing problems with the game too. Hovering over a priest in the Russian campaign would crash the game. The French Campaign had a mission where it would crash upon load, as did the British campaign. I did enjoy a one off instance where a British artillery gun rolled across the map at a high speed, right into my troops. Looked like a plane on the map.
Had bugs where my soldiers couldn't throw a grenade through an open door, where some shells didn't go off (might be a feature, but still infurating), where I click on an enemy to shoot them with a tank and the tank just sits there without moving (yes, it had ammo), where an enemy depot randomly blew up as I was cutting barbed wire next to it. It goes on.
The missions seem really 'samey'. Stealth through here, scout this, destroy this, take these trenches and move up. Seemed to go on and on. Some missions really drag on too.
The controls are so unintuitive, that it's embarrassing. Grouping your troops is the standard make a box and select them, but as far as I could tell, you can't assign them to a number for quick access. Edit - I was wrong, you can assign squads with shift+1, and use hotkeys 1-9 to select them. However, the numbers you assigned aren't displayed on the screen, so I hope you have a good memory. You still have to select them in the described way. Sometimes the game gives you a load of men to command, but you have to waste a load of time sorting it all out. You have to double click on the group to go to them, and there's no easy way of telling the location of what group you have selected other than actually finding them and looking at them. This makes it so hard to actually form a strategy of where to place them. They could have highlighted them on the map, could have let them have assigned numbers and show the numbers on the map. But no, we're stuck with this.
All in all it's been an infuriating experience, with moments of entertainment. I spent a lot of the time swearing and wondering how the hell the AI could be so stupid. A WW1 strategy could be great, but this game has been ruined by utterly incompetent developers, developers that care more about bleeding money from consumers through DLC than actually putting in the work to make this game amazing.
Avoid this game. If a friend buys it for you, disown them as a friend and beg Valve to remove it from your library.

Overall, the game is fun, but it is a bit repetitive. I liked the fact that there was variety: some fights were hand-to-hand, and some involved gunplay, and it was lighter on the gunplay. The brutality of some of the finishing moves was fun and their frequency was wisely limited so it didn't get dull. Fighting with weapons was garbage; what do you mean you can't block a weapon with another weapon??
The city looked pretty nice, but there was zero optimization going on. I played most of the game at 30 fps; I understand that this "definitive edition" is to blame for the just-okay frame rate. With the number of mobs that could be onscreen at once, the city didn't feel isolated, but it certainly didn't feel densely populated.
I never felt like I was completely in control of Wei. I hated the fact that the run button was the same as the jump button. I prefer the way special moves are done in the Batman games, by pressing multiple buttons simultaneously. I'm not a fan of this X-X-X-Y nonsense. I'm a fan of Street Fighter, but not Mortal Kombat.
Vehicle controls were straight crap. With all of the games that incorporate driving, you would think the developers would have learned something. Whether with cars, motorcycles, or boats, you're guaranteed to tool around HK with a scowl on your face.
The story felt like a movie. It is your run-of-the-mill cop kung fu story, but I give it a B because I dig those kinds of movies.
Like most games of this type, you get a whole lot of game for your money. Hong Kong is a pretty big map, and there are plenty of quests and collectibles. I did almost everything in the game, and I had fun exploring. I don't give it an A for value because after I finished it, I didn't care to play it again.
(Note to self: uninstall Sleeping Dogs.)

The Surge is a game I have very mixed feelings on. Gameplay wise it's great, but the balancing of the game feels very odd. The beginning and end are fine, but the middle is easily the hardest part of the game, at least with my with build: operator class rig (light armor) and one handed weapons. Many of the enemies at this stage have ranged weapons capable of high damage in addition to melee attacks capable of hitting 90+% of my health. This continued from around the 3rd to 4th boss, and then got better. To minimize frustration at this point in the game I would stack at 2-3 health and heal mods and definitly upgrade your armor which is something I didn't really do early in the game.
The level design is good for the most part and filled with shortcuts back to the operations, which acts similarly to the bonfires in Dark Souls. Now and then however it can be extremely frustrating with enemy placement or not being able to find where to go, because the areas can look a bit similar.
The leveling system is very comparable to Warframes. As you level using the scrap enemies drop you gain power capacity which is used to slot in mods and armor. This system works well for the most part, but can also make the leveling feel a bit dull.

The combat feels very souls like with a few small changes. First of all after you target an enemy you can further target individual limbs, which may or may not be armored. As you attack you gain energy which can be used for all manor of things, such as using injectable items, using drone abilities, and most importantly cutting off limbs, which is how you aquire many of the armor and weapons in the game. instead of strong and light attacks you have horizontal and vertical attacks which can be mixed together for combo attacks, as well as doing bonus damage versus certain limbs.
My first playthrough took just over 20 hours, which while on the shorter side I think it's fine as the game does have replay potential with different weapons and ng+. Personally I would recommend this game full price if you think you can deal with the high difficulty towards the middle of the game, and if not definitly on sale if this seems like something you would like.

Also, be warned that every time you enter operations the game assaults you with country music.

I really like The Surge so far and find it much more accessible than Dark Souls and even viable for casual players. I've only played 7 hours and just passed the second area but feel compelled to write a review due to my highly positive experience. The following points are notes on the game and don't reflect the full experience
Positive:
Great implant system. It benefits multiple types of play. You could have 9 health injections, focus on passive boosts, or my preferred method of using energy. I currently don't use finishing moves, except to extract specific parts, and instead use the energy for healing or increasing damage. You can disable enemy health HUD and remove all health injections in return for more health and higher damage
Excellent energy system lets you specialize
You're always progressing. Weapon type skills, for example staff, one-handed, or double-rigged, increase as you use those weapon types. Even on a bad run you've still progressed
Instant heals keep the game fast
Good exploration. There's many hidden areas and paths to gain items and shortcuts. Once you've unlocked a shortcut it stays unlocked, allowing you to bypass most enemies and get further. Inventory and items are saved so you can dash to the item and die. Travel often takes too long though - a negative
Neutral:
Time limit to reclaim scrap. When you die you lose scrap - and only scrap. You're given a limited time to it, unlike Dark Souls. This will be a negative to some but I don't mind it because, at least in the first two areas, the time limit isn't a major concern
Enemies can kill you in one move. There's times where I die on the first enemy in the area. You need to play smart. This is good but casual players will get frustrated by stun locks
Boss battles are okay
Negative:
Progression walls. I left the first area at level 35 core. The next and final level is 45, which feels currently unattainable until later in the game. This is done for balancing and new game plus, but then why let players reach second to last by the first area?
Cycling implants. If you want to go from health injection to damage boost you have to cycle through all your implants - which may be difficult in combat. Hotkeys should be available for keyboard
Enemy encounters aren't great for the most part.
Inventory isn't interesting. You get a bonus for wearing a full suit of the same armor, so there's no mixing of armor pieces. Using one weapon is beneficial, so you aren't likely to switch often. Drones don't add enough for experimentation and energy is often better used elsewhere. So far the only consumables I've seen are scrap packs
Blocking isn't useful. It constantly drains stamina, locks you, and doesn't prevent many attacks. It takes too long to activate and doesn't block non-targeted enemies. Dodging is always better if available. This could be fixed by making activation quicker and allowing you to block non-targeted enemies
Fighting multiple enemies is hard and tedious. A better tactic is baiting one at a time using your drone or running away. Better blocking would help

The Surge is, overall, a pretty good game. So why can't I reccomend it? Difficulty spikes. The game, as currently balanced, has points where no matter your gear, you have to proceed through multiple enemy encounters without a single mistake. And that would be okay if the category of mistake didn't include "RNG decided the attack that normally hitstuns an enemy isn't going to this time, but the hitstun animation plays". The animation locks and generous input buffering break down to put you in situations where you can't avoid taking a hit, and enemies hitstun is much more reliable, and they can 2 shot you. It leads to a game with severely frustrating areas that block progress and make it very hard to git gud - the indicators for a safe hit and an unsafe one are identical.
Otherwise, this is a massive step up from the developers previous titles, I don't regret having bought it, and I hope they can tweak damage a bit, but I'm looking forward to what they do next. Soulsborne die hards should enjoy quite a bit, even if it's not quite up there with From's series.

It follows the Dark Souls formula in many ways, but manages
to be original and refreshing
Pros:
-Combat is fast and responsive, encouraging dodging more than blocking
-Leveling System is unconventional, fits the setting and is well thought through
-You will not have to struggle to make sense of basic mechanics
-You can fully respec at any point in the game, since the whole system is equipment-based
-Sub-areas are heavily interconnected
-Crafting system is engaging and encorporated fluidly into gameplay, without forcing you to
deliberately halt your progress to to side-work
-graphics are solid
Cons:
-Focus is on manuvering the environment and defeating mobs, not on big bosses, which are well made, but rarely occur
-Story isn't as deep and philosophical as in Dark Souls, although the atmosphere is still very good
-Mobs deal heavy damage and getting 2-hitted by common enemies can be frustrating, until you manage
to adapt to the flow of combat

All in all, the Surge is a well made action-heavy RPG with interesting, fresh elements.

I've been anticipating the Surge for some time. After the End of the Souls series, something fresh would be great.
I knew for a new IP from another dev, to fill DS's shoes, would be TALL order. Even with that in mind The Surge dissapoints me.
The main reasons:
- Combat is slow and unfair. You have the same rig / weapons as enemies. You upgrade them. You are not undead. But somehow, you are slower, need to hit enemies 4 times to kill them, while they kill you in 1-2 hits most of the time.
- Dodging and Blocking is not very effective. The hitboxes are often poor. Your moves / combo's / executions move you around, often off edges / into acid / toxins. It makes chosing your arena a bit too important, slowing down gameplay further.
- The level design gets too complicated halfway through the second area. You'll get lost all the time, and shortcuts were once THE way to move forward, but now you are forced to get through 5 minute hikes through / past enemies to get to the boss. Feels like the Devs got confused building the layout too.
==
Pro's:
+ Graphics are fine, performance is great even.
+ Sounds like a factory, voice acting is okay I guess
+ Some outdoors areas look nice, interwoven levels.
+ The gear combat gimmick is a nice new touch.
+ No statpoints but Core Power and implants
==
Cons:
- Combat is not balanced, because your weapons are your enemies weapons and movesets are not.
- Armor / health doesn't really benefit you much. The way I see it, there are only two valid playstyles
- Weapon variation is a little poor.
- Tthe weapon proficiency system and how hard it is to travel back effectively, makes it near impossible to switch weapon style after about 200minutes of the gameplay time.
- Fitting more gear in Core Power might leave you farming the same route a couple of times. And then some more to actually progress.
- Bosses feel random and replacable. You don't see them coming and the areas feel like the way back to base. Prepare to lose 30 minutes of exploration / farming to them. (Because you'll probably won't find you way back to the arena in 2:30-4:00)
- Bosses seem to have a timer. I died literally to nothing after fighting them for about 10 minutes. Might have been major hitbox one-shots.
- The game features some very lame one-shots on you. No amount of armor / health will help you.
- You have to be careful where to pick a fight. You'll go over the edge or will get attack by more than two "normal" enemies and you'll probably die.
- If your weapons are too good, it's impossible to cut of new equipment.
- Boss weapons are the best in class early game.
- Only 5 bosses.
- You'll get lost a lot in this game.
- You'll find tons of  insignificant 'hidden' items, but shortcuts are often easy to miss. Or not that "short".
- Very little lore to go on. A ton of the voice logs are repeats. Sometimes things are intrestingly detailed and then suddenly anticlimactic.
- Pointless (no reward?) side-quests. Bugged side-quests too.
==
Graphics: 8/10
Sound: 7/10
Gamplay: 3/10
Longivity: 4/10 (18-40 hours - some NG features)
Verdict: "Meh" 6/10 - if you enjoy a slower Souls-lite with more mazelike levels and futuristic settings, and think getting one-shotted by enemies is fine, and boss design is overrated.

Overall. The Surge does a great job of fixing what was wrong with "Lords of the Fallen" and be a better game.

The Surge is clearly a game that has garnered a divided reception.
One group claims this game is a Dark Souls knock-off; that its cheap and shallow and doesn't do anything new. The other group sees the game as something more, a spiritual successor to Dark Souls, that only on the surface, imitates Dark Souls' combat, but improves upon it with more action, more utility, more combat depth and most importantly more FUN.
Is this game fun? That's the question you seek to answer by sifting through these reviews. In a word, is it fun? OH HELL YES. Yep, that was three words. With the RB, RT buttons giving you Vertical and Horizontal attacks, utilizing a potential 16 combos, (4 combo slots, 2 moves = 16) socketable "implants" (some hot swappable, some not) that give you useful powers, much needed health and stat boosts, and other interesting abilities, the game goes far beyond Dark Souls' slash, slash, dodge and repeat gameplay. It's a high-speed, action-packed gameplay loop that will have you scratching your head thinking "was I ever really as good as I thought I was?"
SMALL SPOILERS AHEAD: Did I mention the ability to target the appendages of your opponents that create a meta-game within itself? Once you start the game, you realize the whole company property of the job you just accepted has gone haywire, with brain-fried zombie-humans wearing half-broken sets of armor. Powered-up exosuit zombies. Just let that sink in for a sec. So you see an enemy, target him and a blue shield icon pops up: armored. The right stick allows you to switch targeting to arms, legs, the body or head, showing which parts are unarmored and which are. Go to town on the unarmored parts? More damage and more stun on the enemy. Pick an armored appendage and here's where the game gets good: focusing on an armored part of the body allows you to HACK IT OFF, potentially dropping that piece of armor for you! And it goes deeper than that, that's just the quick and easy explanation.
Now onto Level Design. People are saying the levels are "small, cramped" that somehow also is a "running simulator" Let me address this: Dark Souls never had wide-open level design, if you remember. Sure it had a handful of semi-open areas, like forests and swamps, but areas Dark Souls was for the most part linear and claustrophobic, with winding corridors and lanes that funneled you in one specific direction. Now compare that to The Surge: a game that is somewhat claustrophobic with corridors and lanes, that DOESN'T funnel you in a specific direction. In The Surge, you are exploring but there's not ONE way that seems apparent. It's not easy to determine how to continue through the level, like in Dark Souls. In fact, a lot of the game is you figuring out where the hell you came from and how to get further. People would cry out now "RUNNING SIMULATOR!!!!". See, there's this thing called Shortcuts. Shortcuts are hidden through the levels that let you easily get to far ahead places so you don't have to fight through the same 50 guys to get back to where you were. The game does a very good job of hiding some of these shortcuts and connecting everything in your head is almost as tough as the combat. I really enjoy piecing together the level bit by bit, finally celebrating at my mastery of understanding once I realize "man, I could've just dropped down here!"
tldr; Combat is more involved and fulfilling than Dark Souls, with super hard AI that requires patience and learning (nothing is cheap, it's all easily beat with tactics and skill), epic levels and bosses, deep RPG mechanics, and some really fulfilling POW, KABOOM, WHAM combat moments that make the game supremely fun and rewarding.

I don't write many reviews, as I tend to go overboard. However, I want to write this up for people on the fence for this game. Hopefully I'll help someone out as to whether or not this game is for them.
So let's get the basics out of the way first. People are going to compare The Surge to Dark Souls and the like. This is a fair comparison, and I understand why they do it. However, the game plays a little more like Bloodborne than Dark Souls. It encourages you to be aggressive. You build up energy which enables you do spend that on things like consumables, executions and etcetera. It has a dash dodge rathen a roll dodge. You gather tech scrap (souls) to upgrade you equipment and your characters power core. You can also lose said scrap if you die on your way to recover it.
If you're still intrigued then let's move on. But let's do a little history session first.
Back when the original DOOM came out there was no FPS. And whether you want to believe it or not, it was not classified as one. Instead it helped kickstart the sub-genre of action games to become what we now know as FPS. So why am I saying all this? Because of the rise of the Dark Souls series, we now have another DOOM like situation. There is no official term for this sub-genre but the popular verbiage is Souls-like. With games like Lords of the Fallen, Salt and Sanctuary and now The Surge, a new sub-genre of Action RPG is emerging. And just like not all FPS games are the same, this applies here too. These games share the basic concepts of Dark Souls, but usually have their own twist on it.
I didn't realize steam reviews have a character limit, so let me bullet-list my positives of the game:
Now for the "juicy" parts. Hopefully I can help someone out there decide if this is a Buy at Full Price, Wait for a Sale, or Skip. This might be a wall of text so strap yourself in.
Let's start off light. There is an aspect of the blocking system that the game teaches you early on that I have a problem with. It involves holding the block button and then pushing the right stick up (to jump up) or down (to duck down). I only have a problem with this because it is weakly implemented and honestly doesn't even need to be in the game. If you want to duck first and then jump the second attack (or vice versa) you have to basically complete the first animation and then press block again, and then you the second action. If I could just hold the block button the whole time and switch between the two it would be much better. However, there are more enemies that attack too quickly to even think about doing this in any practical way. This should either be removed or reworked to make it a more viable option.
Second, the level design can put people off during their first playthrough. I understand this, and respect this opinion when people state it. My NG+ playthrough was much more enjoyable than my first since I knew the lay of the land. But this shouldn't be the case. I fear people will be too frustrated with the game afterwards to even think about doing NG+ and on. You can and will get lost at times. The levels can be a big web of tunnels, areas and shortcuts. And it's sad because I feel the game is even better once you get to the NG+'s.
The "lack of variety" in the areas can put some people off. I got over this quickly by putting myself into the mindset that I'm walking around a huge facility that people built and worked in. It's only natural that environments like this can look the same because of this. But I get why people don't like it.
I can understand the frustration with the weapon proficiency system. I can see why people feel shoe-horned into a certain weapon type. This can lead to people getting burnt out by using the same type of weapon for the whole game instead of exploring different types. BUT, I feel the system is necessary for NG+4 and on so you can still get incrimental doses of attack power after upgrading equipment to the max Mk (Being Mk. XX). And after I got a lot more comfortable with the combat it wasn't so bad to get different weapon types up to snuff, even in NG+. But most people will not want to do this, which is understandable.
The story isn't the best around. Don't expect Dark Souls series intricate webs of stories here. But if you don't care then it's a great game to kill stuff in nevertheless.
There are atleast two parts of the game that have a big spike of difficulty. It can be frustrating to some people. But it needs to be brought up because of the nature of the situation. But, just like the level design, I felt everything was fine and fair once I got into NG+. They could have done with a more gradual increase of difficulty much like Dark Souls however. I think this is caused by the emphasis on the normal enemies rather than the bosses. As each one almost feels like a mini-boss most of the time. Not to be confused with "bullet-sponge" enemies however. As these are not.
Upgrading equipment can get VERY expensive. Had I known this going into NG+ I would have upgraded everything to (almost) max level before moving on. Once in NG+ you can not upgrade from say, Mk. II to Mk. V. It forces you to upgrade directly to Mk. VI. And it accounts for the costs it would take (scrap wise) to do so. So going into NG+ and wanting to upgrade a set of armor I stopped using earlier to Mk. VI was super expensive.
Overall, I enjoy playing The Surge. Sure it has it's problems. But it's the best Souls-like to come out in my opinion. I can only get so far into Lords of the Fallen before getting bored. I'm not big into the 2-D attempts like Salt and Sactuary. But maybe I'm just burnt out on 2-D games as I grew up with the NES/SNES/Genesis.
Look, all in all, if you're a fan of Dark Souls, don't go in with that mindset. This is definitely it's own game within this new sub-genre of games. It brings with it new ideas to keep it fresh enough. And it borrows ideas from the best to keep it familiar. The game plays more like Bloodborne with it's encouragement to be aggressive due to the energy system. But it's also mixed with Lords of the Fallen, just more polished and way less sluggish. It feels weighty, but in a good way this time. And at the end of the day, man does it feel damn good to rip off the arm of an enemy that's been giving you a hard time.

I once tried Dark Souls. After playing Dark Souls 3 for a couple of hours I was like no way, I can't handle grinding games like that. And then I heard about this game. Ignored it at first since it looked just like Dark Souls, but then the gameplay videos started to pop up. I was like whatever let me check that out. The graphics and the setting looks interesting weapons looked awesome and then I noticed something. It wasn't as punishing as Dark Souls. For example you can store your Tech Scrap in your Base (The thing you need to level up). Then there is another thing called energy which you can convert to health or execution power, which provides more resources or call a helping drone. And after that I was like f*uck it I'm gonna buy this. Tried it and I'm totally happy about it. It's still Challenging where you can die in 2 hits or if you get caught up in a combo. But if you want you can run still back to your base and store everything you have collected. The enemies spawn again it you go back tho. And the gameplay feels a lot like Bloodborne since you dodge a lot around and totally ignore blocking, because it uses a lot of stamina and you get hit hard if you can't block the second or the third attack.
So yeah if you like this kind of game I would absolutely recommend it. If you tried any Souls game and found it too punishing you should check this one out. And if you're in neither group give this game a chance. It's from a small company who made a really good Souls-Like game and who also has his own good ideas.

Endless Sky wasn't appealing to me at first and I didn't want to get it, but after a week of my friend threating to shoot me in the face I decided to give it a whirl. I will never regret that day that I got this game, never.

Endless sky can be quite humorous at times. Examples are of having conversations with people (not real people(This game ain't multiplayer)) when jokes are told or other funny stuff. I can't explain it all.
Well, this is where I end my review, unfortunetly. I hope you at least try this game, and not just for 5 mins! More like 2 - 3 hours! BTW: It's kinda hard to start the campaign, you will need to read some guides.

One of the best MMORPG's I've ever played, hands down.
I only have 200~ hours on steam, but that doesn't include my playtime on PS3 and PS4 which amounts to a total of roughly 3 weeks of total playtime.
So for the actual game I'd highly reccommend it, there is so much QoL that's put into the game, teleports are available to any town you've visited before very early in the game, chocobos are available at ~lvl20, 1 character can play every job so it virtually eleminates the need to make a second or third character, and it's as easy as changing your weapon to correspond to the class you want. Controller support is FANTASTIC. I've played on and off since ~2.3 and I've never felt the need to switch to a keyboard and mouse from a PS control.
The Story and soundtrack is easily the best i've seen from an MMO, it's a full fledged Final Fantasy with an epic story and a beautiful soundtrack with new and familiar tracks.
The Gameplay is great too, the varied jobs each have unique traits and abilities with the 3 core roles Tank, DPS, Healer. While early on in the game the lack of skills can get a little boring, with a party it's much easier to get through content both in difficulty and just getting over the early game solo grind. There is a large amount of dungeons to play that are unlocked through the main story and the Duty finder makes it easy to get a party for most dungeons.
Dungeons after Haukke Manor (~lvl 28) are all very different from one another, each with it's own different mechanics that you need to figure out to finish the dungeons and then boss fights can get intense. There's no penalties for your party wiping so you're encouraged to keep trying until you figure it out.
My biggest problems with the game are really the slow start in the beginning and how bad the queue times can be for DPS classes. While endgame and expansion content is fantastic the beginnning of the main  game can be boring by yourself, and unless you have a friend to play with or a FC to help you through the early content it's easy to just give up. My second biggest problem is the Duty Finder times for DPS, sometimes up to a full hour on the content that isn't run very much. it's easy to mitigate this of course, if you have a tank or healer in your party you can be matched fairly quickly.

This is an interesting game, For a subription driven envronment, it really is quite immersive. The world is gigantic!
Previously, i've been as a player of today's gaming, very weary of mmo's typically due to the abuse of microtransactions. However this game does not appear to have anything other than the purchase of game time. Which is remarkable.
Having played a few recently established titles of this particular genre, i very much noticed that microtransactions were an almighty pain in the backside, making the game very much pay2win. Though this one doesn't appear to use those. Which is as i stated brilliant. I've been a long-time of SE's work and i'm proud to say that they're delivering a solid service here.
let's run through the posotive notes :
- A regularly updated server
- Great connectivity with no llagging or disconnecting issues
- Brilliantly detailed environments and optimized really well, i'm using an FX-8350 & 1050T,  everything is maxed with utterly no stutters. The cpu load is balanced, so multitasking is still possible. Game will dial down it's load when you happen to be using other applications. which is very handy.
- Gamepad support***, this coming from a player of DC online, the triggers are conveniently set up as quick commands and these may be modified via drag and drop, which is very useful and much less confusing.
- A fully working map which is helpful for finding destinations during quests.
- Good rewards for completing quests, including gear and weapons.
- Pleasant community
- Lots of character development options
I've only played the game for a relatively short time, but i like it. It's an mmo in which you are free to explore openly and there appears to be something to do as the constant. This is especially good for players alike myself, who like to explore and learn the ins and outs of different mechanics, good for completionists to be frank.
There's only one single bad note i found :
- Waiting for instances (i.e. bosses), it may seem a little arduous, but at least you are free to roam and complete quests as you are waiting for these. Sort of neutral.
In a nutshell, it's very much alike world of warcraft, but with better peripheral support for controllers. XB1 and 360 controllers will work perfectly.

It's almost good; it has a lot of potential, but doesn't deliver.  Maybe their next attempt at a soulsbourne-like will be good.  Or maybe my standards are too high from other soulsborne games.
The intro was a neat idea, but didn't accomplish anything; being able to walk (and hop a little) was not significant.  This guy was on an empty bus, walked into an empty (except for some security guards, presumably preventing him from running) building; of course it was a terrible idea.
The main character is a non-silent protagonist, but he's extremely boring.  The whole point of a non-silent protagonist is to have an interesting character!  And if the main character is so boring and non-essential to the game, why not have character creation?
Similarly, character customization is almost non-existent. "Leveling up" just opens up the number of "equipment" slots that you get (1 every ~10 levels).  A slot might be used to give you 3 heals ... or +30 max health.
Enemies and fights are very boring; they are nearly identical with simple patterns (and some poorly telegraphed moves).  Perhaps to compensate (and artifically increase difficulty), dodging/avoiding attacks is rather unfair.  I often got hit because dodges seems to have no i-frames; to compensate, I just baited out their (almost-identical) attacks, hit the enemy twice, then dodge away, repeat.  The same strategy for every enemy.  Two enemies at once means run or die.

This game is 20/10. If you wasted countless hours (or days) playing Minesweeper only to be frustrated when you have 1 mine left with an equal probability of being in multiple cells, YOU NEED TO PLAY HEXCELLS.
The elegance of this game is the simplicity of it's concept. Your only goal is to find the occupied cells. Hexcells will give you very limited information to accomplish that goal while giving you all of the information you need to find every single cell with absolute certainty.  If you ever need to guess in this game then you literally still have alot to learn.  This is not a guessing game, it's a pure logic puzzle that is AMAZING!

Its essentially the same game as the previous Hexcells, but now it has the restart puzzle feature i mentioned i wanted. They also added the infinitely generated puzzle feature. Nice.
The game is essentially minesweeper with better defined rules, less rng, and paths that go off on thier own that aren't shaped like squares. This means you can work through your checklist of math rules a certain row has, and once you finish that row the new information you have will help you solve other rows of the equation. The branching paths were cool, but sometimes the puzzles got so big that it took a really long time to work through a branch and once i was done i would still have like 5 other paths to work on, which can be pretty exhausting.
The repeat in mechanics really knocks the game down a peg. A big part of why a puzzle is interesting is because it's new; having to work with new problems and rulesets is a big part of why the game is fun. The more i play this puzzle game, the less i enjoy it because it feels exactly the same as the last game.
The no mistakes requirements to unlock new levels also really got on my nerves this time around. Making players constantly have to resolve puzzles they already worked through is frusterating and i found it to be a big turn off from the game. Once i finshed a row of hexes, i was thinking thank god, now i can finally attempt one of the other dozen paths that are in this level.

Review Edit
I've decided to update my review with a pro's and cons list, with additional details to address many other reviews, mostly negative falacies as I see them.
Pros
-Tactical Gameplay (strategic breach and clear, cover)
-No Class System (you pick and choose all your gear)
-Typical FPS Controls (it will feel natural to you)
-Squads (make a team with friends and hop in to win)
-Decent Map Design (you are given multiple approaches and choices to how you attack/defend)
Cons
-Only 2 Maps (though the devs say they are working on more)
-Takes Awhile To Get A Game Going.
More Discussion
Optimization
Is the game optimized well? I'm not going to lie, it can be better. Is it as bad as a lot of the negative reviews make it out to be? No. On default medium setting, I am able to run the game at smooth frame rates (60fps) with a Celeron G1620 2.7GHz Dual Core CPU and HD 7770 1GB GPU. My CPU is below the listed requirements for the game, and yet I still run it fine at this time.
Matchmaking
Is it a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to get in the game? It wasn't initially, when a bunch of the negative reviews sprouted up saying it was. Now is a different story, you'll find yourself waiting awhile. Personally, I blame ignorant individuals who just wanted to bring this game down with misinformation.
Updates
There is a lot of complaints with the devs not making updates. There have been minor updates, but seeing as the game has been out for less then a month, and only has a 4 man team, large updates will take a bit of time.
WarZ/ISS Team
To my understanding, the dev team is Nacho Games, a 4 man team comprised of ex HAWKEN devs. The Producer Free Reign are the developers of WarZ/ISS, though it has been mentioned that they have no input on the creative process for this game. If them being the producer worries you, avoid the game, don't do what others did and bash this game because of it.
RS:S Ripoff
Seriously people, it's 2015, every game in this day and age is a ripoff of another game. The only differences in the majority of cases are the fact that they're programmed seperately, and contain different graphics. You can go and make what you think is a completely original game tomorrow, and I promise you, I'll list a bunch of games it's a ripoff off, whether art style, mechanics, characters, and so on.
My Final Verdict
I enjoy the game for what it is, I've had a lot of fun with it, and I hope things pick up again so I can have more. It would be great to see people buying the game, but on the same note, I won't reccomend buying it simply due to the fact you may not get to play much. My advice, wait for a sale, when more people may consider buying it, increasing your odds of enjoyment, and saving some cash.

Previously, i've been as a player of today's gaming, very weary of mmo's typically due to the abuse of microtransactions. However this game does not appear to have anything other than the purchase of game time. Which is remarkable.
Having played a few recently established titles of this particular genre, i very much noticed that microtransactions were an almighty pain in the backside, making the game very much pay2win. Though this one doesn't appear to use those. Which is as i stated brilliant. I've been a long-time of SE's work and i'm proud to say that they're delivering a solid service here.
let's run through the posotive notes :
- A regularly updated server
- Great connectivity with no llagging or disconnecting issues
- Brilliantly detailed environments and optimized really well, i'm using an FX-8350 & 1050T,  everything is maxed with utterly no stutters. The cpu load is balanced, so multitasking is still possible. Game will dial down it's load when you happen to be using other applications. which is very handy.
- Gamepad support***, this coming from a player of DC online, the triggers are conveniently set up as quick commands and these may be modified via drag and drop, which is very useful and much less confusing.
- A fully working map which is helpful for finding destinations during quests.
- Good rewards for completing quests, including gear and weapons.
- Pleasant community
- Lots of character development options
I've only played the game for a relatively short time, but i like it. It's an mmo in which you are free to explore openly and there appears to be something to do as the constant. This is especially good for players alike myself, who like to explore and learn the ins and outs of different mechanics, good for completionists to be frank.
There's only one single bad note i found :
- Waiting for instances (i.e. bosses), it may seem a little arduous, but at least you are free to roam and complete quests as you are waiting for these. Sort of neutral.
In a nutshell, it's very much alike world of warcraft, but with better peripheral support for controllers. XB1 and 360 controllers will work perfectly.

This game tries its hardest to be an enjoyable experience but falls too short in too many areas for me to recommend it to anyone. The visuals are fine, the setting is interesting, and it comes close to a strongly satisfying core gameplay but the biggest problem is that it comes close but never goes further.
The proficency system asks you to choose one type of weapon and stick with it for the rest of the game unless you want to have a good ol' time grinding enemies and this wouldn't be a problem if the depth of the weaponry was more than it is, but unfortunately it feels shallow. Most enemies have a specific pattern that falls into "slow guy with big thing" "fast guy with two stabby things", "medium slowish guy with a big stabby thing" or "robot whose AI can be abused by circling to the right" so most of the in-game encounters settle into using one combo repeatedly except for the rare encounters which warrant more thought.
On top of this the game has a problem with hitboxes (I have not checked any other reviews this is personal experience only) and it throws enemies at you that use poorly explained/telegraphed moves, which in itself isn't the worst thing in the world, but just adds to the mess of fights that had potential for stand out moments.
The biggest thing I feel also needs to be pointed out is that the developers of this game love to talk about the similarities between their games and the "soulsborne" series and honestly it is an unfair comparison they are forcing on themselves, certain game mechanics aside the pacing and battle to battle experience for this game and Lords of the Fallen are much more "duel" focused as any individual enemy can kill you in 2-3 hits with almost any of their attacks and the progression of your strength never really feels significant.
Also a few quick hit dissapointments before ending this:
-very few bosses, I won't say a specific number for anyone looking to play but honestly for how lackluster the bosses are I expected there to at least be more of them
-lack of main character personality, if you are going to go with a narrative where the player character has a given name and presumably a story to why they ended up in a nightmare scenario, why not use that
-I already touched on this but I just have to mention it again, why are there so few options for weapon types and literally no variety in combos within those weapon types
-The backtracking element, this is pretty minor since most of the backtracking is non-essential and the primary story backtracking is fairly like/non-obnoxious, but it honestly just felt unnecessary
I do wish I could recommend this game because despite all the negativity in the review it does come close to being a very enjoyable if flawed experience and I was excited to see how a sci fi take on the slower paced action rpg genre that has become popular in the past few years would play, but it falls too short in too many different places.

This product is technically just a nicer interface for NetHack, but I'm gonna review NetHack at this point, since people are buying it to play NetHack.
In summary:
NetHack's gameplay is archaic.
The game is for masochists.
The game is full of RNG instakills.
You're incentivized to not minmax (which is insane, minmaxing is one of the largest reasons people play RPGs), since every single item (be it equipment or consumable) is more often cursed than not.
Some examples of that:
Put on that unidentified necklace? Worst case: you die because it's cursed and it strangles you. Best case: it does something beneficial, but you don't know what, because it's not identified.
Drink from that fountain? It might heal you, but you might also instantly die.
Pray to the gods? They might save you, but you might also instantly die.
Drink that potion? ... you get the pattern by now.
Unless beating your head against a wall repeatedly sounds like fun to you, you won't have fun with NetHack.

I got this a while back since I love sandbox games; the creativity and building anything you want has always been a draw in this type of game.  I saw that it looked a lot like Minecraft, but I also love Minecraft with countless hours spent on it, so I thought "why not?"  I finally got around to trying it out tonight.
I assumed that although it looked much like Minecraft, it would certainly have its own claim to fame; it couldn't possibly be simply an identical product.
After about twenty minutes of playtime (tops), I said to myself: "Self, you made a terrible mistake here."
The short, simple version of the problem is that it really is identical to Minecraft, except in every way that makes Minecraft stand out.
If there's a method of crafting, I didn't figure it out in the time I played.  It's possible there's an outside wiki with instructions for crafting things, but if you have to chase down a guide for the most simple of functions, there's a problem with your game.
For some reason, I had to pick up every bit of ground clutter I came in contact with, so by the time I logged out I had something like 700 random pieces of grass, flowers, mushrooms, and whatever else I ran across (literally) while I explored.
There also doesn't seem to be a biome system, as I spent the majority of my time running in a straight line trying to see what else there might be (to be fair, trying to find a reason to not be annoyed that I paid for this tripe), and I got nothing but 20 minutes of identical biome landscape.  In my case this was a sort of rolling hills with scattered birch trees, which gets old after a while.  If there is a biome system, each one must be some sort of MASSIVE to not be able to escape the first one in 20 minutes of running straight west.
So that's my very disappointed summary of a game that I'd hoped would be a good MC-style sandbox but turned out to be a lot of nothing really.  I will still look for updates and may occasionally check back to see improvement as the game is early access still, but until there are drastic changes, my review stands as is.

It's free, it can be a ton of fun, and it has heart. For that I recommend you give it a try.
But be warned, it is not a polished game in some respects. Combat balance is problematic and it's easy to miss out on the engaging, but rather linear main story. Once you do get going with it, it can be a heck of a lot of fun and is full of surprises but until you get going on it, you may feel like there is just nothing to do in the game. (I know I did!)
Once I sorted out there was this huge story I was missing (by reading about it online) I got it sorted and found the game a huge delight. Then, I ground out a big pile of credits trading and finally got into the ship building and combat side of the game, also a ton of fun, but not really accessible when you start out, not unless you are willing to get killed with a lot of trial and error to figure it out.
Quick tips for new players to get the most enjoyment...
0. Never say "no" to a quest. Often you can never get it again and most of the quests are lots of fun, especially the main story line.
1. Pick the trade ship to start or possibly the shuttle, but the trade ship is best
2. Until you get some real potent ships, running away is your best combat option! Fast ships stay alive, slow ones die horribly!
3. Grinding trade routes is the easiest way to make an initial stake to buy a decent combat ship
4. If you want to get into making money in combat, you need to think like a wolf, stay out of heavy firefights, pick off lone or crippled targets, run at the first sign of a real threat. Only when you get to late late game and can trick out any ship with alien technology, run a giant fleet etc, can you hope to take on greater numbers or safely go one on one with a similar sized ship.
5. The fastest money is from stealing gear from disabled enemy ships, but you need both good weapons and decent cargo space on the ship.  Capturing ships seems like a good idea, but usually is not a great money maker.

2D Overhead Space Trading and Combat! Yes!  This game is great, which is weird, because it is so simple. It harkens back to a time when graphics were not nearly as refined as they are today, and thus the gameplay relies heavily on the story.  Some of that story is given to you in the form of quests, other parts of that story come from inside of your brain.  Remember when you were a kid and you played spaceship games away from a computer? This game will get your imagination going.
There are some negative aspects.  Many of the ships are slow, jumping from system to system can get tedious (especially because the sound each ship makes while doing so is exactly the same), and there is a serious balance issue that may prevent all but the most hardcore among us from completing the 'main' storyline.
However, this is a free (as in freedom) open-source game that seems to be reasonably easy to mod.  It is enjoyable and easy to sink some time into. It is based on the Escape Velocity series which was originally designed for Macs and those games were amazing as well.  Do yourself a favor and download this one...you may love it!

I have played 30 hours of the game to its conclusion and tried to do as much of the side quests as I could. Here's what I think.
This is a bad game. The only reason I played it to completion was because this game is so frustrating, janky and overall broken that I refused to let it beat me.
To begin, hitboxes in this game make absolutely no sense. There are times where you attack a target at the same time they attack you, only to see your attack go through their model and "miss" while theirs connects successfully. There are other times when you should be invincible while dodging (I-frames) yet the game ignores this and hits you anyway.
Second, are the weapons. Many of the weapons have a string of attacks depending on how many times you hit the attack button, standard fare. The issue comes with many weapons having a longer string of attacks than expected. For example, the game's "heavy weapon" known as "single rigged" weapons have an incredibly long wind up and take quite a bit of stamina. You are locked in this very long (for a souls-like game) animation which leaves you wide open for characters of equal attack speed to hit you. If you press the attack button once more after your first attack you are now locked into a follow up 2 hit combo that you cannot cancel. This has killed me more than it has helped me.
If the issue was only present for the single rigged weapons, it would be fine. However, I also tried what the game considers the "dual daggers" of the game, or "twin rigged" weapons. They hit fast but they do not hit hard. In order to be effective, multiple hits in the same chain are required. However, this also locks you into many combo animations and since these weapons have very little stagger power, the enemy can just power through the hits and hit you...hard.
This isn't the end, however. You, the player, are also gimped from the start and right through most of the game. There were many times where I had a powerful weapon that landed a 3 hit combo only to realize I've only taken a fourth of the target's health. On the other hand, even the fast hitting/low damage enemies were two, three-shotting my character.
This is made far worse by the targetting system this game has. There is no "free targeting" as the auto-target system immediately locks on when you first attack an enemy. This gets worse if there is more than one target. On top of that, the camera, when locking on breaks itself should the target sidestep past you, dodge or move quickly.
Then, there's the bosses. Good lord this is the part I believe was never playtested. The difficulty of each successive boss vastly shifts. First boss, P.A.X is actually a good way to test your skills as it challenges you based on everything you've learned up to that point. Second boss, however, Firebug is more frustrating than fun due to its incoherent, random AI and hitbox (as explained before).
Third boss, Big Sister is a giant assembly plant that gets easy once you realize  you need to un-target each limb on each phase, everytime you attack. That way, you can see what's around you without the camera having a seizure. The fourth boss,  The Black Cerberus is just a dude. Nothing hard about it, nothing interesting about it, it is the Wood Man of The Surge. And finally, the fifth and final boss (that's right, only five) Rogue Process. The boss has two phases. The first one is punishingly difficult while the second one is a joke. The difficulty shifts between bosses is so large it makes a terrible experience.
And lastly, there are the quests. I was not able to finish one of them due to a bug in the game which did not drop the item from a mob that I needed to complete it. I spent a good amount of time resetting the game, killing the speicific mob, even making sure I was doing it right by checking forums and youtube videos of the quest. Another quest had me bringing an drug to another NPC which, later, was supposed to activate an event but never did.
To sum up. Don't buy this game. Deck13 had a great idea that is horribly executed. Their second attempt at a "souls-like" game is better than their first, Lords Of The Fallen. Sadly, this feels like two steps forward, one step back. Maybe in the future, their next attempt will be a fair, and enjoyable one. And if you need another reason, not to get it. This game is so bad, it compelled me to write my second review on Steam, ever.

Aliens Warm, the sequel to the smash hit Aliens Cold, takes a dramatic turn for the series that used to focus entirely on freezing and thawing exobiological samples delivered to the player's science lab by gruff space marines who looked like they just got back from a more exciting video game. In Aliens Warm, the player plays the role of the second tier of scientists, and they spend their time retrieving these frozen samples, thawing them, and attempting to isolate undamaged strains of DNA. These are then recombined in synthetic membranes which are fed a mix of xenoproteins so that alien cells can develop. It's all pretty boring, and you'd probably be better off waiting for the sequel, Aliens Hot, where we'll actually get to regulate the free radical count in the growing cells by modulating the tensor field supplementing the aqueous membrane that forms around the cytoplasm! So yeah, hold out for that.

Burstfire has promise. It takes a new spin on the classic 5v5 firefight over an objective by allowing the defending team to fortify the position with destructible barriers and fortifications while the attacking team seaks out the objective. On the surface, it's great.
The problem is in the details. There is no persistent lobby, after each 5v5 round, you have to find a new lobby. One round and then you find new people to play with. It keeps the teams shuffling in the sense that you really don't ever have a team.
The loadout offers a handful of assault rifles, sniper rifles, pistols, explosives, and 10 seconds to pick your loadout. It gives tooltips that, when 10 seconds is ticking, might as well be essays about the history of the gun, there is no time to do anything but pick one. The first gun I picked, with a scope granted, took up over half the screen when sprinting. I was quick to find a new favorite gun.
Time just seems to be the issue in balance. You don't have a lot of time to play with your team before the shuffle of lobbies, you don't have time to pick equipment, and you don't have time to talk to each other. But it makes up for this in making you wait for everyone to join your lobby and load each phase of the fight.
In the state that it's in, I can't recommend it as more than a time waster for a single person. Don't expect to make friends when you'll be with people for 5 minutes tops before leaving into the pool of potential players.

This game sets out to do one thing and it does it well, Base Management.
Your aim is simple, you want to progress through tech and research until you can launch a rocket to space. But standing in your way is the resources you need and the local alien "Friends"
If you enjoy learning the base rules the game works on, and then using that knoledge to plan and create a production chain then you will likely enjoy factorio, at its core factorio is a problem solving game, you need resources in order to do research, so you can then eventually launch a rocket, but you must balence your resource gathering, gather too much too quickly and the Pollution you create may just anger the locals enough to send them knocking at the front door.
the game is highly modable, and already has a good comunity making those mods, its still being updated with a weekly "Friday Facts" info snippet. and its ingame tutorials do a good job of explaining the game rules too you. this isnt a game that you will finish in 5 mins, but the puzzle aspects make it perfectly rewarding when those 3 hours you spent setting up a train to transport iron ore to your main base while protecting it from aliens.
TL;DR If you enjoy the base building aspects of minecraft, and the strategy of the likes of civ or Age of Empires then you will likely enjoy Factorio

Fond memories of this as a browser game led me to believe that Madagascar would be the cause of my frustrations. This time it's Greenland that distrust everyone and close their port at the slightest whiff of any symptoms.
The game is educational on both the infection spread and the geography of the world. And probably anger management.

Once you've got a rough strategy going (and playing games on casual unlocks helpful extras) of sneaky sneaky, kill 'em all before they can even think about starting a cure, you'll appreciate the subtle differences of the different plague types. Then will begin to find the game much more enjoyable and will start developing your own favourite techniques, such as, mega hordes of zombies invading the irritating surviving country, nasty symptom combos and mind control.
The save function is useful as well, in case something doesn't go quite right or you just want to boot up a 100% infected world and wipe them out in whatever way you see fit. Whilst the world menus seemed useful, I didn't find myself using them much. Maybe they just need a little more polish. Who knows?

When I was younger, I played a game called Escape Velocity, and I couldn't get enough of it. Exploring, trading, fighting off pirates, dabbling in a little politics across a divided galaxy, eventually playing with plugins to add other people's ideas and build in ones of my own, it was all incredible fun.
Looking at Endless Sky, I was skeptical: that was twenty years ago, times have changed, technology has advanced. But it was free to play, so why not see if I was wrong?
There shouldn't have been any doubt. Maybe you can find prettier graphics while you fight or ship goods for thin profit margins in EVE Online, maybe there is more space to explore in No Mans Sky, but the style of game Endless Sky taps into (and does so perfectly) seems to stand the test of time.
There are changes, of course... the passage of time DOES mean it can bring nicer graphics to the table than its predecessors, for one, and I've found the information layed out in the UI is more accessible than in the various iterations of EV, but (other than the absence of slot machines in Endless Sky's port cantinas) everything seems an improvement.
If anyone out there was a fan of the Escape Velocity games, I cannot recommend this one enough... and if you never got a chance, this is a great opportunity to do so.
