I'm going to start off by saying that this game is amazing.
A lot of people are comparing it to Dark Souls, which I can understand. However, it's also much more than 'Dark Souls in a Sci-fi setting'. The game has a bigger emphesis on the 'trash' mobs. There are only 4 bosses in the entire campaign. This is not a bad thing. The 'trash' mobs are in themselves quite challenging and can be quite relentless. Add on top of that a constantly changing area.
There are technically only 4 or 5 areas. The starting area is fairly straightforward. The next area you get to, is where I spent the majority of my time. It's very big with lots of shortcuts back to this game's equivilant of a campfire: The Ops. This particular level changes a lot though. It feels dynamic and the game as a whole keeps throwing new challenges at you, even in areas you thought you knew.
Add on top of that a progression system, which encourages exploring. The developers chose a Castevania aproach for quite a few of the 'secrets' in this game as well. Backtracking is essential, if you want to get all the loot the game has to offer. There are also conventional secrets that you can get to by either jumping, having a keen eye or just stumbling upon them. I have yet to find any ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t 'hit a wall and it disappears' secrets.
The combat is great. You can use both mouse & keyborad and a controller. I haven't tried a controller personally, but I know it can be done. The mouse & keyborad controls are excellent, and every key is rebindable! I've also been able to run the game at a full 60 fps, if not higher, for the entire game.
tldr;
This is a great game. It reminds me a lot of Dark Souls, but it also diverges away from it in key areas. It's not a clone, but it's got clear inspiration from Dark Souls. I personally liked this game enough to complete it in 3 days. The campaign is about 30 hours, I did a lot of looting, but I didn't find all the secrets. Moreover, there's a new game+ mode.
Buy this game if you're at all interested in the premise. It's bloody great, even if it is a bit pricey.
EDIT:
I've now played a bit further in NG+. I feel like the game doesn't scale well in NG+ and becomes way too easy. I have just beaten the third boss. It took me 3 hours to get to this point in NG+, where in the first run-through I spent 20 hours doing the same.

Emily Is Away is a minimalistic story-focused game taking place on a Windows XP operating system and an Instant Messaging (IM) client. After completing the game in its half-hour story, you'll be left feeling as hollow as you were when you were in your late teens/early twenties.
The game, taking place throughout the mid/early 2000s, brings you to a pre-Facebook world where IM'ing was both the norm AND what was cool. The aforementioned Windows XP design, combined with old sign-in sound effects, recreates this time and technology eerily well. It helps that a lot of the avatars you can choose are based on real album covers, movie posters, t-shirt designs, and other pop culture references of the time. Right from the getgo, it looks authentic and will at least get a chuckle out of you for its amusing dedication to a time that most of us are too embarassed to think about. Moreover, its authenticity will lend itself to the very familiar feelings the story will bring out of you.
And boy, you will feel very angsty by the end of this.
Throughout the game, you talk to your friend Emily via the IM client in short spaced-out bursts, starting from when two of you graduate from high school. The setting provides a perfect in-universe reason for why this story uses an IM interface and a great foundation for watching how your friendship evolves.
The game prompts you with three responses at a time in order to keep your half of the conversation going. When you choose one, you "type" it out by pressing any key on your keyboard until the response is finished and then hit the send button. It's a nice quirk to emulate the typing, even if you don't really type the response yourself.
This is where some of the game's more interesting (and terrifyingly real) quirks come into play. As you "type" responses, you can see your character backspace to correct typos, change word choices, and rephrase entire sentences from the player's end of the chat box. The changes in word choices, and even entire sentences, represent your character's hesitations or second thoughts or true feelings. It is authentic to how we can think about and dwell on what to send through a chat/text message for moments, trying to think of the best response and "drafting" something to say, before actually sending it.
In other words, the game creates the tension people get when they see "so and so is typing a message" in the client... from both sides of the conversation. Since the game makes you "type" everything out, you're forced to look at your response letter by letter, punctuation by punctuation. The weight of your words will ride on your neck and you'll have to live with how your words affect Emily's responses.
The only characterization and exposition you'll get out of this will be from the chats, and each chat session with Emily is very short. It's up to you to fill in the blanks based on the chats (
). What's not told or said in the chats still lend themselves greatly to the narrative, living up to the game's minimalistic style and recreating how it feels to make sense of old, possibly contextless conversations from your own text/social media messages.
And this all remains a fun (albeit depressing/emotionally frustrating) endeavor because the writing is believable. Smileys, all lowercase letters, "lol," and other typographic details portray these chats exactly as you'd expect. More importantly, this makes Emily seem real and creates emotional investment on your part. You don't have to like how the story plays out or how the characters progress, yet you'll still find yourself identifying with such imperfect, immature, confused, possibly malicious young adults. The game will still keep your attention because it gets under your skin, crawls into your heart, and breaks it while compelling you to see things through to the end.
I'd criticize the game for being short and having few endings for a game full of
different meaningful speech choices, but I can see why the game's brevity and
leave such a great impact. Had the game overstayed its welcome
, the game would wear itself out and fail to relate to emotions we've all surely felt in the internet age.
While this game isn't for everyone, it's a free game that is very confident in its presentation and is humble with itself. It certainly didn't turn into a pretentious interrogation/critique of online communication or a campy meme-filled romp about the 2000s, and this game could've easily veered in one of those two directions.
Instead, it's one of the most unique and clever (FREE!) experiences of 2015. It's worthwhile, even if it hurts you so badly that it drives you back to the mid 2000s bands who comforted your bleeding heart.

Nethack is an incredibly difficult tile-based roguelike. The game is always different every time you play, and being a roguelike, death is permanent. Each playthrough tells a tale of how horribly your player character dies, (or lives, if you escape the dungeon, or actually BEAT THE GAME) and because of the random nature of the game, you are going to die in many different sadistic and stupid ways. For instance, see that pretty amulet lying on the floor?
Overall, I find this game both very fun and challenging. There are free versions of nethack available in the form of ascii and tiled, top-down versions, so if you're not sure about it, I recommend getting either one of those versions first before playing.

I'm extremely pleased with this title, and it seems to have come out of nowhere. As a PC gamer I haven't had much luck with the Souls-like genre, but a sci-fi version was too good to pass up, and I'm really glad I grabbed it.
The combat system is excellent. Meaty, thoughtful, you have to consider your attacks and pay close attention to every oponent. The difference between an easy enemy and a deadly one isn't some slider setting or whether or not its a 'boss' of some kind, it's how well you know them and how carefuly you've chosen your weapon and when to strike.
There's a big emphasis on learning the oponents, the terain you're fighting on, and especially your own movesets. Each weapon, even within one of the 5 weapon classes behaves differently. Heavy and Single-Rigged weapons can turn you into an engine of destruction, but commiting to an attack leaves you unable to defend yourself if you chose the wrong time to strike. Getting caught in a heavy attack against one oponent, only to have a second appear from around the corner becuase you didn't pay attention to your surroundings can result in a quick death.
Though the game certainly seems punishingly difficult at first, you can quickly learn how to take advantage of the many opportunities the game offers you to turn the situation in your favour. Customize your gear and implants to maximize health and healing to slug it out with enemies. Increase your stamina to be able to dodge them till the perfect opening appears and then strike. Go with a heavy-hitting weapon and goliath armor to make sure that when you connect, you can stagger and stun-lock your oponents, or choose increased attack speed armor and fast-hitting single-handers or twin-rigged weapons to tear through oponents quickly while having the flexibility to avoid damage. Use high-HP but limited-use heals, health-regen, or a heal triggered by using 'energy' which you gain by succesfully landing hits on your enemies. You have many options to customize your combat style to your liking.

After seeing a few first impression videos I thought the game looked promising. I was looking for something similar to the soul series and its also clear that it was something that the developers where set out to do.
The game functions the same way in its core, but a lot clunkier. Attack seems to always connect if they are thrown in the targets general direction and you are also unable to pass through the hitbox of an other enemy.
But seeing as this game was made on a lower budget, you have to expect a lower level of combat.
My issues with the game are it's core design choices.
- Weapon proficiency, Who thought it was a good idea to add XP bars to your weapon? The souls game's have always been about experimenting. You're not going to start leveling up a new weapon mid game, grinding and gimping yourself for hours just to see if you like a new thing.
- Impact, poise damage is now amplified by the heavier armor you wear, meaning that you are forced to move slowly if you want to hit hard, again less choice to the player.
- Farming components, if you want to upgrade or create a new armor set, you need cut of the corresponding part of the enemy, how ever you wont get materials from hitting the enemies unarmored weak spots. So the game goes out of its way to encourage you to play smart, but then wont reward with any of the materials you need to progress in the game for doing so. Meaning that upgrading your gear is a slow slug fest.
- Lots of back tracking with no fast travel feature.
- No recall feature, the game actively goes out of its way to scum bag you out of losing your "souls", it will make you jump in to holes, it will lock doors behind you and with all this they had the decency to put your "souls" on a timer, so if you're not fast enough they are gone for good.
The game has a high degree of artificial difficulty, that it's so unfair, unpredictable and with a very slow grind.

I've played this game for nearly four years, on and off, before getting it on Steam when my harddrive died.
This game is not for the casual gamer, or anyone with high blood pressure.
You will laugh, you will cry, and more than anything, you will die a lot. In all of my time playing I've only ascended one time, and only with the help of bones files (random drops from previously slain characters) and thoroughly studying nethack wiki.
I have two tips:
One, start with melee heavy characters like knight, barbarian, or valkyrie. They are much easier to play, before you get used to the trickier classes like wizard and tourist.
And most important... don't get attached to your pets. Ever. It will lessen the pain.

NetHack itself is cool. And while Vulture adds much-needed graphics to NetHack, it doesn't do that great of a job with the interface.
1. Not all possible commands are exposed, so you still need to know the keyboard controls to NetHack, or at least have a reference
2. The interface is cumbersome to use. If I want to shoot a monster it takes multiple mouse clicks. Something as basic as shooting should be a single click, or keystroke
3. The interface doesn't remind the player of what keystrokes correspond to what commands. That in my opinion is the biggest failure of Vulture. I could tolerate Vulture as a crutch until I learned all the controls. But since Vulture doesn't teach me what the controls are it's not useful for learning purposes.
Vulture is kind of lazy, it's a shell over the controls NetHack already has and does the bare minimum to present those controls. The UI should have been designed independently of whatever the controls are for Nethack.

TL;DR - Emily is Away is a masterfully crafted nostalgia simulator for all of us who got the chance to experience the magic of IM software like MSN Messenger (Later rebranded into Windows Live Messenger), or AIM/AOL, ICQ with added note of that bittersweet tingly feeling of someone asking you that "Can I ask you something, but you might hate me." question. I would wholeheartedly reccomend it to everyone who wants to experience a nostalgia rush for free.
I like this game a lot. I do. I feel like it speaks to me, because I started using MSN when i was 10 and it kind of phased away in favor of Facebook and other mobile messengers when i was around 18. I made friends through the use of IM software, sent gigabytes of music, videos and images even though i had a sh*tty internet connection and spent hours just typing like mad. When it all kind of went away I wasn't really aware of how much I am going to miss it.
When i started playing this game it all started coming back to me. And it felt so good.
And then came the inevitable, bittersweet ending. To say that I expected anthing else, I would be lying. This exact thing happened to me with almost 95% of people I kept in touch (daily) once over this kind of software.
Honestly, I would reccomend this to any person who was a teenager that used IM software in the period when that software was "in". Believe me, spend a hour of your time and relieve some of your memories you didn't even know you missed :)

A few promising features were half implemented but went nowhere. Others, like religion, trading, burial based on religious preferences never materialized.
The bare bones structure is there, but for a game that tried to be Dwarf Fortress (DF-9, heh), it's missing alot. One resource to collect, there won't be any traders or materials to trade for. If you look at it as a tower defense game, it can sort of work, as random waves of boarders and raiders can test your defenses and one bad hull breach can doom your entire base, but that alone isn't worth it.
Exploration and randomly generated content is nonexistant. You get hostile raiders, meteor showers, maybe 12 different canned derelict ships will appear to explore, and immigrants. Features that never materialized: Sending citizens on missions to nearby planets, traders. You'll see it all in ~2 hours.
Overall I mostly enjoyed this game on the potential that it'll get better and seeing the new content in the monthly updates that used to come. It's not really worth it as a finished product.

Personally i always have a open mind for new hardcore ARPG games, partially because DS's combat system is kinda plain for me, but i do enjoy challenging gameplays. The Surge managed to construct a new style of combat system, including new move sets, damaging system and targeting system. The combat system itself i would say it is a huge success, since i am dodge main i do have a pleasent time using light armors taking down human enemies within seconds, the block does not work well, however i actually never tried to block so i will skip on that.
Yes the combat experience is not perfect, since i hate dealing with robots, they are either too meat or requires too much repetititve work such as trying to get to the back and backstabs them, and they do not move like humans, they basically make 360 turns according to how they like, and the movesets are sometimes too fancy that makes your can't dodge in time, still overall speaking i think TS does have a fluent combat experience, with fancy movesets that gives player a more refreshing look comparing to DS.
The level design might be the main problem, since every level looks the same and feels the same, basically factory or ruin, and unlike Nioh or DS or BB, which all 3 of them managed to make every level looks different and refreshing even though it follows the same theme or age or style, but TS failed to do so, which is why i was not really motivated to play constantly, in DS i might explore a little bit of the new level after the boss fight even i decided to go play other games or go to sleep, well TS, i just takes a quick look, knowing it looks same, bank all my scrap and go take a break, especially i am really not a fan of factories and underground.
I always appreciate small and young studios because they are always dare to make changes, in TS they added bank system, added limits to recover scraps and added body dismemberment, and a lot of new small stuff. For all the small stuffs, i don't think they made the game easier or harder, it's just about how much effort should i put in or how should i put it, neither other hardcore ARPG have to take the small stuffs, i mean i definetly hope that you can bank souls in DS but still that's how small stuffs made games different from one another, and i certainly not hoping that all the game uses the same stuff.
Overall, i do recommend Hardcore ARPG lovers to try out TS, just to feel the new stuff. Hardcore ARPG is a small circle and i do truly thank TS for bringing new stuff to it.

Edit: It has been pointed out that my complaints for Vulture (after my 1 hour of gameplay) may be incorrect.  Some of the things listed in the comments I thought I had tried and had no success, but I can't go back to check as I no longer have the game.  Please take the comments below into account before deciding on purchase. I stand by my "No" recommendation as I still think Nethack is best in it's original form, but take the specific complaints with a grain of salt.
---
As with all graphical interfaces that have been tacked on the top of Nethack, Vulture suffers from enough flaws to make it unusable for anyone that is familiar with the game.  Several major flaws made this unplayable as a Nethack game:
1) cannot eat corpses from the floor.  Huge problem as you had to pick them up, and become stressed, in order to eat. This is a huge problem as eating then takes may more turns and makes a hard game even more difficult.
2) no way to throw a corpse/tripe to your pet.  This is a must for training.
3) pet is a constant annoyance to what is an otherwise nice mouse-click based movement system.
4) notifications of items on the floor seem to be suppressed, and with the 3D walls, make it easy to miss things.
5) graphical icons are never as clear as the original Nethack ASCII characters.  Could eventually learn them, but feel it's not worth the effort at this point.
These are some of the big annoyances I found in just an hour or so of play.  Having the interface limit my choices was very unworkable.  If you aren't familiar with Nethack, you may not miss the flexibility, but it will still kill you.
I've been playing Nethack off and on for 25ish years.  I've tried a lot of graphical interfaces for it over the years and have been disappointed by all of them.  I was hoping from the positive reviews that this one might work out, but it is still unusable for any serious play.  Not to say it didn't have good points, it does.  The menus are nice, inventory is workable, it made some of the meta commands more accessible and the mouse movement is really nice.  Ultimately, Nethack is such a rich, deeply rewarding game that if Vulture is the ONLY way you will play it, get it and try it out.  But if you really want to experience Nethack, do it in the original ASCII, it will be well worth your time to learn it.

Vulture for Nethack is a graphical overhaul of Nethack - essentially larger tiles on an isometric map.
I think anyone who likes RPGs should experience Nethack, and Vulture is the prettiest way to play it. Vulture still has quite a steep learning curve, so patience and a bit of reading will go a long way.
If you haven't played Nethack before getting Vulture first read the Nethack Guidebook (
) to see if Nethack is something you're interested in.
Vulture replaces the sample screenshots in the Guidebook with static isometric tiles (as shown in the Steam store screenshots).
After you've taken the time to familarize yourself with many Nethack commands and been desensitized by frequent horrible death you'll find a game of surprising depth and challenge.
Okay - The graphics are of Vulture are (as yet) modest (no animations, modest resolution), but still a big step up from the original ASCII nethack or 2D graphical tiles. I started laughing out loud the first time my wizard (Orcdalf) started hallucinating in game - something that's merely annoying when I'm playing the traditional 2D interface with small tiles seems appropriately ridiculous when playing in isometric Vulture.
My suggestion is to go into the interface options and drop wall opacity down to 0.4 or so, and also switch to "half height" walls. This helps to stop the isometric walls obscuring ground objects.
Poor - The music seems straight out of 1990s midi, and other token environmental and combat sounds are simple.
Poor - The UI is a work in progress (DarkArts are working on a GUI and graphical overhaul). As is it seems possible to perform most actions in the game with just a mouse - but it's usually much easier using the traditional (esoteric) Nethack keyboard commands.
I did find myself using the mouse menus more than I expected in my test run of Vulture - so they do come in handy (probably as much as the Windows or X versions of 2D Nethack).
About 50 levels :). Wikis are packed full of spoilers for Nethack or brave (and headstrong) adventurers can persist in discovering new (probably unpleasant) features on every play through..

This one is a hidden gem.  It doesn't need flashy cool graphics or innovative features, because the subject of the game is inherently simple: you are a border agent in a fictional communist nation.  That's it.  The game starts out simple, and you'll think you've mastered it after the first day passes in-game.  But then, it gets harder.  A lot harder.  Just like any government agency, they constantly shift the rules and ask you to be on the lookout for different things that you hadn't even noticed before.  You'll have to get every detail right, because every mistake you make will cost you money at the end of the day, and could potentially make you or your family struggle for warmth, or food, or both.
The most interesting part of this game is that you truly get to understand what it's like to live the life of another person, warts and all.  Most of us react in shock and disgust at the thought of a border agent taking a bribe to look the other way for a certain person.  But through this game, you see that such an offer may be very difficult to refuse, especially when you feel very concerned for your family, or underappreciated by your superiors, etc.  Very few games would even consider looking at such a mundane existence as their topics, but this game does it, and it does it extraordinarily well.  I can see that I'm going to enjoy this one for years to come, when all the other "flash in the pan" games are long forgotten, because there's a very timeless quality to its design that won't fade with newer graphics or improved UI.  It's unapologetically old-school, and I wouldn't have it any other way.  Highly recommended.

Where do I even start with this game?

I didn't even mind spending money on subscriptions and expansions for my friends because I wanted people to play with.
Pros:
- The Aesthetic is gorgeous, even at lower settings.
- The free trial lets you level up a character to level 30, which is nice for newbies to try it out before purchasing it.
- The music is amazing, just like every other Final Fantasy game.
- The story seems cool I guess, (I've skipped most of the cutscenes)
- The ability to choose what you want to do, I.E. becoming a full fledged crafter, gatherer, or dungeoning. There are so many things you can do, and it's your choice on what you want to do next.
- So much content in the core game (Disregarding Stormblood and Heavensward)
- The community is extremely nice.
- Housing
- Transmogrify
- Trials (Fighting summons from numerous FF games)
- Being able to Dye almost any piece of equipment.
- Minions and Mounts
- The character customization is nice as well, it's not extremely in depth like Black Desert Online but it's pretty cool to see your character in every single cutscene there is.
Cons:
- Some Dungeons are underwhelming / annoying to navigate if you're new to the dungeon.
- Some Bosses are very gimmicky.
- Cutscenes can be extremely long, and there are a ton during some dungeons.
- Escort missions (Not mandatory, so it's not too bad)
- Some classes feel very underwhelming.
Combat:
- I felt like this is it's own category cause it's such a big portion of the game. And what I would say about it would be that, sometimes, it's not super impressive. Especially regarding some classes in the very beginning of the game. However, later in the game, when you're able to learn new abilities, it's much more fun and more engaging because you're able calculate a rotation that would benefit you and your party members the best.
I've spent so much time on this game, and I plan on spending so much more, and I'm still not even halfway done with what I want to do in the game.

This is actually my very first review of a game since signing up for steam when they gave away Left for Dead 2 for free and since I dont really delve that deep into a game except for its gameplay and story(if theres singleplayer) so expect more of an opinionated artice regardless of my hours played.
When I first saw this game on my exploration queue I thought to myself "Finally, a WW1 theme game". When i visited the store page I saw a lot of negative reviews I had second thoughts about even getting this game and decided to do some outside research and stuff (cause sometimes the reviews are old or something else). So after watching many videos on youtube and finding out about the little graph showing what you get with what you pay (I guess most of the nega reviews were just from the early stages of this game) and also the last sale I decided to take the risk and buy it mainly because I enjoy games like these.
So far its been maybe less than a week and I have yet to regret that decision. The single player is a bit challenging Ill admit and sometimes it gets to the point of frustration but I dont really mind. With so many games nowadays basically "spoonfeeding" players, its kind of refreshing to play a game that really challenges you and doesnt quite let you steamroll through it (even on rookie setting it can be a bit hard when you dont take the time to think and strategize) even though there are times I wanted to punch my laptop. As for the multiplayer, Ive only been able to play one game (because im a mac user, please dont judge *sad face*) it was an enjoyable experience for me (mainly because my team mate, who mind you was a fellow noob, cooperated with me and helped out as much as he could) until i ended up crashing out, maybe due to the performance setting on my game but nontheless it was fun and I want to do more of it. There is a bit of a learning curve however but once you get the proper feel of the game and its flow (which im still trying to do) then you yourself can be a badass general of an empire.
A few things annoy me however, such as the Ai of your troops sometimes not acting the way you want them to act, the vague mission descriptions for some missions of single player and the long pauses at times during the cutscenes but these are minor things and dont really ruin the experience of the game. It would be nice though that they would patch out some of these issues but it could be me.
all in all, if youre into strategy games then by all means, do buy this game and the deluxe package as it contains everything from the single player missions to the multiplayer. This is basically one of the best deals you'll ever find on Steam. Cthulhu Saves the World is fun, jRPG inspired game, that parodies almost everything it can. It's filled from top to bottom with pop-cultural references and jokes.
It has fairly clean, pixelated art-style and 8bit soundtrack and sounds... oldschool-ish.
As for the fighting system, which takes majority of the game - there isn't much depth in it, but it isn't a problem - there are up to 30 encounters in one dungeon. With such number, even most dedicated strategists would give up, not reaching even half of the game. Instead, game goes for less tactical, fast combat, that still requires some thought, where setting up actions for every member of a party, during one turn takes less than 15 seconds. Because of that, game can (for the most part) get away with its repetitive combat and while it's still a problem, it's nowhere near as big of a problem, that it would be, if they decided with something more complex and time consuming.
Beating the game takes around 8hrs... maybe more. After that you unlock 4 "new game+" modes. And it isn't just some simple "play the game with stats from previous game". There is one gamemode, where you play new character, meet new people - which means, new jokes, new dialogue lines. There is one character only mode, there is hardcore gamemode, where you get underpowered characters and finally Overkill - where you level up extremely fast.
There is also developer's commentary implemented into a game and full bestiary, that shows and describes many monsters and characters you can meet in game.
Finally, you get the game with Breath of Death VII and everything for less than 2€. Totally worth it!

The "Infinite" mode, as I saw in some other reviews, appears to be repeative. And it is.
Here is a quick answer for those who are bothered by this problem.
These "random" stages, as you can see on the generating page, are generated from a certain seed.
If you don't understand what this seed stands for, don't bother. Just FYI, a certain seed can only generate one certain pattern of Hexcell puzzle. This explains why you sometimes see repeated puzzles. Well, I guess the one you see most times is the one generated by those zeroes, lol.
Anyway, I am not able to explain the algorithm how a Hexcell puzzle is generated from a seed. But you still have 10^8, which is eight hundred million, puzzles to enjoy in total (they may not be as challenging tho). So I believe it is worth having this interesting game collected in your library.

When people talk about "Rogue-likes" this is the game that *almost* started it all.  It's effectively the follow-on to the original ASCII "Rogue" game. It's pretty ancient.  A good number of you probably weren't even born when NetHack came out.
Here's the TL:DR version:If you want a VERY in-depth and brutal dungeon exploration game, where you will die A LOT, then this really is the one you want to play.
Here's the full version:
This is an interface update to a game that's been around (and in almost constant development) since about 1987.
It was, then, a top-view text game, where a wall might have been expressed with a block: █  and your character was an @.  The floors were all full-stops, and there were so many key-commands to do things that you just got lost.
Vulture for Nethack is a graphical update to the original game. It turns those ASCII characters into isometric graphics, and takes some of those awkward keypress commands and puts them into menus to make them easier to get at.
If you want some kind of comparison... this is the great, great, grand-daddy to games like Dungeons of Dredmor. It is far FAR more complex and involved. There are so many more things to do, discover, learn and... frankly, get killed by.
Vulture's graphics are certainly an improvement on the original Nethack (unless you're a purist) but they're not even close to as good as Dredmor's. There's no animation to speak of, appalling sound, and the isometric is a bit icky in narrow corridors - but the strength of this one is the game itself, and if you're a fan of the dungeon-exploration style game you'd be doing yourself a great dis-service not to get this one.

Vulture (now Vulture for Nethack) has been my preferred NetHack front-end since I discovered the game a few years ago. Tried Falcon's Eye, which was a mess and abandoned years ago. This is a complex, deep and cleverly done game with an even nicer set of graphics upcoming which is already more than worth the asking price.
Word of warning: Don't expect to wing it and be coddled through to a win... Most players haven't EVER 'won' (accomplished The Ascension), but even getting halfway there is a huge accomplishment.  This is a taste of true old school gaming. Be prepared to die - A LOT -, maybe play in exploration mode or Wizard mode and maybe even do some reading at NetHack wiki. The nice thing about NetHack is that no matter how many "spoilers" you read, you won't spoil the game. There's always something new, something unexpected. If you master even the basics (which is itself a feat), Vulture for Nethack is endlessly replayable. Literally.

This game is basically a super enhanced version or copy of the "free to play" game Pandemic 1/2. I discovered Pandemic when I decided move to San Diego, California for a few months. My Marine buddy that I had went to high school with was stationed at Marine Corps Air Station Miramar (formerly the Top Gun Naval Academy... yup, from the movie) and he said that if I needed a long vacation that I was more than welcom to come live with him at his condo in Cali... For free (FOR FREE)!!! All I needed was to bring my Dj skills so that I could score a temp job spinning at a local Marine hang out (for spending money)! Like anybody in their right mind, I said yes and touched down in San diego the very next week. The first 2-3 weeks was unbelievable. My dj gig wasn't going to begin until the begining of May and I moved in with Chris on April 1st. so I spent almost a month of doing nothing but driving around San Diego and soaking up a lot of southern California sun. Durring the day Chris worked at the Marine base and I was left at home with nothing but free time. This was the first time in a very long time that I could be on a computer and stay on a computer for however long that I wanted. I didn't have a computer back in Louisville, and Chris had 3 of them (In my experience Marines have tons of money since they virtualy have no bills... Uncle Sam floats their tab). Needless to say I spent a lot of time on the computer getting reaquainted with long lost skills. It had been years since I had this opportunity. I used to have a computer back in the day. Then I got divorced and everything changed. It was durring this long trip to Cali that I had discovered Facebook and free to play games (The year was 2009).
The first game that I had come across and the game that I played the most was Pandemic 2. I had tons of free time those first 3 weeks and if I wasn't at the beach I was at the condo playing Pandemic and friending long lost friends on Facebook. Pandemic was at first very creepy. Making a plague or disease and killing off every living person on the planet took a while to get used to. As Plague Incs hardest area to kill off is Greenland, Pandemics hardest land mass was Madagascor. I was always able to wipe out everything except that little pesky island off the East coast of Africa. Every time, it didn't matter what I tried or the order I tried it in... That little damn island would always stay uninfected! Plague Inc. offers all of the same techniques that Pandemic offered except they take those steps and techniques and push them, tweak them and do everything they can to make the game as graphically appealing and more robust as Paddemic could ever think of being. Sure the concept of Plague Inc. is the same concept as in Pandemic but Plague Inc. offers you a more fluid and content driven experience. Plaque Inc. is deep with statistics, charts and all of the information you could think of for you to use in creating your deadly, destroy all plague. In this game the little extras make a huge difference and play a significant part in doing your dirty work. Turn out the lights and put your headphones on and It is basically like having your own little "bad-guy" hide out, lab and database all rolled into one. The realism gets really cool if you have either 2 or 3 screens. When I am sittinng in my chair and looking at all of the eye-candy that Plague Inc. puts on the screen I sometimes rub my hands togeather and do the bad-guy laugh. Sometimes I do this while slowly petting my dog! Just kidding... I don't do that. At least not every day. I can completely understand why our homeland security team would want to have a sit down with the devs of the game... It really does feel like you are in the driver seat of creating a deadly plague. This is hands down one of the best simulators that I have ever played. Simulators for me usually tend to be kinda boring as they usually move slow and are not that entertaining. Plague Inc. however moves at the perfect pace and all of the statistics and updates that play out in real time as your plague spreads are very interesting and entertaining. This game does a very good job when it comes to details... Like they say... "The Devil is in the details"! In plague, the devil really is in the details because it is the details give you the ability to kill off the planet and destroy humanity. Strategy is key and plays an important part if you want to successfully annihilate life as we know it. As of yet there isn't a tutorial so if you are not familiar with this type of game then you might have a rough time figuring out the basics. My advice is to go play Pandemic 2. Doing this will give you a spot on idea of how Plague Inc. plays out. If you like Pandemic 2 then you will love Plague Inc.
Although Plague Inc. is in early access it plays like a finished product. At least to me it does. I guess thats because I am comparing it to Pandemic 2. When put side by side, both games play almost exactly the same except Plague Inc. takes everything Pandemic does and greatly expands it... Which is why Plague seems like a polished game to me. It plays so fluid for an early access game. On sale it is definately worth it, but for the price... I am not exactly sure. Although I really like the game I often times passed it up because I could always play Pandemic for free if I was in a killing type of mood. Although I haven't spent that much time playing the game I know the game is solid because it plays like Pandemic (which is a really solid game) Just seeing all of the extra content that this game offers and already knowing how the game functions lets me know that this game rocks and the short time that I played it just proved me right. If you are not sure about the game, go play Pandemic 2. If you like that game, then imagine Pandemic with better graphics, more detailed statistics, extra in-game content and a gazillion different ways to mutate your plague and destroy the world!
So... Would I recomend this game for you to buy? On sale most definately! For full price... Only if money isn't an issue and you happen to have a lot of it. For me, money is always an issue so I am usually careful when buying games. I already knew how this game was going to be and that was the only reason that I bought it. If I had never have played Pandemic 2 I would have never bought Plague. I hope this has helped you in your decision. Remember... If you have any doubts about Plague Inc. Go play Pandemic 2! Seriously, Pandemic plays almost exactly like Plague and will give you a total whats up on Plague Inc. Here is a link to play Pandemic 2

Note: The 40 hours I have played this game does not do this review justice. I played this game for much longer when it first came out on the tablet.
This is probably one of the funnest casual games I have ever played. I'm not quite sure why it's still in early access, maybe because the developers want to ensure the game has all of it's features included in the final product (multiplyer, scenario creator, etc...) which only gives credence to my recommendation.
Premise:
You are a disease trying to infect, and ultimately destory mankind. The disease will eventually be discovered and a cure developed. You must race against the clock (the cure in most cases) to eradicate the human race or be eradicated yourself.
Pre-Game Features:
Once you select your Single Player game mode type (Main Game, Custom Scenarios, Official Scenarios, or Speed Run (Multiplayer is currently being developed)) you are given a choice as to which type of disease you would like to use. Bacteria is immediately available but, up to 9 more become unlocked as you play the game. I do not remember if Virus is available at the beginning or not since I have unlocked everything. Note: Each disease has it's own special abilities i.e. Bacteria can survive better in extreme climates which you have to spend DNA points to unlock.
Next you choose modifications to your genetic code. There are 5 sections to choose from, each with 5 options that modify things from transmission rate in certain climates to mutation chance. Most genes will need to be unlocked by beating the game. Once you have selected 1 modification from each section it's time to play the game. Note: Gameplay can last about 10 minutes on the lowest difficulty. I have had games last quite a bit longer depending on the disease chosen and other factors. You will learn to hate Greenland and New Zealand.
Gameplay:
The GUI presents you with a map of the world with boats and planes traveling from one country to another. Once you start you select which country you would like to start in by clicking on it. DNA points are the "currency" of the game, or rather the "Exp" which are spent on more modifcations, or upgrades to your pathogen. DNA points are acquired by popping red bubbles that appear when a new country is infected, orange bubbles that randomly appear, and infecting/killing people.
Once you have enough DNA points to upgrade, you may open another GUI with 4 tabs at the top and 3 very important progress bars near the bottom, "Infectivity", "Severity", and "Lethality".
The Progress Bars:
Infectivity Bar: This is how infectious your pathogen is. The higher the bar, the faster the pathogen will spread.
Severity Bar: Probably the most important bar to keep an eye on. To sum it up, the higher the bar the more people will freak out about the pathogen. This includes taking actions such as shutting down land and sea borders, cure research funding, and other measures to slow you down. The other 2 bars also contribute to these sorts of reactions, along with many other factors but not nearly as much as the Severity Bar. Also, the higher the severity, the more DNA points you get for infecting people.
Lethality Bar: This is a measure of how lethal your pathogen is. The higher the bar, the faster people die. Don't start killing people too early or they will die before they can infect other people!
The Tabs:
Overview Tab: This tab is pretty self-explanatory which provides basic information, but it also has a visual graphic of the current physical state of your pathogen. The more upgrades to your pathogen, the more the graphic changes.
Transmission Tab: Spend points here to increase infectivity. Many options are available that work in their own specific ways. For example, "Insect 1" increases infectivity, especially in hot climates with a chance to mutate symptoms from the Symptoms Tab.
Symptoms Tab: This is your bread and butter. Early upgrades increase infectivity, and sometimes lethality and severity. Higher tier upgrades are downright deadly.
Abilities Tab: Each pathogen has its own special abilities, but most of them share other abilities such as increasing resistance to hot and cold and drug resistance.
Once you have spent the points and return to the main map screen, you may start to see the color of the countries around the world begin to color red. You will gain more points and develop your pathogen and hopefully annihilate the planet.
Pros:
- Lots of pre-game options to customize your pathogen
--- Unlockable gene modifiactions and pathogens increases replayability
--- Several difficulty modes
- Simple and easy to use interface
- Game isn't too long or too short
- Super high replayability
- Consistently being updated
- Zombies are awesome!
Cons:
- Can get repetitive
- Some difficulty modes/pathogen combinations can frustrate you. Some games can last several hours by reloading previous saves or starting over
Neutral:
- No multiplayer, but is in the works
- Official scenarios don't really add much depth
- Some pathogens are too easy
- Can get fast paced as you start popping bubbles left and right. However, the ability to pause detracts from this

After playing over 1000 hours of this game, I can safely say that this is hands down the best MMO you will ever play.
Let's begin:
The music is superb. It's just like all the final fantasy games before it, and the soundtrack is always fitting while playing. I never once thought a song seemed out of place or anything like that.
The story is basic TO BEGIN WITH. But once you hit around level 20 or so, it starts getting very interesting, as you begin fighting primals (essentially gods) and the Empire, the main threat in the storyline.
The gameplay is fantastic, and there are sever different classes to play, each having one or two jobs branching off of them. For example, Arcanist begins as a DPS caster, but then at level 30 goes into either a Healer role with Scholar or a stronger DPS role with Summoner. I've never once gotten bored with the gameplay, and it just keeps bringing me back for more. Then there's also gathering and crafting classes, and those are also very enjoyable. They're constantly updating the game to add new content, and there has never been any shortage of things for me to do. But let me say, this game can get pretty grindy. That's really not a big deal, though.
The visuals are stunning. They blended a cartoony/anime-esque style with realism, and got something really good looking, and this definitely works in the game's favor. For example, I've been playing this game for nearly two years now, and I've never once gotten tired of the visuals. They never seem tiring or seem to age poorly.
Lastly, the community is top-notch. I rarely ever see anyone rude or disrespectful. Everyone is simply here to have fun. Everyone helps each other out, even if they don't know each other. Many times I've simply gone into a city and asked for a crafter to help me with something, and I've always gotten one nearly immediately.
All in all, get this game as soon as possible. It's an experience you won't want to miss.

SNES-esque RPG starring H.P. Lovecraft's famous monster, Cthulhu. There's a lot I don't like about RPGs in general, but this one manages to correct a lot of the most frustrating aspects of other RPGs:
-Allies are fully healed after battles, rather than leaving you barely limping along only to be killed in the next random encounter. (Battles are still quite hard though! MP is not fully restored after each battle, so use it wisely.)
-Only a limited number of random encounters will occur in each area before they are "turned off." You have the option to manually begin a battle with monsters if you still want to fight in a "finished" area.
-You can save any time, anywhere! (Outside of battles of course.)
Good humor, entertaining characters, and a bizarre plot that manages to make sense despite how odd it is. You won't find much that's better for the $3.00 price tag (and that $3 also includes Breath of Death VII, another RPG from the same company - this game is basically $1.50!).

Dark Souls of the Future? Take a harsh difficult, giant bosses, ressource-loss on death and shortcuts to the "bonfire" and you'll answer "yes". But this game is so much more and different. Unique crafting/upgrading, mods, interesting storytelling, executes, hit-boxes, combos,... I encountered just one short sound-bug with one of the NPCs who would repeat one phrase again and again till the conversation is over.... and one minor lightning-bug with the hologram and the wall behind it.
Edit after clear:
So after 20hours I cleared the storyline. I didn't rush but I didn't sniffed out every single (secret) location either. After the ending I searched if there are alternate endings and discovered many people that give a bad impression about the game just by reading a summary of the storyline. I enjoyed every minute and I'm glad I didn't spoiler myself with the story because the magic of this story goes with the unknown "what the heck is happening" and the search for answers. Look it up at the internet and you ruin the game for yourself... congratulation!
Back to my review which won't change a single step because The Surge was satisfying from the very beginning to the very end. The ending itself was somewhat okayish but better judge for yourself once you get there. I for myself, once I finished writing this commentary, will start a NewGame+ to discover the very last bits of secrets I left behind at my first walkthrough.
If I had one thing to mention that is clearly a bad move from the game then it's getting stuck in the story after "Black Cerberus" because you didn't find one specific thing in a showcase.

it fits every time but maybe one or two more tracks wouldn't hurt

it's not packed with hours of conversations but you get the feeling of the missing informations you looking for. If you didn't spoiler yourself you get sucked up by the story. The ending could be better but that's my point of view

Dark Souls had it's fatality moves but they were real hard to pull of. The Surge is all about fatality and it fits so well with the crafting system as an excuse to pull it of as much as possible.

Warren, the dude you play, hasn't much deepnes in his character. But that's okay because The Surge Story isn't much about solving thing with "character". You're not commander shepard to save the galaxy with questionable speeches but with iron and blood. The most of the few NPCs are your everyday dudes you meet on the streets but it fits into the story because you are on the "streets" out there.
Happy hunting, everyone!

Hexcells Infinite is back with the same formula but with a ton more content. Aside from the 36 campaign puzzles (that sprinkle in a few tutorials to explain the core concepts) Infinite has an infinite more (well, 999,999,999 mode to be more precise). Obviously infinite mode gives the player a lot of value and replay ability as most of these puzzles (I've done 60 of them) take between 2-15 minutes. The option to use the date as a seed is a nice touch for daily playing.
Infinite added a much needed save feature: maintaining the progress of your current campaign or infinite level. I say needed because some of the campaign levels can take a long time to solve (a few clock in at well over an hour during first playthrough). This also resets all the available information which is great if you accidentally or foolishly turned off some vital clue.
I give credit to the sound design. Aside from the pleasant music, revealing hexes produce one of several different musicle cues. It's just a nice touch to engage the player and give a bit of variation.
My only complaints are that highlighting columns and particularly blue hexes) to give information can sometimes make it difficult to see elements of the game. Several times the faint flashing  against the white backdrop almost blends in which may lead to mistakes. As for mistakes, while there is no guessing in the game, it can be a bit of a chore to put an hour into a level only to have a misclick force a restart (but no one said achievements are supposed to be easy).
Hexcells infinite gives some strong improvements over past iterations while keeping the core mechanics in tact. There is a ton of value for this game at any price for those looking for a challenge.
Smart, intuitive, difficult. This (and the other two Hexcells) should be played in order and enjoyed to the max.

Given how many hours I've put into this over the years though, I don't mind handing over a couple of pounds to reward them for making what is probably the best Nethack mod that exists.  It's great for new players, but still completely accomodating for the experienced.
It's a bit rough around the edges, there's no animation or visual effects, and the game just quits out once your run is over.  There's also no SLASH'EM mode!  (Although I guess that's a seperate project, maybe the workshop can take care of it)
All in all, it's a lot of fun, and you could easily play it for over ten years without beating it.

I suspect that if you asked a large random sample of people to rate this game on a scale from 0 - 100, you would find the mean to be above 50, maybe around 75, and the standard deviation to be unusually small compared with most other games. That's my theory as to why this game has such a high rating on Steam (96% at the time of writing). It's a good game, but there is absolutely no way it deserves such a high rating. Not even when hell freezes over.
The gameplay is centered around the collection of equipment-- guns, mainly. Most of the guns in the game are randomly generated, and it works well. They each have different characteristics, and each gun manufacturer (guns have a brand as one of their characteristics) has its idiosyncrasies. The quality of generated guns scales with the level of the enemies in the area where they generate, and consequently, as you proceed through the game, your existing guns will inevitably become obsolete, even if they were a few standard deviations above the average quality of generated guns at the time you found them. This forces you to always be on the lookout for new equipment, and to be ever-engaged in upgrading your arsenal. This formula works well! And it doesn't feel like a kick in the pants because your existing guns don't degrade; they're still as good as they were when you found them. It's just that the enemies in new areas are becoming harder.
The gun physics are good. It's not like Fallout 3 where the chance to hit enemies is based on the roll of a die. Ugh. In this game, the physics are so reliable that you can hit a moving enemy in the head with a sniper rifle from a great distance, taking into account the bullet travel time (which varies across weapons by the way!). Fantastic.
The script and story of this game are truly terrible. The writers do not know how to write relateable or realistic characters. Everything is very black-and-white, and childlike. The lack of realistic complexity in the writing also shows through what I think is supposed to be humour. Apparently the writers of this game thought it was funny that the 'bad guy' of the game calls you up and says "butt-stallion". Later in the game, they make an attempt at humour by calling an enemy "bonerfart". Yeah. That's the childish level of humour in this game. In fact, it's such simpleton humour that even as a child I wouldn't have found it funny. The attempts at humour are really jarring and try-hardy, to the point where its cringiness is a significant detriment to the game. It's annoying and, amazingly, even
to listen to the attempts at humour made. Which is why I listen to music while playing this game; so I can drown out the non-medy script.
Let's give the childish black-and-white bad-guy-good-guy story a pass. The main villain of the game is not even remotely threatening, because he is written as the most childish and immature character of them all. Throughout the game, the villain contacts you directly through the radio and talks to you. He doesn't say anything threatening or unnerving, he just says things like "butt-stallion" as noted above. Having heard nothing from the villain through the radio at all would have GREATLY increased the player's fear of him. I would have wondered what he was plotting, whether he could outsmart me, how he's using his arranging his virtually infinite military power to destroy you. Instead, you learn that he has the mind of a child. Wow. Such threat.
This is the main fault with the script-- the fact that it is largely composed of non-medy. However, pretty much every part of the writing is terrible.
For instance, your character shows up to the planet of Pandora in search of a vault full of treasure (very shallow motivation but that can work well if your character has a character arc throughout the game!). However, when you arrive at the main hub of the game (where your allies are), everyone immediately lauds you as a hero because of the fact that you're a vault hunter.
?????????????????????
There are a trillion questions here which fill your mind.
All of those questions arose from a single, simple event in the game: arriving at Sanctuary. You cannot possibly imagine the vast ocean of nonsense contained in the script and story of this game. It is unfathomable. And look, plotholes are fine. But this is different. This is
. I get that this game is not about the story, but you have to at least care about the characters. Heck, you at least have to care about the main thrust of the game: eradicating the villain.
The game/script does nothing to make me care about anything. To the writers' credit, they did attempt to make you dislike the villain, though. They portray him as having performed cruel experiments on people and animals. But it's so exaggerated and out-of-place with the rest of his childlike demeanour that it's totally unbelievable.

Would you break the rules at a border check to reunite a family?
Would you approve dangerous people with legitimate passports?
Would you put yourself and your family at risk to help someone else?
Would you help someone if it meant risking outbreak of disease?
Papers, Please isn't a game that forces a particular issue or crams such things down your throat (e.g. Press F to Feel), but it does introduce you to some pretty interesting scenarios (with no definite correct response) during your time at the Arstotska border check. Surrounding these questions, however, is a very entertaining 'paper simulator' that sees you checking documents for inconsistencies and approving or denying entry. Overall, the game provides a suprisingly rich experience and your actions throughout lead to a variety of different endings (I think 20 in all), providing a lot of room for replaying the game (especially after unlocking endless modes).

One of the greatest Fantasy MMORPGs I've ever played in my life. It's been over a year and a half and I'm still playing, mainly because i haven't done everything in it, which you actually can without the use of alternative characters.
-What I like most of all:
-The Main Scenario stories are very engaging as they truly represent your progression along in the journey. A majority of the game's content is unlocked by working through the Main Story Quests. (Unless you decide to buy the Story Skip items from the Mog Station to move far closer into Stormblood.)
-All Jobs/Classes are available for the player to accept and freely switch at any time you want. It used to be where you need to have certain classes at a specific level to have the more advaced version of the starting classes to gain new skills, now you just need to have your current class at lvl 30 to get the next job instead!
-Leveling up may still be grindy in some aspects, but dungeon duties give a good helping hand on a daily basis.
-Crafting and Gathering Jobs are their own individual professions.
-The community is large in almost every world with friendly people backing you up.
--What I have "small" issues with:
-If you are playing this for the sake of housing aesthetic, you're gonna need to be incredibly patient. Luxury will cost you heavily in this game.
-It's difficult to find an even ground if you're playing with friends that are new to the game and you're too far in. FFXIV shows progression when msotly done single handedly. Not being able to share quests or level appropriate dungeon duties becomes a bummer when your friends haven't unlocked the content yet.
-My most biggest upset is how SquareEnix's customer service is incredibly flawed, that if one thing messes up with your account, you may end up completely boned and starting over with a different account. Their security methods are way too precise, making you wish you had written down your details just in case of one small mistake. Such a great game doesn't deserve such lousy service.
Overall:
FFXIV is a game that is definitely worth it's monthly fee, even for uncertain newcomers. It gets much better when you find a good place among the player community, in free companies, as you journey through Eorzea with an axe, a staff, a bow, or even a skillet to mark your identity among the millions doing the same. There's so much to do you'll spend weeks to months or even years doing it all.
My Personal Score: 9/10

I’m writing this review because I believe this game needs an honest, non-biased review. I have played this game for a few hours (28+) and am currently about half way through NG+, and sure I have a private profile and 1 VAC ban (for CoD: Advanced Warfare), but that should hold no weight here because this game has no Multiplayer and it was over two years ago.
First a little background, I have played Demons Souls, Dark Souls 1 – 3 (including all DLC) and Bloodborne, Salt and Sanctuary, Titan Souls and a few other “Souls Like” games, I feel as if I have some background and some depth as a gamer to make a review here. Before I played this game, I revisited Lords of the Fallen, by actually playing through some of the game again, just to be able to compare the gameplay and the maturation of the developer as this is their second attempt at a Soul-type game.
Cons:
-	Low Mob Variation. However, it’s somewhat understandable given the constraint of the story. Keep in mind, you are at the CREO facility, so what would you honestly find here? Well, the crazy workers, security personnel, and the automated robots so not really sure what folks were wanting here, you can’t just toss in crazy abortions like you would find in Dark Souls, it wouldn’t make sense wouldn’t fit, and it also doesn’t make sense yet to send in outside entities yet because nothing has truly gone awry at this point (no spoilers).  One point here, the mobs will get more attack variation as the game progresses, for example, the tripod jumpy mob will have an electroshock attack later in the game, when in the beginning, it does not.
-	Limited Armor/Weapons EFFECTS. Read this correctly, I am very content with the amounts of weapons and armor in the game, it’s the effects that are disappointing. You have 3 armor subtypes (Goliath (heavy), Sentinel (medium), Lynx (light)) and 5 weapon subtypes (1h, single rigged, dual rigged, heavy-duty and staffs each having at least 4 to choose from if you collect them all (both the unique boss weapons as well), so I feel the amount in each is fine, but what about special effects to give Warren that extra edge? The armor has special effects if you wear the full set and some of the boss weapons have an elemental effect if you get the 2.0 version (dmg from them is a moot point), but the bonuses from them are negligible at best (even the Drone ones), you gain more by mix and match to be honest. This can be patched!
-	Implants Do Not Scale with NG+. This is a HUGE issue. The game gets increasing harder, the implants needs to get increasing better… Don’t give V.1 implants when upgrading the Rig to V10 or higher, that makes no sense. True, they scale with level, but once the hard cap is reached, that’s it, there is also an implant space cap, so if you are going to NG+++ and the MOBs are progressively getting more HP and hitting harder, Warren needs better implants. An example would be Implanted Electrodes V.2 (which is the highest you can get btw), they do 36 energy restore, currently I have 120 energy (Vanadium E cell V.5 and V.3), I have 2 equipped, so when I pop it off, I restore 72 energy, I would have to equip 3 (which I have but with my current build it would be harmful) to fully restore my energy, but if a V.3 or V.4 would be introduced, it would solve high that issue especially for NG+ and beyond play. This can be patched!
-	Bosses. Very underwhelming. I like the idea of specific fighting tactics for a 2.0 weapon, however those tactics are already on the web, so they are no longer a secret, however, only having 5 in a game like this is very disappointing, I felt very, confused is the best word I can use here as to the bosses, especially for a game like this.
Pros:
-	Level Design. In a game like this, gone are the days of the lazy gamer who needs a waypoint icon to show them exactly where to go and exactly what to do and when they get lost allowing a warp back to start over (of course you kind of know where you have been due to no mobs being present). Adds a new thought to should I go there and do that right now, or should I wait, it’s the risk vs. reward mind set. This game makes the player engage their brain and figure things out, explore, use the tools at your disposal to find things. It fit the story as well, many will disagree here but if you honestly think about it, it does, Warren is at the CREO facility, it’s going to look the way it does, they aren’t going to have some strange exotic designs here, just facility structures with joining auxiliary tunnels, kind of like any other building you go into in real life, if you look at them.
-	Story. It was good, it was real, it was honest. I was able to find all the voice logs and hear all the emails, the story unfolds rather well if you listen to them all. Warren is just a guy, nothing special, in a failing world, goes to the one place where he thinks he can get a break, CREO. Gets a job, goes in, gets his rig (in a messed-up way), wakes up and everything has gone pear shaped. He has no special skills, no god like powers, nor should he. He doesn’t know who to trust, doesn’t know anyone from Adam, first person he finds is Sally, who says he has to help fix everything? Ooohhhhkkayy… What would you do? They give you choices, and they do affect the side questing and the main quest from my experience (again no spoilers). You don’t get OP, and the game doesn’t allow you to nor was it designed that way, you are the under-dog, and the game reminds you of that the whole way through, and I liked that.
-	Synergy. What I mean by this is, implants/Drone/Gear. Using the proper gear drone and implants together will create some good synergy. I have seen some streamers find it, and I myself have found it as well, this is something that really comes down to player preferences (builds), but the Developers have put enough in the game currently to synergize with each weapon/armor type.
-	Mob attack Variations/Increasing attack pools. When you begin the game the mob attacks are limited, but as you progress, they mobs become more aggressive and more attack types unlock and they gain more skills. One example is what I mentioned in the Cons area with the tripod jumpy mob gaining the electroshock stun wave attack later in the game, another example is the security guys, at the beginning they have limited attack pools, but at late game, they have stun darts and a ground stun attack they don’t have at the beginning of the game. I believe this happens after you get finished with R&D, in NG+ its right out of the gate.
Summary: If you are looking for a Souls-Type game that is going to scratch that itch for you, this really isn’t that game, because if you go into this game with that mindset, you will become disenchanted and be left with a bad experience. If you are looking for a game with a different take and a challenge that has room to grow, then, this may be that game for you, but that’s up to you on if you want to experience the game, don’t go on my or any other single person’s opinion as the end all buy or not buy decision maker. Also, it will become easy to fall into the meta for this game with attacking (jump jousting, dash back) and get very bored mid-game, I would advise experimentation with what I talked about concerning synergy with weapons/armor and drones to avoid this because this can become a factor with your overall game experience. I hope this helps in some in your decisions, thank for taking the time to read.

I'm kinda mixed on this game.
I'm going to mark "No" because it has a $50 price tag.  If it's in the $30-$35 range I'd say go for it.
It's souls-like game, there's no doubt there.  The 1 on 1 combat can be fun and engaging and the ability to cut off limbs, and the finishers are really good improvements on a combat system like this.  The way the game lets you "Farm" the "Armor" is also an interesting aspect (as long as the drop-rate isnt significantly lowered).
However, this is kinda all the game has going for it.  The cons kinda come in after:
> Combat vs more than one enemy can sometimes feel really cheesy since dodging isnt reliable.
> The levels feel really small and cluttered, with only one "Checkpoint", but what feels like WAY too many shortcuts.
> You die, you drop your "Souls", but now you have timer for "Increased difficulty" to get your "Souls".
- What does this add to the experience?
- Is it to be able to subtly brag that "Our game is harder than <Dark/Demon> Souls" ?
> There's a limited amount of weapons and armor (6-ish types of weapons, and about the same for armor variants)
- There's no real customization for your armor, be it Logos/Decals/Colors.
- If you enjoy the "Fashion-Souls" aspect, you wont find it here.
> The "Majority" of the play time spent in this game comes from replaying the same content over and over.
>  Like the Souls series,  you spawn with no clue of what's going on, and no real direction or desire to move forward in the story.  (IMO, a terrible and lazy copy/paste choice here, I still dont know why they went that route - probably because the if you found out what the real story is early on, you'd of lost interest much faster.)
> There's only a few bosses, which could be a pro or con depending on who you ask.
> Like "Lords of the Fallen" it feels like it's a badly re-skinned Souls-lite, instead of being it's own thing.
- It's "Futuristic, not "Sci-Fi" IMO, but it's still a boring story, a bit of repetition, and limited content.  It could have been released as an "Xbox Arcade Title" with the amount of actual content there is.
- In short, if the combat aspect of the game doesnt hook you, there's nothing here for you.
I could be wrong, but how this is set up, it really seems like a 1-off title:  *The AI has "taken over", in the 'Work Factory' you play in*, and I just dont see how this would be "Repeated" for a "Franchise" on a larger scale more than once.
TBH, I think they could of done this game, but instead make you play as "Customized Pilot" or "Generic Robot" against "Robots/Mechs/Andriods" where you could integrate parts onto your Robot/Mech the same way they do here.
At least with that route, they could of wrote a more interesting or uinique world/story, but that's just my opinion.

2 things:
1. The game get exponentially worse late game, and NG+ is terrible.
2. Use QUICK SAVE / QUICK LOAD (F5/F8) to avoid a lot of pain/cheese.
