To put into perspective, I have about 70 hours of game time and have stepped into NG+ before beginning to write. This review is also cut short, as it is my first steam review, and I was not aware of the word count limitations. There should be -pages- more. This game deserves "Mixed Reviews" status at best, and most positive reviews on here have not even hit mid game!
I will begin by saying that after considerable thought, I do not recommend this game. I am an extensive "Souls Like" fan and I am no stranger to extreme difficulties and challenges associated with games like these into NG+7 difficulties, which require finesse, patience, skill and (at times) a bit of luck. Before we begin, the TLDR: More cons than pros. The cons include Story, gameplay, level design, AI, difficulty, balance, and more.
STORY- (Spoilers)
The story of The Surge is confusing and common sense details leave lots of questions.
The entire time playing, there is a sense of panic and a need to escape. Warren very much wants to get out of there and survive - Only midway through the game do we realize that Warren is not trying to escape and find a way out, but is moving closer to the center of the facility for no reason. When I realized story wise that Warren was trying to (for whatever reason) get to the root of it all, it was well into the game.
As I navigated through the gritty catwalks and cooridors (Get used to it, the same textured hallways), I would frequently hear radio calls that had panicked figures talking about a killer on the loose who was breaching security, slaying scientists and being an absolute ruthless menace. As these were all none of the things I thought I was doing, I thought there was a enemy character we would be introduced to later. When I discovered it was supposed to be me, I just couldn't wrap my head around it. Confusing.
There were times where gold story elements could happen - A prominant char hangs himself later on, and the audio log at his feet is yet another ramble from a character not even them! Wasted potential.
The story is barely existant - You will be forced to listen to looped CREO PSAs on monitors that ultimately tell the same thing every time. Get used to hearing them, and the "safe room" music on loop as you navigate and backtrack.
You will navigate the same textured cooridor and elevators all through the game, with little variety to the biomes you play through. Enemies will retexture and be reused at every turn. You will be backtracking to every area multiple times.
Combat- feels clunky and similar to Lords of the Fallen, but a bit better. The targetting of individual body parts to sever schematics and crafting materials at first feels very refreshing. Enemies however, if they have an armored part you wish to sever, has hyper armor - You do not. Even attacks with the heaviest of weapons results more often than not with you being animation locked and unable to dodge. Swinging around a hammer that was bigger than my opponent did not even stagger the lightest of armored enemies. Attacking armored parts with lighter gear (Such as dual rig claws) is frustrating and extends combat into tedius amounts of time. Attacking unarmored areas however, give satisfying levels of damage and stagger.
Each weapon had a variety of nicely animated combos. Unfortunately, comboing is a liability in this game. The game punishes you with enemy hyper armor, resulting in successful combos you perform leaving you open to punishing (nearly one hit kills) normal attacks that stagger you. Keep in mind, you must target the armored sections to get gear. For me, this meant ditching my claws outside of lunge attacks because as beautiful as the combos were (And god, are they pretty) seeing anything past the first 2-3 hits meant almost certainly that you were trading blows - and losing the exchange.
The Combo system is also incredibly frustrating. Attack patterns will lock you into place with no way to cancel the animation to get out of the way. At one point I realized that the combos would automatically begin additional attacks without prompting; swinging a heavier weapon with two attacks resulted in an unwanted third attack extending the animation by solid seconds - more than enough to get you killed by the most trivial of enemies. "Getting good" at the combo system required me to poke and prod enemies, rather than engage in a fun fight.
"Dodging" is non existant. There is nothing to keep you safe from the enemy aside from a lunge to the side or back - Neither of which have iframes, all of which require an immense amount of stamina to perform if you follow up with any sort of attack. If your character is knocked to the ground, you are vulnerable to attack and will frequently get killed as you slowly stand to your feet.
Armor and Equipment is a tragedy. There are a good number of weapons, though their actual variety is lacking with few things to make them unique. The Boss Weapons are extremely unique (All 5 of them..) however unless you read spoilers and strategy guides (Or have dumb luck) you will likely never see them. I was thrilled to get the Firebug claws from the second boss, and was dismayed when I discovered that there is a SECOND weapon that drops instead if you fulfill a specific condition. Otherwise, you get a garbage "Unenchanted" version of the weapon.
Let me begin this part by saying that I feel very strange about this boss loot mechanic. On one hand, I was delighted to tail chop in Dark Souls, and I LOVE loot, especially rare loot. But for whatever reason, the mechanic in this left me feeling incredibly cheated. There is no way outside of playing through the game a second time at NG+ to attempt the weapon drops, and the methods to obtain them really can't be known unless you have prior knowledge. It should make the loot feel rarer, but it feels more like the Devs tricked me into having to replay rather than feel accomplished because the loot you get is TERRIBLE if you get the mundane version.
There is a total of 5 bosses. Five. And one of them is a normal enemy who uses the first boss as a rehashed minion.
Armor is a mess. Heavy armors have less protection than light, require more power, and have useless effects. Even "Fashion Souls" is impossible because the armors require too much power to use your implants unless at much higher levels. Defense is also a negligible stat, offering virtually no protection the higher you go. (Naked vs full top tier heaviest  NG armor resulted in no noticible defense)
Difficulty - Struggle is at the core of games like these, but the difficulty is so artificially inflated. Light attacks against you cleave entire health bars, the AI aimbots their attacks to the point where they will baseball slide in a complete circle to track you. Enemies will lunge and arc mid flight and track you around corners. AI pivots on the spot (You cant) with faster attacks than you, so perfect dodges often are rewarded with the attack just turning to you.
This game only feels difficult because it is blatantly imbalanced, hamstringing you with animation locks, cheesy AI and bewildering hitboxes. This is not even a matter of player skill. You have every QA facet of the game against you, and shows the developers lack of testing or ability to balance. It is when you get your foothold and "get good" that the real problems with the game will be noticed. I promise you that.
AI- This sums the AI up -

The first few hours were made to impress, with the rest of the game lazily made. There is some good stuff here, but broken and meaningless quests, bad story, unpolished combat, 5 bosses (With a rehash!), confusing story, unbalanced mechanics and terrible AI are not worth the price of admission.
NG+ has extras, if you can bring yourself to play it a second time. There is so much more to say but I'll simply say this. Do not buy this game. Avoid it.

As someone who joined in the first week when the game was released as open beta, left for a  while, returned, left again aaaaaand returned again, I think I can do a review of this game.
First of all, you may read on other reviews that the game is dying despite decreasing player base. Well, I believe it WAS dying. Since the player base seems to have increased from 1 year ago to now. I see a lot of new players, new guilds, and a lot of ppl online! - Ok, now I can start the usual review.
I've tryied some other MMOS when I left this game, but I came back! - Why??
This game community is awesome! People are overall really nice and help new players with stuff, it's very easy to forma parties for PvE, there is a good PvP system and there are ALWAYS ppl playing PvP. - So it's really hard to be forced to play alone, as in some other games.
There are LOTS of Guildes which you can chose from! There it THE Top Guild, with maxed lvl players ONLY, there are some other Elite Guilds, there are the Nacionality Guilds, like Russian or Brazilian Guilds, Small Guilds, Big Guilds, Active Guilds, Unactive Guilds and Ok Guilds(ENMITY yay!).
Basically, there is a Guild for everybody! - Sometimes they require you hit lvl 20, 30 or even lvl 60(max) to join one, but it's actually easy to get to lvl 30 by youself. But the sooner you get to a Guild, the sooner you can ask veteran players for tips more often! - As a lvl 50 who left for a long time I sometimes ask my lvl 60s friends who are still playing lol.
About it being a Pay to Win game, it is not! - Maybe if you want to defeat the Top Guild You HAVE to spend some money since some been playing the game since it released and they have AN ENOURMOUS AMOUNT OF TIME of effort by playing the game! - But you can pretty much hit lvl 60 by not paying a cent! - Sorry Katuri! - But the  grinding GETS faster when you pay real money to it! - You can also pay for it in Gold(game currency)! But it's not very cheap. The top players who don't pay real money do it! So here's my first tip lol(I should do it more often). So, I don't agree it's a pay to win game, because there are a lot of new players on the game and just a  small amount of those paid real money.
On the other  hand, why not paying real money at some point? You are playing a very good game for FREE! The first two packs are actually decent priced considering the quality of the game. The third it's like VERY GOOD, but it's more than I would pay for the game, if it wasn't free.
The graphics are not THAT GOOD, it may be a little childish for some, but considering MANY other MMOS that have been releasing, this one has a really nice graphic! The maps are really good as well, some quests are tyring, others are not, the game has a REALLY COOL item upgrading/ recipe/ Seal making/ stuff like that/ market System! Everything well planned and It's even possible to reset your skills WHENERVER you want(as long as you've reached lvl 20)! - If you pay one kind of in game currency of course. The game does not punish the player base who works and studies, because when you leave the game for a certain time, there will be a 2x xp bonus for quite some time, depending on the time you were gone, and it seems that the highest lvl you are, the biggest time the bonus will work for you - it seems that way, but I have not confirmed this yet. The mobs are well made, graphically and functionally, also give us drops that makes sense. I love the class/ skills system,  very good, with lot of options to chose from - not as much as tree of savior, but just enough! You can also  have many characters to your account, which means you can make a character of every class to see which you like most to play with. There are some forced PvP areas, which I really enjoy  it!
The bad things about this game are the LAGS, it LAGS SO HARD at certain times! Since last patch it was almost impossible to play with my sorcerer(maybe because I use a lot of skills), but same does not happens with my other characters who don't use as much skills when I go farming. - But it's something they can fix and they do some server maintence(if I didn't write this word right, sorry, not first language and I had a blank on how to write it). Also, the time you spend grinding and how expansive stuff are, if you expect you'll get lvl 60 fast and be a top player fast, forget it! You may hit lvl 60 on record, but it takes a LOT of grinding to it. You may spend over 2 weeks on a single lvl at a certain point of the game! lol. - Right now I'm lvl 50 for 1 year! But I left for 1 year so it does not count much haha! Another bad point is the walking! AAh the walking! The game requires a LOT of time by walking from place to place. There are the instant teleports, but they cost gold, and at certain points of the game, you don't have gold for that! So, good luck on walking. Mounts are only efficient for knights, other classes can't attack from mount. And not real money mounts are not very efficient(fast), but they help a bit. Or you can also make a seal on your shoes that increase your speed! And use certain items. The space on the bag is a real struggle as well, but you can live with it and you can buy reales to buy those slots!

Great game, fun times, but ♥♥♥♥ all this game is hard.
And it's not a good kind of hard, it's an RNG based hard. You could do things right, you can follow a build guid on how to win with a particular plague. But still lose because Greenland closed their port before you got on there, or your virus mutates into a "scary" disease and work on the cure goes nuts before you've infected even a quarter of the population. All RNG.
It wouldn't be bad if the game wasn't so time invested, but you spend a lot of time on your plague, just to not be able to infect some island state, even with upgraded plague birds, or airborne particles.
This breaks the gameplay, sure you can just start again, but after playing for 30 min just to watch as your plague dies out by killing 99% of humanity, but Japan is still alive on their own island of protection.
Sure it's realistic enough that if they close their islands borders they'd be more likely to survive. But from a gameplay perspective, the game should just say "Game Over an island closed their borders before you infected it." That's what is actually happening, but it neglects to tell you.
Sure there's strategies to defeat RNG, and for the most part they work but some situations are rendered extremely hard, or impossible, simply because RNG is always there.
I can't really reccommend people buy this game, there's a tablet version if you wanna try it. But until they work out the RNG issues within the game, which they probably never will thinking that it's ok that the hardest difficulty not only requires you to go online and follow instructions, and those instructions will still only give you a 10% pure luck based chance of actually winning.
There's little strategy here, it's a build order, so playing the same plague more than once is kind of repetitive. You can't really react to what people do. I still love the old ASCII/Tilebased graphics of the original but this is a nice little isometric coat of paint thrown on for the people who absolutely cannot stand ASCII graphics I guess.  Anyone unfamiliar with NetHack should realize this is one of the huge stepping stones that set the foundation for all the roguelikes we see nowadays and often at times the benchmark at what people compare most modern-day roguelikes to. The game is unforgiving, relentless and even in death you will at times find humor in it since there are so many ridiculous ways you can die.  The game just like NetHack closes upon death and the final scoreboard which IS annoying as heck when you want to play it again and you have people messaging you "having problems?  it says you're loading up Vulture for NetHack like once every minute or two".  A minor inconvenience that I'm used to.
In short, if you want NetHack on Steam with the graphics presented to you in the screenshots then the price is reasonable considering the hundreds if not thousands of hours I've spent on the original game, and in those many hours I never really got very far, yet still pushed onward hoping I could see something new or die a whole new ridiculous way.  If you have absolutely no clue what NetHack is but enjoy dungeon-based roguelikes then I'd say you owe it to yourself to play this or some iteration of NetHack.  Just do yourself a favor first and go over the manual and study all those commands, you'll be glad you did.

We all know Nethack is a good game, so this review is covering Vulture in specific. Out for 3 years already, Vulture finally makes it way onto Steam for the same price as the Desura release.
This is a tile and graphical interface for the game "Nethack", making it easier on the eyes and on the controls as it can be controlled with the mouse, using keyboard hotkeys for shortcuts.
The game opens with no main menu and instead asking your characters name. Similarly, when you die or otherwise end the game, the game closes and requires to be started back up through Steam to play again. You are quickly greeted with some rather off-key music, the volume of which cannot be controlled in the game and must be done through volume mixer. It's very possible to start new games and be unable to leave the first room due to the random dungeon layout. The art style is very inconsistent, at one point It spawned me with an anime robot girl sprite that looked like it was ripped from something else, another time I'd spawn as a very poor 3-d model of a Tourist. Came across a Magic Marker, which was actually just a huge .png of a Sharpie someone had taken from Google. Fountains don't seem to work. There's no real way to examine items you've picked up.
Despite all these things I still kept trying it. It's really nice to have some art associated with things so it's easier to tell what things are at a glance, but I find it hard to recommend to someone over other games or tile packs. Has a really nice 90s Freeware feel to it, so there's that. Avoid if you don't like stolen art, bad music and restarting for the 30th time because you can't leave the first room.

One of the greatest Fantasy MMORPGs I've ever played in my life. It's been over a year and a half and I'm still playing, mainly because i haven't done everything in it, which you actually can without the use of alternative characters.
-What I like most of all:
-The Main Scenario stories are very engaging as they truly represent your progression along in the journey. A majority of the game's content is unlocked by working through the Main Story Quests. (Unless you decide to buy the Story Skip items from the Mog Station to move far closer into Stormblood.)
-All Jobs/Classes are available for the player to accept and freely switch at any time you want. It used to be where you need to have certain classes at a specific level to have the more advaced version of the starting classes to gain new skills, now you just need to have your current class at lvl 30 to get the next job instead!
-Leveling up may still be grindy in some aspects, but dungeon duties give a good helping hand on a daily basis.
-Crafting and Gathering Jobs are their own individual professions.
-The community is large in almost every world with friendly people backing you up.
--What I have "small" issues with:
-If you are playing this for the sake of housing aesthetic, you're gonna need to be incredibly patient. Luxury will cost you heavily in this game.
-It's difficult to find an even ground if you're playing with friends that are new to the game and you're too far in. FFXIV shows progression when msotly done single handedly. Not being able to share quests or level appropriate dungeon duties becomes a bummer when your friends haven't unlocked the content yet.
-My most biggest upset is how SquareEnix's customer service is incredibly flawed, that if one thing messes up with your account, you may end up completely boned and starting over with a different account. Their security methods are way too precise, making you wish you had written down your details just in case of one small mistake. Such a great game doesn't deserve such lousy service.
Overall:
FFXIV is a game that is definitely worth it's monthly fee, even for uncertain newcomers. It gets much better when you find a good place among the player community, in free companies, as you journey through Eorzea with an axe, a staff, a bow, or even a skillet to mark your identity among the millions doing the same. There's so much to do you'll spend weeks to months or even years doing it all.
My Personal Score: 9/10

Totally not worth the money they ask, and it's a subscription based MMO.
I did enjoy myself in the first month by doing only the main quests. That is why i subsrcibed. But a month in, i hit the Heavensward level limit and began doing other things and then it hit me : other than the main quest, everything else in the game is bad. I'm paying a subscription fee, then why do i have to see things like these :
- There is no bank, only servants with 100 slots each, and only 2 are free, the others are added as paid service (monthly subscription to this too, PER servant).
- There is no AH, everything goes trough the servants.
- Servant interaction menus are unintuitive and require too many clicks to be able to do anything
- Character inventory is ridiculously small and is quicly filled up even when simply doing main quests.
- Vanity items such as Glam sets (gear with specific appearance) take up inventory space. Good luck if you want to collect them all.
- Crafting is incredibly hard to work around. I like the complexity of recipes since many recipes depend on other crafting jobs recipes, but the way crafting is done is too complex and frustrating that most of the time i simply wanted to abandon crafting the items and just get on with my quests instead. Crafting anything requires time. God forbid if you want to mass produce some item, like parts used in many other recipes (ie wood logs, ore ingots...)
- When i tried leveling up my characters secondary jobs, because most players were doing high level dungeons, most of the time when i didn't have a ready guild party i had to wait long time to find a party, even as a healer or tank. One time i waited for 4 hours, stayed till i got a party just to see how long it would take.
- There is housing, but there is limited number of slots, so unless you're incredibly lucky to stumble upon a free slot, you can only spend all your time teleporting between housing areas trying to find a free slot.
All in all, after playing many MMOs, this one pales in comparison. Even more so because it's a SUBSCRIPTION MMO. I've seen non subscription MMOs with better game experience than this. I can't honestly recommend this game to anyone unless they're an absolute fan of Final Fantasy franchise. Even then i'm not sure they would like it.

This game is a perfect stress reliever for me. The music is blissfully serene, and the puzzles are both enjoyable and almost entirely logical with very few blind guesses involved.
Gameplay wise it's largely Minesweeper based infused with a dash of Picross-style logic. It may seem a little daunting at first but the rules are explained very well and it quickly becomes second nature.
If you like logic puzzles then you can't go wrong with this game, especially for the price. While there aren't technically an infinite number of puzzles (and the generated puzzles will occasionally feel same-y due to using the same logic patterns) there are more puzzles here than you could possibly play in a lifetime.

Yes, it is similar to minesweeper, but it has many more dimensions of logic than minesweeper which make it significantly more interesting, challenging and rewarding.  I've completed like five out six levels so far, and I find it actually a little too challenging and often get stuck for longer than is fun.  It is, however, very rewarding when you complete a level.  One important thing to know: YOU NEVER HAVE TO GUESS.  There's always enough information to KNOW what is the right move.  If you think it's too arbitrary because you're guessing all the time, then there's another level of logic for you to discover.  If you enjoy hard puzzles, this is for you.  If you enjoy very casual games, this might be harder than you would like.
Very relaxing, fun and challenging without being tedious. Recommended for everyone who likes puzzles.

Great game, fun times, but ♥♥♥♥ all this game is hard.
And it's not a good kind of hard, it's an RNG based hard. You could do things right, you can follow a build guid on how to win with a particular plague. But still lose because Greenland closed their port before you got on there, or your virus mutates into a "scary" disease and work on the cure goes nuts before you've infected even a quarter of the population. All RNG.
It wouldn't be bad if the game wasn't so time invested, but you spend a lot of time on your plague, just to not be able to infect some island state, even with upgraded plague birds, or airborne particles.
This breaks the gameplay, sure you can just start again, but after playing for 30 min just to watch as your plague dies out by killing 99% of humanity, but Japan is still alive on their own island of protection.
Sure it's realistic enough that if they close their islands borders they'd be more likely to survive. But from a gameplay perspective, the game should just say "Game Over an island closed their borders before you infected it." That's what is actually happening, but it neglects to tell you.
Sure there's strategies to defeat RNG, and for the most part they work but some situations are rendered extremely hard, or impossible, simply because RNG is always there.
I can't really reccommend people buy this game, there's a tablet version if you wanna try it. But until they work out the RNG issues within the game, which they probably never will thinking that it's ok that the hardest difficulty not only requires you to go online and follow instructions, and those instructions will still only give you a 10% pure luck based chance of actually winning.
There's little strategy here, it's a build order, so playing the same plague more than once is kind of repetitive. You can't really react to what people do. The UI is just not designed to allow you to have full control over your plague. Especially when it comes to they plagues like "Simian" and "Necroa" It adds some semblence of strategy, but darn if they'll work on making the UI show all the information that you need.
All in all, the UI needs a serious update, the game play needs an overhaul to move away from the Tablet based "pop bubbles" gameplay and RNGeezus. Until the developers actually make a game worth playing on your PC, avoid at all costs, not worth your time, not worth your money, and not worth washing your hands.

This game has one of the best core combat systems I have ever seen.  Weapons feel weighty but not entirely unwieldy, actions are fast but require commitment, and if you ♥♥♥♥ up you can die in nothing flat.
Enemy variety and environmental variety is mildly lacking if you're used to Dark Souls, but individual enemies are higher quality and harder to beat than the ones Fromsoft serves up.  The dog-like enemies introduced in the second area, for instance, managed to pose a challenge to me all the way to end-game.
There are only five boss fights, but all of them are at least reasonably challenging and interesting designs.  The devs didn't feel the need to toss in "filler" boss fights, it seems.
Levels are insanely complicated, full of secrets and side-paths.  There's only one Ops station (this game's version of a Dark Souls bonfire) per major area, meaning that every level is crammed to the brim with shortcuts back to Ops instead of new stations.  One Ops station manages to actually serve as the checkpoint for TWO sections of the game, including two of the five bosses.
It's got a good story, but it is told in a very different way from the Souls series - it's much more traditional RPG feeling.  Tastes may differ, but I personally really enjoyed picking up audio-logs and talking to NPCs to discover what was going on.
Overall, 8/10 would recommend to anybody who liked Dark Souls for the combat.

So I like The Surge. Combat is fun and challenging.
But there is a big problem with The Surge compared to Dark Souls.
In Dark Souls, you *REALLY* want to get your XP (souls) back to the base because your character will become more powerful for it.
In The Surge.... not so much. In The Surge, *you* the player are getting better at beating the mobs but your character doesn't really improve that much from run to run. This makes any particular run feel less worthwhile, and it means dying just not that big a deal. I didn't really need that XP anyway, because there wasn't much I could do with it.
The other problem with The Surge is a lack of character variety. In Dark Souls you can build a lot of different viable characters. You can build wizards, you can build clerics, you can build warriors,  you can build rogues, etc.  In The Surge, your character variant is determined 100% by the weapon selected and so yes technically there are different character types. But it isn't enough, ultimately you're a melee warrior.
Overall, the game has great feel, good combat, it has a certain fun to it, but it is never quite comes together like how Dark Souls does.
I'll give it a 6 out of 10 so a recommend but just barely. Only if you absolutely love these types of games and you've played Dark Souls to death.

If you can get past some levels feeling cramped, maze-like, and a bit samey in addition to a story that is light, vague, and scattered, what you are left with is a fun, challenging but achievable souls-like, encouraging exploration and discovery with a viscerally-impactful, methodical combat system, an awesome loot acquisition mechanic, and plenty of surprises around every corner.
Put on your exoskeleton, grab a massive steel beam formed as a greatsword, and go loot what you sever... and remember, no button mashing!

This game is by the Lords of the Fallen people and shows that they've learned a lot in the years since that particular "soulslike".   Unfortunately, it's not enough.   It starts off really promising but it all falls apart in the second half just like Lords of the Fallen did.
The Surge is plagued by just bad design decisions, such as overly labrynthine levels consisting of similar looking hallways and giving many enemies the ability to do ranged stun attacks.   Combine this with frequent railroaded sections where your ability to backtrack is taken away and trash enemies that are obscene damage sponges and what was really fun at the beginning becomes a horrible slog in the second half.
I was ready for something new and sci-fi (and colorful!) but this game really would benefit from being even more soulslike than it shipped.   I really wanted to like this game and was thoroughly enjoying myself up until about halfway through the "R&D" level where it just got lazy with encounter design and re-use of assets and it just gets worse from there.    At the end, everything can kill you with a good 1-2 hits, while you will have to continually hit them a dozen times with a fully upgraded weapon in an unarmored spot to take them down.   That's not "challengingly hard" that's just blatantly artificial in difficulty.
But there's a really good first half of a game here, wait for it to be at least 50% off.

Edit: I did beat the game now, and can safely say that after the strong opening areas everything proceeds to go downhill until the very end. The final boss is kinda allright tho.
TLDR:  The surge is not bad per se. I would actually say the first half of the game is pretty decent. After that, however the game falls apart rapidly and becomes a massive, frustrating mess. This,and a series of absolutely baffling design decisions make me not want to recommend this game.
This game prides itself in being a hardcore action RPG with high difficulty in a sci fi setting. And for the first two areas that formula works rather well. You dodge the mad shells that were you collegues, swinging around industrial equipment, chopping off body parts in a sprawling environment that invites you to explore and finding shortcuts that take you back to the ops that act as checkpoint. That part is fun.
As soon as you kill the first boss however you will realize that your enemies suddenly got massively upgraded. They no longer stagger. Their attacks will kill you in 1-2 hits. Their health pools got inflated. This sadly is the theme for the rest of the game. Your enemies' power level will rapidly increase while the growth of your character is heavily gated by upgrade materials. Leveling up your power core will barely do anything for you. This will lead to weird situation where you wail on your enemies with an industrial hammer the size of a man and barely scratching them only for them to power through your onslaught and deliver an enemic looking kick that will drain about 80% of your health.Sounds about right.
Speaking of enemy power- it is hillarious how effective their armor is. Armored body parts will gain up to 60% damage reduction and higher stagger resistance. This actually plays very well into this game's main mechanic of targeting specific body parts, as it directly encourages you to actively go for unarmored spots. This only gets incredibly weird when you get your hands on those armor pieces, and all of a sudden a piece of protective gear that could stop anti armor weaponry beforehand now has the defensive capabilities of a wet sheet of paper.
Damage in itself is also handled rather poorly. Dmaage types are split into three different physical attributes and a somewhat enigmatic 'elemental' stat. Elemental covering everyting from toxic gas to getting set on fire.  Since phyiscal attacks are allways a mix of all three damage types ,there is no real feedback to which physical damage types are more efficient against which enemies, making the distinction somehwat pointless. Not as pointless as the elemental damage stat however. You see- the first wepaons that will deal elemental damage are available pretty much after you beat the second boss. On twin rigged and staff type weapons which most people wont have used extensively. Also it is AT THIS VERY POINT the game will throw mostly robots and humans in HAZMAT suits at you. Both of which are highly resistant to elemental damage.
Level design also takes a massive nose dive after the second boss. Open areas get traded for series of linear corridors with the occasional box shaped room thrown in. With the occasional really bad misstep. Like that one instance where a shortcut back from ops will lead you onto a small patch of dirt surroudned by acid and enemy ambushes waiting on both sides. Also enemy placement tends to go a bit overboard later on, making you fight groups of enemeis that can kill you with 2-3 hits frequently. This,paired with very long walks makes getting back to a point you died at a chore.  After dying you will, as it is expected of these types of game, drop all of your currency which you can pick back up when you get to where you died. For some reason the devs decided to add a timer of 2 Minutes and 30 seconds to this process. If that timer runs out, your scrap is invariably lost. Between this and the massive amount of slow but powerful enemies, you will soon realize that simply running through the and ignoring a lot of the encounters is the best way to progress through the later levels. Also, expect a lot of 'lunge ambushes' where an enemy is covneniently placed out of your view behind some boxes or a doorframe only for the to hit you with a very powerful unblockable lunge attack if you walk past them. This is realtively likely to outright kill you. Dying to those allways feels incredibly cheap, but every area has at least one of those hidden somewhere.
The area where this game fails the msot however,are its bosses. Only one of them is somewhat decent. There is only five of them in the entire game. And one of them is used twice. But in hindisght that might have been for the best, as the ones they did come up with are all among the worst bosses i have ever fought. Every single one of them has periods of invulnerability where you need to wail on some part- or in one case another enemy entirely- in order to even make the boss vulnerable. This serves only to drag the fight out as long as possible. To add insult to injury here, every boss also deals massive damage to the point of them easily oneshotting you. Every single boss encoutner feels like a long, drawn out grind only designed to tire the player out until they make a simple mistake that immediately kills them. They aren't tests of skill but rather long, drawn out contests of atrition. And if that wasn't bad enough, every single boss also has a hidden prerequisite you have to fulfill in order to get their best weapon drop, which msotly consists of the player handycapping themselves.
All in all- the game confuses being 'hard' with incredibly handycapping the player and making them jump through tedious and frustrating hoops. There was potential in the beginning but terrible boss fights and a large amount of cheap deaths sour the experience to the point of it turning into a slow and frustrating grind.

EDIT:  So after a bit more playing, I realized why exactly I don't like the game.
1.  No matter what level you get, or how good of gear you get, the enemies are not scaled consistently - meaning - at level 1 you will get 3 shotted by everything around you and your guns will only do 10% dmg.  At level 75, you will still get 3 shotted and only do minimal dmg.   There's no real feeling of progression.  I don't want to be able to run around and breathe on an enemy and have it die, I want the challenge, but what's the point of having xp/levels if they don't amount to anything?  (Dead Island did what borderlands tries to do much better!)
2.  There's no concentration.  You run into an area with badguys and it's an all out brawl fest.  There's too much going on around you; explosions, other players' skills, enemies coming from all angles - there's absolutely no way to keep a goal in mind, which leads into...
3.  Every time you pick up a quest, it automatically activates it (instead of storing it for organized questing).  You leave base for one quest, and end up starting, and only half finishing, 19 other quests before you realize you were supposed to be doing one thing...

5.  Bottom line the game just seems like a complete jumbled up mess with no organization and no push from the devs to actually play it. There's no telling where they're going, what they're playing with, and there's absolutely no way to keep track of what's going on...

Alright, I think I'm far enough into the game at this point to give an honest review. Keep in mind that you may disagree, and that's fine. I want to start by saying that I have a max rank (Lv. 60) character and a guild I've personally founded by myself. I do love this game, it's very addicting. It's your tradional point and click MMORPG that reminds me a lot of how Vanilla WOW was back in the day difficutly wise.
You can explore a wide variety of beautiful locations, quest with friends, tinker with whatever build you're making at the time, or just goof off and explore. If you're more of a PVP player the game offers duels with other opponents in safe zones. On top of that you can also compete in Castle Sieges, Arena, and Battleground, all of which are aimed at people who love PVP, as you'll be fighting other well geared opponents. I can say with confidence that you can hit level cap with no Premium and it's not a necessity, though it does make the game easier and a lot more enjoyable. I've given you the good, now I'm going to give you the bad.
While everything up to level cap isn't pay to win, everything afterwards is. Now don't mob me on my post for saying this, it's true.
1. To compete with the best players in the server PVP wise, you need great gear. Upgrading gear past a certain point requires very deep pockets as the odds of successful improvent start to go lower and lower, and finally hitting 1% after a certain point. This requires you to buy many Red Stones and Runes of Preservation.
2. Sealing. Not only is getting the seal you want hard, but then getting the seal you want Orange is outrageous. You must have very deep pockets  to do this with every piece of gear, as well as unbelievable luck.
3. Cards. If you want Monster Cards you're going to have to put an insane amount of grind in and hope you get super lucky, or buy them off of the market for an insane amount of gold. Some of them aren't that steep while I've seen some go as high as 150 Million Gold.
So in conclusion, while this game is free to try and it's completely possible to hit lv. cap without paying a single penny, if you plan to stick around and get serious about PVP you're going to be shelling out a good deal of money, or spending many many hours end game grinding for the gold you need. So, maybe not necessarily pay to win, more like pay for convenience.

The bag slots are in absurdly short supply, so you'll have to sell almost everything you loot from enemies just to make room for more loot.
The negative points aside, the character customization is somewhat detailed with face and hair styles, visible equipment, and suit items.  You can also choose either gender for any of the four character classes, rogue, archer, warrior, and mage.  I created one of each class and mostly stuck with the cute girls but gave the male mage a go and was surprised by how good the outfits and poses are.  Everything just looks good.
The downside to the aesthetics is the camera doesn't tilt low enough for them to matter most of the time.  You are always looking at everything from a bird's eye view.  If you were thinking it would be like Torchlight, you're in for some disappointment.  The movement controls also suck.  Characters are slow and can't attack from a stationary position, making the long range attacks somewhat useless unless you find some kind of obstacle to lock the AI behind.  That brings me back to my RuneScape days and reminds me how awesome that game was, compared to this anyway!

First off, I'm not saying the game is bad in any way, it is well made. But if you are looking for smaller micromanagement style missions that Soldiers: Heroes of WW2 has, this is not it.
Dev comment: "game should be about big dirty and bloody battles, not about stealth."
<original review>:
Pricing of this game is not the issue. To get everything you pay 32 euros, check the "Read me before you buy".
The problem for me with this game is that there are no individual soldiers. Even if there is, you have no time for them. You simply have too many men to control to have time for your soldiers. Soldiers: Heroes of WW2 was based on managing and caring of individual soldiers, not more than 5 or six at a time. With that amount in RTS you can still care for their well being, health, ammunition and actually about placing them in good positions.
Also in this game (maybe more realistic but not very playable) your soldiers die immediately from one hit. Before you had health that allowed even some sort of "dash to safety". This might change with difficulty level but again SHoWW2 level of difficulty is very had even with health / bandages / revive.
How Battle of Empires does good or better if compared to old skool Soldiers: Heroes of WW2? Graphics is nicer, some enhancements in inventory system. The controls are a step up from SHoWW2 as well as Direct Control with WASD now.
However all the around 12 missions we tried, most of them started with maybe 4-30 units in command and map full of other allies. The mission? "Defend against a large enemy" or "attack the enemy trenches". This proves difficult and not much fun when your framerates start to drop and you start to lose focus of individual soldiers. Now I get the idea developers were after: WW1 was much like this, big groups running towards each other. But surely there were some more covert fights also where you could have only smaller number of troops? There could be missions with focus on smaller units but I couldn't find any.
I understand they want the big fights but this engine is not the right one for this. Already with Men of War the focus started to widen too much from the individual soldier:
Well, like their name says:
Soldiers: Heroes of WW2 (about individual soldiers, heroes)
- The best game with this engine!
Men of War
- Already men, not man. Good game, not so much stealth missions. Already started to have too large fights
Battle of Empires
- Like the name says big battle between empires, no focus on individual soldier
My advice to developers is:
with GEM engine, please create games more focused on individual soldiers.

If someone understand the game...
... it wouldn't be me. I mean, the plotline is just Starship Troopers without the big army and the corporation hiding the truth. But anyway, it seems that the Swarms is a hate story with mankind when reading the biography of the characters.
Anyway, you're just arriving a mining colony not answering calls, you already know that there was a problem, else you wouldn't be here and you have to get through to understand how they got swarmed by the aliens. You're beginning in the landing bay to finish into Timor Station, with a baby nuke bomb to escort. You're passing by the surface, by the reactor room or the residential area with labs locked down without forgetting your little trip in the sewer and the famous cargo elevator scene where everyone is shocked by a famous lag that is just in reality a slow motion scene.
The plot isn't really evolved by the PDA, seeing how short are the levels and the time you don't have to read them. So if at first glance, I was pleased by the turn of the events in-game, the lack of information prior the incident is just being making something amiss. I'm perhaps too used to Doom 3, Max Payne, FEAR or Legendary where you get a lot of clues about what's happening or how you got into the nightmare.
So the gameplay isn't intuitive at first: you'll have a time to adjust to that. If moving is just being the hardest part, the rest is really simple (not if you're not knowing all the keys): you just shoot swarms, you heal people if you're medic, you hack computers if you're tech.
Because you can choose between eight characters, two by classes, with special weapons. Everyone is unlocking the same weapons but not every class can use them. I'm explaining: the Officer is typically your common character you're meeting in the game: not heavily armed, without real speciality. The Specialist is the Heavy Weapon guy, carrying heavy miniguns. The Medic is the doctor you're going for if you're wounded, only him can carry enough health for everyone. The Tech is just your hacker, he's the only that can break into computers or some locked doors. If the Tech is really needed, having him dead is making the mission restart.
You have to earn XP for leveling up and getting unlocks. Everything is determined at the end of the mission, with the stats of it, if you earn achievements (or if you repeat them - for example, you already have the one with healing an infected marine but you can still earn XP for it if you keep healing people with parasites) or with the difficulty of the mission.
Alien Swarm isn't really the game with magnificent tracks, apart the sounds from the Swarms, the voices for the Marines or the music track indicating that you're gonna be swarmed or under adrenaline effect, you have nothing. No music menu, no music in the lobby leader, just random sounds. It's maybe a free game but it could have been given some good music. After all, play a game from Ben Crosshaw or Grundislav Games and you have always a serious soundtrack.
I must say that for a free game, the graphics are good, without real graphic glitches. As you're seeing all from top down, you need to recognize the Marines: white is for Medics, yellow for the Techs, green for the Officers, Blue for the Special Weapons and each of them has a different design, so, it's really easy to recognize them. The enemies are also well done, as the levels. The only little negative point are the bodies around the base, that are looking like nothing. Apart that, each level is adapted to his name, so, you're in a residential area (with labs near), you'll find offices but also a gaming room, sleeping rooms, bathrooms, etc.. If you're in the sewers, you'll be walking in water for example.
In other words, Alien Swarm, despite my initial reluctance to play it (it's not a FPS, I was just getting the hat), managed to chase my fears, to surprise me and to make me love it, even if it will never be the same love I'm carrying for my FPS games. So, I recommend it to any people searching for a good co-op game.

Before I start this review, I wanted to recommend "Tetrobot and Co." to those who look for intellectual challenges. It's a far superior puzzle game than the Hexcells trilogy, and is a game that actually challenges your problem solving skills.
Now onto Hexcells Infinite.
The idea of different types of hints comparing to minesweeper is refreshing, there are 3 types of additional hints besides the number of adjacent blue hexes:
1) Number of blue hexes in a column
2) Consecutive or non-consecutive blue hexes in adjacent hexes/column
3) Number of blue hexes in 2 hex radius
However the freshness of new ideas runs out extremely quickly, and there will be no more new mechanics from that point on - the game becomes extremely repetitive, with few exceptions.
There are 2 methods the developer adopts to make this game challenging:
1) Reduce redundant information to bare minimum, by giving you non-blue hexes with question mark instead of an actual number. In my eyes, all this does is to make the levels long, and extremely unsatisfying to solve. It doesn't really pose interesting challenges, instead it just creates dead ends and forces you to move to somewhere else. When you have a board with over 400 hexes, it gets extremely annoying and frustrating to click on that one non-blue hex only to see a question mark.
2) Create extremely large levels that take over half an hour to complete (if your goal is to make 0 mistakes) - or significantly longer if you are not a fast thinker. Many levels include completely independent sections which would have served much better as multiple smaller levels. Instead of keep creating interesting mechanics, the only variation becomes the overall shape of each level. It's quite sad to see a promising idea dying so quickly, it's like a novel with amazing first 3 chapters, but 20 more boring and mundane long chapters after, ruining the entire book.
The way this game works, is for the player to slowly exhaust all the available information to determine which ones are blue hexes. But because there are only 4 types of information, it really doesn't require that much problem solving skills or creativity. Most later campaign levels feel like chores, and you are forced to do them slowly. At some point you might be forced to take a guess, and seeing the 0 mistake jumping to 1, ruining your perfect record, is quite infuriating.
The game has nice audio, however there are some minor technical issues:
1) Regardless of which monitor is selected to play the game in windowed mode, the game would always launch across all monitors. If the developer wanted to, this bug can be easily fixed in minutes.
2) If you click really quickly, sometimes clicks won't register.
In conclusion, I wouldn't recommend this game to any of my friends.

Let me start off by saying, I have found some serious issues with the game that need to be addressed. So its a thumbs down for me.
Where to begin even... I wont waste your time explaining what this game is about or other games it compares to, thats already been done ad nauseum by literally everyone else and their mom. So straight into the meat of it then.
The blocking and dodging system is garbage. And even if its just because I havent figured out how to work it right or whatever, its still garbage. I have 12 hours into this game, lots of progression, a couple boss fights in, and I still cant block simple attacks and then sometimes, for no reason, I seem to block... like what is going on??
The attacking system is also garbage... I press the button once to swing my weapon and I end up throwing 3 or 4 combo swings, sometimes to my very own peril, often times with plenty of tech scrap on the line.
Leveling up does not increase your max health, so even at a super high level, the level 1 mobs can still one or two shot you, and oh, believe me, they will.
Speaking of mobs... the AI is absolutely horrible. I have not actually encountered a single mob that I have actually HAD to fight in order to progress in the game. I only end up fighting with them because I feel like I should have to... not that I actually do have to... which is super weird... Its completely broken in this regard. Literally the only time you HAVE to fight an enemy is when its a boss (obviously) or when one of the mobs like the ARC bot bugs out and literally blocks a super small pathway and gets stuck there.
Speaking of the ARC bots bugging out and blocking your path, the enemies are constantly bugging out. Sometimes you hit them with a certain weapon and weird things happen where the enemy goes flying or skidding across the room from a simple light attack... its very wonky and feels terrible when it happens. When an ARC bot bugs out and blocks your path, usually cornering you, usually you cannot even attack it. You will die. Its cheap, and poorly engineered.
The game is poorly optimized... I am running 4 GTX 680s, and an overclocked i7 4770k, with 32gb of ram, and I can only get away with 45fps on high settings. 20fps on ultra. To compare, Dark Souls III (and just about every other game I have) runs perfectly on maxed out settings.
Very little weapon and armor variety. Other games in this genre usually feature a multitude of tech paths you can choose... this game only has two paths, and very little variety to be discovered in the game world. What this means is, very little replay value. There are also no game changing decisons to be made either. So a play once, is a play 100 times.
Some things I do like about this game, is the theme, the animations, the level design (pure brilliance) and some elements of the otherwise terrible combat system such as the feel of the weapons having impact and weight. But with that being said, a "Very high impact" weapon will stagger enemies, unless you hit them in the wrong frame, then they will just power right through your massive hit on them like it was a paper airplane chipping their forehead.

Cthulhu Saves the World is an interesting game.
On the outside it looks like a simple turn-based rpg trying to copy classic rpgs like Dragon Quest, but with much more cheesier and non-proffesional graphics.
But this game is a gem. On the inside it all comes together to make a very entertaining game.
It has several innovations: Everytime your character levels you get to choose the improvement the character gets, you can only fight a certain amount of monsters in an area before you stop randomly encounter any more(with a option to keep fighting if you want), you get combo points for hitting enemies over time which you can then use on special moves to do large amounts of damage which when combined with the fact enemies get stronger every turn means each battle goes by pretty fast.
Long story short, if you like old rpg games like Dragon Quest or Final Fantasy then this is a good buy, especially with the cheap price and being bundled with a similar game.

Even if it wasn't so awfully cheap and bundled together with another little game that is good in its own right, this is a hilarious take on Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos. Basically what he would have done if he had wanted to parody himself. If you like cosmic horror stories, but think that they should be a little bit more upbeat and less gritty, then this is the game for you.

Vulture (once called Vultures Eye) is, simply put, a fancy skin for one of the most legendary games ever created, Nethack.

In my opinion, Nethack is the greatest of the second generation roguelikes, and the pinnacle of what it is to be a roguelike. Just a glance at the
will show you just how complex this game is. And the random little reactions certain items have, the times you realize some random piece of junk can actually save your life... this is where Nethack really shines. Little things you pick up along the way (and through multiple runs) eventually make you a hardened, if not always successful adventurer. That lizard corpse you carry at all times, that sprig of wolfsbane, the bundle of unidentified wands, it all reminds you of the times you were less cautious, less knowledgeable of this world you are now a part of.

Vulture makes the game incredibly accessible for those with a bit of patience. If you have been at all enamored with any of the titles spawned from the recent resurgence of roguelike games, and are looking for something more substantial, I can wholeheartedly recommend this product.

(Of course, if you feel up to it, you can just dive in to the unaltered game for free. Though be prepared for ASCII.)

My POV is that we use the term rogue-like/lite only because it was the first. But like most firsts to a thing it was a later version from someone else that did it best, and for me Nethack was that verion. If you played Nethack, this is Nethack. It's just a graphic overlay to Nethack to step beyond the ascii a bit, but it is not it's own game, it is Nethack.
Anyone who wants to know what it is they are talking about when they use the term rogue-like should for sure either play rogue or better yet play this. I've known plenty of people who've played it, but few who've beaten it. Any game that can be bested  in a single sit, or any regularity by someone is not a very rogue-like game in my eyes. Expect more losses than wins if you choose to delve into these dungeons in seach of the Amulet of Yendor. Games like this are what get the hadrcroe lable from me, and there is a reason they do not make a lot of games like this anymore. It's a more niche audiance that's going to get in for the level of punishment and unfrogiving nature of NetHack. If you thought Dark Souls was hardcore, you might have to alter your scale of assesment if you go a few rounds with this beater of buttocks.

Nethack. This game means a lot to me. Since I discovered this gem some years ago it has always had something new to show me nearly every time I give it a go. It has been years and I have never ascended but I grow closer everytime I create a character. There is so much to learn in this game and the mouse interaction and menu screens in this version make that a lot easier though at this point I prefer to use the key commands since I know them by heart. This game takes time and patience and is an incredibly deep game. I believe this game has the longest history for development which has been shared among many fans over the years since the 80s. This is the original "roguelike" as Nethack refers to its development. This is a "hack" of the original Rogue by way of the "net" when the internet was still in its infancy and only available to those in Universities or those who worked for telephone companies and is still under ongoing development by the community to this day. This interface makes Nethack more user friendly for first time users and may be a good starting point for those interested, however, this game has always been completely free and is available at
. Give it a go and if it is your kind of thing then it is sure to keep you busy for years to come.

If you ever wanted to try the classic roguelike NetHack but was terrified because of the ASC II graphics and interface, you should try Vulture. Vulture is an graphical interface for NetHack. It makes the game much more user friendly and give you that 90's RPG feel with the isometric visuals.
The goal of the game is to go down 50 floors, find the amulet of Yendor and go back 50 floors to exit the dungeon. NetHack is hard, like really HARD, but with a lot of humour, so you never get too overwhelmed.
There's hundred ways to die in NetHack, and believe me, it's fun discovering them. On my first playthrough I drank water from a fountain, was transformed into a lynx and was killed by monsters spawned from a cursed chest.
If you enjoy pure roguelikes (turn-based) you can't go wrong for U$ 2.99. My only advice is: read the manual (specially chapter 9.2 - interface options) to learn how to properly configure resolution (yes, you can play with true 16:9 aspect ratio), sounds, etc, and know more about the game itself.

I have played a lot of the original Nethack with no graphics or simple tiles. It's a great game. I think the best thing that happened was when I met my older characters ghost and it killed me.
This is great for people who don't want to learn ten thousand key combinations to do things. It just makes playing Nethack easier, and it's really good for what it does.

All of the customization parts are faction-based, and the factions are very well spread out. In other words, to build the best ship, you are actually required to transcend the entire galaxy to collect the parts you need. Some can't even be bought. Instead, they have to be stolen off other ships, which adds even more difficulty to building "ideal" ships.
The only thing I don't like is the heavy limitations on engine/weapon setups. Weapons, you're limited not only by what your ship can carry and how many weapon ports it has, you're also limited on how much "weapon space" you have, if the other two werent limiting enough. Engines, same thing, minus the weapon ports. What if I wanted to create a rideable missile, or simply put stronger weapons on my ship? You are allowed to put on as much shielding as you want though, which I find odd compared to the weapons/engines. Last I knew, shields were more important than engines in heavy combat. (I did modify a ship to have a few hundred engines though, and steadily dropped to <5fps as the stars zipping by merged into a massive white background. I was going a few hundred thousand units/second on a game intended for ~900 tops, lol)

Literally the only time you HAVE to fight an enemy is when its a boss (obviously) or when one of the mobs like the ARC bot bugs out and literally blocks a super small pathway and gets stuck there.
Speaking of the ARC bots bugging out and blocking your path, the enemies are constantly bugging out. Sometimes you hit them with a certain weapon and weird things happen where the enemy goes flying or skidding across the room from a simple light attack... its very wonky and feels terrible when it happens. When an ARC bot bugs out and blocks your path, usually cornering you, usually you cannot even attack it. You will die. Its cheap, and poorly engineered.
The game is poorly optimized... I am running 4 GTX 680s, and an overclocked i7 4770k, with 32gb of ram, and I can only get away with 45fps on high settings. 20fps on ultra. To compare, Dark Souls III (and just about every other game I have) runs perfectly on maxed out settings.
Very little weapon and armor variety. Other games in this genre usually feature a multitude of tech paths you can choose... this game only has two paths, and very little variety to be discovered in the game world. What this means is, very little replay value. There are also no game changing decisons to be made either. So a play once, is a play 100 times.
Some things I do like about this game, is the theme, the animations, the level design (pure brilliance) and some elements of the otherwise terrible combat system such as the feel of the weapons having impact and weight. Alright, so first off I want to say I have a bias towards games like this. I have spent many hours in DS, DS2, DS2 scholar, DS3, Bloodborne, and Lords of the Fallen. I recently beat the surge after 21hrs of gameplay so now I think I can give my opinion.
This game has some of the most fun combat I have ever seen in this type of game. Pulling or cutting someones limbs off for their gear is simply fantastic each time. The jumping and ducking mechanic when used on certain enemies feels incredibly rewarding when pulled off. However, this game has 2 glaring problems that makes it more of a chore than entertaining.
The first deals with the enemies themselves, now there are alot of LOTF esk features in this game such as The Champions rage bar, the "soul" multiplier, and the reviving enemies. However, this game has the exact opposite problem LOTF had. LOTF had really simplistic enemy designs with basic attack patterns (Think Dark Souls Lite) but its bosses seemed cheap and unfair at times usually leading you to cheese them out to progress. The Surge has the most ridiculous mobs I have ever seen. Most of the mobs in this game can 1 shot you regardless of armor (have tested fully upgraded LYNX and RHINO, on average the RHINO can sustain 1-2 more hits with a HUGE movement penalty). The bosses however are pretty fun, a little predictable but a fight you know will be tough but can still come out the victor. (Except 1 boss, random camera angle switch? What is this Nier Automata? lol)
Most of the small enemies are 10x tougher than ANY boss in this game and even other DS titles. Imagine if all the small mobs in bloodborne were replaced with Gascoigne (If any of u have played bloodborne). Its cool at first but after a while it becomes tedious to die to a new enemy youv'e never seen and have to fight ALL the mobs to get back to one guy and figure out in 3 secs what he did to kill you and how to dodge it. Im NOT against fighting an enemy multiple times to figure out how he works and eventually defeat him but if I have to fight 30 Gascoignes to get to the ONE guy I wanna fight it becomes very unfun. This leads me to the Duck/Jump feature. This feature works on 2 enemies throughout the entire game. Ones a Mini boss and the other is a regular mob. Pulling off one of these moves during an enemies attack and pushing in for a stun is fantastic! It makes you feel incredible, but it is utterly useless since you are given so much stamina that dodging left or right is safer and more consistant (Think of bloodborne... wow this game is kinda like that in terms of movement).
The second one I probably should have mentioned first but Im not re-typing this thing. The main problem with this game is the actual level design. I dont mean the interconnectivity, ive always enjoyed interwoven maps. I mean the color/art behind it. All of the areas minus the first and part of the... third I think... are the same mechanical industrial factories. Now I KNOW this is the style they are going for but to connect all the areas they use "tunnels" with lifts and doorways. The problem is the tunnels all have the same black tunnel/yellow guard rail design. They are almost impossible to tell apart from one another especially the dim lit ones. So on top of having to retrieve your lost "souls" from the new guy that one shot you while you were blocking, you have to navigate endless coridors all the same color and figure out where the ♥♥♥♥ to go. I really would have loved these tunnels to be color coded (think mirrors edge style) so I could tell one areas tunnels from the next since they are in all the areas. Ill be honest, the caticombs in LOTF was my least favorite area in the game, it was very similar in design and I would get lost down there all the time (Im not the best navigator) but I have completed all the DS games including bloodborne without an issue so im not that bad. Besides DS2, I did look up a guide for that one... Anyway Ill wrap this up with the pro's in a final thoughts paragraph and TL:DR for those that dont wanna read this... I know I wouldnt.
Final Thoughts (MY OPINION): This game has ALOT to offer with fleshed out combat, an interesting world, and weird people you meet along the way. Its problems  lie in its repetitive art design/impossibly hard to navigate levels (Though I am not the best navigator), along with standard mobs that could be end game bosses. I really enjoyed the first 10 hrs of this game up until the 2nd boss. The weapons were interesting although few in nature along with armor sets not really giving you much in terms of actual armor lol. The injections/implants system is a really cool idea that kinda changes up the way you play without having to include a class system. All-in-all if you guys loved bloodborne/a really fast DS than this game might be for you. I would wait for a sale tho, as someone who isnt very good but has played all the DS games, I beat this in 21hours when most of that was me trying to navigate the nightmare hellscape that is The Surge. I would wait for a sale, this game was fun but not $50 fun. Its definitly better than lords of the fallen but id wait till its around $30. I doubt Ill go back to it unless they add some different or more interesting weapons and maybe tone down the 1 shots. Also PC port is good! I5 and 1060.
TL:DR- This game is essentially SciFi BloodBorne, Fast satisfying combat, Fun Bosses, Interesting story, Regular mobs that can out DPS all the bosses in this game, and hard to navigate levels due to repetitive art (could be me though). I think $30 is a good price.
Hope this helps! Let me know if you have any questions!
BTW: This is MY opinion. Feel free to have your own! (rating it down until it drops in price) sux theres no, "its ok" rating lol.

First off, I'm really loving this game. Disclaimer: I haven't played any Souls games, so I don't know how they compare. Would I recommend it to everybody? No, not quite. Not that it's a bad game but because it's not for everyone. It's very hard and you will die a lot. You have to learn the enemy's patterns and how to properly approach the combat. If you rush in and try to combo enemies to death by button mashing, you will lose every time. Button mashing is absolutely not an option here. You have to learn the combos and choose your attacks wisely because if you just spam attacks, you'll get locked into combo animations that may get you killed. You have to choose and commit to your attacks. With that said, the combat system if very flexible and fair. If you die, it's pretty much your fault. Only a couple times did I feel that my death was unfair. Don't fret too much about dying though, you only lose your collected scrap, which you get from every kill and can be farmed again. When you die, you can collect your scrap again if you make it back to your body within the time limit of about 2min. Killing enemies along the way adds to the timer as well, and generously so. I've never once had an issue getting back to my scrap within the time limit...but I have died on my way back, losing 5k scrap or so in the process. It will happen, it's frustrating, but you move on. Everything else you collect though from implants (abilities and stat upgrades) to weapons, armor, and crafting components are all saved right when you pick them up, so when you die, you still have those. This system is very nice as the only thing you lose is the most abundant resource in the game that you can get from anywhere, so although you can get set back a little if you lose a bunch, you can always make it back, like the difference between your paycheck getting lost in the mail and you breaking a priceless keepsake.
Overall, I really like it. I have about 15hrs of playtime and just beat the second boss and got to the third area. The combat is great and really reminds me of Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild in some respects. Locking onto enemies and dodging/parrying work pretty similarly, as well as needing to keep your distance and lunge in for strikes in between enemy attacks. Even the way enemies can power through your attacks to do some facial deconstruction is very similar. The way you unlock shortcuts also feels kinda like a Zelda dungeon.
A tip for people to avoid some potential frustration. Don't just go with whatever weapon has the highest damage number. Attack speeds and combos are super important. The first powerful weapon you get from the first boss has a very high damage value compared to the rest, but it's so slow that you will probably have trouble with more agile enemies. I'd recommend experimenting with different weapons and, like BotW, don't just specialize in a single weapon type, otherwise you'll probably have trouble with some enemies.

Never played NetHack? Well, previously, there was only one excuse for that; aversion to ASCII-based graphics.
Now there is no excuse. You cannot seriously call yourself a gamer until you have played NetHack.
NetHack is a game where experimenting is both rewarding and punishing. To say there are a million ways to die in NetHack is an understatement; you WILL die. A lot. I encourage liberal experimentation for your first hundred or so games. This will result in them being over very quickly, and, as a result, you'll learn 100 ways to die and 100 things not to do.
NetHack is THE quintessential roguelike. Heck, NetHack is the second choice for the very definition of roguelike (the first choice being Rogue itself). It's filled to the brim (and above) with content. Paired with the permadeath that defines roguelikes, this gives NetHack a legitimately enormous replay value.
NetHack is BLOODY HARD. As stated before, you will die. A lot. A whole lot. You have to go down roughly 50 floors, with each and every one teeming with foes that can and (given half a chance) will kill you. Then you have to go back UP those 50 floors. This 100-floor fact gets really scary when you see just how easy it is to die on the first few floors.
That being said, NetHack is also fair. It's been postulated that every game generated is winnable, played by a sufficiently experienced player. There are people that can win many games in a row. Given enough time, you can become one of those people.
Do you, for some reason, not have $3 to pay for this? Google NetHack. There are plenty of ways to play the ASCII version (which, besides graphics, is the exact same thing) for completely free. (The graphics are totally worth it though.)

Vulture brings the quintessential Roguelike, Nethack to life with an updated user interface and graphics. Roguelike has been a heavily abused buzzword in the gaming industry for the past few years plus. "Hey, look! Something random happens in this game...it's a Roguelike!"
No...no it is not. Knock it off you.
That's not to say I don't play many of those games too but this game is more deserving than any other on Steam to be called a true Roguelike.
Vulture isn't perfect and still retains Nethack's learning curve for the uninitiated but more improvements are coming, including a massive update to the graphics, interface, music and more. There's also a fine line in Nethack in regards to the "spoilers." I would encourage players to try playing on Wizard Mode before reading the big book of Nethack spoilers.
P.S. You're gonna die...a lot.

Vulture for Nethack is a great dungeon crawl. You start with a character and class that you choose or via random selection and try not to die! This may sound easier than it is to achieve. The dungeons are brutal. You start with limited equipment and armor . From room to room and level to level you never know what you will encounter. Will it be an easy floor with plenty of shops and money or will you be shot with a wand of death by an unsuspecting gnome lord?
This is a game that makes you use every bit of knowledge and cunning you have just to get from level to level. You are given spells, wands, potions and various other items to try and best every creature and puzzle you encounter. Good luck try not to make your God angry and always remember to post your YASD! (Yet Another Stupid Death)
Overall this is one of the best games I have played in years. It is a game I have come back to over and over. It has massive replay ability. I highly recommend giving it a shot.  Here are a few tips : Always know where your towel is, Never eat while satiated, Dont F with Shopkeepers, And do try not to genocide yourself.
Good luck and Enjoy!

Vulture for Nethack makes accessible to the gaming public
one of the most original, challanging, and intriguing games
of all time.
Nethack was originally released in 1987 with ASCII
graphics. In it, the player must traverse scores of randomly
generated dungeon levels in order to locate the Amulet of
Yendor and return it to his Deity's altar on the Astral Plane.
The game is notoriously difficult and has an almost infinite
replay value. However, it's poor graphics and obscure interface
has kept it beneath many gamers' radar.
Vulture has changed nothing about Nethack but the graphics
and interface. The graphics are attractive and set a sort of
Dungeons and Dragons mood. The mouse-driven interface is smoothe
and intuitive, the drop-down menus are self-explanatory and helpful,
and the music, sound-effects, and occasional animations bring the
game to life.
Nethack is now more accessible to the new player, and only the
most die-hard fan of the old ACII graphics is likely to object
to the beautiful improvements that DarkArts Studios has made
to the way this game is played.
