The main premise of the mechanics - that all "weapons" (all named as if they are programming functions) can also be used as modifiers for other weapons, applying some trait that is reminiscent of its effect as a weapon, or can be slotted to gain some sort of personal passive buff related to the function's use as a weappon - is interesting, but needs some refinement before I would call it successfully implemented.  The game drowns you in options.  I'm not that far into the game, but with the 9 functions I have collected so far, the number of possible combinations, between 4 weapon slots, 5 modifier slots between those, and 1 passive slot, is mind-numbingly large.  I understand wanting to encourage experimentation, but I feel like I've been put to work at one of Thomas Edison's laboratories, expected to iterate through every possible permutation to try and find the best one.  Which you have to do, because the penalty for not being optimal is apparently ludicrously high.  I would be fine with not every combination of functions slotted as weapons, modifiers, and passive buffs being equally as powerful or useful, but during my play I have more than once barely made it through a fight after losing multiple lives.
Which is its own problem, because the functions *are* your lives.  Every time you get knocked to 0 life one of your functions gets burned out, and cannot be used until you've made it to a specfied number of "Access Points", which makes it impossible to do anything like experiment when half of the things you're trying to learn how to use are unusable for large stretches of the game.  All because you hadn't found the magic formula when you turned the corner and bumped into the next wave of dudes.
In a game that seems bound and determined to force you to try new combinations over and over and over again, you would think the game would allow for the reallocation of functions whenever you wanted, but this is not the case with Transistor.  Remember those "Access Points" I referred to earlier?  Those are the only places you can modify your loadout.  This, combined with the game forcing you to finish every combat by locking you into a sort of arena for every confrontation, which never seems to include one of these Access Points, you have better hope your build is optimal for what you're facing, otherwise you're going to be stuck using unfamiliar functions to try and eek your way through the next few combats, so that you can hopefully get to enough access points to get the original list of functions back.  Only *then* can you try experimenting, making modifications to your original build to try and find out why that pack of dudes you ran into turned you into mincemeat, and what changes you might make to keep yourself out of the grinder next time.
I am sure I could go online and watch a few hours of poorly edited youtube video explaining how everything works, and maybe afterwards be able to piece together something that works for me.  Also, I am sure I could find a few fan-made wikis for the game, and after trying to read through them find out enough information about function effects and combinations to be able to better optimize my build.  Never mind that it is poor game design to force someone to *leave the game* to figure out how to play said game, it is even worse to force them out of your game just so they can learn how to get through the game.
In short, the game has too many possible combinations of weapons, modifiers, and passives, and the penalty for a less-an-optimal combination is too steep, limiting access to the main story behind a wall of senseless experimentation and iteration.  I remember hearing it said that the developer's previous game, Bastion, lacked interesting gameplay, in part due to a lack of options available for weapons and abilities.  I fear that my ptoblems with this game stem from the devs' response to this criticism, and I feel it only makes this game worse, swinging wildly far past the point of balance, making the gameplay tedious and boring.  Maybe they could have solved this by giving you the option of letting the game pick a loadout for you.  It wouldn't need to be the best of all possible combinations, but if it were, say, at the midpoint of the optomization spectrum for the next encounter, you coukld not only go into the next fight/set of fights not only knowing what you might need to get through them, but also be given hints as to what awaits, allowing the player to try and infer how to use these assigned tools to win the next encounter.  Instead, you have to hit up youtube and the vast stacks of Wikia just to get through the damn game.
In the face of this, I cannot in good conscience suggest anyone purchase this game.

This was my first foray into the hexcells series. I'm not much of a puzzle game fan though I really like logic problems which this definitely caters to. It's super interesting to see how the puzzles develop over time as you learn more and more principles about the mechanics of the puzzles. I also like that there's only one right answer but multiple ways to go about solving the puzzle; you can go at your own pace and take any direction you wish. If you get stuck, just look at a new area of the puzzle and you might have new information since your last visit.
The instructions to hexcells are a little vague, so definitely take your time on the first instruction puzzle of each series and don't worry about finishing without mistakes the first go around. The most important lesson is that marking hexes grey can sometimes be just as important, if not more important, as marking hexes blue. Keep that in mind and you'll have a great time.
If you are new to the hexcells series -- this is the one to get. I haven't tested the other standard levels, but this one offers longterm replayability that the other two games don't by adding a custom levels feature.
/r/hexcells and /r/hexcellslevels are great tools for finding cool community-created levels as well as installing plugins to make applications of the levels faster and easier. Hexcells Infinite also comes with a new puzzle a day and a random puzzle feature. I will warn you that the random hex puzzles are rather easy to complete, often giving a ton of information for free without needing any moves, and don't give the same satisfaction completing them that finishing the base set does. I will definitely be purchasing the other two hexcells games to get my puzzle fix soon.
As for value, I beat 36 included levels in about 11 hours according to steam, though I've played the game sometimes without launching steam so I'm not sure if it tracked everything. I'd say the total is closer to 20 hours for the base levels, and I expect to probably sink another 20 or so hours playing custom levels and the new daily puzzle. For $5 that's a steal, I paid like a buck and a half on sale which is highway robbery.
To the developer, if you made new levels in a DLC I'd definitely buy it! I would also humbly suggest a way to play this in the dark like SquareCells has, spent a lot of late nights burning my eyes out with this game :)

The thrid in the Hexcells series, Hexcells Infinite is a refreshing addition to this line of minesweeper inspired puzzle packs. The original Hexcells was refreshing and fun whilst Hexcells Plus was, at times, exceedingly tedious with some of the puzzle designs. The tedium of Plus--as generally caused by a little too much "mucking around" with the blue cell counter mechanics on some puzzles, is not replicated in Hexcells Infinite. Hexcells Infinite, unlike it's predecessors does have some capacity for random puzzle generation. Although, thus far, the randomly generated puzzles are not as complex as many of the prefab puzzles in the "story set"--for lack of a better term--they remain fun and the seed system does afford sufficient depth of puzzles able to be generated to afford extensive diversionary and casual replay value.
The soundset remains relaxed and in sync with the previous titles and the controls remain identical as well.
My greatest irritation remains with perfecting each puzzle--which is to say, the instant one makes a mistake, to erase that mistake one must start the entire puzzle from scratch. This is perfectly fine, in terms of design overall, but I have found myself, at times, forgetting which button tags a blue cell and which uncovers a yellow cell--resulting in stupid mistakes and thus having to redo an entire puzzle from scratch. An undo function, allowing for a single mistake to be back-tracked once per puzzle would remove the occassional misclick irritation of having to restart a puzzle you already know how to do but were "clumsy" in regards to inputs.
Overall, this is an excellent program, surpassing it's two predecessors in replayability, and would be enjoyed by any fan of minesweeperesque puzzle games. Definately worth a buy--especially when the full series goes on a sale.

100 hours later, here is what this MMO is like,
Pros:
- Very good story
- Solid, methodical gameplay
- Methodical dungeons and raids
- Ability to switch classes on the fly
- Excellent crafting system
- Very good graphics compared to most MMOs
- Very good community that is less toxic than most other online communities
- Amazing expansions that are definitely worth the price
- Leveling is a tad bit less frustrating than most MMOs
- Sheer amount of content that will keep you up at night
Cons:
- So. Many. Fetch. Quests. (within the main story questline itself)
- Main story is very long. This is not normally a bad thing and the main story is very good overall but the amount of fetch quests just makes no sense sometimes
- You must complete extremely long main story questlines within ARR (the base game) before you can access the expansions. Again, not normally a bad thing but the fetch quests will frustrate you sometimes
- Again, the community is very good but you will definitely ecounter a small number of elitists at the end game content that are worse than elitists of other games
Overall, I would give this game a 9/10. It is one of the best MMOs I have ever played, second only to 2007 Runescape.

I speak for the Stzeam Version only. I was never a Fan of getting locked to the Steam Version. As for the Community. It is one of the best. Many other Players are mostly willing to help, if you need some help. But there will be some Who are still bad apples. They will blame People for doing to less Damage or failing on Mechanics. But over all the Comunity is much more mature.

The only Con i hope will fix over time are the low resolution Armor Textures, especially on older pieces from ARR, since they had to support the PS3 up till Stormblood release (what dropped and is no longer an issue).
My Game times speaks for itself how much time i spent allready in this Game. There is more than just PvE Raiding stuff you can do.
As typical for an MMO'S you have Dungeons and raids, with Omega being the next Raid coming out in a few days as this review is written.
Then there are so called Hunts in the Open World. Those are your Rare Monster Spawns what reward you different things.
Then you can do also on the Open World Events what are called F.A.T.E.'s. Those are you Guild Wars 2 like Events where you do different things.
Then you can take part in Treasure Hunts. You can gather maps what you decipher and kill some mobs before looting the Chest. On the higher Tier Maps (usualy the one you need at least 4 People) you have a chance to spawn a Portal what leads to a Treasure Vault.
Then there is also the Deep Dungeon. It is a part of this Game where you get into a Randomized Dungeons and try to clear it. It have a entire own Leveling System bound to it and nothing of your Gear and so on will count in there only the 2 Stats you wil given inside. Right now we have the Palace of the Dead what can beated by Random Groups, put together with the automated Duty Finder, to Floor 100. If you wanna takle Floor 101-200 you have to gather some Friends  and hope you never get a complete Group wipe at any of the floors.
Also there is PvP in this Game. It is not as popular like you GW2's and WoW's, but with the latest COMPLETE overhaul of the PvP System it certainly is going to a good direction of it. Where it was before a unbalanced mess of Gear stats and total ability bloat, you have now a unified System where you don't have to worry about gear anymore and the Abilities are cut down to some one them, making it more of a skilled gameplay instead of who presses the most buttons of the time. But there are still some flaws with some Jobs being totaly overtuned, what can be now much better worked on, since it is totaly indepentend to the PvE side of the Game.
Then at last but certainly not least there is the crafting and gathering.
Both have their own little system bound to it. With Crafting you mostly will try to get an higher Quality Item out of it, since it boosts the stats on it.
As Gatherer you have little controll if you get High Quality Items from it, you rather bound to certain Timers for rare Materials to gather.
Both got also with Havensward a new System implemented whatr is used to get massive amounts of XP during Leveling from 51-70 and on 60 and 70 for get new Recipes, Locations for new nodes, some gear options and crafting Materials.
For crfating you have certain amounts of Skills for each Crafter what will help you not only to finish the item you want to craft, but also to increase the Quality of it.
As gatherer you mostly try to use your skills foreither increasing the chance to gather it, get a higher procentige on the chance to get HQ items out or imcrease the amount you gather with one swing. Also you don't compete with other players for the same nodes, since everyonehave it's own spawn of it. That counts also for the rare timed Nodes. You will often see many people will gather the same node at the same time.
Over All you are in for a treat. The Main Story will guide you through the game and will give you a good story along the Way. Just keep in mind that the beginning is tuned for people who NEVER played a MMO before and you will feel it.

When Final Fantasy XIV first came out, it sucked. The developers just didn't know how to make a MMORPG and had completely neglected the MMO part. Their solution? Pull the plug on it in the most epic way possible (See the "Answers" trailer; that was the last thing players of the original game saw before servers shut down), after which they relaunched a whole new version of the game where the critical faults of the original game had been adressed.
The game takes place five years after the cataclysm which happened during the shutdown event of the original game. The people of Eorzea are still recuperating from the devastation caused by the dragon Bahamut, but the neighbouring Garlean Empire, antagonists of the original game, are done licking their wounds and again sets its sights on conquering Eorzea, and if that wasn't enough, creatures all over Eorzea are summoning ancient spirits called Primals, who indoctrinates their victims into being their zealous followers. That's where you come in. You must assist the people of Eorzea to get back on their feet and rise up against the invading forces standing on their doorstep.
The game is pretty forgiving for newcomers who never played the original game, and people are more than willing to recount what has happened before, during and after the Calamity in the original game. You get pointers during the opening minutes of the game explaining how the game works and how to play it. Furthermore, there is a myriad of other players who are happy to respond to questions, give advice and help you get started. If you have trouble, all you need to do is ask.
The gameplay is pretty standard. There is nothing new to this game that haven't been done before in other games, but Squenix have managed to polish it down to near perfection. The one thing that's bothering me is the UI. The hotbars of the mouse and keyboard interface have unneccessarily wide spaces between them by default, and only two of them have key commands. If you need more, you'll have to go into the settings. This game also supports various controllers, and while the controller interface was a nice effort, it just comes off as clunky, and your skills will not have enough room in the controller hotbar, forcing you to constantly switch back and forward between hotbars, which can be quite annoying.
The graphics is, other than the story, where the game truly shines. Everything looks fantastic in game, and while it's not as pretty as the original, where the graphics were so advanced it severely limited the amount of other players visible (the worst thing you can do in an MMO), you will still get a wonderful experience exploring the vast lands of Eorzea and its surroundings.
All in all, it's a pretty run-of-the-mill MMORPG. Don't go into it expecting something new, but what it does it does really well, and the community is one of the better ones. Does it deserve the monthly subscription cost? That is entirely up to you. A free trial lets you try the game out before you buy it, allowing you go experience the base game and reach level 35 (which is halfway to the current level cap), currently without any time restriction.

If you ever enjoyed any RPG on the NES you owe it to yourself to step into the world of Cthulhu.  A very enjoyable experience.  And did I mention this company is going to finish the Penny Arcade series!

Cthulhu Saves the World plays much like the old-school NES and Super NES party-based RPGs, where you control the individual actions of a party of characters in battle.  However, unlike a lot of RPGs, it doesn't bog down in a ton of statistical details and lots of different kinds of armor and weapons.  Certainly, there are upgrades as you go along, but you don't have to buy a helmet, breastplate, greaves, shield, and boots to defend your character well; it's very much a pick-up-and-play type of RPG.  This isn't to say it isn't challenging, however; later battles may drive you nuts until you find just the right party and strategy to succeed.  The story is also engaging, and there is a lot of humor throughout.  Some conversations are downright funny, and even the narrator gets involved.  Character profiles are also winners.  One boss is literally a black hole; the profile says, "Now we're just getting silly."  Don't let the low price tag fool you; Cthulhu Saves the World is a great game.

This game is not just a sci-fi Dark Souls. The progression mechanics, crafting/upgrading/weapons/armor, NPCs, environments, and enemy mechanics, just to name a few things, all feel fresh and set the game apart. The combat falls somewhere between Dark Souls and Bloodborne, leaning more towards Bloodborne. Those who face-tanked or shield-♥♥♥♥♥d their way through the Dark Souls games and try to use those tactics here will have a bad time. You can still circle strafe most of the mobs to bait whiffs, but some enemy weapons and attacks actually require you to dodge at the right time or really move around in order to succeed. It seems to me that the people who are claiming you die in one or two hits after the first level neglected to upgrade their armor, or might not have even bothered to get a full armor set at all. It takes some time to acquire, craft, and upgrade armor and weapons, but that is what the game requires. There is far less of an emphasis on boss fights, and more of an emphasis on exploring the levels. To get the most out of the game requires a good amount of looking around for areas you may have missed, and a little bit of grinding in areas you've already been. The large interconnected levels are very fun to explore and the unlockable shortcuts system fits in perfectly with their designs. The lack of multiplayer is a bummer, but as a single-player experience it works very well. I did encounter a few inconsistencies with the first boss's attack boxes, and some of the enemies do have some "cheap" attacks, but the game is very fair and well polished overall. I'm not one to often do reviews at all, if anything this is my first one. I'm a little bit ways into the game and I've just to say, to whoever developed this game, good job.
I see a lot of people comparing this game to Dark Souls, and quite frankly, yes, it has a lot of elements similar to Dark Souls, but with its own little twist. One of my most enjoyable things to do in the Souls series was to collect weapons and armor sets to be a fashionable undead knight.
And whilst some armor sets are cryptic, which I found rewarding due to how they were hidden, The Surge's system of systematically ripping the armor straight from your enemies limbs is just such fan service for me. It's great. Being able to mix and match what you want, and yank a weapon from the enemy just to beat the snot out of his friend with it moments later is truly a blast.
Breaking away from this whole "Dark Souls" comparison, in all honesty, the setting, the story and the environment is giving me the most nostalgic chills back to Bioshock 1 and 2. I can't explain it without you going through the game and finding all the little audio logs like I am.
I don't want to droll on for too much longer so I'll just conclude it here. The setting and the look of everything, and how the enemies function is very appealing to me. And the combat is crisp enough to keep me engaged.
If I'm going to nitpick at something which does dissapoint me, it's that there's only 5 "bosses" but due to the large amount of unique mini-bosses strewn around I'll only give it a slap on the wrist.
Overall, if you loved Bioshock as much as I did and want to feel some nostalgia in the form of a Souls style game, pick this up, you might just be surprised.

The main premise of the mechanics - that all "weapons" (all named as if they are programming functions) can also be used as modifiers for other weapons, applying some trait that is reminiscent of its effect as a weapon, or can be slotted to gain some sort of personal passive buff related to the function's use as a weappon - is interesting, but needs some refinement before I would call it successfully implemented.  The game drowns you in options.  I'm not that far into the game, but with the 9 functions I have collected so far, the number of possible combinations, between 4 weapon slots, 5 modifier slots between those, and 1 passive slot, is mind-numbingly large.  I understand wanting to encourage experimentation, but I feel like I've been put to work at one of Thomas Edison's laboratories, expected to iterate through every possible permutation to try and find the best one.  Which you have to do, because the penalty for not being optimal is apparently ludicrously high.  I would be fine with not every combination of functions slotted as weapons, modifiers, and passive buffs being equally as powerful or useful, but during my play I have more than once barely made it through a fight after losing multiple lives.
Which is its own problem, because the functions *are* your lives.  Every time you get knocked to 0 life one of your functions gets burned out, and cannot be used until you've made it to a specfied number of "Access Points", which makes it impossible to do anything like experiment when half of the things you're trying to learn how to use are unusable for large stretches of the game.  All because you hadn't found the magic formula when you turned the corner and bumped into the next wave of dudes.
In a game that seems bound and determined to force you to try new combinations over and over and over again, you would think the game would allow for the reallocation of functions whenever you wanted, but this is not the case with Transistor.  Remember those "Access Points" I referred to earlier?  Those are the only places you can modify your loadout.  This, combined with the game forcing you to finish every combat by locking you into a sort of arena for every confrontation, which never seems to include one of these Access Points, you have better hope your build is optimal for what you're facing, otherwise you're going to be stuck using unfamiliar functions to try and eek your way through the next few combats, so that you can hopefully get to enough access points to get the original list of functions back.  Only *then* can you try experimenting, making modifications to your original build to try and find out why that pack of dudes you ran into turned you into mincemeat, and what changes you might make to keep yourself out of the grinder next time.
I am sure I could go online and watch a few hours of poorly edited youtube video explaining how everything works, and maybe afterwards be able to piece together something that works for me.  Also, I am sure I could find a few fan-made wikis for the game, and after trying to read through them find out enough information about function effects and combinations to be able to better optimize my build.  Never mind that it is poor game design to force someone to *leave the game* to figure out how to play said game, it is even worse to force them out of your game just so they can learn how to get through the game.
In short, the game has too many possible combinations of weapons, modifiers, and passives, and the penalty for a less-an-optimal combination is too steep, limiting access to the main story behind a wall of senseless experimentation and iteration.  I remember hearing it said that the developer's previous game, Bastion, lacked interesting gameplay, in part due to a lack of options available for weapons and abilities.  I fear that my ptoblems with this game stem from the devs' response to this criticism, and I feel it only makes this game worse, swinging wildly far past the point of balance, making the gameplay tedious and boring.  Maybe they could have solved this by giving you the option of letting the game pick a loadout for you.  It wouldn't need to be the best of all possible combinations, but if it were, say, at the midpoint of the optomization spectrum for the next encounter, you coukld not only go into the next fight/set of fights not only knowing what you might need to get through them, but also be given hints as to what awaits, allowing the player to try and infer how to use these assigned tools to win the next encounter.  Instead, you have to hit up youtube and the vast stacks of Wikia just to get through the damn game.
In the face of this, I cannot in good conscience suggest anyone purchase this game.

I really wanted to like this game.  I think the Great War is a section of history that has been passed up quite a bit, and an RTS looked like the perfect way to do this.
This game doesn't do a very good job.
Not counting the fact that literally half of the game is DLC, Battle of Empires does not present a good portrayal of the Great War.  It feels too clean, and nothing feels like it has any impact.  Artillery is weak, compared to the absolutely devastating thing it actually was.  Machine guns have trouble cutting down the swaths of soldiers that come at them.  It doesn't feel like the First World War.  And gameplay wise, it's pretty boring.  It's pretty much exactly Men of War, just in WWI.
Also the voice acting is absolutely horrendous.  You couldn't find anyone to give a half-decent impression of a Russian soldier?
I guess I'll have to wait for another WWI RTS to show up and see if it piques my interest without disappointing me like this one.

Much more entertaining than the mobile origin would suggest. It's not a a game rich in detail, but it offers surprisingly deep gameplay and plenty of replayability. At first it's very easy to "win", but as you unlock more and more strains the difficulty increases and the end game, if you could call it that, is actually pretty challenging.
There's plenty of variation between the strains, and they all have their own personality. I was surprised by how much the flavor texts could shift the feel of the game, and even on a more technical level most strains offers something unique. Some TLC is needed for the news feeds of the individual contries (they get repetetive and you rarely bother looking at them untill you've almost won), and it would be nice if the game offered a little more graphical variety, but in the end it's not a game about graphics. Also, the feeds are hidden unless you select the country directly, so the repetition is not as big of a problem as it could have been.
It may not be a future classic, and it can be shallow from time to time, but it's a perfect game for when you want to play something but you don't have the energy to get very invested. I find myself coming back to it a lot.

First you mine. Then you get machines to mine for you.
Then you research new technologies. Then you get machines to research for you.
Then you build a factory. Then your factory builds factories for you.
There's always something to do in Factorio, which is why most of the top reviews talk about it like it's crack.
I thought they were exaggerating too, until I spent played it for 36 hours straight the day after I got it.
Worried that it's too complicated for you? It's not. Ultimately, Factorio boils down to a very simple concept: Combining resources to make new, better resources. That said, if you're the kind of player that wants a highly efficient and organized factory, you could spend hours planning, tweaking, and working out ratios in your head.
Either way, Factorio is absolutely worth your time and money. 5/5

Murderlands 2, awww where to begin!
As with my last review i shall be splitting this review into four different segments (Each based off the game in question), the segments shall be
General Gameplay
Mulitplayer
Story
Downloadable content and expansions.
As Tiny Tina would say "LET'S HAVE OURSELVES A MUTHA-HUMPIN' TEA PARTYYYYYY"
GENERAL GAMEPLAY.
This game happens to be one of the smoothest and well-build games i have ever played, the movement is tight and responsive and aiming is fair and challenging, i also love the extra immersion bonus how the camera height for each character is changed depending on thier height, (Example, Salvador has the smallest, I think Krieg has the highest).
Each class is fun and extremely different and each having a special move to make you feel like a total murder machine, for example.
Axton (The commando) has a deployable Sabre Turret which he tosses like a grenade, this turret starts off slow-firing and with only one single cannon but can be upgraded to feature, Missle Pods, Dual Cannons which fire Slag bullets, Longbow upgrades that let the Turret teleport across the map with a single throw, A copy of your shield, and SO much more!
Of course now on to the main humor point for borderlands, GUNS! There are....Just...SO MANY GUNS! With the random weapon generator i can assure that you will NEVER hold two of the same gun at any time in your many playthroughs, these can range from simple pistols that shoot regular bullets, to automatic flaming sniper rifles, to submachineguns that fire more than one element and oooogh, gotta calm down.
General gameplay? 10/10. This game as i have said is a smooth and crisp example of refinement and engineering.
MULTIPLAYER.
Nothing to say here, it's just like the singleplayer, works just as well too!
Multiplayer? 8.5 out of ten. My ONLY problem with this is that some players can make changing zones a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ but with friends it's a completely flawless experience.
STORY.
Ahh what a great time to grab a gun.
The story is simple but deceptively complex, beginning as four strangers on a train arrive on a seemingly violent and horrible planet named "Pandora" where you are immediatly almost killed! Who would have guessed, the story continues as you grab some guns, grab some allies, grab some loot, grab some quests, and let yourself get swamped with all the fun you'll have. I found the story can be a little at times BUT this point has been made Null due to my playing this game through for probably the 30th time. Fun, entertaining and with great iconic characters that all deal out humor, cash and quests.
Story? 10/10. Nothing else to say, it's simple yet complex, barren yet full of things, can be boring but springs to life with each chance to pull a trigger.
DOWNLOADABLE CONTENT AND EXPANSIONS.
Well well, Now to the fun part! This game features some of the most brilliant and hilarious (And rewarding) Dlc i've ever seen (Along side FALLOUT: New Vegas)
My favourite bieng "Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon Keep", this expansion has the new four vault hunters beat the "Slamma Jamma" out of a hyperion informant downstairs while the rest play the borderlands version of D&D, "Bunkers and Badasses", the whole DLC is narrated by the people actually playing the game, the whole map and all it's segments are D&D themed and full of 4th wall breaks.
Not to mention the two new included heroes. The Mechromancer and The Psycho, who are both hilariously unique and powerful. My favourite quote from Krieg (Psycho) bieng "I LIKE MY LOOT LIKE I LIKE MY BABY STEAKS! RARE!"
DLC 9/10, Some are shorter than others but it is all together a brilliant and funny experience.
FINAL ROUNDED SCORE: 9.6/10.

The game has more than lived up to my expectations. Though not as massive as a Souls game, there is a lot more going for it in my opinion. The additional combat mechanics help make the game feel more interesting than the now stale Dark Souls formula. Options and Advance Combat mechanics also exist for people looking for a more slightly challanging experience. The smaller scope also means everything feels more focused and balanced than anything I've experienced in a Souls Game. There are also a lot of Quality of Life improvements over the Souls games that greatly reduce the grind and eliminate almost all of the painful RNG. The combination of a tighter focus and shorter length makes New Game+ much more appealing to someone like me who has a tendancy to try everything out and then subesquently get burned out on the game and not want to bother with NG+.
So far, the game crashed twice for me, so overall I'd say it's pretty stable. With the frequent autosaving, it really had no impact on my game. I tend to play brawler games with a controller, so I can't really say how the M+K controlls work for it.

I usually don't review things until I thoroughly finish them, but I've already enjoyed this game much more than most. The combat is fluid and responsive, the level design is a tad confusing but once it clicks it makes so much sense, and the enemy design is simple but complex enough to warrant a playthrough or two.
EDIT:
100 levels later and one playthrough complete. Gosh this game feels good to play. They really use the few things they have in the game to their advantage. At a 50 dollar asking price, I really would say this game is worth it. Despite this my ultimate reccommendation is to get it on a sale for about 35 dollars or so, the game is a beautiful, tragic, and neat blend of a game.

I'm approaching this as someone who'se never played a proper 3D Souls-like before, although I played enough 2D Souls-Likes to know what I'm getting into. I'll keep this short.
*Combat mechanics are good early, but fall apart towards the end as everyone describes. Every button hit after the first attack sends the character into a (painfully slow) combo animation that can't be cancelled. Uncancellable combos suck hard at the end game, where enemies attack harder than the player and are often capable of one hit kills if not blocked or dodged.
UPDATE: The game has been patched and the endgame is alot more forgiving now. Instead of 1-shotting the player, later enemies more reasonably 3 or 4 shot the player. The hard hitting attacks are now telegraphed better, and blocking is much more reliable.
Animations are also somewhat cancellable with blocks and are more responsive to dodges, now.
*No ranged weapons in the game, end game enemies come with healing/strength increasing drones that absolutely must be taken out first. Player has a Drone that can attack at range, but it's powered by a guage that only fills up while you're fighting, so more often than not you find yourself needing to get beaten down just to try and take out the enemies buff drone. Overall, the drones hiding behind mobs, and the flamethrower guys are the bane of endgame corridor fighting.
*Story sucks. It wants to be System Shock, but nothing makes sense and audio logs and convos talk in generalities that don't go anywhere. An entire in-game area is basically a plot thread that comes to a dead end.
Despite all that, I don't really regret the purchase, it's a decent gear grindy game where you get power armor and smack sh*t down (EXTREMELY satisfying and weighty smacking sh*t down, the combat feels right.) Not having played other Souls games, I probably don't know any better though.

I've slept on this Papers, Please game for quite a while imagining it to be a drab, Orwellian-esque indie title that would be a chore to play. And sure, while all of the themes one would come to expect with a game of this premise are there, the gameplay itself is an utter joy to contrast the oppressive world of Arstotzka.
Papers, Please essentially boils down to a puzzle game of increasing difficulty where it's your duty to spot inaccuracies of various documents provided by those who want to pass through the border to the glorious country of Arstotzka where you, having been selected by your government through a labor drawing, have been entrusted with the keys to the proverbial kingdom. As the days press on you'll find yourself struggling through the day-to-day difficulties of feeding your family whilst being a morally responsible (or reprehensible being, if you so choose) agent in a world that encourages you to scrap by in any way you can, with border regulations increasingly tightening and less than scrupulous individuals both trying to evade the regulations that you must follow, or elicit your favor through bribery and pleas of help, stand firm for the glory of your homeland, do what you must to see your family through the nightmare of an Orwellian state, or hell maybe even stage a revolution.
A wholly unique, at times intriguing and an overall engrossing play. Papers, Please is a can't miss indie title, join me in the glory of Arstotzka comrades for we must keep our borders safe.

Bought this game in early-access because I'm a big fan of this period and I haven't been so let down since Aliens: Colonial Marines came out. What I thought would be an interesting RTS turned out to be little more than an expensive mod for AS2. I have three main problems with this game:
1) The campaign, which is 95% of the reason I bought this game since multiplayer is terrible and there isnt a 'fight against AI' option is terrible for the amount you pay. The levels are poorly done and very often what should be interesting and exciting campaigns become repetitive and dull. Some battles, like the Marne in the French campaign are great, but seriously who wants to spend two missions helping a handful of Russian officers evade small patrols of Germans and *spoiler alert* spend a mission hiding a flag? Where is the Battle of Tannenberg? Stalluponen? The Battles of the Masurian Lakes? A lot of missions are poorly scripted too, voices don't kick in when they're supposed to or cutscenes activate when they shouldn't- a good example of this was in the Ivangorod mission where in the middle of a fierce firefight the game loaded a cutscene out of the blue. This cutscene involved several soldiers being attacked and shot down by germans whilst they continued to have a calm conversation about what they'll do when the war ends.
2) The voice acting is terrible. And I mean terrible. When I bought this game the French soldiers had a strong Eastern European accent, which I could forgive because it was early days and they'd obviously patch it later.  Which they did, to my horror. When I next loaded the game, their accents had been replaced by British ones- trust me when you hear soldiers using french slang in thick london accents you can't help but laugh. The voices are as awful as the unit animations. The Russian accents are pretty good, but thats all the praise I have.
3) The DLC is getting out of control. I payed for the early-access with the promise of German and British campaigns, as well as the ones that came with it. And once again I got shafted. Do they seriously expect me to pay a tenner to get what they offered me when I payed for this game? Ten pounds for two more campaigns of bad accents, dull missions and more inevitable soul-crushing frustration at what I've become by buying their goddamn DLC. Seriously this has to stop- it's like paying for a sandwich to be told that the fillings will cost you the same price again. If they hadn't demanded more money via DLC, I could have even forgiven some of the other faults.
tl;dr Poor scripting, bad cutscenes, doesn't bring anything new, poor animations, overpriced DLC, don't waste your money

-Some mechanics are unexplained or explained far too late.  Why am I halfway through the second area before I get a tutorial prompt letting me know I can dodge and counter-attack high or low attacks?  How much benefit am I getting out of weapon proficiency scaling?  How can I tell which attacks are blockable?  Seems really inconsistent.
-The high contrast industrial lighting in most places looks great and adds atmosphere, but at times it can make it hard to see your character and close enemies when standing in shadows.  This is especially problematic as you need to be able to see the enemies initiate their attacks.  I raised the gamma level but it still is hard.  Some more ambient lighting would be nice.
-Rig-mounted lights are terrible for all but one suit I have found.  The scarab suit gives an omnidirectional glow which is handy in the dark.  The rest are spotlights that can only point directly ahead.  I would have prefered to use the drone for light - it could hover above and behind the player to illuminate a larger area in exchange for not having access to its attacks while the lights were on.

The Surge is good.
Flaws? Yes.
I played dual blades which is the fastest weapon type in the game. I felt strong, agile and fragile due to wearing armour that was the most mobile. I was one-two shot often If I allowed myself to be hit but I always felt like it was fair. Combos and consecutive hits feel good, staggering enemies and feeling like you have power in your hits.
You level up, you unlock implants (stims,max health,max stamina, stamina consumption rate etc) at specific levels. You get stronger as you level up. You get exosuit upgrades that have increased implant slots but require more levels to use them.
It's linear but you know what you're getting. seeing you're 5 levels or so away from unlocking a new implant slot which allows you to use the one that gives you an additional 3 medkits or even more scrap from enemy kills. That's the type of progression The Surge has.
You
get forced into using a specific weapon type. This is because each weapon type levels up with use and weapons have scaling on these levels which means more damage. So you're going to feel like you need to use one weapon to take advantage of the system. I can understand the system but with leveling a second weapon type feeling too tedious I just ended up sticking to one.
I really enjoyed the level design to be honest. It's a factory sure but what is anyone expecting? You'll often feel lost and no clue what part of the level you are in but It doesn't feel wrong or bad. It feels like you're the guy that just started his first day at CREO and has no clue where things are.
It's all in a factory but it does change aesthetics in various levels and its quite grim to look at but feels like it was crafted with being connected in mind and making sense in some way that you can appreciate.
I felt a lot of tension in this game as some parts are claustrophobic and there's often a lengthy period between finding a shortcut to the safe area and when the place you're in looks nothing like where you just came from and you're low on stims you will feel so relieved when you see a sign pointing to Operations (basically bonfire)
-Not many weapons
-Enemy types (Felt like it could've done with just a few more)
-Low number of bosses 5 and they were all rather easy) but they were fun don't get me wrong.)
-Boss difficulty vs standard enemies (normal enemies pose more threat than bosses, not a bad thing. I'm merely meaning that the bosses felt too easy.)
-The tiny hole beside the train near the end of the game
-Enemies respawn but don't really have a reason for it(?) other than just copying souls mechanics

Let me give you the most honest opinion of this game: As a guy who finished Demons Souls, Dark Souls 1,2,3 and Lords Of The Fallen + DLC's. The graphics are amazing, the ambiance as well. It really fits into the Sci-fi theme this game has and it's downright gorgeous just check some screenshots. Combat is fun, each weapon has it's own finishers and it switches between fast paced and slow paced depending on your rig and weapons. Because most weapons and armors are industrial based it has a sense of weight around it, level design is complex and follows the same pattern as the first Dark Souls being layered but it also is zone based like Lords Of The Fallen. The conveince system is perfect, just like any Souls game you always find a way to traverse the map. Storyline is handed through the envoirement and other grafity and signs on the walls. Is it harder than Dark Souls? In some cases no in others yes especially the mobs and boss fights which do a lot of damage and find some way to get the upper hand. Is it a Dark Souls clone? No it is not. Does it fit in the same category as Dark Souls also known as ,,Soulslike'' yes it is very much a ,,soulslike'' game but it has it's own originality.

The price tag and initial 10% discount was a foreshadowing of what to expect. I am a huge dark souls fan and while similar this game doesn't come close. Dark souls is challenging and rewarding, well thought out and punishing. This game is thrown together with the intention of making money off a target audience. It is clunky and the enemies have no depth. The world is very linear, only one thing to do...but open so you get to run around over and over until you find some random switch. . Hard to really say if it gets any better, as I am still very early in the game.  I just don't feel the urge to continue.
I could see this game being good with another year of development. As of now I cant recommend it.

Gameplay overview
Burstfire is a tactical squadbase fps brought to you by Nacho Games. The primary game mode of this game consists of 2 teams attacking/defending an objective that randomly spawns in one of the four set locations on the map. Players are given immediate access to a wide variety of tools (drones, barbed wire, breaching charge, etc) to play around with.
Each round, you are allowed to choose a primary and secondary weapon, 2 grenade types, and 2 tools to bring with you. Initial phase consists of 60 seconds where the attacking team spawns in ball drones to scour the map and mark the objective along with any traps the other team has placed. The defending team spends this time placing traps down and preparing. After this comes the execution phase, where both teams try to either wipe out the other team or complete the objective. The defending team still has the option of placing traps during this phase, but they are at risk of getting shot while trying to do so.
The concept of the game is great albeit with some really big restrictions on play-style. Unlike Rainbow Six Siege, you can only breach walls at certain points. These are marked by a giant grey slab in the wall. While they are usually more than enough points of entry than allocated traps, it's still a minor annoyance. Another huge gripe I had with the game is the fact that if the defending team leaves the building, they immediately get marked as a red outline that the attackers can see through walls. I have no clue why they did this. Breaching charges can break walls but they can't be placed on wooden planks blocking the windows; you need special grenades to do the trick (once again... makes no sense...).
The visual presentation is solid ,albeit, a bit lacklustre. Everything still looks slightly blurry despite playing on max settings.  Some guns lack the ummph that you would normally expect when shooting them. Rounds are extremely fast usually lasting 5-10 minutes max. As far as I can tell, all weapons, scopes, tools and such are unlocked at start to give you full access. There are currently only 2 maps (?)... maybe more that I haven't encountered. I've played this game through its E3 alpha and look forward to playing more. Overall, if nothing else it's a great game that caters to a niche genre. Its slow paced action brings me back to the days of Rainbox Six and SWAT 4. I recommend this game as  a budget time burner until Siege comes out.

Do give this game a try, If nothing else, it is open-source and free.
However, it is much more than just that, and I'd like to thank all those who have participated in the game's creation and subsequent updates for keeping a level of quality that is very high indeed.
So, in a nutshell, this game is a top-down Escape Velocity-like venture into the great darkness, where you will find intrigue, wealth and combat in abundant quantity. The game looks fantastic and is very steamlined - in a way that makes it easy to navigate the menus and understand what is going on, at any time.
However, while the game boasts very high-quality graphics, performance, and exceptional writing, I have a few gripes with the way combat works : basically, there is no skill involved, nada, just the way you outfit your ship. Out of money means out of options, and dogfighting or missile-dodging is very awkward due to the way ships move around. Capital ships are king, overclassing every other by being not just tougher, but much more powerful and faster, too.
With that in mind, and it can make some parts of the game feel tedious, you are provided with many options with which to customize your ship and tinker all you want. Once you start making money, it's very easy to gain more and more money-mentum and get what you want.
What does it for me, then, besides the overall quality and effort put into this lovely game, is the story and writing. The galaxy isn't a familiar place for humanity yet, and the more time you spend mucking around doing random things, the more mysteries you'll uncover - not necessarily solve, though. The writing feels very alive and well-documented, and although you are sometimes little more than an onlooker to unfolding events, it always does its best to push you, to keep you wanting for more.
And if you like striking out into the unknown, boy does the game have its ways of rewarding you.
And this is what space games are about : going out of your way to reach the next riddle, because you have a vague feeling of it being there.
Endless sky does it very well. And with every update, I fire it up, and it feels good taking the old lady for a ride into the sea of stars, to stir stuff up and find out more, and more, and more...

Three months ago I wrote a negative review for royal quest after rewriting my original positive review. I will now go on to expand that negative review.  My last review ended with me summarizing that Royal Quest is pay to win. Which it is, however, it gets worse. The admins, and mods in charge of the forums online are corrupt and protect people at the top of the food chain in game that have cheated their way there. To help people understand the game and the background of what i'm saying i'm going to give a very fast breakdown of all the different levels and parts of the games.
levels 1-20 = having fun, playing casually, (taking the bait)
levels 20-40 = more challenge, figuring out your class and game goals (getting hooked)
levels 40-50 = sinking more time & money into the game you didn't expect (you can't turn back now)
levels 50-59 = hoping that the max level 60 will change the game for you (being disillusioned)
level 60 = looking to get in a top guild, throw all your time & money at the game (your fate)
so all in all how Royal Quest works is this: it lies to you in the beginning, and then once you've invested too much time and money into it to leave, it forces you to join a top guild to succeed. which isn't inherently bad if it weren't for the background corruption of the game. and that corruption boils down to this: monster cards.
there is a special item in game that are called monster cards. essentially these cards are very hard to get and make your gear and character very strong. however, there are normal monster cards and then Elite/Boss monster cards which are the hardest monster cards to get but also the strongest. Now when you get to level 60 typically the last thing you do before finishing your character is finding all the normal and Elite/Boss monster cards you need.
However it came to light that the leader of one of the strongest guilds in the game had fabricated the majority of his Boss cards some time in past. And to top it off when someone tried to call him out on it, their account was permanently banned. Since that time, people have avoided openly talking about that incident for fear of being permanently banned.
but it gets better. That corrupt guild leader then became a moderator. And as a moderator in any medium your responsibility is to be objective and help the players in the game you moderate. However this corrupt moderator went around and instigated arguments with players (because that's the type of guy he is) and then would chatban people who hurt his feelings.
Recently I was one of those people that got temporarily banned for arguing with him after realizing how corrupt he was. The interesting thing is there are in game rules where you're not allowed to discredit those in authority. however, every single forum post or in game conversation that shows evidence of moderators abusing their power magically gets removed. so when they ask for evidence to our insinuations they know we dont have alot because they took away most of them.
To make you smile even more, after this recent happening of me and my friends arguing with the corrupt moderator, i messaged the admin about the whole incident and was promplty temporarily banned for discrediting the corrupt moderator. I then made a forum post about the whole situation and how the moderator was corrupt and broke the silence on all the wrongdoings of the mods and administration and was promptly banned from making forum posts.
TL;DR:
-this game is dying because of corrupt moderators and admins abusing their powers to cover up illegal stuff they did in the past and only care about the top guilds that those corrupt people are a part of.
-There is no way to prevent the people in authority from abusing their powers so they do it all the time and you get punished for even trying to stop them.
-don't play this game if you want to have fun. don't play this game if you're bored. don't play this game at all. play WoW or guild wars 2, or Tera. literally any other MMORPG.

I've always liked the idea of MMORPG's, yet I always struggle to connect with them for the long term. There is no doubt that this genre is a huge time sink.
However, Final Fantasy XIV is a love story to a series that I grew up with and plays so well off what that franchise has built. With the release of Stormblood, this game has hit the upper echelon of story-telling within the genre. A Realm Reborn played it safe, Heavensward allowed the game to explore its identity and add some darker tones, and Stormblood took full advantage of all that came before it to make a compelling cast of characters really shine in a genre that often times relegates its story deep into the background.
Beyond that, the dungeons and raids are well designed, a lot of fun, and require a team of players that know what they are doing. Stormblood also made PvP relevant, so... that's nice.

A brilliant parody of old school JRPGs that also manages to be a damn fine game in it's own right.  Also, you get to be Cthulhu.  Highly recommended.

You play Cthulhu on a quest to regain your eldritch powers. The only way to do this is to become a hero by traveling around the world map, visiting fantasy towns named after Mythos locations, and laying the smackdown on your Great Old One brethren. Along the way you pick up several party members (one of whom seems to represent some kind of cameo; the game certainly seemed to expect me to recognize her).
The combat is full-on Dragon Quest. The enemies line up in front of you and you ATTACK / DEFEND / MAGIC / ITEM etc. The combat system is tweaked to be more user-friendly than similar games from the 1980s, and there are other conveniences (like being able to save anywhere) that eliminate most of the frustration factor.
The only downside is that this DOES make the game pretty easy. Completing it unlocks another mode called Cthulhu's Angels, where the title character stays on the sidelines but you start with three party members. I didn't play that far in this mode, but it seems significantly more difficult (and, bless, features its own separate story traversing the same locations).
Easily worth $3. Great humor, and wicked fun!

This game is absolutely brilliant, and hilarious at the same time. I love the characters and their dialogue; i've laughed out loud plenty of times. The game took me just under 12 hours to beat. The battle system requires careful planning at times in order to win. You have to prioritize enemies and skills. Lots of party members to pick up and switch out based on your play style. There are some annoyances in the game, but nothing that prevents you from having a great time. The worst part about the game is the maze-like dungeon design; you will get lost and spin around in circles. Luckily, there is a maximum number of battles for each dungeon, and then you'll stop getting random encounters, meaning you can wander the maze freely to find all the loot and make it to the end. Dungeons feel twice as big as they need to be. Also, after beating the game there are bonus game modes to play. I can't recommend this game enough!

Haven't finished it yet, but being a Dark Souls veteran I'd like to point out that the team behind Lords of the Fallen has taken a huge step forward. While the latter was not a bad game, it became obsolete really fast and wasn't as enjoyable from a certain point on.
The Surge on the other side got me hooked for a variety of reasons:
+ Great combat/Loot system
+ Difficulty throughout the game is consistent (mobs become more difficult gradually and you won't get stuck at a single boss for hours while dashing through the area mobs)
+ Intense and creepy-ish atmosphere
The negatives can be summed-up to a general lack of weapon/armor variety and a somewhat sluggish blocking mechanic.
Money well-spent for me - can be polished further, but this one is a keeper I'll revisit.

I've been looking forward to this game for a while and it has been well worth the wait. It definitely has every bit as detailed and brutal a combat system as dark souls. It's very obvious they got their inspiration from those games. I like that it feels like it expands on the combat system in it's own way. Not just with the limb targeting and finisher move system that allows you to rip body parts and exo-suit pieces off your enemies-but also with the blocking/evading system that feels much better than the souls games ever did. Not only is combat faster paced, but it's more varied given that you can't just block enemy attacks by holding the block button and facing them-you actually have to anticipate where your enemy will strike and either block or evade there. But even beyond that, the counterattack system lets me feel like even more a badass and even more immersed in the combat by letting me counterattack immediately after blocking/evading. The better enemies use it too and it makes it almost feel like playing against a human player-especially given their unpredictable AI.
I've been playing for many hours now and haven't found an enemy yet that doesn't seem to have multiple methods of attack. from lying in wait to ambush me mid-combat with someone else, to attacking aggressively the moment they see me, to waiting for me to attack to dodge my moves and attack me mid-combo like i try to do to them. the zombified enemies in the first level seemed dumb in comparison to the zombified and more humanlike enemies i've found since then.
The game also seems to have some side quests scattered throughout the maps. The maps themselves, despite being blandly factory-like in color scheme and layout, have been fairly large in my opinion. I've just explored the first 2 quite extensively so far in an attempt to familiarize myself with the layouts and landmarks i use to navigate my way around this facility. They both have a fair amount of shortcuts that I've come to expect and appreciate from games like these-even more so given that there is no real way to quick travel back to base to save your tech scraps.
That's another thing-this game's main currency appears to be tech scrap. nothing wrong with that-in fact, i even like it. especially when i can store it at the safe zone in each level so i don't lose it if i die. Doing so resets the combat multiplier that give more tech per kill, but also resets all the enemies, allowing you to practice and farm. When you die with tech on you, you have a certain amount of time from when you leave the base to get it. killing enemies adds to that time, or you can try to sprint past all of them to get it. personally, i like to kill along the way, adding more to my combat multiplier as well as my overall tech amount. To help you out even further, there are various tech scrap items you can use from your inventory that sometimes drop from enemies or have a chance of spawning around the zones. You can stockpile them seemingly indefinitely, or use them and bank them right there at base like i like to.
Ripping armor off of enemies yields an initial schematic for that armor piece so you can build it later, and later will yield gear parts to help upgrade those specific pieces of armor. Meaning torso pieces upgrade torso pieces, arms upgrade arms, and so on. It looks like every weapon and armor piece can be upgraded 4 levels and enemies with higher level gear will drop higher level loot to help keep upgrading your exo-suit. meaning it's not very helpful to grind in areas you've already been to if you're looking to upgrade your current gear further. you have to keep pressing on and unlocking the new areas. from what i've seen-i could end up being proven wrong if i get my power cell upgraded enough.
The exo-suit itself can be upgraded to allow you to do more with it. Beyond just unlocking new areas or side quests outside of combat, levelling up the power cell allows you to wear heavier armor, use better implants, and unlock more implant slots. With a wide array of implants to choose from-and the better armor obviously locked away behind higher power cell costs, you'll want to keep upgrading your rig. Some of the implants can only be swapped at base and other can be swapped out in the field-allowing for instant customization depending on what situation you're walking into or what weapon you're planning to use for the upcoming fight. the game encourages you to use different weapons for different enemies (there's no single weapon that is going to be great against every enemy.) and i think that's part of why they have the weapon proficiency mechanic in the game at all. to reward players to who keep using different weapons and penalizing players who try to do it all with just one and then realize late game that they need a different weapon against this new foe or cluster of enemies.
Some of the injectable implants can be stacked for more uses-such as the various healing ones-which is much appreciated in new areas when you don't know what you're going to come up against or how to survive fighting it. Because that leads me to my main reason for recommending this game-it's brutal. BRUTAL. Pretty much any enemy can kill you in just a few hits-if not in just a single combo. That sense of fear and requirement of near perfection is something i feel the souls games lost towards the end in an attempt to make it too accessible. this game is not for everyone. If you do not learn to fully utilize the advanced combat system, you're gonna have a bad time. This game plunks you down in a merciless world, but gives you all the tools you need to survive in it. Use them and abuse them or it will use and abuse you.
Spoiler Alert:
The CREO security guards at the start and throughout the second area don't seem to respawn, so if the armor piece you need isn't on them, keep going back to base and refreshing. i made the mistake of killing the last 2 in the same fight and missing out on the torso piece. don't make my same mistake.
Ignore that-they DO respawn later in the game and you run into more with that armor as well. Still, it's a good chance to get it early. Also, the better rigs with the extra implant slots really add to the depth of the combat. a wide range of stat effects are possible with 16 slots and the many implants.

I would love to recommend this game to people. I like it's ideas and the setting is what made me buy it. I do not regret buying it since it hits a very niche place for me which means I can justify the purchase. However, I don't think this game will ever be a big hit and there are a lot of things that make me scratch my head while I play it. I never raged as much as I do at this game which takes me back to when I was young playing video games, not for good reasons.
This for me is the whole reason I bought this game. I am a HUGE sci-fi fan and one of the reasons why I play Fallout so much is because of the Power Armor. To me this was a major win but is very niche as well seeing as that is probably not why most players will come to this game.
I was worried when I first saw the game that it would not have a modular armor system built in. What I mean by that is, if you equipped the Rhino set it would be the entire rig not just a section of armor. Now that is not without it's faults. I will go on much like others have.
This is a huge problem. While the actual system of combat is fun, fluid, and enjoyable to watch; the enemy design wasted all of it's potential. The art design of the enemies is fantastic but the only things that makes the enemies scary is their overwhelming power scale compared to you. They all 1-3 hit you, humans are acceptable but every robot I run away from. If the more...nuianced mechanics of the game in the dodging, blocking, and parry worked the robots would be enjoyable to fight. However, the dodge mechanics only work on a simplistic level when combined with human reaction and control scheme. There is no way that their jump up or crouch mechanic would be easy to do with their current implemitation. They use these hard to use features to substitute high and low block which means block does not work against 90% of the enemies you will want to block and you can't even block like they show in their trailer when warren stops the rhino from killing him. If Warren were to try and block that attack in-game he would have died.
Simply put there is very little. So much so that I will not be playing this game after I beat it unless they change a lot or add something worth coming back for. The "way" you play your character will be dictated by your early decisions and due to the profeciency system you will not be using other weapon types unless you are willing to grind. You will find due to enemy difficulty that you will not be using any of the unique traits of your weapons and armor might as well not have bonus's and be purely cosmetic. Weapons are the only thing that make a noticable difference in your survivability. I find I only pick armor based on the set bonus. Such as the Liquidator armor makes the enemies in R&D, Biolab, and first visit to the waste disposal area much easier to deal with. The armor therefore has situational value not overall gameplay value. I just do not see how my first character will play differently from my next if I decide to play again.
I think how Souls (since that is the comparison game) does it is fantastic. You have intimidating enemies that are easy to fight (most of the time) once you get past the face value of the enemy. Then you have a few like the classic black knights who are meant to keep a permanent challenge in the mobs so you stay on your toes. However the way The Surge handles the enemies is like every enemy is a black knight that you encountered before you are supposed to. As stated before every enemy 1-3 shots you with robot enemies being mostly immune to your damage unless you hit them where they are vulnurable. So for example the generic security bought you encounter there is only it's eye otherwise even with leveled up gear it only takes 5-8 damage from you hitting it's outside. While this makes you feel like you are truly trying to kill a tank with a power tool this does not make for compelling combat when you have this security bought tacked on top of 3-4 security guards who flip around and 2-3 shot you. It is nigh impossible to fight multiple enemies without getting ganked by one you can't see off camera. I just entered the production facility for the third time and now there are security guards stacked on each with these robots eveywhere. I no longer feel any desire to play the game since this makes it night impossible to do any of the compelling parts of the combat system without dying. When it came to me this is the future enemy standard I just gave up, not out of rage but despair that the game was no longer enjoyable for all I will be doing is dodging away until I can do one stab and then dodge again.
This is the part that makes me feel like I am playing an old school 3rd person adventure game. Often when you are in cramped corridors or on platforms with no guard rails you feel like you are more fighting the camera then the enemy. Too many times did I run off the edge or fell off due to prolonged animations for attacks or dodges or just not seeing it due to the camera tweaking out. This does not happen much any more and games so this is why I think of it as a bad. I will put as a disclaimer though that as I have grown I have narrowed my taste in games and therefore may not have just been encountering these games.
I would only recommend this game to people like me, who are really into Sci-fi/Robot games and want a decent adventure game in this niche setting. If it didn't reisde in a narrow setting I would say this game was not worth the price however given it's uniqueness I will say it is up to the buyers progitive, which is how it is always anyway. This game is not for everyone which is why I do not recommend it in this review.

This game has such a good concept but in the end it falls flat.
The first 5~ish hours of this game were very enjoyable, however as i progressed further into the game it became glaringly obvious where the issues where, its trying so hard to be another souls game but it falls flat on its face.
..:: Combat ::..
The combat in the surge feels fantastic, weapons feel very different and actualy feel like they have weight and impact to them, ive seen a plethora of people moan about slow weapon being useless, but they are wrong, i have been using a single riged heavy weapon its sure slow, but if you use the full lynx set it has a very good attack speed, and considering as of right now, my damage on it is over 100 i can smash most enemies in the area i am located in seconds. If i switch to a smaller weapon of even dual the difference is huge.
..:: Perfromance ::..
This game runs fantastic im running with 12gb of ram, a i7-3770 ( not OC'd) and a gtx 960 even at max setting im getting 60fps in nearly every area. Im yet to have any crashes though ive heard of others having them.
..:: Graphics ::..
Visually this game is very pretty while it may not be the most advanced graphicaly it still looks damn good for its setting and the animations on the player and enemies and bosses are brilliant.
..:: Gameplay ::..
You can store your tech-scrap( Souls ) in the medbay so you dont have to carry them around.
..:: Story ::..
Good luck with that, the story if very flat none of the NPC's are really that memorable, and neither are any of the bosses
..:: Bosses ::..
The bosses are in any way interesting or mechanicly fun, they are tedious and boring, hit Limb X, stagger boss, Rinse repeate ( having only killed 3 bosses, and currently on the fourth ) Oh and you have to hit the boss on the specific area when you stagger them else you do 0 damage.
..:: Standard mobs ::..
Early on the mobs are quite tricky but manageable, however as soon as you get further into the game it changes from manageable to pointless, the mobs in this game only serve to either be used to farm for upgrades ( which are useless to some degree) or to make pointless fights with, if you want to actually progress in the mid to late game its much easier and faster to just speed run strat and ignore every mobs and press the buttons, also pressing buttons and entering the animations for that makes you IMMUNE to all damage.
Add to this that most if not all mobs have hyper armour and can just smash you to bits even if you are attacking them, and with the fact some of them have weapons you cannot obtain because they are ranged. you can quickly turn a trade for scraps into death.
Want to kill mobs and progress to the boss to get Scrap, dont bother, they can literaly 1-2 shot you even in tank gear, you will end up wasting most if not all of you healing before you even reach the boss even if you have been through the area several times. Its just not worth the time unless you are farming limbs.
..:: Upgrading Gear ::..
The concept is great, remove X limb to find that limb and use it to improve your own parts. However this can take several hours, espcially if you are farming for specific gear because the mobs dont always have the armour on them you want/need, and if you dont lop off X limb, good luck getting upgraded!
Upgrading your gear, makes you very marginally more stronger, now were talking small ammount you gain almsot no health only what i assume is akin to armour. if you upgrade your weapon sure you will do more damage but that aint going to stop the mob  smashing you to bits in seconds.
..:: Combat ::..
Blocking, there is literaly 0 reason to ever block, heck you can hold block and your R-stick up or down to jump or duck from an attack but mobs attack and dart around so fast and the fact blocking makes you stand still, it has 0 use, its far easier and far safer to dodge.
..:: Misc ::..
There are only 5, yes FIVE bosses in the entire game, ive seen people beat this game in 16 hours.. for a £40 game that ammount of content is shocking, that price tag is far to high considering the replayability for this game is almost 0, sure there is NG+ but aside from maybe new mob placment and being able to upgrade your gear higher there is nothing new.
5/10
Whilst the game has so many glaring problems, the combat is fun, if this game was £20 it would be worth the price tag, right now this game is far to expensive for what you get, and has far to much artifical difficulty, and lack luster bosses.

I think the majority of negative feelings people have towards this game come from the fact that it compares itself to Dark Souls, which is one of the best games of all time, so it compared negatively. This is a shame because The Surge is a truly unique experience, legitimate criticisms can be made, the frequency of one-hit-kill attacks is disappointing and the length is not ideal. Looking at this game alone though it offers one of the best melee combat systems with incredible hit detection and a variety of interesting weapons. The Surge is an open world, third-person, action game with a focus on scavenging, exploration and tactical melee combats taking place in a post-apocalyptic, dystopian, setting. Here's my review about this great game.
The player rides an exokeleton that makes exploration, fighting and survival possible in the game setting, and that exoskeleton is the key to all gameplay. The game revolves itself around melee combats, from where you obtain the majority of resources and items you need in order to upgrade and acquire new gear. Combat in this game is, perhaps, the best executed part, because of its complexity, yet short learning curve. The player is able to target individual body parts to inflict damage specifically to a more vulnerable limb, or damage and cut it down in order to scavenge their armor pieces or weapons and be able to use them. The player is able to dodge or block attacks and lock on enemies (which prompts the body part targeting option), so melee fighting can be executed tactically for the best desired result possible.
Defeated enemies drop tech scrap, the main currency and crafting material in the game, it is used to develop and upgrade your exo-suit, as well as improve its Core Power, which is the energy required in order to equip certain gear. This is basically the leveling system in the game, so there is no skills or perks to choose from when you level up.
Enemies range from the weak and slow enemies to the powerful and tough bosses, so do not expect to always win. The point of the game is to fight tactically, without brainlessly bashing the attack button. Even the weakest enemies are capable of quickly dropping you if you don't properly plan and time your attacks. Dying also makes you drop your current tech scrap (allowing the player to go back and recover it at the place it was dropped within a certain time limit), and since it can only be banked at certain places, the player must evaluate the risk-reward aspect before rushing to explore each section of the world.
The game is labeled as open world, and indeed it is, but level designs are not exactly fit to allow the player to explore each and every place and since there is no abilities such as climbing or jumping (there is actually a jumping mechanic, but it is very limited and can only be used at certain locations), it pretty much forces you into mostly linear paths, but that isn't what the game is all about anyway. Exploration is still encouraged, though.
There is also a crafting element, providing the player the ability to fabricate gear, provided schematics for them are currently available.
It is also possible, provided enough power is available, to create any combination of weapons and body parts in order to construct unique exo-suits, suiting any need.
The concept is rather interesting for a game set in a post apocalyptic scenario (a theme we all know it's been overused to the point of becoming a cliche). A tech company finds itself in the role of saving humanity from a world torn by war and lack of resources, and this is the justification behind the transformation of the protagonist from a wheelchair tied man to a walking living weapon. Very interesting.
