Emily is Away. Aside from being a massive throwback to Windows XP and old IM'ing clients, it's also possibly the most realistic and soul crushing story I have had the pleasure of experiencing.
Without giving too much away, you play as yourself talking to Emily, your highschool friend over an IM client. It is clear you have feelings for Emily but are too afraid to show them.
The dialogue is extremely well written, if a bit guilt inducing and for the first time in quite a while, I actually cared about the character of Emily and was seriously offended when she said someone else was her best friend. I'm not even offended when that happens in real life, yet this game somehow brought it out.
--SPOILERS AHEAD---
The game (to my knowledge) has two endings, neither of them particularly good. Theres the bad ending where everything you attempt to type about feelings and your relationship are backspaced out and replaced with menial chitchat as an excuse to keep the converstaion going with her giving copy paste answers until you decide to leave and the really bad ending where she leaves pretty much as soon as you start talking.

Sleeping dogs is an open world game that ends up feeling like a mix of the Batman games and Grand theft Auto. You play as an undercover cop trying to take out a top ranking figure in the Triad, the biggest mobsters in china. The game features all the hallmarks of a good cop story, morality choices, trying to keep undercover, and realizing that the side you are trying to destroy may be less evil than the side you serve.
Yes, you see guns in trailers. No, you shouldnt get used to them. This is a melee combat game that plays like the Batman Arkahm series games. You will be bashing peoples heads into air conditioners, punching them senseless, and flinging them into silly "Death scene" areas. There are guns, but you dont get them forever and you essentially never just "spawn" with one. This games focus is almost entirely on driving and melee combat.
The game comes with all the original's DLC, which is good for the most part (The horror themed one is so derpy that Im discounting it here). The DLC where you get to play as a beat Cop, rather than an undercover cop, is pretty sweet, and makes me wish for a reverse GTA where you play as cops in an open world game. Shame its such a small part of this game, but still.
Overall, this is an open world game that did not get the same love longstanding series like GTA did. That being said, its not a bad game at all and I recommend the heck out of it, especially if you live on games like GTA or batman (And if you prayed and hoped for a mix of both? this is your game)
If i had to point out some negatives, i'd say that the combat gets extremely repetetive once youve gotten passed the 9000th fistfight (People who played the Arkham series know exactly what im talking about). The games lack of guns is a blessing and a curse, given its nature as a beat em-up, guns would ruin a large part of the game. That being said, it feels like they should either of included more, or just not included them. The gun running segments are some of the least fun in the game because the weapon system is just so poorly made in comparison to the fighting system. Incorporating the system used in "I am alive" (A game where guns are extremely rare, and are used to ward enemies off or control them more than they are used to kill) Would have made the gun system fit better with the melee system.

An incredible game I was playing when I didn't have internet for a year and half.
From when I've last played here is my review.
These are my main points about the game.
Logisitics, transporting resources: by hand (man), convator belts, car (manual), train, flying robots (automated).
Power, supplying power: steam, solar.
Basic resources: water, coal, iron, copper, oil.
Enemies: aliens
Victory: fly rocket to space with satellite
Personal review.
At the start of the game I was completely overwhelmed at the idea of creating infrastructure perfectly to automate resources going in and out like a real factory. I kept restarting and I kept recreating until I had found my niche of how I wanted to play. From the game on it gets massive and then the aliens start to come but at that point they are just more annoying than dangerous. I've played at least 200 hours as I wasn't connected to the internet but it was some ride. After finding my niche it was mostly a waiting game, however at that point I couldn't help but wonder when I would run out of resources and if I did expand how would I connect it to work with everything else. Then it kept spiraling out of control, things were clogging up and things had to be rebuilt. In terms of maintenance and design this game is bang on for making you work. As you work your way up the tech tree and building manifest, processed resources become more important and harder to process due to limited supplies of oil. As well the time it takes to process certain items become a burden in the long run and you soon realize there is no waiting game it is a matter of mass production per time. The game has huge replay value which is why I played for this long. The game has less emphasis on the dangers of the planets as the aliens are generally all the same and attack you due to the polution you create which is based on the fact your expanding. Overall great game.
Some of its flaws:
Tutorial was basic enough to get you going but there are some things that are bit confusing such as train lights.
Bigger variety of weaponry, defences etc.
Bigger variety of enemies.

Contrary to what other reviewers have said, you do not ever need to guess with Hexcells Infinite. I will admit to not completing many of the generated levels yet,though each so far has required nothing more than logic.
As such, Hexcells is a near perfect puzzle game. Infinite improves upon the previous two games not just by providing a near endless number of generated levels to play, but by improving nearly every other aspect of the game.
The UI is friendlier; you can have just the 'click' sounds, with or without the music, expanded hexes are more clearly distinguished against others.
This installment is by far the hardest. The previous two start off easy and work up to much more difficult puzzles, this is no different, but some were so large and challenging that I have sat there staring at the screen for hours in single puzzles.
If you like minesweeper and hate ever having to guess, get this game. My only recommended game on steam with a library of over 300!

This is a very well thought out, polished game.  The best part is it doesn't have the most frustrating part of minesweeper since you very very rarely have to *guess* where a blue tile/bomb is.  Speed running in it is different than minesweeper since you have to look all over the board for info about the area you are working on.  There are more rules to it than minesweeper.  I beat the game and make few mistakes, but after the playtime shown for me, I could still improve my times by 2x after more practice.  So yes, it's a great game that develops some skill even beyond basic logic and arithmetic.

If you read somebody saying that there is luck involved in this game, it's simply not true.  All the puzzles in this game can be solved by logic alone.
As somebody that has a lot of anxiety, this game is an absolute go-to for relaxing.  Imagine minesweeper and sudoku combined in a way that feels nothing like those two games.  It's a very zen-like experience.  That's not to say that it isn't tough.  It is!  I love this game quite a lot and cannot recommend it enough.

Hexcells is a minesweeper with 0% luck and 100% guess, hexagons instead of squares and (far) better graphics. The rules are quickly and efficiently explained, leaving you to focus on solving the puzzles.
As the third and last installment of the Hexcells serie, the game mechanics remain the same as the previous Hexcells but new puzzles are introduced as well as the ability to save and quit in the middle of a puzzle (very welcome for the harder ones) as well as a random generator of puzzles.
This latter feature adds infinite replayability altough the random puzzles are never as well-thought (i.e. hard) as the ones from the game developpers.

The Surge is an open world, third-person, action game with a focus on scavenging, exploration and tactical melee combats taking place in a post-apocalyptic, dystopian, setting. Here's my review about this great game.
The player rides an exokeleton that makes exploration, fighting and survival possible in the game setting, and that exoskeleton is the key to all gameplay. The game revolves itself around melee combats, from where you obtain the majority of resources and items you need in order to upgrade and acquire new gear. Combat in this game is, perhaps, the best executed part, because of its complexity, yet short learning curve. The player is able to target individual body parts to inflict damage specifically to a more vulnerable limb, or damage and cut it down in order to scavenge their armor pieces or weapons and be able to use them. The player is able to dodge or block attacks and lock on enemies (which prompts the body part targeting option), so melee fighting can be executed tactically for the best desired result possible.
Defeated enemies drop tech scrap, the main currency and crafting material in the game, it is used to develop and upgrade your exo-suit, as well as improve its Core Power, which is the energy required in order to equip certain gear. This is basically the leveling system in the game, so there is no skills or perks to choose from when you level up.
Enemies range from the weak and slow enemies to the powerful and tough bosses, so do not expect to always win. The point of the game is to fight tactically, without brainlessly bashing the attack button. Even the weakest enemies are capable of quickly dropping you if you don't properly plan and time your attacks. Dying also makes you drop your current tech scrap (allowing the player to go back and recover it at the place it was dropped within a certain time limit), and since it can only be banked at certain places, the player must evaluate the risk-reward aspect before rushing to explore each section of the world.
The game is labeled as open world, and indeed it is, but level designs are not exactly fit to allow the player to explore each and every place and since there is no abilities such as climbing or jumping (there is actually a jumping mechanic, but it is very limited and can only be used at certain locations), it pretty much forces you into mostly linear paths, but that isn't what the game is all about anyway. Exploration is still encouraged, though.
There is also a crafting element, providing the player the ability to fabricate gear, provided schematics for them are currently available.
It is also possible, provided enough power is available, to create any combination of weapons and body parts in order to construct unique exo-suits, suiting any need.
The concept is rather interesting for a game set in a post apocalyptic scenario (a theme we all know it's been overused to the point of becoming a cliche). A tech company finds itself in the role of saving humanity from a world torn by war and lack of resources, and this is the justification behind the transformation of the protagonist from a wheelchair tied man to a walking living weapon. Very interesting.
I don't know what engine this game uses, but the landscapes, light effects, particles and overall details are handcrafted and very beautiful. Helps a lot with immersion.

I purchased this game when it was still in Early Access for the full price (was $25 when I bought it).  Developers promised a lot of things, new features, customization, and a vast amount of gameplay.  Unfortunately, none of these promises were delivered.  I bought the game because I enjoyed Double Fine's Brutal Legend.  They seemed like a trustworthy developer that could get a fun quirky game done and make it worthwhile.
After months of no updates and no communication I began to lose heart.  The minimal amount of playtime (logged 0.6 hours) was due to the lack of a tutorial (which they have since added, and it's sub-par) and (I assume) a bug that prevented my characters from entering the base I built.  I started another game, and again they wouldn't enter the base I built and ended up suffocating.  Started another game and I finally got them to enter the base, and that's where more bugs appeared.  Just read the forums to get an idea of how frustrating the bugs are and how broken the game is, despite it getting a full release.
Very disappointed in Double Fine.  Their lack of communication regarding the game's development, refusal to be honest with people who bought their product (e.g. not letting us know they planned to stop development and leave the game as is), and the fact that they had the gall to release the code and tell the community that if they like the game, then they have to fix it.  Come on.
To conclude, I'd say avoid this game, it will receive no further updates, and as it stands it's an incomplete mish-mosh of ideas.  Even for $12 I'd say skip it.  Hopefully they update Gang Beast, which I also purchased before this fiasco, although it hasn't received an update since the day I bought it (2 months ago).
Update: Source code has been released...and there are still parts of the code that are hidden, as one person on the forum mentioned, the Oxygen Recycler.  One of the most basic units of the game.  It's used to prevent your base from losing oxygen, thus preventing everyone from suffocating.
Update #2: Price has changed to $20.01 (from the sale price of $12), and that's about it.  Tried playing the game again and it wouldn't let me complete the tutorial (was not allowed to place a second airlock door where it indicated).  Still have yet to build my own base.  They supposedly also fixed some bugs on October 30th.  This is what one user had to say:
"crlsniper Nov 1 @ 2:30pm
Glad to see your working on fixes, though the bigest fixes need to be AI fixes, Mostly for doctors and security. I lost an entire base just because none of the doctors would go help people who where incapacitated, neither would soldiers go arrest and move raiders who where incapacitated either."
Multiple counts of the same complaint.  Furthermore, despite where you establish your base, you will have near constant attacks from pirates/raiders.
Some brave souls have attempted to mod the game (essentially having to rebuild the game from the ground up), check this thread out:
It outlines a lot of the bugs and problems with the game, such as faulty oxygen recyclers (e.g. too many people in a room would cause dramatic decreases in oxygen no matter how many recyclers you had, thus everyone in that room eventually would suffocate).
Update #3: Free copies of Hack n Slash were provided to buyers of this game (myself and a few others received a copy), however it strikes me as more of a political ploy than a genuine apology.  This is because people who purchased Hack n Slash got a copy of this game.  As far as I know, Hack n Slash purchasers weren't spat upon and kicked to the curb by Double Fine, so this move makes no sense to me.
And of course I'm not eligible for the new refund policy, since I purchased this game over a year ago.  GFY Double Fine.
Not an acceptable way to treat ones customers. For shame, double fine. For shame.

Sleeping dogs is an open world game that ends up feeling like a mix of the Batman games and Grand theft Auto. You play as an undercover cop trying to take out a top ranking figure in the Triad, the biggest mobsters in china. The game features all the hallmarks of a good cop story, morality choices, trying to keep undercover, and realizing that the side you are trying to destroy may be less evil than the side you serve.
Yes, you see guns in trailers. No, you shouldnt get used to them. This is a melee combat game that plays like the Batman Arkahm series games. You will be bashing peoples heads into air conditioners, punching them senseless, and flinging them into silly "Death scene" areas. There are guns, but you dont get them forever and you essentially never just "spawn" with one. This games focus is almost entirely on driving and melee combat.
The game comes with all the original's DLC, which is good for the most part (The horror themed one is so derpy that Im discounting it here). The DLC where you get to play as a beat Cop, rather than an undercover cop, is pretty sweet, and makes me wish for a reverse GTA where you play as cops in an open world game. Shame its such a small part of this game, but still.
Overall, this is an open world game that did not get the same love longstanding series like GTA did. That being said, its not a bad game at all and I recommend the heck out of it, especially if you live on games like GTA or batman (And if you prayed and hoped for a mix of both? this is your game)
If i had to point out some negatives, i'd say that the combat gets extremely repetetive once youve gotten passed the 9000th fistfight (People who played the Arkham series know exactly what im talking about). The games lack of guns is a blessing and a curse, given its nature as a beat em-up, guns would ruin a large part of the game. That being said, it feels like they should either of included more, or just not included them. The gun running segments are some of the least fun in the game because the weapon system is just so poorly made in comparison to the fighting system. Incorporating the system used in "I am alive" (A game where guns are extremely rare, and are used to ward enemies off or control them more than they are used to kill) Would have made the gun system fit better with the melee system.

Hexcells is a fantastic series that you should definitely play.
It is reminiscent of Minesweeper, but the puzzles can be solved deterministically with no random chance or luck involved, only clever inferences based on each cell's surroundings.
The game starts off simple, but getting a perfect score on the later levels approach crushing levels of difficulty as you're asked to mentally juggle more and more possibilities - or you can just use a guide. :P
Hexcells Infinite introduces randomly generated levels in addition to the set of handcrafted ones already present... but the results are basic. The rules for the generator tend to produce puzzles that are pretty easy to solve and can only compensate for their lack of it by making them larger in scale.

With an overwhelmingly large amount of time in this game, and 720 of the random levels completed as of this review, I can assure that this game is one of the best ending games to a series of games. There isn't a single level you can't complete with guessing as you'll always have one move you can logically make, though it can be obscure. As always, even the 36 "story" levels prove to have an equal difficulty curve, albeit steeper than the previous two games. For anyone who wants a well-made puzzle game that can also prove calming, I suggest this one as well as the previous two. Though, this game allows you to change the controls, so superior game goes to Infinite.

Fun game for those who like Mine Sweeper or other logic solving games.  Slightly more complicated rules for hints, there's the rows/columns hints that isn't present in Mine Sweeper.
There's also pleasant ambiance music, soothing and easy to listen to while solving.  Doesn't mesh well if you're in the hasty mind pushing yourself to beat best times.  But when you're just playing the game and relaxing, it is wonderful.
I recommend the Hexcells Infinite version because you can generate random puzzles to play.  The other versions in the Hexcell series (including this one) all have pre-made maps for you to play that are deliciously complicated and ramp up in difficulty.  But once you've beaten the premade's, you've beaten them.  You'll get your money's worth on each game, but you may not want to go back to the premades for some time.  Having a huge amount of random generated puzzles to tap whenever you want to play a fresh game?  Delightful.

Legend of Grimrock is as old school as it gets, and thats a good thing. Puzzles range from easy to hair rippingly hard, combat is balanced (if you know what your doing), and overall I get the same feeling of excitement I did when i was younger watching my dad play these games.
If you've ever played Lands of Lore or Eye of the Beholder, pick up Legend of Grimrock. It's a blast from the past for nostalgic real-time dungeon crawlers, and so far Ive loved every minute of it.

So, this game is a typical dungeon crawler but it can also play like a first person point-and-click adventure at times, mostly when doing puzzles.
The story here is that a team of four prisoners did something to♥♥♥♥♥♥off the king so badly that he wanted to chuck all of them into Mt. Grimrock, and it is up to you to guide them to their freedom, or perish. There's a couple of races and classes, each with their own abilities and skills, so you can customise your Fighters, Mages or Rogues to some degree.
The puzzles are quite simple, although some of them takes some trial and error (or some looking around) to solve, not to mention that there's secrets. Gameplay 's not much to write home about and can be quite difficult to get used to if you've never played a dungeon crawler or haven't done so for a while.
Overall, the game's good enough to last you a few hours, and the promise of a level editor (in alpha at time of writing) brings more potential longevity to the table. Worth a look.

Only played for an hour, but it's free so an hour of fun should justify a positive review.
It's a classic trade-escort-survive-missions 2D space game with newtonian physics. Nothing new as such, but very well done and, as said, free.
Production values are very high, it runs extremely efficiently even on a total potato, and great care has been taken to maximise quality of life - new line for emphasis:
This game DOES NOT WASTE YOUR TIME.
You can launch it in a second flat, get to play with one click and no waiting, and immediately start planning business and flying around. You can plan the most efficient mission composition because the menus are designed to be extremely helpful, highlighting navigational and ship type restrictions, possibilities for multiple missions and so on. You don't waste time with docking manoevers, lengthy jump charge-ups, landing animations, cutscenes or any other of that tripe that so many games parade in front of you. It's seriously just second-to-second gameplay; you can meaningfully play this game even if all you have is five minutes.
The visuals are nothing special, just standard cliché'd spacecraft = aircraft ships, and space is mostly full of visually busy but physically meaningless asteroids and such. But it's well done for what it is, and the sound design is good too, highlighting important events with chunky audio so you don't miss anything. It's not big on getting you attached to your ship, crew, or business partners, so don't expect any personalisation options, fleshed-out storylines or characters. Your ship is a visually identifiable bunch of stats - but those stats are entirely visible and you have a number of options for tweaking them via equipment, so again gameplay is very good on that end.
The business aspect of the game seems like the central gameplay area, and it's very streamlined while still giving you some calculations and decisions to make. Balancing risk and reward, mortgages, interests, profit margins, ship upgrades, cargo capacity, fuel, protection from pirates and so on gives you plenty to do, while keeping it all simple enough to not make it a chore.
I haven't played it long enough to judge it on the amount of its content, but it's free so if you like what you heard so far you should just go and do that yourself.

I've tried to write this review many times and keep deleting what I wrote, so I've decided to go with a pros and cons list for simplicities sake (NOTE: I have not beaten the game and do not intend to due to my complaints listed below) Lets start with the positives:
PROS:
-Runs very well in terms of FPS and general performance (Obviously this differs from PC to PC, but the game seems to be optimzed well)
-animations are fluid and are satisfying
-combat, for the first few hours of the game, is fun and enjoyable and you can really see what the developers were going for with the limb targeting.
-the overall aestetic of everything is fleshed out well.  The industrial mecha vibe is strong throughout and the weapons and armor designs are great
-The intropart of the game, before you get your powersuit, felt really natural and enjoyable and i wish other games had interesting opening like this.  It made me wish the story was better.
-Despite what i'm about to say in the cons, this is a (mostly) fun game.  It feels unique in its combat and deserves and purchase when i goes on sale.
CONS:(Where to start...)
-Characters are dull and meaningless and voice acting is meh.  None of the NPC were very interesting at all and really had no bearing on the part of the story i played.(Coming from Dark Souls where the community is spoiled with wonderfull charcters and voice acting, I guess it was foolish of me to expect that level of quality right off the bat)
-Hit dettection felt wonky at times.  To be fair, most of the time it was ok, but i would have liked a bit more consistancy.
-Most weapons in the game felt unuseable. The combat in this games is fast, which is a good thing. However, several of the weapon classes felt as if you were moving through a swamp while the enemies were spinning circle around you pummeling you to death.  Dont get me wrong, the moves sets for each weapon were interesting and fun to mess around with, but some were just too slow.  Its a shame because the single rig, which has you strapped with one huge blade one your arm had some of the coolest designed weapons, but had and abysmal moveset.
-There is no satisfying feeling of progression.  Leveling up your rig lets you equip more plug-ins sure, but they really dont feel very impactful due to reasons ill get to later.  So if leveling up is lame, how about upgrading gear? Is that satisfying?
-Gear Upgrades feel pointless.  While the weapons upgrades did allow you to progress easier thorugh a level due to the dmg increase, the armor upgrades had not effect on gameplay at all. The heavy armor felt the same as the light armor and only a few set bonuses were actually worth anything. Id say about 2 out of (i think)6 armor sets in the game felt useful. Not only that, but the materials used to upgrade gear needs to be grinded off of your enemies via the limb system.  Its not too bad, but it turns the limb targeting into more of a chore than I think it should be. Enough about armor.
-Most enemies, outside of the first few hours, will at most 3 shot you.  This is what really killed my fun.  I would spend an hour or so trying to grind to level up my gear only to go back to a troublesome enemy and still get oneshot.  The worst offender of this is the security gaurds. You meet them releativly early in the game and they push your♥♥♥♥♥♥in, but you think "oh ok, this must be an enemy I come back and fight later".  You'd be half right.  The games wants you to fight them when you first meet them for a side quest and they destroy you until you learn to cheese them, BUT when you come back later, several more hours into the game with better gear mind you, they will still 1 or 2 shot you.  Most of the enemies you come across can do this and it just gets old after you die to a random jobber for the millionth time.
-Enemy and check point placement is brutal.  Enemies first.  Im used to cheeky placement of enemies from Dark Souls, however in this game, when the lock on system is horedous, fighting more than one enemy seems literally inpossible. Dodging and managing one enemy who can 1 shot you is hard enough, but 2 or 3 ( or at this one part 5) thats crazy.  Each enemy can have hyper armor so even if you connect with one enemy in a group the others could just push right through you. To touch on shortcut placement really quick, the 2nd area, might be the WORST haul through an area with the least amount of short cuts ive ever played in my life.
-Combat becomes boring and unfun. In order to deal with some of these outrageous enemies you have to resort to BS methods of damaging them and abandon the not-so-useful, but still cool, combos the game trys to getyou to use.  Too many enemies are armored, which essentially means, they will ignore your combos and attack you anyway.
-The game feels like it has conflicting ideas.  The combat seems to work best in medium sized spaces with 1 or 2 enemies to deal with, and the first few hours feels good, cause thats mostly where youre fighting the enemies.  After that tho, the game has you funnling down literally pitch black air vents where it demands you fight an enemy that is as wide as the pathway so you can get past. Most of the later sections of the game have these small corridors and mobs of enemies to deal with that fly in the face of making the game feel good.
-"Soul Drop" Much in the same way DS does it, when you die you drop your tech scrap and you have to go get it before you die again.  However, what this game didnt figure out is how to place that care package in a reachable spot and not in the middle of nowhere.  In this game, the scrap drops exactly where you died, not a few seconds before, not on the platform you were on right before you fell, but exactly at the point where you die.  I had a death marker that was just floating in mid air because the ground dropped out and dropped me into a bottemless pit.
A few Minor complaints:
-The dialouge would play over itself or an audio log would cut out important plot dialouge.
-If you're gonna have an NPC in the world, dont have enemies stay agro'd when talking to them.
-in my 20 hours playing i only ran into 3 boss fights.  On fight was just a guy who after taking a bit of dmg would just run away and call in a previous boss to fight. It happens 3 times in that fight alone.
-If youre gonna have a dodge move, put a fair amount of i-frames in.
-if youre gonna have a block, make it so it works and not so every enemy can just hit you throught it.
-I would have liked more weapon or armor variaty.  The discovery of new armor and weapons was really cool, i just wish it didnt become obsolete so quickly.
I could go on probably for a bit and im sure i had more complaints, but its 3 o'clock at night and my saltiness over this game is wearing out.  Overall, I find my self severely dissapointed in this game.  I wanted something that could take up my time like DS did. I honestly wish i could return it.  I probably wont beat it, and if i do beat it, I certainly will never play it again.  This game had several ideas it was playing with and many of them just didnt pan out.
Final Verdict: 3/5

Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition is often referred to as the Chinese/Japanese GTA. I hope that we can put this common misconception aside and look at this game as it is. The game brings so much more to the table. It has a hacking system, good melee combat , free running, mahjong poker, classical music & chinese pop on the radio and even karaoke. That's not the surprising part, the surprising part to me was that it brought as much as GTA IV and combine it with so much more side stuff. To give you an idea how much there is, there is about 30% story and the rest of it is all side stuff. And when you are thinking that you are done with everything you can call contacts to unlock even more side content, at the moment 32 hours in, I did just about did half of the whole package.
The fighting system is both smooth on keyboard and mouse as it is on controller. The main fighting style in the city is kung fu, and anyone seems to master it, and the game loves to shed light upon this style to make players use it . What I mean with that is that gun fights are going to be there but they are going to be scarce. There are loads of combinations to unlock in fighting to make you even more of a powerhouse. They even added realistic sounds to the fighting, whenever we are doing a finisher which is breaking an arm for example sounded so realistic that it reminded me from when I dislocated my shoulder. It sounded so similar that I got goose bumps from it. Some kinds of fighters grab you from behind and hold you in a uncomfortable position to escape from but it is so hard to escape from that it's annoying. Another minor disadvantage is that the heavy and weak attack is set to the same key which I thought made the combinations a bit harder than they should be.
The story starts off pretty straight forward and linear but eventually I got attached to the main character as you get to understand him. You play Wei Shen, a returning Hong Kong citizen, which had connections with the Sun On Yee triads from his childhood. Upon his return he got arrested because of crimes he commited in the United States. Since he has connections to the triads he has to infiltrate into the gang and destroy the gang from inside out. This includes betrayal, killing, investigations on people and even hacking to achieve your goal. Most of the side mission also are about the police work you can do. The main character really was well fit into the story, most of the time you could not even tell if he was instinctivily making decisions in the gang or he was doing it to succeed in his mission to destroy the gang. In the end the story takes a few interesting turns which came out of nowhere but it turned out very good.
In the past you could buy the version without the DLC's but I looked into it and they seemed mandatory since that version is not available anymore. There are two extra stories, obviously smaller than the main story.
The first DLC is called Nightmare in North Point which is set after the main story as a horror story. It includes ancient Chinese myths like the Jiang Shi folklore. The combat is also pretty engaging because every fight gets more intense with an extra difficulty added. For me this DLC is equally good content as the main story.
The second DLC is called Year of the Snake which is set right before Chinese New Year. Here you have to do cop work to defeat a terrorist cult trying to bomb the city and most of it's citizens. It was more of a cat and mouse game than the suposed investigation on the cult. Some of the missions initiated with searching within an area which was just as easy as finding the odd looking guys in special suits. I wish they had made that more intense. What I also noticed is that unlike in the main story of the first DLC is that Wei was very quiet which I did not like, I would have loved some conversations even if it just was filler.
All in all a real thrill to play and even worth trying out if you favor GTA above anything. If the fighting style sounds like you would enjoy it or enjoy the combination they pulled off with the police work and the triad crimes you really should try out this game. However you shouldn't pick this up if you do not prefer melee combat.

There are some games that are genuinely addictive but, this is one of those games where you feel like it's not a time waste of nothingness. Sometimes I can just get so absorbed in Hexcells that I lose track of time. The ambient music, the blinding light of the screen can keep you glued to your seat for minutes deciphering some of these puzzles. The logic of this game is wonderful something similar to that strange Windows game Minesweeper only no annoying little bombs that end the game when you hit it. The Hexcells series has been a fun and relaxing way for me to pass the time. The calm ambience and minimalistic structure of the games makes it easy to keep coming back to whenever you have a little time to kill. Infinite makes things far more convenient with the save feature, especially once you start getting into the really meaty and challenging puzzles later on. That was my only real complaint about its precessors, and it makes a world of difference in Infinite.
While the randomly generated puzzles aren't quite as challenging as the expertly crafted stages, it's a nice feature that adds more playability to the game. I find that I spend more time testing speed over accuracy, whereas the main puzzles really encourage you to fill your cells in carefully (if you want to get the completionist achievements, anyway!).
I think the only thing that has given me trouble is just how easy it is to misclick, particularly when you're on a roll. Luckily, the game doesn't penalize you for errors and allows you to finish each puzzle regardless of how many you make.
Overall, a fun and simple game does what it sets out to do: scratching that puzzle itch in a quick and conveninent manner. I really appreciated the amount of creativity and challenge that was put into some of the game's main puzzles and I think it'd be worth playing them through again sometime.

This is the third in a series of puzzle games, with this one being the clearly superior production out of the three.  I say this because, like the first game, it gives a short tutorial level for any of the gameplay mechanics that are necessary to play the game.  However, unlike the first game, which developed these aspects much more gradually with several easy levels, this game starts applying these ideas at more advanced difficulty and application quite quickly.  This is a good thing in my view, since like all of the other games in the series, each one only has 36 designed levels for you to solve.  If too much time is spent walking the player through the gameplay, not enough time can be spent on levels that challenge all of the aspects the player had to learn to make it that far.
The last few levels were quite challenging, and I was happy to tackle and master them.  All of them could be solved logically without guessing, but it took me some time working out what combination of information available to me would let me click or destroy the next block.  One aspect I was immensely thankful for was that the developers put in a level save feature, so whatever progress you made already could be saved for later, giving you a chance to take a break and come back to the place you had got stuck on.  You could jump inbetween levels, making progress until you hit a roadblock, and then switch your focus somewhere else.  It helped me tremendously.
What ices the cake for me and gives this title the most value out of the others is that there is a puzzle generator for this game.  Very similar to how you can find websites to solve nigh infinite combinations of Sudoku puzzles, you can generate all of the puzzles you could ever want to do for this game.  The only flaw is that the puzzles are immensely easier than the ones with a human touch, and there's no way to select if you want a smaller, easier puzzle or a larger, more difficult puzzle.  It's all randomly generated with no way to set parameters for the puzzle you get (unless you look up specific codes, if there would be any of those listed somewhere in the first place).  Either way, I have enjoyed the trilogy, and can always come back to this one in the series if I want to play new puzzles.

First you mine. Then you get machines to mine for you.
Then you research new technologies. Then you get machines to research for you.
Then you build a factory. Then your factory builds factories for you.
There's always something to do in Factorio, which is why most of the top reviews talk about it like it's crack.
I thought they were exaggerating too, until I spent played it for 36 hours straight the day after I got it.
Worried that it's too complicated for you? It's not. Ultimately, Factorio boils down to a very simple concept: Combining resources to make new, better resources. That said, if you're the kind of player that wants a highly efficient and organized factory, you could spend hours planning, tweaking, and working out ratios in your head.
Either way, Factorio is absolutely worth your time and money. 5/5

I love Bastion, and I'd heard such great things about Transistor. After having just replayed Bastion, I decided to dive in and give it a shot. While it is undeniably a Supergiant Games product, it doesn't try to cash in on Bastion's success with a copy-and-paste successor. The music, audio and writing are all still top notch. The graphics and style, while different, still ooze a sort of cold charm.
And the combat system. It's a simply but brilliant mashup of action and turn-based usage on an isometric grid. That makes it sound bloated, but it's not. It's elegant, but leaves enough room for clever strategy and rotations of your Functions to make even the most challenging battles seem breezy with some changes in your approach.
And the story is beautiful. I daresay it outdoes Bastion here, if not in the other categories. This game has solidified Supergiant Games as one of those devs I'll buy from without question, at least until I'm disappointed.

A sort of "pick your own story" game, in which you select what to type, having conversations with a friend named Emily. It's a nice read, and at times it might make you feel like you're writing to a real person. The story, as I said, follows two characters, one of which is Emily, and the other is you. You both went to school together, and this game starts during the last year of High School, and goes on to the last year of college, with each chapter being about each year. It's also quite short, and free.

An emotional game that has a young guy and gal talking to each other using an old-school chatting box. The game revolves around these two young individuals during high school and college years, and takes us on a ride of questions, suspense, and understanding. What I most experienced about the game is the bonding and the relatability this game has. This little gem circles around one simple, but important, term: Friendship.
As many older people know (I'm talking mainly high schoolers/colleges), not all friendships last forever, and this game takes a fantastic direction of that, creates a story, and sprinkles all kinds of emotions. I, for one, actually felt stunned when certain situations happened, and some I understood because I'd had that in my own life. That's one of the biggest reasons I love this game:
. I've always been a fan of a game that makes me feel immersed with the characters. I mean, you don't even see the characters at all! They're just letters and sentences on a screen, but the feelings are real, as if you can hear the struggle of a personal bonding with someone that doesn't even exist!
I found this game charming. If you like a free, good short story with a side of feels, this game is perfect!

TLDR below. I can't believe I played this thing for 30 hours. The fact that it is free to play has nothing to do with it either, because there have been many other free to play games that I ended up playing not any longer than 5 minutes. Or even some paid ones.
But I love the "open world space" context and I love science fiction, and I love spaceships. I love trading, decision making, route planning, and some minimal combat. I like rogue-like, risk taking, random generation. All of these are in the game, and it's surprisingly addictive. If I start a session in this, I can't leave it for at least 3 hours straight. It makes you plan things, think, reason, order, panic, get nervous etc. If a game makes me feel this way, I call it a good game. At least it's always one of the main points when I'm grading a game.
+ Tiny game size (seriously wtf)
+ Open world with many MANY different star systems and planets/moons/space stations (I couldn't unlock the whole map in 30 hours and had more than 50 systems explored already) ((the edges were still unexplored. however close I got, there would always be some new system on the edge))
+ Insane variety of ship types (more than 30 I guess)
+ Serious in-depth customization of ships (such that I couldn't even completely explore all of the possibilities)
+ More on customization: engines, shields, weapon types, ammo types, steering, hyperdrive, crew, bunks, cargo, the heat production of your setup, power consumption, generators, speed, and MORE to customize. Seriously wtf
+ Banks are everywhere on every system but shipyards are rare, so it's a good thing to not be safe all the time
+ Game gets procedurally more difficult as you start posessing a more powerful fleet (but it doesn't punish you unfairly ever)
+ Different mission types (not just shoot this, carry that, get paid) though I understand why some people might still see it that way. I didn't. I had my fun. It's everyone's own opinion.
++ You can pay off pirates if you're a rich♥♥♥♥♥merchant xD
- OK, graphics are not bad but everything feels like just an image file. This is not exactly a con, as some people might be into this sort of thing in the first place
- Sound effects can get a bit repetitive the longer you play (though they are not horrible)
- You can sometimes get stuck between a rock and a hard place (marooned on a planet with vicious pirates just outside waiting to eat my corpse) ((got past them in 15 tries though)) So can be frustrating at times.
- You can sell back your ships for their FULL value. ALWAYS. Any add-ons are also sold for their FULL value. Say that you have a ship you bought for 1 million credits. You modified it further with 200,000 credits. You flew it around, up and down the whole galaxy. Engaged in combats, repaired and refueled it. Hauled cargo and carried passengers. You did this for two years. And you can still enter any shipyard and sell that old♥♥♥♥♥freighter for it's FULL 1,200,000 credits value. This is kind of bad, because it doesn't ever put you in harm's way money-wise. It shouldn't work that way imo.
- Unclear story, if there is one (there may not be, but it felt like there was one. still i couldn't even start it in 30 hours. i was way too busy having fun trading and expanding the fleet)
So, the final verdict is: extremely addictive if you're into this sort of trading simulation with complex ship customization as well as minimal combat and a little rogue-like frustrations. I am a space trading enthusiast so this was a pure gem for me. Too bad the graphics were on a budget. Because if it weren't, and it was online, it would compete with Eve Online. Has the same concept, only with a smaller world and less content in general, also no multiplayer. But like I said, I am a single player person most of the time and enjoyed this thing for 30 hours. So it was cool for me.
Buy your first ship. Start carrying cargo (or shoot pirates) ((or become one)) and start paying your credit debt. Then buy more ships. Apply for more loans and buy more ships. Carry bigger things further apart. Start making real money. Customize your ships so you are better suited for longer and more dangerous space travel. Expand your fleet. Put more bunks so you can carry whole colonies to far away systems. Expand expand expand. Earn more money! Don't know what to do with that much money? Buy more insane ships or even more cargo space!! Where does it stop? I don't know! All I know is that my girlfriend found this game stupid, but I spent 30 well-fun-had hours on it.
I would say, give it a try, since it's free to play and has the size of an immature watermelon.

Building on the long line of the Battlefield series, Bad Company 2 continues the focus of Bad Company 1’s team tactics, cover destruction, and vehicle usage. There are 4 classes, which you get weapons for by playing as the class and scoring points. Those points also go towards improving your soldier rank, which occasionally gives you certain global unlocks as your progress. The game’s cover system focuses on making most cover destructible to a certain degree, and new to this game are certain destructible buildings.
But let me warn those that enjoy more death match style games: This is heavily reliant on team strategy. In this way, the game can be frustrating at times, but also very rewarding when you use actual tactics to out maneuver the enemy. With at least one more map pack and an expansion releasing soon, Bad Company 2 may not live up to the greatness of Battlefield 2, but it more than delivers a delicious team based shooter for $20.

This is my next favorite puzzle game. You're going to hear comparisons to Minesweeper, but I can assure you that the differences are enough that you might love this game even if Minesweeper isn't your thing.
That's certainly the case for me. To start with, there is never a need to guess. Every puzzle has all the clues you need. Now, admittedly, guessing can sometimes be fun and fulfilling, but this is the kind of game where if you fail, it isn't because of the random flip of a coin, but because you didn't pay close enough attention.
That's what I love about this game: It is a pure logic test that does great things for exercising your brain. The first couple of worlds introduce you to the rules. After you've got the rules, though, the priceless part of the game is the random puzzle generation that will make a seemingly endless stream of puzzles.
It isn't without problems, though. The music gets to be a bit much, fortunately you can turn it off. There are surprising UI elements missing. You can't advance through the game numbers (seeds) in a linear fashion, unless you're willing to remember your 8-digit numbers yourself. Even so, I'm not sure how random the random system really is, since I SWEAR I've replayed some of the games.  Some players might appreciate a hint system.
All that aside, though, it is a very enjoyable puzzle game, and is likely to go on my list of puzzle games that take all my time.

The Surge surprised me quite a bit. It's a great fresh take on the "Kick Your Butt So Hard It Hurts... So Good!" formula. I'm a huge fan of Lords of the Fallen, the Souls series of games, Nioh, and Bloodborne on PS4.
The Surge is not a perfect game, and to make this quick here's a list of Pros and Cons.
PROS:
- Leveling system is very straight forward and unique
- Implant system leaves a lot of room for customization and tweaking
- The combat is even more skill based with the limb targeting
- Crafting that is straight forward and gathering the resources is directly tied into the limb targeting system which is so smart
CONS:
- Story is kinda meh so far (Minus the opening cinematic and playable cutscenes which were awesome and engaging). After a great opening, the story just seems to melt away as you hack and slash your way through the enemies.
- Enemies are very similar and attacks seem much more predictable.
- Game seems much easier than Lards of the Fallen and basically all the other games of this type.
Definitely enjoying my time with The Surge and if anyone was on the fence, I'll say I'm glad I didn't wait for a sale or price drop. Definitely worth the money so far.

Let me lead with this, I have not beaten this game. Frankly I do not have the desire to. I bought this game hearing that it was the quintessential, Sci Fi, Souls-like(or lite) experience. This is absolutely true in many regards.
-There is a rest area that you refill a limited pool of healing items in. There you also level up and pick your upgrades.
-There is an emphesis on finding shortcuts in the area during your progression through it.
-You collect a form of "currency" that upon one death, you drop them on the spot. If you can make your way back, you can retrieve them, if not they vanish.
-And above all of this, the game is difficult.
But that last one is where the game loses me.
Difficulty in the Souls games has almost always felt...   fair. Like if I died, it was easy for me to say, "Okay, yeah I messed up there". But this game has a lot of issues where I just feel outright cheated when I die.
For starters, the dodge doesn't seem to have invulnerability frames. Which, in a game like this, is sort of important.
"Why don't you just block then?'" Because that doesn't work an inexcusable amount of times. A fair amount of enemy attacks are just straight up unblockable.
"So the dodge is sketchy and the block is worthless, okay fine. I'll just play super offensively." Oh how preciously naive I was. The enemies will, frame perfect, initiate attacks with hyper armor and hard counter you. By the way even with heavy armor and quite a lot
of health, "trash mobs" can two shot you.
On top of all of this there are varying issues with tracking enemies with lock on and hit boxes (for you and the enemies).
The enviroment is not without its flaws either. It's almost impossible to really tell where you are in relation to anything. So shortcuts aren't something you can seek out. You just sort of happen across them and maybe recongnize the area you're in. Hard to tell because most areas look pretty similar. That probably has more to do with the game taking place in a factory, and to a lesser extent, poor level design.
Also, there was an section in the second area where there is a hallway coated in some acid or something. There was almost no way to get through this without taking damage, because there were 2 enemies that would refuse to let you kite them out of it. So you have to fight them in not even toenail high acid that would shred you over time, while fighting two enemies that can two shot you, and immediately afterwords fight a boss in the next room.
I hate to use the term "artificial difficulty" because it had always sounded like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ excuse as a souls player, but my god this game thrives in it.
It's just hard for me to justify the money I put into this game. Had it been $20 or so, I might have been okay with the various blaring issues this game has, but $50? No, absolutely not. I can't in good conscious recommend this game.
(Thank you to everone who has taken the time to read my review! If you purchased the game afterwards and enjoyed it anyway, GOOD, I hope you continue to enjoy it. If my review kept you from buying it, I'm glad I could save you the $50. That said, if you're still on the fence about getting it, there are people who review games for a living that can explain things much better than I can. The one I watched was from Total Biscuit. Thank you to everyone who commented as well. Even the people who have nothing better to do than ♥♥♥♥♥ at negative reviews for a game they already bought, honestly why are you here? I might give it another chance when I'm feeling a bit more patient, but for now my opinion stands. Classic case of "Mad cuz Bad" I suppose.)

Not much can be added here that other reviewers have not already touched upon.
Positives:
+ An incredible soundtrack (This seriously cannot be overstated).
+ The art style, visuals, and voice acting are also very, very good.
+ The combat mechanics are unique and allow for multiple ways of approaching the same problem.
+ The story is interesting (However, see the point below).
Negatives:
- There is a lot that goes into the combat, and I can see how it may not be for everyone. Although it has these elements, it is not very action-oriented (e.g., run in, slash, dodge incoming attacks), and seems to reward players for planning attacks and escape routes out ahead of time. The game has a Turn mode that allows for this, though you are not required to use it and, in some cases, I found it beneficial not to use it against some enemies.
- The game is fairly short.
- The story can be convoluted. I think the creators tried their best to keep it coherent while still dropping the player into a world that feels like it has been around for a while, not holding the player's hand throughout the game, and maintaining an air of mystery about the events unfolding. However, I also think the story would have benefitted from being longer.
There's more to say, but nothing that other reviewers haven't already discussed. Personally, I like the story and the combat system. It allows customization options for attacks and how to fight enemies, in general. It is the first game I played that sports a Turn/planning mode (I'm sure others exist, I just haven't played them), and I was a fan of it. It sets it apart from other games, including Bastion. However, another commenter mentioned that they found the combat to be more precise and appropriate for a keyboard+mouse than for a controller, and I agree completely.
If you haven't already played Transistor by now, it is worth the cost. It also appears to periodically go on sale quite often, providing even more reason to give it a chance.

One of the main issues is COMBAT. Combat, combat, combat.
Imagine yourself in this scene: You just got through a horde of weaker enemies, being able to destroy them with one combo from your weapon. You're feeling happy, good, even ecstatic. You can take on anything.
In the distance, (Or rather, down a narrow corridor. Much of the level design in this game is made to look like a Dead Space level, which WAS Third person, but an FPS at a way closer scale. Often times, rooms'll be too closed in. Also, levels tend to look the same ALL the way through.) you see a stronger-looking enemy. You just went through a horde of weaker ones, so this one shouldn't be so hard. You run up and begin hacking, using your memorized combo pattern.
Until you see that the enemy doesn't stagger, and instead begins to swing it's big♥♥♥♥♥hammer at you.
You frantically hit the dodge button, thinking "I can dodge out of the way while he leaves himself open, and strike from the back!" However, your character has different plans. He's stuck in the middle of his combo, hacking and slashing as doom looms above his head. You smash your dodge button over and over, as impending death comes crashing down on your poor character's head.
After you open your eyes again, you sigh a breath of relief. He's alive, but has about 95% of his hit points gone from ONE HIT. But wait. Even though the other enemy didn't stagger, and he has the same armour as you, your character has fallen to the ground! The enemy looms closer, and swings his giant ♥♥♥♥ing hammer again down on your character's balls.
The staggering and combo-locking in this game hurts, especially when levels as long as these with no checkpoints are implemented. If you get into a combo, you CANNOT get out of the special move, which often doesn't do any more damage than a regular single-hit move.
And staggering is absolutely broken. No matter what weapon you use, be it heavy, light, or two-handed, an enemy will rarely stagger, and even then, not for long. However, your character will stagger and fall at the slightest hit, no matter how much heavy♥♥♥♥♥armour he's wearing.
I can forgive everything else, such as the basic, closed in, boring levels; Non-changing enemies (Literally, in my first 6 hours, and maybe even beyond, I've seen only two different main enemies, just with different skins or armour, but same weapons.); And even random holes in the ground when most of the ground is shaded in black anyway (You'll have a light to turn on, but it doesn't point down).
But the issue of combat in a SOULS-LIKE game should've been fixed early on. Too much back-tracking to a death that I didn't deserve because my character decided to get himself locked.
Some of the pros, however, are:
+ The cool♥♥♥♥♥limb dismemberment mechanic. Gawd damn, it's cool when it goes into slow motion to show you ripping off a head, tearing a body in half, or slicing a limb off.
+ The pleasant look of environments, weapons, armour. Pretty much everything in this game is aesthetically pleasing and nice to look at.
All in all, I'll give it... a 5/10. Not fun after a while, but I'm still gonna finish it to the end to get some cool slow-mo snapshots for my computer wallpaper.
TL;DR   I don't recommend it for anyone looking for a good Souls-game, a good combat game, or an interesting experience.

As a big fan of the Souls series I was excited for this game. I played through and had a decent time with Lords of the Fallen so I had come to expect a Souls like that might be a bit slower and rougher around the edges. However, that is not this game.
The most critical failure of the game is the combat. It feels slow and sometimes downright unresponsive. Slower weapons have extremely long wind-ups and consume laughably large amounts of stamina. Fast weapons have decent attack speed and stamina consumption but have no stagger and will allow enemies to power through your attacks.
The previous issues could be ignored were it not for the addition of forced combos and poor hitboxes. I would often find myself trying to hit an enemy twice only to find my character swinging for a third time and taking an enemy attack that I had intended to dodge away from. Couple that with the poor hitboxes where often swinging at an enemy directly ahead will result in a miss and recieve an attack from an enemy that you would've otherwise staggered.
In short the acceptance of death from your own failures in a Souls title gives way to frusteration of death from poor mechanics in this title. Instead of being hard but rewarding, this game leaves you feeling like you only won because things happened to fall into place.

Wow. That ending. It's like I got stabbed in the heart. I was NOT expecting that at all. This game really messed with my head for a good two days because the ending left me so conflicted. Never have I felt so happy and sad for a video game character at the same time. Wow.....just........snap, that was such a good game.
As for a REVIEW, I was really impressed by Transistor's mechanics, story, art (!!!) and music (!!!). Especially the last three. When I play a single-player game, I want a game that will give me a great, well-thought-out tale that keeps me interested through the whole experience. There was just enough details in this game to keep me running around with my killer thumb drive that had the souls of my enemies (and random strangers) installed into it, yet enough ambiguity to keep me curious.
I love the simple RPG-like mechanics of being able to update the Transistor with the digital souls of my enemies, and even make the game intentionally harder for more XP. The ability to pause time and pull a 2250 version of Sherlock's "mind planning" thing was also awesome, and I found the creative side of me piqued as I installed bloatware into the processes that dared to subscribe me to a service I had no interest in. Chucking processes into the recycle bin of a USB has never been so fun!
Oh my goodness, and the aesthetics, both visually and aurally; that just blew me away. Usually when I screenshot a game, it's because I'm like, "Hey, I did a thing!" and think that someday a human being will come into my life that will actually care about the image I captured. Not this game. No, I found myself taking plenty of screenshots because they would make great wallpapers for my computer. It's just so gorgeous, and the speakeasy techno-jazz music unexpectedly just adds to the mood like no other. Maybe it's because of this game I like "Say U Wont" by Brasstracks so much, because Darren Korb proved to me that Jazz and Electronic can get married and all sorts of wonderful kids running around the house like "Old Friends", "Stained Glass" and "Coasting". They're nowhere near as redneck as their cousins from the Bastion, such as "A Proper Story" or "In Case of Trouble", but they are still part of the same family where good ol' Darren somehow finds a way to make Electronic work with pretty much any music style.
So yeah, if you like going hog-wild on freaky, white programs with a massive thumb-drive that just so happens to have your boyfriend's soul in its motherboard to the sound of surprisingly satisfying electro-jazz, then this is your game.

An incredible, crushing, sense of what it might be like to live in the worst of times.
Papers Please tasks you with the role of  border guard in a fictional Eastern European dictatorship. Your job is to check the visas of people trying to enter the country, trying to keep up with the constantly changing and confusing laws of your country while deciding who is lying and who deserves to get in. On top of that you only get payed for people processed, so good luck feeding your family and keeping the heat on if you let yourself get paralyzed by sob stories and complicated run-arounds! The chunky pixel aesthetic and crushing but catching soundtrack really help sell the mood and are a treat. This game is fun, but it will make you feel bad. It is worthy playing. Check it out.

I loved the Playstation 2 version back in the day so i had to get this in the last sale.
Based on the great series from the UK comic 2000AD, You're a genetically engineered super soldier in a future war.
It's a third person shooter with satisfying combat and a surprising amount of options on how you want to take on each wave of enemies. The controls are responsive, you can enter and exit cover, switch weapon modes and use gadgets with ease. The graphics still look pretty decent and character models are chunky and well detailed and the gun sounds are loud and meaty.
Being a game from 2006 it does feel a little clunky by modern standards but controls perfectly with keyboard and mouse and runs just fine on Windows 10 when there are some games which are newer which don't even do that!
It's a straight forward, no nonsense shooter from the glory days before every game had to be a 50 hour open world grind fest and sometimes that's all you need.

The Legend of Grimrock is fantastic. It's a throwback to the old dungeon crawls, but with a twist. While the movement is tile based, the combat is real time. What this allows the game to do is something that I haven't had an RPG do since I was a child: Instill fear. When you make a movement mistake, you're back against a wall, hacking/casting at a baddie that you know is going to kill you in 5 seconds, trying desperately to keep up the attack while managing your inventory to find potions.. it's a unique experience.
It's about 15ish hours playthrough with no replayability atm, but the level editor is coming out soon. One of my favorite games of 2012 so far.

Not much can be added here that other reviewers have not already touched upon.
Positives:
+ An incredible soundtrack (This seriously cannot be overstated).
+ The art style, visuals, and voice acting are also very, very good.
+ The combat mechanics are unique and allow for multiple ways of approaching the same problem.
+ The story is interesting (However, see the point below).
Negatives:
- There is a lot that goes into the combat, and I can see how it may not be for everyone. Although it has these elements, it is not very action-oriented (e.g., run in, slash, dodge incoming attacks), and seems to reward players for planning attacks and escape routes out ahead of time. The game has a Turn mode that allows for this, though you are not required to use it and, in some cases, I found it beneficial not to use it against some enemies.
- The game is fairly short.
- The story can be convoluted. I think the creators tried their best to keep it coherent while still dropping the player into a world that feels like it has been around for a while, not holding the player's hand throughout the game, and maintaining an air of mystery about the events unfolding. However, I also think the story would have benefitted from being longer.
There's more to say, but nothing that other reviewers haven't already discussed. Personally, I like the story and the combat system. It allows customization options for attacks and how to fight enemies, in general. It is the first game I played that sports a Turn/planning mode (I'm sure others exist, I just haven't played them), and I was a fan of it. It sets it apart from other games, including Bastion. However, another commenter mentioned that they found the combat to be more precise and appropriate for a keyboard+mouse than for a controller, and I agree completely.
If you haven't already played Transistor by now, it is worth the cost. It also appears to periodically go on sale quite often, providing even more reason to give it a chance.

Take a simple game mechanic that is deceptively deep, add gorgeous art and attitude, and top it off with a wonderful soundtrack, and you have Transistor.  If you loved Bastion you'll love this game.  If you haven't played Bastion either, what are you doing with your life!?

Wow. That ending. It's like I got stabbed in the heart. I was NOT expecting that at all. This game really messed with my head for a good two days because the ending left me so conflicted. Never have I felt so happy and sad for a video game character at the same time. Wow.....just........snap, that was such a good game.
As for a REVIEW, I was really impressed by Transistor's mechanics, story, art (!!!) and music (!!!). Especially the last three. When I play a single-player game, I want a game that will give me a great, well-thought-out tale that keeps me interested through the whole experience. There was just enough details in this game to keep me running around with my killer thumb drive that had the souls of my enemies (and random strangers) installed into it, yet enough ambiguity to keep me curious.
I love the simple RPG-like mechanics of being able to update the Transistor with the digital souls of my enemies, and even make the game intentionally harder for more XP. The ability to pause time and pull a 2250 version of Sherlock's "mind planning" thing was also awesome, and I found the creative side of me piqued as I installed bloatware into the processes that dared to subscribe me to a service I had no interest in. Chucking processes into the recycle bin of a USB has never been so fun!
Oh my goodness, and the aesthetics, both visually and aurally; that just blew me away. Usually when I screenshot a game, it's because I'm like, "Hey, I did a thing!" and think that someday a human being will come into my life that will actually care about the image I captured. Not this game. No, I found myself taking plenty of screenshots because they would make great wallpapers for my computer. It's just so gorgeous, and the speakeasy techno-jazz music unexpectedly just adds to the mood like no other. Maybe it's because of this game I like "Say U Wont" by Brasstracks so much, because Darren Korb proved to me that Jazz and Electronic can get married and all sorts of wonderful kids running around the house like "Old Friends", "Stained Glass" and "Coasting". They're nowhere near as redneck as their cousins from the Bastion, such as "A Proper Story" or "In Case of Trouble", but they are still part of the same family where good ol' Darren somehow finds a way to make Electronic work with pretty much any music style.
So yeah, if you like going hog-wild on freaky, white programs with a massive thumb-drive that just so happens to have your boyfriend's soul in its motherboard to the sound of surprisingly satisfying electro-jazz, then this is your game.

You know, I wouldn't picture myself a fan of turnbased RPGs; mostly because I usually find them boring and a lot of the stories in them are well,  a tad too anime-y for my tastes. This game turns that old paradigm over on its head. It looks the quivering mass of RPG ness and turns it into a gibbering blob of bossness. It makes the turn based system fun, exciting, and challenging with the monster's strength increasing each turn, thus putting a nice stress on the player to get the battles done quickly. And the addition of a combo system adds extra layers to the gameplay, like an oniony layercake. Basically, gameplay wise, it takes all the stuff I usually loathe about turnbased stuff and removes or improves those mechanics to keep things exciting. Entertainment, that's a big thing this game is about! If it isn't the gameplay that keeps you interested its definately the silly story the tongue n' cheek humor. It's bundled with Breath of Death! This game to me has many flaws and many positive points.
We've seen thousands of "ball" physics games, in which you have to make your way through many different levels, using different kinds of weapons/balls, working your way out by timing shoots, creating your mental scheme, anticipate the position of the enemies when you have blown up one or two barrels/crates/bombs and so on.
I mean, there's a lot of these games.. physics puzzle games are one of the most played category in Flash websites and not only.
This game has some rare features: a button to speed up the level (there are balance games in which you have to wait minutes to see your ball slowly moving XD), a feature that makes your ball re-start when it's been stuck for 30 seconds and a general "lethality" that you have, so that you can drop enemies over yourself and they'll die by getting in contact with you.
But there are also many flaws. First of all you absolutely can not play this game in windowed mode, 'cos the game screens often are so big that you can't even understand where you are and where are the triggerable floors/bombs and so on. Moreover, physics here seems a little bit "random".. hence the fact that no one has still written a walkthrough XD On many level it seems that it's more a matter of luck the direction your ball takes.. or that the timing isn't so important, since you get in one way or another to the same endpoint.
Graphics are nice, but they're too much "predominant" - these kinds of games need the focus only on the player, the enemies and most of all the things you can trigger: you must see at first glance where are the bombs, where are the enemies located, which tiles you can remove in order to make your path, and this sometimes on Zombie Ballz is difficult to forecast, so you need many trial and error (by the way why space is the key for restarting and not R?! XD).
The developers are the same ones of Save Jesus, which was to me much better; many things are exactly the same, like the different balls you can use and the graphics style.. but Save Jesus was more beautiful and good looking than this one, for sure.
Some reviewers said that this one is better than the Zup! series but really, it's a different kind of puzzle games and even if you compare the two, Zup! is way better than this. This could be compared to awesome games like Cover Orange or Vampire Physics. And this one fails every contest.
But overall, it's still enjoyable and I think it doesn't deserve a negative review. Just bear in mind that if you like this genre of games, there are dozens way better.

This did not disappoint. The sheer number of things you can do when approaching a firefight make this a real gem.
Some of the most glaring issues are as follows:
1. It's pretty short at about 6 hours on normal. I don't mind short games because, obviously, the richness of the experience is more important, and I think Rogue Trooper delivers when it comes to experience. Your mileage may vary.
2. The controls are a bit clunky. Rogue has to swivel around a point if you want him to turn around, and this makes it very annoying to position him for a jump across a chasm; I died about four times in the game, and three of those times were due to me accidentally doing a combat roll into a canyon. The actual interface for selecting weapons and equipment will probably take you a minute.
3. The game's easy. The enemy AI will cower at your approach, let's put it that way. It's unlikely that you'll die or reach any fail states through lack of action.
4. Not enough enemies to fight. Rogue Trooper really suffers due to there being so few things to kill. There's a good variety of enemies, many of whom compel you to change up your tactics to defeat them, but when the fight is over in 10 seconds because you shot up a gas tank on a truck, it feels like the Norts just aren't allocating the amount of ground troops to stop you that they maybe should be. This negates from the core feeling of the player being some stealthy, deadly commando.
7/10 I think is the average rating this game got; I can't fault that but I could understand 5 or 6 out of 10.
If you catch it on sale, don't even think about it, add it to your cart. At full price, it's just a matter of if you like slightly older-style games, or have real megaboner for blue people.

"A bit clunky".  It's a phrase that appears repeatedly in other reviews and I think it fairly sums up the game.
For me "Rogue Trooper" as effectively a "straight" war story with a sci-fi setting was one of 2000 A.D.'s less interesting strips.  Partly because instead of setting it up thematically as a re-reun of the American Civil War (which would have suited the names of the warring factions) in attitudes and actions it's America Vs Russki Commie Fascists in space.
Like "Judge Dredd vs Judge Death" made by the same developer it reasonably accurately portrays the hardware from the comic strip and is actually truer in spirit and primary characters to  the comic strip than Dredd was.
It's very old fashioned for its 2006 release date - linear levels, graphics,  and cut scenes from a game five years older.
It also glitched out on me (Windows 10) once with the entire upper half of a key character vanishing and getting me stuck as a result.  Despite being linear some of the maps aren't easy to follow but there's a good online Walkthrough.  You'll thank me for the spoiler that when you enconter them mobile armour (think Ripley's loading apparatus in Aliens or eight foot high Transformers) you need first to incapacitate them with an electro grenade AND THEN run up to them and finish them off by pressing "E".
This is where the game's biggest clunk occurs.  Grenades can have a system of throwing them which involves setting one up, adjusting the landing location, and then pressing fire which makes them very clunky indeed under fire and makes heavy armour particularly lethal.  Generally the game is survivable because you can manufacture your own health kits at a rough cost of looting two dead Norts which is a bargain.  That's offset by levels where you are targeted by accurate enemy at long range necessitating reloads with the benefit of hindsight.
Why the positive review then ?  Firstly on sale you should be able to pick the game up for £1.50 - £3.00.  At those sorts of prices it's a good game for the money.  And whilst "Rogue Trooper" isn't my favourite 2000 A.D. strip the conversion here is accurate enough and the source material works spectacularly well as a game setting.
