I cannot recommend this title in its current state. There are some changes that could be made to improve it, and if that ever happens it will become a recommendation from me. The game captures the dark souls experience in a crude way, but misses all the nuances that soulslike will have to really recapture the feelings that games like dark souls 1 captured.
The balancing and improvement system for weapons and armor is really skewed. The weapon classes lack advantages/disadvantages for each class, and there are some that are just head and shoulders better than others in every way. Armor bonuses are simple "x% better/worse stat with y protection stat" and don't seem to make a noticeable difference.
Progression in terms of improvement of gear is very simple, requiring you to simply have enough scrap and spare parts to upgrade gear. However, this is gated extremely hard by the fact that the spare parts required don't drop until you are in the right area. Ex: To upgrade sword mk1 to sword mk2 you need upgrade part mk2. This continues with mk3 and mk4. These higher mk parts cannot be acquired until a certain area of the game, meaning your gear is essentially locked to a certain upgrade mk until you can progress. This wouldn't be a problem if the enemies weren't simply the same types with higher scaled numbers. This means that instead of feeling better with your upgrades, you feel like you are just on par. Not upgrading means you will just die faster/not kill as fast. The titanite system in souls allows you to focus your improvements, and the enemy types are varied and can involve timing and outplay to win fights. This is just simply not the case in this.
Overall, this is a very rough-around-the-edges soulslike. There are simple balance changes that could be made revolving around weapons and armors (upgrading, advantages/disadvantages of classes) to improve the experience overall and give a more rewarding feeling to playing. However, the lack of enemy diversity is a big problem, especially with how it comes down to simply more hp/damage instead of varied attack patterns and learning. As it stands right now, you go into a new area and get devastated simply because your gear is scaled for the last area and have to grind until you are back on par. This is not enjoyable once you fall into this routine and does NOT capture the core feeling one gets from a soulslike.

I should probably point out that, despite my eventual dismay about this game, I actually enjoyed the first 5-10 hours of The Surge. However, in the end, the game delivers merely an idea, and fails to live up to most of the sums of its parts.
The idea within the combat system of targetting body parts, and your moveset being different depending on what you are targetting is pretty cool. It was very well realized in the first two levels with the normal enemies. However, as the game goes on you begin to realize barely any of the combos and attack tactics will ever work. Most enemies later on can only be taken on with cheesy methods of dash stabbing, slide tackling, and general hit and run tedium. There is no robust parry and evasion (you can dash, but i-frames are terrible, and blocking is so clunky and unresponsive, with a terrible add-on of having a jump and duck mechanic which is borderline impossible to utilize) system, especially on the enemy's part. Instead, the developers just load them up with adamantine poise levels, and the magic ability to hit way faster than you ever can, with the force of Thor's hammer, staggering you to kingdom come. Later on you get enemies firing flamethrowers and grenades, while you hopelessly try to close the gap with your melee weapons, and they insta kick you down chunking half your health... bleh.
Character progression is so horrible it's soul destroying. Upgrading is tragically linear and gated, there aren't enough weapons, and even if there were, there is a terrible weapon proficiency mechanic (presumably added when the devs realized there would be no motivation to actually kill mobs anymore i.e: the only part of the game worth a damn) that more or less limits you to one weapon type.
Level design I found very interesting with the shortcut unlocking, but the design is so uniform and indistinctive that from the second level onward you will have no notion of where you are going, and out of frustration will probably miss areas. There really should have been a metroidvania style map here.
All in all, there is just no drive for the player to keep coming back once he or she hits the brick wall of tedium. The combat system needs reworking, and I just wish Deck 13 would hire someone to make a more robust and responsive sense of melee combat that works within some semblence of balance. Even if you could find your way to enjoying the stilted rules of combat here, there is nothing else driving you forward other than just plodding your way through the environment to get to the end of the game.
The Surge is a really good idea on paper, with a pretty tragic implementation.

Apparently changes have been made to the combat so I'm going to give the game another run in due time.
Meanwhile, I have stopped looking at review comments and won't be engaging any further. Thanks for anyone who has had an inch of common sense in their replies. For the git gud crew, I'll just copy and paste an earlier reply here --

As someone who hasn't played the from software games for more than a couple of hours (mostly because of the horrid pc port of the first dark souls and because of how clunky keyboard controls were in those) I find this to be a nice point of entry in the genre. Unlike the games it was inspired from, the pc port is good and the game is perfectly playable with keyboard and mouse.
the good:
- the combat feels... right. The character moves as you'd expect and there is quite a bit of depth to weapon, armor and movement interaction.
- I personally enjoy the theme, it has a nice sci fi horror vibe and you get a friggin exoskeleton.
- YOU GET AN EXOSKELETON
- the level design is complex and ingenious, with plenty to explore and different ways to approach certain encounters
- the enemies are quite varied and the bosses are intimidating
the meh:
- I encountered some bugs, nothing gamebreaking but in one occasion I got stuck in an area that I could access but not escape. Fortunately quitting and loading the game placed me very close to where I got stuck but outside the dreaded area.
- occasionally the framerate dips, I have yet to understand what causes this but I believe it has something to do with the loading of some areas. It generally doesn't happen during combat.
- the music in the OPS centers (bonfires) gets annoying after a while
- the ingame crafting and equipment menus are a bit clunky, it's not always clear what the advantages of certain weapons and pieces of armor are until you wear them and check the full stats. You can also craft things that are completely useless (for example a second chest piece identical to the one you have), the game will not warn you and you'll have wasted resources.
Most of these are pet peeves and minor problems in my opinion so the game gets a solid recommendation from me.
-post-patch update-
The update fixed a lot of issues (none gamebreaking but still) and in particular the block mechanic is much more usable now. This change reduces much of the frustration some of the more challenging enemies offered while still not making the game trivial. Now it's perfectly viable to stand still and parry an attack rather than just having to dodge everything.
While it feels a little content light, what it does have is very well done. Brings back a lot of memories of playing similar games from my childhood, while having a more modern look.

SHORT ANWSER- Overall, I think the game is very fun to play, has much potential, and would love to see multiplayer integrated in.
STORY- The main "story" starts off with you walking into a bank to get a loan for your very own ship. It's your responsibility to pay off your debt by what ever means possible. There is more story but only being a few hours in game(I've been playing offline so my play-time much higher than what is shown) I still have much to descover.
SHIPS- After signing off you have the choice of 3 starting spacecraft in your price range: A small shuttle used for light cargo and passenger ferry, a cargo hauler, and a small fighter-craft. Which one you choose decides what jobs you will be doing to pay off your debt. (There are dozens of diffrent ship classes and variaty so don't be dissapointed). As you pay off your debt and aquire more credits, you can buy larger, more expensive ships to suit your needs. Every ship in the game is unique and handles differently, and each one is fully customizable(Weapon sytems, cargo holds, radio equipment, ect.)
MECHANICS- One of the games high points are the ammount of different mechanics you have access to. You can request loans and build up your credit score(A great feature imo, so the better your score the more money you are entitled to). You can hail friendly ships for help (Fuel/repair), boad enemy vessles and add steal their cargo(Or the entire ship). along with these, you can map out different routes to solar systems across the galaxy. My favorite feature is the ability to make your own fleet and have escort ships to protect you.
NPC SHIPS- Nearly every place you go will have some amount of space traffic. It is very cool to see diffrent fleets, cargo ships, and shuttles all going about their bussiness across the galaxy. One thing that new pilots need to worry about are raiders and pirate ships. You can be attacked at any time, so If you don't have good weapon systems, powerful engines or are lucky enough for a friendly faction to save you you will get disabled and boarded (Unless you pay a $30,000 bribe)
PLANETS- Another great part of the game is that EVERY planet and space station you visit has its own little back history and photographt of it's surface. Not every planet is the same, so if you need some weapon upgrades or new modules, then you will need to keep track of what planets have the services you are looking for. Some planets have no life on them so If you land thinking you can refuel you are sorely mistaken (This caught me off-gaurd a few times).
COMBAT- The only thing that is a bit tricky in ES is the combat. Ships although futuristic, still behave a bit like modern day craft, so unless you can afford upgrades to your engines or have a speedy ship that deals a lot of punishment, combat isn't reccomended.

Fantastic game. It's been a long time since I played something that actually hooked me into it for more than an hour. Probably because this game has a mix of many things that I enjoy. Kung-Fu, open-world games, another culture, a great story, and it's actually a finished game.
Everything from the characters to the environment drew me in. Missions are exciting, driving is also fun and responsive (trade-off being it's kind of twitchy), the game is pretty well optimized and reflections are also very good everywhere. Sleeping Dogs has a good balance of drama-filled violence with more steady and relaxing missions in-between.
I would actually be willing to replay this whole thing again very soon. And I never say that about any game. I always have to wait at least a year or so to touch it again just so it feels kind of new.
For such a great game though it also has more bugs and lacking features than I thought it would. A lot of it is simple stuff too that shouldn't take too long for a developer to sort out or add. Some things are:
AI talking with hand gestures but there's a rifle in that hand, crashes during police missions, scripted chase events where the enemy would be stuck behind an obstacle, cars usually don't honk if you get dangerously close to them especially in the opposite lane, cops don't give a crap if you're destorying propery, my firearm randomly disappears when holstered, and sometimes if you're trapped in a bear hug you can't get out cause the game thinks you have to kick someone away first.
Anything else that isn't intentinal is usually hilarious and makes the game more amusing. Like the flag girl getting wrecked by the other cars at the start of a race.
I like how the hacking and break-in elements to this game are relatively easy but not completely pointless. I hate spending more time than I have to to break into something in other games. Either because it's too hard or I don't want to do the extra work to figure out something so miniscule to the overall game. that usually will ruin it for me. But Sleeping Dogs does just fine with this.
I just wish the DLC was much better. Both can be beaten in just over an hour each. The zombie one was just stupid because all your doing is beating up hopping zombies and undead main characters. Although Wei had more badass fight moves in that one. The cop one I thought was better but again it didn't really offer much. I was also hoping the Zodiac Tournament was going to be some tough journey of defeating fighters one by one until I became champion, cause that one had it's own intro to it. But again this felt like it was cut way short. If more work was added to all these areas then this would be my number one game, and it almost is. Despite all this, I couldn't be more glad to play Sleeping Dogs.

Stody-wise this is a powerful experience in a unique world, with lots of possible themes to interpret. It's the narration of Bastion with the exposition of Dark Souls (although fleshed out: using your abilities in different ways unlocks chunks of the backstory attached to each ability) and the general sort of vaugeness that, if you engage with the world, can lead to all sorts of interesting interpretations.
As for the gameplay, they found a way to add interesting gameplay to the usual isometric fighter. While Bastion kinda played itself, this game has more discrete encounters that play as follows: stop time and go on a rampage with abilities, and then run around scared for a couple seconds until the time-stop recharges. Some of the other reviews mention that the mechanics are sorta goofy, and they are, but it's in a way that works consistently. Some enenies will move/blink out of the way in the middle of your combo. Some abilities will break your combos with their secondary effects. If you keep this in mind and take the estimated damage outputs with a grain of salt, the system works fine.
The real gameplay draw for me is the "character building". You're similar to a MOBA character, with innate passives, 4 moves, and possibly passives for the moves. You then get a list of abilities and you can decide which are which, throwing together a cohesive kit from all sorts of options. For example, there might be an AoE skill, which can be used as an ability to deal AoE damage, or an ability's passive to make it deal AoE damage, or a character passive to add some AoE to all abilities. You can throw together pretty crazy kits (and since you need to try all the skills in each role to get their lore, you have incentive to reinvent your kit every couple of minutes). As well, running out of health "overloards" whichever ability you put the most of your power budget into, which means you can't use it for a couple fights, and have to finish the current fight without it. Not only does this mean that you need to build your kits with multiple lines of attack in mind, but unless you're getting through fights relatively unscathed you'll be reworking your character pretty frequently, and I love this.
One last thing to note, the "balance it yourself" mechanic has been brought over from Bastion; you can opt into extra difficulty in exchange for a little extra exp. I'd recommend turning it all on, since the kit building really shines when you're getting knocked around a bit. Except, and this is important, turn it off if you're having trouble with the final boss. The end of the game is really strong narratively, unless you break all immersion by stubbornly throwing yourself against that wall to the point that you're not even paying attention to the narration. The final battle isn't Sans and I'm pretty sure it isn't balanced around the "limiters", blow through it and watch the ending.
tl;dr great game if you liked the narrative style of Bastion or you've ever theorycrafted characters for a MOBA. Learn from my mistakes and do the final boss without the "extra difficulty" mechanics, he's there for the narrative not a Sans type of challenge.

I'm not going to give a detailed evaluation of the whole game. The music is fantastic, the story is enchanting (if VERY awkwardly implemented by having to unlock half of it with skill use).
I want to talk about how dull I find combat. Especially progression.
The game's enemy variety is based on incomparables. It's not about high defense and low defense, etc.; it's about strange behaviors. Some enemies teleport after being hit. Some go in and out of stealth. Some make others immune as they live. Some don't allow you to start a turn when you're too close.
You skillset, too, has many strange properties, BUT you still defeat enemies mainly by dealing damage*. There's no longterm resource management** (your health immediately refills after battle). In that sense? There's no reason not to try to deal as much damage as possible as quickly as possible. Charming or stunning enemies has less impact compared to RPGs with longterm resource management (like, the MP cost of blinding an enemy making up for the MP cost of healing yourself after battle when they hit with physical attacks). Getting hit doesn't matter unless that hit kills you.
*Enemies drop cores after they die that turn into small, weak enemies if not immediately collected. But they're small, weak enemies, so...
**... except when your health bar hits zero, when your main attack skills one by one until you have no more and reach game over. Skills recharge after every 2 new save points found. You'll have more skills than you can meaningfully equip. You can restart a battle at any time with no consequence. So, the punishment for failure is very light.
They address this by using "Limiters", which are mods in the game that also give you EXP bonuses.
THE PROBLEM is that the EXP bonuses are so small (2% or 4% each) for drastic effects (like reducing your total equipment cost by a third or doubling damage you recieve). It doesn't pay off for me.
To compare: in a game like TWEWY, the drop rates for pins (attacks) increases DRAMATICALLY as you up the difficulty or manually lower your level. You can sell pins for money, too. So, playing the game in a more difficult way rewards you more frequently with more gameplay options through new attacks/money that you turn into more attacks and equipment. Higher difficulty=more options=more ways to engage with game=more fun.
This game asks you to double the damage against you for a 2-4% EXP bonus with a Limiter. It's still completely managable this way, BUT how is that a proportionate reward for doubling damage? How about 16% percent more EXP for making the game disadvantegeous for me in 5 unique ways? Keep in mind, leveling is the only way you gain skills outside of a few handed to you by the narrative. So, for every 6 levels I'd get without Limiters, I get an extra skill with them on? After all that time? And I'm only level 10 at hour 8? It just FEELS bad.
I'm getting tired of all my old skills BEFORE I get new ones, long after using each recently acquired skill fully to unlock more story. I'm still merely dealing as much damage as quickly as possible after realizing most of the unique skills don't help me achieve that. Unique skills aren't useless, but they sometimes have overlap in utility with more straightforward, more spammable skills (i.e., why would I use 1) a skill that draws enemies closer to me when and only deals damage at maximm range paired with 2) a close-range move, when it's about as turn/damage efficient to use ONE long range, barrier-penetrating move?). There are many examples. This is bad design.
So, I'm either entirely unchallenged, or I'm making the game harder and longer but not proportionately more interesting. Moment-to-moment, this game's making me bored with its gameplay more than it's dazzling me with it presentation and unique, figurative story.
EDIT: Beat the game at 9 hours. Problems with gameplay didn't change. I leveled up twice after the game ends with a dense gauntlet of fights... after I'd already settled into core, cheesy strategies.
EDIT: Recursion (New Game+) is much more fun. I wish this was in the second half of the game/an optional hard mode at the start.

While I have only played a short bit so far, I can say that the puzzle aspects of this game are fairly interesting. Gameplay is (as others have noted) reminiscent of Sudoku and Minesweeper. The puzzles themselves arent very hard, and to my knowledge have no life system other than the fact that you get rewards based on how few mistakes you make. This system works very well and is very easy to understand the mechanics of the game with its "do it to learn it" tutorials.
This game has my praise as being a simple brain teaser, and I recommend it for this reason. It does its job and it does it well. Everything else below this is annoyances I have however, as this is a game about following the limited rules, and trying to do as well as possible. Some of the rules introduced, however, limit your ability to use your brain however and this peeves the hell out of me.
An annoying point for this system is that 1 mistake might be no lost points in some levels, while other more difficult puzzles might be that 2 mistakes is 2 lost points. Another issue I have with this is the need for guessing, in a system that gives its credits based on mistakes made. This game REQUIRES you to guess all the time, even in the first few levels even. And what I mean by guessing is that instead of intellectually plotting out your course, you are required to take a stand and say "well at least its just 50/50." And this is exacerbated by the "?" buttons. There is a level where there are ROWS of these unknown buttons, making it impossible to go around and therefore impossible to know how to move on without guessing. Turning this puzzle game of intelligence into a bit of a♥♥♥♥♥♥ And then theres the fact that the blocks you fill in as correct dont have numbers on them too. Meaning that if you are in a choke a couple blocks wide and you only get fillers then you have no way of moving forward, yet again forcing you to GUESS!

Love the Hexcells games. The Infinite mode is exactly what I've always wanted, so much fun to play a random map while listening to The History of Rome podcast.
While the later levels bogged me down simply cause I didn't want to start writing with a sharpie on my monitor, I still appreciate this Minesweeper/Sudoku puzzle game.

At times unbelievably frustrating - and then so very rewarding when you figure stuff out. Highly addictive, great piece for winding down from a hectic day. If the puzzles start to get too hard for your taste, take a break with the infinite puzzles: they're easier than the last main puzzles, but still require thinking.

I was enjoying the game, until world 3-4. At that point, the rules were violated twice in the same puzzle (-3-). This drove the point home of an earlier puzzle where there was an entire solid block of ? cells, requiring me to randomly click and memorize the pattern for the replay. I suppose it would be possible to map the entire puzzle out and model it based on how many pattern cells are remaining, but for a "casual puzzle game" I wouldn't be expecting something like that actually be required to proceed.
The game is created fairly well, the principles and mechanics are great, but the world puzzles are badly planned out.
I did not try the Infinite portion, and since it is the biggest advertised part of the game, perhaps that is the key feature. But I can only imagine that something procedurally generated will be pertinent to the other issues experienced.

Don't let the idea that you can purchase premium currency with in game gold fool you, this game is pay 2 win.
If you're high level (50+), you can earn enough gold to pay for a premium membership (or royal blessing, as it's called), but there's much more to be had with premium currency. More backspack in your tiny backpack? Pay up. Per item type (equipment, loot, potions, quest items). Would you like to revive instantly? Pay up. Fast travel for no gold? Pay up. Pet collars? Pay up. In fact, you're constantly nagged with functionality that requires you to either get a premium membership or pay a one time fee in premium currency. Constantly.
If you don't have a premium membership, you receive a lot less gold, experience and loot. Your resurrecting sickness lasts seven times longer, and much much more.
The game itself is alright. There are tons of different spells, and different classes really do feel like different classes. Some quests are unique and interesting, but most are fetch, deliver or kill quests. The PVP wasn't well thought through, and can be tedious at times. Most areas look similar, and enemies are not very unique in the way they act.
The chat is horrendous and unintuitive. This leads to very little chatter over the airways and a sort of isolated feeling, as if you're not really in an mmorpg.
Overall, the relentless pushing to get you to pay up spoils most of the fun, especially since your basic account is so limited it's hard not to feel pressured into spending money. I can't recommend it.

There is something inherently strange about this game. It plays nothing like it looks. It's the average person at the bar that you just can't get a good look at but every once in a while they turn around and your heart skips a beat. What is it about this person that is so enthralling? You have to go up and talk to them regardless of what your friends think. Turns out you have the most amazing conversation ever and watch the sun come up in the parking lot, not once making a single move on them. You go home happy, revitalized and content, patiently waiting for them to text you.
On the surface it appears to be a management simulator, chock full of interesting things to do, with equally as many ways to do them. Beneath the surface lies something that I didn't expect, something that didn't quite sink its teeth into me until around 20 hours in; there is always a better way to do things and you will dream about them regardless of how often you play. Belt systems can be merged, split and re-routed in a million different ways, smelting grids can be reformatted to minimize their footprint but maximize their output. Electricity becomes an art as you weave power lines aesthetically around your base being extra careful not to create a criss-cross which, while functional, looks terrible and we can't have terrible looking things in our base...
You start to grow content with your output, making mental notes of how you would like to move things around to make room for future upgrades. You sit back and enjoy your creation and how well everything is running. Suddenly, a red exclamation point shows up next to your toolbelt...hmmm, what's that? Your map shows it as well. You mouse over it, thinking that maybe you ran out of power or something simple, then it happens...
The biters are ripping through your iron mining in the northwest corner of your base! They are shredding metal like hot butter. The miners are taken out and the biters turn their sights on you. With almost supernatural speed they race toward you, fangs wet with a taste for blood. You have only a pistol to protect you. 10 measily bullets because you didn't spend the research points to get weaponized. The screen goes red and your stats are shown.
You vow to do things better. You will be ready the next time they attempt to breach your walls. Your factory will be stronger. You will be faster. They will be deader. This means war.
This game....is amazing.

Legend of Grimrock is a 3D first person tile-based dungeon crawler with real-time combat. Blending elements of Wizardry, Ultima Underworld(s) and Arx Fatalis it's a solid entry into a very small corner of the RPG world where releases are few and far between.
You begin as a party of four prisoners thrown into a dungeon atop a mountain. A place, as the game cleverly puts it, "Only remembered when things need to be discarded or forgotten." There are no towns, no merchants and very little feeling of respite.  Your map and the food, torches, alchemy reagents, spell scrolls and equipment you'll find are worth more than gold to a naked, starving group of prisoners who must battle their way to the bottom of the mountain for any hope of escape. Standing in your way are 13 floors of deadly creatures and cleverly designed traps and puzzles.
Though the environment and enemy variety is limited the game is beautiful, and though the skill system is brutally restrictive in what you can achieve it's still a good crawl with lots of secrets to be found.

This is a hard, hard, HARD dungeon crawler, but there's clearly a lot of thought put into it. It's basically old-school with new graphics, but the way it does so is awesome. This game will require trial and error, patience, and actual thought, so be prepared for that. Definitely worth playing!

This is like going back to high school after you've graduated from the university. The old school is back with this game, bringing old memories with it. Legend of Grimrock successfully resurrects titles like Eye of  The Beholder, Wizardry, Dungeon Master, and the list goes on... If you are nostalgic about old school dungeon crawl, get Grimrock.
Full of puzzles, a great throwback to classic American dungeon crawls on old pcs and the SNES. Loads of content with player made support.
If you liked any of the old 4 party dungon crawlers like Eye of the Behlolder or Ultima, you will like this. Updated graphics and  N E S W nostalgia.

Final Fantasy XIV is a fairly fun game. I've played a lot of MMO's , WoW being my favorite out of the bunch. Though I recommend and play this game, I still think it needs a few things talked about.
First lets talk about the classes. When you make your character in ff14 you will be stuck with that one character, which is pretty cool. You are capable of switching classes and setting gear presets anytime and anywhere. This works well, though I do recommend you take your time and choose your primary class wisely, because once you do a quest its gone forever. This means when you go and level another class you will have to grind the levels. They try to make this easier with increased experience but it still can be a long and tedious grind. Once you reach a higher level you will learn about another type of class. Each minor class has what I'm calling a primary class. For example if you are a rogue, you can become a ninja. This however requires you to level up a second class. In this example the second class would be pugilist. Of course this primary class has its own benefits and story line which is really cool.
The combat, in this game is frankly boring. If you have played any other MMO in your life other than free browser ones then you will probably agree to a certain extent. FF14 is a cross platform game and that means the game has to be dumbed down a bit for consoles. This translates to many parts of the game, but my primary gripe is with the long Global Cooldown on most skills. You do an awful lot of standing around in ff14 waiting to be able to cast another spell. You do get used to this, but its something of a big drawback for others and myself. The dungeons and raids in this game are a bit of a tossup. Most of them are incredibly easy. However a few of them are mind numbingly difficult. Difficulty in this game comes down to two factors. The first is mechanics which require the entire party to know the fight and do their part to not screw things up. For example one boss has four pillars in the center of the map. If the pillars break too much from being hit by AOE or special pillar breaking mobs then about halfway through the fight everyone will wipe. Pretty simple stuff if you break it down, like kill mobs that spawn, and stay away from the pillars until certain attacks happen. Yet I've wiped countless times in that dungeon. The second type of difficulty in this game is the lack of common sense mechanics. There are dungeons and raids in this game with boss fights that you simply will not figure out on the fly and will need to either be told or lookup before fighting it. This is a cool thing because you get some cool boss fights, on the other hand its infuriating to wipe because of some nonsensical mechanic.
If you are someone coming into this game to play directly with a friend(level with them), you may have a bad time. This game plays more like a single player RPG with a chat room. When I played with a friend we constantly had to disband the party to do our own instance scenarios. This happened so much that we just decided to level seperately.
The questing system is also something you should know about. Quest in this game are less about killing mobs until you get X amount of item to return to someone. Instead there is a lot of relay quests. Someone will tell you to take something to someone, then that someone will tell you to take it to someone else and that repeats or youll be asked to go back to the original person. There are plenty of combat quests where youll need to kill like 5 of this and or 3 of that. However this game feels like it jerks you around alot. They dont play around making you do these relay quests either. You will travel across the map multiple times to do these. This makes it nice that they add in teleport nodes around the map, but frankly it becomes more of a chore than grinding mobs till you get the required items. You are also forced to do dungeons. This bothers me a bit, as I like to mainly just quest up to the end game dungeons because I play DPS and dont want to sit in que for a long time to then trudge through one of their 30 minute dungeons. Early on this isnt too bad, but around lvl 50 you are going to do alot more dungeons and it becomes very tedious.
This game also has an incredible amount of dialogue. Everyone wants to talk and have a story, even the most patient person may break from the amount of dialogue boxes. Most of the dialogue in this game isnt voiced. Some of the main quest ones are, but only a handful.
The story for this game seems interesting and there is alot of it to take in. I didnt care much for the main story as much but the side stories and other character stories were interesting and fun to partake in. Like any other story there are plot holes and things here and there but overal its a nice backdrop to the game itself and it feels like your partaking in a world.
Overal the game is fun if maybe a bit slow. Its a fairly pretty game, though it has nothing on games like Black desert or Archeage. There are houses available for players and guilds. The guild houses are nice. I dont know much about player houses, as I have yet to buy one. You get retainers in this game wich go out in the world and gather items for you. It isnt a big perk, just a cool think to have. The community is also friendly and more oriented to RP and talking. Though this can be a bit of a drawback in dungeons. Healers and tanks simply dont do their jobs sometimes because they wanna chat. I felt Like I had to mention that because it happens frequently in this game, and I've never experience it in others. Though you have to pay monthly to play, this has to be my second favorite MMO. I wanted something for when WoW became a bit too boring to play for a while, and this was the best one I could find.
TLDR:
If you are someone who hates dialogue and slow combat this game is not for you.

The Surge is an interesting stab at the 'Souls - like' subgenre. Unlike Lords of the Fallen, which I immediately stopped playing, there is enough in The Surge to keep my attention. Below I'll list what I liked/dislike.
Likes:
Combat - The combat in The Surge is weighty and feels good. Dodging feels quick and responsive. I really enjoyed the severing mechanic. Overall the combat is solid and more importantly, fun.
RIGS - I like the idea of RIGS and bolting parts on to them. The Surge made me feel like Matt Damon in Elysium... So that's a plus.
Loot - Tying loot to where you attack is interesting and executed fairly well. I like that I can look at an enemy and say "Okay, what part do I need?"
Levelling - Kind of a mixed feeling here. I like that there aren't a ton of stats to level and that implants play a crucial role, but the weapon proficiency idea is pretty bad.
Dislikes:
Environment - I found the environments to be pretty bland and forgettable. Never had a real wow moment.
Combat - The combo system is pretty annoying at times. There is no way to action cancel, so starting a combo means you're fully exposed to death. I also found some of the boss hitboxes to be pretty bad/inconsistent.
Warren/NPCs - I'm okay with having a fixed character, but make them interesting. The Surge's characters are boring and poorly acted. I ended up wishing I could've created my own character instead.
Levelling - Weapon proficiency is just bad. This is one of the more horrible design decisions.
Loot - I wish there was more loot to collect and more interesting RIGs
Having hated Lords of The Fallen, The Surge has been a pleasent surprise. While it is not amazing, there is enough here to actually have me intrigued as to what Deck13 does next. If you're looking for a 'Souls - like' that takes the genre into a different direction. Pick up The Surge.

Stody-wise this is a powerful experience in a unique world, with lots of possible themes to interpret. It's the narration of Bastion with the exposition of Dark Souls (although fleshed out: using your abilities in different ways unlocks chunks of the backstory attached to each ability) and the general sort of vaugeness that, if you engage with the world, can lead to all sorts of interesting interpretations.
As for the gameplay, they found a way to add interesting gameplay to the usual isometric fighter. While Bastion kinda played itself, this game has more discrete encounters that play as follows: stop time and go on a rampage with abilities, and then run around scared for a couple seconds until the time-stop recharges. Some of the other reviews mention that the mechanics are sorta goofy, and they are, but it's in a way that works consistently. Some enenies will move/blink out of the way in the middle of your combo. Some abilities will break your combos with their secondary effects. If you keep this in mind and take the estimated damage outputs with a grain of salt, the system works fine.
The real gameplay draw for me is the "character building". You're similar to a MOBA character, with innate passives, 4 moves, and possibly passives for the moves. You then get a list of abilities and you can decide which are which, throwing together a cohesive kit from all sorts of options. For example, there might be an AoE skill, which can be used as an ability to deal AoE damage, or an ability's passive to make it deal AoE damage, or a character passive to add some AoE to all abilities. You can throw together pretty crazy kits (and since you need to try all the skills in each role to get their lore, you have incentive to reinvent your kit every couple of minutes). As well, running out of health "overloards" whichever ability you put the most of your power budget into, which means you can't use it for a couple fights, and have to finish the current fight without it. Not only does this mean that you need to build your kits with multiple lines of attack in mind, but unless you're getting through fights relatively unscathed you'll be reworking your character pretty frequently, and I love this.
One last thing to note, the "balance it yourself" mechanic has been brought over from Bastion; you can opt into extra difficulty in exchange for a little extra exp. I'd recommend turning it all on, since the kit building really shines when you're getting knocked around a bit. Except, and this is important, turn it off if you're having trouble with the final boss. The end of the game is really strong narratively, unless you break all immersion by stubbornly throwing yourself against that wall to the point that you're not even paying attention to the narration. The final battle isn't Sans and I'm pretty sure it isn't balanced around the "limiters", blow through it and watch the ending.
tl;dr great game if you liked the narrative style of Bastion or you've ever theorycrafted characters for a MOBA. Learn from my mistakes and do the final boss without the "extra difficulty" mechanics, he's there for the narrative not a Sans type of challenge.

I'm not going to give a detailed evaluation of the whole game. The music is fantastic, the story is enchanting (if VERY awkwardly implemented by having to unlock half of it with skill use).
I want to talk about how dull I find combat. Especially progression.
The game's enemy variety is based on incomparables. It's not about high defense and low defense, etc.; it's about strange behaviors. Some enemies teleport after being hit. Some go in and out of stealth. Some make others immune as they live. Some don't allow you to start a turn when you're too close.
You skillset, too, has many strange properties, BUT you still defeat enemies mainly by dealing damage*. There's no longterm resource management** (your health immediately refills after battle). In that sense? There's no reason not to try to deal as much damage as possible as quickly as possible. Charming or stunning enemies has less impact compared to RPGs with longterm resource management (like, the MP cost of blinding an enemy making up for the MP cost of healing yourself after battle when they hit with physical attacks). Getting hit doesn't matter unless that hit kills you.
*Enemies drop cores after they die that turn into small, weak enemies if not immediately collected. But they're small, weak enemies, so...
**... except when your health bar hits zero, when your main attack skills one by one until you have no more and reach game over. Skills recharge after every 2 new save points found. You'll have more skills than you can meaningfully equip. You can restart a battle at any time with no consequence. So, the punishment for failure is very light.
They address this by using "Limiters", which are mods in the game that also give you EXP bonuses.
THE PROBLEM is that the EXP bonuses are so small (2% or 4% each) for drastic effects (like reducing your total equipment cost by a third or doubling damage you recieve). It doesn't pay off for me.
To compare: in a game like TWEWY, the drop rates for pins (attacks) increases DRAMATICALLY as you up the difficulty or manually lower your level. You can sell pins for money, too. So, playing the game in a more difficult way rewards you more frequently with more gameplay options through new attacks/money that you turn into more attacks and equipment. Higher difficulty=more options=more ways to engage with game=more fun.
This game asks you to double the damage against you for a 2-4% EXP bonus with a Limiter. It's still completely managable this way, BUT how is that a proportionate reward for doubling damage? How about 16% percent more EXP for making the game disadvantegeous for me in 5 unique ways? Keep in mind, leveling is the only way you gain skills outside of a few handed to you by the narrative. So, for every 6 levels I'd get without Limiters, I get an extra skill with them on? After all that time? And I'm only level 10 at hour 8? It just FEELS bad.
I'm getting tired of all my old skills BEFORE I get new ones, long after using each recently acquired skill fully to unlock more story. I'm still merely dealing as much damage as quickly as possible after realizing most of the unique skills don't help me achieve that. Unique skills aren't useless, but they sometimes have overlap in utility with more straightforward, more spammable skills (i.e., why would I use 1) a skill that draws enemies closer to me when and only deals damage at maximm range paired with 2) a close-range move, when it's about as turn/damage efficient to use ONE long range, barrier-penetrating move?). There are many examples. This is bad design.
So, I'm either entirely unchallenged, or I'm making the game harder and longer but not proportionately more interesting. Moment-to-moment, this game's making me bored with its gameplay more than it's dazzling me with it presentation and unique, figurative story.
EDIT: Beat the game at 9 hours. Problems with gameplay didn't change. I leveled up twice after the game ends with a dense gauntlet of fights... after I'd already settled into core, cheesy strategies.
EDIT: Recursion (New Game+) is much more fun. I wish this was in the second half of the game/an optional hard mode at the start.

The basic story of the game is that you control Red, a beautiful young singer whom was attacked by the Camerata, losing her voice in the process. Escaping backstage, she finds and wields an extravargently crafted sword referred to as
, a weapon with the ability to hold the consciousness of the deceased and be the "brush" that crafts the city of Cloudbank. An above average and largely overlooking third person shooter based on a series of graphic novels about a genetically engineered super-soldier fighting baddies on another planet. All your supplies must be crafted-- ammo, grenades, health, upgrades-- using scrap scattered around the levels or salvaged off dead bodies. The graphics are nothing to write home about, but they get the job done.
My biggest complaint would be the lack of context for the story-- where am I? Why are the Norts fighting the Southers? What is that giant black-hole-looking thing in the sky? The cutscenes are well choreographed and do a proper job leading you into the next set-piece, but I wanted to know MORE about the universe.
Also, I wish the game were longer. This is more of a compliment than a complaint, though. The levels themselves feel just long enough and the game features many memorable quirks and twists on standard gameplay to make it a memorable experience. Sniping an enemy's air tank and watching him run around in a frenzied panic never gets old.

If Sim City 2k, Minecraft, Transport Tycoon and Dwarf Fortress had a beautiful, bugfree baby, and that baby only inherited the best features of its parents, it would still suck♥♥♥♥♥compared to Factorio.
Jokes aside, this game is really well-made and you can tell that the creators care about quality. Despite its alpha-status, it's already practically bugfree and heavily optimized. It can handle huge factories even on outdated hardware, and if that is not enough, the next update (0.15) will bring even more optimizations.
The Gameplay itself is addictive to say the least. Many strategy and planning games let you automate at least some things, but not too much because the developers probably thought that it would take away the fun. Well, Factorio let's you automate literally everything, and guess what: (clever) automation is more fun than anything!
Buy this game, it's worth every penny.

Factorio is an interesting game. While it has many of the tropes that permeate the industry these days (open-world, survival(ish), crafting elements, etc.) it takes the role of a problem-solving game moreso than a survival one.
At first glance the gut reaction may be "Oh it's like Minecraft or Terraria" but the satisfaction of Factorio comes from efficiency.
The extensive list of machinery available to the player allows for rather ridiculous level of automation, and in fact utilizing this automation to the fullest makes your quest to launch a rocket into space a much easier and much more rewarding experience.
It felt like a grind at first, but when I joined a random Multiplayer server to check it out I was shown how many different ways I could be approaching that grind to be more optimal. It may not be everybody's cup of tea but quickly after that I became hooked on setting up splitting conveyor belts and assemblers to turn things like Lab Research and Steel Production into a completely autonomous process.
Being able to hit the Research hotkey and select a new upgrade without worrying even slightly if my Labs were fueled was empowering. Walking up to a box packed to the brim with Steel Beams when I needed them was awesome, especially since I just set up a system to make that box happen and walked away to do other tasks.
It's a hard sell at first, but if you're a person that enjoys organization and takes joy from watching a complex Rube Goldberg Machine that YOU created work perfectly and create the end-result you were hoping for, Factorio is going to be a game you'll want to check out.
The addition of multiplayer servers adds a lot, as you can access them to get tips from other players, look for new ways to design your factory, or set up a party of friends attempting to achieve the Rocket Launch goal as quickly as possible in the procedurally-generated world.
Overall, it's not a game for every single person out there, but it fills a unique niche somewhere in between the Minecraft/Terrarias and games like Infinifactory, and that's pretty rad.

The only problem being every attack past the first press, is insanely dangerous and there is no benifit. This mean to play effectivly and without risking everything on the enemy actually being staggered, you get to kill the enemy slightly faster.
Otherwise the best tactic is to jump attack an enemy then move back, again and again until the fight is over.
To further emphesise how ♥♥♥♥ed up the combo system is, ill give the example of the duel wield weapons... ALL OF THEM, if you press Right trigger 3 times you do 3 pretty quick attacks, good, easy to dodge the almost instant enemy attacks. However if you press 1 more time, just 1 more time, you are then locked into a 4 or 5 hit combo, that have no stagger on enemiers. Couple this with the fact that with the agile exo suit, you can take about 3-4 hits from weak enemies and stronger enemies 2 shot you.

One of these is a robot scrapper, it has a huge shield infront and has perfect tracking when not attacking. This means the only way to do more thant 5 dmg is to wait for 2 of around 6 attacks, and hope to god it isent standing somewhere you ant get behind it. Then try and dodge, run  or shimmy your way behind it to get an attack or 2, Repeat 5-6 times, then fight the next one. No incentivy to try and out play it, there is no other way to defeat it.
Most of the enemies also have tracking when attacking, even enemies that jump at you will move mid air and hit you if you dodge a bit too soon. And since your dodge is about 5 cm and dosent show any indication of i-frames, its a pure luck if you actually dodge something or not.

Well what can i say!
After putting in a solid 20 hours into The Surge i feel like i can definitely give my review and oh boy is it positive!!!
I came into this game with no expectations as that is how i like to begin the journey of new games to hit the scene and i must say im extremely impressed with what i have seen and played so far!
From the get go it got me hooked. I love the combat system, for me it's faultless. I have seen a few reviews saying you should be able to cancel attacks mid way through and at first i agreed but now i see it as if you just go into a fight spamming keys/buttons and die because you couldnt cancel and dodge an attack in time then that is your own fault.
The Surge is pretty unforgiving in that way, if you aren't willing to learn and adapt to each type of enemy and treat each as your last you are going to pay for it over and over again until you feel like throwing your monitor out the window in a fit of rage!
Don't get me wrong the game is not easy, it is most definitely challenging which is a good thing.
Enemies will surprise you even the ones you have fought countless times, never just try rush your way through a section just because you have been through it many times as it will bite you in the backside. Patience and good timing is the way to play and if you have played souls most people will be able to adapt pretty well and quickly in that regard.
As for graphics, the game looks supurb at max settings and is optimised extremely well. I have held steady frames the entire game time ive played so far so i am mighty impressed with that.
Sound also is really great, from the different ground types you step on, the sounds of exo suits moving, weapons colliding with enemies and of course yourself and all the way through to the enviroments and speech is nice and crisp.
Enviroment setting for me personally i really enjoy the look and feel of it. It changes quite a lot through the different area's you need to navigate through and the interconnectivity with all the shortcuts through each area is extremely well done so that's another thumbs up from me there.
Story, so pretty much you are just trying to find out what the hell has happened, i dont really want to go into it due to the possibility of spoiling it for others so i will just leave it at that. It's interesting and has me continuing on and on and on through a million deaths to find out everything.
I have only encountered one bug so far and its extremely minor i dont even care and that was a drone that went invisible just before i attacked it but i was still able to target and destroy it so it is nothing to really complain about.
So all in all i most definitely recommend this game. but i must say do not go into the game expecting dark souls, yes it has a lot of souls vibes coming from the gameplay but take into mind The Surge is it's own GAME!!! enjoy it for what it has to offer and im sure you will enjoy the game as much as i am!
Thanks for reading and i hope this review inspires many more people to jump on deck of this amazing game!

This game brings back so much nostalgia from playing the original Escape Velocity by Ambrosia software. I remember playing  EV on my Dad's Mac LC III back in 1996. I had spent countless hours building up my empire, taking over planets and trying to rule the galaxy. It looks like I'll have my chance to do that all over again!
For the time I have spent so far, the execution for Endless Sky has been fantastic. The mechanics are very similar to Escape Velocity but there are some nice additions to the hotkeys and the ways that the game is able to interact with them...it's just smarter and more intuitive. The writing is incredibly charming and well thought out. There is a lot of detail and lore that has been created for those that enjoy that. I've just found out that the writing is open-sourced and those who wish to can contribute on the git-hub page (very cool). There seems to be a good group of writers who have been contributing to the details of alien species, other planets and their biomes/exports/civilizations etc.
The difficulty level is easy at the beginning but ramps up relatively quickly. Those who encounter pirates and aren't quick to escape or hail a friendly ship may get blown apart pretty quickly if they aren't familiar with the controls and mechanics. There is also a fair bit of grinding to get your credits rolling which can be even more painful at the beginning due to the loan you have to pay off from acquiring your starter ship. Although these come across as negatives, they do come hand-in-hand with the genre and it's "predecessor."
My only feature request: Cloud Saves. I would love to be able to easily pick up where I left off while on a laptop without having to manually maneuver saves around.
If you like space/sim/exploration/story with a decent skill ceiling, this game is for you.

Hell of a game. Highly, highly recommend.
The original production was meant to be another True Crime game, but the original developer fell through and they sold the game to a new developer who set it in Hong Kong. Knowing its a True Crime game, you can see the similarities. The rogue-like undercover cop with a rough history being a big sign.
Hong Kong looks amazing in this game, especially on extreme graphics settings. The cars handle pretty well, definitely an arcade style with a great variety too. From supercars and fast saloons to scooters and work vans. The hand-to-hand/melee weapon combat is very Batman Arkham Asylum, and the firearms are decently well done. Somewhat hard to come by outside of missions (until you unlock the ability to get them out of cop cars).
The three XP systems (Cop, Face and Triad, in ascending order of difficulty) take a bit of getting used to and can offer a steep learning curve. But the same could be said about any other game. Sleeping Dogs wiki and the IGN page became my best friend for a while there.
There is A LOT to do in side missions, which help with some of the XP. Everything from collectables and combat, to favours and side stories. It takes a fair bit of time to complete them all, but you get a sense of accomplishment from doing so! A gritty main plot where the lines really do get blurred, you start to question which team you're rooting for. Very rich story. So much so, a film was announced earlier this week starring one of Rogue One's actors in the leading role. Adding another well-known name to the already significant names that do voices in the game (such as Kelly Hu and Emma Stone, to name a few).
Sleeping Dogs goes on sale quite regularly, and its a spectacular deal when you get it on sale, but I'd happily pay full price for a game like this.

In brief: fun FPS, decent storyline, good cutscenes. Very linear, perhaps a little dated, but pleasantly varied and satisfying. No online multiplayer these days.
On the hideously poisoned and war-scoured planet Nu-Earth a genetically-engineered supersoldier known as Rogue Trooper fights in the endless war between Norts and Southers. The atmosphere is deadly to unprotected humans and the ordinary footsoldiers must fight in cumbersome pressure suits, but the Genetic Infantrymen (GIs) are immune to the poisons in the air and strut out without so much as a shirt on their supermanly blue chests. The game begins with the first deployment of the GIs and the ♥♥♥♥♥torm which immediately ensues.
The gameplay is fairly typical snap-to-cover shooter fare. Rogue packs a pistol and assault rifle at the outset and acquires additional weapons including grenades, mines and a mortar. The weaponry is powerful when correctly used, and choosing the right gun for the situation is very important when the game gets hard. Use of emplaced weapons is sometimes optional and sometimes obligatory, and there are a couple of levels in which Rogue boards a vehicle and uses its guns in a duck-hunt fashion. These sections, despite their on-rails pace, give the player a break from the game's exploration and resource-management angles.
The game's resource is scrap, salvaged from dead enemies and flyblown junkpiles. The resource system explains how Rogue manages to keep himself supplied whilst operating in enemy territory, and is the game's only major departure from the comic-book setting. Scrap is converted into supplies by Bagman, Rogue's biochipped backpack.
The biochips are a key feature of the storyline. Their job in the comic was to provide dialogue opportunities for a character defined by his lone wolf status; they also exercise some control over Rogue's gear, allowing them to make a material contribution to fights. In the game each biochip offers unique features including a decoy mode; notably, Gunnar in the (you guessed it) gun can act as an independent sentry and provides an auto-aim function which makes the weapon very powerful indeed. With a little practice it's possible to get every Nort infantryman with a headshot or tankshot, even when Rogue's on the run. The tankshots are very satisfying as the oxygen tanks inexplicably blow up after a second or two and send the luckless Nort flying.
The opening levels walk you through the basics of Rogue's gear, and once you get the hang of it the combat can seem easy, even on the hardest setting. The real challenge at the higher levels is in the scarcity of resources, a restriction which obliges you to conserve ammo and explore the game's tactical possibilities. Most situations can be approached in multiple ways; stealthy murders bring scrap bonuses and a fun little cut-scene of Rogue snapping a neck or plunging in a dagger.
At the easier levels it's possible (and fun) to just blaze headfirst through pretty much everything. Level structure is essentially linear with some alternate pathways and the AI, whilst not stupid, is predictable enough. Note that there's no manual reloading, something which I guarantee will annoy you when you're sniping. The game's also quite short – less than 10 hours to complete the campaign, probably a lot less if you try.
The story, told in biochip banter and game-engine cutscenes, is one of its great strengths. The voice-acting is very good and the script is solid, as it should be – it's written by Gordon Rennie, who scripted the second run of the original Rogue Trooper in 2000AD. The cutscenes are very well produced and really transcend the limitations of the engine with inventive camerawork and striking characters. Some players have remarked on the game's lack of boss fights, as most of Rogue's major opponents are dispatched during a cutscene; for me this wasn't a problem as Rogue's key enemies are all physical weaklings in comparison to him, so mano-a-mano boss fights would seem forced and implausible. The climactic all-in fights in the game's later stages are enjoyably chaotic as it is.
Multiplayer I can't say much about as it's no longer available for online play, Eidos having shut down their RT servers several years ago. LAN play is possible and the multiplayer maps can be played with AI enemies.
Overall: fun game, if you're a 2000AD fan who plays shooters buy a copy without delay.

The idea of choice and consquence is so fundamental to this game that it's almost impossible to review it without spoiling the options (and in some cases, lack thereof). But I'll try...
: Realistic, believable character interactions. The gameplay mechanics are built seamlessly into the conversation. It's both satisfying (as a player/gamer) and a gut-wrenching (as a human being) to see what the player character chooses to edit or delete, before sending their messages. I also loved the palpabale tension when you see Emily typing -- and then deleting -- parts of a critical message.
On a more shallow note, there are plenty of fun Easter Eggs with the user icons and achievements.
: I expected the game to have some kind of invisible "relationship meter" -- if you dealt with Emily the "correct" way, it would unlock
, but no. It seems like there's no way around the player character's
.
I tried so many different approaches on repeat playthroughs: stereotypical "nice guy", detached/apathetic, stalkerish (concerned about Emily's welfare but judgemental of others), as much of an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ as I could be -- the end results vary only slightly.
It's not enough to break the game -- and I still liked the experience enough to pay for it. Really looking forward to what this dev can accomplish on a larger budget.
: Not directly game-related, but an observation from reading community posts:  it's kinda painful to realize how many people already feel nostalgic about the mid-2000s.
Also, the unrealistic expectations that some players have about Emily's behavior. I personally thought that she acted reasonably in just about *every* scenario I played -- like a normal person in her early 20s who isn't completely sure about what she's looking for.

The Hexcells games involves a much improved and varied Minesweeper style gameplay compared to the standard Minesweeper clones that are nearly everywhere (including the standard Minesweeper installed on most Windows computers).
Hexcells improve on the basic Minesweeper format in quite a number of different ways that change up the Minesweeper gameplay by adding different alternative ways on locating the mines. I won't spoil the fun of working them out for you though.
Speaking about the new and different ways of locating the mines, the main campaign of pre-defined set levels slowly introduce these new mechanics to players while explaining the methods you can use these to solve the puzzles. This starts with the basics so that even a novice easily start to play and goes all the way up to some really challenging tests towards the end with the final puzzle taking hours to complete. Luckily this game auto saves constantly so you can ways come back to where you left off.
Hexcells Infinite is probably the best of out the 3 current Hexcells games due to the new Infinite mode (that wasn't in the previous 2 games) which randomly generates new levels so there's always something to come back to or continue on after the main campaign is completed.
As you can see in the screenshots on this store page it has a nice minimalist look with both light & dark setting so that you're not blinded by that white blackground all the time.
It runs very well on any PC that I've had no matter the specs low or high. Variety of resolution settings which all seem to work great and a nice window mode setting so you can play while doing something else (like watching a movie or TV show, etc).
The only improvement I could think of was if the Infinite mode had some more generation settings so you can generate a puzzle more to your liking rather then it being nearly completely random.

After playing through Dark Souls 3 on all available platforms (Xbox One, PS4, and now PC), I think i can safely recommend this game to anyone that appreciates the Dark Souls franchise. Listed below are the Pros and Cons that i have found so far during my time playing The Surge.
Pros:
- Feels like Dark Souls and Space Marine had a child and this was the result.
- A nice clean and easy to use UI.
- The game looks amazing and captures the Dark Souls Sci-Fi feel.
- Battles require thought beforehand, charge in recklessly and get rekt.
- The game has a decent weapon variety (one hand, two hand, staff, one rig, two rigged).
- Proficiency levels make weapons stronger as you increase it.
- Armor looks amazing and has set bonuses once all six pieces are equiped.
- A lot to explore in each of the levels.
- Nice execution effects on enemies.
Cons:
- Wonky hitboxes make you feel cheated when you die.
- Enemies seem to have hyper armor (all enemies).
- Enemies hit very hard and do a lot of damage (a lot of times i get two shot).
- Leveling up the power core only increases your power capacity.
- Most of the implants seem lack luster and do not do a lot.
On the Fence:
- Grindy (pro or con pending on the type of player you are).
A lot of the Cons can be overlooked as long as you play smart. The "On the Fence" item could be a Pro or a Con depending on the kind of gamer you are. If you like grinding scrap and mats you'll love this game however if you don't then count that as a Con. So far I am enjoying the game, and would rate it a 7.5/10. If the creators can fix the hitboxes and the raw strength of the enemies i would give it a 9/10.

Let me answer your questions.
Is this Sci-fi Dark Souls?
yes, yes it is.
Is the combat as complex as DS?
A little simpler but different enough to make it interesting. The armor, implants, and tactics you use make the biggest difference.
Is it as Dark as DS?
No not really. The lore and story is dark but not enough to make you want to dye your hair black and comb it over one eye, then wonder if anyone would miss you if you killed yourself. The actual scenery is colorful and interesting to look at.
Is it as hard as DS?
It is in that it will quickly punish you for any mistake you make. It does reward you for exploring everywhere, and for being careful yet aggressive. Five hours in, The Surge slices out a very specific cross-section of the Dark Souls games -- high-fidelity melee combat against difficult enemies, looping, labyrinthine level design, and a high-risk currency system. A grungy, industrial sci-fi setting completes the package.

I don't know if it's the setting, or the general atmostphere of this game, but something about it is just really cool and special. (Some of you may know that I enjoy reading crime fiction set in the underworld of Japan so this game has a pretty similar feel to it which makes it stand out to me.) You might find games like this that have better open worlds, but this game does a lot to make almost every experience unique and fun and if you spend enough time watching through the cutscenes and piecing the bits together you'll probably come to like the story as well.
As far as gameplay is concerned the hand-to-hand combat is amazing as is the shooting. Driving about is whacky and wonky especially the race and chase sequences, but it is still enjoyable and hilarious at times especially the takedown slides you can do with cars. There's also a lot to do; police missions, triad missions, races, helping out vendors and triad members, exploration and cool seemingly random events with rewards. There's also lots of little mini-games which actually seem to belong in the game, and are used well, instead of just being thrown in for the sake of 'amusement'.
I like the bright, busy and noisy streets of Hong Kong and there's really plenty to enjoy here if you stick with it.

This is a pretty unique little gem of a free MMORPG with a somewhat deceptive item shop.

Everything in this game is purchaseable with ingame currency, including the premium currency itself. It is expensive, but you can buy it with in game gold.

Summary:
-8 classes to choose from (4 in the beginning)
-a variety of ways to min/max your attributes
-crafting is very important and the only way to get best items (so far)
-item shop is very very optional
-lots of PVE content, but mostly traditional MMORPG grindy stuff
-encourages grind with rewards...lots and lots of rewards
-a million ways to customize your character to your taste stats wise
-okayish graphics and good sounds effects
All in all, this is by far one of the better free MMORPGs I played in a long while and has a very fair item shop that is very non intrusive.
I definitely recommend this to the fans of the genre and especially those old school players that miss some of the older MMORPGs

No it's not Dark Souls and that's a good thing. As someone who played Bloodbourne and the Dark Souls trilogy in it's entirety, i thoroughly believe that Deck13 made a great addition and alternative to the "Souls-like" genre/games.
My personal highlight of this game is it's great combat. All attacks feel very meaty and impactful. You really get the feeling of beeing a badass mofo in a futuristic exo-skeleton crushing your enemies with a huge hammer. Provided you don't overestimate yourself, because this game is as dificult and merciless as the games by FromSoftware. The Scurge puts a greater emphasis on fighting "regular" enemies rather than spectacular bosses. Regardless of your gear or level you still will be absolutely destroyed by your run-of-the-mill enemies, which i personally enjoyed but some people seem to view as a balancing issue. Similar like the Souls-Games you avoid damage by either blocking or dodging atacks. Although the latter option is the more reliable. Since this game has no shields (at least to my knowledge) there are only a handful of atacks that you can block without taking noticable punishment. Unfortunately the game doesn't explain which atacks are actually blockable, so this might lead to some trial and error related frustration in the beginning. But there's a unique twist about the blocking in the Scurge. While blocking you can either duck underneath an atack or hop above an low attack. The timing to pull this off is similarly tight as the parry mechanic in the Souls-game and those "mini dodges" can be followed up by powerful counter atacks. But since this is much harder to pull of correctly than your average parry it is oh-so more satisfying. The dodge mechanic works similarly as in Bloodbourne, where you esentially make a little jump in a direction where you want to go. This works and feels just as great as in Bloodbourne and when timed perfectly you will avoid pretty much all harm.
Purely by comparing the core combat mechanics i actually prefer the Scurge over the Souls-Games (it's heresy, i know...), but the feeling of combat is obviously something very subjective and cannot be potrayed by words accurately.
The only mechanic related to combat/character customization i very dislike is the Attack Proficiency System: Basically a Elder-Scrolls-like mechanic where you do more damage with a weapon type the more you use it. I really don't get why this mechanic is in the game since every other aspect of customization invites you to experiment with your build as you go.
There are no Requirements you need to fullfill stat-wise on any Armor or Weapon. The only "stat" you level up in this game is your core power. Every piece of armor/mod/consumable consumes a certain amount of core power, so you simply design your build around the idea of managing your currently available core power. This system seems very simplistic at first glance, but allows great variety in how you want to play your character. I personaly always like to play the Souls-Games with all types of different builds, and since FromSoftware likes to put odd restrictions regarding respecs, i really enjoyed Deck13's approach.
Even though this game definitely falls behind it's competitors in terms of variety in scenery and enemy design, the game is still very pretty for a sci-fi setting mainly consisting of metal corridors.
I still think that this game is great take on the Dark-Souls-Formula and is a must-buy for every Dark Souls veteran, who is willing to question some design desicions that are so engrained in our beloved Franchise.
Im looking forward for Deck13 future work and hope that they will fix the present issues with the game.

What's the most important part about a game where you're fighting 99% of the time?  The combat : )
As a long time Souls fan, I've had to adjust to different playstyles/speeds/weight within that series, so why shouldn't a game by another dev feel different?
I started with lighter rig/suit, and picked a fairly fast One-Handed weapon (Vibro cutter or something), and the combat is very responsive...  Sometimes it feels like dodging is a bit too OP, since it's fast, and having picked a faster weapon, I can dodge as needed.  Like with other games in this genre, going full R1 spam will get you hit/killed, so timing your attacks is critical (which is what I love about these games).  I tested a slower version, and some dual wield options, and they're too slow, or too little damage, for me to make a switch, but the variation in playstyle is nice.  The second boss weapon is especially neat, and hot : )
The trade-off between attacking vs energy vs energy abilities is great...  The 'use energy to heal' Implant should have come as a starter (though you can get it very early), and feels like must have.
The map layouts are also great...  Each map is very interconnected, and if you can map it in your head, you have clues as to where your next shortcut is.  But as a first time through, not knowing the map, it's scary at times when you're down to 0 heals, and you just want to find that shortcut back so that if you die (and you should always die, instead of running back to heal, to keep your multiplier happy), you don't lose all your souls... er... Scrap.
Which reminds me of the one surprisingly bad thing I dislike about the design.  When you die, you drop your Scrap, and have 2.5m to run back... That timer is stopped in elevators (but not lifts), and increases as you kill stuff on the way...  All that is good, and gives a feeling of urgency (which may make you take risks that turn out bad or great), but when the timer ends, the Scrap is gone (unlike LOTF where the value counts down over time).  If you accidentally enter a boss room, before opening a shortcut, you may have a LONG trip back to miss out on that scrap.
The story is a bit unwieldy at times, but, given the genre, it's still a 15/10 relatively.  It is told, like many shooters, so if you like those, like I do, it's all good : )
The User Interface is also soooo much better than others in the genre...  Takes a bit of adjustment initially, but makes so much sense afterwards...  The ability to 'bank scrap' is also great.
