This is going to be a relatively long review so here's a TL;DR.
This game is great fun if you like space trade sims, and it's only going to get better. And it's free. What more could you ask for?
Pros:
-Fun Time sink
-Takes less processing power to run than Chrome
-Huge amount of customization
-Huge Galaxy to explore
-Huge amount of freedom
-FREE
-Open source
-Obligatory: "Better than No mans Sky"
-Did I mention it's FREE?
Cons:
-Only one story means it can get boring for some.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Now, for those that want a much more long winded review, Carry on at your own risk.
When I was a kid, my grandmother had an old iMac G3 at her house with tons of games and stuff on it. Games like Wolfenstein 3D, Beachhead 2000, Kid Pix, Bugdom...and the one I spent over 100 hours on, EV Override. I loved that game I would sit there for the entire day at that obsolete piece of tech and tap away at the keyboard, destroying Vonian Frigates, Hunting renegade Helians, Alliying with the various alien races to the north, and getting my money stolen by that dastadly "Cap'n Hector" (I only had the shareware version...a 30 day free trial that expired many years prior to when I started playing it)
I loved that game, It just plops you down in a crappy little shuttle, and says: "Alright, You wanna be an Explorer? Trader? Courier? Pirate? UE Pilot? UE Blockade runner? Ambassador? Vonian ally? Conqueror of the galaxy? Because you can do that...Or you could do none of it.
Some storylines would give you access to new ships, new items, new missions, change your relationships to the other governments, All this stuff blew mind as a little 10 year old. And that's not even going into the vast amounts of ships and upgrade tech you could buy
After my grandmother passed and that computer thrown out, I had I huge craving to find a game like EV override again. I checked the Ambrosia official website to it, and to my dismay, they are still charging the same amount they were back in 1998. Okay, so it's only 15$, but I'm not too pleased that they still have the balls to not drop the price, and there's no guarantee that it would work on windows 10. I did some more digging and after much deliberation, I came across this. Endless Sky.
A "Spiritual Successor" to the venerable EV series. It claims to have the core that made the EV series fun, and I can say, it does. I installed the game, accepted my loan, and was plopped down in a crappy shuttle and told to earn my living. And thus my adventure began.
If there's a good way I can describe Endless sky while being able to validate my lengthy intro in this review, It's that this game is basically diet EV Override/Nova. Not that that's a bad thing. I'll get into that later. Basically, take what I wrote up about Override, and take the following things out.
-Multiple storylines/jobs
-All the alien races (Endless sky only has the "Hai" if I gather correctly)
-A main antagonist faction (That being the vonians in EV)
-The ability to pluder credits and fuel from disabled ships...Not sure why that's left out...
-A pilot Permadeath "Hard mode"
Now, in place of those things (Currently) add these:
-More intuitive controls, such as: Auto Aim, Auto Jump, auto...route planning(?)
-More intuitive UI
-More intuitive Fleet controls
-Refined graphics
-Still alive and being updated
-Asteroid mining is said to come soon
-Temperature and energy bars. Different ways to evalute your combat strats
-The amount of crew you have plays more of a role here. No longer just a percentage booster for capture, but for how many of your crew will survive the encounter. And you really don't wanna let the die.
-FREE
So, this game doesn't have the meat to it that EV has, but in return it's mechacnially better. Now, if by chance, the devs decide add the features that I listed as missing, then I will be one happy camper, but until then, I'm content as is. I would like more storylines though...joining the Navy instead of the Rebels would be a nice start. Then the ablity to pluder fuel and credits
About the game as is, Here are some things I would like to see tweaked:
-Make it so bounty hunter missions don't spawn the all the target ships spawn in the same system. I make my living as a Pirate hunter, so I accept a ton of bounty missions at once, later go into another system, and am immediately bum rushed by all of the pirates from the missions I accepted. (Apparently "Near system X" actually means "In system Y") Maybe make it so the pirates will jump around actually near System X instead of just sitting in System Y until I find them. Make them feel more alive.
-Maybe something's wrong with the "Casualty rate if you attack" because more than a couple times, I've had a 0.1-0.2 predicted crew loss and then proceeded to lose 2 crew members for whatever reason. Unless I'm not reading something correctly
...
That's pretty much it from me in terms of what I can say to tweak. I'll jump in more and see what else I can find.

There is something inherently strange about this game. It plays nothing like it looks. It's the average person at the bar that you just can't get a good look at but every once in a while they turn around and your heart skips a beat. What is it about this person that is so enthralling? You have to go up and talk to them regardless of what your friends think. Turns out you have the most amazing conversation ever and watch the sun come up in the parking lot, not once making a single move on them. You go home happy, revitalized and content, patiently waiting for them to text you.
On the surface it appears to be a management simulator, chock full of interesting things to do, with equally as many ways to do them. Beneath the surface lies something that I didn't expect, something that didn't quite sink its teeth into me until around 20 hours in; there is always a better way to do things and you will dream about them regardless of how often you play. Belt systems can be merged, split and re-routed in a million different ways, smelting grids can be reformatted to minimize their footprint but maximize their output. Electricity becomes an art as you weave power lines aesthetically around your base being extra careful not to create a criss-cross which, while functional, looks terrible and we can't have terrible looking things in our base...
You start to grow content with your output, making mental notes of how you would like to move things around to make room for future upgrades. You sit back and enjoy your creation and how well everything is running. Suddenly, a red exclamation point shows up next to your toolbelt...hmmm, what's that? Your map shows it as well. You mouse over it, thinking that maybe you ran out of power or something simple, then it happens...
The biters are ripping through your iron mining in the northwest corner of your base! They are shredding metal like hot butter. The miners are taken out and the biters turn their sights on you. With almost supernatural speed they race toward you, fangs wet with a taste for blood. You have only a pistol to protect you. 10 measily bullets because you didn't spend the research points to get weaponized. The screen goes red and your stats are shown.
You vow to do things better. You will be ready the next time they attempt to breach your walls. Your factory will be stronger. You will be faster. They will be deader. This means war.
This game....is amazing.

The Surge is a science fiction themed Souls-like.
-Combat that feels good -- weapons have weight (but not too much weight) and executions are brutal. If you enjoyed Souls combat but felt that there wasn't enough weight behind each hit, and liked Bloodborne dodging, this offers a similar experience.
-Interesting body part targeting system/weapon system. Focus on hitting enemy body parts and cut them off when you have enough energy to get armor and weapons.
-Industrial complex theme (also listed under cons) -- each area has a believable setting and flows from one area to the next. Weapons and armor fit the theme very well.
-Few bosses (also listed under cons) -- The Surge is less about boss fights and more about 'trash' mobs -- every mob that you would consider 'trash' in a Souls game is dangerous and should never be underestimated. However, each boss brings its own gimmick that most of the time can be ignored past the first phase of the fight. One reviewer mentioned that the Firebug required you to chop off all its limbs -- however, once you chop off 3, phase 2 begins, and the boss can be taken down without further loss of limbs by targeting the main body.
-Implant system allows you to change your build to suit each area or your own playstyle. Collecting implants found throughout each level is highly recommended.
-Typical Dark Souls-esque storytelling. There is a main story that you can follow, but will barely make sense unless you go looking for audio logs and pay attention to the environment.
-Graphics are crisp and the lighting is excellent, with a brightness slider for those that find it too dark.
-Energy meter used for various actions, such as operating companion drone, using implants, and executions on enemies, always feels relevant and rewards aggressive tactics.
-Few bosses (5). Most people consider bosses to be the highlight of a Souls-like. Unfortunately, there aren't that many bosses in the game.
-Industrial complex theme -- due to the setting, many rooms can feel similar -- it's up to you to remember where to turn and how to get to different areas.
-Not much music.
-Heavy armor may have too many penalties -- in a game that relies on dodging and rapid stamina regen, slowing down stamina regen is a harsh penalty. Medium or Light armor are far more managable.
-One or two late game enemies have annoying hitboxes on their attacks. If you've played FromSoft titles and have fought dragons/wyverns, you'll get a general idea of what I'm talking about.
-Scrap (souls) timer -- upon death, you drop your scrap and there will be a timer counting down the seconds until your scrap vanishes. This timer can be extended by 20-30 seconds per enemy killed. I didn't notice a huge difference in how I played the game in regards to the scrap timer. Sometimes I killed every enemy on the way to my dropped scrap and I ended up with 3+ minutes on the timer. Other times, I ran past everything and got to my scrap with a minute left.
-Voice acting -- Not terrible, not great. Mostly average. Some people will enjoy it, others won't.
-No guns -- While no guns makes sense for the setting, it does seem strange that only drones and very select enemies get ranged attacks. Your only ranged attack comes in the form of a personal drone.
Worth a buy if you liked the Souls games, but this is very much a different beast. Go in with an open mind and you'll probably enjoy it. In terms of buy/sale -- 35-40 dollars seems like a good price. Anything lower is a steal!

For someone who doesn't want to read the whole review, here's a short version. The game is fun whilst being hard, but it's easy reloading makes it the fun hard rather than hard hard. There's so much customisation for your ship and fleet that you'll never want to stop trying to upgrade and there's the option to conquer the entire human race.
Recommend this game? Yes, because there's few games where it can be fun farming aliens, stealing their FTL Drives, Computers, Power Reactors, Cooling systems, and pretty much anything they have that you want. Or other things such as taking over the entire human race, meeting friendly aliens and then giving the warmongering members of their race Jump drives and profiting of off their raids, or building a fleet capable of destroying anything.
The game is astoundingly fun, but hard at the same times, see below for more on this. The controls are hard to master, I recommend you turn on auto-aiming before you even start the game, given than your going to be dog fighting other fighters at the start, and your hard-point lasers don't track targets. Once you get past the difficulty of the start and have your starting debt paid off, the game starts to get going, with player able to amass a massive fleet, if they can afford it. I personally took great fun in a smaller fleet equipped with the best equipment I could find. Buy a ship from one part of the galaxy and equip it with the best weapons there, then head ealsewhere to upgrade the reactor and engines, then elsewhere to upgrade it's shields.
Eventually you'll end up in an "upgrade triangle" as you end up earning enough cash on one lap to buy a new ship and have to do the whole thing again.
When you finally break out of the loop by starting the main story line, you end up fighting for the rebellion and attacking the Republic. This immediately breaks your upgrade loop as everyone now hates you, apart from the shield guys, but to get to them you have to go all the way through the heart of the Republic and carries the feeling of complete suicide. So you have to hope that you can keep your best ships alive, while only losing the cannon fodder ones. Realistic? Yes. Fun to play as you watch the last of your Osprey medium warships blows up? Noooooo. That's one of the three issues with the story, heres the other two:
The missions themselves are more varied than just fetch, deliver, or escort quests. Theres still a lot of those, but at least the main quest line is somewhat different. Though the scouting missions are absolute torture. They should be renamed "Destroy every ship at this star system by yourself, as there's no way any ship can sneak through the enemy forces there and we're to lazy to even try and help you."
The other issue is the narrative combat missions at the start of the mainline story line. At this point the game wants to paint the image of the player in a small ship still, say a fighter or a light warship. Me? I showed up in the Bactrian, the best human ship in the game and a small fleet, after previous play throughs had taught me that showing up to the rebellion in a light warship was a one-way ticket to suicide-ville. As it stands, the player has to have about 50mil credits invested in ships otherwise they get steam-rolled by republic ships. And then it's a coin toss as to whether you survive the mission as chances are the enemy will focus fire on you, your shields go down in two seconds and a minute later your now a gaseous vapor in orbit of the star. So I would say that needs rebalancing.
After the main story line ends, the player is turfed back out onto the galaxy, and can now go about building a giant fleet to subjugate all of humanity. I know there's some story beyond this, but then it becomes a hunt for clues as to where the next fragment begins.
All in all a very enjoyable game, that can be played on a laptop or Macbook without a proper mouse.

Ok- Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition. I'm not sure what makes it 'definitive' aside from coming with (DLC?) Year of the Snake, and the other one. You know, the one with the jianshi. I bought the game while it was on sale, and boy do I not regret it. I love crime-sort of games like Saints Row and Yakuza, and even though I've only got 5 hours under my belt, here's my run down:
Graphics:
-I'm running them on medium- and they're not too terrible. Not the best, but not terrible. What threw me off were the character models- they were uncanny to say the least. I keep Wei under the facemask and forget for the most part.
-Night/Day and rain effects. I gotta say, I'm a sucker for them. Gives different impression of the city. The rain actually felt like rain to me (though I am comparing it to the rain from Mafia III)
-You can dress your home boy
Gameplay:
- The A (or X in my case) sprint feels pretty natural considering speed, but really offputting in terms of animation. Dude runs like he has a ferret in his pants.
- Combat felt nice and satisfying when hits connected, and for those who like beyond button mashing, there are an array of combos that'll make you feel like a martial arts wizard. I for one enjoyed the parrying and the ability to interact with the environment with your take downs. Beat a man into a garbage bin? Check, yeah.
- Side missions are pretty rinse and repeat, as are main missions after a while. Go here, beat up some thugs, get some story, drive. If you've played Saints Row 2- imagine that level of needing to drive. And there are no fast travel options unless you choose to go by taxi.
- Speaking of driving, the controls feel smooth until you mess with the camera. ♥♥♥♥ that noise- you want to back up? Well enjoy some front-back flipping as you do so to make the job that more annoying.
- Solid ambient dialogue even if the voices, when not speaking cantonese(?), felt like they were really pushing the accent.
- The streets can get kind of repetative, but it is what it is. Would have loved to see more buildings you could enter and interact with like in GTA5.
- Skill trees, my guy.
-Morality- in a way. More like: be a thug (triad skill tree), or be a thug with courtesy (cop skill tree).
- Pretty good humor to break the mood away from constant "Grr, Mr. Mean Triad Undercover Guy Going Through♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;
Rundown:
- If you're looking for stunning graphics, this may not be the place if you plan on oogling the characters
- Enjoyable gameplay despite janky camera issues once and a while when you drive (back up- I guess just never miss a turn?)
- Repetative missions, but with an overall decent story flow
- Nice characters, nice dialogue
- I repeat- you get to cloth ya' boy.
A good investment when on sale- when not... maybe wait for it or something unless you really need to fuel your SR/GTA game-style addiction.

Ever wonder what it would be like in a video game if your gun could talk to you? How about your helmet and backpack? Well, Rogue Trooper's premise is basically that. You play as a cloned super soldier whose toughness cannot be contained by the confines of clothing or armor, and get orbital drop-pod'd into a warzone on an alien planet that has pretty much gone to hell with your squad and a whole bunch of other Dr. Manhattan lookalikes. Naturally, things go awry, one thing leads to another, your three squadmates become a part of your equipment, essentially possessing your gun, helmet, and backpack, providing abilities such as setting up as a turret, deploying a hologram, crafting new upgrades, and most importantly, banter. The gameplay holds up despite the age, controlling much like any other third person shooter with added cover mechanics to boot. Your playstyle is restricted only to your imagination, for the most part: whether you want to move from cover to cover shooting dudes in the head, sneak around and stealth kill enemies from behind, set up your gun to act as an automated turret while you flank, distract foes with a hologram as you snipe from afar, among other possibilities, is entirely up to you.
As with almost every other game in existence, Rogue Trooper does have its flaws, however. Controls can be finnicky at times and can take some getting use to (most jarring being how blind-fire is a contextual action instead of simply firing without aiming when in cover), the campaign is rather short and feels like it ended far too quickly, your possessed equipment's chatter can get repetitive and sometimes annoying, and the multiplayer mode is, to my knowledge, entirely dead unfortunately (although you can still play either of the two multiplayer modes alone). The biggest issue I had however was one particular mission stuttered the framerate so low that a dolphin could count the frames per second with one flipper. Granted, I play on a toaster of a laptop, but up until that point, the framerate for the game was decent enough to play. It made the game impossible to play, to the point that I had to go about finding a way to skip the mission entirely. That may not be the case for all users, but it was what affected my experience the most personally.
All in all, Rogue Trooper is a damn fun game and has aged well. If you like third person shooters, a neat story with interesting background lore (you can even unlock encyclopediac entries on almost everything you encounter in the game), the unique nature of your equipment talking to you, the thought of having blue skin, or the comic series of the same name, Rogue Trooper may interest you.

You too Double Fine?
An Early Access game falls short again but this time it is a pretty well known developer that decides to under deliver.  DF stated that it simply wasn't making enough money to warrant continued development and from a gamer's perspective, there's not much of a game to warrant purchasing, especially at the $25 price range. What we have here is a stalemate in which both parties lose. Gamer's lose money and the developer loses face.
As it stands, Spacebase DF-9 does let you create a base and manage some resources, it does have some random events to throw at a player so that the game isn't completely boring however, there are no end game type things to work towards, no objectives to ultimately strive towards.  In five hours, a player can pretty much run into everything the game offers and after that, the game will just keep repeating itself.
The lack of gameplay issue is compounded by the fact that the beta phase of game testing is being skipped over entirely.  DF is going to tack on a tutorial, wrap up some issues and then release the code in hopes that modders will run with their..un-game and make it better.
What was supposed to be a game that was to be in continuous development over the next five years with gameplay tweaks and additions is now kicked out the door in its current shape. I guess in space, no one can hear you break promises.

"Rogue Trooper" is a third-person cover-based shooter with fun gameplay mechanics, a decently long campaign, and atrocious AI.
Based on the same-titled graphic novel and with the game garnering a sort of cult-like status with plenty of player statements testifying to its uniqueness, in reality I was expecting more.
Not worth repeating. Generic army conspiracy story of the most basic kind, told via poor cinematics (both in terms of actual graphics and directing). DO NOT believe the ones saying about how good the plot is, because it's not.
Good, but dated. The game is from 2006, after all. For the setting, which is basically a wasteland planet, you get a decent amount of variety in level designs.
Meh. Nothing special, really. A few good score tracks.
The most important part of the game, its saving grace in a sense. Your character is really three soldiers in one, given that he installs biochips with his dead comrades' personalities into his equipment. This gives you a variety of options when engaging the enemy. Since the levels are completely linear, this gives you the possibility to truly choose your approach in an organic way: stealth, guns-blazing, or a combination of the two. Neither gameplay style is forced on you at any time. This is good, but...
... on the other hand it's also not that good. Neither approach features any reward at all. Even in the stealth-based missions, it's completely the same if you just pull out your big guns and start unloading. going Rambo is almost always the easiest way to get through a level (since the game on HARD is really not that hard at all), and by the later levels I ditched the sneaking altogether because...
... the AI is so damn stupid, you just want to blow them all to hell for being such dumbasses. You take out a soldier, and his companion standing a few feet next to him won't notice anything. You take out the whole area, blow things up. No one else comes to you, and you're thinking: "OK, with all the shooting, everyone who was here would've come out. The area is cleared." And then you round a corner and find a solider casually facing away from you, oblivious because, well, he was around the corner and didn't register a thing.
Also, the game has no boss fights, really. And all the killings of the main bad guys is done via cutscenes. This takes a certain sense of accomplishment away from you, the player.
Finally, the campaign mode on HARD will last you about 8-10hrs. The last difficulty called MASSACRE is locked initially. The game has no collectibles or achievements of any kind, so there's no true replayability.
A game whose only saving grace is the novelty in the gameplay where you can choose on how you approach the level. Everything else is average, or below average. Recommended only under these conditions:

The boss fights in the surge are different to the boss fights in dark souls as they are both difficult but for varied reasons. In dark souls, the boss fights are based on skill, reaction time and learning the move sets of the bosses. In the surge the boss fights are all based on gimmicks which is frustrating as a boss should be beatable just from damage alone. Take Firebug for example, to defeat the boss all its legs must be broken off by damaging them individually. After a leg is damaged enough the boss will stagger and you are meant to attack the joint on the leg to break it off, if you attempt to attack any other point on the boss then you won’t deal any damage. Also, the legs on the boss are treated as separate entities by the targeting system so switching between legs is random which is annoying.
The combat in the surge is ok but could be improved, it feels like it is designed for 1v1 however there is many times where you must take on multiple enemies at once. The blocking/ducking mechanism is too slow to be effective in combat as many of the enemies are faster than you. The AI for the enemies is based on your input which is ridiculous as it constantly puts you at a disadvantage against everything which makes you not want to play the game.
You are going to be farming a lot as no matter what armour or weapon you have, in the next area the enemies will be stronger. It isn’t like dark souls in the sense that you can find a set of armour early on and stick with it, you are constantly going to be changing and upgrading your build.
Throughout the game there will be many areas that you can’t proceed through as you aren’t at a high enough level. This seems to be a very cheap way to increase the length of a playthrough when it doesn’t serve any other purpose. There are many enemies that are placed in extremely annoying places just to make you die more.
After finishing this game there wasn’t a sense of accomplishment, just disappointment.

Took me about 125 hours(Casual) to beat a Realm Reborn(7th Umbral Era), not including 7th Astral Era and expansions.
---------------
Pros:
-The world is beautiful and well detailed.
-Guilds, buy a house, have a wedding, ride a chocobo etc...
-Awesome community for new players
-The quests and the main story were fantastically written and gave the player a reason why he/she needs to fight in this dungeon or raid unlike WoW which makes you question "Why am I doing this?".
-There are plenty of classes to choose from such as a few: WhiteMage, BlackMage, Scholar, Warrior etc...
-Each class has its own unique traits to help the party
-Unlike most MMORPG, you can have 1 character be any class in the game! With no extra fees! It takes only a few seconds to change into another class if you don't like the original one you picked!
-The developers listen to the community and are constantly updating the game to make it better.
Cons:
-Waiting for a dungeon could take up to 30 minutes depending what level you are, especially if you just started playing. Because most people are like two expansions ahead.
-Some quests can be annoying because it makes you run all over the map for a brief conversation.
-Sometimes a quest has actual voice actors, but majority of the time it is just reading....and reading....and more reading. You will get use to it though.
-New Players & Expansions
-New players who want to play with their friends in the new expansion (StormBlood) have to complete the whole story of a Realm Reborn(7th Umbral Era and 7th Astral Era). Which is fine. However, you also have to beat their other Expansion Heavensward as well. To avoid this, you could pay $25 to skip the campaign, not including the additional $40 Expansion, and $15 a month (BTW you need to rank your character up to level 60 to play StormBlood)
----------------------
All and all, get the game if you love MMORPG. I promise you won't regret it, especially if you have a friend.

Possessing the most deep and complex story ive run into on an mmo, the main scenario for Final Fantasy is a joy to witness and has even brought a tear once or twice. Though I play this game as a Final Fantasy title first and formost, the game manages to be more then that. In a world where mmorpgs come out every year and usually fail to be notable for not iterating on the idea of the genre, this one manages to do well without trying to deviate from the standards for mmos that have been put in place since Everquest and made standard by Warcraft. It doesnt innovate so much as refines the gameplay the genre is known for while telling a top notch story the series has been known for in the past. Though the game possesses a great deal of "grind" its hard to count it as a strike against it when the grind I found was mostly spent completing the story quests beyond the level cap. While I hate that they hit my scholar with the nerfbat like a hyperactive child who found the candy jar with Stormblood, I still find this game a pure joy to play with its great story, excellent controller and traditional countrol scheme. At the very least try this game and hear the kind of tales Final Fantasy used to be known for once again!

I can understant the idea of creating a new visual novel trying to undertake the emotions and atmosphere of an early 2000's relationship, especially a seemingly long distance one. However, in practice here, it is not fulfilling the task. The first playthrough of the game feels good, it feels like the game has fulfilled the task.
If you never wish to play past this point, you can possibly feel accomplished in something, but you never will. After all, what about the other endings?
There essentially aren't any. This is an example of a visual novel gone wrong.
In a way similar to the Walking Dead Season 1 game, the ending won't change based on your choices. Maybe the words spoken will, but the overall outcome is completely set in stone. The difference between that game and this game (besides the clearly obvious) is that TWD had plans to use your choices in another game, and there they were fulfilled.
This game does not fulfill your choices. You will ALWAYS be denied by Emily, whether or not you were a♥♥♥♥♥♥or not.
Try and get into a relationship and hang out AT ALL when she brings up the idea? She thinks you're a creep and just want to bang. Tell her you don't want her over, and she says you were never there for her.
Nothing you do in this is the right choice. There is no good ending, and I suppose that's what the creator intended the game to be; this emotional roller coaster that ends in the ♥♥♥♥ing toilet. But it's not good. Don't get me wrong, this is the type of game I've been waiting to see for a while, but the way it was executed here is not in a good way. It however a free game, and while I don't recommend you play it, the first experience is a fairly decent one. So go ahead, download it, play it, and get a depressing glimpse at what could have been a good game.

Your job is to run a checkpoint on the border of two countries, approving or denying the entry of people to the country. While this may seem pretty cut and dried, a lot of times you will find decisions that play on your moral compass. The consequences of your decisions are usually viewed in the paper the next day. There are 20 different endings in all based on the decisions you make in-game, and along the way you will meet very memorable characters. The game has an amazing feel to it and certainly was worth every hour I put into it, and I plan on playing it much more to unlock all the endings. If you find that you really enjoy the technical aspect of checking papers and stamping passports like me, when you're all done with the story you can play endless mode too.

I do not normally write reviews, but I purchased this game having sunk hundreds of hours each into every souls game from demon souls through the ringed city. I also very much enjoyed Lords of the Fallen, by this same developer, despite the criticisms. I love challenging video games.
This looks like a good game, but it is not a good game. People are saying it is good because they're not realizing how bad the game gets as you play on. This is not a game where you can face tank. This is not a game where you need to git gud. This is a game that you have to cheese your way through. You'll feel disappointed after you play it for a while, because you'll eventually realize that you cannot play with skill.
1. This doesn't feel like an RPG. You can level from 1 to 100 and you literally get no stronger. The leveling system doesn't exist. It exists, but it doesn't do anything. Is that an RPG to you?
2. The weapon system is pathetic. It isn't "get strong, use strength weapons" or "get dexterity and use dex weapons." No, you have to grind with the weapon to make it viable. If you find a new weapon but you're not proficient in it, you have to grind that weapon for hours to make it viable.
3. The trash mobs (the game is basically nothing but trash mobs) hit like a truck and they do so in a gimmicky fashion that leaves you dieing not because you made a mistake but because the trash mob enemies have insta-turn and insta-kill. The only game "playstyle" that works is to find a big weapon that does impact damage, hit once and then run/dodge away and repeat. That's the combat in this game. You can't play with skill. You have to cheese. It might look like as you play on it will get better. No, it won't.
4. Because the junk mobs are so hard, the game consists of running past the enemies. Running scared from enemies (I'm not talking about sneaking) is not a fun game mechanic. Since leveling up does not increase anything and you don't have the resources to fight every enemy since they have insta-kill and rapid tracking abilities, you will end up running through areas just to try to find items and open doors.
5. The combat system is terrible, but it is made worse by the level design and game assets. The environments are the same. Not only is it boring, but it is hard to play when all you see are environments that look the same. Where are you? You're in the same area with the same assets as the previous area that looked the same but wasn't where you need to be. Not fun.
In short, I played it for slightly over 2 hours. I had buyer's remorse. I asked for a refund. This is the first game I've ever asked for a refund of and steam was kind enough to approve. Keep an eye on your play time so that when you realize that this is a nicely wrapped chocolate covered stinker that you can at least not end up with buyer's remorse. I played, didn't like it and got my money back. In other words, I'm happy. The only reason I wrote this review is because I don't want you to get taken on a game that looks like it could be good but isn't.

This is what you are getting and you should have heard it by now; this game is very very similar to Dark Souls. I didn't really know that going in, but I enjoy Dark Souls to a degree, so I have been enjoying this one.
The combat feels fresh. You have to build a whole rig suited to weapons and play style and each piece can make a huge difference. However, this game woops you so hard. Even Dark Souls 1 didn't woop me this hard. Not really a good thing imo, but I really can't bust it for that either. Just know, the game is very very difficult. It punishes you every chance you give it.
There is a story, for those of you who parrot paid, bs, reviewers like IGN (Ignorant, Greedy, Ninnies). Is it the best story, no. Has it got me wondering what happened and driving me forward? Yes. Does it have intrigue? Yes. The only issue here is this; the game is so difficult and so punishing and it takes so long to progress, that what would be a pretty good story can get lost if you aren't paying attention. Especially to the videos, audio logs, and conversations in the world.
Is this better than Dark Souls? No probably not, but that just depends if you like sci-fi or fantasy better. It's different enough to make it good enough for a buy, but ultimately it boils down to a very similar experience to the brutal Dark Souls games.

I've just played through Rogue Trooper for the first time and it is nothing if not a bit of a strange one. Look at that release date: 23rd of May 2006. I almost can't get my head round it. This is a game released two years after Half-Life 2 and yet so much of it feels so much older. Primarily because it looks so much older but also because the levels are so clearly demarcated by stats summaries and cut-scenes. That aspect of it feels pre-Half-Life, never mind pre-Half-Life 2. A clue to why it has these throwbacks is because although this was released six months after the Xbox 360 hit the shelves it was only ever released for PC, PS2 and Xbox (and much later Wii) and was clearly fighting against the limits of those two ageing consoles. And yet in spite of this the game has aged very well.
Crucially everything that was good about the game in 2006 is still good now. It is still pleasingly varied in terms of the gameplay. The guns still stand up and feel like they pack a punch. There is also a very pleasing amount of freedom regarding how levels are approached. It is all very linear but there is almost always a choice as to whether to go semi-stealthy, cover-based or all guns blazing. It also doesn't overstay its welcome. At the time as a full priced game I think it would have felt rather too short but today it feels about right. I don't think I'd want to spend that much more time staring at that few polygons and for the price I paid I'm more than happy with this little slice of history.
One final word of warning through. The game is keen on its non-interactive cutscenes which often feel like they steal the most dramatic moments from the player. Every significant villain is defeated in a cutscene rather than at the players hands and that just isn't very satisfying. Still a good game and one with some unique features that will likely be of interest to fans of the shooter genre.

But if you don't let her visit you, she's bitter and claims that you didn't have to pick between her and Emma (despite the fact that she wonders why you didn't make moves on her in high school in that same conversation obviously blurring the lines between your friendship) Emily starts dating Brad (or Travis) without telling you and when she's broken up, she expects you to put your relationships on hold for her sake. The biggest irony is if you tell her that you don't want to talk in Chapter 4, she'll tell you that you should think about someone other than yourself but I don't think there's a single instance where Emily ever considered your feelings or didn't try to bend you to do what she wanted.
The more I did playthroughs, the more I hated Emily and the more I realized that she's a very realistic character. We've all had relationships with someone, the "could we" or "can't we" emotionally volatile relationships and I think this game accurately portrayed years of emotions into such a short playthrough. I think worst of all is your relationship with Emma. Emily creates just so much baggage and using so many tactics to guilt you and make you feel awful for living your life, you're unable to move on and pursue Emma, who eventually (justifably) gets tired of waiting for you. I know I personally have been in that situation, longing for someone but being stuck to the emotions and will of someone else, having feelings stagnated. It stressed me out that when the protag doesn't get with Emma, I understood why...
Anyway, it was definitely worth the playthroughs. The game made me think, it's quirky at times and I love the unlockable icons. WIll certianly make you feel and honestly question why do we romantically pursue the people we do sometimes.
TLDR// 10/10 would abandon Emily again
The bottom line is Emily could be bi-polar.
Much like talking to that high school crush on AIM back in the day. No matter what you say or do she'll always choose that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, Brad.
I did enjoy this game, but it did make me somewhat depressed because it reminded me of similar situations that I have experienced in life, so tread lightly.

Possessing the most deep and complex story ive run into on an mmo, the main scenario for Final Fantasy is a joy to witness and has even brought a tear once or twice. Though I play this game as a Final Fantasy title first and formost, the game manages to be more then that. It doesnt innovate so much as refines the gameplay the genre is known for while telling a top notch story the series has been known for in the past. Though the game possesses a great deal of "grind" its hard to count it as a strike against it when the grind I found was mostly spent completing the story quests beyond the level cap. While I hate that they hit my scholar with the nerfbat like a hyperactive child who found the candy jar with Stormblood, I still find this game a pure joy to play with its great story, excellent controller and traditional countrol scheme. At the very least try this game and hear the kind of tales Final Fantasy used to be known for once again!

It was fun at first, and sending waves of copy-pasted soldiers into the meat grinder in the editor is hours of entertainment, but I can't recommend this game just to save others from dissapointment.
I'll start with the elephant in the room, the devs are almost cartoonishly greedy it seems. They've cut the legs off the game to sell to us as DLC. It's analagous to selling someone a car, and then selling them a season pass that includes the rear-view mirror, the trunk door, and the two rear wheels.
Otherwise, the game fails to in any way captre the brutality of the first world war. This is do in part to the failing of the Gem engine to be able to accurately portray this, but nonetheless I expect more to that end from a project of this scale. Trench Warfare was frequently brutal hand to hand combat, but all this seems to depict is lazy potshots at one another from across no mans land. Artillery is frequently so weak it's virtually useless, failing to do any significant damage before the enemy has a chance to bandage themselves. The addition of horses was interesting at a glance, but the soldiers can't do anything from horseback, so attempting to make cavalry charges just results in a lot of dead horses. Hardly spectacular. Gas is rarely used in the campaign, and it's always a cutscene, watching a trenchful of your men just die without any kind of reaction. Nobody puts on the gasmasks that are clearly in their inventory, no body attemtps to run or seek shelther from it. It's like gassing mannequins.
All in all, a very poor depiction of World War One. Look elsewhere.

You know, after 7 of my friends and I bought this game and all "played together" every waking moment for 7 days (to die) straight, I have to say...
This is probably the loneliest MMORPG out there.
I haven't played ALL of the big name MMORPGs, but this game just feels... so damn lonely. We were all in a Discord chat together talking, hanging out, and discussing the game, but only for about an hour -- at most -- did we ever actually do anything together, and that was all of us just messing around with the duelling option. Other than that, the experience is completely solo. All the real people in-game just feel like extensions of AI that cluttered up my screen and took up CPU usage. I mean, you literally do nothing with anyone else. Nothing. Endgame is a different story, but through the levelling and exploration and crafting process, there is zero player interaction, unless you want to waste in-game energy points messaging in chat, that is.
I convinced all my friends to buy this game in hopes of all of us playing and interacting and questing and raiding together, but this game disappointed me in that regards to a point where I would not reccomend this game to anyone looking to play with their friends or to socially interact in any meaningful way for at least 50-60 hours (if you don't just treadmill grind your way to level 55 as fast as possible and try to join a guild, anyway). Even then, the interaction extends to your guild, at best.
To me, the whole point of an MMORPG was to interact, socialize, and roleplay with your friends and the community, but this game taught me, more than in any other MMO, that nowadays this isn't a must-have in today's MMOs.

There is a no way I could recommend this game. And to be honest, I have absolutely no idea why Final Fantasy XIV Online is still so popular and loved. This is one of the most boring MMO's I've ever played.
In the 30 hours of playing this game I hade no fun with it. And I mean zero fun. Sure, the graphics, character creation and general looks of the game are very fine and pleasing, but the gameplay, oh my god. Speaking as a MMO veteran, this combat system is one of the most braindead executions I've ever experienced in a game like this. It's not a joke when I say, I almost fell asleep while tanking a dungeon. There seems to be absolutely no challenge or difficulty in the early game. But what is worst is the Global Cooldown Timer for abilities, which is whooping two seconds. All you do in combat is pressing 1... Then 2. Then 3, maybe. Then 1 again. Every two seconds. While sidestepping once in a while, that your health doesn't fall under 90% from an enemy telegraphed skill. Snoooooore. Wanna know what the biggest challenge of this game was? Setting up your account on the Square website. Oh, you know what I'm talking about.
The quests you receive are a joke. I had exactly three types of quests in this time of playing. #1 Run from point A to B, than back to A, or maybe do some emotes to a NPC in between. #2 Run to A and kill X amount of enemy. #3 Guide this NPC to point A. But you have to make an emote every 30 feet, to get this guy moving. Are you ducking kidding me?! They seem to be the standard type of quests, but due to this combat system everything feels so unbelievably slow and boring. Besides that, the start of the game is you running around your first town for around 2 hours, doing fetch quests without any combat. All text tutorial. Great. Padding. That's the keyword here.
People tend to praise the story in this game. I have no idea what they're talking about. Cutscenes are just as unentertaining as the combat. Animations look wonky, there is no interesting story to be found here in the early game, and the voice acting, oh my god! I can't believe that these people received a paycheck for this performance. They sound worse than voiceactors for commercials, I'm not kidding. But when you don't hear these horrible actors, you hear nothing at all. Normally you have sighs, grunts or murrs from characters, to show the player what this NPC sounds like. Not here, most cutscenes are completely mute, you're just clicking through textboxes.
A lot of fans of this game will probably argue now - "Well, sure it's not as good in the beginning, duh! You have to play to the higher levels and endzones to have better combat, story and more challenges!" I've read this pretty much everywhere. The early game sucks, endgame is better. My question is, why in the world should I press myself through 60 hours of mind numbing grinding and gameplay I'm not enjoying in the slightest, to get to the good part? When you're eating a cake, you don't want to munch through a yucky burned crust on the outsides to get to the slightly better inside. There are so many other free MMO's who do this job way, way better. And even if this is the case that the game gets better, most people were saying that the game becomes cool with Heavensward, the first big addon. So I have to pay more money to get some fun out of it. Plus the monthly fee of course. Ya, no way I subscribe to this.
No. Way. Dude.

Factorio takes the cake and eats it single-handedly in front of you. Then orders you cook up a fresh batch since he’s always hungry for more. Playing this game, you’ll be able to summarize it almost like a love-hate relationship. Stressful at times, but too good to pass up or abandon. Wube Software managed nearly the impossible on Steam. (Re)Invent a subgenre I thought was long since been declared dead and buried. The kind of strategy game that features just the right amount of base management and resource gathering, without being tagged as “real time strategy”. Not by its classical definition, at least. You don’t control an army per se, even if you shall be forced to fight for your life and in defense of the machines you shall construct. Think Industrial Giant 2 except you’re not running a business, instead focusing on escaping a strange planet.
Who said a game about in-depth industrial processes can’t be fun? Our story begins with the lone survivor of a crash landed spacecraft. The silent type of astronaut/engineer/MacGyver that shares some of these traits with every gamer’s favorite space engineer, Isaac Clarke. But I’ll just call him “Bob”. So what does out good pal, Bob, do once he finds himself within an inhospitable, foreign and far away place? Does he phone Home, fail and then crawl into a corner and weep at his sorry fate? Nope, he industrializes the living hell out of his foster planet, in the noble pursuit of building a new spacecraft capable of facilitating his escape. As you can imagine, the local wildlife ain’t too happy to concede defeat and allow our resourceful spaceman to revive and actually bring about what shall really look like the Third Industrial Revolution in regards to scope and complexity, if not in sheer size.
Just take a good look at the game’s screenshots from its Steam Store page. If you’d been an alien lifeform inhabiting that planet, you’d probably try to kill Bob too. But our protagonist is both determined and crazy enough to let no one and nothing stop him from achieving his goal. While focusing on the rocket, he won’t hesitate to build and make good use of anything from drones, tanks, laser turrets and trusty ol’ trains, in his attemps to defend the resource greedy machines while tinkering away at the many crucial components required by a spacecraft.
If you think the road ahead is gonna be both long and tough to complete, rest assured I’m here to…confirm your fears. You’ll be facing an uphill battle against increasingly aggressive aliens (which almost resemble the Zerg from Starcraft) and industrial machinery which requires some degree of automatization. You start off barehanded and stranded, but it doesn’t take long before you craft a pickaxe and start mining for the first metal ore pieces, stones and coal to literally fuel your struggle for survival. In-game tips are always present and the tutorial featured in the first few missions is more than welcome. You’ll need all the help you can get and creativity plus intuition will always play crucial roles, as you have to become as efficient as the machines you are creating.
On some campaign maps, you’ll find space at a premium but at least you can easily deconstruct structures and assets with the option of repositioning them at will. In more than just one way, your battle to escape can be regarded as a metaphor for humanity’s own struggle to always evolve and adapt. You start off with the help of steam (First Industrial Revolution), then electricity (Second Industrial Revolution) only to move on quickly towards complex circuit boards and the increasingly independent machines that only lack true artificial intelligence, from being self-aware and able to build/maintain themselves without human interference. Are you kickstarting the Third Industrial Revolution or just creating a small scale Skynet? All of this while destroying the planet step by step with the rapid industrialization and its inevitable by-product, which is pollution itself. Congratulations!
If all that sounds complicated or simply grim, that’s because it really is so. I glanced over the reviews written by other Factorio players here on Steam and simply looking at their playtime, I realized that I couldn’t reach dozens or hundreds of hours into this game, even in 6 or more months. It is an addictive game, I get it. I simply would lack that kind of patience which I sincerely find noteworthy, in those which possess it. And the title surely isn’t helped by the fact that it looks nearly like the tycoon games from 15 years ago and somehow with even fewer sounds. Before you start throwing rocks at me, understand that I’d never choose quality graphics over quality gameplay but a balance is needed in everything we accomplish.
Take into consideration that the game for all its plain looks, still is feature rich, complex beyond its own good and offers a sandbox mode for truly passionate builders to quite literally unleash the mad genius lurking within them. I still find Factorio a bit on the overpriced side, since it’s an Early Access game. But as always, your choice counts in the end. It is humanity’s story in a nutshell. Relentless determination followed by greed and sacrifices in pursuit of bettering ourselves at any and all costs.

It's being made by friendly, helpful developers and is 3 times cheaper than this one for at least 10x the content.

First of all I have already beat up the game and the NewGame+. And I have 94% of all achievements.
I am recommending this game ,but not for this price point  (50 euro)!  WAIT FOR A DISCOUNT 25-30 euro.
Ok , The Surge. This game has a lot of small problems . Its good souls-like game. There are no cheap shots from any enemy's. You can notice every attack before it has happened . This is both good and bad. In the start this game will crush you like a bug if you try to go full on Rambo , but after the 2/3  this game starts to be too easy. If you play rational most of the enemy's wont even hit you. The best strategy in this game is to just hit and run your enemy's. Cuz if you mess up they will 1 or 2 shoot you. They are combos in this game but overall they can be very dangerous if you don't know when you use them. And probably most of the times you will die cuz you started the combo, but the enemy stagger has over and he will hit you for a ton of DMG . But overall the hole combat system is fun and you can use all of the weapons on the fly. Although I can say that later on  the fast attacking weapons are starting to suck cuz the time to kill the mobs is x2 and that means that they have x2 chance to kill you as well. And in a game that every mob can 1/2 shot you that's a problem.
The upgrading gear system was really nice. I knew what I need to do to get the next mark (lv) of weapon/armor without any RNG ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. If you need 3 more pieces of arm gear to UPG you just go out and cut off some arms and you have it .I love it.
I have seen a lot of negative stuff about the map design but I think people are just stupid. The maps are soo liner that 95% of the time there is no way you can get lost. You just need to pay attention a bit. Overall for me the map design was ok . The shortcuts ware often enough that I had no problems with progressing through the map , but they ware not that often to make dying mechanic meaningless. And you can never be sure are you willing to push a bit more with a lot of scrap(souls) to find next shortcut or you have to go back and bank it .
The story in this game is very much souls-like . You can find only pieces of a big story puzzle and probably you will miss some of the pieces but at the end of the game you will have an idea what is the story. Overall the story is not great , but I think it will make your imagination run wild questions about the missing pieces of story ...for a time.
Ok here comes the big stinker for me : NG+ . The NG+ just doesn't  bring anything interesting at all. It puts from time to time on the map a bit more hard hitting mobs and that's it. With knowing where is every mob and where to go  I had no problems beating up NG+ . To be hones I got bored ,cuz for me the game had become too easy. There is nothing new in the NG+.  And that is BIG BIG PROBLEM for a 20-25 hour game.
About how the game is running .The Surge for me did run like a charm. I had stable FPS on the best quality and never I end up on a game breaking bug that will ruin the game for me. Probably the biggest problem is when you execute there is a good chance that you can fall in a insta dead hole in one of the areas.
Overall I am recommending this game to everyone that is looking for a souls-like game. And the syfy style makes this game feel fresh and new.  But probably its best to wait for a sale on this game. For a 20-30h game with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ NG+ I just cant recommend the 50 euro price tag. But I think when this game hits 25-30 euro this is easily a must buy .
My personal score for this game is 8/10. This is nice start for syfy souls-like game series. And i cant wait to see what they will do if there is a sequel.

Summary- I loved playing the game, but then the flaws became more and more apparent. 6/10
This game is the easy mofe for Dark Souls that i have been looking for. You can store your currency at any time to avoid loosing it and there is a quick save/load feature with F5/F8. That's all i ever wanted. Going without healing at ops or dying can increase your scrap multiplyer to 3x to decrease grinding too.
Combat, OK. Weapons feel appropriately weighty. Movement is deliberat and controls are tight. Every time i died i knew it was my fault (Except for the last boss). There were points in the game where i died multiple times, but at no point did i feel angry at the game. I lost 20k scrap (little over 2 levels at the time) one time and didn't even feel bad. By the end of the game i was running around with 80k before even concidering going back. The final boss is too big, you target it's limbs but the camera stays in the same place. This makes all jump and sliding attacks very finiky. I counted well over 50 missed attacks because a slide was never executed. I was fighting the camera the entire time. Early game enemies also do way too much damage, this needs to be scaled back.
A more contraversial move The Surge makes though is that it removes all skills and massively simplifies things. You have a  core power level and your armor and implants take power. Nothing stops you from changing your loadout (at the medbay) at any point. This removes a large part of the difficulty in Dark Souls. I appreciate the ability to customize my loadout to he situation i find myself in though, so i see this as a plus. Then again, at one point your health just stops going up. What point is there to a heal that does 320 when your health never naturally goes above 200?
Map- I love how it folds in on itself. While the map itself is huge, shortcuts make it feel small at the same time. Signs are all over the map to help you know where you are at any time, but more needed to be done. I had no idea where the 4th area was, and the 5th and 7th areas were complete mazes. Even with 4 hours of trying, I never even got to the 3rd floor of the final area.
Inplants. Im going to be honest, not a lot of variety here. I would have liked to see more varriation here. There's injectables to power up attacks and another ones that increase weapon proficiency but that's pretty much it for weapon focused inplants. There are energy based implants, energy which can be used to restore health, execute damaged enemies, use an injectable, or to attack with your drone. Other than that, you can have 24 healing items if you find them and want to do so, or increase your maximum health/power core level. There needs to be more variety here.
Weapons classes each have a unique moveset that you either like or don't like. I was disapointed to see that all three of my single-rig weapons have the exact same moveset. Weapon streangth scales with proficiency, and as you find a move set that you like, you will naturally gravitate towards one weapon. This means that the weapon class you choose in the first area will likely out perform all other weapons. It's dissapointing to get a new weapon, only to have your current weapon be better. This game is truly an underrated classic. I know that is heared alot thease days, but that is the truth. Rogue Trooper is based of the comic series of the same name.Taking place in the future, you take control of the sole surviving "Genetic Infantryman". Rogue. The G.I.s were engineered to survive un-aided in the heavily poisoned and acidic atmosphere of Nu-Earth, the focal point of the war between the Norts and Southers. Betrayed by a general, the GI's were all but eradicated. Rogue was the exception. Thanks to a failsafe during their creation, the GI's have a Bio-chip implated at the base of the neck. The Chip downloads a GI's personality upon death for transport in another GI's gear (Mainly: Helmet, Rifle and Backpack) For cloning upon return. Armed with his dead comrades, Rogue stalks the hellhole of Nu-Earth for the traitor. But enough about the plot, what about the gameplay? At it's simplest: Rogue Trooper is a cover-based third person shooter. However that does it no justice. The main "gimmick" is that your squad is your equipment. Gunnar has a wide variety of firing modes. From Rifle to Sniper to Mortar to SAM. He even has a Sentry function. Helm is specialized in hacking and creating a holographic decoy. Finally, Bagman can supply you with Micromines and anything else you need. If you've got the salvage for it that is. Yes, you supply yourself with grenades, ammo, medpacks, and Upgrades. Whether you enjoy running and gunning, sneaking, or ambushing this game has got you covered.

Far too overlooked Sci-Fi-shooter with an interesting setting, fresh mechanics, good ideas, a good handfull of gadgets, an excellent sniper rifle, satisfying snipe and/or stealth AND shooting elements, a nice little revenge-story and enough gameplay freedom and variety to keep you interested! Buy!

An interesting character. He's young and feels betrayed. He makes it his life mission to take down the man who exterminated his kind. Pretty straight-forward person, but his ironically-named buddies (biochips stored in his equipment) make playing singleplayer more of a variaty. Voice actor was pretty good at playing the character.
Pleasing both the serious and silly audiences, the rifle "Gunnar" is cocky and sarcastic. Think of him as a little bit of Deadpool mixed in with FPS Doug (the "BOOM! HEADSHOT!" guy). Makes remarks on your shots and combat skills, and is always eager to kill some Norts.
A tough guy with the ability to recycle any salvage you aquire into health and ammo. Also upgrades weapons. This guy is really helpful during combat. He automatically reloads your gun for you in the middle of a firefight and applies a medpack to replenish your health when you get low. Instead of relying on your health and ammo bar, Bagman announces when you get close to running out or dying. Great addition to the game.
He's a middle-aged character, among the 3 Biochips. He can hack computers, drive vehicles and provides a radar for you. I don't think he talked as much as the others, but he was really lively when piloting a vehicle. Removing him for computer hacking and driving removes your radar, making you rely on plain sight and instinct while he does his work. Great challenge.
The villain that causes Rogue to go, well... rogue. You don't really see his face during the beginning of the game, until you catch up with him for the first time. After that, you'll never forget him. He acts like a stereotypical general or other high-ranking men in the Army & Navy. Runs from the protagonist, sends his little army men to fight his battles and even hides behind a shield and watches people die! Totally makes sense. Hahaha.
Good singleplayer. Collecting salvage and upgrading weaponry was pretty fun. They also give you a few ways to handle a situation. "1. Go in guns-a-blazing or 2. Sneak around, silently killing Norts like a blue ninja." You have the tech and knowledge to help you with both solutions. And characters that provide comic relief!

So this will be one of the very few games that actually made me to write an review.
Royal Quest is a definitely FUN mmo to play! Altough it's lacking balancing hard, especially between ranged and melee classes.
It's a game that features a freedom of building your character (i will mainly focus on mage-sorcerer as i play one). As a sorcerer you can go pve-solo build, pve-support, pve-pvp or purely pvp way.
There are three main weapons for a mage and it is spellbook - cheap but medicore ranged attack, scythes - high atk close combat and bracelet+orb combo - medium damage but tons of def (i use bracer+orb). But that's not the end of it, you also got 4 talent trees which specializes in different range of enchantements to your playstyle. On top of that we got equipement that can be imbued with special seals and slots that can fit cards that gives dozens of enchantements. The range of how you want to play is quite diverse which i really like! :)
There is no "true crafting" as you could see in other mmos, there is no craft leveling, all you have to do is get a proper recipe and resources that are needed for an item and just craft it. It sounds simple but getting those items requires either lots of gold or lots of grind.
Now let's go to badies of this game.
The amount of grind is helluva big, without premium it would take me ages to get to 31lvl (as iam now) and i already can feel like even with 2x exp and all that it will still be quite long before i hit 60 (note that i preffer solo style untill i reach like 50).
The game is not exactly p2w but it has it's aspects, even tough everything can be purcharsed with normal ingame money, to get this money without any help you either grind like mad or just buy premium currency and sell premium stuff, either way will let you achieve what you want. I personally bought dlc from steam store and im happy with it.
It's quite unballanced game, especially very hard start for all melee classes, if you have no money then go mage or archer, both of them got healing spells and can kite harder mobs in early, unlike other melee classes, ofc it's not easy, it still requires skill but it's still much easier than lets say, DK which i started with and dropped at 24 lvl (it took me 2 days to get to 24 on dk and 1 day to get to 24 on mage)
Overall i would score this game 7/10, it would be 10/10 if melee classes would be optimized better way.
Hope i helped!

1. Global Map Movement
You can use the Map feature to left click on the point you want to run to and your character will run to the location accordingly. No need to keep left clicking all the way.
1. Pay to Win
3500 Reales for $100.
Here's a list of core mechanics you can buy with cash
1. Bag slots x 1 for 9R. (Inventory space, another core mechanic)
2. Arena Tickets x 10 for 29R
3. Maiden's Ticket x 20 for 29R (They are selling 20 town portal scrolls for $0.80, a bloody core mechanic)
4. Ambrosia x 20 for 9R (Heals 100% Health, Energy and Mana over 5 seconds, Elixirs can be bought with cash too)
5. Card of Chaos for 399R (Weapon Insert : Attacks with Chaos Element Weapons deal increased damage to all other elements. This is an item advantage)
6. Royal Blessing x 30 for 319R (All experience gain increased by 50%, Item find increased by 50%, Town Portal Skill and 4 other buffs)
If this isn't Pay-to-win, I think the developers are delusional.

Boring as hell. The most generic backtrack quests that I have seen. Fetch quest galour.

3 servers. Elgore, Iris, Kabuk. 2 are offline and 1 has a low population.

Constant advertising for you to sign up for a premium account.

It was way past midnight when the famous philosopher Wube Software LTD started working on this game that he finished in just under 8 hours inside a dirty garage all by himself and without any experience in producing any software. Once he had finished, majorly dehydrated and inconveniently dressed, he was the proud independant producer of the first ego shooting RTS puzzle action adventure RPG simulation. He swore that he would never corrupt it by making it early access without ever publishing it officially, took a zip of his fourty-second coffee this night and pressed the release button.
That was the day Factorium appeared out of nowhere and without any announcement. It crashed into people's world, changed their view of things and had almost all players reconsider their life choices by the new philosophy that just entered their mind.
The meaning of FactorTheGame, the stunning story, the beautiful voice-acting, infamous AAA-graphics, its participation in the philosophical debate of today with its radical new ideas and approaches is something that is far beyond what you can cover in a review. However, in the next few hours and days, I will give it a try.
It all started in 1935, Lincoln Elldalek and Herbert Hollick-Cumberdale started the first Antarctia flight over the entire continent in the history of man. They saw the deadly beauty and the dangerous sharpness of the almost endless desert of ice. Their emotions and their thoughts surely were beyond anything us lesser beings can imagine nowadays, where there are no comparable riddles left to be solved.
Nietzsche said that god is dead and that we killed him and that is surely what he meant by that. The philosophy of FactsUnited, a game that is circled around building up something that does need everything to function automatically, is something so complicated, so beyond comprehension that it might stun you when you first experience the value of yourself and what you mean to the world.
You start off as a regular worker inside a complex society on some alien-infested planet. Your daily job is standing around and make sure the sinister aliens don't smell your red boxes on the map so that they don't come over and attack you.
Then you start building the first energetic perpetuum mobile by placing a self-fueling burner miner on some coal that will continue to run forever as long as there is coal to mine and due to the effectiveness you sadly end up with overflow which then leads to new dangerous developments like the first idea to produce red test tubes automatically and your damnation begins.
Minutes, hours, days, weeks, months, years, centuries, millenia pass and you build up something that is so automated, so perfect, that it can stay online forever. It will continue to do what you build it for as long as the entropy in the universe is below 1, as long as there is some sort of concentrated energy available in the entire universe.
You then start to realize that what you build is very similar to what Nietzsche said, only in a whole new perspective. You are the god and the machines are the ones speaking the idea out. They killed you, even though you were the one who created them. You were their god and now that they function automatically, the only redundant thing, the only thing that no longer has any purpose neither in the system that you created nor in the greater universe and all infinite parallel universes around you, is you, the player.
You made something so great and so automated that it's independant of its own creator. The creator, you, have only one action left that might give you a temporary feel of being something of note: Destroy what you created and make yourself needed again.
What value does your life contain when even though you are capable of developing entire worlds you can not find anything of note to do? Is your entire existance only necessary to create something that is then independant of you so that you have to destroy it to be necessary again?
Those are the actual questions that Factorissimo arises. It's less than a game than a metaphysical dissertation around the usual concerns of existentialism, along with a harsh portion of cosmic pessimism as already know it illustrated by Eugene Thacker.
The horrors of the world-in-itself, as Thacker put it, are brought to life in FactsReloaded, where you face the aliens that want to eat your brains and suck out ear juice because you are destroying their environment. Doesn't this make the insane contrast between you as creator and you as demolisher even more obvious? Not only that all you can create is imperfect until you automated it to a point where it does not need you, you also are not able to accomplish that without crashing the reality of lesser beings than yourself, stealing their world, stealing their ressources and killing them using a fatass German Panzer that - ironically - built from
ressources.
Factorheyo is an existentialistic philosophy around creating something destructive that you have to destroy in order to prevail with your own significance. Or in other words - what meaning does your product have, when you are of no meaning at all? What value does your yes have, when you are not willing to let action follow it?
If you are able to face those questions, if you are able to live with the knowledge that might suck you into the depth of nihilism, if you are capable of enduring despite the pressure of
riding down your self-esteem, then go forth and read Funtorio.
I do however suggest that if you want to maintain happiness in your life, it's better to not ask questions and not touch this society-endangering masterpiece that is Fact. Keep your eyes closed and continue to imagine that validity and genesis are directly connected to each other.
It's a lot healthier for our very human mind to do that instead.

I'm really enjoying this game so far! The limb targeting for new gear and for materials to level your gear is a really cool touch to the tried and true Souls formula. Like Lords of the Fallen, there is a timer to get your Tech (souls), but each kill you get on your way to retrieve your souls will increase the timer creating a really cool risk/reward. There is an energy meter that  is seperate from your stamina that lets you do really cool things like hacking off limbs in spectacular fashion or heal yourself to allow to fight longet before needing to replenish your health potions. Mixing and matchin armor on your arms and legs allows flexibility in what you want to do in the game as far as fat rolling, etc. All your stats are on the gear you use. You level your rig that allows you to equip more/heavier gear and equip more mods that increase your health or energy. You aren't putting anything into specific stats. You can even bank your Tech so you won't lose them if you die if you just have a lot and know a boss is coming up soon. The only concern I have is the length of the game. After six hours I beat two out of the five bosses. But there were a lot of doors in the two areas I have completed that I couldn't get into because my level wasn't high enough so there is a reason to go back to earlier areas to explore some more even once you beat the boss. Also of note is there is no multiplayer or online functionality at all. That's fine with me as I never engaged with anything multiplayer related in any souls game and it kind of adds to the isolation feel of the world that you're trying to survive in, so it fits in a way.

The Surge is a compelling take on the Souls-like genre that adds new combat mechanics and a new twisted setting to the field. The gritty sci fi setting is incredibly engaging and fresh, while the fast paced and intuitive combat make the game incredibly fun to play. The original Souls games are my favorite games of all time, and the Surge does justice to the genre and succeeds in adding new and fresh elements to the scene.
I highly recommend this game to any who love the Souls series, or any who like challenging RPGs and fast paced action combat!

I'm not really an authority on Souls games. I've puttered around in DSII a bit, and after several years have only recently gotten anywhere close to the end (I think?)
So rather than comparing this to a Souls game, or referring to it as a "souls-like", or whatever, I'll just say: I really like this game. It does what it set out to do and it does it well.
The combat is really fun and instantly addicting. It's super satisfying when you get it, and then it gets harder, in a good, not-arbitrary way (so far, I'm not all that deep into the game yet).
It's hard. It's not "I want to kill everyone and then myself" hard, but it's hard enough to make you think twice before getting greedy.
The incentive to fight the hard way is really cool: attack armored bits to earn more scrap and maybe a blueprint for a forklift-tine-turned-arm-stabby that would impress Ripley.
I've read some lambasting of the setting and of the story...well, the setting is neat as hell, and the level design is thoughtful and cool. It's very satisfying to take a risk and go down the spooky corridor with all the spooky dudes to find you've made a shortcut all the way back to the medbay and can now cash in all those sweet scraps.
As for story--and I know the souls series is supposed to be superduper deep lore-wise, etc--I don't think it's all that lacking when compared to a souls game. The latter are already intentionally vague, and Surge relies on this too. So what? I'm not in it for the story in the end man. I want to chop up fellow denziens of the dystopic cyberpunk future and probably go through a bunch of♥♥♥♥♥♥just to still find myself under the heel of the big ole sci-fi corporation.
Hopefully reality will bcome similar to this game someday, and I can become a corporate shill / scab turned mindless cybernetic murder fiend.
